macro.name: Observation in classroom, playground and clinic
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.8
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accurate and objective documentation

▸  CORU 3.1
     Be able to gather all appropriate background information relevant to the service user's health and social care needs

▸  CORU 5.31
     Conduct a range of assessment methods safely and ethically, adapting and re-evaluating their application as appropriate

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.1.1
     Have sensible regard for individual clients' moral and cultural values.

▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Observation is the only assessment method that shows you the child in the environment the referral is actually about. A WISC-V tells you about a child in a quiet room with one adult and no competing demands — which is not where the difficulty is happening. Everything a teacher describes is mediated through their interpretation; observation is your one chance at unmediated data. It is also the method most often done badly, because it looks like something anyone can do.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The four methods and what each is for
     Narrative (running record) — you write continuous prose about what happens. Strength: captures sequence and context you did not anticipate. Weakness: you cannot quantify it, and your attention drifts to what is salient rather than what is frequent. Use it first, when you do not yet know what you are looking for.
Timed interval sampling — you divide the observation into fixed intervals (commonly 15 or 30 seconds) and record whether the behaviour occurred in each. Strength: gives you a percentage you can compare before and after an intervention. Weakness: tells you nothing about why. Use it when you need a baseline.
Event sampling (frequency count) — you count each occurrence of a defined behaviour. Strength: exact counts for discrete, countable behaviours. Weakness: useless for continuous states like off-task. Use it for hitting, calling out, leaving the seat.
ABC recording — for each occurrence you record what came immediately before (antecedent), the behaviour, and what followed (consequence). Strength: the only one of the four that generates a hypothesis about function. Weakness: slow, and you will miss things while writing. Use it when the referral question is why.

▸  Why the method must be chosen before you go
     If you arrive without a method you will default to narrative, and narrative confirms whatever you already believed. Choosing beforehand forces you to operationalise the behaviour — to turn 'disruptive' into something you could count. That operationalisation is half the assessment. If you cannot define the behaviour tightly enough to record it, the referral question is not yet clear, and that is worth discovering before you spend an hour in a classroom.

▸  Reactivity, and what to do about it
     Your presence changes behaviour. Children perform, or freeze, or seek your attention. This is not a flaw to eliminate but a variable to report. Two practical moves: stay long enough that novelty wears off (the first ten minutes are usually unrepresentative), and observe on more than one occasion where possible. In the report, say what you think your presence did. A sentence such as 'Over the first ten minutes the pupil looked towards me repeatedly; this reduced thereafter and the data below are drawn from the remaining period' is more credible than pretending you were invisible.

▸  Looking at the environment, not only the child
     The referral names a child, but the data you need is relational. Count how many times the teacher directs an instruction at this child compared with a peer. Note where the child is seated and what they can see. Note the transition points — most difficulties cluster at transitions rather than during tasks. If you leave with data only about the child, you have produced a within-child account by default, and your formulation will follow it.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Sharp, P., Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2015). Educational psychology in practice: Observation. In Frederickson & Cline, Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity (3rd ed.). Open University Press. — the chapter on assessment methods.

▸  Department of Education and Skills (2017). Continuum of Support: Guidelines for teachers. NEPS. — read the section on classroom support, so you know what you are observing against.

▸  CORU (2023). Standards of proficiency for educational psychologists. Standards 3.1, 3.2, 5.31.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Recording interpretation as description — 'he was frustrated' is an inference; 'he pushed the worksheet away and put his head down' is an observation. Write the second and infer later.

✗  Observing only the target child, and producing a within-child formulation by accident.

✗  Generalising from one lesson. One maths lesson on a Friday afternoon is not a profile.

✗  Not agreeing an introduction, so the child is singled out or told something untrue.

✗  Choosing narrative every time because it requires no preparation.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You recorded what happened accurately but could not say why you chose that method.

▸  GRADE 4
     Method chosen and applied correctly; description and interpretation separated; context recorded alongside the child.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can name what your method was blind to, you observed across settings, and your observation answers the referral question rather than describing everything.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the methods
     [3–4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The four observatio

macro.name: Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.2
     Be able to modify and adapt communication methods and styles, including verbal and non-verbal methods, to suit the individual service user, considering issues of language, age, culture, beliefs and health and/or social care needs

▸  CORU 3.1
     Be able to gather all appropriate background information relevant to the service user's health and social care needs

▸  CORU 5.2
     Demonstrate a critical understanding of relevant biological sciences, human development, social and behavioural sciences and other related sciences, together with a knowledge of health and wellbeing

▸  CORU 5.12
     Know the psychological theories of education, human development, learning and teaching and their application in children, young people and adult learners

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.1.1
     Have sensible regard for individual clients' moral and cultural values.

▸  PSI 1.1.3
     Convey respect for and abide by prevailing community mores, social customs, and cultural expectations in their scientific and professional activities.

▸  PSI 1.3.5
     Ensure at least the following are understood: purpose and nature of the activity; mutual responsibilities; likely benefits and risks; alternatives; consequences of non-action; the option to refuse or withdraw at any time without prejudice; the period the consent applies to; and how to rescind consent.

▸  PSI 1.4.1
     Seek as full and active participation as possible from others in decisions which affect them.

▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The developmental history is the only source of data covering the first five years, and it is the difference between a profile and a snapshot. It is also the point at which the parent decides whether you are someone they will tell the truth to. Rushing it costs you the information and the relationship at once.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What the history is actually for
     You are looking for three things. First, timing: when did each domain come online, and were they in step with each other? A child who walked at 11 months and said first words at 30 months has an uneven profile, and unevenness is more informative than delay. Second, trajectory: has the gap widened, narrowed or stayed constant? A constant gap suggests a stable difference; a widening gap suggests the demands are outpacing the skill. Third, discontinuity: was there a point at which something changed, and what else was happening then?

▸  The domains, and the order to take them in
     Pregnancy and birth — complications, prematurity, birth weight, time in special care. Early motor — head control, sitting, crawling, walking. Speech and language — babbling, first words, two-word combinations, and crucially whether anyone was worried. Social and play — eye contact, joint attention, pretend play, interest in other children. Self-care — feeding, sleep, toileting, dressing. Medical — illnesses, hospitalisations, hearing and vision checks, medication. Education — preschool, transitions, previous schools, supports already tried.
Take them in roughly this order because it is chronological and parents can follow it. Do not jump around; a parent who loses the thread gives shorter answers.

▸  Why sleep, feeding and self-care are the ones people skip
     They feel intrusive and they are not obviously psychological. They are also where the most useful information often sits. Persistent sleep difficulty affects attention, mood and learning, and is treatable. Restricted eating can indicate sensory difference. Delayed self-care with intact motor skills points somewhere different from delayed self-care with motor difficulty. Skipping these three is the commonest gap in trainee histories.

▸  Asking about strengths first, and why it is not politeness
     Opening with what the child is good at does two things. It gives you data you will need for the recommendations — you cannot build on a strength you never asked about. And it tells the parent that this is an assessment of a whole child, not a catalogue of deficits, which changes what they are willing to tell you for the next hour.

▸  Handling disclosure without losing the interview
     Parents disclose bereavement, separation, their own mental health, and sometimes safeguarding concerns. The move is: stop the schedule, acknowledge it plainly, ask one follow-up if it is relevant to the child, then signal the return — 'thank you for telling me that. Can I come back to the early years for a moment?' Do not rush past it and do not abandon the interview. If it crosses a child protection threshold the duty is immediate and separate from the assessment.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Carr, A. (2016). The handbook of child and adolescent clinical psychology (3rd ed.). Routledge. — the chapter on intake interviewing.

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2015). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity (3rd ed.). Open University Press.

▸  PSI (2025). Code of professional ethics (5th rev.). Clauses 1.1.3 and 1.3.5 on respect and informed consent.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Reading questions off a schedule for the first time in the room.

✗  Skipping sleep, feeding and self-care because they feel intrusive.

✗  Accepting 'normal' or 'fine' as an answer without a follow-up.

✗  Taking the history with the child present when the content is sensitive.

✗  Letting the supervisor lead every time — only leading earns a rating of 3 or above.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You covered the schedule with the supervisor leading and the content was complete.

▸  GRADE 4
     You led it, covered every domain including the uncomfortable ones, and followed up ambiguity.

▸  GRADE 5
     You led it, the parent raised something you had no

macro.name: Structured interviewing of teachers and SET
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.1
     Be able to gather all appropriate background information relevant to the service user's health and social care needs

▸  CORU 5.13
     Know the structures and systems of school, community and social settings in which educational, health and social care services are provided for children, young people and adult learners

▸  CORU 5.14
     Know the impact of structures and systems in which educational services are provided on the development of children, young people and adult learners at individual, group and organisational levels

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The teacher holds the comparison data you cannot get anywhere else — how this child compares with thirty others doing the same task in the same room. They also hold the intervention history, and without it your recommendations will repeat what has already failed.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The Continuum of Support, and why you must place the child on it
     NEPS operates a three-level model. Classroom Support is what the class teacher does within ordinary differentiated teaching, planned and reviewed informally. School Support adds targeted intervention for a smaller group, with a written support plan and a review cycle, usually involving the SET. School Support Plus is individualised, often drawing on outside professionals including you, with a detailed plan and formal review.
The level matters because it tells you what has been tried and what the school's next move can realistically be. Recommending School Support for a child already at School Support Plus tells everyone you did not ask.

▸  Allocation versus deployment
     Since 2017 special education teaching hours are allocated to schools on a profiled basis rather than per diagnosis — so a diagnosis does not generate hours. How the school then deploys those hours is a separate decision made internally, and two schools with identical allocations can deploy very differently. When you ask about support, ask both questions: what does the school have, and how has it chosen to use it.

▸  Getting a referral question that can be answered
     Referrals arrive as descriptions, not questions — 'concerns about progress in literacy'. Your job is to convert that into something answerable: is the difficulty specific to literacy or part of a broader profile; is the current intervention appropriate and being delivered as intended; what should happen next. Write your version in one sentence and read it back. If the teacher does not recognise it as theirs, you have not yet got the question.

▸  Asking what has been tried, without it sounding like an audit
     Teachers often expect to be judged. Frame it as information-gathering: 'What have you already tried, and what did you notice when you did?' The second clause matters — it invites observation rather than justification, and it often produces the most useful data in the interview, because a partially effective intervention tells you more than a failed one.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Department of Education and Skills (2017). Continuum of Support: Guidelines for teachers. NEPS.

▸  Department of Education (2017). Circular 0013/2017: Special education teaching allocation. — cite the circular number, not 'guidance'.

▸  NCSE (2014). Delivery for students with special educational needs. — background on the allocation model.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Assuming nothing has been tried.

✗  Not requesting attainment data until after you have met the child.

✗  Taking the referral wording at face value.

✗  Interviewing the person who is available rather than the person who knows the child best.

✗  Not agreeing what feedback the school will get, so expectations diverge.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You gathered what you were asked to gather.

▸  GRADE 4
     You clarified the question, established the Continuum level, and read the attainment data first.

▸  GRADE 5
     You arrived knowing what the school had already tried, and your question was one the teacher recognised as theirs.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the school system
     [5–6 hours for the first school  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     How SET allocation works, what the Continuum of Support levels are, and what a school can offer at each.
     How you build it: Read the Continuum documents. Map one school properly.

     ·  Place the child on the Continuum of Support
          you have it when: You know the stage before you recommend anything
          [NEPS Continuum of Support]

     ·  Ask what has already been tried and what happened
          you have it when: You did not assume nothing had been tried
          [CORU SoP 5.13]

     ·  Ask about presentation across the timetable
          you have it when: You know whether it varies by subject or teacher
          [CORU SoP 5.14]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Getting the right information
     [Habit, not hours  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Clarifying a vague referral, finding the right informant, and getting the data you need in advance.
     How you build it: Write the referral question in one sentence before every meeting and check it with the teacher.

     ·  Clarify the referral question with the person who raised it
          you have it when: You can state it in one sentence they recognise
          [CORU SoP 3.1]

     ·  Request standardised attainment data in advance
          you have it when: You read it before meeting the child
          [CORU SoP 3.1]

     ·  Ask who knows this child best in the school
          you have it when: You found the right informant, not the available one
          [CORU SoP 3.1]

     ·  Agree what feedback the school gets and when
          you

macro.name: WISC-V administration to proficiency standard
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.6
     Demonstrate safe and effective implementation of practical, technical and clinical/professional skills

▸  CORU 5.21
     Establish, maintain and conclude a professional relationship with a service user, safely and ethically, recognising and managing professional boundaries

▸  CORU 5.31
     Conduct a range of assessment methods safely and ethically, adapting and re-evaluating their application as appropriate

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.4.3
     Respect the right of individuals to discontinue participation or service at any time, and be responsive to non-verbal indications of a desire to discontinue.

▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 3.3.6
     Take all reasonable steps to ensure tests and assessment methods are only used by those qualified and trained to do so.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The WISC-V is the instrument you will be judged on most directly — there is a proficiency examination, and administration errors are visible on the protocol to anyone who reads it. It is also the instrument most likely to be over-interpreted. Learning to administer it is a few weeks of work. Learning what it does and does not tell you takes the full three years.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What the test is built on
     The WISC-V is organised around the Cattell–Horn–Carroll (CHC) model, which proposes broad ability domains beneath general ability. The five primary indices map onto CHC constructs: Verbal Comprehension (crystallised ability, Gc) — acquired verbal knowledge and reasoning; Visual Spatial (Gv) — perceiving and manipulating spatial relations; Fluid Reasoning (Gf) — novel problem solving with minimal prior knowledge; Working Memory (Gwm) — holding and manipulating information briefly; Processing Speed (Gs) — speed and accuracy on simple visual tasks.
The separation of Visual Spatial from Fluid Reasoning was the major change from WISC-IV, where both sat inside Perceptual Reasoning. It matters because a child can be strong at spatial construction and weak at abstract reasoning, and the older structure hid that.

▸  Start points, reverse rules, discontinue rules
     Start point: where you begin, determined by the child's age, with a lower start if ability is known or suspected to be low. Reverse rule: if the child fails at or near the start point, you administer earlier items backwards until the criterion is met, establishing a true basal. Discontinue rule: after a specified number of consecutive zero scores you stop, because further items would yield nothing and cost the child confidence.
The rules vary by subtest. There is no general rule to learn — the work is per-subtest memorisation. The reason hesitation is what an examiner watches for is that hesitating tells them you are computing the rule rather than knowing it, and a child notices the pause.

▸  Querying, prompting, and where the line is
     A query is a permitted follow-up when a response is ambiguous or incomplete — usually 'tell me more about that'. The manual specifies which responses may be queried and with what wording. A prompt is a permitted reminder of task demands. Neither may be used to steer the child toward a better answer.
Over-querying is the commonest integrity failure and it comes from decency — you can see the child nearly has it. Every unpermitted query inflates the score and invalidates the comparison to the norm sample, because the norm sample was not queried that way. If you realise you have over-queried, note it on the protocol and flag it in the report.

▸  Confidence intervals and why point scores mislead
     Every obtained score contains measurement error. The confidence interval expresses the range within which the true score probably lies — typically reported at 95%. An FSIQ of 97 with a 95% interval of 92–102 is not meaningfully different from one of 103 with an interval of 98–108, though the point scores look different. Report intervals. Writing 'his IQ is 97' is both technically wrong and practically harmful, because schools act on the number.

▸  When an index is not interpretable
     If the subtests contributing to an index differ substantially from each other (the manual gives the critical values), the index is an average of unlike things and describes no real ability. In that case you report the subtest-level pattern and say the index is not interpretable. This is a genuine skill and it separates a psychologist from an administrator.

▸  The clinical half
     Scores are half the data. The other half is how the child approached the task: did they plan before starting or dive in; what happened after failure; did they ask for help; did they check their work; was performance affected by time pressure specifically. Write behavioural observations for every administration, including practice ones, and compare them against the scores afterwards. That comparison is how the clinical eye develops.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Wechsler, D. (2016). WISC-V UK administration and scoring manual. Pearson. — chapters on administration and standard procedure.

▸  Wechsler, D. (2016). WISC-V UK technical and interpretive manual. Pearson. — chapters 1 and 2 for the theoretical structure.

▸  Flanagan, D. P., & Alfonso, V. C. (2017). Essentials of WISC-V assessment. Wiley.

▸  PSI (2025). Code of professional ethics. Clause 3.3.6 — tests used only by those trained to do so.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Over-querying to help a child succeed.

✗  Continuing past a discontinue rule out of kindness.

✗  Paraphrasing instructions

macro.name: WIAT administration, scoring and interpretation
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.2
     Be able to justify the selection of and implement appropriate assessment techniques and be able to undertake and record a thorough, sensitive and detailed assessment

▸  CORU 3.3
     Be able to determine the appropriate tests/assessments required and undertake/arrange these tests

▸  CORU 5.6
     Demonstrate safe and effective implementation of practical, technical and clinical/professional skills

▸  CORU 5.32
     Interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data, within relevant conceptual frameworks, to inform case formulation and psychological intervention planning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 4.2.2
     Take due care to avoid misrepresentation, exaggeration, distortion or errors in reporting assessment results, research findings or service effectiveness, and act quickly to correct any such error.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Attainment testing answers a different question from cognitive testing: not what can this child do in principle, but what have they learned. The interesting data is in the relationship between the two, and that relationship is the most misused finding in educational psychology.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Choosing subtests, and why you must justify omission
     A full battery is rarely warranted. Select for the referral question: word reading and reading comprehension for a literacy referral; numerical operations and maths problem solving for numeracy; spelling and written expression where writing is the concern. Write your rationale before you assess. If you cannot justify the battery beforehand, the battery is wrong — and a report reviewer will notice that you tested everything rather than deciding anything.

▸  The ability–attainment discrepancy, and its limits
     A gap between measured ability and measured attainment was once treated as diagnostic of a specific learning difficulty. It no longer is, for three reasons. Regression to the mean makes some discrepancy statistically expected. The discrepancy model identifies children late, because a young child has not yet had time to fall far enough behind. And it systematically misses children whose ability score is itself depressed by the difficulty — a child with a reading difficulty scores lower on verbal subtests because of reduced print exposure.
What a discrepancy does tell you is that attainment is out of step with other functioning, which warrants explanation. It does not by itself name the explanation. Say that in the report.

▸  Basal, ceiling and the mechanics of scoring
     Attainment subtests use basal and ceiling rules rather than the reverse-rule structure of cognitive subtests. Establish the basal by working backwards until the required consecutive correct responses are obtained; stop at the ceiling after the required consecutive errors. Score the same day, while you can still read your own handwriting and recall ambiguous responses. Check every raw-to-scaled conversion: a single transcription error changes a composite, and composites are what people act on.

▸  Curriculum-based measurement as an alternative
     Standardised attainment tests tell you where a child sits against a norm group. They do not tell you whether an intervention is working, because they are insensitive to short-term change and cannot be repeated frequently. Curriculum-based measures — brief, repeatable probes drawn from the curriculum — are better for monitoring. Use the standardised test to establish the profile; use CBM to track progress. Knowing when not to reach for the standardised instrument is part of the competency.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Wechsler, D. (2017). WIAT-III UK administration and scoring manual. Pearson.

▸  Fletcher, J. M., Lyon, G. R., Fuchs, L. S., & Barnes, M. A. (2019). Learning disabilities: From identification to intervention (2nd ed.). Guilford. — the chapter on identification models.

▸  CORU (2023). Standards of proficiency. Standards 3.2, 3.3, 5.32.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Administering the full battery because it is there.

✗  Treating a discrepancy as a diagnosis.

✗  Reporting point scores without intervals.

✗  Leaving scoring to accumulate until the end of the week.

✗  Not noticing a score that contradicts everything else and reporting it anyway.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Scores are correct and reported as points.

▸  GRADE 4
     Battery justified in writing, intervals applied, discrepancy interpreted cautiously.

▸  GRADE 5
     You reported ranges and said what the gap does not prove.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Selection
     [2 hours, then 10 minutes per case  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Which subtests answer which question, and what omitting one costs you.
     How you build it: Write your rationale before assessing, for five cases.

     ·  Select subtests matched to the referral question
          you have it when: You can justify omitting what you omitted
          [CORU SoP 3.2 · 3.3]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Administration
     [6–8 hours  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     Standard administration of reading, spelling and numerical subtests.
     How you build it: Three supervised practice administrations.

     ·  Administer to standard
          you have it when: Errors would not change the composite
          [CORU SoP 5.6]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Scoring
     [6–8 hours, then 45 min per protocol  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     Raw to scaled conversion, composites, confidence intervals.
     How you build it: Score three protocols by hand before using software. Have all three checked.

     ·  Score the protocol the same day
          you have it when: Scoring is not left to accumulate
          [CORU SoP 2.8]

     ·  Check every raw-to-sca

macro.name: Synthesise findings from multiple sources into one profile
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.4
     Be able to analyse and critically evaluate the information collected in the assessment process

▸  CORU 5.27
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accessible and accurate reports — devised in collaboration with service users, as appropriate — that are suitable for the intended audience and context of their use, in order to communicate and justify professional opinions made

▸  CORU 5.32
     Interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data, within relevant conceptual frameworks, to inform case formulation and psychological intervention planning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
This is the section that separates a report from a test-results printout, and it is where most trainee reports lose marks. Anyone can list scores; the psychologist's contribution is the judgement about what they mean together.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Convergence, divergence, and weighting
     Lay every source on one page: cognitive profile, attainment, observation, parent report, teacher report, the child's own account. Mark where they agree and where they do not. Convergence across independent sources is your strongest evidence. Divergence needs explaining — and the explanation is often the finding. Where you weight one source over another, say which and why. 'The teacher report and classroom observation converge; the parent report differs, which may reflect the different demands of the home setting' is a defensible sentence.

▸  Writing integration rather than a list
     The failing structure is: here are the WISC results, here are the WIAT results, here is what the teacher said. The reader is left to synthesise, and they will not. The working structure is a paragraph that begins 'Taken together, these findings indicate…' and then names the pattern, followed by a sentence naming what does not fit. If you never write a sentence containing the word 'however', you have probably smoothed something away.

▸  Not suppressing disconfirming evidence
     PSI clause 4.2.6 requires you not to suppress evidence that disconfirms your conclusion. In practice the suppression is rarely deliberate — you form a view early and stop noticing the data that does not fit. The countermeasure is procedural: before writing, list what your formulation does not explain. If the list is empty, you have not looked.

▸  Limitations, and why every report needs one
     A limitations paragraph states what the assessment did not cover and what that constrains. Typical content: domains not assessed, single-occasion data, instruments normed on other populations, information not available. It costs five minutes, it evidences CORU 1.2 and PSI 2.3.1 directly, and it is absent from most trainee reports. It is the cheapest mark in the portfolio.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Reporting test by test and calling it integration.

✗  Never writing a sentence beginning 'however'.

✗  Omitting the limitations paragraph.

✗  Weighting a source without saying you have done so.

     You listed each test in turn.

▸  GRADE 4
     An integration section exists, names convergence, and includes limitations.

▸  GRADE 5
     The reader is not left to do the synthesis; divergence is named and explained.

     [Habit — 30 minutes per case  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]

     How you build it: Draft one and have it torn apart in supervision. It is the hardest thing to learn from written feedback alone.

     ·  Write an integration section rather than a list
          you have it when: The reader is not left to do the synthesis
          [CORU SoP 5.27]

     ·  Ask whether the profile answers the referral question
          you have it when: You noticed if it did not

macro.name: Phonological and literacy measures
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.3
     Be able to determine the appropriate tests/assessments required and undertake/arrange these tests

▸  CORU 5.28
     Be able to critically evaluate the theory and application of a range of assessment methods used in educational psychology to identify psychological, educational and developmental needs at individual and group levels

▸  CORU 5.32
     Interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data, within relevant conceptual frameworks, to inform case formulation and psychological intervention planning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Literacy referrals are the largest single category you will meet in Irish primary schools. The assessment is only useful if it leads to a specific intervention, which means you need to know both the reading model and what the schools on your patch can actually deliver.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The simple view of reading
     Reading comprehension is the product of decoding and language comprehension — not the sum. If either is near zero, comprehension is near zero. This gives you four profiles: good decoding and good language (typical); poor decoding and good language (dyslexic profile); good decoding and poor language (poor comprehender, often missed because they read aloud fluently); poor at both (mixed).
The profile determines the intervention. Phonics for a poor decoder is appropriate; phonics for a poor comprehender is a waste of the child's time. Establishing which you have is the point of the assessment.

▸  The phonological deficit hypothesis
     The dominant account of developmental dyslexia holds that the core difficulty is in representing and manipulating the sound structure of language, which impairs the mapping between graphemes and phonemes. Three measures are standardly taken: phonological awareness (can the child segment, blend and manipulate sounds); rapid automatised naming (how quickly can they retrieve familiar labels — a naming-speed deficit is partly separable from a phonological one); and phonological working memory (non-word repetition, digit span).
The double-deficit hypothesis proposes that children weak in both phonological awareness and naming speed have the most severe difficulty — worth checking rather than assuming a single cause.

▸  Specific versus general
     Before concluding a specific difficulty, check the cognitive profile. A child whose reading is weak alongside generally low measured ability has a different picture from one whose reading is weak against average or above ability. Neither is more deserving of support, but they call for different interventions and different expectations. Do not write 'specific' unless you have checked.

▸  From profile to provision
     Write the recommendation before you look at the programme list, then check what the school holds. A structured, cumulative, multisensory phonics programme delivered four times weekly for twenty minutes by the SET, reviewed at six weeks, is a recommendation. 'Recommend phonics support' is not. Specify who, how often, how long, and when it will be reviewed.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Hulme, C., & Snowling, M. J. (2013). Developmental disorders of language learning and cognition. Wiley-Blackwell.

▸  Snowling, M. J., Hulme, C., & Nation, K. (2020). Defining and understanding dyslexia. Oxford Review of Education, 46(4), 501–513.

▸  Department of Education and Skills (2017). Continuum of Support: Guidelines for teachers. NEPS.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Recommending phonics for a poor comprehender.

✗  Concluding a specific difficulty without checking the cognitive profile.

✗  Reporting composites without saying what they do and do not establish.

✗  Recommending a programme the school does not have and cannot get.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You named the profile without linking it to provision.

▸  GRADE 4
     Battery administered and scored correctly; profile interpreted against the cognitive picture.

▸  GRADE 5
     The recommendation follows visibly from the finding and the SET could start on Monday.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · The reading model underneath
     [4–5 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The simple view of reading, the phonological deficit hypothesis, and what a dyslexia profile actually looks like.
     How you build it: One chapter on reading development plus one on dyslexia. Write a half-page summary of each.

     ·  Explain why phonological awareness matters for reading
          you have it when: You can explain it to a teacher without notes
          [CORU SoP 5.12]

     ·  Distinguish a specific difficulty from a general one
          you have it when: You check the cognitive profile before concluding
          [CORU SoP 3.4 · 5.17]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Administering the battery
     [5–6 hours  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     CTOPP-2 or equivalent — timing, error recording, scoring the composites.
     How you build it: Two supervised practice administrations, then score both by hand.

     ·  Administer phonological awareness subtests to standard
          you have it when: Administration is fluent and timing accurate
          [CORU SoP 5.6]

     ·  Administer rapid naming tasks accurately
          you have it when: You timed and recorded errors correctly
          [CORU SoP 5.6]

     ·  Score the phonological composites correctly
          you have it when: Composites calculated and checked
          [CORU SoP 5.6]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Turning a profile into advice
     [Habit per case  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Linking what the profile shows to an intervention the school can deliver.

macro.name: Social communication screening measures
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.2
     Be able to identify the limits of their practice and know when to seek advice and additional expertise or refer to another professional

▸  CORU 5.24
     Identify and apply knowledge of the intersecting forms of diversity of service users, working in an inclusive, sensitive and equitable manner

▸  CORU 5.28
     Be able to critically evaluate the theory and application of a range of assessment methods used in educational psychology to identify psychological, educational and developmental needs at individual and group levels

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Screening sits at a boundary you must be clear about: you are not diagnosing, and in Ireland the diagnostic pathway usually runs through a Children's Disability Network Team. Being precise about what a screen entitles you to say protects the child from a premature label and protects you from practising outside competence.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Screening, assessment, diagnosis — three different things
     A screen is a brief instrument designed to sort a population into probably-worth-looking-at and probably-not. It is optimised for sensitivity at the cost of specificity, which means false positives are expected and acceptable. An assessment is a fuller individual investigation. A diagnosis is a formal determination against criteria (DSM-5-TR or ICD-11), usually multidisciplinary for autism.
A positive screen entitles you to write: this child's presentation warrants further assessment, and here is the pathway. It does not entitle you to write that the child is autistic, and you should say so explicitly in the report.

▸  What the common instruments do
     The SCQ is a 40-item parent questionnaire derived from the ADI-R, with a commonly used cut-off around 15, though the manual's guidance and local practice vary. The SRS-2 gives a dimensional measure of social responsiveness rather than a yes/no, which is often more useful clinically. Neither is diagnostic. Both rely on a single informant's recall, which is their main weakness.

▸  Why questionnaires and observation disagree
     A parent reports across years and settings; you observe for forty minutes in one. Disagreement is normal and informative. If the screen is positive and you saw nothing, consider: masking, a structured setting that supports the child, or a parent reporting anxiety-driven behaviour that has a different source. If the screen is negative and you saw a great deal, consider a parent without a comparison point, or behaviour specific to the school context. Report the disagreement rather than choosing a side.

▸  Atypical and masked presentation
     Autistic girls are identified later and less often, and the reasons are partly instrumental — the screening items were normed on samples that were predominantly male. Presentations that are commonly missed include: social difficulty that looks like shyness or anxiety; intense interests in socially typical topics; and camouflaging, where the child consciously imitates peers and is exhausted by it. A negative screen in a girl with a strong parental concern is a reason to look further, not to stop. The same logic applies to late identification in children whose difficulty was previously attributed to something else.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Rutter, M., Bailey, A., & Lord, C. (2003). Social Communication Questionnaire manual. Western Psychological Services.

▸  Psychological Society of Ireland (2022). Guidelines for psychologists working with autistic people.

▸  Lai, M.-C., & Baron-Cohen, S. (2015). Identifying the lost generation of adults with autism spectrum conditions. The Lancet Psychiatry, 2(11), 1013–1027.

▸  HSE (2023). Progressing Disability Services: CDNT referral pathways. — know the local route.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Writing anything that reads as a diagnosis.

✗  Relying on the questionnaire alone.

✗  Treating a negative screen as reassurance when parental concern is strong.

✗  Not knowing where a positive screen goes next in this service.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You administered it and reported the result.

▸  GRADE 4
     Screen integrated with observation; limits stated; pathway named.

▸  GRADE 5
     You wrote that a screen is not a diagnosis, considered masked presentation, and the family left knowing the next step.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing what a screen is
     [4–5 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The difference between screening, assessment and diagnosis, and what a positive screen entitles you to say.
     How you build it: Read the SCQ manual's validity section. Then read the PSI Autism Guidelines 2022.

     ·  Recognise the limits of a screening instrument
          you have it when: You said in writing that a screen is not a diagnosis
          [CORU SoP 1.2 · PSI Code 2.3.1]

     ·  Know the onward diagnostic pathway in this service
          you have it when: You could name where a positive screen goes
          [CORU SoP 1.2]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Administering and integrating
     [3–4 hours  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Completing the screen with an informant and combining it with observation.
     How you build it: Complete three with parents, then compare each with your own observation.

     ·  Administer a screen with a parent
          you have it when: You explained what a screen can and cannot tell them
          [CORU SoP 2.1]

     ·  Integrate screening data with direct observation
          you have it when: You did not rely on the questionnaire alone
          [CORU SoP 3.4]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Recognising atypical presentation
     [3 hours, once  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     How autism presents diffe

macro.name: Behavioural and emotional rating scales
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.3
     Be able to determine the appropriate tests/assessments required and undertake/arrange these tests

▸  CORU 3.4
     Be able to analyse and critically evaluate the information collected in the assessment process

▸  CORU 5.32
     Interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data, within relevant conceptual frameworks, to inform case formulation and psychological intervention planning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 4.2.2
     Take due care to avoid misrepresentation, exaggeration, distortion or errors in reporting assessment results, research findings or service effectiveness, and act quickly to correct any such error.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Rating scales give you something no other method does: the same construct measured by two people who see the child in different settings. The disagreement between them is usually more informative than either score alone, and it is routinely thrown away.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What the common instruments are
     The SDQ is brief, free, widely used in Ireland, with parent, teacher and self-report versions covering emotional symptoms, conduct, hyperactivity, peer problems and prosocial behaviour plus an impact supplement. The Conners forms focus on attention and hyperactivity. The BASC-3 and ASEBA are broader and longer. Choose for the question: the SDQ for a general screen, a focused instrument where the referral is specific.

▸  Elevated versus clinically significant
     Standardised scores are usually banded — average, slightly raised, high, very high — with the bands set by percentile in the norm sample. An elevated score means unusual relative to the norm group. It does not mean disordered, and it does not license a diagnosis. Say which band and what it means in plain words, and avoid reporting a T-score without translating it.

▸  Reading informant discrepancy
     Cross-informant agreement on child behaviour is modest — correlations around 0.3 to 0.4 between parents and teachers are typical. This is not measurement failure; it reflects genuine setting specificity. A child rated high at home and average at school may be managing all day and releasing afterwards, or may be supported well at school. A child rated high at school and average at home may face demands at school that are not present at home. Both patterns are findings. Report them as information about context, not as one informant being wrong.

▸  The child's own voice
     Self-report versions exist from around age 11 for the SDQ and younger for some instruments. The child's own account is required by CORU 2.3 and by Article 12 of the UNCRC, and it frequently diverges from both adults. Where a self-report is not age-appropriate, you still need the child's view — obtained in conversation and quoted directly in the report.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Goodman, R. (2001). Psychometric properties of the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 40(11), 1337–1345.

▸  De Los Reyes, A., et al. (2015). The validity of the multi-informant approach to assessing child and adolescent mental health. Psychological Bulletin, 141(4), 858–900.

▸  United Nations (1989). Convention on the Rights of the Child, Article 12.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Reporting a T-score without translating it.

✗  Treating an elevated score as a diagnosis.

✗  Averaging informants, which destroys the most useful finding.

✗  Omitting the child's self-report where one was available.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You reported both informants separately.

▸  GRADE 4
     Correct instrument, correct scoring, bands translated into plain words.

▸  GRADE 5
     Discrepancy treated as data about context, and the child's own account included.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Choosing the instrument
     [3 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Which scale for which question, which informants, and what each is normed on.
     How you build it: Compare SDQ, Conners' and ASEBA on one page. Know what each is for.

     ·  Select the right forms for informant and age
          you have it when: Parent, teacher and self-report chosen appropriately
          [CORU SoP 3.3]

     ·  Include the child's own self-report where age-appropriate
          you have it when: The child's account appears alongside the adults'
          [UNCRC Art. 12 · CORU SoP 2.3]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Administering and scoring
     [3–4 hours  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     Briefing informants, chasing returns, scoring and converting.
     How you build it: Do three sets. Score by hand once.

     ·  Explain to informants how to complete them
          you have it when: Forms come back usable
          [CORU SoP 2.1]

     ·  Score and convert to standardised scores
          you have it when: Scoring is checked
          [CORU SoP 5.6]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Reading discrepancy
     [Ongoing  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     What it means when parent and teacher disagree, and why that is data rather than error.
     How you build it: Bring one discrepant set to supervision and be talked through it.

     ·  Analyse informant agreement and discrepancy
          you have it when: Discrepancy treated as data about context
          [CORU SoP 3.4 · 5.32]

     ·  Distinguish elevated from clinically significant
          you have it when: You know what the cut-offs mean and say so
          [PSI Code 4.2.2]

macro.name: Adapt standardised procedure and record the adaptation
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.8
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accurate and objective documentation

▸  CORU 5.31
     Conduct a range of assessment methods safely and ethically, adapting and re-evaluating their application as appropriate

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

▸  PSI 4.2.2
     Take due care to avoid misrepresentation, exaggeration, distortion or errors in reporting assessment results, research findings or service effectiveness, and act quickly to correct any such error.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Standardisation is what makes a norm-referenced score meaningful, and rigid adherence can make the assessment meaningless for the child in front of you. Knowing which adaptations preserve validity and which destroy it — and recording either honestly — is a genuine competency, not a workaround.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What standardisation buys you, and what it costs
     A standard score compares this child to a norm sample tested under specified conditions. Change the conditions and the comparison weakens. That is the cost of adaptation. The benefit is that a child who cannot access the task under standard conditions produces a score that measures their access, not their ability. Both errors are real; the judgement is which one you are making.

▸  Adaptations that preserve the comparison, and those that do not
     Generally preserving: a break between subtests; repeating an instruction where the manual permits; adjusting the physical environment (lighting, seating, noise); allowing a fidget object; moving to a different room.
Generally compromising: extending a timed item; rephrasing an instruction in your own words; providing a prompt the manual does not permit; changing item order within a subtest.
Where an adaptation compromises the comparison, you may still make it — but the score is then descriptive rather than normative, and you must say so.
This is a general principle rather than a rule to apply blindly: check the specific manual, and if a given adaptation is not addressed there, take it to supervision rather than deciding alone.

▸  Reasonable accommodation as a legal duty
     Under the Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 a service provider must do all that is reasonable to accommodate a person with a disability. That duty applies to your assessment. It does not oblige you to produce a valid standard score by any means — it obliges you to make the assessment accessible, and to be honest about what the resulting score means.

▸  Recording, and why it must be contemporaneous
     Annotate the protocol at the moment the adaptation happens, not afterwards. Write what you did, when, and why. Then in the report state the adaptation and its effect on interpretation: 'Two breaks were taken at the child's request. Standardised timing was preserved and scores are considered valid.' Or where it was not preserved: 'Instructions for Block Design were rephrased. This departs from standard procedure and the score is reported descriptively rather than as a normative comparison.' Written a week later, the same sentence is a reconstruction.

▸  Being willing to stop
     PSI clause 2.3.3 requires terminating an activity that is more harmful than beneficial. An assessment that is distressing a child and producing invalid data meets that test. Stopping is a defensible professional decision; continuing to get a complete protocol is not. Record the decision and the reason.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Equal Status Acts 2000–2018. — the reasonable accommodation provisions.

▸  PSI (2025). Code of professional ethics (5th rev.). Clauses 2.3.3 and 4.2.2.

▸  Wechsler, D. (2016). WISC-V UK administration and scoring manual. Pearson. — the section on testing the limits.

▸  CORU (2023). Standards of proficiency. Standards 5.31, 2.8.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Adapting and not recording it.

✗  Recording it afterwards from memory.

✗  Reporting an adapted score as if it were normative.

✗  Pushing through distress to complete the protocol.

✗  Deciding alone on an adaptation the manual does not address.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You adapted, but wrote it up afterwards.

▸  GRADE 4
     Adaptation chosen proportionately, annotated at the time, effect on validity stated.

▸  GRADE 5
     You were willing to stop, and said so in writing.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing what adaptation costs
     [2–3 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Which adaptations preserve validity, which invalidate a score, and how the manual treats each.
     How you build it: Ask your supervisor for three examples and why. Read the manual's section on testing the limits.

     ·  Choose an adaptation proportionate to the need
          you have it when: Break, rephrase, reorder or discontinue, chosen deliberately
          [CORU SoP 5.31 · Equal Status Acts]

     ·  State the effect on validity in the report
          you have it when: You said whether scores remain interpretable
          [PSI Code 4.2.2]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Noticing and deciding in the moment
     [Builds with practice  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Recognising when standard procedure has stopped working, and being willing to stop entirely.
     How you build it: Write a note after every administration on what you noticed and when.

     ·  Recognise when standard procedure is not working
          you have it when: You noticed early rather than at the end
          [CORU SoP 5.31]

     ·  Record the adaptation at the moment it happens
          you have it when: Annotated on the protocol, not reconstructed
          [CORU SoP 2.8]

     ·  Re-evaluate whether to continue at all
          you have it when: You were willing to stop
          [PSI Code 2.3.3]

macro.name: Learn the four frameworks for practice
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.1
     Be able to communicate diagnosis/assessment and/or treatment/management options in a way that can be understood by the service user

▸  CORU 5.29
     Know and apply educational psychology theory and systemic, ecological and problem-solving frameworks related to assessment methods

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
A framework is not a form to fill in. It is a decision about what counts as an explanation. Choose Monsen and you have committed to making your reasoning visible and falsifiable; choose the Interactive Factors Framework and you have committed to showing causal layers interacting rather than listed. Trainees who skip this step do not end up frameworkless — they end up using an implicit one, usually a within-child deficit model absorbed from report templates, and they cannot defend it when an examiner or a parent asks why the formulation looks the way it does. Your 4 August review named assimilating multiple sources as a development area. That difficulty is almost always a framework problem rather than a data problem.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Monsen's Problem-Analysis Framework (Monsen & Frederickson, 2008)
     A hypothesis-testing cycle: gather information, generate competing hypotheses, test each against the evidence, state the conclusion and what would disconfirm it. Its strength is that reasoning is inspectable — another psychologist can follow your steps and disagree at a specific point. Its weakness is that it is slow, and it can produce a tidy account of a messy situation by quietly dropping the hypotheses that did not resolve. Use it when the referral question is contested, when informants disagree, or when a previous formulation has not held.

▸  The Interactive Factors Framework (Frederickson & Cline, 2009; after Morton & Frith)
     Four levels — biological, cognitive, behavioural, and environmental — with arrows showing influence between them. Its strength is that it forces you to show interaction rather than list contributors, which is precisely the gap named in your review. Its weakness is that the arrows are easy to draw and hard to justify: an arrow is a causal claim and needs evidence. Use it for developmental and learning presentations where biology, cognition and environment are all live.

▸  The Constructionist Model of Informed and Reasoned Action, COMOIRA (Gameson & Rhydderch, 2008)
     Puts change, not diagnosis, at the centre, and treats every account — yours, the teacher's, the parent's, the child's — as a construction rather than a report on reality. Its strength is that it handles disagreement without deciding who is wrong, and it keeps the child's own construction in the formulation. Its weakness is that it can float free of data if you are not disciplined. Use it in consultation-led work and where the adults around the child hold incompatible views.

▸  Carr's model (Carr, 2015)
     A clinical-psychology formulation structure: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors, mapped across a developmental history. Its strength is that it handles timing — why now, why this child, why it persists. Its weakness is that it is individual-centred and can under-weight the classroom. Use it where onset and maintenance matter, such as school avoidance or emerging mood difficulty.

▸  What choosing actually involves
     The referral question chooses the framework, not your preference. Ask: is the difficulty contested (Monsen), multi-level and developmental (IFF), a disagreement between adults (COMOIRA), or a question about onset and maintenance (Carr)? Write the answer down before you collect data, because the framework determines what data you need. Choosing afterwards is decoration.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Monsen, J. J., & Frederickson, N. (2008). The Monsen et al. problem-analysis framework. In B. Kelly, L. Woolfson & J. Boyle (Eds.), Frameworks for practice in educational psychology. Jessica Kingsley. — read the worked case, not just the model.

▸  Gameson, J., & Rhydderch, G. (2008). The constructionist model of informed and reasoned action (COMOIRA). In Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle (Eds.), Frameworks for practice in educational psychology. Jessica Kingsley.

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity (2nd ed.). Open University Press. — the chapter presenting the Interactive Factors Framework.

▸  Carr, A. (2015). The handbook of child and adolescent clinical psychology (3rd ed.). Routledge. — the formulation chapter.

▸  Kelly, B., Woolfson, L., & Boyle, J. (Eds.) (2008). Frameworks for practice in educational psychology. Jessica Kingsley. — the editors' introduction is the best single account of why frameworks matter at all.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Naming a framework in the report without using its structure. If you cite Monsen and the report contains no competing hypotheses, you have cited it decoratively and an examiner will see that immediately.

✗  Choosing the framework after the data is collected, to fit what you found. That is not formulation, it is retrospective justification.

✗  Using the same framework on every case. If every referral suits the Interactive Factors Framework, you are not choosing — you are defaulting.

✗  Treating the four as interchangeable. They make different claims about what an explanation is. Being able to say what each one leaves out is the test of whether you understand them.

✗  Not asking your supervisor which framework they use. Supervisors have defaults too, and knowing theirs tells you how your reports will be read.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You can name the four

macro.name: Name and apply one framework to each substantial case
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.5
     Be able to demonstrate sound logical reasoning and problem solving skills to determine appropriate problem lists, action plans and goals

▸  CORU 5.29
     Know and apply educational psychology theory and systemic, ecological and problem-solving frameworks related to assessment methods

▸  CORU 5.32
     Interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data, within relevant conceptual frameworks, to inform case formulation and psychological intervention planning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The gap between knowing a framework and applying one is where most Year 1 reports fail. A report that lists findings — scores, then observation, then parent view, then teacher view — is a catalogue, and a catalogue leaves the reader to do the formulation. Applying a framework means the structure of your report is the structure of your reasoning, so a reader can see not just what you concluded but how, and can disagree at a named point. CORU 5.32 requires you to interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data within relevant conceptual frameworks. The phrase 'within relevant conceptual frameworks' is doing real work there.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Letting the framework structure the document
     If you have chosen Monsen, your report has a hypotheses section, and each hypothesis has evidence for and against. If you have chosen the Interactive Factors Framework, your report has levels and states the interactions between them. Do not write a standard report and add a framework sentence to the introduction. The test: delete the framework's name from your report — would a reader still be able to tell which one you used? If not, you did not apply it.

▸  Showing reasoning step by step
     Write the inference, not just the conclusion. Not 'John has a specific learning difficulty in reading' but 'John's word reading is at the 4th percentile while his Verbal Comprehension Index is at the 55th. The gap is not explained by instruction, as he has had two years of structured phonics, nor by attendance, which is 94%. The most parsimonious remaining explanation is a specific difficulty in phonological processing, supported by his score on [measure].' The second version can be argued with. That is the point.

▸  Including the child's own construction
     Every framework in the handbook has a place for the child's account, and it is the most commonly omitted element in trainee reports. Ask directly: what do you think is hard? what helps? what would you change? Then put the answer in the formulation, not in a decorative quote box. If the child's account contradicts the adults', that contradiction is a finding — see the skill on distinguishing primary from secondary needs.

▸  Citing it properly
     Name the framework and give the citation in the body of the report, not a footnote. 'This formulation is structured using the Interactive Factors Framework (Frederickson & Cline, 2009), which considers biological, cognitive, behavioural and environmental contributors and the interactions between them.' One sentence, early, then deliver on it.

▸  The one-hour rule
     Budget an hour per case for formulation, separate from writing. Formulation done while typing the report becomes narration of the data. Sit with the data, choose the framework, sketch the structure on paper, then write.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Monsen, J. J., & Frederickson, N. (2008), as above — specifically the worked example showing hypotheses tested and rejected.

▸  Cameron, R. J. (2006). Educational psychology: The distinctive contribution. Educational Psychology in Practice, 22(4), 289–304. — on what psychological reasoning adds beyond description.

▸  Woolfson, L., Whaling, R., Stewart, A., & Monsen, J. (2003). An integrated framework to guide educational psychologist practice. Educational Psychology in Practice, 19(4), 283–302.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  The framework appears in the introduction and nowhere else.

✗  Conclusions stated without the inferential step that produced them, so a reader can only accept or reject the whole report.

✗  The child's view recorded as a quotation but not used in the formulation.

✗  Formulating while writing, so the report narrates the assessment in the order it happened rather than in the order the argument needs.

✗  Hedging everything. A formulation that commits to nothing cannot be wrong, and is therefore useless to the school.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     The report presents findings accurately but the formulation is a summary of them.

▸  GRADE 4
     A named framework structures the report, the reasoning is visible, and the child's construction is included.

▸  GRADE 5
     The reasoning can be challenged at specific points because you have shown where it could fail, and you state what evidence would change your conclusion.

          you have it when: It appears by name with a citation
          [CORU SoP 5.29 · 5.27]

          [CORU SoP 5.32]
