macro.name: Distinguish primary from secondary needs
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.5
     Be able to demonstrate sound logical reasoning and problem solving skills to determine appropriate problem lists, action plans and goals

▸  CORU 3.6
     Be able to demonstrate an evidence-informed approach to professional decision-making, adapting practice to the needs of the service user and drawing on appropriate knowledge and skills in order to make professional judgments

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Almost every referral arrives with the secondary need on the form. Schools refer for behaviour, and the behaviour is downstream of an unidentified reading difficulty. They refer for anxiety, and the anxiety is downstream of an unmet language need. If you formulate the presenting problem you will recommend an intervention for a symptom, it will not work, and the school will conclude that psychology does not help. Distinguishing primary from secondary is the single highest-value move in the whole formulation competency, and it is mostly a matter of asking what came first.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Generating more than one hypothesis, properly
     Two is the minimum and they must be genuinely competing — not 'dyslexia' and 'a specific difficulty with reading'. For a child referred for classroom behaviour, competing hypotheses might be: (a) an unidentified literacy difficulty makes independent work aversive, and the behaviour is escape-maintained; (b) the behaviour is attention-maintained and independent of task difficulty; (c) the classroom's demand level is developmentally inappropriate for most of the class and this child is the one who protests. Each predicts different data.

▸  Using timing as evidence
     Ask when each difficulty began, and get the answer from more than one source. If the behaviour predates the literacy difficulty, literacy is not driving it. If the behaviour began in second class, when independent written work started, that is strong. Developmental history is the instrument here, and it is why the parent interview matters more than trainees usually assume.

▸  Using the situational spread
     A primary difficulty shows up wherever its demand is present. A secondary one is tied to the context that provokes it. If the behaviour occurs in literacy and maths word problems but not in oral maths, PE or art, reading is implicated. If it occurs everywhere including yard, it is not task-driven. This is what the comparison observation is for.

▸  Recording the hypothesis you rejected
     Write it in the report: 'An attention-maintained explanation was considered and is less consistent with the pattern, because the behaviour did not occur during whole-class oral work where adult attention was equally available.' This is the single line that most distinguishes a grade 5 report from a grade 3. It shows you tested rather than assumed.

▸  Holding uncertainty honestly
     Sometimes the sequence genuinely cannot be established — records are missing, the child moved schools, the informants disagree and neither is more reliable. Say so, say what it would take to resolve it, and recommend accordingly. 'The direction of the relationship between X and Y cannot be established from the available information. A review after one term of targeted literacy support would clarify it.' That is a stronger report than a confident guess.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity — the chapters on identification and on behaviour, read together.

▸  Carr, A. (2015). The handbook of child and adolescent clinical psychology — predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors.

▸  Snowling, M. J., & Hulme, C. (2012). Annual research review: The nature and classification of reading disorders. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 53(5), 593–607. — for the literacy-to-behaviour pathway specifically.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Formulating the referral question rather than the problem. The referral question is a hypothesis someone else has already made.

✗  One hypothesis, tested for confirming evidence only.

✗  Treating co-occurrence as causation. Anxiety and reading difficulty appearing together does not tell you the direction.

✗  Never writing down what you rejected, so the report reads as if only one explanation was ever entertained.

✗  Forcing a primary/secondary distinction when the evidence does not support one, because it makes for a neater report.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You identify the needs present and describe them accurately.

▸  GRADE 4
     You generate competing hypotheses, test them against the data, and state which need is primary.

▸  GRADE 5
     You record the rejected hypothesis and why, and where the sequence is genuinely unclear you say so and specify what would resolve it.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Generating alternatives
     [Habit — 20 minutes per case  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Producing more than one explanation before settling on any.
     How you build it: Write three hypotheses for every case for one month. It becomes automatic.

     ·  Generate more than one hypothesis
          you have it when: An alternative was genuinely considered
          [PSI Code 4.2.6 · CORU SoP 3.5]

     ·  Record the hypothesis you rejected and why
          you have it when: The rejected one appears somewhere
          [PSI Code 4.2.6]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Testing against evidence
     [Ongoing · one case a fortnight  ·  Weeks 7–12

macro.name: Consider the likelihood of co-occurring conditions
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.4
     Be able to analyse and critically evaluate the information collected in the assessment process

▸  CORU 5.15
     Know psychological models related to the cognitive, behavioural, emotional, social and learning development of children, young people and adults in educational, health and social care services

▸  CORU 5.17
     Know psychological models related to the factors that hinder the fulfilment of potential and achievement among children, young people and adults, in order to identify needs and address barriers to learning and development

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Co-occurrence is the norm, not the exception, and diagnostic overshadowing is the most common way children get missed. Once a child has an autism diagnosis, their reading difficulty gets attributed to autism and never assessed. Once a child is identified as having a general learning disability, their anxiety is treated as part of the picture rather than as something treatable. Your job in a formulation is to consider a second presentation as routine rather than as a special step, and to weigh the evidence for each separately.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The pairings you should expect
     ADHD and specific learning difficulty co-occur at rates commonly reported between 30 and 50 per cent. Developmental Language Disorder and literacy difficulty are strongly associated. DCD co-occurs with both ADHD and DLD. Autism co-occurs with ADHD, with anxiety, and with intellectual disability. Anxiety accompanies most unidentified learning difficulties of long standing. Know the rates approximately, and check them in a current source before citing a figure in a report.

▸  Diagnostic overshadowing, and how to resist it
     The discipline is procedural rather than attitudinal. When a child arrives with an existing diagnosis, write down the difficulties that diagnosis does not explain, before you begin. If a child with autism cannot decode, autism does not explain the decoding — assess it. If a child with a general learning disability has attainment well below the level predicted by their cognitive profile, the discrepancy is a finding, not noise.

▸  Twice-exceptionality
     High ability plus a specific difficulty produces average attainment and a child who looks unremarkable while working several times harder than their peers. It is missed constantly because screening is attainment-based. The signal is a large discrepancy within the cognitive profile — strong verbal reasoning, weak processing speed or working memory — with attainment sitting between them. Look at index scatter, not just the composite.

▸  Weighing each separately
     Do not let evidence for one condition carry the other. Build the case for each independently: what would establish it, what evidence is present, what is absent. Then state what would be needed to establish the second presentation — which is often a referral rather than a conclusion you can reach yourself.

▸  Knowing what is not yours to diagnose
     As a trainee educational psychologist you do not diagnose ADHD, autism, or any medical condition. You describe the profile, note what it is consistent with, and refer. Writing 'this profile is consistent with an attentional difficulty and referral to [service] is recommended for diagnostic assessment' is correct. Writing 'John has ADHD' is outside your competence, and PSI 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 are explicit about that boundary.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity — the chapters on specific difficulties and on co-occurrence.

▸  Kaplan, B. J., Dewey, D. M., Crawford, S. G., & Wilson, B. N. (2001). The term comorbidity is of questionable value in reference to developmental disorders. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 34(6), 555–565. — on why the pairings are not accidental.

▸  Pennington, B. F. (2006). From single to multiple deficit models of developmental disorders. Cognition, 101(2), 385–413.

▸  NCSE guidance on twice-exceptional learners, and the NEPS Continuum of Support materials on identification.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Stopping at the first explanation that fits.

✗  Attributing every difficulty to an existing diagnosis.

✗  Missing high ability because attainment is average.

✗  Citing co-occurrence rates from memory. Check them — figures vary widely by study and an examiner may ask for the source.

✗  Diagnosing. You describe and refer.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You note an additional difficulty when it is obvious from the data.

▸  GRADE 4
     You consider a second presentation routinely, and weigh the evidence for each separately.

▸  GRADE 5
     You state explicitly what would be needed to establish the second presentation, and you name the boundary between description and diagnosis.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the common pairings
     [3–4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Which conditions commonly co-occur in this age band, and roughly how often.
     How you build it: One page listing the eight commonest pairings and their approximate base rates.

     ·  Know the common co-occurrences in this age band
          you have it when: SLD with ADHD, anxiety masking autism, and so on
          [CORU SoP 5.15 · 5.17]

     ·  Consider twice-exceptionality
          you have it when: High ability masking difficulty was considered
          [CORU SoP 5.17]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Weighing separately
     [Habit per case  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Not letting one explanation absorb everything.
     How you build it: For each case, ask what this for

macro.name: Analyse risk and resilience
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.3
     Be able to act in the best interest of service users at all times with due regard to their will and preference

▸  CORU 1.12
     Understand and be able to apply the limits of the concept of confidentiality particularly in relation to child protection, vulnerable adults and elder abuse

▸  CORU 5.17
     Know psychological models related to the factors that hinder the fulfilment of potential and achievement among children, young people and adults, in order to identify needs and address barriers to learning and development

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
A formulation that records only what is wrong produces recommendations with nothing to build on. Protective factors are not a courtesy paragraph — they are the material the intervention is made from, because an intervention that runs through an existing strength is the one the school will actually sustain. Separately, and more seriously: this is the skill where you must know the point at which risk stops being a formulation matter and becomes a safeguarding one. Your 4 August review named risk management protocols as a development area. Know the threshold before the day you need it, not on it.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Risk factors at three levels
     Child level: developmental difficulty, chronic illness, early adversity, communication difficulty. Family level: parental ill health, bereavement, separation, housing instability, income strain, caring responsibilities. Community and school level: unstable placement, repeated changes of teacher, discrimination, low expectations, poor peer group, distance from services. Gather across all three or you will produce a within-child formulation by omission.

▸  Protective factors that are genuinely present
     The test is evidence, not optimism. 'Supportive family' is not a protective factor unless you can say what the family does. 'Good relationship with the SNA' is one if you observed it, or if the child named that adult when asked who helps. One reliable adult, one area of competence, one place the child chooses to go — these are real and usable. Write them specifically enough to build on.

▸  Building the recommendation on a protective factor
     If a child reads willingly with one particular teacher, the intervention is delivered by that teacher or explicitly models her approach. If the child's strength is oral reasoning, the access arrangement is a reader before it is anything else. This is what turns a list of strengths into a formulation that does work.

▸  The safeguarding threshold, in practice
     You are operating under Children First and the school's Designated Liaison Person route. The threshold is not a judgement call you make alone. If a child discloses harm, if you observe injury, if you have a reasonable concern about welfare, or if a child indicates intent to harm themselves or another — you stop, you do not continue the assessment, you tell your supervisor the same day, and you follow the DLP route. This does not replace your own duty: if you are a mandated person (confirm your status with UCD), a report must reach Tusla as soon as practicable — jointly with the DLP or by you (Children First Act 2015). PSI 3.3.4 requires you to act to stop or offset serious harm even where a confidential relationship is involved. CORU 1.12 requires you to apply the limits of confidentiality in relation to child protection. Neither leaves discretion.

▸  What to do in the first hour
     Write down what was said or seen, verbatim where possible, with the time. Do not question the child further — that is not your role and it can compromise a later process. Tell your supervisor. Tell the DLP. Record who you told and when. Then record what you did, because your own record is the thing that protects both the child and you. Rehearse this sequence before you are in it; on 22/05/2026 you managed a disclosure at Grange, and that day is evidence for this skill.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Children First: National Guidance for the Protection and Welfare of Children (DCEDIY, current edition) — and your NEPS service's own protocol, which is the one that binds you day to day.

▸  Masten, A. S. (2014). Global perspectives on resilience in children and youth. Child Development, 85(1), 6–20. — on ordinary rather than exceptional protective processes.

▸  Rutter, M. (2012). Resilience as a dynamic concept. Development and Psychopathology, 24(2), 335–344.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), clauses 3.3.4 and 1.3.14 — read the actual wording, it is on the Reference sheet.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Listing risk and never using it in the recommendations.

✗  Listing protective factors that are aspirational rather than observed.

✗  Continuing an assessment after a disclosure because it felt rude to stop.

✗  Recording a concern in your own notes and not telling anyone that day.

✗  Treating risk analysis as a section of the report rather than as something that can interrupt the work at any point.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You identify risk and protective factors and record them.

▸  GRADE 4
     You gather across child, family and school levels, and at least one recommendation is built on a protective factor you evidenced.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can state the safeguarding threshold and the exact sequence you would follow, and your formulation shows how risk and protection interact over time rather than as two lists.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the factors
     [3 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The established risk and protective factors at individual, family and school leve

macro.name: Account for the biopsychosocial context
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.2
     Demonstrate a critical understanding of relevant biological sciences, human development, social and behavioural sciences and other related sciences, together with a knowledge of health and wellbeing

▸  CORU 5.5
     Be able to identify and understand the impact of governmental, organisational, community and societal structures, systems and culture on health and social care provision

▸  CORU 5.14
     Know the impact of structures and systems in which educational services are provided on the development of children, young people and adult learners at individual, group and organisational levels

▸  CORU 5.16
     Know psychological models related to the impact of family structures, culture, community, organisations and systems on cognitive, behavioural, emotional, social and learning development

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Which model of disability you are working from determines what you recommend, whether or not you have ever named it. A medical model locates the difficulty in the child and produces recommendations aimed at the child. A social model locates it in barriers and produces recommendations aimed at the environment. A biopsychosocial model holds both and is what CORU 5.2, 5.14, 5.16 and 5.5 collectively require. Most trainee reports are medical-model by default because the assessment tools are child-focused, and the report follows the tools.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Naming the model you are using
     Write it down before you start. If you are working from a biopsychosocial model, your report has to show the environment doing something, not just appearing in a paragraph. The question that exposes a default medical model: if the environment changed and the child did not, would any of your recommendations become unnecessary? If the answer is no, you have written a within-child report.

▸  Biological and developmental contributors
     Birth and developmental history, hearing and vision status, sleep, chronic illness, medication and its timing, genetic conditions, early intervention received. Note particularly: a history of glue ear during the infant classes is a live hypothesis for a literacy difficulty presenting at eight, and it is routinely missed because nobody asks about hearing four years after it resolved.

▸  Family, culture and community
     Home language and the amount of exposure to the language of instruction, literacy practices at home, parental experience of school, migration and displacement, community resources, and the family's own construction of the difficulty. For a child assessed through an interpreter, this is not background — it changes what the scores mean, and the report must say so.

▸  The school environment as a contributor, not a backdrop
     Class size, teaching approach, how much of the day is independent written work, staff turnover, the Continuum of Support level and whether what is documented is actually happening, physical environment, acoustics, seating. The gap between the support recorded in the Student Support File and the support observed in the room is a finding worth stating plainly.

▸  Writing the levels as interacting
     The move that separates a grade 5 from a grade 3 is showing influence, not listing contributors. Not 'John has a phonological processing difficulty. John's class has 29 pupils. John's first language is Ukrainian.' Instead: 'John's phonological processing difficulty is compounded by a class size which limits individual feedback, and by the fact that instruction is in his second language, so that errors which would ordinarily be corrected within a lesson persist uncorrected. Each factor alone would be manageable; together they account for the size of the gap.' That sentence is a formulation. The first version is a list.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity — the opening chapters on models of disability, read before anything else in this skill.

▸  Bronfenbrenner, U., & Morris, P. A. (2006). The bioecological model of human development. In Handbook of Child Psychology (6th ed.). Wiley.

▸  Engel, G. L. (1977). The need for a new medical model. Science, 196(4286), 129–136. — the original biopsychosocial argument, short and still worth reading.

▸  Oliver, M. (2013). The social model of disability: Thirty years on. Disability & Society, 28(7), 1024–1026.

▸  NEPS Continuum of Support guidelines — the Irish policy frame your recommendations have to land inside.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Writing a within-child report while believing you hold a social model.

✗  Listing environmental factors in a context paragraph and never referring to them again.

✗  Not asking about hearing history, and attributing a literacy difficulty entirely to phonological processing.

✗  Treating English as an Additional Language as a footnote rather than as something that changes the interpretation of every verbally mediated score.

✗  Recommending only what the school already does, because you did not examine the environment closely enough to see what is missing.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You record biological, family and school information in the report.

▸  GRADE 4
     You name the model you are working from and show the levels contributing.

▸  GRADE 5
     You show the levels interacting, you state which interaction accounts for the size of the difficulty, and at least one recommendation targets the environment rather than the child.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the models
     [3–4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The social

macro.name: Educational interventions in literacy
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.8
     Be able to evaluate intervention plans using appropriate tools and recognised performance/outcome measures along with service user responses; revise the plans as necessary and where appropriate in conjunction with the service user

▸  CORU 5.33
     Be able to critically evaluate the theory and application of evidence-based intervention methods — at individual and group levels — in educational, health and social care settings

▸  CORU 5.34
     Design intervention(s) on the basis of available data, evidence-informed professional judgement, formulation and service user perspective

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

▸  PSI 3.1.2
     Monitor and evaluate the effect of their professional activities, record their findings and, if appropriate, communicate new knowledge to others in the field.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
A report that identifies a reading difficulty and recommends 'targeted literacy support' has done half a job and the weaker half. The school already knew the child could not read. What they need from a psychologist is which component is broken, which intervention addresses that component, at what intensity, for how long, and how they will know whether it worked. CORU 5.34 requires intervention designed on the basis of available data, evidence-informed judgement and formulation — which means the intervention must follow from your assessment, not from a list of what the school already owns.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The components, because the intervention follows the component
     Reading is not one thing. Phonological awareness, phonics and decoding, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension are separable and a child can fail at any one of them with the others intact. A child who decodes accurately but slowly has a fluency problem and phonics instruction will not touch it. A child who decodes fluently and cannot answer questions has a comprehension or vocabulary problem. Identify the component before you name a programme.

▸  What works, by component
     Phonological awareness and decoding: systematic, explicit, synthetic phonics, taught to mastery — this is the most robust finding in the literacy literature. Fluency: repeated reading with feedback, and paired reading. Vocabulary: direct instruction of a small number of words taught deeply, not lists. Comprehension: explicit strategy instruction — prediction, clarification, questioning, summarising — modelled then gradually released. Ireland-specific: UFLI and the NEPS literacy materials are what schools are likely to have; know them well enough to say whether what the school is doing matches the component you identified.

▸  Specifying rather than recommending
     A usable recommendation has five parts: what, who delivers it, how often and for how long per session, over what period, and what will be measured. 'Daily 20-minute structured phonics delivered by the SET in a group of no more than three, for one term, with progress monitored fortnightly on non-word reading' is a recommendation. 'Literacy support' is a wish. Intensity is the variable schools most often get wrong and psychologists most often leave unspecified.

▸  Measuring it
     Choose the measure before the intervention starts and take a baseline. Use something sensitive to short-term change — curriculum-based measurement, words correct per minute, non-word reading — not an annual standardised test, which will not move in a term and will tell you nothing. Set the review date in the report. CORU 3.8 and 5.37 both require you to evaluate and revise, and you cannot revise what you did not measure.

▸  Knowing what the evidence does not support
     Coloured overlays and tinted lenses for reading difficulty, learning-styles matching, and most commercial 'brain training' packages do not have the evidence base their marketing claims. You will meet schools using them. The professional move is not to denounce but to redirect: acknowledge the effort, state plainly what the evidence supports, and offer the alternative. PSI 4.2.2 requires you to avoid misrepresenting the effectiveness of services.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  National Reading Panel (2000). Teaching children to read. NICHD. — the component structure and the evidence for each.

▸  Ehri, L. C. (2005). Learning to read words: Theory, findings, and issues. Scientific Studies of Reading, 9(2), 167–188.

▸  Snowling, M. J., & Hulme, C. (2011). Evidence-based interventions for reading and language difficulties. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 81(1), 1–23.

▸  EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit — reading comprehension strategies, phonics, and one-to-one tuition strands, each with cost and effect estimates.

▸  NEPS Continuum of Support guidelines and literacy resources.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Recommending a programme without identifying which component is impaired.

✗  Leaving intensity unspecified, so the school delivers fifteen minutes a week and concludes the intervention does not work.

✗  Choosing an annual standardised measure to monitor a one-term intervention.

✗  No baseline, so no way to attribute change.

✗  Recommending only what the school already does, because you did not ask what else exists.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You recommend an intervention appropriate to a reading difficulty.

▸  GRADE 4
     You identify the impaired component, name an intervention with evidence for that component, and specify intensity, duration and deliverer.

▸  GRADE 5
     You specify the monitoring measure and review point, you can cite the evidence for your choice, and you can say what you would do if the first term shows no change.

8 · BLOCKS A

macro.name: Educational interventions in numeracy
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.4
     Be able to analyse and critically evaluate the information collected in the assessment process

▸  CORU 5.33
     Be able to critically evaluate the theory and application of evidence-based intervention methods — at individual and group levels — in educational, health and social care settings

▸  CORU 5.34
     Design intervention(s) on the basis of available data, evidence-informed professional judgement, formulation and service user perspective

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Numeracy is the poor relation in educational psychology practice — less research, fewer programmes, less confident practitioners — and trainees often avoid it by writing a generic maths recommendation. But the developmental sequence in number is well described, and knowing it lets you say where a child actually is rather than that they are behind. That is the difference between a recommendation a teacher can act on and one they cannot.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  How number develops
     Subitising, then counting with one-to-one correspondence, then cardinality (understanding that the last number counted is the quantity), then number comparison and the mental number line, then part-whole relations, then derived facts and strategies, then formal procedures. A child who has not secured cardinality cannot meaningfully do addition, and drilling addition facts will not help. Locate the child in this sequence before recommending anything.

▸  Separating the sources of failure
     A maths word problem failure can be a reading problem, a working memory problem, a number sense problem, a procedural knowledge problem, or anxiety. These need different interventions and the assessment has to distinguish them. Give the same problem orally and in writing; give a calculation with and without the language wrapper. The difference is the finding.

▸  What the evidence supports
     Explicit teaching of strategies rather than drill. Concrete–pictorial–abstract sequencing, with the concrete stage not rushed. Number-line work for magnitude and comparison. Small-group explicit instruction for children behind their peers. Manipulatives used to represent structure, not as an activity in themselves. Maths anxiety, where present, needs addressing alongside the instruction, not after it.

▸  Placing it on the Continuum of Support
     Name the level: Classroom Support, School Support, or School Support Plus. This is how Irish schools allocate resource, and a recommendation that does not name a level leaves the school guessing. If you are recommending School Support Plus, say what makes it that rather than School Support — usually intensity, individualisation and the involvement of outside services.

▸  Being honest about the evidence base
     The numeracy intervention literature is thinner than the literacy one and the programmes have weaker evidence. Say so in the report rather than implying more certainty than exists. PSI 2.3.1 requires you to be mindful of the limits of psychological data and techniques, and a limitations sentence about the numeracy evidence base is a mark of competence, not a weakness.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Gersten, R., Chard, D. J., Jayanthi, M., Baker, S. K., Morphy, P., & Flojo, J. (2009). Mathematics instruction for students with learning disabilities. Review of Educational Research, 79(3), 1202–1242.

▸  Dowker, A. (2004). What works for children with mathematical difficulties? DfES Research Report 554.

▸  Butterworth, B., Varma, S., & Laurillard, D. (2011). Dyscalculia: From brain to education. Science, 332(6033), 1049–1053.

▸  EEF Improving Mathematics in the Early Years and Key Stage 1, and Improving Mathematics in Key Stages 2 and 3.

▸  NEPS Continuum of Support guidelines.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Generic maths recommendations that do not locate the child developmentally.

✗  Not separating the reading load from the calculation load.

✗  Recommending drill for a child who has not secured cardinality.

✗  Omitting the Continuum level, so the school cannot allocate.

✗  Implying the numeracy evidence base is as strong as the literacy one.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You recommend numeracy support appropriate to the difficulty.

▸  GRADE 4
     You locate the child in the developmental sequence, separate the sources of failure, and name the Continuum level.

▸  GRADE 5
     You cite the evidence and state its limits, and your recommendation specifies the instructional approach rather than a programme name.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing how number develops
     [4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     Number sense, counting principles, fact retrieval and the concrete–pictorial–abstract sequence.
     How you build it: One chapter on numeracy development. Write the CPA sequence out in your own words.

     ·  Know concrete–pictorial–abstract sequencing
          you have it when: You can explain it to a teacher in two minutes
          [CORU SoP 5.33]

     ·  Distinguish fact retrieval from conceptual difficulty
          you have it when: The recommendation targets the right one
          [CORU SoP 3.4 · 5.34]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Placing it on the Continuum
     [3 hours  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Knowing which level of support a numeracy recommendation belongs at.
     How you build it: Map one school's numeracy provision across the three levels.

     ·  Recommend at the right point on the Continuum
          you have it when: Level stated
          [NEPS Continuum of Support]

     ·  Specify what success would look like
          you have it when: A teacher would know wh

macro.name: Wellbeing interventions at class and group level
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.33
     Be able to critically evaluate the theory and application of evidence-based intervention methods — at individual and group levels — in educational, health and social care settings

▸  CORU 5.36
     Apply safe and ethical intervention(s) appropriate to the goals and purpose identified in intervention plan(s)

▸  CORU 5.40
     Work collaboratively with other professionals — including teachers, other school staff and multi-disciplinary teams — to build capacity among those responsible for the delivery of interventions

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Working at class and group level is where educational psychology does something a clinician cannot, and it is the competency Irish trainees evidence most thinly — your own review named systemic work as a development area. A universal or targeted group intervention reaches thirty children for the cost of one assessment. It is also where the risk of doing harm through a badly designed group is real and under-discussed.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The tiers, and choosing the right one
     Universal (whole class or whole school), targeted or selective (a group identified as at risk), and indicated (individual). Universal programmes have small effect sizes across many children; targeted groups have larger effects on fewer. The choice is not about severity alone — it is about whether the difficulty is shared. If a third of the class has the difficulty, a targeted group misidentifies a classroom problem as a child problem.

▸  What the evidence supports
     Social and emotional learning programmes delivered with fidelity produce modest but real gains in wellbeing and in attainment. Fidelity is the variable that predicts whether they work — poorly implemented SEL produces nothing. CBT-informed anxiety groups for children have reasonable support. Mindfulness in schools has mixed evidence and some trials showing no effect or harm in adolescents; do not present it as established. Friends for Life and similar manualised programmes are used in Irish settings — know which your service uses.

▸  Facilitating a group without doing harm
     Screen who is in it. A group of children with the same difficulty can normalise it or can amplify it — deviancy training is a documented risk when grouping children with conduct difficulties. Set ground rules with the group rather than for them. Manage disclosure: a child may disclose in a group and you have no control over what the other children repeat. Say at the start what you will do if someone tells you something that worries you, in the children's own terms.

▸  Leaving it behind
     The intervention that ends when you leave has failed. Build in the school staff from the first session — co-facilitate, then hand over, then review. CORU 5.40 asks you to build capacity among those responsible for delivery. Write the handover into the plan at the start; it does not happen if it is an afterthought.

▸  Evaluating a group
     Pre and post measures on the children, a fidelity check on the delivery, and a teacher or facilitator view. Something as simple as a validated brief measure at week one and week eight will let you say whether it worked, and gives you a practice-based research output — which is another of your named development areas, met by the same piece of work.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Durlak, J. A., Weissberg, R. P., Dymnicki, A. B., Taylor, R. D., & Schellinger, K. B. (2011). The impact of enhancing students' social and emotional learning: A meta-analysis. Child Development, 82(1), 405–432.

▸  Dishion, T. J., McCord, J., & Poulin, F. (1999). When interventions harm: Peer groups and problem behavior. American Psychologist, 54(9), 755–764. — read this before you run any group.

▸  Kuyken, W. et al. (2022). Effectiveness of universal school-based mindfulness training. Evidence-Based Mental Health, 25(3). — the trial that complicated the mindfulness story.

▸  Weare, K., & Nind, M. (2011). Mental health promotion and problem prevention in schools: What does the evidence say? Health Promotion International, 26(S1).

▸  Department of Education Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Running a targeted group for a difficulty that is actually classroom-wide.

✗  No fidelity check, so you cannot tell whether the programme or its delivery failed.

✗  Grouping children with conduct difficulties without considering deviancy training.

✗  Not setting out disclosure rules with the children at the start.

✗  No handover, so the work ends when the placement does.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have contributed to a group intervention.

▸  GRADE 4
     You chose the tier deliberately, screened membership, and co-facilitated with school staff.

▸  GRADE 5
     You evaluated with pre and post measures and a fidelity check, handed over to staff, and can state what you would change.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the evidence
     [4–5 hours, once  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     Which whole-class wellbeing programmes have an evidence base, and how strong it is.
     How you build it: Read one review of school-based wellbeing programmes. Note which are used in Irish schools.

     ·  Know the evidence base for what you recommend
          you have it when: You can cite it
          [CORU SoP 5.33 · 5.41]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Group facilitation
     [6–8 hours  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Running a session with a class rather than an individual — pacing, managing participation, adapting live.
     How you build it: Co-facilitate twice with the teacher before leading a

macro.name: Foundations in counselling skills
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.2
     Be able to identify the limits of their practice and know when to seek advice and additional expertise or refer to another professional

▸  CORU 5.18
     Know psychotherapeutic models relevant to educational psychology and critically evaluate these as they are applied in practice

▸  CORU 5.21
     Establish, maintain and conclude a professional relationship with a service user, safely and ethically, recognising and managing professional boundaries

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

▸  PSI 3.4.3
     When referring a client, maintain support and responsibility for caring until contact has commenced with the agent to whom referral was made.

▸  PSI 3.4.4
     Give reasonable notice and make reasonably certain that discontinuation will cause no harm to the client, before discontinuing services.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
You are not a therapist and Year 1 is not therapy training. But every parent feedback meeting, every pupil interview, every difficult consultation runs on counselling micro-skills, and without them you will get thin information and damaged relationships. The other half of this skill is knowing precisely where your competence ends — PSI 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 put that boundary in writing, and crossing it is one of the more serious things a trainee can do.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The micro-techniques, and what each is for
     Open questions get an account; closed questions confirm a detail. Reflection of content shows you heard; reflection of feeling shows you understood and is the one trainees skip. Summarising at intervals lets the person correct you, which is how you avoid building a formulation on a misunderstanding. Silence — three to five seconds after an answer — produces more than any follow-up question, and is the hardest to tolerate. Practise silence deliberately; it feels far longer than it is.

▸  Reflecting feeling without labelling
     'That sounds frightening' is a hypothesis offered for correction. 'You're anxious about it' is a label applied. The first invites 'no, more angry actually', which is information. The second closes it. Tentativeness is not weakness here — it is the technique.

▸  Knowing your limit, concretely
     You can listen, contain, and help someone think. You cannot deliver therapy, treat a mental health condition, or work with trauma. If a parent begins disclosing their own mental health difficulty, your job is to listen, acknowledge, and signpost — not to take it on. If a child's disclosure moves toward trauma, you stop and refer. Write the referral routes out in advance so that in the moment you have a name to give rather than a vague suggestion to see someone.

▸  Solution-focused technique as the usable middle
     Solution-focused approaches are widely used in Irish educational psychology, are within trainee competence with supervision, and are well suited to school work. Scaling questions, the miracle question, exception-finding and identifying what is already working give you a structure for a pupil interview that is both useful and defensible. You have already used this framework at Roscommon; build it deliberately rather than incidentally.

▸  Ending well
     Signal the ending before it arrives — 'we have about ten minutes left'. Summarise what was said and what happens next. Be explicit about what you will and will not do, and what will be written down and who will see it. An unclear ending leaves a parent expecting contact that is not coming, which does more damage than a blunt but clear one.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Egan, G., & Reese, R. J. (2021). The skilled helper (11th ed.). Cengage. — the standard text for the micro-skills.

▸  Ratner, H., George, E., & Iveson, C. (2012). Solution focused brief therapy: 100 key points and techniques. Routledge.

▸  Rogers, C. R. (1957). The necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change. Journal of Consulting Psychology, 21(2), 95–103.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 2.2.2, 2.2.3 and 2.2.4 — the competence boundary in the Code's own words. Full text is on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Kelly, B., & Perkins, D. F. (Eds.) (2012). Handbook of implementation science for psychology in education. Cambridge University Press.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Filling silence.

✗  Labelling feeling instead of offering it tentatively.

✗  Drifting into therapy with a parent because the conversation went there and it felt unkind to stop.

✗  Not knowing the referral route, so the signpost is vague.

✗  Ending without saying what happens next or what gets written down.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You use open questions and can conduct an interview that gathers information.

▸  GRADE 4
     You reflect feeling tentatively, tolerate silence, summarise to allow correction, and can state where your competence ends.

▸  GRADE 5
     You use a named approach deliberately, you recognise in the moment when a conversation is moving outside your competence, and you redirect and refer cleanly.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · The micro-techniques
     [8–10 hours plus practice  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Open questions, reflective listening, summarising, silence, scaling.
     How you build it: One skills course or text. Then practise each deliberately, one per session.

     ·  Use open questions and reflective listening
          you have it when: The young person speaks more than you do
          [CORU SoP 5.18]

     ·  Hold silence without filling it
          you have it when: You waited
          [CORU S

macro.name: Write recommendations naming the Continuum of Support level
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.8
     Be able to evaluate intervention plans using appropriate tools and recognised performance/outcome measures along with service user responses; revise the plans as necessary and where appropriate in conjunction with the service user

▸  CORU 5.34
     Design intervention(s) on the basis of available data, evidence-informed professional judgement, formulation and service user perspective

▸  CORU 5.35
     Identify and evaluate the characteristics of school organisation and culture in order to contribute to school development that enhances the participation and wellbeing of all learners

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

▸  PSI 3.1.2
     Monitor and evaluate the effect of their professional activities, record their findings and, if appropriate, communicate new knowledge to others in the field.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The Continuum of Support is the structure Irish schools use to allocate resource. A recommendation that does not name a level is a recommendation the school cannot action, however good the psychology behind it. This is the most concrete Ireland-specific skill in the intervention competency, and it is the one that determines whether your report changes anything.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The three levels, precisely
     Classroom Support: led by the class teacher, differentiation within ordinary teaching, documented in a Classroom Support Plan. School Support: additional targeted input from the SET, usually small group, with a Student Support File and review dates. School Support Plus: individualised, higher intensity, typically involving outside professionals, with a detailed plan and formal review. Know which documentation each level generates, because naming a level implies that paperwork.

▸  Naming the level and justifying it
     State the level and say what makes it that level. 'School Support Plus is recommended because the difficulty has persisted across two terms of School Support at [described intensity] without measurable change, and because input from occupational therapy is required.' A level named without justification gets downgraded by whoever allocates.

▸  Writing recommendations that actually happen
     The features that predict implementation: addressed to a named role rather than 'the school'; specific about frequency and duration; achievable with resources the school has or can get; sequenced, with a small number first; and with a review date. Five actionable recommendations beat fifteen aspirational ones. Ask yourself for each: who does this on Monday morning?

▸  Building in evaluation
     Every recommendation needs a way of knowing whether it worked. Add one line: 'review at the end of term 2 using [measure]'. This takes five minutes, satisfies CORU 3.8 and 5.37, and is the single most commonly omitted element in trainee reports.

▸  Writing for the actual reader
     The report is read by a parent, a class teacher, a SET and possibly a SENO. Write so each can find their part. Avoid unexplained test names and percentiles in the recommendations section — the findings section is where the technical detail lives. CORU 5.27 requires reports suitable for the intended audience, and PSI 1.2.8 requires communicating in language the recipient understands.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  NEPS Continuum of Support: Guidelines for Teachers, and the associated resource packs for primary and post-primary.

▸  NCSE guidance on the allocation of special education teaching resources.

▸  Department of Education circulars on the SET allocation model — check for the current circular rather than relying on an older one.

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity — on the relationship between assessment and provision.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Not naming a level.

✗  Naming a level without justifying why it is that one rather than the one below.

✗  Fifteen recommendations, so none are prioritised.

✗  Addressing recommendations to 'the school' rather than a role.

✗  No review point, so nothing is ever evaluated.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Your reports contain recommendations relevant to the findings.

▸  GRADE 4
     You name the Continuum level, justify it, address recommendations to roles, and specify frequency and duration.

▸  GRADE 5
     Recommendations are sequenced and small in number, each carries a review point and measure, and the section is written so a parent and a teacher can each act on it.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the Continuum
     [5–6 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     What classroom support, school support and school support plus each mean in practice.
     How you build it: Read the NEPS Continuum documents. Map one school onto them.

          you have it when: The level appears in the text
          [NEPS Continuum of Support]

     ·  Check the school can actually resource it
          you have it when: You asked before recommending
          [CORU SoP 5.35]

     [20 minutes per case  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]

          [CORU SoP 5.34 · PSI Code 2.3.2]

macro.name: Observe and deliver parental feedback sessions
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.1
     Be able to communicate diagnosis/assessment and/or treatment/management options in a way that can be understood by the service user

▸  CORU 2.14
     Understand the need to work in partnership with service users, their relatives/carers and other professionals in planning and evaluating goals, treatments and interventions, and be aware of the concepts of power and authority in relationships with service users

▸  CORU 5.27
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accessible and accurate reports — devised in collaboration with service users, as appropriate — that are suitable for the intended audience and context of their use, in order to communicate and justify professional opinions made

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.3.4
     Provide, in obtaining informed consent, as much information as a reasonable or prudent person, family, group or community would want to know before deciding — in language they understand, taking reasonable steps to ensure it is in fact understood.

▸  PSI 1.4.1
     Seek as full and active participation as possible from others in decisions which affect them.

▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The feedback session is where the assessment becomes real for the family, and it is the part of the work most likely to go wrong in ways that cannot be repaired. A parent who leaves confused will not implement anything; a parent who leaves feeling judged will disengage from the school. It is also the moment where you find out whether your formulation survives contact with the person who knows the child best.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Structuring the session
     Open by checking what they already know and what they want from the session — this takes two minutes and reshapes everything after it. Give the headline finding early, plainly, before the detail; parents sit through explanation waiting for the verdict and hear none of it. Then the supporting detail. Then what it means practically. Then recommendations. Then questions, with real time left. Check understanding by asking them to say back what they will tell their partner.

▸  Translating scores into meaning
     Never lead with a percentile. 'Out of a hundred children her age, about ninety would read more accurately than she does at the moment' is a percentile made human. Or compare to demand: 'she can hold about three pieces of information at once, and the instructions she is given in class routinely contain five'. If you use a number, explain what it is a number of.

▸  Holding the room when it goes difficult
     Parents cry, get angry, disagree, or go silent. None of these require you to fix them. Pause. Acknowledge plainly — 'this is hard to hear'. Do not fill the silence with more findings. If a parent disagrees with a finding, that is information: ask what they see that is different. Sometimes they are right and you have missed something. If a parent becomes angry, it is usually about the system rather than about you; do not defend the system reflexively.

▸  Managing the school's presence
     Feedback sessions often include a teacher or SET. That changes the dynamic — parents may not say in front of the school what they would say alone, and the school may have a stake in a particular outcome. Decide deliberately who is in the room, and consider offering the parent a few minutes separately. CORU 2.14 asks you to be aware of power and authority in these relationships.

▸  Interpreters
     If an interpreter is needed, brief them before the session: no summarising, no editing, first person, and tell them the technical terms that will come up. Address the parent, not the interpreter. Allow roughly double the time. Say in the report that the session was conducted through an interpreter and what that means for interpretation. CORU 2.5 requires you to recognise when a professional translator is needed — you did this repeatedly at Boyle, and it is strong evidence.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity — the chapters on working with families and on assessment in a second language.

▸  Buckley, J. A., & Epstein, M. H. (2004). The Behavioral and Emotional Rating Scale-2: Providing a comprehensive approach to strength-based assessment. California School Psychologist, 9, 21–27. — on strength-based feedback.

▸  Tervalon, M., & Murray-García, J. (1998). Cultural humility versus cultural competence. Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, 9(2), 117–125.

▸  HSE guidance on working with interpreters in health and social care settings.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 2.1, 2.2, 2.5 and 5.27 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Leading with scores.

✗  Delivering all the detail before the headline, so the parent hears none of it.

✗  Filling a silence after difficult news.

✗  Defending a finding a parent disputes instead of asking what they see.

✗  Addressing the interpreter rather than the parent.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have observed and contributed to feedback sessions.

▸  GRADE 4
     You structure the session, translate scores into meaning, and check understanding.

▸  GRADE 5
     You hold the room when it goes difficult, manage the school's presence deliberately, and work effectively through an interpreter.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Structuring the session
     [3 hours plu

macro.name: Observe and then contribute to teacher consultation
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.22
     Be able to critically analyse the factors that influence therapeutic and professional relationships, including power dynamics between the practitioner and service user

▸  CORU 5.38
     Know and apply a range of consultation approaches at individual, group and organisational levels

▸  CORU 5.40
     Work collaboratively with other professionals — including teachers, other school staff and multi-disciplinary teams — to build capacity among those responsible for the delivery of interventions

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 2.3.3
     Terminate an activity when it is clear the activity is more harmful than beneficial, or when it is no longer needed.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Consultation is how one psychologist reaches more children than they could ever assess, and it is the activity Irish educational psychologists spend most of their time on. It is also a distinct skill with its own models, not just a meeting. The BPS treats consultation as a competency in its own right; the Irish documents fold it into other competencies, which means it is easy to do a whole placement without ever learning a model.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Learning one model properly
     Pick one and use it repeatedly rather than sampling several. Problem-solving consultation follows a sequence: problem identification, problem analysis, plan design, implementation, evaluation — and the evidence says problem identification is where consultations succeed or fail. Solution-focused consultation starts from exceptions and preferred futures. Collaborative consultation positions you and the teacher as joint problem-solvers with different expertise, which is usually the right stance in a school.

▸  Problem identification, which is most of the work
     The presenting concern is rarely the workable problem. 'He's disruptive' becomes workable when it becomes 'he leaves his seat during independent written work, about four times in a thirty-minute period, mostly in the second half'. Getting from the first to the second is the consultation skill. It takes questions, not suggestions, and it usually takes longer than the teacher expects.

▸  Question technique
     Questions that open a consultation up: when does it not happen? what have you already tried and what happened? what would you see instead if this improved? what do you think is going on? The last one matters — teachers usually have a hypothesis and are rarely asked for it, and it is often right. Avoid 'have you tried', which reads as an implied criticism however it is meant.

▸  Staying out of the expert role
     The pull toward being the person with the answer is strong, especially when you are a trainee and want to be useful. Resist it. A solution you supply is a solution the teacher owns less, implements less faithfully and abandons sooner. Your expertise is in the process and in the psychology; theirs is in the child and the classroom. CORU 5.40 frames this as building capacity.

▸  Closing the loop
     Agree who does what by when, write it down, send it within twenty-four hours, and set a review date. Ten minutes. Consultations without a written record and a review date evaporate, and the teacher concludes that psychology is talk. Your review named record-keeping and write-up of consultations as a development area — this is the habit that addresses it.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Wagner, P. (2000). Consultation: Developing a comprehensive approach to service delivery. Educational Psychology in Practice, 16(1), 9–18.

▸  Sheridan, S. M., & Kratochwill, T. R. (2007). Conjoint behavioral consultation: Promoting family-school connections and interventions. Springer.

▸  Wagner, P. (2008). Consultation as a framework for practice. In Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle (Eds.), Frameworks for practice in educational psychology. Jessica Kingsley.

▸  Gutkin, T. B., & Curtis, M. J. (2009). School-based consultation: The science and practice of indirect service delivery. In Handbook of School Psychology (4th ed.). Wiley.

▸  BPS Standards for the Accreditation of Doctoral Programmes in Educational Psychology (2023) — the consultation competency, which the Irish standards do not separate out.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Accepting the presenting concern as the problem.

✗  Offering solutions before the problem is defined.

✗  Asking 'have you tried', which teachers hear as criticism.

✗  Never asking the teacher what they think is going on.

✗  No written record and no review date, so nothing follows.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have observed consultations and contributed to them.

▸  GRADE 4
     You use a named model, you spend real time on problem identification, and you record actions and review dates.

▸  GRADE 5
     You stay out of the expert role, your questions demonstrably shift the teacher's framing, and you can evidence a consultation that changed classroom practice.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Learning one model
     [4–5 hours plus practice  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     A structured consultation model with named stages you can follow.
     How you build it: Read one model properly. Follow it explicitly for five consultations.

     ·  Use a named consultation model
          you have it when: You can say which one
          [CORU SoP 5.38]

     ·  Contract at the start
          you have it when: Both parties know what this meeting is for
          [CORU SoP 5.38]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Question technique
     [Ongoing  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Asking so the other person generates the solution.
     How you build it: Ask your supervisor to count how many solutions you supplied.

     ·  Ask questions that open rather than close
          you have it when: The teacher generated the solution

macro.name: Familiarise with SET provision and allocation
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.13
     Be aware of current data protection, freedom of information and other legislation relevant to the profession and be able to access new and emerging legislation

▸  CORU 5.5
     Be able to identify and understand the impact of governmental, organisational, community and societal structures, systems and culture on health and social care provision

▸  CORU 5.13
     Know the structures and systems of school, community and social settings in which educational, health and social care services are provided for children, young people and adult learners

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.8
     Speak out if the policies, practices or regulations of the organisation within which they work seriously ignore or oppose any principle of this Code.

▸  PSI 3.4.5
     Contribute where appropriate to the co-ordination of client services to avoid duplication or working at cross purposes — maintaining adequate records and communicating with other providers.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
You cannot recommend into a system you do not understand. If you do not know how special education teaching hours are allocated, your recommendations will ask for things the school cannot give and will not ask for things it could. Schools read that as a psychologist who does not know how schools work, and it costs you credibility you then spend the rest of the placement earning back.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The allocation model
     SET hours are allocated to schools as a block under a profiled model, not per child and not per diagnosis. The school decides internally how to deploy them. This has two consequences that matter for every report you write: a diagnosis does not generate hours, and recommending 'additional SET time' asks the school to take it from another child. Say what the hours should be used for, not that there should be more.

▸  Who decides what
     The principal and the SET team deploy the allocation, usually through a support plan review. The SENCO or SET coordinator holds the overview. The SENO handles applications for SNA access and for special class or special school placement — a different process from SET hours, and one trainees routinely conflate.

▸  SNA access is about care, not teaching
     SNA support is allocated for significant care needs, not for learning support. Recommending an SNA for a child with a reading difficulty is a category error and will be refused. If you mean adult proximity for safety, say that and say why.

▸  Reading the school's own documents
     Ask to see the Student Support File and the school's SEN policy. The gap between what the file records and what you observe in the room is one of the most useful findings available to you, and it is invisible unless you ask.

▸  Keeping current
     Circulars change. Check the current Department circular rather than relying on what you were told last year, and check before you cite anything in a report. CORU 1.13 requires you to be aware of current legislation and to access new and emerging legislation.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  NCSE — guidance on the special education teaching allocation model.

▸  Department of Education circulars — check for the current SET allocation circular.

▸  NEPS Continuum of Support: Guidelines for Teachers.

▸  Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs (EPSEN) Act 2004.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Recommending 'more SET hours', which asks the school to take them from another child.

✗  Confusing SNA allocation with teaching support.

✗  Assuming a diagnosis generates resource.

✗  Citing an out-of-date circular.

✗  Never asking to see the Student Support File.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You know that SET hours are allocated to schools rather than to children.

▸  GRADE 4
     You can explain the allocation model, the roles of SENCO, principal and SENO, and the SNA criteria.

▸  GRADE 5
     Your recommendations are written to fit the allocation model, and you use the gap between documented and observed support as a finding.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · The allocation model
     [4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     How SET hours are allocated to schools and what determines the figure.
     How you build it: Read the current SET allocation circular. Name the circular number.

     ·  Understand how SET hours are allocated
          you have it when: You can explain the model to a parent
          [CORU SoP 5.13]

     ·  Cite the specific circular rather than 'guidance'
          you have it when: You name the circular number
          [CORU SoP 1.13]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Deployment in practice
     [3 hours  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     How a school actually uses what it is given, which is a different question.
     How you build it: Ask two SET coordinators how they deploy. Compare.

     ·  Know how the school deploys what it has
          you have it when: Allocation and deployment are different things
          [CORU SoP 5.14]

▸  BLOCK 3 · The wider structures
     [2–3 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The SENO role, the NCSE, and what each can and cannot do.
     How you build it: One page on who does what. Know who to contact for what.

     ·  Know the SENO route and what the NCSE can do
          you have it when: You know who to contact and for what
          [CORU SoP 5.5]

macro.name: Map the school's organisation of supports
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.13
     Know the structures and systems of school, community and social settings in which educational, health and social care services are provided for children, young people and adult learners

▸  CORU 5.35
     Identify and evaluate the characteristics of school organisation and culture in order to contribute to school development that enhances the participation and wellbeing of all learners

▸  CORU 5.40
     Work collaboratively with other professionals — including teachers, other school staff and multi-disciplinary teams — to build capacity among those responsible for the delivery of interventions

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.8
     Speak out if the policies, practices or regulations of the organisation within which they work seriously ignore or oppose any principle of this Code.

▸  PSI 3.4.5
     Contribute where appropriate to the co-ordination of client services to avoid duplication or working at cross purposes — maintaining adequate records and communicating with other providers.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Two schools with identical allocations produce completely different outcomes, and the difference is organisation. Mapping it tells you whether the child's difficulty is a child difficulty or a delivery difficulty — and if it is the latter, an individual intervention will not fix it. This is the clearest example of working at a level above the child, which your review named as a gap.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What to map
     Who is on the SEN team and who leads it. How children are identified and by whom. Withdrawal versus in-class support and the ratio between them. Group sizes. How plans are written, reviewed and by whom. How information moves from SET to class teacher and back. What happens at transition points within the school.

▸  How to gather it without it becoming an inspection
     Ask as curiosity, not audit. 'How does it usually work when a teacher is worried about someone?' gets you the real process; 'what is your identification procedure?' gets you the policy. You want the real one.

▸  Reading the pattern
     If every child is withdrawn in groups of six for the same programme regardless of need, the organisation is doing the deciding, not the assessment. If plans are written by the SET and never seen by the class teacher, nothing will generalise. These are findings, and they belong in the report — carefully worded, but there.

▸  Feeding it back without blame
     Describe rather than judge: 'support is currently organised by year group rather than by need, which means [named child] is working on material above his current level.' Offer one change, not five. Schools implement one.

▸  Recording it as systemic work
     Log it as systemic change, not as casework. Trainees do this work and then file it under assessment, which is how Systemic Change ends up thinly evidenced.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity — the chapters on whole-school approaches.

▸  Fullan, M. (2016). The new meaning of educational change (5th ed.). Teachers College Press.

▸  Wagner, P. (2000). Consultation: Developing a comprehensive approach to service delivery. Educational Psychology in Practice, 16(1).

▸  Department of Education — Looking at Our School: A Quality Framework.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Asking for the policy and believing it describes the practice.

✗  Mapping and never using it in the formulation.

✗  Feeding back five changes.

✗  Wording it as criticism of named staff.

✗  Logging it as casework.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You can describe how the school organises support.

▸  GRADE 4
     You gathered it systematically, and the map informs your formulation.

▸  GRADE 5
     You identified a delivery-level factor, fed it back in a way the school could act on, and logged it as systemic work.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Mapping accurately
     [6–8 hours for the first  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     Recording what actually exists at each Continuum level in this school.
     How you build it: Do one school thoroughly. The first takes six hours; later ones take two.

     ·  Map each Continuum level against provision
          you have it when: The map is complete and accurate
          [NEPS Continuum of Support]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Finding the gap
     [2 hours per school  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Identifying where the continuum breaks down in this school.
     How you build it: Compare the map against what the Continuum expects. The difference is the gap.

     ·  Identify a gap in the continuum
          you have it when: You named one
          [CORU SoP 5.35]

     ·  Say what would close the gap
          you have it when: You proposed something the school could do
          [CORU SoP 5.35]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Giving it back
     [2 hours  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Presenting the map to the school so it is used rather than submitted.
     How you build it: Offer a twenty-minute slot at a staff meeting.

     ·  Present the map back to the school
          you have it when: It was used, not just submitted
          [CORU SoP 5.40]
