macro.name: Visit a range of special education settings
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.13
     Know the structures and systems of school, community and social settings in which educational, health and social care services are provided for children, young people and adult learners

▸  CORU 5.39
     Work as part of a multi-disciplinary team in order to actively contribute to the integrated delivery of interventions at individual and group levels

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.8
     Speak out if the policies, practices or regulations of the organisation within which they work seriously ignore or oppose any principle of this Code.

▸  PSI 3.4.5
     Contribute where appropriate to the co-ordination of client services to avoid duplication or working at cross purposes — maintaining adequate records and communicating with other providers.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
You will be asked whether a child needs a special class or a special school, and you cannot answer that honestly if you have never been in one. PSI 3.3.6 requires that experience in educational settings includes special education — it is a requirement, not enrichment, and you currently do not meet it.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What counts
     A special class attached to a mainstream school, a special school, an early intervention class, and where possible a post-primary special class. These are different environments with different populations; one visit does not cover the category.

▸  What to look at
     Staffing ratios and how adults are deployed. The curriculum actually in use — L1LP, L2LP, or an adapted mainstream curriculum. Communication systems in use and whether they are used consistently by everyone. Sensory environment. What integration with mainstream looks like in practice rather than on paper. Where pupils go afterwards.

▸  The question you are really answering
     Placement questions are about fit between a child's needs and what a setting can provide, not about severity. A child may need a special class for communication support and mainstream for maths. Seeing settings lets you write about fit rather than about category.

▸  Checking your own assumptions
     Most trainees arrive with a view about special provision, usually absorbed rather than examined. Notice yours. CORU 5.44 asks you to reflect on how your own values shape your practice, and placement questions are where those values have real consequences.

▸  Arranging it
     It will not happen unless you ask in week one and get a date. Put it in the Appendix 1. Ask your supervisor which settings the service works with most, and go to those.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Accreditation Standards (2022), 3.3.6 — the settings requirement.

▸  NCSE — policy advice on special schools and classes.

▸  NCCA — Level 1 and Level 2 Learning Programmes.

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009) — the chapters on inclusion and placement.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Treating one visit as covering special education.

✗  Observing the children and not the system.

✗  Writing placement recommendations without having seen the setting.

✗  Not examining your own assumptions about special provision.

✗  Leaving it unrequested until it is too late.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have visited at least one special education setting.

▸  GRADE 4
     You visited a range, observed curriculum, staffing and communication systems, and can describe how they differ.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can write a placement recommendation framed as fit between need and provision, and you can name your own assumptions and how you checked them.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Arranging them
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Knowing which settings exist locally and getting access early.
     How you build it: List every special setting on your patch in week two. Request visits immediately.

     ·  Arrange visits early in the placement
          you have it when: Booked in the first weeks
          [Handbook Table 3]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Knowing what to look at
     [2 hours to build the schedule  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     Structure, staffing ratios, communication supports, sensory environment, therapy integration.
     How you build it: Take the same observation schedule to every setting so you can compare.

     ·  Observe structure, staffing and communication supports
          you have it when: You can describe how the setting works
          [CORU SoP 5.13]

     ·  Talk to therapy and SNA staff, not only teachers
          you have it when: You spoke to the people delivering
          [CORU SoP 5.39]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Recording it as evidence
     [10 minutes per visit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Logging each visit separately so it counts for Table 3.
     How you build it: One Appendix 5 entry per setting, tagged with age band 5.

     ·  Log each visit separately in Appendix 5
          you have it when: Each setting is its own entry
          [Handbook Appendix 5]

macro.name: Attend service team meetings
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.11
     Be able to express professional, informed and considered opinions to service users, health professionals and others in varied practice settings and contexts and within the limitations of confidentiality

▸  CORU 2.16
     Understand the role and impact of effective interdisciplinary team working in meeting service user needs and be able to effectively contribute to decision-making within a team setting

▸  CORU 5.5
     Be able to identify and understand the impact of governmental, organisational, community and societal structures, systems and culture on health and social care provision

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.8
     Speak out if the policies, practices or regulations of the organisation within which they work seriously ignore or oppose any principle of this Code.

▸  PSI 3.4.5
     Contribute where appropriate to the co-ordination of client services to avoid duplication or working at cross purposes — maintaining adequate records and communicating with other providers.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Team meetings are where you learn what the service actually is — its priorities, its pressures, how decisions get made, who holds what. They are also the only routine opportunity to practise contributing professionally among colleagues rather than in supervision, which is a distinct skill and one CORU 2.16 names directly.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Attending as participation, not observation
     Sitting silently for a term is a wasted term. Prepare one thing to contribute — a case question, a resource you found, an offer to take something on. Small and specific is better than impressive.

▸  Learning the service's shape
     Note the referral pathway from arrival to closure, the waiting times, the caseload sizes, what gets prioritised and why, and which other services are frequently involved. This is the knowledge that makes your recommendations realistic and it is not written down anywhere.

▸  Contributing without overreaching
     As a trainee your contribution is a question, an observation or an offer — not a verdict on service design. 'Can I ask how a referral like that usually gets prioritised?' is useful to you and unthreatening to everyone. Save opinions on how the service should run until you understand why it runs as it does.

▸  Multi-disciplinary meetings specifically
     Different professions formulate differently and use the same words for different things. Listen for where the disagreement actually is — it is usually about the model, not the facts. Your contribution is the psychological formulation, stated plainly and without jargon, and the reasoning behind it.

▸  Recording it
     These count as placement activity and evidence CORU 2.16 and 5.39. Log them with date, type and what you contributed, not just that you attended.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 2.15, 2.16 and 2.17 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Frost, N., & Robinson, M. (2007). Joining up children's services: Safeguarding children in multi-disciplinary teams. Child Abuse Review, 16(3).

▸  Hall, P. (2005). Interprofessional teamwork: Professional cultures as barriers. Journal of Interprofessional Care, 19(S1).

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Attending silently for a term.

✗  Not learning the referral pathway, then writing unrealistic recommendations.

✗  Offering opinions on service design as a trainee.

✗  Using psychological jargon in a multi-disciplinary meeting.

✗  Logging attendance without logging contribution.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You attend team meetings.

▸  GRADE 4
     You prepare a contribution, and you can describe the service's referral pathway and priorities.

▸  GRADE 5
     You contribute a formulation in a multi-disciplinary setting in language others can use, and you can name where professional models differ.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Understanding the service
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     How casework is prioritised here and what the service can and cannot offer.
     How you build it: Ask directly how the queue is determined. Write down the answer.

     ·  Understand how casework is prioritised here
          you have it when: You know what determines the queue
          [CORU SoP 5.5]

     ·  Note what the service can and cannot offer
          you have it when: You know the limits before recommending
          [CORU SoP 5.5]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Contributing
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Saying something useful in a room of more experienced people.
     How you build it: Prepare one contribution before every meeting. Even a question counts.

     ·  Prepare something to contribute
          you have it when: You spoke
          [CORU SoP 2.16]

     ·  Contribute a psychological perspective
          you have it when: You added something another discipline would not
          [CORU SoP 2.11]

macro.name: Learn consultation models
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 4.5
     Understand the importance of and be able to seek professional development, supervision, feedback and peer review opportunities in order to continuously improve practice

▸  CORU 5.38
     Know and apply a range of consultation approaches at individual, group and organisational levels

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.8
     Speak out if the policies, practices or regulations of the organisation within which they work seriously ignore or oppose any principle of this Code.

▸  PSI 3.4.5
     Contribute where appropriate to the co-ordination of client services to avoid duplication or working at cross purposes — maintaining adequate records and communicating with other providers.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Consultation is the main delivery mechanism of Irish educational psychology and it is the competency the Irish standards fold into others rather than naming — so it is entirely possible to do a placement without ever learning a model. The BPS names it as a competency in its own right. Knowing a model is the difference between a conversation and a method.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Why a model at all
     Without one you will default to advice-giving, which is the least effective form of consultation and the most likely to be politely ignored. A model gives you a sequence, a stance, and something to fall back on when the conversation goes sideways.

▸  Problem-solving consultation
     Problem identification, problem analysis, plan design, implementation, evaluation. The evidence consistently shows problem identification predicts outcome — most failures happen because everyone agreed too quickly about what the problem was.

▸  Solution-focused consultation
     Starts from exceptions and preferred futures rather than causes. Scaling, the miracle question, amplifying what already works. Fast, well suited to teachers under time pressure, and the framework you already used at Roscommon.

▸  Collaborative and conjoint models
     Collaborative consultation positions you and the teacher as equals with different expertise. Conjoint behavioural consultation brings parent and teacher into the same process, which is powerful where home and school are giving contradictory accounts.

▸  Choosing and sticking with one
     Learn one properly this year rather than sampling four. Name it in supervision, use it repeatedly, and notice where it fails. Competence comes from repetition with reflection, not from breadth.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Wagner, P. (2008). Consultation as a framework for practice. In Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle (Eds.), Frameworks for practice in educational psychology.

▸  Sheridan, S. M., & Kratochwill, T. R. (2007). Conjoint behavioral consultation. Springer.

▸  Gutkin, T. B., & Curtis, M. J. (2009). School-based consultation. In Handbook of School Psychology (4th ed.).

▸  BPS Standards for Accreditation (2023) — the consultation competency.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Defaulting to advice-giving.

✗  Sampling several models and mastering none.

✗  Rushing problem identification.

✗  Using a model's techniques without its stance.

✗  Never naming which model you used, so it cannot be evidenced.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You can name several consultation models.

▸  GRADE 4
     You use one model deliberately and repeatedly, and name it in your records.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can say what your model is poor at, and you choose a different approach when the situation calls for it.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Problem-solving consultation
     [4–5 hours plus practice  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     The stages of a structured problem-solving model and what each is for.
     How you build it: Read one account properly. Follow the stages explicitly five times.

     ·  Learn a structured problem-solving model
          you have it when: You can name and follow its stages
          [CORU SoP 5.38]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Solution-focused approaches
     [3–4 hours plus practice  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Scaling, exception-finding, preferred future questioning.
     How you build it: One short text. Then use scaling in three consultations.

     ·  Learn a solution-focused approach
          you have it when: You can use scaling and exception questions
          [CORU SoP 5.38]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Choosing between them
     [2 hours reflection  ·  Ongoing all year  ·  Study]
     Knowing which suits which situation, and being able to say why.
     How you build it: After five of each, write a half-page on what each gave you.

     ·  Ask your supervisor which model they use
          you have it when: You know whether they were trained in it
          [CORU SoP 4.5]

     ·  Follow one model explicitly for a set of consultations
          you have it when: You can say what the model gave you
          [CORU SoP 5.38]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN
No full chapter yet.

10 · REFERRAL AREAS THIS SKILL SERVES
▸  5.4 Concerns about early development
     full entry under 2. Structured interviewing of parents for developmental history

▸  5.6 School and access factors
     full entry under 24. Familiarise with SET provision and allocation

11 · WHERE THE EVIDENCE GOES
Table 2 area 4 · Table 3 category 7 · EDUC42700 Organisation of Supports and presentation

12 · LAW AND POLICY
Education Act 1998 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018

13 · YEAR AND HOW IT EXTENDS

macro.name: Deliver the good practice presentation
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.8
     Know the basic principles of effective teaching and learning, mentoring and supervision

▸  CORU 5.20
     Know and communicate the role of educational psychologists in providing evidence-based psychological services across educational, health and social care settings, focusing on supporting the psychological and educational development of children, young people and adult learners through assessment, diagnosis, formulation, intervention, prevention, advocacy, consultation, training and research

▸  CORU 5.40
     Work collaboratively with other professionals — including teachers, other school staff and multi-disciplinary teams — to build capacity among those responsible for the delivery of interventions

▸  CORU 5.41
     Be able to critically analyse, appraise and evaluate psychological and other relevant contemporary research to inform evidence-based practice

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.8
     Speak out if the policies, practices or regulations of the organisation within which they work seriously ignore or oppose any principle of this Code.

▸  PSI 3.4.5
     Contribute where appropriate to the co-ordination of client services to avoid duplication or working at cross purposes — maintaining adequate records and communicating with other providers.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Training delivery reaches more people than casework ever will, and it is the activity where your review named a strength — interpersonal communication and delivery of training. Build on it. CORU 5.40 asks you to build capacity among those responsible for delivering interventions, and a presentation is the most direct way to do that.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Choosing a topic that comes from the work
     The best topics come from a pattern you noticed across cases — three referrals for the same misunderstanding, a resource nobody knew existed. That is practice-derived training and it lands differently from a generic slide deck.

▸  Pitching it to the audience
     Teachers want something usable on Monday. Every section should end with what to do, not what to know. Cut the theory to what is needed to make the practice make sense, and put the rest in a handout.

▸  Evidencing what you claim
     If you say an approach works, cite something. PSI 4.2.2 requires you not to misrepresent the effectiveness of what you offer, and a training audience will act on what you tell them. Be as careful about overclaiming in a presentation as in a report.

▸  Evaluating it
     A three-question form at the end: what will you do differently, what was most useful, what was missing. This takes two minutes, gives you evidence for the portfolio, and turns a presentation into a small piece of practice-based research — which covers a development area you are otherwise short on.

▸  Leaving something behind
     A one-page summary beats fifty slides. People keep one page.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 5.8, 5.20 and 5.40 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Joyce, B., & Showers, B. (2002). Student achievement through staff development (3rd ed.). ASCD. — why training alone rarely changes practice without coaching.

▸  Kirkpatrick, D. L., & Kirkpatrick, J. D. (2006). Evaluating training programs (3rd ed.). Berrett-Koehler.

▸  EEF — Effective Professional Development guidance report.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  A topic chosen because it interested you rather than because the school needed it.

✗  Theory-heavy with no Monday-morning action.

✗  Claiming effectiveness without evidence.

✗  No evaluation, so no portfolio evidence.

✗  Fifty slides and no handout.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have contributed to delivering training.

▸  GRADE 4
     You chose a practice-derived topic, pitched it to the audience, and left a resource behind.

▸  GRADE 5
     You evaluated it, can report what changed, and can say what you would do differently — treating it as practice-based research.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the content
     [6–8 hours  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Study]
     The evidence base for whatever you are presenting on.
     How you build it: Search properly, appraise five sources, use three.

     ·  Cite current peer-reviewed evidence
          you have it when: The evidence base is visible
          [CORU SoP 5.41]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Presenting to professionals
     [4–5 hours  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Pitching to teachers rather than examiners — translating every technical term.
     How you build it: Rehearse once in front of someone who is not a psychologist.

     ·  Pitch it at teachers rather than examiners
          you have it when: Every citation is translated
          [CORU SoP 5.40 · 5.8]

     ·  End with three things the school could do this term
          you have it when: Actionable, not aspirational
          [CORU SoP 5.40]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Capturing the impact
     [1 hour  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Getting feedback that evidences you built capacity.
     How you build it: Hand out a five-question feedback slip. File the results.

     ·  Collect and file feedback from the school
          you have it when: You have evidence it built capacity
          [CORU SoP 5.40]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN
No full chapter yet.

10 · REFERRAL AREAS THIS SKILL SERVES
▸  5.6 School and access factors
     full entry under 24. Familiarise with SET provision and allocation

11 · WHERE THE EVIDENCE GOES
Table 2 area 4 · Table 3 category 7 · EDUC42700 Organisation of Supports and presentation

12 · LAW AND POLICY
Education Act 1998 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018

macro.name: Build rapport with a child during assessment
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.2
     Be able to modify and adapt communication methods and styles, including verbal and non-verbal methods, to suit the individual service user, considering issues of language, age, culture, beliefs and health and/or social care needs

▸  CORU 2.3
     Recognise service users as active participants in their health and social care and be able to support service users in communicating their needs, choices and concerns

▸  CORU 5.21
     Establish, maintain and conclude a professional relationship with a service user, safely and ethically, recognising and managing professional boundaries

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.8
     Be acutely aware of the need for discretion in recording and communicating information, so as to prevent it being interpreted or used to the detriment of others: not recording information which could lead to misinterpretation; avoiding conjecture; clearly labelling opinion; and communicating in language the recipient can understand.

▸  PSI 1.4.1
     Seek as full and active participation as possible from others in decisions which affect them.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Rapport is not politeness, it is measurement validity. A child who is anxious, bored or suspicious produces scores that underestimate them, and you will then build a formulation on a number that is wrong. Everything downstream — the recommendation, the resource, the placement — rests on whether the child engaged.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The first three minutes
     Introduce yourself in a sentence they can repeat. Say plainly why you are there, what will happen, how long it will take, and that there will be things they cannot do because the tasks get harder for everyone. Say what happens to the information. Then ask if they have questions and wait.

▸  Reading state and adjusting
     Watch for withdrawal, guessing, fatigue, and the shift from effort to compliance. Standardised administration is not negotiable, but breaks, order within permitted limits, and encouragement between items are. Know exactly what the manual permits before you need to use it.

▸  Adapting, and recording the adaptation
     If you deviate, record what you did and why, and state in the report what it means for interpretation. An adaptation recorded is a professional judgement; an adaptation unrecorded is an invalid administration. CORU 5.31 requires adapting and re-evaluating as appropriate — appropriate includes writing it down.

▸  Children who refuse
     Refusal is data. Note what was refused, when, and what preceded it. Do not coerce. Stopping and returning another day produces better data than a completed protocol obtained under pressure, and it protects the relationship the school has to keep.

▸  Ending
     Thank them specifically. Tell them what happens next and who will be told what. Children worry about this more than adults assume, and an unclear ending can undo a good session.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Sattler, J. M. (2018). Assessment of children: Cognitive foundations (6th ed.). — the chapters on establishing rapport and on observing test behaviour.

▸  WISC-V UK administration and scoring manual — the sections on rapport, breaks and permitted queries.

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009) — on assessment conditions and validity.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 5.21 and 5.31 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Starting the first subtest within two minutes of meeting the child.

✗  Not explaining what happens to the information.

✗  Pushing through visible fatigue to finish the battery.

✗  Adapting without recording it.

✗  Ending without saying what happens next.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You establish a working relationship and complete the assessment.

▸  GRADE 4
     You explain purpose and confidentiality in the child's terms, read state, and use permitted adjustments.

▸  GRADE 5
     You adapt deliberately and record it with its implication for interpretation, and you can justify stopping an assessment.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Meeting them where they are
     [2 hours plus observation  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Practice]
     Register, pace, physical positioning, and what to say first.
     How you build it: Watch your supervisor's first two minutes with three different children. Write down what they do.

     ·  Meet the child at their level, literally and in register
          you have it when: Not talked down to or over
          [CORU SoP 2.2]

     ·  Explain what will happen and why
          you have it when: The child could repeat it back
          [PSI Code 4.3.1]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Giving real agency
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Offering choices that are genuinely the child's, and responding when they decline.
     How you build it: Build two real choices into every session. Notice what happens.

     ·  Give the child a real choice early
          you have it when: Something was actually theirs to decide
          [PSI Code 1.4.1]

     ·  Notice and respond to reluctance
          you have it when: You adjusted rather than pushed on
          [CORU SoP 5.31]

     ·  Ask the child what they think would help
          you have it when: The child's view was sought
          [UNCRC Art. 12]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Closing
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Ending so the child leaves feeling competent rather than tested.
     How you build it: Have a closing line you use every time. Watch how they walk out.

     ·  Close so the child leaves feeling competent
          you have it when: How they walk out
          [CORU SoP 5.21]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN
No full chapter yet.

10 · REFERRAL AREAS THIS SKILL SERVES
▸  3.1 Conf

macro.name: Communicate with school staff, SENCO and principal
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.13
     Understand and be able to discuss the principles of effective conflict management

▸  CORU 2.17
     Understand the role of relationships with professional colleagues and other workers in service delivery and the need to create professional relationships based on mutual respect and trust

▸  CORU 5.13
     Know the structures and systems of school, community and social settings in which educational, health and social care services are provided for children, young people and adult learners

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.8
     Be acutely aware of the need for discretion in recording and communicating information, so as to prevent it being interpreted or used to the detriment of others: not recording information which could lead to misinterpretation; avoiding conjecture; clearly labelling opinion; and communicating in language the recipient can understand.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The school decides whether your recommendations happen. A psychologist who is easy to work with and clear gets implementation; one who is late, vague or appears to be inspecting does not. This is not politics — it is the difference between a report that changes something and one that is filed.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Knowing who does what
     The principal decides and allocates. The SENCO or SET coordinator holds the overview and usually the documentation. The class teacher has the daily relationship and will deliver most of what you recommend. The SNA often knows the child best and is asked least. Address each accordingly.

▸  Arriving well
     Confirm the day before. Arrive early. Sign in. Say how long you need and keep to it. Bring your own equipment. These are small and they are most of your reputation in a school.

▸  Communicating a difficult message
     Sometimes the finding implicates the provision. Lead with shared purpose, describe rather than evaluate, and offer one change. 'He is working on material above his current level, so most of his day is spent on tasks he cannot access — could we look at the level of the work?' is sayable. 'The differentiation is inadequate' is not, and it will end the relationship.

▸  Managing disagreement
     Teachers sometimes disagree with findings, and sometimes they are right. Ask what they see. CORU 2.13 covers conflict management and the technique is the same as in consultation: get to the specific observation behind the position.

▸  Closing the loop
     Send a short written summary of what was agreed within a day. It prevents misremembering, gives the school something to act from, and evidences the record-keeping your review named as a development area.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 2.11, 2.13, 2.15 and 2.17 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Wagner, P. (2000). Consultation: Developing a comprehensive approach to service delivery.

▸  Stone, D., Patton, B., & Heen, S. (2010). Difficult conversations. Penguin.

▸  NEPS Continuum of Support guidelines — the shared language schools already use.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Treating 'the school' as one entity.

✗  Arriving late or without equipment.

✗  Delivering a provision-level criticism as a criticism.

✗  Defending a finding instead of asking what they see.

✗  No written follow-up.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You communicate professionally with school staff.

▸  GRADE 4
     You address the right person for each purpose and follow up in writing.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can deliver a message that implicates the provision without damaging the relationship, and the school acts on it.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the roles
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Who does what in an Irish school and who to approach for what.
     How you build it: One page: principal, deputy, SENCO, SET, class teacher, SNA. What each can decide.

     ·  Know who does what in this school
          you have it when: You approached the right person
          [CORU SoP 5.13]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Negotiating a shared question
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Getting agreement on what you are all trying to answer.
     How you build it: Write the question and read it back. Adjust until both agree.

     ·  Negotiate a shared referral question
          you have it when: Both parties recognise the question
          [CORU SoP 2.13]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Repairing
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Going back after a difficult conversation.
     How you build it: Make the second contact within a week. Always.

     ·  Manage disagreement rather than avoiding it
          you have it when: The disagreement was addressed
          [CORU SoP 2.13]

     ·  Maintain the relationship afterwards
          you have it when: You went back
          [CORU SoP 2.17]

▸  5.5 Involvement of other services
     full entry under 27. Attend service team meetings

macro.name: Give feedback to parents on assessment findings
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.1
     Be able to communicate diagnosis/assessment and/or treatment/management options in a way that can be understood by the service user

▸  CORU 2.2
     Be able to modify and adapt communication methods and styles, including verbal and non-verbal methods, to suit the individual service user, considering issues of language, age, culture, beliefs and health and/or social care needs

▸  CORU 5.27
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accessible and accurate reports — devised in collaboration with service users, as appropriate — that are suitable for the intended audience and context of their use, in order to communicate and justify professional opinions made

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.8
     Be acutely aware of the need for discretion in recording and communicating information, so as to prevent it being interpreted or used to the detriment of others: not recording information which could lead to misinterpretation; avoiding conjecture; clearly labelling opinion; and communicating in language the recipient can understand.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
This is where the assessment becomes real to the family and where it is most easily wasted. A parent who does not understand the findings cannot advocate for their child, and parental advocacy does more over a school career than any single recommendation you write.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Headline first
     Parents wait through explanation for the verdict and hear almost none of it. Give the finding plainly in the first two minutes, then the detail, then what it means, then what happens next.

▸  Plain language as a professional obligation
     PSI 1.2.8 requires communicating in language the recipient can understand. Replace percentile with a comparison to peers; replace working memory with holding information in mind while doing something with it. If you cannot explain a finding without the technical term, you do not yet understand it well enough to report it.

▸  Strengths that are real
     Lead with a strength, but only one you can evidence from the assessment. Invented strengths are heard as consolation and undermine everything else you say.

▸  When the parent disagrees
     Ask what they see that is different. Parents have far more data than you do. A disagreement is either information you lack or a difference in what the behaviour means — both are worth the time, and neither is resolved by repeating the finding.

▸  Checking it landed
     Ask them to say back what they will tell someone else. It is the only reliable check, and it routinely reveals that the central message did not survive.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 2.1, 2.2 and 5.27 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 1.2.8 and 4.3.1 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2009) — on working with families.

▸  Tervalon, M., & Murray-García, J. (1998). Cultural humility versus cultural competence.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Leading with scores.

✗  Using technical language and checking understanding with 'does that make sense?'

✗  Inventing a strength.

✗  Repeating a finding a parent disputes.

✗  No check that the message landed.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You deliver findings accurately to parents.

▸  GRADE 4
     You lead with the headline, translate into plain language, and check understanding.

▸  GRADE 5
     You handle disagreement as information, and the parent leaves able to explain the findings to someone else.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Preparing
     [20 minutes per session  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Knowing the order and having the plain-language version ready.
     How you build it: Write the first three sentences and the three hardest translations before every session.

     ·  Prepare the structure before the meeting
          you have it when: You knew the order you would take
          [CORU SoP 2.1]

     ·  Use plain language and check understanding
          you have it when: You checked
          [PSI Code 4.3.1]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Leading with the person
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Describing the child rather than the scores.
     How you build it: Write two sentences about the child that contain no numbers. Open with those.

     ·  Lead with the child, not the scores
          you have it when: The child is recognisable in your description
          [CORU SoP 5.27]

     ·  Name strengths specifically
          you have it when: Not generic praise
          [CORU SoP 1.3]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Managing distress
     [2 hours, then practice  ·  Ongoing all year  ·  Practice]
     Slowing down rather than pushing through.
     How you build it: Ask your supervisor what they do. Have your own two sentences ready.

     ·  Hold distress without rushing past it
          you have it when: You slowed down
          [CORU SoP 2.2]

     ·  Leave the parent with something concrete
          you have it when: They know what happens next
          [CORU SoP 2.16]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN

12 · LAW AND POLICY

macro.name: Keep case notes to service standard
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.13
     Be aware of current data protection, freedom of information and other legislation relevant to the profession and be able to access new and emerging legislation

▸  CORU 2.8
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accurate and objective documentation

▸  CORU 2.10
     Be aware of and comply with local/national documentation standards including, for example, terminology and signature requirements

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.8
     Be acutely aware of the need for discretion in recording and communicating information, so as to prevent it being interpreted or used to the detriment of others: not recording information which could lead to misinterpretation; avoiding conjecture; clearly labelling opinion; and communicating in language the recipient can understand.

▸  PSI 4.2.5
     Take care in communicating their knowledge, findings and views to clearly differentiate facts, opinions, theories, hypotheses and ideas.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Case notes are a legal record, disclosable under GDPR subject access and potentially in court. They are also the thing your review named — record keeping and write-up of observations and consultations. Notes written on the day take minutes; notes reconstructed take hours and are visibly reconstructed.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What goes in
     Date, time, location, who was present, what was done, what was observed, what was decided, what happens next and by whom. Factual and contemporaneous.

▸  Separating observation from inference
     'Left his seat four times in twenty minutes' is observation. 'Was not engaged' is inference. Record the first and label the second as your view. PSI 1.2.8 requires avoiding conjecture and clearly labelling opinion — this is the clause that protects you when a note is disclosed.

▸  Writing as though it will be read by the family
     Because it may be. Subject access requests are real. Would you be comfortable with the parent reading this sentence? If not, rewrite it — not to hide the finding, but to state it professionally.

▸  Storage and retention
     Follow NEPS protocol on where notes live, how they transfer, and how long they are kept. Do not keep identifiable material on a personal device. PSI 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 and the GDPR minimisation principle all apply, and this is the area where trainees most often slip through convenience.

▸  Same-day discipline
     Write in the car before you drive off. Eight minutes, accurate, done. This single habit addresses the development area more than anything else in this skill.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 1.2.6, 1.2.7 and 1.2.8 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 2.8, 2.10 and 1.13 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Data Protection Commission — guidance for organisations on subject access and retention.

▸  General Data Protection Regulation — Article 5 principles.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Writing up in bulk days later.

✗  Recording inference as observation.

✗  Writing something you would not want the parent to read.

✗  Identifiable material on a personal device.

✗  Recording what was discussed but not what was decided.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You keep case notes.

▸  GRADE 4
     Written the same day, separating observation from inference, covering decisions and actions.

▸  GRADE 5
     Your notes would withstand a subject access request, and you can state the retention and storage rules you are working under.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the standard
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     This service's format, terminology, signature and retention requirements.
     How you build it: Read the records policy in week one. Ask for three sample notes.

     ·  Use the service's format and terminology
          you have it when: Notes match the service standard
          [CORU SoP 2.10]

     ·  Store and transfer records lawfully
          you have it when: Nothing identifiable on a personal device
          [GDPR · CORU SoP 1.13]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Writing defensibly
     [2 hours plus audit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     Fact separated from opinion, no conjecture, opinion labelled.
     How you build it: Have one week of notes audited by your supervisor early, while the habit is forming.

     ·  Separate fact from opinion and label opinion
          you have it when: A reader can tell which is which
          [PSI Code 1.2.8 · 4.2.5]

     ·  Avoid conjecture
          you have it when: You did not speculate in the record
          [PSI Code 1.2.8]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Writing them at all
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     The discipline of same-day recording.
     How you build it: Block fifteen minutes after every contact. Defend it.

     ·  Write the same day
          you have it when: Notes are contemporaneous
          [CORU SoP 2.8]

     ·  Record consent, contacts and decisions
          you have it when: The file shows what you did and when
          [CORU SoP 1.15]

macro.name: Produce the psychological report to countersigning standard
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.2
     Be able to justify the selection of and implement appropriate assessment techniques and be able to undertake and record a thorough, sensitive and detailed assessment

▸  CORU 5.27
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accessible and accurate reports — devised in collaboration with service users, as appropriate — that are suitable for the intended audience and context of their use, in order to communicate and justify professional opinions made

▸  CORU 5.32
     Interpret, synthesise and critically evaluate assessment data, within relevant conceptual frameworks, to inform case formulation and psychological intervention planning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.8
     Be acutely aware of the need for discretion in recording and communicating information, so as to prevent it being interpreted or used to the detriment of others: not recording information which could lead to misinterpretation; avoiding conjecture; clearly labelling opinion; and communicating in language the recipient can understand.

▸  PSI 2.3.1
     Be mindful, when making decisions based on psychological data and techniques, of the limitations of such data and techniques.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The report is the artefact that outlives you on the case. It is read by parents, teachers, SENOs and sometimes other services years later. Countersigning standard means your supervisor can put their name to it — which is a higher bar than 'accurate', because they are staking their registration on your reasoning.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The structure that works
     Reason for referral and the question being answered. What was done and when. Findings by source. Formulation, using a named framework. Recommendations by Continuum level, addressed to roles. Limitations. Review point. If your report has no limitations section it is not at countersigning standard.

▸  Answering the referral question
     Read it again before you write the conclusion. Reports routinely describe a child thoroughly and never answer what was asked. If the question cannot be answered, say so and say why.

▸  Integration rather than listing
     The findings section can be organised by source. The formulation cannot. It must name where sources agree, where they conflict, and what you make of the conflict. This is the single biggest difference between a grade 3 and a grade 5 report.

▸  Limitations that are specific
     Not 'all assessment has limitations' but 'the WISC-V was administered in English, which is [child]'s second language, so the Verbal Comprehension Index is likely to underestimate his reasoning; this is discussed in the interpretation.' Specific limitations demonstrate competence. Generic ones demonstrate a template.

▸  Writing for countersignature
     Send it with the raw data and your scoring. Expect substantial edits on the first few and treat them as teaching. Ask which changes were accuracy, which were house style, and which were reasoning — the third category is where the learning is.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 5.27, 5.32 and 3.2 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Sattler, J. M. (2018). Assessment of children — the report-writing chapters.

▸  Monsen, J. J., & Frederickson, N. (2008). The problem-analysis framework — for the formulation section.

▸  NEPS report templates and house style — ask your supervisor for the current version.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  No limitations section.

✗  A formulation that lists findings in the order they were collected.

✗  Not answering the referral question.

✗  Recommendations with no Continuum level or named role.

✗  Treating supervisor edits as corrections rather than teaching.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You produce a complete, accurate report.

▸  GRADE 4
     It answers the referral question, uses a named framework, and carries specific limitations and a review point.

▸  GRADE 5
     It integrates sources including where they conflict, and requires only house-style edits from your supervisor.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the template
     [3–4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     This service's structure and what belongs in each section.
     How you build it: Read five reports by experienced EPs in this service before writing your first.

     ·  Know the countersigning standard before drafting
          you have it when: You asked at the start
          [CORU SoP 2.10]

     ·  Proofread against the service template
          you have it when: No score or name errors
          [CORU SoP 2.8]

▸  BLOCK 2 · The four sections that carry the marks
     [Ongoing · 2–3 hours per report initially  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Tool rationale, integration, formulation, limitations.
     How you build it: Draft each separately and have each critiqued once.

     ·  Include a tool rationale
          you have it when: It is there
          [CORU SoP 3.2]

     ·  Include an integration section
          you have it when: Not a list of tests
          [CORU SoP 5.27 · 5.32]

     ·  Name the framework in the formulation
          you have it when: Named and cited
          [CORU SoP 5.29]

     ·  Include a limitations paragraph
          you have it when: Every report, no exceptions
          [PSI Code 2.3.1]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Writing for use
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Recommendations and language pitched at the person who will act.
     How you build it: Read it aloud. Anything you stumble over is badly written.

     ·  Write recommendations a teacher could act on Monday
          you have it when: Specific, resourced, dated
          [CORU SoP 5.34]

     ·  Quote the child's own words
          you

macro.name: Adapt written communication to the audience
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 2.2
     Be able to modify and adapt communication methods and styles, including verbal and non-verbal methods, to suit the individual service user, considering issues of language, age, culture, beliefs and health and/or social care needs

▸  CORU 5.25
     Select, evaluate and revise communication approaches to promote inclusive communication appropriate to the context of practice and the intended audience

▸  CORU 5.27
     Be able to produce clear, concise, accessible and accurate reports — devised in collaboration with service users, as appropriate — that are suitable for the intended audience and context of their use, in order to communicate and justify professional opinions made

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.8
     Be acutely aware of the need for discretion in recording and communicating information, so as to prevent it being interpreted or used to the detriment of others: not recording information which could lead to misinterpretation; avoiding conjecture; clearly labelling opinion; and communicating in language the recipient can understand.

▸  PSI 4.3.1
     Respect the right of clients and research participants to receive an appropriate explanation of the nature, purpose and results of investigations, assessments and research findings, in language they can understand.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The same findings have to reach a parent, a class teacher, a SENO and sometimes a consultant, and a single register cannot serve all of them. CORU 5.25 and 2.2 both require adapting communication to the audience — and in practice this is what determines whether your work is used.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Knowing each reader's question
     Parent: what does this mean for my child and what happens now. Class teacher: what do I do on Monday. SENCO: what level of support and what documentation. SENO: what is being applied for and what evidence supports it. Another professional: what did you find and how confident are you.

▸  Layering one document
     Rather than writing four documents, layer one: a plain-language summary at the top, technical detail in the body, role-addressed recommendations at the end. Most readers read the first page and the recommendations — put the load-bearing content there.

▸  Writing the summary last and hardest
     The one-page summary is the most-read and least-drafted page in most reports. Write it after everything else, and cut every term you have not explained.

▸  Adjusting for reading level and language
     If the report will be read through an interpreter or by a parent reading in a second language, shorter sentences and no idiom. State in the report that it was prepared with that in mind. You did this at Boyle for a report issued in Ukrainian — it is strong evidence and should be logged.

▸  The test
     Give the recommendations section to someone outside psychology and ask what they would do first. If they cannot say, rewrite it.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 2.2, 5.25 and 5.27 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 1.2.8 and 4.3.1 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Plain English guidance — NALA guidelines for writing for the public.

▸  Harvey, V. S. (2006). Variables affecting the clarity of psychological reports. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 62(1).

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  One register for all readers.

✗  Technical terms in the recommendations section.

✗  Writing the summary first and never revising it.

✗  Idiom in a report read through an interpreter.

✗  Never testing readability on a non-psychologist.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Your written work is accurate and professional.

▸  GRADE 4
     You layer the document and write recommendations addressed to roles in plain language.

▸  GRADE 5
     You adapt deliberately for reading level, language and interpreter use, and record that you did.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Identifying the reader
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Knowing who this is for before you write a word.
     How you build it: Name the primary reader at the top of every draft. Delete it before sending.

     ·  Judge who will read this and what they need
          you have it when: You can name the primary reader
          [CORU SoP 5.27]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Producing more than one version
     [2–3 hours to learn  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     A report and a plain-language summary, or a report with an accessible section.
     How you build it: Write one plain-language summary for a real case. It takes forty minutes the first time.

     ·  Change register between family and professional audiences
          you have it when: Two versions read differently
          [CORU SoP 2.2 · 5.25]

     ·  Produce an accessible or plain-language version
          you have it when: It exists where it is needed
          [Equal Status Acts]

     ·  Check the young person could read what is written about them
          you have it when: You considered them as a reader
          [UNCRC Art. 12]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN

macro.name: Garda vetting and Children First certification
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.12
     Understand and be able to apply the limits of the concept of confidentiality particularly in relation to child protection, vulnerable adults and elder abuse

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
This is the gate. Without vetting in place you cannot be alone with a child, and without Children First training you do not know what your legal obligations are. It is administrative and it is also the point at which you become a mandated person under statute — which is a change in your legal position, not a formality.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What vetting covers and does not
     Garda vetting discloses convictions and specified information. It is not a character reference and it does not expire in a way that lets you assume it transfers. It is held by the organisation that requested it. Moving from Roscommon to Cavan may require re-vetting through the new service — check in week one rather than discovering it when a school asks.

▸  Children First training
     Complete the Tusla e-learning module and keep the certificate. It explains the categories of abuse, the reporting thresholds, and the role of the mandated person. Do it before placement, not during.

▸  What being a mandated person means
     Under the Children First Act 2015 a mandated person must report knowledge, belief or reasonable suspicion that a child has been, is being, or is at risk of being harmed, above defined thresholds, to Tusla. This is a legal duty, it sits alongside the school's DLP route rather than replacing it, and it does not depend on your supervisor agreeing.

▸  Knowing the school's route too
     Every school has a Designated Liaison Person. Get the name for each school you work in, on your first visit, and write it somewhere you will find it under pressure.

▸  Keeping the paperwork
     Certificate, vetting confirmation and dates go in the portfolio. It is evidence and it is also the thing UCD will ask for.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Children First Act 2015.

▸  Children First: National Guidance for the Protection and Welfare of Children (DCEDIY).

▸  Tusla Children First e-learning module.

▸  National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Acts 2012–2016.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Assuming vetting transfers between services.

✗  Leaving Children First training until mid-placement.

✗  Not knowing you are a mandated person under statute.

✗  Not having the DLP's name for the school you are in today.

✗  No certificate in the portfolio.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Vetting and training are complete and evidenced.

▸  GRADE 4
     You can state what being a mandated person requires and the threshold for reporting.

▸  GRADE 5
     You know the DLP for every school on your caseload and hold both the statutory and school routes clearly.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Getting cleared
     [1 hour of admin, weeks of waiting  ·  Before placement  ·  Habit]
     Submitting vetting early enough and completing the training.
     How you build it: Submit the moment you have the form. It takes weeks, not days.

     ·  Submit vetting early enough to clear before day one
          you have it when: Cleared, not pending
          [National Vetting Bureau Acts]

     ·  Complete Children First training and file the certificate
          you have it when: Certificate dated before placement
          [Children First Act 2015]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Knowing what it obliges you to do
     [3–4 hours, once  ·  Before placement  ·  Study]
     Thresholds, what mandated means, and that the duty is personal.
     How you build it: Read Children First National Guidance thresholds properly. Not the summary.

     ·  Know the Tusla reporting thresholds
          you have it when: You can state what reaches the threshold
          [Children First National Guidance]

     ·  Know you are a mandated person and what that means
          you have it when: The duty is personal, not delegable
          [Children First Act 2015]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN

macro.name: Complete service induction
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.9
     Understand the role of policies and systems to protect the health, safety, welfare, equality and dignity of service users, staff and volunteers

▸  CORU 1.13
     Be aware of current data protection, freedom of information and other legislation relevant to the profession and be able to access new and emerging legislation

▸  CORU 3.13
     Be able to comply with relevant and current health and safety legislation and guidelines

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.6
     Take all reasonable steps to ensure tests and assessment methods are only used by those qualified and trained to do so.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Induction is where you learn the things that are never written down and that everyone assumes you know — where records live, how referrals arrive, what the lone-working policy is, who to ring. Skipping it does not save time; it moves the cost to the first day something goes wrong.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What to cover
     IT and systems access. Where case files are stored and the rules for taking them out. Referral pathway from arrival to closure. Health and safety, including lone working and travel. Expenses and mileage. The service's risk and child protection protocols. Who covers when your supervisor is absent. Data protection practice specific to the service.

▸  Lone working specifically
     You will drive alone to schools you do not know and sometimes visit homes. Know the service's lone working policy — who knows where you are, what the check-in arrangement is, what to do if a visit feels unsafe. CORU 3.13 and 3.14 cover establishing safe environments for practice, and this is the part trainees never think about until it matters.

▸  Reading the protocols rather than being told about them
     Ask for the documents. A summary from a colleague is not the protocol, and if something happens you will be held to what the protocol says.

▸  Writing your own induction note
     One page: systems, key names and numbers, protocols and where they live, the referral pathway. You will consult it for a month and it is portfolio evidence of CORU 1.9.

▸  Doing it again at Cavan
     A second service means a second induction. Different systems, different protocols, different DLPs. Do not assume the Roscommon induction covers it.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 1.9, 1.13, 3.13 and 3.14 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Your NEPS service's induction pack, risk protocol and lone working policy — ask for them in week one.

▸  Safety, Health and Welfare at Work Act 2005.

▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 3.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Treating induction as a formality.

✗  Being told about protocols rather than reading them.

✗  Not knowing the lone working arrangement.

✗  No record of what induction covered.

✗  Assuming one service's induction covers the next.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You completed induction.

▸  GRADE 4
     You hold the protocols, know the referral pathway, and recorded it.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can state the lone working and risk procedures without looking them up, and you repeated induction properly at the new service.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · The safety layer
     [2–3 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Health and safety, lone working, home visit procedure.
     How you build it: Ask for the induction checklist in writing. Work through it.

     ·  Complete health and safety and lone working induction
          you have it when: You know the procedure for a home visit
          [CORU SoP 3.13 · 3.14]

▸  BLOCK 2 · The people layer
     [1 hour, week one  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Who the DLP is, who to contact for what, and how urgently.
     How you build it: Write the names and numbers on one card. Keep it with you.

     ·  Identify the DLP by name in week one
          you have it when: Written down, not looked up later
          [Handbook §6.2]

     ·  Learn the referral and risk pathways
          you have it when: You know what happens after you refer
          [CORU SoP 1.2]

▸  BLOCK 3 · The records layer
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Where records live, for how long, and what you may and may not do with them.
     How you build it: Read the information governance policy. Ask what the retention schedule is.

     ·  Learn the records, IT and information governance policy
          you have it when: You know where records live and for how long
          [GDPR · CORU SoP 1.13]

     ·  Ask which tools you may administer independently here
          you have it when: Agreed in writing in the Placement Plan
          [PSI Code 3.3.6]

9 · FULL CHAPTER, WHERE WRITTEN

macro.name: Obtain informed consent and assent
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.3
     Be able to act in the best interest of service users at all times with due regard to their will and preference

▸  CORU 1.15
     Be able to gain informed consent to carry out assessments or provide treatment/interventions and document evidence that consent has been obtained

▸  CORU 1.16
     Be aware of current legislation and guidelines related to informed consent for individuals with lack of capacity

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 1.2.9
     Inform those to whom they offer services about legal limits on confidentiality where appropriate.

▸  PSI 1.3.5
     Ensure at least the following are understood: purpose and nature of the activity; mutual responsibilities; likely benefits and risks; alternatives; consequences of non-action; the option to refuse or withdraw at any time without prejudice; the period the consent applies to; and how to rescind consent.

▸  PSI 1.3.10
     Seek willing and adequately informed participation from any person of diminished capacity, and proceed without consent only if the activity is of direct benefit to that person.

▸  PSI 1.4.3
     Respect the right of individuals to discontinue participation or service at any time, and be responsive to non-verbal indications of a desire to discontinue.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Consent is the largest single section of the PSI Code — twenty clauses in 1.3 alone — and it is the one trainees treat as a signature. It is a process, it is ongoing, and it is the clearest example of a legal and ethical requirement that can invalidate everything downstream if it is not right. An assessment without valid consent is not a flawed assessment; it is one that should not have happened.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Consent is a process, not a form
     PSI 1.3.1 is explicit: informed consent is the outcome of a process of agreeing to work collaboratively, not the signing of a form. The signature records the process; it does not constitute it.

▸  What must be understood
     PSI 1.3.5 lists it: purpose and nature of the activity, mutual responsibilities, likely benefits and risks, alternatives, the likely consequences of non-action, the option to refuse or withdraw at any time without prejudice, the period the consent covers, and how to rescind it. Work through that list rather than trusting a template to have covered it.

▸  Who consents, and assent
     In school settings a parent or guardian consents for a child. The child assents — meaning they agree, in terms they understand, and their refusal is respected. PSI 1.4.3 requires respecting the right to discontinue and being responsive to non-verbal indications of wanting to stop. A child who has gone silent and stopped trying has withdrawn assent even if they have not said so.

▸  Third-party referrals and multiple relationships
     PSI 1.3.19 requires clarifying the nature of multiple relationships when services are at the behest of a third party — which a school referral is. Say who asked for this, what will be written, who will see it, and what the limits of confidentiality are. Say it to the parent and to the child.

▸  Capacity and re-consenting
     PSI 1.3.10 and 1.3.11 cover diminished capacity. And consent is not permanent: if the work changes materially — a different assessment, a new purpose, a report going somewhere unanticipated — go back. CORU 1.15 requires documenting that consent was obtained; documenting it once at the start does not cover a changed purpose.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), section 1.3 — all twenty clauses, full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 1.15 and 1.16 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015.

▸  NEPS consent forms and service guidance — use the current version.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Treating the signed form as the consent.

✗  Not explaining the limits of confidentiality to the child.

✗  Continuing when a child has withdrawn assent non-verbally.

✗  Not clarifying who asked for the assessment and who will read it.

✗  Not re-consenting when the purpose changes.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You obtain and document written consent.

▸  GRADE 4
     You work through what must be understood, obtain assent from the child, and explain confidentiality limits.

▸  GRADE 5
     You treat consent as ongoing, re-consent when purpose changes, and can cite the clauses behind each step.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing what consent requires
     [4–5 hours, once  ·  Before placement  ·  Study]
     The twenty clauses in PSI Code 1.3 and what each obliges you to cover.
     How you build it: Read Principle 1 in full. Build your own consent script from it.

     ·  Explain purpose, process and who will see the report
          you have it when: In plain words, before anything begins
          [PSI Code 1.3.5]

     ·  State the right to stop or withdraw
          you have it when: It was mentioned
          [PSI Code 1.3.5]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Confidentiality and its limits
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     What you may not keep confidential, and saying so before it matters.
     How you build it: Write your own sentence for explaining limits to a child and to an adult. Use it every time.

     ·  State the limits of confidentiality before disclosure
          you have it when: First, not after

macro.name: Recognise and act on child protection concerns
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.12
     Understand and be able to apply the limits of the concept of confidentiality particularly in relation to child protection, vulnerable adults and elder abuse

▸  CORU 3.12
     Be able to carry out and document a risk analysis and implement effective risk management controls and strategies; be able to clearly communicate any identified risk, adverse events or near misses in line with current legislation/guidelines

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
This is the one where getting it wrong is unrecoverable. It is also the one trainees rehearse least, because it is uncomfortable to think about. You have already managed a disclosure — at Grange on 22/05/2026 — which means you know this is not hypothetical.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What you are looking for
     The four categories in Children First: neglect, emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse. Indicators may be disclosure, observed injury, behaviour, or something a third party tells you. You do not need to be sure. You need reasonable grounds for concern — that is the threshold, and it is deliberately low.

▸  Receiving a disclosure
     Listen. Do not promise confidentiality — you cannot keep it, and saying so at the start of any session is why that matters. Do not ask leading questions or investigate; that is not your role and it can compromise a later process. Let the child say what they say, then stop.

▸  The sequence, exactly
     Stop the activity. Record verbatim with the time, as soon as possible. Tell your supervisor the same day. Follow the school's DLP route. As a mandated person, report to Tusla where the threshold is met — this duty is yours and does not transfer to the DLP. Record who you told, when, and what was agreed. Then write your own account of what you did.

▸  What not to do
     Do not wait for supervision. Do not decide it is probably nothing. Do not investigate to find out whether it is serious enough. Do not record it only in your own notes. PSI 3.3.4 requires acting to stop or offset serious harm even where a confidential relationship is involved — the Code removes the discretion you might feel you have.

▸  Afterwards
     Bring it to supervision even though it is resolved. Write it up as a dilemma entry. Expect to feel unsettled; that is ordinary and is what supervision and PSI 4.1.2 exist for. A managed disclosure is significant evidence for this competency and should be written up, not left as a line in a day log.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Children First Act 2015 — particularly the mandated person provisions.

▸  Children First: National Guidance for the Protection and Welfare of Children (DCEDIY).

▸  Tusla — making a report, and the thresholds.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 3.3.4, 1.2.5 and 1.3.14 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Department of Education — Child Protection Procedures for Primary and Post-Primary Schools.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Promising confidentiality.

✗  Asking questions to find out more.

✗  Waiting for the next supervision session.

✗  Assuming telling the DLP discharges your own mandated duty.

✗  Not writing it up afterwards as evidence.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You know that concerns must be reported and to whom.

▸  GRADE 4
     You can state the categories, the threshold, and the full sequence including your own mandated duty.

▸  GRADE 5
     You have followed it in practice, recorded it properly, and used supervision afterwards.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Recognising
     [4 hours, once  ·  Before placement  ·  Study]
     Knowing the thresholds well enough to recognise one in the moment.
     How you build it: Read the National Guidance thresholds. Then read three anonymised examples.

     ·  Recognise a concern against the threshold
          you have it when: You knew it when you saw it
          [Children First National Guidance]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Responding in the moment
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     What to do and not do while it is happening.
     How you build it: Rehearse it. Know that you do not investigate.

     ·  Do not investigate or question further
          you have it when: You did not interview the child
          [Children First National Guidance]

     ·  Record verbatim what was said or seen, at the time
          you have it when: Contemporaneous and factual
          [CORU SoP 2.8 · 3.12]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Acting
     [1 hour, week one  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Reporting the same day, whether or not anyone is available.
     How you build it: Know the DLP, the route and the timeframe before you need them.

     ·  Act the same day without waiting for supervision
          you have it when: The duty does not wait
          [Children First Act 2015]

     ·  Report to the DLP and record the time
          you have it when: The file shows who and when
          [Children First Act 2015]

     ·  Bring it to supervision afterwards, not instead
          you have it when: Supervision follows the action
          [Handbook §6.2]

macro.name: Work an ethical dilemma through a decision procedure
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.19
     Understand the principles of professional decision-making and be able to make informed decisions within the context of competing demands including those relating to ethical conflicts and available resources

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Ethical competence is not having good instincts. It is being able to show that you followed a systematic process when the answer was not obvious — which is exactly what PSI 3.6.1 requires and what Appendix A of the Code sets out. A documented dilemma is also the hardest piece of portfolio evidence to fake and therefore the most convincing.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Recognising a dilemma
     A dilemma is not a hard decision. It is a situation where two obligations conflict — confidentiality against welfare, the child's wishes against the parent's, the school's interest against the child's, your competence against the need in front of you. If there is a right answer and it is just difficult, that is not a dilemma.

▸  The seven steps
     PSI Appendix A: define the issues and the parties; scan the Code and identify every relevant clause, plus other guidelines and legislation; evaluate the rights, responsibilities and welfare of all affected parties; generate as many alternatives as possible; evaluate the likely outcome of each; choose, implement and inform; take responsibility for the consequences.

▸  Identifying the parties properly
     Appendix B of the Code gives the categories: the psychologist, direct beneficiary, subject, extended beneficiary, participant, referrer, colleague, contractor, employer, manager, supervisor, employee, the wider profession, other parties, the general public. Trainees typically name two parties when there are six, and the missing ones are usually where the conflict actually sits.

▸  Generating alternatives
     'More the better' is in the Code for a reason. The first two options are usually the obvious binary. The useful option is normally the fourth or fifth — a partial disclosure, a delay with conditions, a consultation before deciding.

▸  Documenting it
     The Code strongly recommends keeping notes at each stage. Write it up as an Appendix 8 dilemma entry: what it was, who was affected, which clauses were in tension, what you generated, what you chose, what happened. One well-written entry evidences Ethical Practice better than twenty routine records.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), section 3.6 and Appendices A and B — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 1.19 — professional decision-making within competing demands.

▸  Bond, T. (2015). Standards and ethics for counselling in action (4th ed.). Sage.

▸  Koocher, G. P., & Keith-Spiegel, P. (2016). Ethics in psychology and the mental health professions (4th ed.). Oxford University Press.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Treating a hard decision as a dilemma.

✗  Naming two parties when there are six.

✗  Generating two options and choosing between them.

✗  Deciding alone when consultation was possible.

✗  No written record, so it cannot be evidenced.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You recognise ethical issues and raise them in supervision.

▸  GRADE 4
     You follow a systematic procedure and identify the clauses in tension.

▸  GRADE 5
     You identify all affected parties, generate genuine alternatives, document the process, and can account for the consequences.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing the procedure
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The seven steps of PSI Appendix A, in order.
     How you build it: Read Appendix A. Write the seven steps on a card.

     ·  Identify the issue and all affected parties
          you have it when: Including ones you would otherwise miss
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 1 · Appendix B]

     ·  Scan the Code for the clauses that apply
          you have it when: You cite clause numbers
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 2]

     ·  Evaluate each party's rights and responsibilities
          you have it when: Each considered separately
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 3]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Working it through
     [3–4 hours to learn  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     Generating alternatives and evaluating them rather than deciding and justifying.
     How you build it: Use it on a hypothetical first. Then on a real one with supervision.

     ·  Generate as many alternative courses as possible
          you have it when: More than two
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 4]

     ·  Evaluate the likely outcome of each
          you have it when: Consequences thought through
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 5]

     ·  Decide and record the decision
          you have it when: Written down
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 6]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Owning it
     [Habit  ·  Ongoing all year  ·  Practice]
     Taking responsibility including where it went wrong, and keeping notes throughout.
     How you build it: Write the Appendix 8 entry the same day.

     ·  Take responsibility for the consequences
          you have it when: Including where it went wrong
          [PSI Code Appendix A step 7]

     ·  Keep notes at each stage
          you have it when: The Code strongly recommends it
          [PSI Code Appendix A]
