macro.name: State and hold the limits of your competence
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.2
     Be able to identify the limits of their practice and know when to seek advice and additional expertise or refer to another professional

▸  CORU 2.2
     Be able to modify and adapt communication methods and styles, including verbal and non-verbal methods, to suit the individual service user, considering issues of language, age, culture, beliefs and health and/or social care needs

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.2.2
     Recognise the boundaries of their competence, and do not exceed these.

▸  PSI 2.2.3
     Offer or carry out (without supervision) only those professional activities for which they have established their competence to practise to the benefit of others.

▸  PSI 3.3.6
     Take all reasonable steps to ensure tests and assessment methods are only used by those qualified and trained to do so.

▸  PSI 3.4.3
     When referring a client, maintain support and responsibility for caring until contact has commenced with the agent to whom referral was made.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The pressure in Year 1 runs entirely one way: toward doing more than you should. Schools want answers, parents want certainty, and saying 'that is outside what I can do' feels like failure. It is the opposite — PSI 2.2.2 and 2.2.3 make it a requirement, and the trainees who get into difficulty are almost never the ones who said no too often.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Where the line is, concretely
     You do not diagnose. You do not deliver therapy. You do not work with trauma. You do not administer instruments you have not been trained on and supervised in. You do not give a score on the day before it is checked. You do not advise on medication. You do not give legal advice about entitlement. Write this list somewhere you will see it.

▸  The phrasing that works
     'That is outside what I am able to do at this stage, but here is what I can do, and here is who does that.' Three parts: the limit, the offer, the route. Said that way it reads as competence, because it is.

▸  Recognising pressure in the moment
     The pull is strongest when someone is distressed and you are the only professional in the room. Notice the pull rather than acting on it. If you are about to do something you have not done before because it seems needed now, that is the moment to stop.

▸  Supervised extension is different
     Doing something new under supervision is how competence grows and is entirely legitimate. PSI 2.2.3 says you carry out without supervision only what you have established competence in — the phrase 'without supervision' is the whole point. Agree the new thing in advance rather than discovering it mid-session.

▸  Recognising impairment in yourself
     PSI 2.5.1 requires you to refrain from practice when your judgement or ability to benefit and not harm others is seriously impaired, and to seek assistance about whether to limit or suspend activity. That is a professional obligation, not an admission, and knowing it exists before you need it makes it easier to act on.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), section 2.2 and 2.5 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 1.1, 1.2 and 1.17 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Scaife, J. (2019). Supervision in clinical practice — on the supervised extension of competence.

▸  Barnett, J. E., Doll, B., Younggren, J. N., & Rubin, N. J. (2007). Clinical competence for practicing psychologists. Professional Psychology, 38(5).

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Giving a score on the day.

✗  Drifting into therapy because the conversation went there.

✗  Administering an instrument you have not been supervised on.

✗  Saying yes because the alternative felt unhelpful.

✗  Continuing to practise while seriously impaired because stopping felt worse.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You ask for help when you are unsure.

▸  GRADE 4
     You can state your limits and decline appropriately with an alternative and a route.

▸  GRADE 5
     You recognise the pull in the moment, extend competence deliberately under supervision, and know the obligation to suspend practice when impaired.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing where the line is
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Publisher levels, service policy, and your own actual competence.
     How you build it: List every tool you hold and its user level. Check against service policy.

     ·  Know your publisher competence level for every tool
          you have it when: You can state it
          [PSI Code 3.3.6]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Saying it
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Naming a limit before being asked, without apologising for it.
     How you build it: Say it once in your first supervision. It gets easier.

     ·  Say early what you are not yet competent to do
          you have it when: Before being asked
          [CORU SoP 1.2 · PSI Code 2.2.2]

     ·  Decline work that exceeds you
          you have it when: You declined
          [PSI Code 2.2.3]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Referring properly
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Handing on without dropping the case.
     How you build it: Maintain contact until the referral is picked up. PSI 3.4.3 requires it.

     ·  Refer on and maintain responsibility until contact is made
          you have it when: You did not drop it at referral
          [PSI Code 3.4.3]

     ·  Include a limitations paragraph in every report
          you have it when: Every one
          [CORU SoP 1.2]

macro.name: Manage workload and your own wellbeing
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 1.18
     Be able to take responsibility for managing one's own workload as appropriate

▸  CORU 1.20
     Be aware of and be able to take responsibility for managing one's own health and wellbeing

▸  CORU 4.1
     Be able to engage in and take responsibility for professional development

▸  CORU 5.45
     Be able to recognise personal emotional responses and the impact of trauma, as identified through professional/therapeutic practice and supervision, and use appropriate tools to develop effective self-care to maintain professional functioning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.5.1
     Refrain from practice when professional judgment or ability to benefit and not harm others is seriously impaired by a physical or psychological condition; and seek competent professional assistance to determine whether to limit, suspend or terminate professional activity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
CORU 1.18 and 1.20 make workload and your own health professional requirements, not personal matters. PSI 4.1.1 requires self-care specifically to avoid conditions that impair judgement, and 4.1.2 requires seeking support when stressed. Your review named monitoring, self-care, workload, pace and volume as a development area — so this is assessed, and it is assessed as competence.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Knowing your actual capacity
     Not what you can do in a good week — what you can sustain across a term including travel, write-up and the unexpected. A school visit is not a school visit; it is travel, the visit, the write-up and the follow-up. Count all four when you plan.

▸  Protecting write-up time
     The most common failure is booking visits back to back and leaving no time to write, which produces the backlog that then becomes the problem. Block write-up time in the diary as though it were a visit. It is the cheapest single intervention available to you.

▸  Saying no with a reason and an alternative
     'I can take that if we move the Thursday visit to next week' is a negotiation. 'I'm very busy' is not. Give your supervisor the information they need to decide — they usually do not know how full you are.

▸  Using the supports that exist
     Adjustments agreed with UCD Access, weekly check-ins, scaffolding and visual supports, joint target setting — these were recommended for a reason and using them is not a concession. Build them into the Cavan contract in week one rather than requesting them in November.

▸  Naming the pace question when it is real
     Your 4 August review recommended half days or alternate days for rest and recovery. A recommendation from a supervisor that is not reflected in the schedule is a live issue and it belongs in writing with UCD and the service, not absorbed quietly. Raising it is an exercise of CORU 1.18 and 1.20, not a complaint.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 1.18, 1.20 and 5.45 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 4.1.1, 4.1.2 and 2.5.1 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 6 — supervision and raising concerns.

▸  Wise, E. H., & Barnett, J. E. (2016). Self-care for psychologists. In APA Handbook of Clinical Psychology.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Counting visits rather than visits plus write-up plus travel.

✗  Booking back-to-back days with no write-up time.

✗  Saying you are busy without giving the detail to act on.

✗  Requesting adjustments only once things are difficult.

✗  Absorbing a scheduling problem rather than naming it in writing.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You complete the work asked of you.

▸  GRADE 4
     You plan realistically including write-up and travel, and negotiate workload with information.

▸  GRADE 5
     You have adjustments agreed in advance and in writing, you monitor your own functioning, and you escalate a structural problem through the proper route rather than absorbing it.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing your numbers
     [2 hours  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Actual caseload, actual travel, actual hours.
     How you build it: Track it for two weeks. The number is usually different from the impression.

     ·  Track your actual caseload and travel load
          you have it when: You know the numbers
          [CORU SoP 1.18]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Knowing your signals
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     What your own early warning signs are.
     How you build it: Write down what you were like the last time you were depleted. Three specific things.

     ·  Recognise your own warning signs
          you have it when: You can name them
          [CORU SoP 5.45]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Acting on it
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Raising workload early and seeking supervision when stressed.
     How you build it: Put one line about your own state on every supervision agenda for a month.

     ·  Raise workload before it becomes a problem
          you have it when: Before, not after
          [CORU SoP 1.18]

     ·  Seek supervision when stressed, not only when stuck
          you have it when: It is required, not permitted
          [PSI Code 4.1.2]

▸  BLOCK 4 · Knowing the formal duties
     [1 hour, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     The seven-day notification and when to refrain from practice.
     How you build it: Read Handbook §5 once. Know it exists.

     ·  Know the seven-day notification duty
          you have it when: You could act on it if needed
          [Handbook §5]

     ·  Refrain from practice where judgement is seriously impaired
          you have it when: You would know and would act
          [PSI Code 2.5.1]

macro.name: Agree and sign the supervision contract
macro.text:
2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The contract is the document that makes everything else enforceable. Without it, the weekly hour is a courtesy that gets cancelled when the caseload gets heavy, and you have no standing to ask for it back. PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 requires a placement contract, thirty minutes of supervision per placement day, observation in both directions, a mid-placement review and two review meetings with written feedback. Those are not favours. Signing it in week one is also the only moment when asking for something feels normal rather than like a complaint.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What you are actually entitled to
     One hour of formal supervision weekly. Thirty minutes per placement day in total, which for four days a week means two hours — the weekly hour plus an hour of informal contact. Observation of you by your supervisor, and observation of your supervisor by you. A mid-placement review. Two review meetings with written feedback. Read PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 yourself before the conversation so you are quoting a standard rather than making a request.

▸  What to put in beyond the minimum
     How and when you contact your supervisor out of session, and what counts as urgent. What happens when they are on leave — who covers, and how you reach them. How disagreements about a case get resolved. What is recorded and who holds it. Whether supervision notes are shareable with UCD. Confidentiality of what you disclose about your own practice. Adjustments you need in order to work well, which you are entitled to raise and which are better agreed in writing at the start than negotiated in October.

▸  Drafting it so it survives a busy term
     Write the day and time of the weekly hour into the contract, not 'weekly'. Name what happens if it is missed — rescheduled within the same week, not dropped. Specify the observation dates in advance if you can, because observations are the item most likely to slip to the end and then not happen. Both of you sign and date it, and you keep a copy.

▸  Raising adjustments without framing them as problems
     The phrasing that works is functional rather than personal: 'I work better with written follow-up after supervision, so I would like a short email summary of agreed actions' is a workflow request. It costs your supervisor two minutes and it protects you from a disputed recollection later. Put the ones that matter in the contract.

▸  The Cavan contract specifically
     This is a new supervisor and a new service. The Roscommon arrangement does not carry over automatically. Agree it in week one, before any casework, and use the opportunity to name the two Table 3 bands — Early Years and Young Adult — in the Appendix 1 at the same time, because neither can be added retrospectively.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Accreditation Standards (2022), section 3.3.9 — the supervision requirements in full. The text is on the Reference sheet, Part B.

▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook Year 1, section 6 and Appendix 8.

▸  Scaife, J. (2019). Supervision in clinical practice: A practitioner's guide (3rd ed.). Routledge. — the chapter on contracting.

▸  Hawkins, P., & McMahon, A. (2020). Supervision in the helping professions (5th ed.). Open University Press.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Not having one, and discovering in March that the weekly hour was never protected.

✗  Signing a template without reading it, so you do not know what you agreed to.

✗  Writing 'weekly' rather than a named day and time.

✗  Leaving observations undated, which is how they end up not happening.

✗  Assuming the Roscommon arrangement transfers to Cavan.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     A contract exists and is signed.

▸  GRADE 4
     You negotiated its content rather than accepting a template, and it names times, cover arrangements and observation dates.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can cite the standard behind each entitlement, and the contract anticipates the situations that usually break supervision rather than only the ordinary case.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing what you are entitled to
     [2 hours, once  ·  Before placement  ·  Study]
     The dose, the review points, the observations — what the PSI and the handbook require.
     How you build it: Read PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 and Handbook §6. Both are short.

     ·  Know the 30 minutes per placement day entitlement
          you have it when: You can state it if the hour slips
          [PSI Accred 3.3.9]

     ·  Know the four components expected
          you have it when: Educative, supportive, evaluative, safeguarding
          [Handbook §6.1]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Drafting it
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Bringing something rather than waiting to be given one.
     How you build it: Draft it before week one. Bring it in.

     ·  Bring a draft to week one
          you have it when: You arrived with something
          [Handbook §6]

     ·  Record day, time, duration and format
          you have it when: Specific, not 'as arranged'
          [Handbook §6]

     ·  Agree how cancellations are handled
          you have it when: Who rearranges, and by when
          [PSI Supervision Guidelines 2024]

     ·  Both sign and date it
          you have it when: It is signed
          [Handbook Appendix 8]

macro.name: Take the weekly supervision hour
macro.text:
2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The weekly hour is the single most protective thing in the placement, and it is the first thing to disappear when a caseload gets heavy. Trainees rarely lose it in one decision — it goes gradually, moved once, then shortened, then merged into a car journey, until it is not happening and nobody has said so. The hour is not a discussion of cases you could have had by email. It is where you find out what you did not know you did not know.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Protecting it structurally
     It is in the calendar as a recurring appointment with a location. It is not the last hour of the day, because the last hour is the one that gets eaten. If it moves, it moves within the same week and you book the replacement before you leave the conversation. If it is cancelled twice in a row, that is a pattern and you name it at the next one.

▸  Using an hour well
     An hour holds roughly three substantive items, not eight. Bring one case you are stuck on, one thing you did that you are unsure about, and one forward-looking item. Case updates that could be an email should be an email. The most valuable minutes are usually spent on the thing you were reluctant to raise.

▸  The difference between supervision and case management
     Case management asks what is happening and what happens next. Supervision asks what you were thinking, what you noticed in yourself, and what you might be missing. Placements drift toward case management because it is more comfortable for both people. If three sessions in a row have been status updates, say so — 'I think we have been doing case management; can we spend this one on how I am finding the work?'

▸  Counting it properly
     Thirty minutes per placement day is the standard. At four days a week that is two hours, of which one is the formal session. The informal hour is real supervision and counts — corridor conversations, a call after a difficult visit, a joint drive to a school. Record it in Appendix 8 rather than letting it go unlogged, because at the end of the placement the log is the evidence that the standard was met.

▸  When it is not working
     Supervision can be insufficient without anyone behaving badly — a supervisor stretched across too many schools, a service in transition. Raise it early and functionally: 'We have had two of the last five sessions. Can we look at how to protect it?' If that does not change it, UCD placement staff need to know, and the handbook gives you a route for raising concerns. Using that route is not disloyalty; it is what the route is for.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Accreditation Standards (2022), 3.3.9.

▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 6.1 and 6.2, and 6.4.3 on trainee concerns.

▸  Hawkins, P., & McMahon, A. (2020). Supervision in the helping professions — the seven-eyed model, which gives you language for what a session is actually attending to.

▸  Carroll, M. (2014). Effective supervision for the helping professions (2nd ed.). Sage.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Letting it move to the end of the day.

✗  Arriving with nothing and treating it as a status update.

✗  Not logging the informal contact, then being unable to show the standard was met.

✗  Deciding a supervision problem is your fault for needing too much.

✗  Waiting until the end of placement to say it was not happening.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You attend supervision when it happens.

▸  GRADE 4
     You protect the hour, arrive prepared, and log both formal and informal contact.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can tell supervision from case management, you redirect it when it drifts, and you raise a shortfall early through the proper route.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Protecting it
     [Habit  ·  Ongoing all year  ·  Habit]
     Treating the hour as fixed rather than movable.
     How you build it: Put it in the calendar as unavailable. Defend it twice and it stops being questioned.

     ·  Protect the hour
          you have it when: It happened
          [PSI Accred 3.3.9]

     ·  Raise it if it slips twice
          you have it when: It is a requirement, not a courtesy
          [PSI Accred 3.3.9]

     ·  Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively
          you have it when: You track the total
          [PSI Accred 3.3.9]

macro.name: Prepare and send an agenda in advance
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 4.3
     Be able to evaluate and reflect critically on own professional practice to identify learning and development needs; select appropriate learning activities to achieve professional development goals; and integrate new knowledge and skills into professional practice

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
An agenda sent the day before changes what the hour can do. Your supervisor arrives having thought about your questions instead of hearing them cold, and the session starts at the substance. It also protects you: an agenda is a dated record of what you raised and when, which matters if a concern later turns out to have been raised early and not acted on. CORU 4.3 requires you to evaluate and reflect critically on your own practice to identify learning needs — the agenda is where that becomes visible.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The fifteen-minute habit
     Same time every week, the day before. Three to five items, each one line, in priority order so that if you run out of time you have lost the least important thing rather than the most. Send it by email so it is timestamped and searchable.

▸  Choosing items that are worth an hour
     Good items share a shape: you have already thought about them and got stuck. 'CS26-02343 — I have two competing formulations and cannot decide which the data supports' is worth the hour. 'CS26-02343 update' is not. Bring the thinking, not just the problem.

▸  Including the uncomfortable item
     The thing you are avoiding raising is almost always the highest-value item. Something you are not sure you did correctly. A case you are dreading. A comment that landed badly. Put it on the agenda in writing, because once it is written you will raise it, and unwritten it will not survive the first twenty minutes of case updates.

▸  Marking what you want from each item
     Annotate: 'for a decision', 'for your view', 'for information'. It takes five extra words and stops the session spending twenty minutes on something you only needed noted. It also tells your supervisor when you are asking to be told what to do versus asking to think it through.

▸  Carrying actions forward
     End the agenda with last week's actions and their status. Two lines. It makes the sessions cumulative rather than a series of unconnected hours, and it produces the record of change that Appendix 6 and the reflective essay both ask you to demonstrate.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 6.2.

▸  Scaife, J. (2019). Supervision in clinical practice — the chapter on preparing for and using supervision.

▸  Carroll, M. (2014). Effective supervision for the helping professions — on the supervisee's responsibility for the session.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Sending it as you walk in, which removes the only benefit.

✗  Items that are status updates.

✗  Omitting the difficult item and then not raising it.

✗  Ten items, so the hour becomes a list read aloud.

✗  Never referring back, so nothing accumulates.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You sometimes arrive with notes.

▸  GRADE 4
     An agenda goes in advance every week, with items that show prior thinking.

▸  GRADE 5
     Items are marked for what you want from them, the uncomfortable item is on there, and actions carry forward so the sessions build.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · The habit
     [15 minutes weekly  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Sending three items the day before, every week.
     How you build it: Recurring calendar reminder. It is administration, not skill.

     ·  Send it the day before
          you have it when: In advance, not on arrival
          [Handbook §6.2]

     ·  Keep it to three items
          you have it when: Focused
          [Handbook §6.2]

     ·  Update on actions agreed last time
          you have it when: You closed the loop
          [Handbook §6.2]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Choosing the right items
     [Ongoing  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Learning to bring what you are avoiding.
     How you build it: Notice which case you did not mention. That is the one.

     ·  Include at least one thing that went badly
          you have it when: Not only successes
          [CORU SoP 4.3 · PSI Code 4.1.2]

macro.name: Keep supervision session records
macro.text:
2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Appendix 8 is assessed, and it is also the only proof that the supervision standard was met. Written on the day it takes ten minutes; reconstructed in June it is visibly reconstructed, and an examiner can tell. More than that, the record is where you can see your own development — a June entry compared with a February one is the clearest evidence of change you will have, and the reflective essay depends on it.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The ten-minute record
     Date, duration, format, who was present. What was discussed, in a few lines per item. What was decided and by whom. What you are doing before next time. Written within the day, not the week. If you write it in the car before you drive off, it takes eight minutes and is accurate.

▸  Tagging against the competencies
     Mark each entry with the competency or competencies it touched. It costs nothing at the time and it means that in December you can answer 'what supervision did I get on systemic change?' by filtering rather than by reading eighteen records. This is also what lets the Log's competency tags do their work — supervision is evidence, not just support.

▸  The dilemma entry
     When an ethical dilemma arises, the record is longer and has a specific shape: what the dilemma was, who was affected, which Code clauses were in tension, what options you generated, what you decided, and what happened. PSI 3.6.1 requires a systematic procedure and the Code's Appendix A sets one out. A single well-written dilemma entry is worth more in the portfolio than twenty routine ones, and Ethical Practice is hard to evidence any other way.

▸  What not to put in
     Supervision records are not case files. Identify cases by reference number, not by name. Do not record third-party personal information that belongs in the case file. Be careful recording your own health or personal circumstances — note that an adjustment was discussed, not the underlying detail. PSI 1.2.6 and 1.2.8 apply to these records as much as to any other.

▸  Getting it countersigned
     Ask your supervisor to sign the records periodically rather than all at the end. A run of unsigned records in June is a problem; a signature each month is administration. The same logic applies to Appendix 4 — you are currently carrying an unsigned 84-day log, and that is exactly the situation to avoid repeating.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, Appendix 8 and section 6.1.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 3.6.1 and Appendix A — the ethical decision-making procedure, reproduced on the Reference sheet.

▸  Scaife, J. (2019). Supervision in clinical practice — on recording.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Writing them up in bulk at the end of placement.

✗  Recording what was discussed but not what was decided.

✗  Naming children in supervision records.

✗  No dilemma entries, leaving Ethical Practice thinly evidenced.

✗  Leaving all countersignature to the final week.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Records exist for most sessions.

▸  GRADE 4
     Written within the day, covering discussion, decisions and actions, and tagged to competencies.

▸  GRADE 5
     At least one full dilemma entry following a systematic procedure, records countersigned as you go, and the sequence shows development over time.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · The record itself
     [10 minutes per session  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     What an Appendix 8 record must contain and how many you need.
     How you build it: 19 for a 75-day placement. Write it the same day.

     ·  Complete a record for every session
          you have it when: 19 for a 75-day placement
          [Handbook Appendix 8]

     ·  Record topics, actions and who does what
          you have it when: Actions are specific
          [Handbook §6.1]

     ·  Get them co-signed
          you have it when: Signed, not just written
          [Handbook Appendix 8]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Tagging it
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Marking which component each session covered.
     How you build it: Four letters in the margin. Ten seconds.

     ·  Tag which of the four components the session covered
          you have it when: E, S, Ev, Sg
          [Handbook §6.1]

▸  BLOCK 3 · The dilemma entry
     [30 minutes when it arises  ·  Ongoing all year  ·  Habit]
     Recording an ethical dilemma using the seven steps.
     How you build it: Write it the same day it happens. It is the strongest ethics evidence you will have.

     ·  Record any ethical dilemma using the seven steps
          you have it when: All seven, from PSI Appendix A
          [PSI Code Appendix A]

macro.name: Observe your supervisor with a client
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.8
     Know the basic principles of effective teaching and learning, mentoring and supervision

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
You learn more from watching an experienced psychologist handle a difficult moment than from any amount of reading about it. Specifically, you learn the things nobody writes down: how they open with a wary parent, what they do when a child refuses a subtest, how they close a feedback meeting that has gone badly. PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 requires observation in both directions, and trainees routinely complete the being-observed half and skip this one.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Arranging it early
     Ask in week one, before the caseload builds. Ask for a specific thing — 'could I sit in on a feedback meeting?' — rather than 'could I observe you sometime', which produces agreement and no date. Get it in the diary. Consent from the family is required and your supervisor arranges that, but you should ask early enough that it is possible.

▸  Watching for process, not content
     You already know what a WISC-V administration looks like. Watch how they manage the room: where they sit, how they handle an interruption, what they say when a child gets a run of items wrong, how they signal that a section is ending. Write down verbatim phrases — the actual words someone uses to decline to give a score on the day are more useful than a principle about managing expectations.

▸  Watching the difficult moments especially
     The valuable minutes are where something goes slightly wrong. A parent becomes upset. A teacher disagrees in front of the parent. A child discloses something unexpected. Note exactly what your supervisor did, including the pause before they spoke. These are the moments you will face and have no script for.

▸  Debriefing while it is fresh
     Ask afterwards about a decision you noticed: 'you changed tack when she mentioned the older brother — what were you thinking?' Experienced practitioners make these moves automatically and often have not articulated them until asked. This question is where most of the learning is.

▸  Recording it as evidence
     This is an Appendix 7 form and it counts. Two of your four Appendix 7 observations can be you observing your supervisor. Complete your section on the day, not in June — the four Roscommon forms are currently sitting with your sections blank, which is the position this habit avoids.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 6.2 and Appendix 7.

▸  PSI Accreditation Standards (2022), 3.3.9.

▸  Hawkins, P., & McMahon, A. (2020). Supervision in the helping professions — on modelling and observational learning in supervision.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Asking vaguely and never getting a date.

✗  Watching the content you already know rather than the process you do not.

✗  Not asking about the decisions you noticed.

✗  Leaving the Appendix 7 form blank on the day.

✗  Treating it as optional because the standard is usually policed in one direction.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have observed your supervisor at least once.

▸  GRADE 4
     You observed with a focus, recorded process rather than content, and debriefed.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can name specific techniques you adopted from the observation and point to where you have since used them.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Arranging it
     [Ask once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Getting it booked in the first weeks rather than the last.
     How you build it: Ask in week one. The handbook says occasional rather than protracted.

     ·  Arrange it in the first weeks
          you have it when: Front-loaded, as the handbook expects
          [Handbook §6.2]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Watching usefully
     [1 hour per observation  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Practice]
     Having a focus rather than watching generally.
     How you build it: Agree what you are watching for beforehand. Write it down.

     ·  Agree a focus before observing
          you have it when: You knew what you were watching for
          [CORU SoP 5.8]

     ·  Record what they did that you would not have
          you have it when: Specific, not general admiration
          [CORU SoP 4.3]

     ·  Ask afterwards why they did it that way
          you have it when: You asked
          [CORU SoP 4.5]

macro.name: Be observed with a client
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 4.3
     Be able to evaluate and reflect critically on own professional practice to identify learning and development needs; select appropriate learning activities to achieve professional development goals; and integrate new knowledge and skills into professional practice

▸  CORU 4.5
     Understand the importance of and be able to seek professional development, supervision, feedback and peer review opportunities in order to continuously improve practice

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 3.5.2
     Facilitate the professional and scientific development of those whose work they supervise by arranging appropriate work experience and offering constructive feedback.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Being observed is the only way anyone finds out what you actually do, as opposed to what you report doing. Reports and supervision both pass through your own account of the session. Observation does not. It is also the most anxiety-provoking part of placement for most trainees, which is precisely why it should happen early and often enough to stop being an event.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Arranging it early and more than the minimum
     Two observations is a minimum, not a target. Early ones are more useful because there is still time to change something. Ask for the first within the first month, on something ordinary rather than something you have over-prepared.

▸  Choosing and naming the focus
     Tell your supervisor what to watch for. 'I want feedback on how I handle the transition between subtests' produces something usable. 'Any feedback welcome' produces general reassurance. Naming the focus also means you are directing your own development, which is what CORU 4.3 asks for.

▸  Being observed on something difficult
     It is tempting to be observed doing the thing you are best at. The observation is worth more if it is the thing you are unsure of — a feedback meeting with a parent who disagrees, an interview with a reluctant adolescent. You are not being marked on polish; you are being marked on whether you can use feedback.

▸  Receiving feedback without collapsing or defending
     Both reactions cost you the same thing: the information. Write it down as it is given, ask a clarifying question, and do not respond to the substance in the room. Sit with it, then come back the following week with what you did about it. That return is the part that gets noticed.

▸  Completing your own section of the form
     Appendix 7 has a trainee section and it is yours to write. It asks what you thought, what you would change, and what you will do differently. Complete it the same day while you can remember the session. You have four forms from Roscommon with the supervisor's half done and yours empty — those are the quickest item on your outstanding list and they are getting harder to write with every week that passes.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 6.2 and Appendix 7.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 4.3 and 4.5 — the text is on the Reference sheet.

▸  Scaife, J. (2019). Supervision in clinical practice — on live observation and on receiving feedback.

▸  Stone, D., & Heen, S. (2014). Thanks for the feedback. Viking. — not a psychology text, and the most practically useful thing written on receiving feedback.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Leaving both observations to the end of placement.

✗  Asking for general feedback and getting reassurance.

✗  Being observed only on your strongest activity.

✗  Defending in the room instead of listening.

✗  Leaving your section of the form blank — the single most common outstanding item.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You have been observed the minimum number of times.

▸  GRADE 4
     You named a focus in advance, completed your section on the day, and acted on the feedback.

▸  GRADE 5
     You chose to be observed on something you found difficult, and you can show a specific change in practice that followed.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Arranging it
     [Ask once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Habit]
     Booking both early rather than scrambling in the final fortnight.
     How you build it: Book both in the first month. Diary them.

     ·  Arrange both observations early
          you have it when: Booked in the first month
          [Handbook §6.2]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Choosing the focus
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Habit]
     Asking to be watched on the thing you find hard.
     How you build it: Name it explicitly when you ask. Rapport, feedback, a difficult consultation.

     ·  Request a focus you find hard
          you have it when: Not administration, which is easiest
          [CORU SoP 4.5]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Receiving it
     [Ongoing  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Practice]
     Taking critical feedback without defending, then acting on it.
     How you build it: Write it down verbatim before responding. Respond next session.

     ·  Receive critical feedback without defending
          you have it when: You listened
          [CORU SoP 4.3 · PSI Code 3.5.2]

     ·  Act on the feedback and say so next time
          you have it when: Something changed
          [CORU SoP 4.3]

macro.name: Raise immediate concerns out of session
macro.text:
2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Some things cannot wait until Thursday. The handbook at section 6.2 requires you to raise crises immediately, and the reason trainees fail to is almost never that they did not recognise the concern — it is that they did not want to interrupt, or were not sure it was serious enough. The cost of interrupting your supervisor unnecessarily is two minutes of their time. The cost of not interrupting them is potentially a child's safety and your registration. These are not comparable.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What counts as immediate
     A child protection or welfare concern under Children First. A disclosure of harm. A child indicating intent to harm themselves or another. An injury you observed. A situation where you believe a child is unsafe. Something you did that you think may have been an error with consequences. A parent or school response that has escalated beyond what you can manage. Anything where waiting three days would change the outcome.

▸  Deciding in the moment
     The test is simple and deliberately low: if you are asking yourself whether this is serious enough to interrupt someone, it is. Trainees systematically under-call, not over-call. Make the call.

▸  The sequence
     Stop the activity. Do not question the child further — that is not your role and it can compromise a later process. Write down what was said or observed, verbatim where possible, with the time. Contact your supervisor the same day. Follow the school's Designated Liaison Person route. This does not replace your own duty: if you are a mandated person (confirm your status with UCD), a report must reach Tusla as soon as practicable — jointly with the DLP or by you (Children First Act 2015). Record who you told, when, and what was agreed. Then write your own record of what you did. Know your service's protocol and the DLP's name for each school before you need them, not on the day.

▸  Acting when you cannot reach your supervisor
     The contract should say who covers. If it does not and you cannot reach anyone, the DLP route in the school still exists and Children First still binds you. You do not get to wait because the person you wanted to call did not answer. Record every attempt to make contact.

▸  Afterwards
     Bring it to the next formal session even though it is resolved, and write a dilemma entry in Appendix 8. A managed disclosure is significant evidence for Ethical Practice and for this competency — you managed one at Grange on 22/05/2026, and that day should be written up as evidence rather than left as a line in the day log.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Children First: National Guidance for the Protection and Welfare of Children (DCEDIY, current edition), and your NEPS service's own protocol.

▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 6.2.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 3.3.4, 1.2.5 and 1.3.14 — on acting where serious harm is possible, and the limits of confidentiality.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 1.12 and 3.10.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Waiting for the next scheduled session.

✗  Continuing the assessment after a disclosure.

✗  Questioning the child to find out more.

✗  Recording it only in your own notes and telling no one that day.

✗  Not knowing the DLP's name for the school you are in today.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You know that immediate concerns must be raised immediately.

▸  GRADE 4
     You can state what counts, and you have the protocol and the DLP route to hand.

▸  GRADE 5
     You have followed the sequence in a live situation, recorded it properly, and written it up as a dilemma entry afterwards.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing what counts
     [1 hour, week one  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Crisis, client welfare concern, ethical dilemma — the handbook names all three.
     How you build it: Read §6.2. Ask your supervisor what else counts here.

     ·  Know what counts as immediate here

macro.name: Contribute to peer and group supervision
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 4.5
     Understand the importance of and be able to seek professional development, supervision, feedback and peer review opportunities in order to continuously improve practice

▸  CORU 5.8
     Know the basic principles of effective teaching and learning, mentoring and supervision

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Peer supervision gives you something one-to-one cannot: the range of what other trainees are encountering, and evidence that your difficulties are ordinary. It is also where you practise presenting a case to people who are not obliged to be kind about it, which is the skill that later becomes multi-disciplinary team working. CORU 5.8 covers mentoring and supervision; CORU 4.5 covers seeking peer review.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Turning up as the whole of the skill, mostly
     Peer supervision is the first thing dropped when a placement gets busy, and it is usually dropped by everyone at once, after which it quietly stops existing. Attendance is most of the contribution.

▸  Presenting a case properly
     Two hours of preparation for a presentation is right. Structure it: the referral question, what you did, the formulation and the framework behind it, where you are stuck, and the specific question you want the group to answer. Bring the stuck part, not the resolved part. A case you have already solved wastes everyone's time including yours.

▸  Contributing to other people's cases
     The useful contribution is a question, not a suggestion. 'What did the child say about it?' and 'what would make you wrong?' open a case up. 'Have you tried X?' closes it down and usually reveals you were not listening. Notice when a group is converging too fast on one explanation and say so.

▸  Confidentiality in a group
     Cases are anonymised — no names, no school names, no detail that identifies. Establish this explicitly at the first session rather than assuming it. PSI 1.2.4 and 1.2.5 apply to peer discussion exactly as they apply anywhere else, and a group of trainees is not a private space.

▸  Recording it
     Peer and group supervision counts toward the supervision requirement and toward CORU 4.5. Log it in Appendix 8 with date, format and what was discussed. Trainees routinely fail to record it and then cannot evidence it.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Accreditation Standards (2022), 3.3.9.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 4.5 and 5.8.

▸  Proctor, B. (2008). Group supervision: A guide to creative practice (2nd ed.). Sage.

▸  Hawkins, P., & McMahon, A. (2020). Supervision in the helping professions — the chapters on group supervision.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Attending irregularly, which ends the group.

✗  Presenting a case you have already resolved.

✗  Offering solutions instead of questions.

✗  Insufficient anonymisation.

✗  Not logging it, so it cannot be evidenced.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You attend peer supervision.

▸  GRADE 4
     You have presented a case with a clear question, and you contribute to others.

▸  GRADE 5
     Your contributions open cases up rather than closing them, you notice group process, and the sessions are logged and tagged.

macro.name: Complete Appendix 6 before and after
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 4.3
     Be able to evaluate and reflect critically on own professional practice to identify learning and development needs; select appropriate learning activities to achieve professional development goals; and integrate new knowledge and skills into professional practice

▸  CORU 4.5
     Understand the importance of and be able to seek professional development, supervision, feedback and peer review opportunities in order to continuously improve practice

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Appendix 6 is one document doing two jobs — the self-evaluation you complete before and after the placement, and the end-of-year reflective essay. The before-and-after structure is the point: the comparison is the evidence of development, and it only works if the first rating was honest. A trainee who rates themselves high at the start has nothing to show at the end.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Rating honestly at the start
     The temptation is to rate high because a low rating feels like an admission. It is the opposite: rating yourself accurately at the start is what makes the end-point credible, and supervisors read an inflated first rating as poor self-awareness, which is itself assessed. If you have never administered a WISC-V, the rating is low. That is what Year 1 means.

▸  A caution about the scale
     The handbook describes the range as running from 'unsatisfactory or not meeting minimal requirements' to 'highly satisfactory or far exceeding minimal requirements', and refers to 'a 1 or 2'. It does not explicitly set out a five-point scale. If you are unsure how many points the scale has, ask rather than assume — and use the handbook's own wording in anything you write.

▸  Setting targets that can be evidenced
     A target is useless unless you can tell whether you met it. 'Improve at formulation' cannot be evidenced. 'Apply a named framework explicitly in four reports, and record the rejected hypothesis in each' can. Write targets so that the end-of-placement comparison writes itself. Your eight development areas from the 4 August review are the obvious source.

▸  Comparing properly at the end
     Put the two ratings side by side and account for each change, including the ones that did not move. A competency that stayed the same is not a failure if you can say why — 'I had no opportunity to work at organisational level this placement, so this rating is unchanged and it is a target for Cavan' is a strong entry. An unexplained identical rating looks like you did not engage.

▸  Timing
     The before version is written before the placement, not retrospectively. If you are completing it for Cavan, complete it in week one and date it. A retrospective self-evaluation is visibly retrospective and forfeits the comparison entirely.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 4.5a and Appendix 6. Read the actual wording of the rating descriptors rather than relying on a summary.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 4.3.

▸  Boud, D., Keogh, R., & Walker, D. (1985). Reflection: Turning experience into learning. Kogan Page.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Rating high at the start.

✗  Writing the 'before' version afterwards.

✗  Targets that cannot be evidenced.

✗  Not accounting for competencies that did not move.

✗  Assuming a five-point scale and writing as though the handbook specifies one.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Both versions are completed.

▸  GRADE 4
     The first rating is honest, targets are specific and evidenceable, and the comparison accounts for each change.

▸  GRADE 5
     Targets are drawn from identified development areas, unchanged ratings are explained with a reason and a forward plan, and the document reads as a genuine account rather than a form.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Rating honestly

     How you build it: Do it before day one and date it. Retrospective ratings measure nothing.

          [Handbook §4.5a]

     ·  Rate honestly, including low
          you have it when: An honest low start shows trajectory
          [CORU SoP 4.3 · PSI Code 4.1.3]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Setting targets

     How you build it: Write them as things you will do, not things you will be.

     ·  Name two or three priority targets
          you have it when: Specific and achievable
          [CORU SoP 4.3]

     ·  Carry the targets into the next Placement Plan
          you have it when: They appear in Appendix 1
          [Handbook Appendix 1]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Comparing

     How you build it: Do the After without looking at the Before first. Then compare.

     ·  Rate again at the end and compare
          you have it when: Movement is visible
          [Handbook §4.5a]

macro.name: Write the reflective learning essay
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 4.5
     Understand the importance of and be able to seek professional development, supervision, feedback and peer review opportunities in order to continuously improve practice

▸  CORU 5.44
     Be able to critically reflect on the 'self' and the ongoing impact of one's own culture, values, experiences, beliefs and biases on their professional/therapeutic practice — utilising supervision to assist in the reflective process — and use such reflection to inform practice

▸  CORU 5.45
     Be able to recognise personal emotional responses and the impact of trauma, as identified through professional/therapeutic practice and supervision, and use appropriate tools to develop effective self-care to maintain professional functioning

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.3.9
     Act to minimise the impact of research activities on participants' personality or their mental or physical integrity.

▸  PSI 4.1.1
     Engage in self-care activities which help to avoid conditions (for example, burnout, addictions) which could result in impaired judgement and interfere with their ability to benefit and not harm others.

▸  PSI 4.1.2
     Seek emotional support and/or supervision from colleagues when feeling stressed or vulnerable due to professional dilemmas.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
The reflective essay is where the portfolio either becomes a coherent account of a year or stays a pile of forms. It is also the place trainees most often write about what happened rather than what changed in them. CORU 5.44 asks you to reflect critically on the 'self' and the impact of your own culture, values, experiences, beliefs and biases — using supervision to assist the process. CORU 5.45 asks you to recognise personal emotional responses and the impact of trauma and develop effective self-care. Those two standards are the essay's actual brief.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What it must cover
     Read section 4.5b before you start and list its requirements. Then note that Appendix 6 does two jobs — the self-evaluation and this essay — so check whether you are writing one document or two. Get that wrong and you will write the wrong thing well.

▸  Writing about difficulty without writing a confession
     The essay needs real difficulty in it, because an account with no difficulty is not credible. But the unit of analysis is your practice, not your private life. The shape that works: here is what happened, here is what I noticed in myself, here is what I did about it, here is how my practice differs now. You are not required to disclose anything about yourself that you do not wish to, and you should not feel obliged to; what is required is that the reflection is honest about the practice.

▸  Showing change rather than asserting it
     'I have developed in confidence' is an assertion. 'In February I administered the WISC-V from a script and could not deviate from it. On 21/04 I administered it independently for the first time, and by June I was adapting administration for a child working through an interpreter and recording the adaptation and its effect on interpretation.' That is change, and it is evidenced by dated entries you already hold.

▸  The ten-minute weekly habit
     Write one paragraph a week, dated, about the thing you noticed. In June you will have thirty-odd paragraphs and the essay will be an editing task. Without it, the essay is written from memory in a week and reads that way. Your Log's 'how it developed the skill' column is exactly this habit, which is why it is worth filling in rather than skipping.

▸  Using supervision as source material
     CORU 5.44 specifies using supervision to assist the reflective process. Quote your own supervision records — a dilemma entry, a piece of feedback you initially resisted, a question your supervisor asked that changed how you saw a case. This also demonstrates that your Appendix 8 records are real rather than reconstructed.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  UCD Professional Placement Handbook, section 4.5b and Appendix 6.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 5.44 and 5.45 — full text on the Reference sheet.

▸  Schön, D. A. (1983). The reflective practitioner. Basic Books. — reflection-in-action versus reflection-on-action, which is the distinction the essay rewards.

▸  Gibbs, G. (1988). Learning by doing: A guide to teaching and learning methods. Oxford Polytechnic. — the reflective cycle, useful as a scaffold if you are stuck.

▸  Bolton, G., & Delderfield, R. (2018). Reflective practice: Writing and professional development (5th ed.). Sage.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Describing what happened rather than what changed.

✗  Asserting development instead of evidencing it with dated examples.

✗  Writing it from memory in the final week.

✗  Avoiding all difficulty, which makes it read as a performance.

✗  Over-disclosing personal material — the unit of analysis is your practice.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     The essay describes the placement and what you learned.

▸  GRADE 4
     It shows change with dated, specific examples, and engages honestly with difficulty.

▸  GRADE 5
     It draws on supervision records, names how your own values and assumptions shaped your practice, and identifies what you would do differently — with a forward plan that connects to the next placement.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Knowing what it must cover
     [1 hour, once  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Study]
     Placement, college sessions and independent study — all three strands, plus challenges.
     How you build it: Read §4.5b. It says challenges explicitly.

     ·  Cover placement, college sessions and independent study
          you have it when: All three strands
          [Handbook §4.5b]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Writing about difficulty
     [Ongoing  ·  Ongoing all year  ·  Habit]
     Naming what was hard and what it cost, without performing distress.
     How you build it: Write the difficult paragraph fir

macro.name: Search and critically appraise evidence
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.3
     Know, understand and critically appraise the principles and applications of scientific enquiry, including the evaluation of treatment/intervention efficacy, the research process and evidence-informed practice

▸  CORU 5.41
     Be able to critically analyse, appraise and evaluate psychological and other relevant contemporary research to inform evidence-based practice

▸  CORU 5.43
     Apply research ethics when planning, undertaking and reporting on research with service users and relevant others in the context of professional practice

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 3.1.2
     Monitor and evaluate the effect of their professional activities, record their findings and, if appropriate, communicate new knowledge to others in the field.

▸  PSI 4.2.2
     Take due care to avoid misrepresentation, exaggeration, distortion or errors in reporting assessment results, research findings or service effectiveness, and act quickly to correct any such error.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
Every recommendation you write is an empirical claim about what will help. If you cannot find and appraise the evidence, you are recommending from habit. CORU 5.41 requires you to critically analyse, appraise and evaluate research to inform practice — on placement, not only in the thesis.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  Searching properly in twenty minutes
     Start with the syntheses: Cochrane, Campbell Collaboration, the EEF Toolkit, What Works Clearinghouse. Then PsycINFO or ERIC with a structured question — population, intervention, comparison, outcome. Use the UCD library proxy so you get full text. Google Scholar is for chasing a known paper, not for searching.

▸  Appraising quickly
     Design first: what kind of question is this and what design answers it? Then sample — who were they and are they like your child? Then comparison — against what? Then effect size, not just significance. Then who funded it and who developed the programme. Five questions, five minutes, and you will reject most of what you find.

▸  Effect sizes as the practical currency
     Roughly: 0.2 small, 0.5 moderate, 0.8 large, though context matters and educational interventions rarely exceed 0.4. An intervention with a statistically significant effect of 0.1 is not worth a school's term. Knowing this stops you recommending things that technically work and practically do not.

▸  Recognising weak evidence that looks strong
     Single studies by the programme developer. Pre-post designs with no control. Testimonial evidence on a commercial site. Very small samples with large claims. Outcomes measured by instruments the developer also created. All of these are common in the intervention material schools are sold.

▸  Keeping what you find
     A simple note per topic — question, what you searched, what you found, what you concluded. You will be asked the same questions repeatedly across a career, and the second search should be faster than the first.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Petticrew, M., & Roberts, H. (2006). Systematic reviews in the social sciences. Blackwell.

▸  EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit — effect sizes with cost and evidence-strength ratings.

▸  Cochrane Library.

▸  CASP appraisal checklists — one per study design, free and quick.

▸  Hattie, J. (2009). Visible learning. Routledge — useful for effect-size intuition, read with its methodological critiques in mind.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  Starting with Google rather than a synthesis.

✗  Reading the abstract and stopping.

✗  Treating statistical significance as practical importance.

✗  Not noticing the developer authored the evaluation.

✗  Searching the same question twice because you kept no note.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     You can find relevant research.

▸  GRADE 4
     You search syntheses first, appraise design, sample, comparison and effect size, and reject weak evidence.

▸  GRADE 5
     You can say how confident the evidence lets you be, and you keep a reusable record of what you searched and concluded.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Searching properly
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]
     Using a database, building a search string, recording what you did.
     How you build it: One PsycINFO session with the UCD library. One hour, permanently useful.

     ·  Frame an answerable question from a real referral
          you have it when: Specific enough to search
          [CORU SoP 5.42]

     ·  Search a database rather than a search engine
          you have it when: PsycINFO, ERIC, not Google
          [CORU SoP 5.41]

     ·  Record the search terms and databases used
          you have it when: Reproducible
          [CORU SoP 5.43]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Appraising
     [4–5 hours to learn  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     Judging a study's quality rather than accepting its abstract.
     How you build it: Use the CASP checklist on five papers. It is free.

     ·  Appraise quality rather than accepting the first result
          you have it when: You judged the study, not the abstract
          [CORU SoP 5.41 · 5.3]

▸  BLOCK 3 · Judging transfer
     [Habit  ·  Weeks 7–12  ·  Habit]
     Asking whether this evidence applies to this child in this context.
     How you build it: One sentence per recommendation: why this applies here.

          you have it when: Transferability considered
          [CORU SoP 5.4]

     ·  Log the search as an Appendix 5 research entry

          [Handbook Appendix 5]

macro.name: Cite evidence for recommendations
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 5.4
     Demonstrate skills in evidence-informed practice, including translation of theory, concepts and methods to clinical/professional practice

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.4.1
     Maintain and develop their professional competence.

▸  PSI 3.1.2
     Monitor and evaluate the effect of their professional activities, record their findings and, if appropriate, communicate new knowledge to others in the field.

▸  PSI 4.2.2
     Take due care to avoid misrepresentation, exaggeration, distortion or errors in reporting assessment results, research findings or service effectiveness, and act quickly to correct any such error.

▸  PSI 4.2.6
     Not suppress disconfirming evidence of their findings and views, and acknowledge alternative hypotheses and explanations.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
A cited recommendation is a different object from an uncited one. It tells the reader the claim is not your opinion, it lets them check, and it is one of the specific features that moves a report from a 3 to a 5. PSI 4.2.6 also requires you not to suppress disconfirming evidence — which means citing honestly, including where the evidence is mixed.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  What to cite and what not to
     Cite the intervention recommendation, the framework you used, and any claim about what typically works. Do not cite the test manual for every score or pad the reference list. Two or three well-chosen citations in a school report is right; fifteen is a literature review nobody asked for.

▸  Citing at the right level
     In a report for a school, cite the synthesis rather than the single trial: 'systematic reviews of structured phonics instruction report consistent benefits for children with decoding difficulties (Snowling & Hulme, 2011)' is more useful and more honest than a single study.

▸  Stating the strength of the evidence
     'There is strong evidence for X' and 'evidence for Y is mixed, and it is recommended here because of [case-specific reason]' are both legitimate. The second is more impressive than pretending certainty, and PSI 4.2.2 requires you not to exaggerate effectiveness.

▸  Handling the intervention with no evidence base
     Sometimes the right thing for this child has no trial behind it. Say so, give the reasoning, and specify how it will be evaluated. That is evidence-informed practice — CORU 5.4 asks for the translation of theory and concepts to practice, not only the citation of trials.

▸  Format
     APA 7th. Get it right; it is the convention your reports and your thesis both use, and sloppy referencing reads as sloppy thinking to an examiner.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 4.2.2 and 4.2.6 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 5.4 and 5.41 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  APA (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association (7th ed.).

▸  EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit — a citable synthesis source for school reports.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  No citations at all.

✗  Fifteen citations in a school report.

✗  Citing a single trial as though it settles the question.

✗  Implying certainty the evidence does not support.

✗  Inconsistent APA formatting.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Your recommendations are reasonable and defensible.

▸  GRADE 4
     Key recommendations are cited at synthesis level and formatted correctly.

▸  GRADE 5
     You state the strength of the evidence including where it is mixed, and you justify and plan evaluation for recommendations with no trial base.

8 · BLOCKS AND MICRO-SKILLS WITH PASS TESTS
▸  BLOCK 1 · Building a reusable base
     [4 hours, once  ·  Weeks 3–6  ·  Study]
     A running reference list of the twenty sources you use most.
     How you build it: Build it once. Four hours. It improves every report for three years.

     ·  Attach a source to every substantial recommendation
          you have it when: There is a reference list
          [CORU SoP 5.4]

     ·  Cite current sources rather than the familiar ones
          you have it when: Recency checked
          [PSI Code 2.4.1]

▸  BLOCK 2 · Citing correctly
     [2 hours, once  ·  Weeks 1–2  ·  Study]

     How you build it: One reference-management tool set up once.

          you have it when: Formatting is correct

macro.name: State how a recommendation would be evaluated
macro.text:
1 · CORU — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  CORU 3.8
     Be able to evaluate intervention plans using appropriate tools and recognised performance/outcome measures along with service user responses; revise the plans as necessary and where appropriate in conjunction with the service user

▸  CORU 3.9
     Understand the need to monitor, evaluate and/or audit the quality of practice and be able to critically evaluate one's own practice against evidence-based standards and implement improvements based on the findings

2 · PSI — NUMBER AND FOCUS
▸  PSI 2.3.2
     Direct their interventions towards clear objectives, and do not persist after the objectives have been met or if it is apparent they cannot be met.

▸  PSI 3.1.2
     Monitor and evaluate the effect of their professional activities, record their findings and, if appropriate, communicate new knowledge to others in the field.

3 · WHY THIS MATTERS
A recommendation with no evaluation is a guess that nobody ever checks. CORU 3.8 requires evaluating intervention plans using recognised outcome measures and revising them; 3.9 requires monitoring and auditing your own practice; PSI 3.1.2 requires monitoring and recording the effect of what you do. This is also the smallest, cheapest route into the practice-based research your review named — one line per recommendation.

4 · TEACHING — HOW YOU BUILD IT
▸  The one line
     'Review at the end of term 2 using [measure], with progress monitored fortnightly by the SET.' What, when, how, who. Five minutes per report and it is the most commonly omitted element in trainee work.

▸  Choosing a measure that can move
     Match the measure to the timescale. Curriculum-based measurement, words correct per minute, frequency counts and brief validated rating scales move within a term. Standardised annual tests do not, and choosing one guarantees an inconclusive review.

▸  Baseline before you start
     Without a baseline you cannot attribute change to anything. Take it before the intervention begins, even if it is three data points over a week.

▸  Single-case design as the realistic option
     You will rarely have a control group. A simple AB design with a stable baseline, or a multiple-baseline across two children or two settings, is achievable within a placement and is a legitimate practice-based research output. This is how the Research competency gets evidenced without a separate project.

▸  Closing the loop
     Go back and look. A recommendation reviewed and revised is worth more in the portfolio than three delivered and abandoned, and it is the only way you learn whether your formulations are any good.

5 · WHAT TO READ
▸  CORU Standards of Proficiency 3.8, 3.9 and 5.37 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025), 3.1.2 — full text on this sheet, Part B.

▸  Kazdin, A. E. (2011). Single-case research designs (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press.

▸  Deno, S. L. (2003). Developments in curriculum-based measurement. Journal of Special Education, 37(3).

▸  Barlow, D. H., Nock, M. K., & Hersen, M. (2009). Single case experimental designs (3rd ed.). Pearson.

6 · COMMON ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
✗  No evaluation line at all.

✗  A measure that cannot move within the timescale.

✗  No baseline.

✗  Assigning review to nobody in particular.

✗  Never going back to look.

7 · RUBRIC — GRADE 3, 4, 5
▸  GRADE 3
     Your recommendations are clear.

▸  GRADE 4
     Each carries a measure, a review point and a named person.

▸  GRADE 5
     You take baselines, use a defensible single-case design, return to review, and revise the recommendation on the evidence.

micro.name: Choose a method suited to the referral question
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Method choice is the single decision that determines whether an observation produces evidence or description. Momentary time sampling estimates how much of the time something occurs; partial interval over-estimates it; event recording counts discrete acts; narrative gives sequence but no prevalence. Choose the wrong one and the number you report answers a question nobody asked.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which method your supervisor picked, and listen for whether they say why. Most experienced practitioners choose automatically and have not articulated it in years.

WRITE DOWN — the referral question in the referrer's words, the method used, the interval length, and whether a comparison peer was recorded.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'you used momentary sampling rather than partial interval — what would partial interval have given you instead?' That one question is where the learning is.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the operational definition on paper before you go in, and drafting the recording grid.

THEY HOLD — the final method decision and the interval length.

WHY THAT SPLIT — definition-writing is where trainees learn fastest and where errors are cheapest to correct. Method choice carries the consequence, so it stays with them one more round.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you choose the method, state your reasoning aloud before the observation, and your supervisor either agrees or redirects.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether your reasoning starts from the referral question or from the method you are most comfortable with. Defaulting to narrative because it feels safe is the commonest trainee pattern.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before we go in, what will you do if the behaviour does not occur at all in twenty minutes?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — choose the method, run it, and bring both the grid and your reasoning to supervision.

PASS TEST — you can say why this method and what another would have missed.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the operational definition sheet, the completed grid, and one line in the report naming the method and why. Log against Assessment and against the referral area.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you report a percentage without naming the sampling method, so nobody including you can tell what the number means.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a colleague, without notes, the difference between momentary, partial-interval, whole-interval and event recording, and give a worked case where each is the right choice.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the target behaviour does not occur during the observation window: report the zero, note the conditions, and say what you would change about the timing rather than reporting nothing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Choosing narrative recording because it requires no preparation, then discovering you cannot answer 'how often' — which is what the school actually asked.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds directly into 'Run a timed interval or event sample accurately' and into the formulation, where the observation is evidence for or against a named hypothesis.
