micro.name: Run a timed interval or event sample accurately
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
An inconsistent interval makes every number meaningless, and an illegible grid means the data exists only in your memory — which is exactly what observation is supposed to replace. Hintze (2005) is clear that psychometric quality in direct observation rests on procedural consistency, not on the observer's experience.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what they use to time it. A silent vibrating timer or a watch, never a phone they might touch. Watch how they mark the grid without looking away for long.

WRITE DOWN — the interval length, how they signalled it to themselves, and how many intervals they ran.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you keep counting when something interesting happens that is not what you are counting?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — recording the comparison peer on alternating intervals while your supervisor records the target child.

THEY HOLD — the target child's record, which is the one that matters.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you get the timing discipline and the grid practice with the lower-stakes row, and at the end you have two records to compare for agreement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you record both rows while your supervisor records independently alongside you.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — drift. Trainees lengthen intervals when the behaviour is not occurring and shorten them when it is, without noticing.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — comparing the two grids afterwards and calculating agreement. Below about 80% and something in your procedure needs fixing before the next one.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — run the full observation and bring the raw grid, not a summary.

PASS TEST — intervals are consistent and the record is legible to someone else. Hand it to a colleague: can they read it?

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the raw grid itself, retained with the case file. Not a typed-up version.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a grid only you can read, or one where you filled gaps afterwards from memory. Both invalidate the data and neither is visible in the final report, which is why it matters that you know.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can set up an inter-observer agreement check for a colleague and calculate it, and you can explain why 80% is the usual floor.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you lose the interval count mid-observation: mark the break, restart the count, and report the two segments separately rather than pretending it was continuous.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Reconstructing missed intervals from memory afterwards. It feels like tidying and it is fabrication.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every quantitative statement you make about frequency, and into the single-case designs in the Research competency.

micro.name: Record antecedent, behaviour and consequence separately
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
ABC recording is the foundation of a functional account — what happened before, what the child did, what followed. The discipline is keeping them separate, because the moment you write the cause into the description you have stopped observing and started concluding, and nobody reading the report can tell where that happened.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words the behaviour column. Listen for verbs and absence of adjectives.

WRITE DOWN — three of their entries verbatim, and note what is in the antecedent column that you would have put in the behaviour column.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide where the antecedent ends and the behaviour begins?' There is no clean rule and hearing them think about it is the point.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the antecedent and consequence columns.

THEY HOLD — the behaviour column, which is the hardest to keep clean.

WHY THAT SPLIT — antecedent and consequence are more concrete and give you the rhythm of the recording without the interpretive trap.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — all three columns, with your supervisor reading your entries during the observation rather than afterwards.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — inference leaking into the behaviour column. 'Got frustrated' is inference. 'Pushed the book away and put his head down' is behaviour.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — pointing at an entry and asking 'what did you actually see that made you write that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — full ABC record, brought raw to supervision.

PASS TEST — you have not written the cause into the description. Read every behaviour entry and ask: could a camera have recorded this?

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the ABC record, and in the report a clearly separated 'what was observed' and 'what this suggests'. PSI 1.2.8 requires opinion to be labelled as opinion.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report where a parent cannot tell which parts were seen and which were concluded. This is the failure most likely to cause harm, because it is invisible and it gets repeated by others for years.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can take a colleague's ABC record and show them, entry by entry, where inference crept in, without it landing as criticism.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the antecedent was not visible: record 'not observed' rather than inferring backwards from the behaviour. An honest gap is worth more than a plausible guess.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'became frustrated', 'was attention-seeking' or 'refused' in the behaviour column. All three are conclusions wearing the clothes of description.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into functional behaviour assessment, into the Interactive Factors Framework at the behavioural level, and into every report where you must separate what you saw from what you think.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Agree with the teacher how you will be introduced
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
How you are introduced determines what you get to see. Introduced as 'someone here to watch Jack', you will observe a child who knows he is being watched and a class that knows it too. Introduced as 'someone here to see how the class works', you observe something much closer to ordinary. It is also an honesty question — the child is told something, and what they are told must be true.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the exact words your supervisor agrees with the teacher, and the exact words the teacher then uses with the class.

WRITE DOWN — both, verbatim. The gap between them is often large and is worth noticing.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you say if a child asks you directly why you are there?' Have a sentence ready before you need one.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the wording and bringing it to the teacher.

THEY HOLD — the conversation itself, and any negotiation if the teacher wants to do it differently.

WHY THAT SPLIT — drafting the words is where you learn; handling a teacher who wants to announce you is a relationship skill that needs one more round of watching.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you agree the wording with the teacher yourself, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you accept the teacher's first suggestion out of politeness. Teachers routinely offer to introduce you as being there for a named child, and agreeing costs you the observation.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'could we say it a bit more broadly, so the class settles faster?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — agree it in advance, by phone or email if the visit is short.

PASS TEST — the child is told something true and is not singled out.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — one line in the observation write-up recording how you were introduced. It belongs in the limitations, because it affects what you saw.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — arriving with nothing agreed, the teacher improvising, and a child knowing they are the reason you are there.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague three forms of words that are true, broad and age-appropriate, and explain why each works.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you have been introduced badly: note it in the write-up as a limitation, and consider whether a second observation is needed before you draw conclusions.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Letting the teacher say 'this is the psychologist, she's here to see Jack' because correcting it in the doorway felt rude.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Observe without altering what you came to see', and into the ethical thread about what children are told about assessment.

micro.name: Position yourself to see without becoming the focus
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Where you sit changes what happens. Sitting at the child's table makes you part of the lesson; standing at the front makes you an inspector; sitting in the flow of the room means children route past you all morning. The aim is line of sight to what you came to see, out of the traffic, and low enough not to loom.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor sits, and how long the class takes to stop noticing them.

WRITE DOWN — the seat chosen, the sight line, and roughly how many minutes until the room settled.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how did you choose that spot?' and 'what would you have done if the only free seat was beside him?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — arriving early and identifying two possible positions before the class comes in.

THEY HOLD — the final choice, and any negotiation with the teacher about moving a chair.

WHY THAT SPLIT — scouting the room teaches you what to look for; the social cost of asking to move furniture is theirs to carry one more time.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you choose and take the position yourself.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you adjust. Trainees sit where they first sat even when the activity moves to the carpet and they can no longer see the child.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a quiet nod toward a better spot when the lesson changes shape.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — position, settle, and move if the activity changes.

PASS TEST — the class settles within a few minutes.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — note in the write-up where you sat and how long settling took. It belongs in the limitations.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — twenty minutes of data collected from a class that was performing for a visitor, reported as though it were ordinary.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can walk a colleague through reading a room on arrival: sight lines, traffic, where the adults stand, where the activity will move to.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when there is genuinely nowhere neutral: stay standing at the back, shorten the observation, and report the constraint rather than the ideal.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Sitting down in the first free chair and staying there for the whole lesson.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Observe without altering what you came to see' and into the reactivity limitation you write in every observation report.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor sits, and how long the class takes to stop noticing them.

micro.name: Observe without altering what you came to see
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Reactivity is real and it is not eliminable — your presence changes the room. The competence is not in removing the effect but in minimising it, noticing it, and reporting it. An observation that does not mention reactivity is an observation whose author has not thought about it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does when a child talks to them, or shows them work, or asks what they are writing. There is a technique to redirecting warmly without engaging.

WRITE DOWN — their exact words to a child who approaches them.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide when to answer a child and when to deflect?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the settling minute at the start, and noting in the margin any moment your presence visibly changed something.

THEY HOLD — managing any child who approaches.

WHY THAT SPLIT — noticing reactivity is an observational skill in itself and can be practised safely; handling an approaching child is a live judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you manage your own presence, including children who approach you.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you engage. Trainees answer children because not answering feels unkind, and then wonder why the child performed for them.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — taking over a conversation you have been drawn into.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — full observation, managing your own presence throughout.

PASS TEST — you can name how your presence may have changed things.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a specific reactivity sentence in the write-up. Not 'observations may be affected by the presence of an observer' but 'Jack looked toward me on four occasions in the first five minutes and not thereafter'.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a generic limitations sentence that could be pasted into any report, which tells the reader you did not actually attend to this.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain reactivity with the evidence behind it, and give a colleague three concrete ways to reduce it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child performs throughout: report it as the finding it is, and arrange a second observation before concluding anything about typical behaviour.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing the generic reactivity disclaimer instead of the specific one. The generic version is a template; the specific version is evidence you were paying attention.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the limitations section of every report, and into Ethical Practice — a child has the right to know what you are doing in their room.

micro.name: Note peer interaction and social positioning
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Where a child sits in the peer group is invisible in any test and is often the thing the referral is really about. It is also the domain where adult report is least reliable — teachers see the classroom, and most of what matters happens at break.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor counts. Initiations versus responses, who approaches whom, how long interactions last, whether the child is included or tolerated.

WRITE DOWN — the categories they used, and any child they recorded as a comparison.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell being alone from being excluded?' They are different and the distinction matters enormously.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — recording initiations and responses for the target child.

THEY HOLD — the interpretive layer: whether what you are seeing is withdrawal, rejection, or preference.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the counting is learnable now; reading the social meaning takes more observations than you have yet had.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you record and offer a reading, your supervisor tests it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you distinguish solitary-by-choice from solitary-by-exclusion. Getting this wrong produces recommendations that make things worse.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what did you see that tells you he wanted to join in?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — yard and classroom, with a comparison peer.

PASS TEST — you can describe where this child sits in the peer group.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — counts plus a described pattern in the report, and the child's own account from a pupil interview alongside it.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'appeared to have few friends', which is an impression, unquantified and unfalsifiable.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a colleague how to observe social positioning without pathologising solitude, and can name the risk of reading adult social norms onto a child.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the yard observation contradicts the teacher's account: treat it as information about setting, not about who is right.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording that a child played alone and concluding social difficulty, without establishing whether they wanted to join in.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into referral areas 4.1 Friendships and social skills, into autism screening decisions, and into any group intervention you design.

micro.name: Note adult interaction and prompting patterns
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
How much adult support a child receives is usually unrecorded and frequently the most important variable in the room. A child who appears to manage independent work may be receiving a prompt every ninety seconds. Nobody has counted, and the Student Support File will not say.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor records prompts, and whether they distinguish verbal, gestural, physical and proximity prompts.

WRITE DOWN — the prompt categories used and the count over a defined period.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you raise this with a teacher without it sounding like criticism?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — counting prompts to the target child.

THEY HOLD — the comparison — how much prompting other children receive, which is what makes the count meaningful.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you get the recording discipline; the comparative judgement comes next.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — both counts, and you offer a reading of the support level.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you notice support that suppresses independence. An SNA completing the task is not the child learning it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what would have happened if nobody had said anything for two minutes?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — counts, comparison, and a characterisation of the support level.

PASS TEST — you have characterised the level of support given.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the count in the report, described neutrally. 'Received eleven verbal prompts during a twenty-minute independent writing task; the comparison pupil received two.'

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — reporting the child's output without reporting the support that produced it, so the school concludes he can do more than he can.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a colleague how to feed this back to a school as a description rather than a judgement, and how to build prompt-fading into a recommendation.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the prompting is clearly excessive: describe, do not evaluate, and offer one change rather than five.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Describing what the child produced without describing the adult input that produced it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into adaptive functioning interpretation, into over-support in GLD, and into every recommendation about SNA deployment.

micro.name: Observe the same child across two settings
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A single observation is a single day in a single room. Hintze (2005) found temporal stability in direct observation is modest, and cross-setting comparison is the cheapest correction available. It is also diagnostic in its own right — DSM-5-TR requires ADHD symptoms in two or more settings, and a child who manages in one setting and not another has a setting problem, not only a child problem.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor decides which second setting to use, and what they hold constant between the two.

WRITE DOWN — both settings, the time of day, the activity type, and what changed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what would you conclude if the two observations disagreed completely?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the second observation, using the definitions and grid from the first.

THEY HOLD — the first observation and the comparison between them.

WHY THAT SPLIT — repeating a method you did not design teaches you why procedural consistency matters.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — both observations, and you draft the comparison.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you held the method constant. Changing interval length between the two makes them uncomparable and it is easily done.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the morning one was thirty-second intervals and the afternoon one was a minute — what does that do to the comparison?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — two settings, same method, written comparison.

PASS TEST — you have not generalised from one lesson.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — both grids, and a comparison paragraph in the report naming what differed between the settings.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report that describes a child's behaviour as though it were a stable trait, based on one twenty-minute window.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain temporal stability and setting specificity to a colleague and cite the evidence.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you only get one observation: report it as one, name the limitation specifically, and say what a second would have told you.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating one observation as characteristic, which is the most common single error in trainee observation work.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into ADHD assessment (the two-setting criterion), into school-versus-home discrepancies, and into the systemic question of whether the difficulty is the child or the setting.

micro.name: Keep description and interpretation separate
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
This is the discipline that makes a report defensible. PSI 1.2.8 requires opinion to be clearly labelled as opinion and conjecture avoided. A report where the reader cannot tell what was seen from what was concluded is a report that cannot be checked — and it will be quoted back for years by people who never saw the distinction.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor's report is structured. Where does 'what was observed' end and 'what this suggests' begin?

WRITE DOWN — two sentences from each section, and note the verbs. Description uses concrete verbs; interpretation uses 'suggests', 'may indicate', 'is consistent with'.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide what goes in the findings and what goes in the formulation?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the description section only.

THEY HOLD — the interpretation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing clean description is harder than it sounds and it is where the habit is built.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you draft both, clearly separated, and your supervisor marks anywhere they have merged.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — adjectives in the description section, and unhedged claims in the interpretation section.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — circling a word and asking 'did you see that, or did you think it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — full write-up with the two clearly separated.

PASS TEST — opinion is labelled as opinion throughout.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report itself. This is the single clearest piece of Ethical Practice evidence available to you.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'he was frustrated and disengaged' in a findings section. Neither is observable; both will be repeated as fact by the next reader.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can take a colleague's draft and show them where the two have merged, with the PSI clause to hand.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a school pushes for a conclusion the observation does not support: state what you observed, state what it is and is not consistent with, and decline to go further.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing internal states — frustrated, anxious, unmotivated — in a section that claims to describe what was seen.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every report you will ever write, into PSI 1.2.8, and into the case-notes skill under Working with Others.

micro.name: Link what you observed to the referral question
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
An observation that describes everything answers nothing. The referral asked something specific, and the observation exists to move that question forward — to support a hypothesis, weaken it, or show that the question was wrong. A thorough description that does not connect back is work nobody can use.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor's observation section ends. There should be a sentence that returns to the referral.

WRITE DOWN — the referral question and the closing sentence of the observation section. Put them side by side.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what did this observation rule out?' Ruling out is as valuable as ruling in and trainees rarely write it.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the closing paragraph that links back.

THEY HOLD — the rest of the section.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the linking paragraph is the highest-value sentence in the section and deserves concentrated practice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you name the hypothesis before the observation and state afterwards whether it was supported.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you named a hypothesis at all. Observing without one produces description by default.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before we go in — what would you expect to see if the referral hypothesis is right, and what would you see if it is wrong?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — hypothesis named in advance, observation run, link written.

PASS TEST — the observation answers something rather than describing everything.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report section, plus a supervision note recording the hypothesis you rejected. A recorded rejected hypothesis is strong Formulation evidence.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — three paragraphs of detail and no statement of what it means for the question asked.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a colleague how to set a testable hypothesis before an observation, and explain why that changes what gets recorded.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the observation disconfirms the referral entirely: go back to the referrer and renegotiate the question rather than assessing on regardless.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Answering a question nobody asked, thoroughly.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds directly into Formulation, and into the Monsen problem-analysis cycle where observation is hypothesis-testing rather than data-gathering.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Prepare the history schedule and read it beforehand
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Reading a schedule for the first time in front of a parent costs you the two things the interview depends on: your attention, which is on the page instead of on them, and their confidence, because a psychologist reading questions aloud looks like a form-filler. Preparation is also what lets you depart from the schedule when something matters, because you know what you can skip.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor holds the schedule at all. Experienced practitioners usually work from three or four headings and a prompt list.

WRITE DOWN — their headings, and the order they took them in. Note where they departed from that order and what triggered it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you skip when time is short?' The answer tells you what they consider load-bearing.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing the schedule and bringing a printed prompt list to the session.

THEY HOLD — the interview itself.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you learn the content without carrying the live judgement about pace and sensitivity.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you interview from your own prepared prompt list with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you look down. Every glance at the page is a second not spent reading the parent's face, and parents notice.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — picking up a thread you dropped because you were finding your place.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — prepared, and working from headings rather than questions.

PASS TEST — you are not reading questions for the first time in the room.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your prompt list, annotated with what you added or dropped. That annotated sheet is good supervision material.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a complete schedule and a thin interview, because you got through the questions without hearing the answers.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can hand a colleague a prompt list and explain why it is ordered that way, and which items are non-negotiable.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the parent takes the interview somewhere unplanned and important: follow them, and come back to the schedule afterwards rather than steering them back mid-sentence.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Bringing the full schedule and working through it in order regardless of what the parent has already told you.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every other micro-skill in this block, and into the Carr four-factor formulation the interview is gathering for.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor holds the schedule at all. Experienced practitioners usually work from three or four headings and a prompt list.

micro.name: Take pregnancy, birth and neonatal history
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Most of the time this rules things out, which is exactly why it is asked. Occasionally it explains a great deal — prematurity, hypoxia, neonatal intensive care, significant jaundice. The skill is asking without implying that you are looking for a cause in the parent, because that is how it lands if it is asked badly.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the framing sentence your supervisor uses before this section. There is almost always one, and it does the work of making the questions ordinary.

WRITE DOWN — that sentence verbatim, and the order of the questions.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a parent gets upset at this part?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the factual items: gestation, birth weight, type of delivery, time in hospital.

THEY HOLD — anything that touches on complications or loss.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the factual items are safe to practise on and give you the rhythm; the sensitive ones need a model first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — the whole section, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — your framing sentence, and whether you slow down when the parent does.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — taking over if a parent becomes distressed, so you can watch how it is handled rather than handling it.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — framed, asked, and recorded proportionately.

PASS TEST — you asked about complications without alarming.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a brief factual paragraph in the report. Brief unless indicated — a long birth history in a report about reading comprehension tells the reader you were filling in a form.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — either skipping it because it felt intrusive, or recording it in detail that serves no purpose and follows the family for years.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague two or three framing sentences and explain what each is doing.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent discloses a pregnancy loss or a traumatic birth: acknowledge, do not probe, move on when they are ready, and note only what is relevant.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking the questions with no framing, so the parent hears 'what did you do wrong?'

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the biological level of the Interactive Factors Framework and into Carr's predisposing factors.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Take early motor, speech and language milestones
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Sequence is the output, not precision. Whether a child walked at 13 or 15 months rarely matters; whether language was delayed before behaviour became difficult matters enormously. Parental recall of milestone ages is moderately accurate at best and improves markedly with anchoring, so how you ask determines whether you get data or a guess.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — anchoring. Listen for 'was she walking at her first birthday?' rather than 'what age did she walk?'

WRITE DOWN — three anchored questions verbatim.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a parent says they cannot remember?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the motor milestones, which are the most memorable and the easiest to anchor.

THEY HOLD — speech and language, where the distinctions matter more and are harder to elicit.

WHY THAT SPLIT — motor gives you anchoring practice on items parents recall well.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — all three domains, anchored.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you accept a bare age. 'About one' recorded as '12 months' is a guess promoted to data.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'was that before or after Christmas?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — anchored throughout, with the child health record book on the table if the parent brought it.

PASS TEST — you have dates or approximations, not impressions.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — milestones recorded with their anchor, and any estimate flagged as an estimate.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a milestone table of round numbers, none of which the parent actually said.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain telescoping and recall bias to a colleague and demonstrate three anchoring techniques.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when recall genuinely fails: record 'not recalled', ask whether another caregiver would know, and do not fill the gap.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking for ages and writing down the answers as though they were records.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the primary-versus-secondary distinction in formulation, and into DLD, autism and GLD questions where onset is diagnostic.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Ask about sleep, feeding and self-care
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
These three are skipped more than any others and they change the whole picture. A child sleeping six hours will present as inattentive, dysregulated and slow on every measure you administer. Feeding and self-care give you the adaptive functioning that a cognitive assessment cannot, and both are the first things to go when a child is under strain.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor asks at all, and how they phrase it so it does not sound like a judgement on routines.

WRITE DOWN — the exact questions, and what they did with the answers.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you raise sleep without it sounding like you are blaming bedtime?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — sleep, which is the most concrete: what time down, how long to settle, night waking, what time up.

THEY HOLD — self-care and feeding, which can touch on sensory difficulties and on family circumstances.

WHY THAT SPLIT — sleep is answerable in numbers and gives you the section without the sensitivity.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — all three, and you follow up rather than accepting 'fine'.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you ask the follow-up. 'Fine' is the most common answer and almost never the whole answer.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what time does he actually fall asleep, rather than go to bed?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — asked, followed up, and used.

PASS TEST — you asked. These are the three most commonly skipped.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — if sleep is short, it goes in the report and it goes in the interpretation. A cognitive profile obtained from a chronically tired child carries a limitation and you must say so.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — administering a full battery to a child sleeping five hours a night and interpreting the processing speed index as though it were stable.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a colleague why these three belong in every history and give the follow-up question for each.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when sleep is severely disrupted: name it, recommend GP review, and state plainly that assessment findings should be revisited if it changes.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Accepting 'fine' and moving on.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into ADHD differential, into adaptive functioning, and into the limitations section of any cognitive assessment.

micro.name: Ask about play and peer relationships
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Play and friendship are where social communication shows itself, and parents see a side of it school never does — birthday parties, cousins, the estate, who calls for them. It is also the domain where a language-focused history misses the point entirely: a child can have adequate language and no reciprocal friendships.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor asks about quality or only about quantity. 'Does she have friends?' gets a yes. 'Who does she play with at the weekend, and what do they do?' gets an account.

WRITE DOWN — the questions that produced detail.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell a child who is content alone from one who wants in and cannot?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the factual mapping: who, where, how often, what activity.

THEY HOLD — the interpretive questions about reciprocity and preference.

WHY THAT SPLIT — mapping is concrete; reading social meaning from a parent's account takes practice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — mapping and quality, and you offer a reading afterwards.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you asked about pretend and imaginative play for younger children. It is diagnostically important and routinely omitted.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'does she play the same game every time, or does it change?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — asked, mapped, and used in the formulation.

PASS TEST — you asked about friendships, not only language.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the parent's account of peer relationships in the report, alongside the school's and the child's own. Where the three differ, say so.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a history that covers language thoroughly and social reciprocity not at all, then a report that cannot address the referral.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague a set of questions that distinguish reciprocal friendship from parallel proximity.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent reports friendships the school does not see: treat the discrepancy as information about setting and about what 'friend' means to that family.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking 'does she have friends?' and recording 'yes'.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into autism screening decisions, into referral area 4.1, and into any group intervention you design.

micro.name: Ask about medical history and medication
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Medication names alone tell you almost nothing. What matters is what it is for, what effect it has, whether it is taken consistently, and whether a dose changed recently — because a dose change three weeks ago can account for the entire referral. Hearing and vision belong here too, and a hearing history during the infant classes is the single highest-yield question most trainees skip.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor follows a medication name. Listen for 'and what difference does it make?'

WRITE DOWN — the medical domains covered, in order, and any question you would not have thought to ask.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which medical question has changed a formulation for you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the list: conditions, hospital admissions, current medication, vision and hearing checks.

THEY HOLD — the follow-up on effect and on adherence.

WHY THAT SPLIT — listing is straightforward; asking a parent whether medication is actually being given requires care.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — list and follow-up.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you ask the glue ear question specifically. 'Any ear infections?' gets 'a few'. 'Grommets, or fluid behind the eardrum, in junior or senior infants?' gets an answer that can reframe a literacy case.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'when was her hearing last checked, and by whom?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — covered, followed up, and used.

PASS TEST — you asked what effect it has, not just its name.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — medical factors in the report only where relevant, and any hearing or vision uncertainty flagged as something to rule out before conclusions are drawn.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — assessing literacy behind an unchecked hearing history, then identifying a specific learning difficulty that may not be one.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a colleague why conductive hearing loss during phonics instruction is a competing explanation, and how to ask about it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a medical factor emerges mid-assessment: pause, recommend the medical review first, and say in the report that findings should be revisited afterwards.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording a medication name with no indication of what it is for or whether it is working.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every differential, into the biological level of the Interactive Factors Framework, and into the limitations section.

micro.name: Open with the parent's own concern, in their words
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The parent's own framing is data you can get in the first two minutes and cannot get later, because once you have asked twenty structured questions they will answer in your terms. Their words also go in the report, and a report that quotes a parent accurately is one they trust.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the opening. Listen for an open question and then silence.

WRITE DOWN — the opening question verbatim, and how long your supervisor waited before speaking again.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how long do you let a silence run at the start?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the opening question and the first two minutes.

THEY HOLD — everything after.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the opening is short, high-value, and safe to practise.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you open and hold the silence.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you fill it. Trainees ask a second question within four seconds and lose the account.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a small gesture to wait.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — open, wait, record verbatim.

PASS TEST — the parent speaks first and you have not led them.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the parent's own words quoted in the report's referral or background section. Their phrasing, not yours.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a background section written entirely in professional language, where the parent's actual concern never appears.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the opening two minutes shape everything after, and demonstrate tolerating silence.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent cannot start: offer a narrower opening ('tell me about a normal school morning') rather than a list of questions.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Opening with the referral form rather than the parent.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into COMOIRA, where the parent's construction is one of the accounts you formulate across, and into the feedback session later.

micro.name: Ask about strengths before difficulties
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Asking about strengths first is not a courtesy. It changes what you get: a parent who has described what their child is good at answers the difficult questions differently, and you end up with a fuller account. It also gives you the material for the feedback session, where a strength you can evidence is worth far more than one you invented on the spot.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where in the sequence strengths come, and whether the parent's answer changes the tone of what follows.

WRITE DOWN — the question used, and at least two strengths the parent named.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a parent cannot name a strength?' It happens, and it is significant.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the strengths question and recording the answers.

THEY HOLD — the transition into difficulties.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the question is easy; the transition needs judgement about pace.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — strengths, then transition.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether the strengths make it into your notes at all, or whether you nod and move on to what you came for.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can you give me an example of that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — asked early, recorded, and used later.

PASS TEST — strengths appear in your notes at all.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — strengths in the report, specific and evidenced, and used in the feedback session.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report that opens with a strengths sentence so generic it could describe any child, which parents read as padding.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why strengths-first changes the quality of a history, and what a parent's inability to name one tells you.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent names none: note it without comment, and return to it later in the session.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking, nodding, and not writing any of it down.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the feedback session, into protective factors in Carr's model, and into the child's own sense of themselves.

micro.name: Follow up an ambiguous answer rather than accepting it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Ambiguous answers are where the information is. 'A few', 'sometimes', 'not really', 'he's grand' are all doors, and walking past them is the commonest way a history ends up thin. The difficulty is that noticing has to happen in real time, while you are also listening, writing and thinking about the next question.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — every time your supervisor follows up. Note what triggered it.

WRITE DOWN — three ambiguous answers and the follow-up used for each.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you notice, in the moment, that an answer was vague?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listening for ambiguity and flagging it in the margin for your supervisor to pick up.

THEY HOLD — the follow-up itself.

WHY THAT SPLIT — noticing and asking are separate skills. Practise noticing first; it is the harder one.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you notice and follow up.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — how many you miss. Expect to miss several and expect that to be the most useful feedback of the session.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — circling back to something you passed.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — noticing and following up throughout.

PASS TEST — you noticed the ambiguity in the moment.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the specific answers your follow-up produced. Those are usually the sentences that end up mattering in the report.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a complete history in which nothing is specific enough to act on.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague the four or five stock vague answers and a follow-up for each.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent is vague because they do not want to answer: notice the difference between not knowing and not saying, and do not press the second.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Accepting 'he's grand' about sleep, friendships or homework.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT

micro.name: Ask about family structure and significant events sensitively
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Family context sits at the environmental level of every framework you use, and significant events — bereavement, separation, migration, illness, a parent's own difficulty — frequently explain timing that nothing else does. PSI 1.2.1 restricts you to information germane to the purpose, so the skill is getting what you need without taking more than you need.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor opens this section and how they handle hesitation.

WRITE DOWN — the framing, and one moment where the parent hesitated and what happened next.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide when to stop asking?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the structural questions: who lives at home, siblings and ages, who else is involved in care.

THEY HOLD — significant events and anything the parent flags as difficult.

WHY THAT SPLIT — structure is neutral; events are not.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — both, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you press where a parent hesitates. Hesitation is a boundary and pressing it costs you the relationship.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'we can come back to that another time if you would rather.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — asked proportionately and recorded minimally.

PASS TEST — you did not press where the parent hesitated.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — only what is germane. A family history recorded in detail that serves no purpose is a data protection problem as well as a trust problem.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — either avoiding the section entirely, so the formulation has no environmental level, or recording family detail that will be read by people it was never meant for.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the germane-information principle with the clause, and demonstrate asking a sensitive question and then leaving it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when something raises a safeguarding concern: stop the interview, follow the protocol, supervisor the same day.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording everything a parent discloses because they disclosed it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the environmental level of the Interactive Factors Framework and into Carr's precipitating and perpetuating factors.

micro.name: Manage emotional disclosure without losing the thread
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents cry in these interviews. It is ordinary and it is not a failure of the interview. The skill is responding as a person, without either brushing past it or abandoning the task — and knowing where your competence ends, because if the disclosure is about the parent's own mental health you are listening and signposting, not treating.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does in the first ten seconds. Usually they stop writing and say something short.

WRITE DOWN — their exact words, and how they returned to the interview afterwards.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know when to stop the interview altogether?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the factual sections, and you observe when emotion arises.

THEY HOLD — the response.

WHY THAT SPLIT — this is the one micro-skill where watching twice is better than doing once.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you respond, with your supervisor there to take over.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you keep writing. Continuing to take notes while a parent cries is the single most damaging thing you can do here.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — taking the conversation if it moves beyond your competence.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — stop, acknowledge, wait, return when they are ready.

PASS TEST — you held both the person and the task.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — nothing about the parent's own distress unless it is germane. Record that the interview was paused if that affected what you gathered.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — either carrying on as though nothing happened, or abandoning the interview entirely and having to ask again another day.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague two or three responses that acknowledge without opening something you cannot hold, and explain where the competence boundary sits.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent discloses their own mental health difficulty or a risk to themselves: listen, do not take it on, signpost specifically, and tell your supervisor the same day.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Continuing to write.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the counselling-skills micro-skills under Intervention, and into the competence-boundary skill under Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Close with what happens next and when
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
An unclear ending is the commonest complaint parents make about psychology services. They leave not knowing what happens, wait, hear nothing, and conclude they have been forgotten. Two minutes at the end prevents it, and it is also where you set expectations you can actually meet.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the closing. There should be a summary, a next step, a timeline and an invitation to ask.

WRITE DOWN — all four, and what your supervisor promised.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you say when you do not know how long it will take?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the summary and the invitation to ask questions.

THEY HOLD — the timeline, because it is a promise.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you should not be promising timelines you do not control.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — all four, having checked the realistic timeline with your supervisor beforehand.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you over-promise to make the parent feel better. It always costs more later than the discomfort it saves now.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — adjusting a timeline you have just given.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — summary, next step, timeline, questions.

PASS TEST — the parent leaves knowing the timeline.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a note of what you told them, so you can check you delivered it. If the timeline slips, contact them before they contact you.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'I'll be in touch', which means nothing and is heard as nothing.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague a four-part close and explain why each part is there.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the timeline slips: contact the family before the date you gave them, with a new date.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Ending with 'I'll be in touch.'

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the feedback session, and into the record-keeping skill under Working with Others.

micro.name: Place the child on the Continuum of Support
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Continuum is how Irish schools allocate. Recommending School Support Plus for a child already at that level, or Classroom Support for one who has exhausted it, tells the school you did not ask. Knowing the stage first also tells you what has already failed, which is the most useful thing in the room.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor asks. Usually not 'what stage is he at?' but 'what does the support look like at the moment?'

WRITE DOWN — the question and the documentation the school produced in response.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when the school does not know what stage a child is at?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking to see the Student Support File and reading it before the meeting.

THEY HOLD — the conversation about what the stage should be.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading the file is where you learn what these documents actually contain, which is often less than their name suggests.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you establish the stage and test it against what you have read.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you accept the school's label without evidence. A child described as being at School Support with no plan and no review is not at School Support.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'could we look at the plan for that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — stage established, evidenced, and carried into the recommendation.

PASS TEST — you know the stage before you recommend anything.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the current stage named in the report, with the recommended stage and why it differs.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a recommendation the school cannot act on because it names no level, or names one already in place.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the three levels, what documentation each generates, and how schools actually use them.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the documented stage and the observed support do not match: describe both, without blame, and make that the finding.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Accepting the label without asking to see the plan.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every recommendation, and into the systemic mapping skill under Systemic Change.

micro.name: Ask what has already been tried and what happened
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Recommending something the school tried last year and abandoned is the fastest way to lose credibility. What was tried, how it was delivered, for how long, and what happened is also diagnostic: an intervention delivered at the wrong intensity that then 'did not work' tells you about delivery, not about the child.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor asks about intensity, not just about what was tried.

WRITE DOWN — the follow-up questions. 'How often?' and 'for how long?' are the ones that matter.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you ask this without it sounding like an audit?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the list of what has been tried.

THEY HOLD — the follow-up on intensity and fidelity.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the list is straightforward; asking a teacher how faithfully something was delivered needs care.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — list and follow-up.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you establish intensity. 'We did some phonics' could mean daily for a term or twice in October.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'roughly how many times a week was that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — asked, quantified, and used.

PASS TEST — you did not assume nothing had been tried.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — what has been tried, at what intensity, and with what result, in the report. Then recommendations that account for it.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — recommending structured phonics to a school that has delivered it daily for a year.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why fidelity and intensity are the variables that usually explain a failed intervention.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when nothing has been tried: say so neutrally, and make the first recommendation the thing that should already have happened.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording that something was tried without establishing how much of it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into intervention recommendations and into the Continuum level you name.

micro.name: Ask about presentation across the timetable
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A difficulty that appears in every lesson and one that appears only in English are different findings requiring different responses. Variation by subject points to task demand; variation by teacher points to relationship or approach; variation by time of day points to fatigue, medication or sleep.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor maps it. Often they ask for the timetable itself.

WRITE DOWN — how the variation was elicited.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what does it mean when it only happens with one teacher?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — mapping the timetable and marking where the difficulty appears.

THEY HOLD — the interpretation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the mapping is mechanical and gives you the raw pattern.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — map and offer a reading.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you ask about time of day. It is skipped, and it is often the answer.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is it different before or after lunch?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — mapped, read, and used.

PASS TEST — you know whether it varies by subject or teacher.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the pattern described in the report. If it varies, the recommendation must address the variation rather than the average.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report describing a child as generally inattentive when the pattern was confined to written work.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what subject, teacher and time-of-day variation each point to.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when it varies by teacher: handle it as a systemic finding, described neutrally, never as a judgement on a named person.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking whether the difficulty occurs, rather than when it does and does not.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the ADHD two-setting criterion, into functional accounts, and into observation planning.

micro.name: Clarify the referral question with the person who raised it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Referral forms are written quickly and often by someone other than the person who is worried. The question on the form and the question in the referrer's head are frequently different, and everything you do afterwards is aimed at whichever one you accepted.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor reads the form back and asks if it is right.

WRITE DOWN — the form's wording and the wording that emerged in conversation.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how often does the real question differ from the form?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the form back and asking what has changed since it was written.

THEY HOLD — renegotiating the question if it has changed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading back is safe; renegotiating scope is a professional judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — clarify and state the question back in one sentence.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you get agreement on a single sentence. Multiple questions mean multiple assessments and you need to say so.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that sounds like two questions — which is the urgent one?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — clarified, agreed, recorded.

PASS TEST — you can state it in one sentence they recognise.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the agreed question at the top of the report, in the referrer's words.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a thorough assessment that answers the form and not the worry.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the referral question governs everything and demonstrate narrowing a vague one.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the question is outside your remit: say so early, and route it rather than assessing around it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Accepting the form as the question.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every subsequent decision, and into the 'link what you observed to the referral question' micro-skill.

micro.name: Request standardised attainment data in advance
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Schools hold group test data you can have for the asking, and reading it beforehand changes what you assess. It can also answer the question on its own, which saves the child an assessment they did not need.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor asks for and how far ahead.

WRITE DOWN — the data requested and what it changed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when the school says it is not available?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — making the request and chasing it.

THEY HOLD — deciding what to do with it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — requesting is administrative; interpreting group test data against an individual profile is not.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — request, read, and let it shape your plan.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you read it before choosing subtests, or after.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'given those Drumcondra scores, do you still need the full battery?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — requested in advance, read, used.

PASS TEST — you read it before meeting the child.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the school data in the report as one source, with its limitations. Group tests are screens, not individual assessments.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — administering an attainment battery that tells you what the school's own data already said.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what group standardised tests can and cannot tell you, and how to weigh them against individual data.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the school data contradicts your own: report both, and treat the discrepancy as information about conditions.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Arriving with no school data and assessing from scratch.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into subtest selection, into the synthesis skill, and into not over-assessing children.

micro.name: Ask who knows this child best in the school
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The person you are given is not always the person who knows. The SET who takes the child three times a week, the SNA who is with them at lunch, or last year's teacher may hold more than the class teacher. Asking takes one sentence and routinely changes the quality of what you get.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor asks, and who they end up speaking to.

WRITE DOWN — the question and the answer.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how often is it not the class teacher?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking the question.

THEY HOLD — arranging the additional conversation if one is needed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — asking is free; adding a meeting to a school's day is a negotiation.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — ask and follow it up.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you act on the answer or note it and carry on with who you had.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'could we get five minutes with her before I go?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — asked, acted on, recorded.

PASS TEST — you found the right informant, not the available one.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the sources named in the report. Who you spoke to is part of the method.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report built on the account of an adult who has known the child six weeks.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why SNAs are the most under-consulted informants in Irish schools and how to include them appropriately.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the best informant is not available: name the limitation in the report.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Interviewing whoever was free.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into source weighting in the synthesis skill, and into Working with Others.

micro.name: Agree what feedback the school gets and when
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Unset expectations produce two failures: a school that chases you, and a school that assumes it is getting something you never intended to give. Agreeing it at the start also forces you to decide what the school actually needs, which is usually less than the full report and sooner.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when in the meeting your supervisor sets this, and how specific they are.

WRITE DOWN — what was promised and by when.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you promise when you do not know the timeline?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — recording what is agreed.

THEY HOLD — making the commitment.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you should not be promising service timelines you do not control.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — agree it, having checked the realistic timeline first.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — over-promising. Schools remember the date.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — adjusting a date you have just given.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — agreed, recorded, delivered.

PASS TEST — expectations set at the start.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a note of what was agreed, and the follow-up email confirming it within 24 hours.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a school that expected verbal feedback in a fortnight and got a report in June.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why interim verbal feedback usually serves a school better than waiting for the report.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the timeline slips: contact the school before the date you gave, with a new one.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving it unsaid.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into record keeping and into the school relationship that determines whether recommendations happen.

micro.name: Understand what each index measures
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
You will be asked to explain an index to a parent within minutes of giving them a number, and a definition read off a manual does not survive that conversation. Understanding also governs whether you interpret correctly: Verbal Comprehension is acquired knowledge and reasoning with language, not vocabulary size; Fluid Reasoning is novel problem-solving, which is why it is less affected by schooling.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor describes an index to a parent. Note that they almost never use the index name first.

WRITE DOWN — one plain-language description for each of the five indices, in their words.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which index do parents most often misunderstand?' It is usually Processing Speed, which people hear as intelligence rather than as speed of simple visual work.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing your own plain-language version of each index and testing it on your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — the parent conversation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — rehearsing the explanation with someone who can correct it costs nothing; getting it wrong in front of a parent costs a lot.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you explain the indices in a feedback session with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you describe what the index measures or what the score means. Those are different and trainees merge them.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — offering a second framing when the parent's face says it did not land.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain all five without notes, adapted to the listener.

PASS TEST — you can explain VCI and FRI to a parent in plain words.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report's findings section, written so a parent and a teacher can each use it. CORU 5.27 requires reports suitable for the intended audience.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report that names indices and reports numbers, leaving the reader to guess what was measured.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the CHC theory the indices rest on, and say what changed between WISC-IV and WISC-V and why.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent asks 'so which one is the real IQ?': explain that the FSIQ is a composite, that it can be misleading where scatter is wide, and why you are reporting GAI if you are.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Explaining an index by restating its name in longer words.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every interpretive statement you make, into the feedback session, and into the EDUC42700 technical analysis.

micro.name: Know what the test does not measure
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The limitations sentence is what separates a competent report from a technically correct one. WISC-V does not measure attainment, motivation, creativity, adaptive functioning, executive function in daily life, or anything about a child assessed in a second language without heavy caution. Saying so protects the child from a number being over-read for years.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the limitations section in your supervisor's reports. Note whether it is specific to the child or generic.

WRITE DOWN — two specific limitation sentences you could not have written yourself.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what has a WISC-V told you that turned out to be wrong?' Every experienced practitioner has one.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the limitations paragraph.

THEY HOLD — the interpretation it qualifies.

WHY THAT SPLIT — limitations are easier to write well than interpretation and they build the habit of hedging honestly.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you draft both and your supervisor marks where you have over-claimed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — generic limitations. 'All assessment has limitations' is a sentence that says nothing.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what specifically about this child makes this score less reliable?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — specific limitations tied to this child and this administration.

PASS TEST — you can say what a WISC-V cannot tell you.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the limitations paragraph. Where English is an additional language, where the child was tired, where administration was adapted — all of it goes here.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report that presents a Full Scale IQ as a fact about the child rather than a measurement under conditions.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain measurement error, confidence intervals and the difference between a score and a construct to a colleague.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a school wants the number to justify a decision the assessment does not support: restate what it measured, restate what it did not, and decline to extend it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A generic limitations paragraph that could be pasted into any report.

micro.name: Apply start points correctly for age and ability
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A wrong start point invalidates the subtest and, if you do not notice, the index it sits in. Start points vary by subtest and by age, and several allow an adjusted start for a child you suspect has lower ability — which is a judgement you have to make before you have any data on them.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor checks the start point or knows it. Note any subtest where they adjusted it and why.

WRITE DOWN — the start rule for each subtest they administered.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when do you start below the age-appropriate point?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — checking the start points on the record form before the session and marking them.

THEY HOLD — the administration.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparation is where accuracy is built, and marking the form is a habit worth having from the first session.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you administer and apply start points yourself.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — hesitation. Looking up a start point mid-subtest tells the child something has gone wrong and costs you rapport.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a finger on the record form pointing at the right item.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — start points applied without reference to the manual during administration.

PASS TEST — you knew the rule without checking mid-session.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the completed protocol. An examiner re-scoring it should see correct start points throughout.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an invalid subtest discovered at scoring, when the child has gone home.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the logic of age-based start points and reverse rules together, since they are one system.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise mid-subtest that you started wrong: complete it, note it, and treat the subtest as invalid rather than salvaging it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Starting at the age-appropriate point for a child who clearly cannot access it, producing a floor effect and a distressed child.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into reverse and discontinue rules, and into the validity of every index.

micro.name: Apply reverse rules without hesitating
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Reverse rules exist so a child who fails at their age-appropriate start point gets credit for easier items they would have passed. Applied late or inconsistently, you underestimate the child. Applied with visible hesitation, you signal to the child that they have failed, which affects everything after.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moment a reverse is triggered. Watch your supervisor's face and hands: there should be no change.

WRITE DOWN — which subtests triggered a reverse and at what point.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you keep a child from noticing you have gone backwards?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — tracking the reverse rule on the form while your supervisor administers, and telling them when it triggers.

THEY HOLD — the administration and the child.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you learn the trigger points without having to manage the child at the same time.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you administer and reverse.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — hesitation, page-turning, and any change in your tone. All three tell the child something.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — nothing visible; they will raise it afterwards.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — reverse applied smoothly and correctly.

PASS TEST — hesitation is what the examiner watches for.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol showing correct reversal.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child who realises they are being given easier questions and disengages for the rest of the session.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why reverse rules exist and demonstrate reversing without a visible break.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child comments on it: answer honestly and lightly, and move on rather than explaining.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Turning back through the stimulus book visibly while the child watches.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into rapport maintenance and into the validity of the subtest.

micro.name: Apply discontinue rules correctly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Discontinue rules protect the child from a run of failure and protect the score from being inflated by lucky guesses. The temptation is to continue past discontinue because stopping feels unkind — and it is the kindest thing available, because the alternative is a child sitting through items they cannot do.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor closes a subtest at discontinue. There is usually a sentence that makes it feel like completion rather than failure.

WRITE DOWN — that sentence.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you ever continue past discontinue?' The answer should be no, and hearing why is useful.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — counting consecutive failures on the form and signalling discontinue.

THEY HOLD — closing the subtest with the child.

WHY THAT SPLIT — counting reliably while also managing a child is genuinely hard and splitting it makes both learnable.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — count and close.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you give one more item 'to end on a success'. It invalidates the subtest and it is very tempting.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a quiet signal to stop.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — discontinue applied exactly.

PASS TEST — you did not continue past discontinue to be kind.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol. A re-scorer should see the discontinue point clearly marked.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an invalid subtest, and a child who sat through six items they could not do.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why discontinue protects both the score and the child, and demonstrate a closing sentence that lands well.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child asks to keep trying: acknowledge the effort, close the subtest, and offer the next one as a fresh start.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
One more item, to finish on a right answer.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into scoring validity and into the child's experience of the session.
