micro.name: Query and prompt only where the manual permits
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Over-querying inflates scores and makes the assessment uncomparable to the norms. It is also the single most common trainee error, because it comes from wanting the child to do well. The manual specifies exactly which responses may be queried and with what wording; anything beyond that is help, not assessment.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — every query your supervisor makes, and check it against the manual afterwards.

WRITE DOWN — the queries used, verbatim.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you stop yourself helping when a child is nearly there?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — marking on the form every response that is queryable, while they administer.

THEY HOLD — the querying.

WHY THAT SPLIT — recognising a queryable response is a separate skill from delivering the query, and it is the one that prevents over-querying.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you query, within the manual.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — queries that are really prompts. 'Can you tell me more?' is permitted; 'are you sure?' and 'think about it again' are not.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a note to discuss afterwards rather than an interruption.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — queries within the manual, recorded with Q on the form.

PASS TEST — you did not over-query to help the child succeed.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol with Q marked. A re-scorer should be able to see every query you made.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a score that reflects your help rather than the child's ability, reported as though it were the child's.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why over-querying is a standardisation breach and demonstrate the permitted wording.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you over-queried: note it on the protocol, flag it in the limitations, and treat the affected score with caution.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Helping, because the child was nearly there and you wanted them to have it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into standardisation, into the limitations section, and into the honesty thread in Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Prepare and check the kit before the child arrives
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A missing block or a lost stopwatch mid-subtest costs you the subtest and the child's confidence in you. Kits get borrowed, pieces migrate, and the only reliable moment to discover it is before the child is in the room.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor checks, and what they check against.

WRITE DOWN — their checklist, or build one from what they touched.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what has gone missing on you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the full kit check and the record forms.

THEY HOLD — everything else.

WHY THAT SPLIT — this one is entirely yours from the start; there is no interpretive component.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — checked and laid out before the child arrives.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you check the stopwatch battery and have a spare pencil. Small, and they are what fail.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — handing you the thing you forgot.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — kit checked against a written list, every time.

PASS TEST — nothing is missing mid-subtest.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — nothing formal, but the absence of incidents is the evidence.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — stopping mid-Block Design to look for a block, and a child who now knows you are not in control of the situation.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague a kit checklist and explain what fails most often.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when something is genuinely missing: omit that subtest, record why, and do not improvise a substitute.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Assuming the kit is as you left it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every administration, and into the professionalism a school judges you on.

micro.name: Set up table and seating correctly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The child must see the stimulus book clearly and you must see the record form without the child seeing it. Sitting opposite creates a test-like confrontation and makes the stimulus book hard to angle; sitting beside makes timing awkward. Corner seating usually solves both.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor sits relative to the child, and how the record form is angled.

WRITE DOWN — the arrangement, including where the kit sits.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do in a room where you cannot get that arrangement?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — setting up the room before the session.

THEY HOLD — administering.

WHY THAT SPLIT — setup is fully learnable in one round.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you set up and administer from your own arrangement.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether the child can see your record form. Children read upside down better than adults expect.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — adjusting your form angle.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — set up so the child sees the stimulus and not the form.

PASS TEST — child sees the stimulus book, you see the record form.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — nothing formal; note in the write-up if the room forced a compromise.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child watching you write down whether they were right.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can describe three workable arrangements for different room types.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do in a bad room: prioritise the child's view of the stimulus, shield the form, and note the constraint.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking whatever table you are given without adjusting it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into rapport and into the validity of timed subtests.

micro.name: Read instructions verbatim
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The norms were built on those exact words. Paraphrasing changes the task, and it happens most under time pressure or when you think the child has not understood — which is exactly when standardisation matters most. If a child genuinely cannot access the instruction, that is a finding, not a problem to solve by rewording.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor reads or recites, and whether the wording matches the manual.

WRITE DOWN — any instruction where you would have been tempted to simplify.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a child clearly has not understood the instruction?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — following in the manual while they administer, marking any departure.

THEY HOLD — the administration.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you calibrate your ear to what verbatim actually sounds like.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you read verbatim with the manual open.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — paraphrasing when the child looks blank. It is almost involuntary.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — nothing in the moment; raised afterwards.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — verbatim throughout, repetition only where permitted.

PASS TEST — you did not paraphrase under time pressure.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol, and any permitted repetition noted.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a score obtained on a task you modified, reported against norms for a task you did not administer.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why verbatim administration is a validity requirement rather than a formality.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child cannot access an instruction: repeat where permitted, record the difficulty as a finding, and discuss in the limitations.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Simplifying the wording for a child who looked confused.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into standardisation, into the limitations, and into the language-difficulty findings a WISC-V can surface.

micro.name: Time accurately while managing engagement
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Several subtests are timed and the timing is part of the score. The difficulty is doing it while also watching the child, recording responses and managing behaviour. Timing that slips because you were settling a child produces a score that is not comparable to anything.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor holds the stopwatch and when they start it. The start point is defined and it is easy to be a second late.

WRITE DOWN — which subtests were timed and any moment timing competed with something else.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do if you have to stop the child mid-item?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the stopwatch, while your supervisor administers and records.

THEY HOLD — everything else.

WHY THAT SPLIT — timing alone is easy; timing plus recording plus managing is the actual skill, and it is built in layers.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — time, record and manage together.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether the watch stops when you look away. It is the most common slip and you will not notice it yourself.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — quietly noting a timing they will raise afterwards.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — accurate timing throughout.

PASS TEST — timing did not slip while you managed behaviour.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — completion times on the protocol, and bonus points calculated correctly where they apply.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — estimated times written in afterwards, which is fabrication however small it feels.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how bonus points work and why a second matters at the top of the range.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when timing is genuinely lost: record it as invalid rather than estimating.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing in a time you did not measure.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Processing Speed and Block Design validity, and into the honesty thread throughout.

micro.name: Record responses verbatim including errors
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Verbatim recording is what makes the protocol re-scoreable and what makes qualitative analysis possible afterwards. A child's wrong answer often tells you more than their right one — a Similarities response that is concrete rather than abstract is a finding you can only see if you wrote down what they said.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how much your supervisor writes. It is more than you expect.

WRITE DOWN — three verbatim responses they recorded that you would have summarised.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a child talks faster than you can write?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — recording verbatim on a subtest they administer.

THEY HOLD — the administration.

WHY THAT SPLIT — recording at speed is a motor skill and needs practice without the cognitive load of administering.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer and record verbatim together.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — summarising. 'Said something about animals' is not a record.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a note beside a response they will ask about later.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — verbatim throughout, including errors and self-corrections.

PASS TEST — another psychologist could re-score from your protocol.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol. This is the artefact your supervisor will actually check.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a protocol only you can interpret, which cannot be re-scored and cannot be defended.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a colleague how to abbreviate without losing the response, and how to use the error analysis afterwards.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you miss a response: mark it as not recorded rather than reconstructing it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording your judgement of the answer instead of the answer.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into scoring accuracy, into qualitative analysis, and into the EDUC42700 technical analysis.

micro.name: Use the record form correctly including Q and P
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The record form is the legal and professional record of the administration. Q marks a query, P marks a prompt, and both must be visible to anyone re-scoring. An incomplete form means an unverifiable score, and it is the first thing an examiner looks at.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the notation your supervisor uses, including anything beyond Q and P.

WRITE DOWN — their conventions.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you always write down that the form does not ask for?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — completing the form's administrative sections and the notation while they administer.

THEY HOLD — the administration.

WHY THAT SPLIT — form discipline is learnable separately and transfers directly.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer and complete the form fully.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — blanks. Every item needs a score, including zeros, and every query needs a Q.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — pointing at a blank.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — complete, legible, correctly notated.

PASS TEST — the form is complete and legible.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the form itself, retained per service protocol.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a form with gaps, where nobody can tell whether an item was failed or skipped.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can audit a colleague's protocol and explain what an examiner looks for.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find a gap at scoring: mark it as not administered and exclude it, rather than inferring a score.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving blanks where the answer was wrong.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into re-scoreability, into record-keeping under Working with Others, and into GDPR retention.

micro.name: Establish rapport before beginning
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Rapport is measurement validity, not manners. An anxious or wary child under-performs across every index, and you will then build a formulation on numbers that describe their state rather than their ability. Five minutes before subtest one is the cheapest investment in the whole assessment.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how long your supervisor spends before starting, and what they talk about.

WRITE DOWN — their opening, and roughly how many minutes passed before the first subtest.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know when a child is ready?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the opening conversation.

THEY HOLD — the transition into testing.

WHY THAT SPLIT — opening is low-risk and high-value practice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — opening and transition.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you start because the clock says so rather than because the child is settled.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — extending the conversation when you were about to begin.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — settled before subtest one.

PASS TEST — the child looks at ease before subtest one.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a behavioural observation note in the report describing how the child presented.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a full battery administered to an anxious child, interpreted as though anxiety were ability.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a colleague why rapport is a validity issue and cite it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child will not settle: stop, reschedule, and record why. A rescheduled assessment is better than an invalid one.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Starting on time rather than when the child is ready.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every score obtained, and into the rapport micro-skills under Working with Others.

micro.name: Explain what will happen in language the child understands
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A child who does not know what is happening is managing uncertainty instead of doing the task. They also have a right to know — PSI 1.4 covers assent, and assent requires understanding. Telling them that some items will be too hard for everyone is the single most useful sentence available to you.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the explanation, and specifically whether your supervisor says the tasks get harder for everyone.

WRITE DOWN — the explanation verbatim.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you adapt that for a five-year-old?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the explanation, in your own words, checked with your supervisor beforehand.

THEY HOLD — the rest.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the explanation is short, rehearsable, and consequential.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you explain and check understanding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you check. 'Does that make sense?' is not a check; asking the child to say it back is.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a simpler version offered.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explained, checked, adapted to age.

PASS TEST — the child could repeat it back roughly.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — note in the report that purpose and process were explained and assent obtained.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child who thinks they are in trouble, or who thinks this decides whether they are clever.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague three age-pitched versions and explain what each must contain.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child asks whether they passed: answer honestly at their level, and never give a score on the day.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Explaining it and not checking it landed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into assent under Ethical Practice, and into the child's experience of every future assessment.

micro.name: Notice fatigue, anxiety or disengagement
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Children rarely say they have had enough. They guess, they go quiet, they stop trying, they get faster and less accurate. Noticing before they tell you is what separates a valid profile from one that measures endurance, and the behavioural observations you record are often more useful to the school than the scores.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor notices and what they do about it. Watch for the moment they decide to offer a break.

WRITE DOWN — the signs they responded to.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what is the earliest sign you look for?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — recording behavioural observations throughout while they administer.

THEY HOLD — deciding what to do about them.

WHY THAT SPLIT — noticing is trainable on its own and is the harder half.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — notice and respond.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you push on to finish the battery. The pull to complete is strong, particularly when the school has given you one slot.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — suggesting a break you had not considered.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — noticed early, responded, recorded.

PASS TEST — you noticed before the child told you.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — behavioural observations in the report, with any effect on interpretation named.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a Processing Speed index obtained in the last fifteen minutes of a two-hour session, interpreted as stable.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can list the early signs and explain how each affects which index.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child is too tired to continue: stop, record what was completed, and reschedule.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Finishing the battery because the room is booked.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into behavioural observations, into the limitations, and into the wellbeing thread in Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Offer a break and record it at the time
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Breaks are permitted and they protect validity. Recording when and where the break fell matters because it affects interpretation — a break between Block Design and Coding tells a different story from a break mid-Coding. Recorded at the time it takes five seconds; reconstructed later it is a guess.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor offers a break so it is not read as a rescue.

WRITE DOWN — the wording and where on the protocol they noted it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you ever break mid-subtest?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — annotating the protocol when a break occurs.

THEY HOLD — the offer.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the annotation habit is worth building first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — offer and annotate.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you annotate at the time or intend to do it later.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a tap on the protocol.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — offered appropriately, annotated immediately.

PASS TEST — annotated on the protocol.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the annotation, and a mention in the report if it affected interpretation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — remembering at scoring that there was a break and not knowing where.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain when a break is and is not permitted and how to phrase the offer.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a break is needed mid-subtest: complete or abandon the subtest by the manual's rule, never pause it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Intending to write it down afterwards.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into interpretation and into the honesty of the protocol.

micro.name: Stop if the child indicates they want to
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
PSI 1.4.3 requires responsiveness to non-verbal indications of wanting to discontinue. A child who has gone silent and stopped trying has withdrawn assent whether or not they said so. Negotiating past that is a consent breach, and it is done routinely and unthinkingly because finishing feels important.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor responds to reluctance, and whether they ever negotiate.

WRITE DOWN — what they said and what happened.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell a wobble from a withdrawal?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — watching for indications and flagging them.

THEY HOLD — the decision.

WHY THAT SPLIT — this is a consent decision and needs modelling before you carry it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you notice and you stop.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — negotiation. 'Just two more and then we'll finish' is negotiation.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — ending the session themselves.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — stopped when indicated.

PASS TEST — you stopped rather than negotiated.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — record that the assessment was discontinued at the child's indication, and what was completed. This is strong Ethical Practice evidence and it is rare.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a complete protocol obtained from a child who wanted to leave, which is invalid data and a consent breach at once.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can cite the clause and explain why a partial assessment is worth more than a coerced complete one.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the school pushes for completion: explain the consent position, offer to reschedule, and do not resume.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
'Just two more.'

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds directly into consent and assent under Ethical Practice, PSI 1.4.3.

micro.name: Close so the child leaves feeling competent
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The child will be assessed again, possibly many times, and how this one ends shapes how they arrive at the next. It also matters in itself — they have just spent ninety minutes being asked things they could not answer, by design.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the closing. Note whether the praise is specific and true.

WRITE DOWN — the closing words, and what the child did as they left.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you say when a child asks how they did?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the closing.

THEY HOLD — anything the child asks about results.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the closing is safe; the results question needs a modelled answer.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close and handle the results question.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — generic praise, and any hint of a score. Never give a score on the day.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — supplying an answer you are searching for.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — specific, true, and clear about what happens next.

PASS TEST — how the child walks out.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a note of what you told the child about next steps, so the feedback session is consistent with it.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'you did great', which the child knows is not true, or a hint at a result which the parent then hears second-hand.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a colleague a closing that is honest, specific and does not disclose anything.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child is upset at the end: stay with it, be honest that some of it was hard, and tell them what happens next.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Generic praise, or letting slip how they did.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the feedback session, into future assessments of this child, and into Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Select subtests matched to the referral question
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
WIAT-III is modular and administering all of it wastes ninety minutes and tires the child. Selection is a reasoning task: which subtests could change your answer to the question asked? Anything that cannot is not neutral, because the child pays for it in fatigue.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which subtests your supervisor selects and whether they say why.

WRITE DOWN — the referral question and the subtests chosen beside it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what did you leave out, and what would it have told you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the selection and your reasoning before the session.

THEY HOLD — the final decision.

WHY THAT SPLIT — your draft gets corrected before it costs the child anything.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you select and justify.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — defaulting to a standard set regardless of the question.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what will Numerical Operations tell you about a reading referral?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — selected, justified, recorded.

PASS TEST — you can justify omitting what you omitted.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the selection and rationale in the report's method section.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a full battery, a tired child, and a report that could have been written from four subtests.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can map referral question types to subtest sets and explain each.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the question changes mid-assessment: add what is needed and record why, rather than continuing on the original plan.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Administering everything because it is all in the kit.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the child's experience, into the limitations, and into efficient practice under caseload pressure.

micro.name: Administer to standard
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The same standardisation logic as WISC-V applies, with one addition: Oral Reading Fluency requires marking errors live while timing, and it cannot be reconstructed afterwards. Written Expression has exact prompt wording and timing that trainees routinely improvise.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor marks Oral Reading Fluency errors while the child reads.

WRITE DOWN — their notation.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you keep up when a child reads fast?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — marking Oral Reading Fluency alongside them, comparing afterwards.

THEY HOLD — the administration.

WHY THAT SPLIT — parallel marking gives you an agreement check without risking the record.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer with them present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — Written Expression prompts, and whether timing holds.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a note to discuss afterwards.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — administered to standard throughout.

PASS TEST — errors would not change the composite.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol, with Oral Reading Fluency marked live.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an Oral Reading Fluency score reconstructed from memory, which is not a score.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can demonstrate live error marking and explain which subtests are most often administered incorrectly.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a timed subtest is disrupted: record it as invalid rather than adjusting the time.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Improvising the Written Expression prompt.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into scoring validity and into the literacy component analysis.

micro.name: Score the protocol the same day
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Scoring decays. Oral Reading Fluency and Written Expression in particular depend on what you saw, and a week later you are scoring your memory. Accumulated unscored protocols are also the commonest cause of the June backlog that makes everything else late.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when your supervisor scores. Often immediately, in the car.

WRITE DOWN — how long it took them.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what goes wrong when you leave it a week?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — scoring the objective subtests the same day.

THEY HOLD — the judgement-based ones.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you build the same-day habit on the easier half first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — score everything the same day, checked by them.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — Written Expression scoring drift. Trainees score generously against the rubric.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — re-scoring one item beside you.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — scored the same day, every time.

PASS TEST — scoring is not left to accumulate.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the scored protocol, dated.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — four unscored protocols in May and no memory of any of them.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why judgement-based subtests decay fastest and demonstrate the rubric.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when same-day scoring is impossible: write your behavioural and qualitative notes immediately even if the scoring waits.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving it until the report is due.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into workload management under Ethical Practice, and into report quality.

micro.name: Check every raw-to-scaled conversion
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A single transcription error moves a composite and the error is invisible in the final report. It will be quoted for years. Checking twice costs five minutes and is the cheapest quality control available to you.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor checks, and how.

WRITE DOWN — their method: second pass, reverse calculation, or a colleague.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever found one?' They will have.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the second check on their scoring.

THEY HOLD — the first.

WHY THAT SPLIT — checking someone else's work teaches you where errors live.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — score and check, with them checking after you.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you check at all once you are confident. Confidence is when errors start.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — finding one.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every conversion checked twice.

PASS TEST — one transcription error changes an index.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol with checking evident.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report circulated with a wrong composite, discovered by someone else.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain where conversion errors cluster and set up a checking routine for a colleague.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find an error after issuing a report: correct it, reissue it, and tell the people who received it. Immediately.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Checking the ones you are unsure about rather than all of them.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into every reported number, and into PSI 4.2.5 on accuracy.

micro.name: Apply confidence intervals rather than point scores
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A standard score of 85 is an estimate with error around it. Reporting it as a point value implies a precision the instrument does not have, and schools and parents then treat a three-point change as meaningful. Confidence intervals are the honest representation and they are in the manual.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor reports scores. Look for ranges rather than points.

WRITE DOWN — two sentences using confidence intervals.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you explain a confidence interval to a parent?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — looking up the intervals and drafting the score table.

THEY HOLD — the interpretive text.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the mechanics first, the explanation after.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — you report with intervals and explain them in feedback.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether the narrative text reverts to point scores even when the table has intervals. It usually does.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — offering the plain-language version of the interval.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — intervals in the table and in the narrative.

PASS TEST — the report does not imply false precision.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the score table with intervals, and narrative that matches it.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report where a school treats a four-point difference as progress.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain standard error of measurement in plain words and demonstrate it to a parent.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when asked for 'the number': give the range, explain why, and do not give a point score to satisfy the question.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
An interval in the table and a point score in the sentence underneath.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into PSI 2.3.1 on the limits of psychological data, and into the limitations section.

micro.name: Compare attainment against cognitive profile appropriately
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Attainment means nothing without an expectation, and the expectation comes from the cognitive profile. But the discrepancy model has real limits — it under-identifies children with lower cognitive scores, which is why current criteria abandoned it as the sole basis for identification. Knowing what the discrepancy does not mean is as important as calculating it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor frames the comparison, and whether they use a formal discrepancy or a descriptive one.

WRITE DOWN — the comparison sentence.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when does a discrepancy mislead you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — calculating the comparison.

THEY HOLD — the interpretation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the arithmetic is straightforward; knowing what it licenses is not.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — calculate and interpret, tested by them.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — over-reading a discrepancy, and missing a child with uniformly low scores who still has a real difficulty.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what would you conclude if both were at the 5th percentile?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — compared, interpreted, and qualified.

PASS TEST — you know what the discrepancy does not mean.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the comparison in the report with its limits stated.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child with low average cognition and very low attainment told they do not meet criteria, when they clearly need the intervention.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why DSM-5 moved away from the discrepancy model and what replaced it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the numbers do not support a label the child clearly needs support for: recommend on need, describe the profile, and say plainly what the criteria do and do not establish.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating the discrepancy as the finding rather than as one piece of evidence.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into specific learning difficulty identification, and into the honesty thread about what tests establish.

micro.name: Notice a score you do not believe and check it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Sometimes a score does not fit anything else you know about the child. The professional response is to check before reporting, because the two likeliest explanations are a scoring error and an administration problem — and both are yours to find.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — a moment your supervisor pauses over a score. Ask what prompted it.

WRITE DOWN — what they checked.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what makes you distrust a score?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — flagging anything that looks inconsistent.

THEY HOLD — deciding what to do about it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — noticing is the skill; the response is a judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — notice, re-score, and decide.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — whether you report a score you privately doubt because re-scoring is tedious.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'does that fit with what you saw in the room?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — noticed, re-scored, resolved.

PASS TEST — you re-scored rather than reported it.

EVIDENCE TO FILE — if the score stands after checking, say in the report that it is inconsistent with other findings and what you make of it.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an anomalous score reported without comment, which the reader then builds on.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the common causes of anomalous scores: transcription, administration, fatigue, and genuine profile variation.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the score is real and does not fit: report it, name the inconsistency, and resist smoothing it into a tidier narrative.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Reporting a number you do not believe because the alternative was more work.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the synthesis skill, into limitations, and into Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Identify where sources converge
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Convergence is the strongest evidence an assessment produces: the same pattern seen by different people, in different settings, with different methods. Triangulation, the idea that agreement across methods beats any single method (Denzin, The Research Act, 1978), is the logic of every integrated report. Get it wrong and you claim agreement that is only surface. 'Teacher and parent both mention attention' is not convergence if one means daydreaming and the other means leaving the seat.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor lines sources up before writing. Many do it on one page: sources down the side, domains across the top. Notice whether they check that two sources describe the same behaviour, or only use the same word.

WRITE DOWN — every source used (interview, rating scale, observation, standardised test, work sample, file) and which domains each one spoke to.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how did you know the teacher's and parent's reports were about the same thing and not just the same label?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building the source-by-domain grid from the file, and marking every cell where two or more sources point the same way, with the specific evidence quoted.

THEY HOLD — the judgement on whether each apparent agreement is real convergence or just shared vocabulary.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the grid is mechanical and teaches you the file. Judging whether agreement is genuine is the clinical skill, and it is the one you will be tested on.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present the grid in supervision and state each convergence aloud: which sources, which behaviour, which setting, how you know they mean the same thing.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — convergence you count rather than check. Three sources that all rely on the same parent report are one source, not three.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the rating scale and the interview both came from mum on the same day — is that two sources?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — build the grid, write the convergent findings into the integration section with each source named in the sentence, and bring it to supervision.

PASS TEST — Convergence is stated rather than assumed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the integration section of the report and the grid as a working paper on the case file. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'all sources indicate attention difficulties' with no named sources, no settings and no check that the behaviours match.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the difference between convergence of label and convergence of behaviour, and why sources that share an origin (the same informant, the same day, the same form) do not independently confirm each other.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find you overstated agreement after the report is drafted: rewrite the sentence to name the actual sources, and weaken the claim to what the evidence carries.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'findings were consistent across sources' without naming the sources or checking they described the same behaviour.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify where sources diverge and say so', 'Judge which source to weight and why', and into Formulation, where convergent evidence carries the working hypothesis.

micro.name: Identify where sources diverge and say so
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Divergence between sources is information, not noise. A child who is described as anxious at home and settled at school is telling you something about context. The cross-informant meta-analysis by Achenbach, McConaughy and Howell (Psychological Bulletin, 1987) found only modest agreement between different types of informant; exact figures are in the paper — check before quoting. A report that smooths divergence away hides the most useful finding and misleads the reader about how certain you are.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words a disagreement between sources in the report. Notice whether they name both sides, or quietly pick one.

WRITE DOWN — each point of divergence in the case: which sources, which domain, which setting, and the likely explanations your supervisor considered.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when the teacher and parent disagree, how do you decide whether it's the child, the setting, or the informant?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listing every divergence on the grid and drafting the possible explanations for each: different setting, different demands, different informant threshold, different time period.

THEY HOLD — the wording that goes in the report, because divergence can land badly with a parent or school who feels disbelieved.

WHY THAT SPLIT — generating explanations is thinking you can practise safely. Wording that will be read by the family carries relational risk.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — draft the divergence paragraph yourself and read it aloud in supervision before it goes in the report.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — divergence resolved by picking the professional source over the parent, or the adult over the child, without a reason. That is a bias, not a judgement.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've gone with the teacher's view there. What would the parent say if they read this sentence?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — identify each divergence, offer at least one explanation grounded in the setting or task demands, and write it into the report in neutral language.

PASS TEST — Discrepancy is named rather than smoothed away

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the integration section of the report, marked in your Appendix 5 entry as the place divergence was handled. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice (PSI Code 4.2.6).

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a profile that reads as if everyone agreed, when your grid shows they did not.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why informant disagreement is expected rather than a problem, and describe the context-based reading of it (De Los Reyes & Kazdin, Psychological Bulletin, 2005, on informant discrepancies).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a family objects that the report calls them wrong: show them the sentence, explain that both accounts are reported as true in their setting, and amend wording that implies blame.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Reporting only the account that fits the hypothesis and leaving the contradicting one out.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Analyse informant agreement and discrepancy' (rating scales), into Formulation, and into Ethical Practice — honest reporting of uncertainty.

micro.name: Judge which source to weight and why
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Sources are not equal, and pretending they are is its own error. A standardised score has known reliability; a single twenty-minute observation may have caught an unusual day; a parent knows the child across years but not in class. Weighting is unavoidable, so the professional task is to make it explicit. An unstated weighting cannot be challenged, and one that cannot be challenged cannot be defended at a review meeting or complaint.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moment your supervisor treats one finding as more telling than another. Listen for the reason: reliability, proximity to the concern, the setting it came from, or how recent it is.

WRITE DOWN — each source, the weight your supervisor gave it (high, moderate, low), and the stated or implied reason.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if the WISC and the classroom observation pointed opposite ways, which would you trust more for this question — and would that change for a different question?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a proposed weighting for each source with one line of reasoning beside it: how reliable, how close to the referral concern, how representative.

THEY HOLD — the final weighting and any sentence in the report that ranks one informant's account below another's.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing reasons makes your implicit weighting visible so it can be corrected. Ranking people's accounts in print has consequences for relationships you do not yet hold.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — state your weighting in supervision before you write the synthesis, and defend it when challenged.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — weighting by status (the psychologist's test over the parent's account) or by convenience (the source that fits your hypothesis) instead of by fit to the question.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the referral question is about the yard. Which of your sources were actually in the yard?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — decide the weighting, write it into the synthesis in one or two sentences, and bring it to supervision already written.

PASS TEST — The weighting is defensible and written down

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the sentence in the report stating which evidence carried most weight and why. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a conclusion that clearly rests on one source, with nothing in the report saying so, so the reader cannot tell what would change it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the criteria for weighting (reliability, validity for the specific question, setting, recency, independence from other sources) and give a worked case where the same source deserves high weight for one question and low weight for another.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when new information arrives that overturns your weighting: say so in an addendum rather than quietly revising the conclusion.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Letting the standardised score overrule everything else because it has a number attached, without asking whether it answers the referral question.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Write an integration section rather than a list', into Formulation, and into defending conclusions at a review meeting.

micro.name: Write an integration section rather than a list
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A report that lists findings test by test hands the hardest part of the job to the reader. Teachers and parents will not integrate a WISC section, a rating-scale section and an observation section on their own; they will skim to the recommendations. Report-writing texts are consistent on this: organise by theme or domain, not by instrument (Lichtenberger, Mather, Kaufman & Kaufman, Essentials of Assessment Report Writing, 2004). An unintegrated report is a common reason for a trainee's report to be sent back.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor's reports are structured. Look for a section headed something like 'integration', 'summary of findings' or 'profile', and see whether it is organised by instrument or by question.

WRITE DOWN — the headings of three of their reports, and one integration paragraph you think works, with why.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when you write the summary, do you start from the tests or from the referral question?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the integration section for a case your supervisor is leading, organised by referral question or by domain, with each claim tied to named evidence.

THEY HOLD — the overall conclusions and the final draft that goes to the family.

WHY THAT SPLIT — drafting integration is where you find out whether you understood the case. Your supervisor carries the conclusions, so an early draft that gets it wrong costs nothing.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the integration section for your own case and bring it to supervision before the recommendations are written.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a list with joining words. 'The WISC showed X. The teacher reported Y. Observation found Z.' is still a list.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'read me the first sentence of each paragraph. Does it make a claim, or name a test?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write an integration section where each paragraph opens with a claim about the child, then gives the evidence from several sources, then says what it means for the referral question.

PASS TEST — The reader is not left to do the synthesis

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report. Name this section in your Appendix 5 entry. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — recommendations that do not follow from anything the integration section said, because the integration section did not say anything.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to rewrite a test-by-test summary into claim-first paragraphs, and explain why this is what makes recommendations defensible.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the findings genuinely do not integrate: say so, name the competing readings, and state what further evidence would decide between them.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Repeating every score again in the summary instead of saying what the scores mean together.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask whether the profile answers the referral question', into Formulation, and into recommendations the school can act on.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Ask whether the profile answers the referral question
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The referral question is the contract. Schools and parents asked something specific, and a thorough report that answers a different question has failed them, however good the psychometrics. It is easy to drift: the assessment finds something interesting and the report follows it. The check is simple and often skipped — reread the question, reread your conclusion, and see whether one answers the other.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor goes back to the referral form before finalising a report. Some print it and set it beside the draft.

WRITE DOWN — the referral question in the referrer's own words, and the one-sentence answer your supervisor's report gives to it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'has a report of yours ever answered a different question from the one that was asked? What happened?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the referral question at the top of the draft in the referrer's words, and a one-line answer to it underneath, before anything else is written.

THEY HOLD — whether the question itself needs to be renegotiated with the school or parent.

WHY THAT SPLIT — checking the fit is a habit you can build straight away. Going back to a referrer to say the question has changed is a consultation decision.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — at the end of your draft, state aloud in supervision: the question asked, your answer, and which section of the report carries it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — an answer that is technically there but buried, or an answer to the question you would have preferred they asked.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if the principal read only your summary, would they know the answer to what they asked?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before sending any report, check it against the referral question and fix it if it does not answer it. If it cannot answer it, say why in the report.

PASS TEST — You noticed if it did not

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report, with the referral question stated at the start and answered in the summary. Note in the Log if the question was renegotiated. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the school rings to ask what the report means for their question.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer how referral questions drift during an assessment, and show the simple check: question, answer, location in the report.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the assessment shows the original question was the wrong one: answer it anyway, then say plainly what you think the more useful question is and why.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Sending a report that is thorough on cognition when the school asked about behaviour in the yard.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into recommendations, into Working with Others — agreeing the question at the start — and into Formulation.

micro.name: State what you did not assess and what that limits
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Every assessment is partial. A report that does not say what was left out invites the reader to assume it was covered — that language was fine because it was not mentioned, or that mood was screened because anxiety was not reported. Stating the limits of your competence and your evidence is a professional obligation (CORU SoP 1.2; PSI Code 2.3.1). Missing limitations are what an external examiner or a complaint will find first.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where in your supervisor's reports the limitations appear, and how they are worded. Some write a short paragraph; some fold them into each section.

WRITE DOWN — every domain relevant to the referral that was not directly assessed in the case, and whether the report says so.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide what goes in the limitations without making the report sound like it achieved nothing?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the limitations paragraph: what was not assessed, why (time, consent, scope, a test not available, the child's state on the day), and what that means for the conclusions.

THEY HOLD — the decision about whether a gap is serious enough to change the conclusions or require an onward referral.

WHY THAT SPLIT — listing gaps is straightforward. Judging whether a gap undermines the conclusion needs experience of what those gaps usually hide.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the limitations yourself and discuss in supervision which of them affect the conclusions directly.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a boilerplate paragraph ('results should be interpreted with caution') that could go in any report and tells the reader nothing about this one.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'caution about what, exactly? Which conclusion would change if you had assessed that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every report you write has a specific limitations paragraph naming what was not assessed and which conclusion that affects.

PASS TEST — A limitations paragraph exists

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the limitations paragraph in the report. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — no limitations paragraph, or a generic one, so the school acts on a conclusion the evidence does not carry.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a limitations paragraph protects the child, the reader and you, and show how to make one specific: name the gap, the reason, and the conclusion it qualifies.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a gap you did not report turns out to matter later: acknowledge it in writing, correct the record, and tell your supervisor before the family hears it from someone else.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A generic 'interpret with caution' line that names no gap and qualifies no conclusion.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Ethical Practice — working within competence — and into onward referral decisions.

micro.name: Explain why phonological awareness matters for reading
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Teachers will ask why you tested sound games when the concern was reading. The answer is the core of the literacy evidence base. The Simple View of Reading splits reading into decoding and language comprehension (Gough & Tunmer, Remedial and Special Education, 1986). Phonological processing difficulty is the best-supported account of why decoding fails (the 'phonological core' view — Stanovich, Journal of Learning Disabilities, 1988). If you cannot explain this plainly, the recommendations that follow will not be implemented.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor explains phonological awareness to a teacher or parent. Note the example they use; most use rhyme, syllables and a spoken word broken into sounds.

WRITE DOWN — the explanation in their words, and any question the listener asked that showed confusion.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you explain the difference between phonological awareness and phonics to a teacher who uses the words interchangeably?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the explanation of phonological awareness in a feedback meeting, prepared in advance and kept to two minutes.

THEY HOLD — linking it to this child's scores and to what the school should do.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the general explanation can be rehearsed and is low-risk. Tying it to a named child's results carries the interpretation, which your supervisor still owns at this stage.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain phonological awareness and its link to this child's reading in a feedback meeting, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jargon ('phonemic segmentation deficit') and overclaiming, such as implying phonological difficulty is the whole story when comprehension or vocabulary are also weak.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a supervisor asking, in the meeting, 'could you give an example of what that looks like in class?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain it to a teacher or parent in plain language, with one example drawn from this child's work, and check that they understood.

PASS TEST — You can explain it to a teacher without notes

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a case note of the feedback meeting. Log against 1. Assessment and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the teacher leaves thinking the answer is more phonics worksheets, or thinking the child cannot learn to read.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the Simple View of Reading, why decoding and comprehension can fail separately, and where phonological awareness sits — citing sources, not from memory of a lecture.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a teacher disagrees ('he knows all his sounds'): separate knowing letter–sound links from being able to manipulate sounds in spoken words, and show the difference with a quick oral example.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Explaining phonological awareness with the child's scores instead of with an example the teacher will recognise in class.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Distinguish a specific difficulty from a general one', 'Interpret a phonological profile in context', and 'Link the profile to what the school can deliver'.

micro.name: Distinguish a specific difficulty from a general one
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A child with weak reading and weak general language or reasoning needs different support from a child whose reading difficulty stands apart from otherwise typical abilities. Current definitions of dyslexia treat it as a continuum and do not rely on an IQ–achievement discrepancy (Rose, Identifying and Teaching Children and Young People with Dyslexia and Literacy Difficulties, 2009). But you still have to know the broader profile — especially oral language — before calling the difficulty specific. Skip that and the recommendation targets the wrong thing.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which information your supervisor looks at before saying a literacy difficulty is 'specific': cognitive scores, oral language, attendance, teaching history, vision and hearing.

WRITE DOWN — the checks they made and any they said were missing.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what would make you say this is a general learning difficulty showing up in reading, rather than a reading difficulty?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — gathering the wider profile: cognitive or language scores, school history, attendance, sensory screening, and whether the child has had adequate teaching.

THEY HOLD — the conclusion about whether the difficulty is specific, and how it is worded.

WHY THAT SPLIT — collecting the context teaches you what the question depends on. The label, or the absence of one, is what the family and school will act on.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present your view in supervision: specific, general, or unclear, and the evidence for each.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jumping from low phonological scores to 'dyslexic profile' without checking oral language comprehension or response to teaching.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's their receptive language like? And how long have they had structured literacy teaching?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — check the broader profile before concluding, and state in the report what that check found.

PASS TEST — You check the cognitive profile before concluding

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the interpretation section of the report, with the broader profile referenced. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report naming a specific literacy difficulty for a child whose oral language is as weak as their reading, so the language need goes unaddressed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why discrepancy definitions were abandoned, what replaced them, and why the wider profile still matters — citing Rose (2009) and your service's own criteria.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the profile is mixed: describe both needs, say which is primary for the referral question, and avoid a label the evidence does not support.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Concluding 'specific' from low phonological scores alone, without checking oral language or teaching history.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Interpret a phonological profile in context', into Formulation, and into Conditions — DLD and literacy difficulty.

micro.name: Administer phonological awareness subtests to standard
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Phonological tasks are presented orally, so the stimulus is your voice. Speak too slowly, stress the wrong sound or repeat an item not allowed to be repeated, and the score reflects your delivery, not the child's skill. Many batteries use recorded audio for some tasks for this reason: CTOPP-2 (Wagner, Torgesen, Rashotte & Pearson, 2013) supplies audio for some subtests. Check your edition's manual for which ones. An inaccurate administration cannot be rescued at scoring.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor delivers oral items: pace, whether they use the audio where the manual requires it, how they handle a request to repeat, and what they do after a discontinue.

WRITE DOWN — the subtests used, the start points, repeat rules and discontinue rules, checked against the manual afterwards.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the easiest way to spoil an elision item without noticing?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — administering one phonological subtest while your supervisor watches, having practised it aloud at least twice beforehand.

THEY HOLD — the rest of the battery and the decision about whether your administration was valid enough to score.

WHY THAT SPLIT — oral delivery is a motor skill that needs practice under observation. Whether a spoiled item invalidates the subtest is a judgement you have not yet seen enough to make.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer the full phonological battery with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — adding sounds (saying 'buh' for /b/), unscripted feedback, repeating items the manual says cannot be repeated, and losing track of the discontinue rule.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a quiet note to check the discontinue rule, or taking over for one item and handing back.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — administer the battery to manual standard, with the audio where required, correct start points and discontinues, and responses recorded as you go.

PASS TEST — Administration is fluent and timing accurate

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the completed record form. Log against 1. Assessment and Table 3 tools.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a discontinued subtest continued, or items repeated against the rules, so the scaled score cannot be interpreted.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can demonstrate clean phoneme production (no added schwa), explain the start, repeat and discontinue rules from memory, and explain why each rule exists.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise mid-battery you broke a rule: note it on the form at that point, decide with the manual whether the subtest is still scoreable, and report the problem if it is not.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Adding a vowel to isolated consonants ('buh' for /b/), which changes the task the child is doing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Score the phonological composites correctly' and 'Interpret a phonological profile in context'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Administer rapid naming tasks accurately
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Rapid automatised naming (RAN) — naming arrays of digits, letters, colours or objects as fast as possible — predicts reading fluency partly independently of phonological awareness. This is the basis of the double-deficit hypothesis (Wolf & Bowers, Journal of Educational Psychology, 1999). The score is a time, often adjusted for errors, so a stopwatch started late or an error not recorded changes the result directly.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — exactly when your supervisor starts and stops the timer, how they record errors and self-corrections, and whether they use the practice items as the manual requires.

WRITE DOWN — the timing rule (when the clock starts and stops), how errors are counted, and whether the test has an error cut-off that invalidates a trial.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do if a child loses their place on the array?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — timing and error recording while your supervisor administers, then compare your times with theirs.

THEY HOLD — the administration and the decision on which timing counts if yours differs.

WHY THAT SPLIT — timing reliability is checkable against another person, so it is the right thing to practise first. Administration adds the load of instructions and managing the child.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer and time the RAN tasks with your supervisor present, timing in parallel.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — timer starts that lag the child's first response, errors missed because you were watching the clock, and prompts the manual does not allow.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — comparing the two times afterwards and asking why they differ by more than a second.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — administer, time and record errors to manual standard, and note anything that affected speed (stammer, naming difficulty, losing place).

PASS TEST — You timed and recorded errors correctly

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the completed record form with times and errors. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a time that includes your instructions, or no record of errors, so the score and any error adjustment are wrong.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what RAN measures and does not measure, why it relates to fluency, and how to time it reliably — with the double-deficit literature cited.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the timing is compromised (interruption, timer failure): note it, do not estimate, and check the manual on whether the trial can be re-run.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Starting the timer on your own instruction rather than on the child's first response, which adds seconds to every trial.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Score the phonological composites correctly' and 'Interpret a phonological profile in context' — especially fluency-focused recommendations.

micro.name: Score the phonological composites correctly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Composite scores are what reports quote and what schools act on, and they are built from several conversions: raw to scaled for each subtest, scaled summed to a composite, composite to percentile and confidence interval. Each step uses the child's exact age on the day. On CTOPP-2 (Wagner et al., 2013), subtests are scaled scores (mean 10, SD 3) and composites are index scores (mean 100, SD 15). Which subtests feed which composite changes with age band, so check the manual for your edition. One wrong table and the whole profile shifts.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor calculates chronological age, which norm table they turn to, and whether they double-check the sum of scaled scores before looking up the composite.

WRITE DOWN — for each composite, which subtests feed it at this child's age, and the table used.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which scoring mistake have you seen most often in trainee protocols?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — scoring the protocol independently, from raw scores to composites, before seeing your supervisor's scoring.

THEY HOLD — the authoritative score, and resolving any difference between your scoring and theirs.

WHY THAT SPLIT — independent double-scoring is the fastest way to find your systematic errors. Your supervisor's version stands until you have shown you score accurately.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — score the protocol and the composites yourself; your supervisor checks it before anything is reported.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — age calculated wrongly (especially borrowing months and days), the wrong age-band table, a subtest summed into the wrong composite, and transcription errors from protocol to report.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — handing it back with 'one of these is wrong — find it.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — score, then check every step a second time on a different day or with scoring software, and reconcile any difference before reporting.

PASS TEST — Composites calculated and checked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the scored protocol with your check marked, and the score table in the report. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a composite in the report that does not match the protocol, found by the family's private assessor or at a review.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can walk a peer through age calculation, subtest-to-composite mapping, and confidence intervals, and explain why a composite is more reliable than any single subtest.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find a scoring error after the report has gone: tell your supervisor, issue a corrected report with the change marked, and tell the family and school what changed and whether the conclusion changes.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Calculating age without borrowing correctly across months and days, and reading off the wrong norm table.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Interpret a phonological profile in context' and into the score table and limitations of the report.

micro.name: Interpret a phonological profile in context
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A low phonological composite shows the child did poorly on these tasks, on this day, compared with the norm sample. It does not by itself establish dyslexia, explain every reading problem, or predict what intervention will work. Interpretation means putting the scores beside reading accuracy, fluency, comprehension, oral language, teaching history and the child's own account. Rose (2009) is explicit that dyslexia is best thought of as a continuum and that response to intervention is part of the picture. Overclaim here and the family leaves with a label the evidence does not carry.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the words your supervisor uses when interpreting phonological scores: 'consistent with', 'suggests', 'is characteristic of'. Note what they will not say.

WRITE DOWN — the other evidence they set beside the scores, and any conclusion they chose not to draw.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what would you need to see before you'd say this profile shows a dyslexic-type difficulty?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the interpretation paragraph: what the scores show, which other evidence agrees or disagrees, and the limits.

THEY HOLD — any diagnostic or quasi-diagnostic language, and how the conclusion is framed for the family.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing interpretation shows your reasoning. Diagnostic language has consequences for school supports and for the child's view of themselves, so it stays with them.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the interpretation and present it in supervision, including one sentence on what the profile does not establish.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — reading scores as causes ('because of her phonological deficit') and ignoring evidence of adequate teaching, attendance, or language.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've said this explains her reading. What else could explain it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — interpret the profile against the wider evidence, and write explicitly what it does and does not establish.

PASS TEST — You can say what it does and does not establish

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the interpretation and limitations sections of the report. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'the results confirm dyslexia' on the basis of one battery, with no reference to the child's response to teaching.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between describing a profile and diagnosing, why phonological scores are one strand of evidence, and how to write both halves: what it shows and what it does not.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent wants a label the evidence does not support: explain what the evidence does show, what support follows from it without a label, and what would need to happen for the question to be revisited.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing that the scores 'confirm' a difficulty rather than that they are consistent with it alongside the other evidence.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Link the profile to what the school can deliver', into Formulation, and into Conditions — literacy difficulty and DLD.

micro.name: Link the profile to what the school can deliver
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A recommendation the school cannot deliver is not a recommendation. Irish primary schools allocate special education teaching under the model set out in DES Circular 0013/2017 (post-primary 0014/2017), within the NEPS Continuum of Support. What is possible depends on staffing, timetable and the programmes staff are trained in. Recommendations should follow from the finding — phonological weakness points towards explicit, systematic phonological and phonics teaching — and be specific enough to act on.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor finds out what the school already offers before recommending. Listen for questions about the special education team, programmes in use, group sizes and timetabling.

WRITE DOWN — each recommendation in their report, the finding it follows from, and whether it names who, what, how often and for how long.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you write a recommendation that is honest about what the child needs when the school can't provide all of it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the recommendations for the literacy section, each linked in one line to the finding it comes from.

THEY HOLD — the conversation with the school about what is feasible, and the final wording.

WHY THAT SPLIT — linking finding to recommendation is reasoning you can practise. Negotiating provision with a principal involves a relationship and service expectations you do not yet hold.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — ask the school what it can offer, write recommendations that fit, and present them in the feedback meeting with your supervisor there.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — generic recommendations ('multisensory approach', 'extra time') that do not follow from this child's profile, and naming a programme the school does not have or cannot resource.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'which finding does that recommendation come from?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write recommendations that each follow from a named finding and that the school has confirmed it can deliver or adapt.

PASS TEST — The recommendation follows from the finding

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the recommendations section and the case note of the school conversation. Log against 1. Assessment, 3. Intervention and 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — ten recommendations copied from a template, none implemented, and a review six months later with nothing changed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how the Continuum of Support and the allocation model shape what schools can do, and how to write a recommendation that names what, who, how often, for how long and how progress will be measured.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the child needs more than the school can give: state the need honestly, recommend what is feasible now, and say who else should be involved.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A list of generic literacy recommendations that could have gone in any child's report.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Intervention — planning and review — and into Systemic Change, where repeated gaps in school provision become a consultation issue.
