micro.name: Recognise the limits of a screening instrument
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A screen finds people who may need a fuller assessment. It does not diagnose. Questionnaires such as the Social Communication Questionnaire (SCQ; Rutter, Bailey & Lord, 2003) or the Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS-2; Constantino & Gruber, 2012) rely on one informant's view and use cut-offs chosen to trade missed cases against false alarms. Sensitivity and specificity vary by sample and age — check the manual and do not quote a figure from memory. A family who hears 'the score was high' as 'your child is autistic' has been misled.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor describes a screening result, in the report and aloud. Notice the words they avoid.

WRITE DOWN — the instrument, the informant, the cut-off, what the manual says the cut-off means, and the exact sentence your supervisor used to report it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever had a screen come back below the cut-off for a child you were sure needed a full assessment? What did you do?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the paragraph that reports the screen, including a sentence saying what a screen can and cannot establish.

THEY HOLD — the recommendation about onward referral, and the conversation with the family.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the wording can be practised and corrected on paper. The onward decision and the family conversation carry emotional weight and service consequences.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — report the screen yourself, in writing and aloud to the family, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — diagnostic language ('scores in the autistic range') and false reassurance from a low score when observation or history raise concern.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor adding, 'just to be clear, this is a questionnaire, not an assessment for autism.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — report every screen with a written statement that it is not a diagnosis, what it does suggest, and what happens next.

PASS TEST — You said in writing that a screen is not a diagnosis

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report paragraph. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a school telling a parent 'the psychologist said he's autistic' because your report said 'scores in the autism range'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain sensitivity, specificity and why cut-offs are compromises, and why a single-informant questionnaire cannot carry a diagnosis.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a screen is being used as a diagnosis by the school or family: correct it in writing, explain the difference, and point to the pathway.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'in the autism range' instead of 'above the screening threshold, which indicates a fuller assessment is warranted'.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know the onward diagnostic pathway in this service', 'Integrate screening data with direct observation', and Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Know the onward diagnostic pathway in this service
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A positive screen with nowhere to go leaves the family holding a worry and no route. In Ireland, autism diagnostic assessment is usually done by HSE multidisciplinary teams — Children's Disability Network Teams, primary care, or CAMHS where there is a co-occurring mental health need — or by private assessment. Assessment of Need under the Disability Act 2005 is one statutory route. Routes, waiting times and who can refer vary by area and change often, so find out the current local position rather than assuming.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor tells a family after a positive screen: who they should contact, who makes the referral, and roughly how long it takes.

WRITE DOWN — the local pathway as your supervisor describes it: team names, referral route, who can refer, whether the school or GP is involved, and any local waiting time they quote.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's changed in this pathway in the last two years, and where do you check it's still current?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a one-page summary of the local pathway for your own use, and checking it with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — advising the family on the route, and any referral made.

WHY THAT SPLIT — mapping the pathway is research you can do alone and it builds your knowledge of the area. Advice to a family must be current and accurate, so your supervisor gives it until you have checked the map.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain the pathway to a family after a screen, with your supervisor there.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — out-of-date information, promises about timescales, and not mentioning interim support the school can put in place without a diagnosis.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor adding what the school can do in the meantime.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name the onward pathway in the report and to the family, accurately for the area, with interim supports alongside.

PASS TEST — You could name where a positive screen goes

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the recommendations section of the report and the pathway summary on file. Log against 1. Assessment and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'the family should seek a diagnostic assessment', with no route named, and a family that does not know where to start.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the Irish routes (HSE teams, Assessment of Need, CAMHS, private), who refers, and the difference between a need-led support in school and a diagnosis-led service.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the pathway is blocked or very long: say so honestly, recommend what the school can do now, and record the gap for your service's systemic view.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Telling a family to 'seek a diagnosis' without naming who, how, or what to do while they wait.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Working with Others — interagency referral — and into Systemic Change, where pathway gaps are raised.

micro.name: Administer a screen with a parent
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents complete screening questionnaires about their own child, often while already worried or defending against a worry. How you introduce it shapes what they report. Some over-endorse to secure help; some under-endorse to protect the child from a label. Explaining what the screen is for, what it cannot tell them, and what happens next is part of informed consent. It also makes the answers more accurate.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor introduces the questionnaire: purpose, how long it takes, how to handle items they are unsure of, and who will see the results.

WRITE DOWN — their introduction as close to verbatim as you can, and any question the parent asked.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you say when a parent asks, before they start, whether a high score means autism?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — introducing the questionnaire to the parent, from a script you have written and checked with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — questions about diagnosis, and any distress that comes up.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a scripted introduction is safe to practise. Questions about what the child 'has' need someone who can answer them in the moment without overstating.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — introduce the questionnaire, answer the parent's questions, and stay available while they complete it, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — leading the parent ('does he do this a lot?') or interpreting items in a way that shifts the answer.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor offering the standard response to an unclear item: 'answer as best you can and we'll talk about it after.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — introduce the screen, explain what it can and cannot tell them, give neutral help with unclear items, and tell them when and how they will hear the results.

PASS TEST — You explained what a screen can and cannot tell them

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a case note recording the explanation given. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent who completed the form thinking the score would give them a diagnosis, and who is distressed or angry when it does not.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the introduction matters for validity as well as consent, and how to answer a parent's questions about an item without shifting their answer.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent becomes distressed or angry during the questionnaire: stop, acknowledge it, offer to finish another time, and record that the conditions may have affected the responses.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Handing the questionnaire over without explaining that it is a screen and not a diagnosis.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Integrate screening data with direct observation', into consent practice in Ethical Practice, and into Working with Others — families.

micro.name: Integrate screening data with direct observation
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A questionnaire records one informant's summary of the child. Observation shows you the child — in the yard, in class, with peers and adults. Each can mislead alone. The screen can be skewed by the informant, and a short observation can catch an untypical day. Guidance on autism assessment consistently requires information from more than one source and setting — check the specific requirements of the guidance your service uses. Relying on the questionnaire alone makes the screen do a job it was not built for.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which settings your supervisor chooses to observe after a screen, and what they look for: initiation, response to bids, reciprocity, play, transitions, sensory response.

WRITE DOWN — the observation focus, the setting, and how the observation was later set beside the questionnaire.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when the screen and your observation disagree, what do you do?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the observation in one setting, with a focus agreed beforehand from the screen items.

THEY HOLD — putting the two together and deciding what it means for onward referral.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a focused observation is a skill you are already building. Integrating it with a screen and deciding on referral is a clinical judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — plan the observation from the screen, observe, and present the integration in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — observing only structured class time when the concern is unstructured social time, and treating 'did not see it' as 'it does not happen'.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the parent reported difficulty at break. When did you observe?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — observe in at least one setting chosen to test what the screen suggested, and write a paragraph that sets the two sources together.

PASS TEST — You did not rely on the questionnaire alone

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the observation write-up and the integration paragraph in the report. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report whose conclusions rest entirely on a questionnaire score.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why screening and observation are complementary, how to choose an observation setting from screen items, and why absence of a behaviour in one short observation is weak evidence.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the two sources flatly contradict: report both, give the likeliest reasons, and let that uncertainty inform the onward referral rather than hiding it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Observing in the setting that was easiest to arrange rather than the one where the concern was reported.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Recognise masked or atypical presentation', into 'Identify where sources diverge and say so', and into onward referral.

micro.name: Recognise masked or atypical presentation
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Some autistic children — often, but not only, girls — learn to hide or compensate for social differences, at great cost to themselves. This is camouflaging, described in Hull et al. (Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 2017). A meta-analysis estimated the true male-to-female ratio nearer 3:1 than the 4:1 often quoted, pointing to under-identification of girls (Loomes, Hull & Mandy, JAACAP, 2017). Screens and short observations may miss these children. The PSI Autism Guidelines (2022) are the reference named for this standard — read them directly rather than relying on a summary.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor asks about effort and exhaustion as well as behaviour: after-school collapse, scripted conversation, intense friendships that break down, anxiety, masking at school and releasing at home.

WRITE DOWN — the questions they ask that go beyond the screen items.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what makes you suspect camouflaging when school says everything is fine?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing a short list of questions on masking and effort for the parent interview and the child, drawn from the literature, and checking them with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — interpreting the answers and deciding whether they warrant onward referral despite a sub-threshold screen.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the questions are the part you can research and improve. Acting on a hunch against a sub-threshold score needs experience of how often that hunch is right.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — ask about masking in interview, with your supervisor present, and bring your view to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — dismissing home reports because school sees no difficulty, and assuming a girl who makes eye contact and has friends cannot be autistic.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what happens when she gets home from school?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — consider camouflaging and late identification in every social communication assessment, and write in the report that you did.

PASS TEST — You considered presentation in girls and late identification

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a sentence in the report on how presentation and masking were considered. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a sub-threshold screen and a calm classroom observation reported as 'no social communication concerns', and a teenager identified years later.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain camouflaging, why screens under-identify it, and what questions surface it — citing Hull et al. (2017), Loomes et al. (2017) and the PSI guidelines.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when home and school accounts are irreconcilable: treat the difference as a possible sign of masking, not a reason to doubt the parent.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking a calm classroom and a sub-threshold screen as evidence against autism in a child who is exhausted and distressed at home.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Analyse informant agreement and discrepancy', into Conditions — autism, and into Formulation.

micro.name: Select the right forms for informant and age
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Rating scale systems come as families of forms for different informants and age bands. Using the wrong one gives you scores compared against the wrong norm group. The BASC-3 (Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015) has teacher, parent and self-report forms by age band. The ASEBA (Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001) has the CBCL, TRF and Youth Self-Report (YSR). The SDQ (Goodman, 1997) has parent, teacher and self-report versions, the self-report for ages 11–17. Check the exact age ranges in the manual you are using before choosing.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor decides which forms go to whom: the child's age, which adults know the child in which setting, and whether the child can self-report.

WRITE DOWN — the instrument, each form used, who completed it, and the age range printed on each form.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which teacher do you send it to when a post-primary student has eight?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — proposing the forms, informants and age bands for the case, in writing, before anything is sent.

THEY HOLD — the final choice of instrument and of informants.

WHY THAT SPLIT — form selection is rule-based and easy to check, so it is the right thing to practise. Choosing the instrument depends on the referral question and on what the service holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — select and send the forms yourself; your supervisor checks your selection before they go out.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a form one band too young or too old for the child, a teacher who barely knows the child, and no self-report where one is available and appropriate.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'she turns twelve next month — which form will you use, and why?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — choose forms matched to the age band on the date of completion, send them to informants who know the child in the relevant setting, and record who completed each.

PASS TEST — Parent, teacher and self-report chosen appropriately

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the method section of the report naming each form and informant. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — scores reported from a form normed for the wrong age band, found when someone checks the date of birth.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the structure of at least two rating scale systems, how to match forms to age and informant, and why the choice of informant is part of the evidence.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the wrong form was completed: do not score it against the wrong norms. Report it as descriptive only, or re-send the right form.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using a form normed for the wrong age band because the child's birthday fell between sending and completion.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Include the child's own self-report where age-appropriate', 'Score and convert to standardised scores', and 'Analyse informant agreement and discrepancy'.

micro.name: Include the child's own self-report where age-appropriate
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Children have a right to express their views in matters affecting them, and those views must be given due weight (UNCRC Article 12). In assessment, that means the child's own account sits beside the adults' — not below it, and not only where it agrees. Internal states such as anxiety and low mood are often under-reported by adults who see only behaviour. Lundy's model of participation — space, voice, audience, influence (British Educational Research Journal, 2007) — is a useful check that the view was heard and acted on.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor introduces a self-report form to a child: who reads the items, how they check understanding, and whether the child is told who will see the answers.

WRITE DOWN — the form, the child's age, how it was administered, and where the child's view appeared in the report.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a child's self-report says everything is fine and every adult says it isn't?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — administering the self-report with the child, reading items aloud where reading is a barrier, and recording anything the child says about the items.

THEY HOLD — how the child's account is weighted and worded in the report.

WHY THAT SPLIT — sitting with the child is direct, supervised practice. Where their view lands in the report shapes the conclusions, which your supervisor still holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer the self-report and write the section presenting the child's view, with your supervisor reviewing before it goes in.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the child's view summarised in one line after pages of adult ratings, or dismissed as 'lacking insight' without evidence.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'where in the report would the child find what they told you?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — include self-report wherever the child's age and ability allow, present it alongside adult reports, and say how it informed the conclusions.

PASS TEST — The child's account appears alongside the adults'

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the findings section showing the child's account in parallel with adult ratings. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report on a thirteen-year-old's anxiety with no self-report and no direct quote from the young person.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain Article 12, Lundy's model, and the practical adaptations — reading items aloud, visual scales, checking understanding — that let younger or less able children self-report validly.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the child refuses or cannot complete a self-report: record that, and gather their view another way — conversation, drawing, scaling questions.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving out the child's own view because the adults' forms were enough to score.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT

micro.name: Explain to informants how to complete them
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A rating scale is only as good as the completion. Forms come back with half the items blank, several boxes ticked on one item, notes in the margins instead of ratings, or completed jointly by two parents without saying so. Each invalidates or weakens the score. Most manuals set a maximum number of omitted items before a scale cannot be scored — check yours. Two minutes of explanation at the start saves a wasted form and a second request to a busy teacher.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor says when handing out or sending forms: the time period to rate, answering every item, one rater per form, what to do when unsure, and the return date.

WRITE DOWN — their instructions, and anything they put in a covering note for teachers.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the most common way forms come back unusable?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a covering note for teacher forms and giving the verbal explanation to parents, checked beforehand by your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether a returned form is valid enough to score.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the explanation is a script you can improve with feedback. Judging validity depends on the manual's rules and on experience of how different errors affect scores.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain the forms to every informant yourself, and check the forms on return before the informant leaves where you can.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — not stating the rating period ('in the last six months'), and not asking the informant to answer every item.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'did you mention the time period? Some of these answers sound like last year.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain the rating period, one rater per form, answering every item, and how to handle uncertainty. Check forms on return and follow up omissions quickly.

PASS TEST — Forms come back usable

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the covering note template and returned forms. Log against 1. Assessment and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a teacher form with twelve items blank, discovered a week later when the teacher has moved on to other work.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why each instruction matters for the score, and write a short covering note that gets forms back complete.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a form comes back incomplete: check the manual's omission rule, follow up the specific items if it is over, and never fill in or pro-rate beyond what the manual permits.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Sending forms without a stated rating period and a request to answer every item.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Score and convert to standardised scores' and into Working with Others — teachers and families as informants.

micro.name: Score and convert to standardised scores
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Most behaviour rating systems convert raw scores to T-scores (mean 50, SD 10) against a norm group chosen by age, sometimes sex, and sometimes a general or clinical sample. Choosing the wrong norm group, missing reverse-scored items, or mistyping into software all change the result without any sign on the page. Hand-scoring invites arithmetic errors; software moves the error to data entry. Either way, what makes the score trustworthy is the check.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor hand-scores or uses software, which norm group they choose and why, and how they check the entry.

WRITE DOWN — the instrument, the norm group, how omitted items were handled, and any validity or response-style index reported.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when do you use combined-sex norms and when separate, and does it change what you conclude?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — scoring the forms independently, including any validity indices, before seeing your supervisor's version.

THEY HOLD — the authoritative score and the choice of norm group.

WHY THAT SPLIT — double-scoring shows your systematic errors quickly. Norm-group choice changes the conclusion, so it is a judgement they keep until you can defend it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — score, choose norms, and present the scores in supervision with the norm group stated.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — reverse-scored items missed, the wrong age band, validity indices ignored, and scores typed into the report wrongly.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — picking one scale and asking you to re-score it by hand in front of them.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — score each form, check the scoring by a second method or on a second occasion, state the norm group in the report, and check validity indices before interpreting.

PASS TEST — Scoring is checked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — scored forms or software printout with your check marked, and the score table in the report. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a clinically significant score reported from a form whose validity index flagged an extreme response style.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain T-scores, norm-group choice, reverse scoring and validity indices, and show a peer a quick way to check software output against the raw form.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a validity index is flagged: do not interpret the clinical scales as if it were not, report the flag, and consider what the response style itself tells you.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Interpreting clinical scales without first checking the form's validity or response-style indices.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Analyse informant agreement and discrepancy' and 'Distinguish elevated from clinically significant'.

micro.name: Analyse informant agreement and discrepancy
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parent, teacher and child ratings routinely disagree. The Achenbach, McConaughy and Howell (1987) meta-analysis found cross-informant correlations were modest, and higher between similar informants than between different types — check the paper for the figures before quoting. Later work argues discrepancy often reflects real differences in how the child behaves across settings (De Los Reyes et al., Psychological Bulletin, 2015, on the Operations Triad Model). Treating discrepancy as someone being wrong throws away information about context.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor lays out scores from different informants: usually side by side by scale. Notice what they say about a scale where home and school differ sharply.

WRITE DOWN — each scale where informants differ by a meaningful amount (your manual may give a guide), and the explanation your supervisor offered.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a parent rates much higher than the teacher, what are the possible explanations, and how do you choose?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building the side-by-side table and listing, for each discrepancy, explanations based on setting, task demands, relationship and informant threshold.

THEY HOLD — which explanation the report adopts, and how it is worded.

WHY THAT SPLIT — generating alternative explanations is safe practice. The wording can make a parent feel disbelieved or a teacher feel blamed.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present the discrepancies and your reading of them in supervision, then draft the paragraph.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — averaging across informants, or writing one informant off as biased without evidence.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's different about the two settings that could make both ratings accurate?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — lay out informant scores side by side, treat each discrepancy as a question about context, and write the likeliest explanation with its evidence.

PASS TEST — Discrepancy treated as data about context

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the rating scale section of the report. Log against 1. Assessment and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'the parent's ratings may reflect heightened anxiety', written with no evidence and read by the parent at the feedback meeting.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why informants disagree, cite the cross-informant literature, and show a peer how to turn a discrepancy into a hypothesis about context that feeds the formulation.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when an informant disputes your reading of their rating: listen, check your interpretation against what they say about the setting, and revise if they have told you something you did not know.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Averaging parent and teacher scores into one number, losing the difference that was the finding.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify where sources diverge and say so', into Formulation — context and maintaining factors — and into Working with Others.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Distinguish elevated from clinically significant
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Rating systems band T-scores, and the bands mean specific things. On the BASC-3, clinical scales at 60–69 are 'at-risk' and 70 and above 'clinically significant' (Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015). On the ASEBA syndrome scales, 65–69 is borderline and 70 and above clinical (Achenbach & Rescorla, 2001). Other instruments use other cut-offs, so check each manual. 'Clinically significant' is a statistical statement about rarity against norms, not a diagnosis. Misusing either term misleads the reader about how concerned to be.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the exact words your supervisor uses for each band, and whether they explain the band in plain language in the report.

WRITE DOWN — the instrument, its band labels and cut-offs as printed in the manual, and the sentence your supervisor used to report an elevated score.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you explain to a parent that a clinically significant score doesn't mean their child has a disorder?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the band label and plain-language meaning beside each score in the draft score table.

THEY HOLD — how the scores are summarised in the conclusion and discussed with the family.

WHY THAT SPLIT — attaching the right label is checkable against the manual. Deciding how much weight an elevated score carries in the conclusion is interpretation.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — report the rating scale results in writing and in the feedback meeting, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'clinical' used to mean 'diagnosed', one instrument's cut-offs applied to another, and at-risk scores ignored because they are not clinical.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor rephrasing: 'what that means is that only about two in every hundred children in the norm group scored this high.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — report each score with the manual's band label, what the band means statistically, and a plain-language sentence, without implying diagnosis.

PASS TEST — You know what the cut-offs mean and say so

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the score table and narrative in the report. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a school acting on 'clinically significant anxiety' as if a diagnosis had been made.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain T-scores, percentiles and band cut-offs, why cut-offs differ between instruments, and why statistical rarity is not the same as disorder.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a score sits just under a cut-off but everything else suggests serious concern: report the score honestly, and let the wider evidence carry the conclusion.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using 'clinically significant' as if it meant 'diagnosed'.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into interpretation and limitations, into Formulation, and into onward referral decisions.

micro.name: Choose an adaptation proportionate to the need
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Some children cannot access a standardised procedure as written: sensory, motor, language, attention or anxiety needs get in the way. Refusing to adapt can breach the duty of reasonable accommodation (Equal Status Acts 2000–2018). Adapting too much means the score no longer means what the norms say. The Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014) separate accommodations, which leave the construct intact, from modifications, which change it. The skill is choosing the least adaptation that removes the barrier.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which adaptations your supervisor uses, and when: breaks, a changed order, repeated instructions, a different seating arrangement, an interpreter, or stopping.

WRITE DOWN — each adaptation, the barrier it responded to, and whether your supervisor considered it an accommodation or a modification.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the smallest change you could have made there, and why did you choose that one?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — planning adaptations before the session from what you know of the child, and writing down why each is needed.

THEY HOLD — decisions made in the room, and whether a proposed change would invalidate the norms.

WHY THAT SPLIT — planning ahead is reasoning you can check against the manual. In-the-moment decisions need experience of how each change affects the score.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer with your planned adaptations and make in-session decisions yourself, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — over-adapting (rephrasing items, extra prompts) out of kindness, and under-adapting out of fear of breaking the rules.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — suggesting a break rather than a rephrase: 'shall we stop for a minute?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — choose each adaptation deliberately from the least-change options (break, rephrase within the rules, reorder, discontinue), and know which ones change the construct.

PASS TEST — Break, rephrase, reorder or discontinue, chosen deliberately

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol annotations and the report's administration notes. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child who was given extra time and rephrased items reported with standard scores and no comment.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain accommodation versus modification with worked examples, the reasonable-accommodation duty, and what each common adaptation does to interpretability.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when an adaptation turns out to have changed the construct: report scores as descriptive rather than normative, and say why.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Rephrasing items to help the child, then reporting standard scores as though nothing changed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State the effect on validity in the report', 'Record the adaptation at the moment it happens', and Ethical Practice.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: State the effect on validity in the report
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Norms describe how children performed under standard conditions. Once conditions change, the reader needs to know whether the comparison still holds. Test publishers' guidance is that non-standard administration must be reported with its likely effect (AERA, APA & NCME, 2014; PSI Code 4.2.2). A score reported without that note tells the reader it means the same as any other score. If it does not, the report has misled them.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor reports adaptations: usually a short 'administration and validity' or 'behaviour during assessment' paragraph. Notice whether they say which scores are affected.

WRITE DOWN — the adaptation, the subtests affected, and the sentence stating whether scores remain interpretable.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when do you decide a score can't be reported at all?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the validity paragraph, naming each adaptation and the subtests it touched.

THEY HOLD — the judgement on whether the affected scores are interpretable, descriptive only, or should be withheld.

WHY THAT SPLIT — listing what changed is a record-keeping task. Whether a score still means something requires knowledge of the test's construct and norms.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the validity paragraph with your own judgement on interpretability, and defend it in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a validity statement that says 'results are a valid estimate' by default, and affected scores left in composites without comment.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that subtest was timed and you gave extra time. Can it go into the index?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for every adapted administration, state in the report what changed, which scores it affects, and whether each remains interpretable against the norms.

PASS TEST — You said whether scores remain interpretable

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the administration and validity paragraph of the report. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an index score built from a subtest you administered non-standardly, reported without comment and used to decide provision.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to judge interpretability subtest by subtest, when to report scores as descriptive, and when to withhold a composite.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise after sending the report that a score was compromised: tell your supervisor, issue a correction, and say whether the conclusions change.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A validity statement that says the results are valid when the administration was adapted.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record the adaptation at the moment it happens', into the limitations paragraph, and into Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Recognise when standard procedure is not working
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Standard procedure stops working in recognisable ways: the child disengages, becomes distressed, cannot understand the instructions, or answers from anxiety rather than ability. The later you notice, the more items are spoiled and the harder the session is to rescue. Early signs are often small — slowing responses, a change in posture, 'I don't know' before the item has been read. Noticing early is what makes a small adaptation enough.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moment your supervisor changes something, and what they noticed just before. Often it is a behaviour you did not register.

WRITE DOWN — the sign, the time, the subtest, and what your supervisor did.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what did you see just before you offered a break?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — watching and noting signs of strain during your supervisor's administration, and comparing your notes with theirs afterwards.

THEY HOLD — deciding when to act.

WHY THAT SPLIT — when you are not administering, all your attention can go on the child, which is how you learn to see the signs. Deciding to act changes the assessment, so it stays with them.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer, watch for signs, and act when you see them, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — pressing on to finish the subtest when the child is clearly struggling, because stopping feels like failure.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a quiet 'how are you doing?' to the child, which gives you the cue.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — notice strain early and act in proportion, and record when and what you saw.

PASS TEST — You noticed early rather than at the end

EVIDENCE TO FILE — protocol annotations with time and behaviour, and the behavioural observations section of the report. Log against 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child in tears by the final subtest, and a protocol with no note of when it started.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can describe the early signs of disengagement, anxiety and confusion, and how to tell them apart, and explain why acting early protects both the child and the validity of the scores.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you missed the signs and the session ended badly: tell your supervisor, check on the child, record it, and judge whether the later scores can be reported.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Pushing through to the end of the subtest because stopping feels like losing the score.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record the adaptation at the moment it happens', 'Re-evaluate whether to continue at all', and the behavioural observations section.

micro.name: Record the adaptation at the moment it happens
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A reconstructed record is not a record. By the time you write up, you will not remember which item you rephrased, how long the break was, or whether you repeated an instruction. CORU SoP 2.8 ties record-keeping to accuracy and timeliness. A protocol annotated in the moment is the only thing that lets you, your supervisor or a later reviewer judge which scores were affected. Without it you cannot write the validity statement honestly.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how and when your supervisor annotates the protocol: margin notes, standard abbreviations, the time written beside a break.

WRITE DOWN — the abbreviations they use and what each means.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's your shorthand for a repeated instruction, a prompt and a break?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — annotating the protocol in real time while your supervisor administers.

THEY HOLD — the administration.

WHY THAT SPLIT — annotating at speed while watching the child is its own skill. Practising it without the load of administering builds the habit before you need both at once.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer and annotate at the same time, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — adaptations made and not written down, and notes added afterwards from memory.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — at the end, 'show me where you wrote down the break.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — annotate every adaptation on the protocol as it happens: what changed, which item, the time. Do not add to the record after the session except as a dated, clearly marked addition.

PASS TEST — Annotated on the protocol, not reconstructed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the annotated protocol. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a validity paragraph written from memory that does not match the protocol, found on audit.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can teach a consistent annotation shorthand and explain why contemporaneous records carry weight that reconstructed ones do not.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you did not record something: add a dated, clearly marked note saying it was written afterwards, and weaken any claim that depends on it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing up adaptations from memory after the session and presenting them as the record.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State the effect on validity in the report', and into Ethical Practice — record-keeping.

micro.name: Re-evaluate whether to continue at all
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Sometimes the right adaptation is to stop. A child who is distressed, unwell, withdrawing assent, or unable to access the task at all is not giving you valid data, and continuing may harm them and their trust in adults who assess them. Assent is ongoing, not a form signed at the start. Trainees often find stopping hardest because it feels like failing the assessment. Stopping well is a professional decision, not a failure.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor stops or reschedules a session, and how they explain it to the child, the parent and the school.

WRITE DOWN — the signs that led to stopping, what was said to the child, and what was planned instead.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the threshold where you stop rather than adapt?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — watching for signs that assent has been withdrawn, and saying so to your supervisor, quietly or at a break.

THEY HOLD — the decision to stop, and the conversation with the family and school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — noticing withdrawn assent is something you can do from the first session. Stopping has consequences — rescheduling, waiting lists, school expectations — that your supervisor manages.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make the call to continue, adapt or stop in your own session, with your supervisor present to support.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — continuing because the school is waiting for the report, or because stopping feels like admitting something went wrong.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'do you want to check with them whether they'd like to keep going?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep checking assent through the session, stop when the child cannot or will not continue validly, and record the reason.

PASS TEST — You were willing to stop

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the protocol note and a case note of the reason and the plan. Log against 1. Assessment and 6. Ethical Practice. Consider Appendix 8 if it raised a dilemma.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a distressed child pushed through the battery, and scores reported as though the session were typical.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain ongoing assent, the signs that it has been withdrawn, and why stopping protects both the child and the validity of the assessment.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a school or parent pushes back on a stopped session: explain that invalid scores would harm the child more than a delay, and offer a plan for completing the assessment.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Continuing a session the child has clearly withdrawn from because the report is due.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Ethical Practice — consent, assent and the child's welfare — and into 'State the effect on validity in the report'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Read all four frameworks named in the handbook
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Handbook §2.1 names four frameworks: Monsen's Problem-Analysis Framework (Monsen & Frederickson, 2008), COMOIRA (Gameson & Rhydderch, 2008), the Interactive Factors Framework (Frederickson & Cline, 2009, after Morton & Frith), and Carr's model (Carr, 2015). The first two are chapters in Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle (Eds.), Frameworks for Practice in Educational Psychology (2008). A trainee who has not read them does not work without a framework. They work with an implicit one, usually a within-child deficit model picked up from report templates, and cannot defend it when asked.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which framework your supervisor's reports reflect, even if unnamed: hypotheses with evidence for and against (Monsen), levels with arrows (IFF), competing accounts held side by side (COMOIRA), or predisposing/precipitating/perpetuating/protective factors (Carr).

WRITE DOWN — for each of three reports, which framework you think it reflects and the sentence that told you.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'did you train in one of the four, or did you come to your approach another way?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading all four in the original chapters, not summaries, and writing one page on each: what it foregrounds, its stages, what it leaves out, what referral it suits.

THEY HOLD — correcting your reading where it misrepresents a framework.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading is yours and cannot be delegated. A supervisor's check catches the common misreadings, such as treating COMOIRA as 'just consultation'.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain each framework in supervision in two minutes, without notes, and say what it foregrounds.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — descriptions that make the four sound interchangeable, and an account of Monsen with no competing hypotheses in it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what does COMOIRA put at the centre that Monsen doesn't?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name all four, their authors and sources, and state in a sentence what each foregrounds.

PASS TEST — You can name what each foregrounds

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your four one-page summaries, kept in your portfolio. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at a viva or examiner's question you can name the frameworks but not say how they differ.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can teach a first-year trainee the four frameworks in one session, with a worked case run through each, citing the original chapters.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you have been working from an implicit within-child model: re-read one current case through a named framework and see what changes.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Reading summaries of the frameworks instead of the chapters, so the stages are remembered but not the reasoning.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify what each framework is good for', 'Identify what each leaves out', and 'Choose a framework deliberately for this case'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Identify what each framework is good for
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Each framework suits different referrals. The Reference sheet (Part C) sets it out: Monsen for contested questions and disagreeing informants; the IFF for multi-level developmental and learning presentations; COMOIRA where the adults hold incompatible views and consultation leads; Carr where onset and maintenance matter, such as school avoidance or emerging low mood. If you cannot match framework to referral, you cannot choose, and you will default.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the referral types your supervisor gets, and how they approach each: which ones they treat as hypothesis-testing, which as consultation, which as developmental.

WRITE DOWN — for each case you see, the referral type and the framework you think would have suited it best.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which kind of referral do you find hardest to formulate, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building a table: referral types down the side, the four frameworks across, with a note on fit for each.

THEY HOLD — correcting fit from their experience of real cases.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the table is reasoning you can do from reading. Experience is what shows where a framework looks right on paper and fails in practice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each new referral, say in supervision which framework you think fits and why, before any data is gathered.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the same answer for every referral, or a choice justified by preference rather than by the referral.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the parents and school disagree completely here. Does that change your choice?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — match each referral to a framework on the basis of what the referral is: contested, multi-level, a disagreement among adults, or about onset and maintenance.

PASS TEST — You can say which referral type suits which

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the fit table in your portfolio, and a line in each case record naming the choice. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — Carr's model applied to a whole-class behaviour consultation, producing an individual formulation of a systemic problem.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a worked referral for each framework and explain why it fits better than the other three.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a case changes character midway, such as a learning referral that becomes a disagreement among adults: say so, and switch framework openly rather than bending the first one.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Choosing a framework because you like it rather than because the referral calls for it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Choose a framework deliberately for this case' and 'Identify what each leaves out'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Identify what each leaves out
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Every framework has a blind spot, and knowing yours is what PSI Code 4.2.6 asks of you here. The Reference sheet names them: Monsen can tidy a messy situation by dropping hypotheses that did not resolve; the IFF's arrows are easy to draw and hard to justify, since each is a causal claim; COMOIRA can drift away from the data; Carr's model centres the individual and can under-weight the classroom. If you cannot say what your preferred framework misses, you will miss it too, every time.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — moments where your supervisor's formulation seems to leave something out: the classroom in an individual formulation, or the child's view in a hypothesis-testing one.

WRITE DOWN — what was left out, and which framework feature made it easy to leave out.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what does your usual approach tend to miss?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing, for each framework, one sentence on what it leaves out and one example of a case where that would matter.

THEY HOLD — correcting your examples.

WHY THAT SPLIT — critique of frameworks is part of your reading. Examples from real cases are where supervisor experience adds most.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for your own formulation, state in supervision what the chosen framework is likely to have missed in this case, and what you did about it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a framework treated as complete, and a limitation stated in general terms but not checked against this case.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you used Carr. Where's the classroom in this?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name the limitation of the framework you used, check whether it affected this case, and say so in the limitations paragraph.

PASS TEST — You can name a limitation of your preferred one

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the limitations paragraph of the report. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an IFF diagram with arrows nobody can justify, and no sentence acknowledging that they are hypotheses.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain each framework's blind spot, give a case where it matters, and show how to compensate for it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the blind spot has shaped a finished formulation: revisit it using a second framework as a check, and revise if the second view shows something the first missed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating your preferred framework as if it had no blind spot.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Make your preferred framework explicit in supervision' and into the limitations paragraph.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — moments where your supervisor's formulation seems to leave something out: the classroom in an individual formulation, or the child's view in a hypothesis-testing one.

micro.name: Make your preferred framework explicit in supervision
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Everyone has a default. Stating yours in supervision lets your supervisor watch for the blind spot that comes with it, and challenge you when the default does not fit the case. Handbook §6 and CORU SoP 5.44 are the references mapped here — read §6 for the programme's expectation of supervision. An unstated default is invisible to both of you, so neither can correct it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about their own theoretical orientation, and whether they do.

WRITE DOWN — the framework you notice yourself reaching for first when you read a new referral.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's my default, from what you've seen of my work so far?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — naming your default framework in supervision, with an honest reason why it is your default: training, comfort, or genuine fit.

THEY HOLD — watching for when the default is being applied where it does not fit.

WHY THAT SPLIT — only you can name your default. Spotting its misuse needs an outside eye.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — state your default at the start of placement, and each time you choose a framework, say whether this is the default or a deliberate departure.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — naming a default and then never departing from it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that's your default again. Did you consider the others?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — your supervisor knows your default without asking, and you flag every case where you use it.

PASS TEST — Your supervisor knows what you default to

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision record. Log against 2. Formulation and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at your mid-placement review, your supervisor notes that every formulation used the same framework, and you had not noticed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why defaults are inevitable, and how stating them in supervision turns them from a blind spot into something checkable.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find you have defaulted on every case: take the last three cases and re-formulate one with a different framework, in supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Never naming your default, so no one can spot where it misleads you.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask your supervisor which they use and why' and into Supervision.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about their own theoretical orientation, and whether they do.

micro.name: Ask your supervisor which they use and why
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Supervisors have defaults too, and yours shapes how your reports will be read and corrected. Knowing whether your supervisor was trained in a framework, or came to their approach through experience, tells you what they will look for and where they are likely to push back. CORU SoP 4.5 is the standard mapped here. It is a legitimate question, and most supervisors welcome it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the framework your supervisor's reports and case discussions reflect.

WRITE DOWN — your guess at their default, before you ask.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which framework do you use most, and were you trained in it, or did you come to it another way?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking the question in an early supervision session, and noting the answer.

THEY HOLD — their answer, and how much they want to discuss it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — asking is yours, and it signals that you are thinking about frameworks rather than just filling in a report. How far to take the conversation is theirs.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — use what you know of your supervisor's framework to anticipate their feedback, and say so: 'I know you'd usually look at this through X; I've used Y because…'

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — adopting their framework to please them rather than because it fits.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'don't use mine because it's mine.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — know your supervisor's framework, whether they trained in it, and how it shapes their reading of your work.

PASS TEST — You know whether they were trained in it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision record. Log against 2. Formulation and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — repeated feedback you do not understand, because you and your supervisor are working from different frameworks without knowing it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why knowing a supervisor's framework matters, and how to raise it without it sounding like a challenge.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when your frameworks conflict on a case: name the difference in supervision and agree which fits this referral, with reasons.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking on your supervisor's framework by imitation, without knowing that is what you are doing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Supervision and into 'Choose a framework deliberately for this case'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Choose a framework deliberately for this case
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The referral question should choose the framework, not habit. The Reference sheet gives the test: is the difficulty contested (Monsen), multi-level and developmental (IFF), a disagreement between adults (COMOIRA), or about onset and maintenance (Carr)? Choose before collecting data, because the framework decides what data you need. A framework chosen after the data is in is retrospective justification. An examiner will see that immediately.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when in the process your supervisor settles on an approach: at referral, after the first meeting, or only at write-up.

WRITE DOWN — the referral, the framework, and the point at which it was chosen.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what in this referral told you which framework to use?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — proposing the framework for a case at referral, in writing, with one line of reasoning.

THEY HOLD — agreeing or redirecting the choice.

WHY THAT SPLIT — making the choice explicit is yours. Their agreement protects the case while your judgement is calibrating.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — choose the framework at referral, plan the data collection from it, and defend the choice in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a choice made after the data, and a data plan that does not follow from the framework.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if you're using Monsen, what are your competing hypotheses before you go in?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — choose the framework at referral, write the reason down, and plan data collection from it.

PASS TEST — You can say why this one and not another

EVIDENCE TO FILE — case record noting framework and reason, and the report. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report that names Monsen but was clearly written first and framed afterwards.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how the referral chooses the framework, with worked examples of each choice.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when new information shows the framework was wrong: say so, change it, and record why, rather than forcing the data into the original choice.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Choosing the framework after writing the report, to fit what you found.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name and cite it in the report' and 'Use the framework's own structure'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Name and cite it in the report
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Naming and citing the framework tells the reader how to read your formulation, and lets them check it against the source. The Reference sheet calls naming the framework in the report 'the marker' for Year 1 formulation. It also shows your reasoning rests on a published model rather than personal judgement alone. A report that uses a framework without naming it hides its structure. One that names a framework without using it is worse.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor names a framework in their reports, and where: the method section, the formulation heading, or not at all.

WRITE DOWN — how it is cited, and whether the citation is APA 7th.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do schools and parents find the framework name helpful, or is it for other psychologists?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — adding the framework name and a full APA 7th citation to the draft, in the method and formulation sections.

THEY HOLD — deciding how much explanation of the framework the audience needs.

WHY THAT SPLIT — naming and citing is mechanical. Pitching it for a parent or teacher readership is judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — name, cite, and briefly explain the framework in plain language in each report.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a name dropped in the introduction with no sign of the framework anywhere else.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you cite IFF. Where are the levels?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name the framework, cite it in APA 7th, and explain it in one plain sentence for the reader.

PASS TEST — It appears by name with a citation

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a formulation an examiner cannot place in any framework, or one that names a framework it does not follow.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why naming the framework matters to different readers, and how to explain each in one plain sentence.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent asks what the framework means: explain it simply in terms of what you looked at and why.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Citing a framework decoratively, with nothing in the report that uses it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Use the framework's own structure'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Use the framework's own structure
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A framework you name should shape the report. The Reference sheet's test: delete the framework's name from your report — could a reader still tell which one you used? If you chose Monsen, there is a hypotheses section with evidence for and against. If IFF, there are levels and stated interactions. If Carr, there are predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors. If COMOIRA, the different accounts are held side by side with a focus on change.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how the structure of your supervisor's reports follows, or does not follow, a framework.

WRITE DOWN — the headings of the formulation section, and which framework stage each corresponds to.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you adapt the framework's structure for school readers, and how?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the formulation section using the framework's stages as headings or clear signposts.

THEY HOLD — how much of the structure is visible in the version sent to the family.

WHY THAT SPLIT — using the structure is the discipline you need to build. How visible to make it for a lay reader is a judgement about audience.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the formulation following the framework's stages, and walk your supervisor through it stage by stage.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a standard report with a framework sentence bolted on.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'take the name out. Which framework is this?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write every formulation so that the framework's stages are visible to a reader who knows the framework.

PASS TEST — The stages are visible rather than implied

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a formulation that could have been written with any framework, or none.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show how each framework's structure appears in a report, with an example for each.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the structure makes the report hard for a parent to follow: keep the structure in the formulation section, and write a plain summary for the family.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing a standard report and adding a framework sentence to the introduction.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Show the reasoning step by step'.

micro.name: Show the reasoning step by step
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A conclusion without visible reasoning cannot be checked or challenged. It can only be accepted or rejected whole. CORU SoP 3.5 and PSI Code 4.2.5 (distinguish facts, opinions, theories and hypotheses) are the standards mapped here. The Reference sheet's worked example: not 'John has a specific learning difficulty' but his percentile scores, what rules out instruction and attendance, and the most parsimonious remaining explanation. The second version can be argued with — that is the point.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor moves from data to conclusion in writing: whether each inference is stated or left to the reader.

WRITE DOWN — one paragraph where the reasoning is visible, and one where it is not.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a parent challenges a conclusion, what do you point them to?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting a formulation paragraph as a chain: finding → what it rules out → what remains → conclusion.

THEY HOLD — testing each link.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the chain exposes your reasoning. Testing it needs someone who can spot the weak link.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the full formulation as visible reasoning and present it in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — conclusions stated as fact, and inference steps skipped because they felt obvious.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'how did you get from that score to that conclusion?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write each conclusion with its evidence, what it rules out, and why the conclusion is the best remaining explanation.

PASS TEST — Someone could point at where they disagree

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the formulation section. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent disputes a conclusion, and the report gives you nothing to point to except the conclusion itself.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to turn a conclusion into a chain of reasoning, and explain why that protects both the child and the psychologist.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when someone points at a link and disagrees: consider it on its merits, and revise if they are right.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Stating conclusions as fact without the inference that led to them.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Generate more than one hypothesis' and 'Test each hypothesis against the data'.

Not started

micro.name: Include the child's construction of the problem
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Every framework in the handbook has a place for the child's own account, and the Reference sheet notes it is the element most often left out of trainee reports. UNCRC Article 12 and CORU SoP 5.11 are the standards mapped here. The child's construction — what they think is hard, what helps, what they would change — should shape the formulation, not decorate it in a quote box. If it contradicts the adults' view, that contradiction is a finding.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor asks the child for their view: the questions, the tools (drawing, scaling, sorting), and where the answer ends up in the report.

WRITE DOWN — the questions, and one example of the child's view changing the formulation.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when has a child's view changed your formulation?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — gathering the child's view directly, using age-appropriate methods, and recording it in their words.

THEY HOLD — how the child's view is weighed in the formulation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — gathering the view is direct work you can do with support. Weighing it against adult accounts is formulation judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — gather the child's view and write it into the formulation, showing what it changed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the child's view in a box at the start, disconnected from the formulation.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if you took the child's words out, would the formulation change? It should.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — ask the child directly, record their construction in their words, and show in the formulation how it shaped your conclusions.

PASS TEST — The child's view shapes it, not just decorates it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the formulation section. Log against 2. Formulation and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a formulation built entirely from adult accounts, with a child quote added for colour.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain Article 12, the methods for eliciting a child's view at different ages, and how to integrate it into each of the four frameworks.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the child's view contradicts everyone else's: treat it as data about how the difficulty is experienced, and let it shape the recommendations.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Quoting the child for colour while building the formulation entirely from adult accounts.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify where sources diverge and say so', into Intervention planning, and into Ethical Practice — the child's voice.

micro.name: Generate more than one hypothesis
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Almost every referral arrives with the secondary need on the form: the school refers for behaviour, and the behaviour is downstream of an unidentified reading difficulty. The hypothesis-testing stance in Monsen et al.'s problem analysis framework (Educational Psychology in Practice, 1998) and the Reference sheet both set two genuinely competing hypotheses as the minimum. PSI Code 4.2.6 and CORU SoP 3.5 are mapped here. One hypothesis, tested only for confirming evidence, produces an intervention for a symptom that will not work.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moment your supervisor first voices an explanation for a referral, and whether a second one follows before any data is gathered. Notice whether the alternatives genuinely compete (escape from literacy demand v. attention-seeking v. a class-wide demand problem) or are the same idea in two phrasings.

WRITE DOWN — every hypothesis named, and for each, the one piece of data that would distinguish it from the others.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which of those did you think was most likely before you went in, and what would have changed your mind?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing two or three competing hypotheses for a live referral before the planning meeting, each with the observation, interview question or test result that would support it and the one that would undermine it.

THEY HOLD — deciding which hypotheses are worth the data collection time on a busy caseload, and adding the one you did not think of.

WHY THAT SPLIT — generating alternatives is thinking you can practise safely on paper. Knowing which ones a school's time can afford comes from years of seeing which turn out to matter.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each new case, bring your hypotheses to supervision in writing before the first school visit, and plan the observation and interviews so each hypothesis gets a fair test.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a 'second' hypothesis that is a relabelling of the first ('dyslexia' and 'a specific reading difficulty'), and a data plan that could only ever confirm the favoured one.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'both of those predict the same thing in the classroom. What would you see if you were wrong?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — at referral, write at least two hypotheses that predict different data, plan a comparison observation or history question that separates them, and record them on the case file before you collect anything.

PASS TEST — An alternative was genuinely considered

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the dated hypothesis note on the case file and the formulation section of the report. Log against 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report for a child referred for behaviour that never asks whether the behaviour clusters around reading tasks, because 'behaviour' was the only hypothesis on the table.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to test whether two hypotheses genuinely compete (do they predict different observations?), and walk through the Reference sheet's three-way example for a behaviour referral, naming the data each predicts.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when data arrives that fits none of your hypotheses: stop, write a new one that does fit, say in supervision that your first set was too narrow, and replan rather than squeezing the data into the nearest fit.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Offering two hypotheses that are the same explanation in different words, so nothing was actually tested.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Test each hypothesis against the data' and 'Record the hypothesis you rejected and why'.
