micro.name: Take a baseline before it starts
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Without a baseline there is no way to attribute change (Reference sheet, literacy), and CORU SoP 3.8 requires you to evaluate what you do. The measure must be sensitive to short-term change — curriculum-based measurement, words correct per minute, non-word reading — not the school's annual standardised test, which will not move in a term. Deno (1985) is the classic source on curriculum-based measurement. Skip the baseline and the review will rest on 'she seems more confident', which cannot tell anyone whether to continue.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which measure your supervisor chooses for which reading component, and how carefully they administer it: timing, passage level, instructions, and the conditions they note so it can be repeated identically later.

WRITE DOWN — the measure, the component it tracks, and the conditions (time of day, who gave it, which materials, any interruptions) so that someone else could repeat it exactly.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how many baseline points do you like to take, and what do you do when the child's scores bounce around from day to day?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — administering the baseline probe (for example a one-minute oral reading fluency passage or a non-word reading list) under your supervisor's guidance, and recording the conditions.

THEY HOLD — the choice of measure where a tool is restricted, and the interpretation of the baseline.

WHY THAT SPLIT — administering a probe is procedural and easy to check. Choosing a measure and interpreting it depends on knowing its sensitivity and limits, which you read in the measure's own manual or source rather than taking on trust.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — choose a measure matched to the targeted component and take the baseline yourself before session one, with your supervisor checking your choice. Take more than one data point if you can, and record the dates DD/MM/YYYY.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the school's annual standardised score used as the baseline; a baseline taken after the intervention has already begun; a measure that does not match the component being taught.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if this intervention works, will this number move in eight weeks? If not, pick another.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before the first session, there is a dated baseline on a measure sensitive to the targeted component, with the conditions recorded well enough that someone else could repeat it.

PASS TEST — There is a pre-measure

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the baseline record attached to the support plan. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at review, the only numbers are this year's and last year's standardised test results; the question 'did it work?' cannot be answered, and the school keeps the child in the group out of habit.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a baseline matters, why short-term-sensitive measures beat annual tests for this purpose, and how to record conditions so the measure is repeatable, pointing a peer to Deno (1985) and the Reference sheet's section on measuring it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when an intervention has started without a baseline: take one now, label it clearly as taken after the start, and be honest in the review about what that does and does not allow you to conclude.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Starting an intervention with no pre-measure, or using the annual standardised test as the only measure.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Set a review point and a measure' and into Research — practice-based evaluation.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Set a review point and a measure
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 3.8 and 5.37 require you to evaluate and revise, and you cannot revise what you did not measure (Reference sheet). PSI Code 3.1.2 is also mapped here. The review date and measure belong in the report, written so that the school can carry them out without you — a trainee leaves Cavan on 18/12/2026, and most reviews will fall after that. A review that only you could run is a review that will not happen.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor writes the review: the date, the measure, who takes it, what will count as enough progress, and what decisions the review will lead to (continue, intensify, change approach, stop).

WRITE DOWN — their wording for the review section and the decision options, and how they decide in advance what counts as progress.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide beforehand what counts as enough progress, so the review is not just a feeling in the room?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the review section: date, measure, who will administer it, and the decision options.

THEY HOLD — the threshold for 'enough progress' and how that is explained to the school and the family.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a threshold needs judgement about what change is realistic for this child. Check the measure's own guidance on expected growth rather than inventing a rate; your supervisor knows what the service uses and what has been defensible in past reviews.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the review section and present it at the meeting, then hand the SET the probe materials and a one-page instruction sheet so they can take the measure themselves.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a measure only you can administer; a review date after you leave with nobody named to hold it; 'progress will be reviewed' with no date at all.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if you were off sick on the review date, could the SET do this from what you have written? Show me the instruction sheet.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every plan has a dated review, a named measure, the role who takes it, and the decisions it will inform, written so that the school can run it without you.

PASS TEST — Measurable by someone other than you

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the plan with its review section, and the instruction sheet you gave the SET. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you leave Cavan on 18/12/2026, the review date passes in February, and nobody in the school knows what to measure, how, or what the numbers are meant to be compared against.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to design a review a school can run alone: a repeatable measure, decision rules set in advance, and a named role holding the date.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the review shows no change: check first the dose actually received and whether it was delivered as designed, then whether the component was right, and only then change the approach — which is what Grade 5 in the Reference sheet asks you to be able to say.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A review that depends on you being there, so it lapses when the placement ends.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Leave the teacher able to run it', into 'Specify what success would look like' for numeracy, and into Systemic Change.

micro.name: Know concrete–pictorial–abstract sequencing
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Concrete–pictorial–abstract sequencing, with the concrete stage not rushed, is one of the approaches the Reference sheet lists as evidence-supported for numeracy. Its roots are usually traced to Bruner's (1966) enactive, iconic and symbolic modes of representation. Most teachers know the phrase; the common problems are moving to numerals too early and using manipulatives as an activity rather than to show mathematical structure. CORU SoP 5.33 is mapped here. If you cannot explain it plainly, you cannot tell whether a classroom is doing it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor or an experienced SET moves a child from objects (cubes, counters, ten-frames, base-ten blocks) to drawings (dots, bar models, number lines) to numerals, and what they check before moving on.

WRITE DOWN — one worked example for one skill, for example subtraction as taking away counters → crossing out drawn dots → 7 − 3 = 4, and the question used at each step to check the link.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell whether a child needs to go back to the concrete stage, or is just using the cubes out of habit?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a one-page CPA explanation with a worked example for a specific skill on your caseload, and checking the wording with your supervisor before using it.

THEY HOLD — the conversation with a teacher whose classroom practice does not fit the approach.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the explanation tests whether you actually understand it. Advising an experienced teacher on their own maths teaching needs a credibility that you build over the placement, and a clumsy first attempt can close the door.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain CPA to a class teacher or SET in a consultation, linked to the child's target skill, with your supervisor present. Show the pictorial bridge, not only the two ends.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jargon; presenting manipulatives as the point rather than as a picture of structure; implying that the concrete stage is only for infant classes.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'could you show her what the pictorial step would look like for this child's sum, using the ten-frame she already has?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain CPA to a teacher, briefly and without jargon, with one example tied to the child's actual target, and say what the teacher should see at each stage before moving on.

PASS TEST — You can explain it to a teacher in two minutes

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the consultation note and your one-page explanation. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the teacher leaves thinking the advice was 'use more cubes', and the child is still counting every cube from one in Fourth Class with no link to the written sum.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain where CPA comes from (Bruner, 1966), why the concrete stage should not be rushed, and how representations carry structure, with one example for place value and one for fractions. Point a peer to the EEF guidance reports on improving mathematics listed in the Reference sheet and read their recommendations on manipulatives and representations directly.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child is stuck at the concrete stage: check whether the pictorial bridge was skipped, and whether the real difficulty is conceptual (cardinality, part–whole) rather than representation.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending 'use concrete materials' without explaining the move through pictorial to abstract.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Distinguish fact retrieval from conceptual difficulty' and 'Specify what success would look like'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor or an experienced SET moves a child from objects (cubes, counters, ten-frames, base-ten blocks) to drawings (dots, bar models, number lines) to numerals, and what they check before moving on.

micro.name: Distinguish fact retrieval from conceptual difficulty
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A child who has not secured cardinality cannot meaningfully do addition, and drilling addition facts will not help (Reference sheet, numeracy). A child who understands number relationships but cannot retrieve facts quickly needs something quite different. Gersten et al. (2009) and Butterworth, Varma and Laurillard (2011) are the Reference sheet's sources on this. CORU SoP 3.4 and 5.34 are mapped. Confuse the two and the child gets flashcard drill for a conceptual gap, or is re-taught concepts they already hold.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor probes strategy rather than accuracy: asking the child to show or explain how they got an answer; watching for counting all from one versus counting on; noticing derived facts ('6 + 7 is 6 + 6 and one more'); giving the same problem orally and in writing.

WRITE DOWN — the strategies you saw, in the child's words, with rough time taken and the errors made.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what exactly did you see that made you think this was retrieval and not understanding?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the strategy interview part ('how did you work that out?') and recording what the child does, word for word where possible.

THEY HOLD — the interpretation, and the decision whether a standardised mathematics measure is needed and which one.

WHY THAT SPLIT — careful observation is something you can do well from the start. Interpretation depends on knowing the developmental sequence (subitising, counting, cardinality, comparison, part–whole, derived facts, procedures — Reference sheet) well enough to place the child in it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — give tasks that separate the two: untimed conceptual tasks (show it with objects, place it on a number line, explain why) alongside a brief timed fact probe, and a calculation with and without the language wrapper. Your supervisor watches.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — reading 'slow' as 'does not understand'; reading correct answers reached by slow counting as mastery; ignoring reading load, working memory or anxiety as sources of failure.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'she got it right — but how? Ask her to show you.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — your report states whether the difficulty is fact retrieval, conceptual, or both, gives the observed evidence for that, and the recommendation targets the one you found.

PASS TEST — The recommendation targets the right one

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the strategy notes and the report section linking evidence to recommendation. Log against 3. Intervention and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — daily times-table drill recommended for a child who still counts all from one to add 4 and 3, who then learns to fear maths as well as not understand it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the developmental sequence in number, what a retrieval difficulty and a conceptual difficulty each look like in a child's behaviour, and which quick tasks separate them, citing Gersten et al. (2009) and Dowker (2004).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a review shows fact speed improved but word problems did not: re-examine the other sources the Reference sheet names — reading load, working memory, anxiety — and re-specify rather than extending the drill.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending fact drill for a child whose difficulty is conceptual, such as unsecured cardinality.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Recommend at the right point on the Continuum' and into Formulation.

WATCH FOR — how your supervisor probes strategy rather than accuracy: asking the child to show or explain how they got an answer; watching for counting all from one versus counting on; noticing derived facts ('6 + 7 is 6 + 6 and one more'); giving the same problem orally and in writing.

micro.name: Recommend at the right point on the Continuum
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Irish schools allocate support through the NEPS Continuum of Support: Classroom Support, School Support and School Support Plus. A recommendation that does not name a level leaves the school guessing how to resource it (Reference sheet). If you recommend School Support Plus, say what makes it that rather than School Support — usually intensity, individualisation and the involvement of outside services. Jumping to the top level because a psychologist is involved can pull resource from a child who needed it more, and can skip what the class teacher could have done.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor asks where the child currently sits on the Continuum, what has been tried at each level and for how long, and how that is recorded in the school's Student Support File or equivalent.

WRITE DOWN — the current level, the interventions tried, their duration and dose, and the outcome, as the school described them.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what would make you recommend School Support Plus rather than School Support for a maths difficulty?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reviewing the Student Support File (with consent in place) and summarising what has been tried at each level, including gaps in the record.

THEY HOLD — any recommendation that moves the child to a different level, especially to School Support Plus, which carries implications for NEPS and outside-agency involvement.

WHY THAT SPLIT — summarising the record is careful reading. Moving a child between levels affects how the school allocates its special education teaching, and your supervisor knows the school's caseload and the service's practice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — state the level with your reasons in the consultation, supervisor present, and include what the class teacher does at Classroom Support level whatever else is recommended.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jumping to School Support Plus because the child was referred to psychology; leaving out the classroom-level actions; naming a level without saying what distinguishes it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'whatever level we agree, what does the class teacher do differently on Monday morning?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every numeracy recommendation names the Continuum level, says why that level rather than the one below, and includes the classroom-level actions that continue alongside.

PASS TEST — Level stated

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report recommendation and the school's updated support plan. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'the school should provide maths support' — the principal cannot tell whether that means a change in class, a place in the SET group, or a referral on, and does nothing until the next contact.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the three Continuum levels, how a numeracy difficulty is placed on them, and why the classroom level never drops out, pointing a peer to the NEPS Continuum of Support guidelines. You can also say, per PSI Code 2.3.1, why a report should admit that the numeracy evidence base is thinner than the literacy one.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the school disagrees about the level: return to what has been tried and its outcomes, agree a time-limited trial at the lower level with a review date, and involve your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Omitting the Continuum level, so the school cannot tell how to allocate the support.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Specify what success would look like' and into Systemic Change — school-level provision.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Specify what success would look like
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 3.8 requires evaluation, and in numeracy, where the evidence base is thinner than for literacy (Reference sheet), a clear local definition of success matters even more. 'Improved number skills' cannot be checked. A success criterion a teacher can observe — for example, 'counts on from the larger number to add within 20 without prompting' — can. Without one, the review becomes a matter of opinion and the child either stays in a group that is not working or leaves one that is.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor turns a finding into an observable target: the behaviour, the conditions, how often it must be seen, and how the teacher will check it.

WRITE DOWN — two or three targets they write, and note which part is the behaviour, which the condition, and which the level expected.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you set a target ambitious enough to matter but modest enough that the child can reach it this term?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting two or three observable success criteria for a child on your caseload, each tied to where you placed them in the developmental sequence.

THEY HOLD — judgement on whether the targets are realistic for the period and the dose agreed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing observable targets is a learnable technical skill. Judging how far a child is likely to move in a term takes experience, and there is no universal rate to look up — check any growth expectation against the measure's own guidance.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — agree the success criteria with the class teacher or SET at the meeting, supervisor present, and check that the teacher can say how they would see each one in an ordinary lesson.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — targets that describe what the adult will do ('will receive support') rather than what the child will do; targets only a psychologist could assess.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'Ms X, if you saw this on a Wednesday, how would you know? What would he be doing?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every numeracy plan has observable success criteria, stated in terms of what the child will do, under what conditions, checked how and by whom, by a stated date.

PASS TEST — A teacher would know whether it worked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the plan with success criteria, and the consultation note where the teacher agreed them. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at review, the teacher says 'he's doing a bit better, I think', the SET says 'not really', and there is nothing written to settle it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to turn a developmental finding into an observable target (behaviour, condition, level, date, checker) and why targets about the adult's input do not count.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the criteria turn out to be set wrongly: revise them openly at the review, record why, and do not move the goalposts quietly to make an intervention look successful.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing targets about the support given rather than what the child will be able to do.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Measure something before and after' and into Intervention review at the next placement.

micro.name: Know the evidence base for what you recommend
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 5.33 and 5.41 are mapped here. The evidence is uneven: social and emotional learning delivered with fidelity produces modest but real gains (Durlak et al., 2011); CBT-informed anxiety groups have reasonable support; universal mindfulness is mixed, and the MYRIAD trial (Kuyken et al., 2022) complicated the story for adolescents (Reference sheet). Grouping children with conduct difficulties carries a documented risk of harm (Dishion, McCord & Poulin, 1999). Recommend what a school likes rather than what the evidence supports and you misrepresent effectiveness — which is where PSI Code 4.2.2 is mapped (read the clause for its wording).

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor answers when a principal asks 'should we do X with Sixth Class?': what evidence they cite, how they phrase uncertainty, and whether they ask what the difficulty is before discussing a programme.

WRITE DOWN — the programme, the claim made for it, the source cited, and any caveat your supervisor added. Note which programmes your service actually uses (the Reference sheet names Friends for Life as one used in Irish settings — check what your service holds).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell a school their favourite programme lacks evidence without losing them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the core sources yourself — Durlak et al. (2011), Weare and Nind (2011), Dishion et al. (1999), Kuyken et al. (2022) — and writing a one-page evidence note for each approach your Cavan service uses, with effect sizes copied from the papers, not from memory.

THEY HOLD — the advice to the school, and any conversation redirecting a school from something it has invested in.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading and summarising is yours to do. Redirecting a school is relational work your supervisor already holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — answer a school's question about a wellbeing programme yourself in a consultation, supervisor present: state what the evidence supports, what it does not, and what fidelity requires, and cite the source.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — presenting mindfulness as established; quoting an effect size you have not read; recommending a targeted group when a third of the class shares the difficulty.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what does the Kuyken trial actually say for this age group? Let's check before we advise.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every group or class-level recommendation you make is accompanied by a citation you have read, a plain statement of the strength of evidence, and any known risk.

PASS TEST — You can cite it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your evidence notes and the consultation record. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you recommend a universal mindfulness course to a post-primary school as 'proven to reduce anxiety', and a teacher who has read the MYRIAD findings asks you where that claim comes from.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the tiers (universal, targeted, indicated), what the evidence supports at each, why fidelity predicts outcome, and the deviancy-training risk, citing the Reference sheet's sources and the Department of Education Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you overstated evidence: correct it with the school in writing, explain what the evidence does support, and tell your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Presenting a programme as effective without having read the evidence, or presenting mindfulness as established.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Co-facilitate rather than only observe' and 'Measure something before and after'.

micro.name: Co-facilitate rather than only observe
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 5.36 is mapped here. Watching a group is not the same as running one: facilitation means managing time, participation, disclosure and the child who will not join in, all at once. The Reference sheet names class and group work as the area Irish trainees evidence most thinly. Co-facilitating with school staff from the first session is also how the work survives your leaving (CORU SoP 5.40). A trainee who only observed has no evidence of the competency at all.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how the facilitator opens a session, sets ground rules with the group rather than for them, handles the child who dominates and the child who says nothing, and what they say at the start about what they will do if someone shares something worrying.

WRITE DOWN — the session structure, the phrases used for ground rules and for the limits of confidentiality in children's terms, and one moment where the plan changed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do in a group when a child begins to disclose something in front of the others?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — one defined segment of each session (the warm-up, an activity, or the closing round), planned in advance with your co-facilitator.

THEY HOLD — the session as a whole, ground rules, and the in-room response to disclosure or distress. A disclosure goes through the child protection route the same day: the DLP is informed and a report made to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty — with supervision afterwards.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a defined segment lets you practise facilitation with a safety net. Disclosure in a group needs a practised response and a clear route.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead whole sessions with the school's co-facilitator, and with your supervisor or the lead facilitator present for at least the first. Agree beforehand who handles distress and who keeps the group going.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — talking more than the children; letting one child set the tone; not stating the limits of confidentiality at the start; the co-facilitator from the school left as a spectator.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — the lead taking over the moment a child starts to disclose: 'thank you for telling us — I'd like to hear more of that with you after the group.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — deliver identified sessions or parts of sessions as a named co-facilitator, with the school's staff member alongside you, with ground rules and limits stated at the start.

PASS TEST — You delivered part of it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — session plans showing your part, a session log, and supervisor feedback. Log against 3. Intervention. No child names in your own Log.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — eight weeks sitting at the back taking notes; the Appendix 5 entry says 'observed group' every week and there is nothing to evidence facilitation.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer how to plan a co-facilitated session, split roles, set ground rules with a group, and state the limits of confidentiality in children's words, drawing on the Reference sheet's section on facilitating without doing harm.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a session runs badly (conflict, a child leaves upset): make sure the child is safe and with an adult, debrief with your co-facilitator the same day, and bring it to supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Spending the whole group as an observer, so there is no evidence you facilitated anything.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Adapt delivery to the group in front of you' and 'Leave the teacher able to run it'.

Not started

micro.name: Adapt delivery to the group in front of you
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 5.36 is mapped here. The Reference sheet says fidelity predicts whether social and emotional learning works, so adaptation is not a licence to rewrite a programme. The skill is adapting the surface — pacing, examples, language, format, seating — while keeping the core components intact. The implementation literature discusses this tension between fidelity and adaptation (Kelly & Perkins, 2012; read the relevant chapters). Deliver a manual rigidly to a group it does not fit and the children switch off; change the core and you cannot tell whether the programme works.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moments an experienced facilitator changes something mid-session — shortening an activity, swapping an example for one closer to the children's lives, moving from talk to drawing — and the moments they deliberately do not.

WRITE DOWN — what was changed, what prompted it (what the children were doing), and whether the change touched a core component or only the surface.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know which parts of this programme you must not change?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the programme manual to identify its core components, and proposing surface adaptations in advance for this group (age, language, literacy level, any child with additional needs).

THEY HOLD — any decision to change a core component or drop a session.

WHY THAT SPLIT — planned surface adaptation is checkable against the manual. Changing core content affects whether the programme is still the programme, and whether the outcome data mean anything.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make adaptations in the moment during your part of the session, with your co-facilitator present, and note each one afterwards.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — ploughing on with a discussion the group has clearly left; or, the opposite, dropping the difficult core activity because the group resisted it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'they've lost the thread — try the drawing version of that activity' or, after the session, 'that change cut the practice step; that one is core.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — notice when the group is not with you, change something on the surface in response, keep the core components intact, and record what you changed and why.

PASS TEST — You changed something in response

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the session log with adaptations noted, and the fidelity record showing core components delivered. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a session delivered word for word from the manual to a group of children who were visibly lost for forty minutes, with nothing noted.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between core components and surface features, how to find which is which in a manual, and why recording adaptations matters for interpreting outcomes.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise an adaptation changed a core component: record it honestly, restore the component in the next session if possible, and note it when you interpret the outcome data.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Either delivering the manual rigidly to a group it does not fit, or quietly cutting core components.

→ Feeds into 'Measure something before and after' and 'Leave the teacher able to run it'.

micro.name: Measure something before and after
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 3.8 is mapped here. The Reference sheet asks for pre and post measures on the children, a fidelity check on delivery, and a teacher or facilitator view — without them you cannot say whether the group worked, or whether a null result reflects the programme or its delivery. A brief measure at week one and the final week is often enough. It also gives you a practice-based research output, which the Reference sheet notes is another development area met by the same piece of work.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor or service uses to evaluate groups: which child measure, which teacher measure, how consent covers them, and how fidelity is recorded session by session.

WRITE DOWN — the measures, when each is given, who gives it, and how the results are reported back to the school.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when the post-measures are no better — do you tell the school the group did not work?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — setting up the evaluation for a group: proposing a brief validated measure the service approves (check the tools list on the Reference sheet and any licensing), a fidelity checklist from the manual, and a short teacher questionnaire.

THEY HOLD — sign-off on the measures and on consent, and how the results are communicated.

WHY THAT SPLIT — setting up is organisation you can own. Choosing measures and agreeing consent for data collection on children involves service policy and ethics your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer the pre-measure before session one, complete the fidelity checklist after each session, and take the post-measure in the final session. In Cavan, plan backwards from 18/12/2026 so the post-measure is not lost to the Christmas break.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — no pre-measure; measures given in different conditions pre and post; outcomes overclaimed from small numbers.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'with eight children and no comparison group, what can you honestly say from these numbers?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every group you run has a pre-measure, a post-measure, a fidelity record and a staff view, and you report the result honestly with its limits.

PASS TEST — There is outcome data, however simple

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the anonymised summary of pre and post data, the fidelity record, and the report back to the school. Log against 3. Intervention and 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an eight-week group ends, the children liked it, and nobody can say whether anything changed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why pre, post and fidelity data are all needed, how to choose a brief measure, and how to state the limits of small-group data without dismissing it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the data show no change or worse: check fidelity first, report honestly to the school, bring it to supervision, and consider — with reference to Dishion et al. (1999) — whether the group composition could have contributed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Running a group with no pre-measure, so no outcome can be shown.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Leave the teacher able to run it' and into Research — practice-based evaluation.

micro.name: Leave the teacher able to run it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet puts it bluntly: the intervention that ends when you leave has failed. CORU SoP 5.40 asks you to build capacity among those responsible for delivery. The sequence is co-facilitate, then hand over, then review, and the handover has to be written into the plan at the start — it does not happen as an afterthought. A trainee on an eleven-week placement is the clearest case: in Cavan you leave on 18/12/2026, and the school keeps the children.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor structures handover: when the school's staff member moves from assisting to leading, what materials they are given, and how the review is arranged after the psychologist steps back.

WRITE DOWN — the handover stages, the materials handed over (manual, session plans, fidelity checklist, measures), and the date of the follow-up review.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which handovers have stuck in your schools, and what made the difference?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing the handover pack: session plans annotated with the adaptations that worked, the fidelity checklist, the measures, and a one-page 'if this happens' guide including the disclosure route (inform the DLP; report to Tusla as soon as practicable).

THEY HOLD — the agreement with the principal about staff time to continue, and the follow-up review after you leave.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the pack is concrete work. Securing staff time is a management decision, and the follow-up needs someone who will still be in the service after 18/12/2026.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — move the school's co-facilitator from assisting to leading over the later sessions, with you supporting, and review each session with them.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — you still leading the final session; a pack left in a staffroom with no conversation; no date for the next run.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'she's ready to lead next week — step back and let her, even if it goes differently from how you would do it.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — plan and carry out a handover so that a named staff member has led sessions, holds the materials, knows the disclosure route, and has a date to run it again.

PASS TEST — Capacity remains after you go

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the handover plan, the pack contents list, and a note of the handover meeting. Log against 3. Intervention and 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — in March, the school says 'the psychologist ran a lovely group before Christmas' and nothing has happened since.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the co-facilitate, hand over, review sequence and why it must be planned at the start, and what a usable handover pack contains.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the staff member cannot continue (moves school, loses the time): discuss with the principal who else might take it on, leave the pack with the SET coordinator, and flag it to your supervisor for the follow-up.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
No handover planned, so the work ends when the placement does.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Systemic Change — building school capacity — and into Working with Others.

micro.name: Use open questions and reflective listening
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Every parent meeting and pupil interview runs on these micro-skills, and without them you get thin information and damaged relationships (Reference sheet). Open questions get an account; closed questions confirm a detail. Reflection of content shows you heard; reflection of feeling, offered tentatively, shows you understood — and it is the one trainees skip (Egan & Reese, 2021). CORU SoP 5.18 is mapped here. This is foundation communication under supervision, not therapy.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the ratio of open to closed questions your supervisor uses in a pupil interview, and how they reflect feeling tentatively ('that sounds like it was really frightening') rather than labelling ('you're anxious').

WRITE DOWN — three open questions and two reflections they used, word for word, and what the young person said next each time.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a young person gives one-word answers to open questions, what do you try next?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — part of a pupil interview (for example, the section on what school is like), using open questions and reflections you have prepared.

THEY HOLD — the rest of the interview, and anything that moves toward risk or distress.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a bounded section lets you practise the technique with support. Anything touching risk — self-harm, suicidal thinking or abuse — goes through the child protection and risk route the same day, and your supervisor holds that until you are practised.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a whole pupil interview or parent conversation, supervisor present, and afterwards count roughly who spoke more.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — strings of closed questions; 'why' questions that sound like blame; labelling feeling; filling the young person's pauses with your next question.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor, gently: 'you said it was hard at lunchtime — tell us a bit more about lunchtime', modelling the open prompt you missed.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — conduct an interview where most of the talking is the young person's, using open questions, reflections of content and feeling offered tentatively, and summaries that let them correct you.

PASS TEST — The young person speaks more than you do

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the interview record (with consent) and a reflective note on your questioning. Log against 3. Intervention. No identifying details in your own Log.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an interview note full of your questions and the young person's 'yeah' and 'dunno'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the purpose of each micro-technique (open question, closed question, reflection of content, reflection of feeling, summary), why tentative reflection invites correction, and where they come from (Rogers, 1957; Egan & Reese, 2021).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a reflection lands badly ('no, I'm not sad'): accept the correction, thank them, and use it — the correction is information.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking a string of closed questions and labelling feelings instead of reflecting them tentatively.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Hold silence without filling it' and into Assessment — including the child's voice.

micro.name: Hold silence without filling it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet says a silence of three to five seconds after an answer produces more than any follow-up question, and is the hardest to tolerate. Rowe's (1974) classroom research on teacher 'wait-time' is a related source — read it for the detail rather than quoting figures from memory. CORU SoP 5.21 is mapped here. Filling silence — the Reference sheet's first listed error — cuts off the thought the young person was about to share and teaches them you will do the talking.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how long your supervisor waits after asking a question or after a young person stops speaking, and what the young person does in that gap. Count silently.

WRITE DOWN — two moments where the silence produced something new, and one where your supervisor judged the silence as distress rather than thinking and responded.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell a thinking silence from a stuck or distressed one, especially with a younger child?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — deliberately practising a count of five after each answer during the interview section you lead.

THEY HOLD — reading silences that may signal distress, withdrawal of assent or something hard to say, and responding to them.

WHY THAT SPLIT — waiting can be practised mechanically at first. Judging when silence has become distress, and what to offer then, is a skill built on experience, and a silence before a disclosure needs a practised response.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — hold silence in your own interviews, supervisor present, and offer a gentle prompt only when the young person seems stuck rather than thinking ('take your time').

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jumping in within a second or two; answering your own question; rephrasing the same question three ways; and the opposite error — leaving a distressed child sitting in silence.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — afterwards: 'you asked about home, she opened her mouth, and you asked about school. What might she have said?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — after questions and answers, wait before speaking; use silence to let the young person continue; distinguish distress from thought and respond to distress.

PASS TEST — You waited

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a reflective note on one interview recording where you held silence and what followed (no identifiers). Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — every pause filled with a new question, and a young person who learns to wait you out.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why silence works, how long it feels versus how long it is, and how to tell thinking from distress, citing the Reference sheet and Rowe (1974).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when silence has tipped into distress: name it gently, offer a break or a different way to respond (drawing, pointing, writing), and check whether the young person wants to stop — respecting withdrawal of assent.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Filling every silence, so the young person never gets to finish the thought.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Use scaling or solution-focused questioning' and into Ethical Practice — recognising non-verbal withdrawal.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Use scaling or solution-focused questioning
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet describes solution-focused approaches as widely used in Irish educational psychology, within trainee competence with supervision, and well suited to school work. Scaling questions, the miracle question, exception-finding and identifying what already works give a pupil interview a defensible structure (Ratner, George & Iveson, 2012). CORU SoP 5.18 is mapped. You used this framework at Roscommon; the aim now is to use it deliberately. Without a technique, an interview drifts into a conversation that may be pleasant but is hard to use.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor introduces a scale (0 to 10, or a visual ladder for younger children), asks 'what makes it a 4 and not a 2?', and asks 'what would one point higher look like?'. Notice how they adapt the miracle question for a younger child.

WRITE DOWN — the exact wording of the scaling and exception questions and the young person's answers.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when would you not use the miracle question with a child?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the scaling segment of a pupil interview, using wording and a visual scale prepared and checked with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — the rest of the interview, and the decision about whether a solution-focused approach suits this young person at all (for example, where there is recent loss or trauma, which is outside your competence).

WHY THAT SPLIT — scaling is a bounded technique you can practise safely. Choosing the approach depends on the formulation and on knowing when a young person's difficulties need more than you can offer.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — use a full solution-focused structure in a pupil interview — best hopes, scaling, exceptions, next small step — with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — using the scale as a rating and moving on without the follow-up questions; pushing past a young person's problem talk so fast that they feel unheard.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you got a 3 — ask what's keeping it at 3 and not lower. That's where the strengths are.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — conduct a pupil interview structured by a named solution-focused technique, adapted to age, and record what the technique produced.

PASS TEST — You have a technique, not just a conversation

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the interview record and a note on the technique used and its adaptations. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an interview note that reads 'chatted about school, seems happy enough', with nothing that can inform a plan.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the core solution-focused techniques, how to adapt scaling for a young child (faces, a ladder, a number line on the floor), and when the approach is not appropriate, citing Ratner, George and Iveson (2012).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a young person answers '0' or 'nothing is working': acknowledge it, ask how they are coping at all, and if risk may be present, follow the risk route the same day and bring it to supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking the scaling question and moving on without the follow-up questions that make it useful.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Recognise when the work exceeds your competence' and into Intervention planning with the young person.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Recognise when the work exceeds your competence
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
You can listen, contain and help someone think; you cannot deliver therapy, treat a mental health condition, or work with trauma (Reference sheet). PSI Code 2.2.2 and CORU SoP 1.2 are mapped here — read the Code's wording on Part B of the Reference sheet. Drifting into therapy with a parent because it felt unkind to stop is one of the Reference sheet's named errors, and crossing this boundary is among the more serious things a trainee can do. Any disclosure of self-harm, suicidal thinking or abuse goes through the child protection and risk route the same day; supervision follows action.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moment in a meeting when your supervisor recognises the conversation moving outside the purpose of the work (a parent's own mental health, a child's trauma history) and how they acknowledge it, contain it and redirect.

WRITE DOWN — the signal they noticed and the words they used to redirect, without identifying details.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how early do you name the limit — and how do you do it without the person feeling pushed away?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing out in advance, for each case, what your role is and is not, and preparing a sentence you can use to name the limit kindly.

THEY HOLD — conversations likely to move into risk, trauma or a parent's own mental health, and any decision about what to do next.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing the boundary is something you can do before the meeting. Holding a person in distress while redirecting them, and judging risk, needs experience you are not expected to have yet.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a meeting where the boundary may be tested, supervisor present; name the purpose at the start, and redirect if the conversation moves beyond it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — continuing because it feels unkind to stop; offering advice on a parent's own difficulties; asking a child questions that open up trauma.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'it sounds like you've been carrying a lot yourself. That matters, and it deserves proper support — can we talk about who could help you with that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — state your role at the start, recognise when the conversation is moving beyond it, name the limit kindly before you are in it, and route risk disclosures through the child protection and risk route the same day.

PASS TEST — You named your limit before reaching it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the case note recording the redirection and any onward action, and the supervision note. Log against 3. Intervention and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent meeting that became a weekly listening session about the parent's own depression, with no referral made.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain where a trainee's competence ends, why (PSI Code 2.2.2, 2.2.3), what the early signals are, and how to name the limit without rejecting the person.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you have already crossed the line: stop, tell your supervisor the same day, agree how to close that thread with the person and where to refer, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Continuing into therapy with a parent or child because stopping felt unkind.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know the onward referral route and use it' and into Ethical Practice — working within competence.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Know the onward referral route and use it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
PSI Code 3.4.3 is mapped here. When a conversation moves beyond your competence, the Reference sheet says you must have a name to give rather than a vague suggestion to 'see someone', and the routes must be written out in advance. In Ireland these may include the GP, HSE CAMHS (usually via GP), HSE Primary Care psychology, a Children's Disability Network Team, and, for any child protection concern, a report to Tusla as soon as practicable alongside informing the school's DLP (telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's duty). Referral criteria and waiting times vary — check each locally. A vague signpost leaves the person with nowhere to go.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor signposts: the service named, how to access it, whether a referral is made or the family self-refers, and how they check the family understood.

WRITE DOWN — for each route: who it is for, how to access it, whether a GP letter is needed, and what the family should expect. Note the service's own list of crisis lines — check numbers there before giving any out.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which referral routes in this area actually work, and which look good on paper?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building a referral route sheet for your Cavan area before the placement starts on 05/10/2026: services, access routes, criteria, and the DLP for each of your schools.

THEY HOLD — decisions to refer, and making referrals on the service's behalf.

WHY THAT SPLIT — compiling the sheet is research you can own. A referral commits the service, needs consent, and relies on your supervisor's judgement about which route is right.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — signpost or propose a referral yourself in a meeting, supervisor present: name the service, explain how to access it, and check the parent or young person knows the next step.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'you might want to talk to someone'; recommending a service without knowing its criteria; forgetting the same-day risk route when self-harm or abuse is mentioned.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the GP is the way in to CAMHS here — would it help if we wrote a short note you could bring?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — when the work exceeds your competence, stop and refer, naming a specific route, how to access it and what happens next; for risk, use the child protection and risk route the same day, then bring it to supervision.

PASS TEST — You referred rather than continued

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the case note of the referral or signpost and the route sheet. Log against 3. Intervention and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent told to 'look into some counselling' who leaves with no name, no number and no plan.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the main referral routes in the Irish system, how to access each, and how to signpost in a way a family can act on.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a referral is refused or the wait is long: tell the family honestly, identify interim supports with your supervisor, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Signposting vaguely ('talk to someone') with no named service or route.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Close the relationship properly' and into Working with Others — interagency practice.

micro.name: Close the relationship properly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet says to signal the ending before it arrives, summarise what was said and what happens next, and be explicit about what you will and will not do and what will be written down and who will see it. An unclear ending leaves a parent expecting contact that is not coming, which does more damage than a blunt but clear one. CORU SoP 5.21 and PSI Code 3.4.4 are mapped here. For a trainee, placement end is a fixed ending: in Cavan, 18/12/2026.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor ends a session and ends an involvement: the signal ('we have about ten minutes left'), the summary, what happens next, and who the family contacts after.

WRITE DOWN — the words used for each part, and anything written down for the family.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you end with a young person who has told you a lot, without it feeling like being dropped?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the summary and 'what happens next' part at the end of a session your supervisor led.

THEY HOLD — ending the involvement with the family and handing on to whoever holds the case after you.

WHY THAT SPLIT — summarising is a learnable micro-skill. Ending a relationship, especially for a trainee who is leaving, means managing expectations and case transfer, which your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — end your own sessions, supervisor present: signal the end, summarise, state what you will and will not do, what gets written and who sees it, and who to contact.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — running out of time and ending abruptly; promising contact you cannot deliver; not telling a young person that you are leaving at the end of the placement.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before you finish, tell him who he can go to in school after you've gone.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — close every session and every involvement with a signalled ending, a summary, clear next steps, what is recorded and who sees it, and a named contact after you leave.

PASS TEST — There was an ending, not a lapse

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the closing case note, the handover note, and the letter or summary given to the family. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent phones the service in January asking when the trainee is coming back, and nobody told her.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the components of a good ending, why an unclear ending harms more than a clear one, and how to plan endings from the start of a time-limited placement.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when an involvement ended without closure: tell your supervisor, contact the family with a clear summary and next step, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Letting contact lapse without a signalled ending, summary and named next contact.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Working with Others — case transfer — and into Ethical Practice — record-keeping.

micro.name: State the Continuum level for each recommendation
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Irish schools allocate support through the NEPS Continuum of Support: Classroom Support, School Support and School Support Plus (NEPS, Special Educational Needs: A Continuum of Support — Guidelines for Teachers, 2007; post-primary guidelines 2010). A recommendation with no level leaves the principal and SET to guess which pot of time it comes from, and the guess is usually the lowest one. Naming the level also tells the school which paperwork follows — a Classroom Support Plan or a Student Support File with review dates.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where in your supervisor's reports the level appears: in a heading above each group of recommendations, in each sentence, or once in the summary. Notice whether they justify the level against what has already been tried at the level below.

WRITE DOWN — for two or three of their reports, each recommendation and the level attached to it, and any recommendation that has no level.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide between School Support and School Support Plus when the school has already been doing small-group work for a term?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the recommendations section of a supervised case with the level stated in each recommendation, and a one-line justification for any recommendation at School Support Plus.

THEY HOLD — the final call on the level, because they know how this school and this SENO respond to each level and what has been agreed at previous consultations.

WHY THAT SPLIT — attaching a level is a mechanical habit you can build now. Judging the level against local history and resource needs knowledge of the school you do not yet have.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the full recommendations section with levels and justifications and bring it to supervision before the report goes out.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a level named without saying why it is not the one below, and a School Support Plus recommendation with no evidence of what happened at School Support first.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've said School Support Plus. What has the SET already done at School Support, for how long, and what changed?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every recommendation in every report you write carries a named Continuum level, with a justification wherever the level is higher than the child's current one.

PASS TEST — The level appears in the text

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the recommendations section of an anonymised report extract, with levels visible. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'X would benefit from additional literacy support' with no level, so the school files it and nothing changes in the timetable.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the three levels, who leads each, what documentation each generates, and why a level must be justified against the one below — citing the NEPS Continuum guidelines rather than memory.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a report has already gone out without levels: send a short addendum to the principal and SET naming the level for each recommendation, and log the correction with your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommendations with no Continuum level, so the school cannot tell which resource they draw on.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Check the school can actually resource it', 'Name who delivers', and into the Student Support File review.

micro.name: Check the school can actually resource it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A recommendation the school cannot staff becomes a line in a file that nobody delivers, and the family reads it as a promise broken. Special education teaching hours are allocated to schools under the Department of Education's SET allocation model (Circulars 0013/2017 primary and 0014/2017 post-primary — check for the current circular before quoting), and the principal deploys them. CORU SoP 5.35 is the standard mapped here. Asking before you write is how you keep recommendations honest.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when your supervisor asks the principal or SET what is possible: before the assessment, during the planning meeting, or after the draft. Notice the questions — how many SET hours are free, which groups already run, whether an SNA is attached to the class.

WRITE DOWN — the resource questions they ask and the answers the school gives, anonymised.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a child needs something the school genuinely cannot provide, how do you write that without setting the school up to fail?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing a short list of resource questions for the SET before the feedback meeting: existing groups, available time, programmes already bought in, staff trained in them.

THEY HOLD — the conversation with the principal about deployment, and any recommendation that the school seek resource from outside, such as through the SENO.

WHY THAT SPLIT — factual questions to the SET are safe for you to ask. Asking a principal to re-deploy staff is negotiation that relies on a relationship your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — check each draft recommendation with the SET before the report is finalised, and adjust wording where the resource does not exist.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — recommending a named programme (for example a specific reading intervention) that the school has never bought, has no trained staff for, or cannot timetable.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before this goes in — did you ask whether anyone in the school is trained in that? Who would deliver it next Monday?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before finalising recommendations, confirm with the SET or principal that each one can be resourced, and record that you asked.

PASS TEST — You asked before recommending

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a note on the case file of the date and who you checked with. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — daily one-to-one precision teaching recommended for a child in a school whose SET time is fully committed, discovered at the review when nothing has happened.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how SET hours reach a school, who decides their deployment, and the difference between recommending within the school's resource and recommending that the school seek more.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child's need exceeds what the school can provide: say so plainly, recommend the achievable version first, and name the route for further resource separately, with your supervisor's agreement.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending an intervention without asking whether anyone in the school can deliver it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name who delivers', 'Name how often and for how long', and 'Limit the number so they can be acted on'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — when your supervisor asks the principal or SET what is possible: before the assessment, during the planning meeting, or after the draft. Notice the questions — how many SET hours are free, which groups already run, whether an SNA is attached to the class.

micro.name: Name who delivers
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
'The school should' is the most common phrase in recommendations and the least likely to be acted on, because it belongs to nobody. Addressing each recommendation to a role — class teacher, SET, SNA, principal, parent — is one of the features the Reference sheet lists as predicting implementation. CORU SoP 5.34 is the standard mapped here. Name a role, not a person, because staff move mid-year.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words the first few words of each recommendation. Many start with the role: 'The class teacher will…', 'The SET will…'. Notice whether parents are given recommendations too, and how those are phrased.

WRITE DOWN — any recommendation in their reports that is addressed to 'the school', 'staff' or nobody, and what they would change.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'why do you name the role rather than the teacher's name, and when would you name the person?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — rewriting a draft set of recommendations so that each begins with a named role and contains one verb that role can do.

THEY HOLD — decisions about which role is appropriate where the school's structure is unclear, for example whether an SNA can be asked to deliver a teaching task.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the rewording is a discipline you can practise at once. Knowing the limits of each role (the SNA scheme is for care needs — check the current NCSE/DE guidance) needs supervision.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the recommendations with roles attached and walk through them with the SET before the report is finalised, asking 'is this the right person for this?'

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — teaching tasks assigned to an SNA, and recommendations addressed to 'home and school' that neither side owns.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who, specifically, does this on Monday morning? If you can't answer, the sentence isn't finished.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every recommendation you write opens with the role responsible for it.

PASS TEST — Responsibility assigned to a role

EVIDENCE TO FILE — recommendations section of an anonymised report extract. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'Visual supports should be used throughout the day' — nobody makes them, nobody uses them, and at review everyone thought someone else was doing it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why ownership predicts implementation, what each school role can and cannot be asked to do, and how to write a parent recommendation that does not sound like homework.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the named role is vacant or on leave: revise the recommendation with the principal, name the covering role, and adjust the review date if needed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Addressing recommendations to 'the school', so nobody owns them.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name how often and for how long', and into 'Agree next steps and who does what' in the feedback session.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Name how often and for how long
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Dose matters: implementation research finds that how much of an intervention is delivered affects outcome (Durlak & DuPre, 2008, American Journal of Community Psychology). 'Regular phonological awareness work' could mean five minutes a fortnight or twenty minutes daily, and the school will pick the version that fits its timetable. CORU SoP 5.34 and PSI Code 2.3.2 are the standards mapped here. Without frequency and duration you also cannot tell at review whether the intervention failed or was never delivered.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor gives frequency (times per week), session length (minutes), and total duration (weeks or until a review date), and where they take the figures from — a programme manual, research, or what the school can manage.

WRITE DOWN — the dosage in each recommendation you see, and any recommendation without one.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'where did the three times a week for ten weeks come from — the programme, the evidence, or the timetable?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — adding frequency, session length and duration to each draft recommendation, and noting the source for each figure (programme manual, published study, or negotiated with the SET).

THEY HOLD — judgement where the evidence-based dose is more than the school can give, and what compromise is still worth recommending.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding the stated dose is research you can do. Deciding how far below it an intervention stops being worth doing is a clinical judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write dosage into every recommendation and explain in supervision where each figure came from.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — invented precision ('15 minutes, four times weekly') with no source, and dosages that add up across recommendations to more SET time than the child could receive.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'add these up for me. How many minutes a week is this child out of class?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each recommendation that involves direct work states how often, for how long each time, and for how many weeks.

PASS TEST — Dosage specified

EVIDENCE TO FILE — recommendations section of an anonymised report extract. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at the review the SET says the programme 'didn't work', and it emerges it ran once a week for four weeks when the manual assumes daily sessions.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain dosage as frequency × session length × duration, why it matters for fidelity (Durlak & DuPre, 2008), and how to find the intended dose in a programme manual.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a review shows the dose was not delivered: record it as an implementation gap, not an intervention failure, and agree a realistic dose before judging effect.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'regular' or 'ongoing' instead of a frequency and a duration.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State how progress will be measured' and 'Set a review date'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor gives frequency (times per week), session length (minutes), and total duration (weeks or until a review date), and where they take the figures from — a programme manual, research, or what the school can manage.

micro.name: Limit the number so they can be acted on
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A class teacher with 28 children cannot act on fifteen recommendations, so she picks the easiest two, which may not be the most important. The Reference sheet's rule is that five actionable recommendations beat fifteen aspirational ones, sequenced with a small number first. CORU SoP 5.34 is the standard mapped here. Prioritising is also a test of your formulation: if you cannot say which recommendation matters most, you have not yet decided what is driving the difficulty.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how many recommendations your supervisor typically writes, whether they number or group them, and whether they mark any as 'first' or 'priority'.

WRITE DOWN — the count per report, and how they handle the extra ideas that did not make the list — an appendix of strategies, a handout, or nothing.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide what to leave out when everything in the list would help?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the full list of possible recommendations, then ranking them by how directly each addresses the formulation and how feasible each is.

THEY HOLD — the cut: which five survive, and whether the rest go in a strategy appendix or are dropped.

WHY THAT SPLIT — generating and ranking is your formulation work made visible. Cutting well needs a sense of what a school actually does with a long list, which comes from seeing reviews.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring no more than five to seven recommendations to supervision, each linked to a named part of the formulation, with the first two marked as priorities.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a long list kept because each item felt worth including, and generic strategies that are not linked to this child's formulation.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if the teacher only did one of these, which one would you want it to be — and why is it number four?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write a recommendations section that is short, prioritised and sequenced, with any additional strategies moved to an appendix or handout.

PASS TEST — Five that happen beat fifteen that do not

EVIDENCE TO FILE — recommendations section of an anonymised report extract. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — two pages of recommendations; at review the teacher has done three, none of them the ones that addressed the core difficulty.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why fewer recommendations are implemented more, how to link each one to the formulation, and how to use an appendix for everything that is useful but not essential.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a school or parent asks for 'everything that might help': give the prioritised list, add the strategy bank separately, and say plainly which items come first.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A long, unprioritised list, so the school chooses the easiest items rather than the important ones.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State how progress will be measured', and into Formulation — linking each recommendation to a hypothesis.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how many recommendations your supervisor typically writes, whether they number or group them, and whether they mark any as 'first' or 'priority'.
