micro.name: State how progress will be measured
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A recommendation with no measure cannot be evaluated, so it continues or stops on impression. CORU SoP 3.8 and PSI Code 3.1.2 are the standards mapped here, and the Reference sheet names the evaluation line as the element most often omitted in trainee reports. The NEPS Continuum expects support plans at School Support and School Support Plus to include targets and review (NEPS Continuum guidelines — read the source for the exact wording). A measure with no named person to take it is not taken.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the measures your supervisor names: a curriculum-based probe, a re-administered subtest, a frequency count, a teacher rating, the child's own scaling. Notice who they name to collect it and when.

WRITE DOWN — for each recommendation, the measure and the measurer, and any that have neither.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you choose a measure the teacher will actually take, rather than the one you would ideally want?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — proposing a baseline and a measure for each recommendation, chosen from what the school already collects where possible (for example standardised test results, reading records, attendance).

THEY HOLD — whether the measure is sensitive enough to show change in the time available, and whether it is fair to ask the school to collect it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — matching a measure to a target is a skill you can practise. Knowing which measures actually move over one term comes from seeing many reviews.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the measure and the measurer into each recommendation and check with the SET that it is realistic.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a full standardised retest proposed after six weeks (too insensitive, and possibly practice effects — check the test manual for retest interval), and 'teacher observation' with no defined behaviour.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what number will the SET write down in March, and what number would tell us it worked?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each recommendation states the baseline where known, the measure, who takes it, and when.

PASS TEST — A measure and a measurer named

EVIDENCE TO FILE — recommendations section of an anonymised report extract, and the agreed measures on the Student Support File where you contributed. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at review everyone agrees the child 'seems more settled', nobody has data, and the support is withdrawn or continued on opinion.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between an outcome measure and an implementation check, how to choose one sensitive enough for a term, and why naming the measurer matters as much as naming the measure.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the measure was not collected: agree a simpler one at review, take a baseline then, and set a new date rather than judging the intervention on nothing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending an intervention with no measure and no named person to collect it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Set a review date', and into evaluation of intervention outcomes.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the measures your supervisor names: a curriculum-based probe, a re-administered subtest, a frequency count, a teacher rating, the child's own scaling. Notice who they name to collect it and when.

micro.name: Set a review date
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Without a date, review happens when someone remembers, which is usually at the next crisis. The Continuum of Support is described by NEPS as a problem-solving cycle of assessment, planning, intervention and review (NEPS Continuum guidelines — read the source for how review is framed at each level). PSI Code 2.3.2 is the standard mapped here. A dated review also protects the child from an intervention continuing for a year after it has stopped working.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor writes an actual date or a term ('end of Term 2'), who they expect to convene the review, and whether they plan to attend.

WRITE DOWN — the review points in their reports, and whether they line up with the school's own Student Support File review cycle.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when you set a review for a school you might not be back in, who makes sure it happens?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — proposing a review date for each case, checked against the school calendar (mid-term breaks, Christmas, exam periods at post-primary), and naming who convenes it.

THEY HOLD — whether the EP attends the review or the school runs it alone, which depends on service time allocation to the school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — picking a workable date is practical and yours. Committing service time to a review is a caseload decision your supervisor makes.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the review date into the report and the feedback record, and put it in your own diary if you are attending.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a date too soon for the dose to have had effect, or one that falls after your placement ends with no handover. Cavan runs 05/10/2026–18/12/2026, so a February review needs a named person in the service.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you'll be gone by then. Who in the school, and who here, will know this review is due?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every report and consultation record you write ends with a review date in DD/MM/YYYY and the role responsible for convening it.

PASS TEST — There is a date

EVIDENCE TO FILE — report and consultation record, anonymised extract. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'to be reviewed in due course', and the next time the child is discussed is a re-referral eighteen months later.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how review fits the Continuum's cycle, how to choose a date that allows the dose to work, and how to hand review over when your placement ends.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a review date passes unheld: contact the school, reset a date, and record in the case file that the original review did not happen.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
'To be reviewed' with no date and no one responsible for convening it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Agree actions with a review point' in consultation, and into the Student Support File review cycle.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor writes an actual date or a term ('end of Term 2'), who they expect to convene the review, and whether they plan to attend.

micro.name: Build at least one on a strength
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Recommendations that only compensate for deficit tell the child, the family and the school that the child is a list of problems. CORU SoP 1.3 is the standard mapped here. Strength-based assessment argues that strengths are also leverage for intervention (Buckley & Epstein, 2004, California School Psychologist). A child who is a confident talker but a weak reader may learn more through oral rehearsal before writing than through more of the reading she already avoids.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor's recommendations use any strength found in the assessment, and how — as a route into the difficulty, as a role in class, or as a source of confidence.

WRITE DOWN — the strengths named in the findings of their reports, and which of them reappear in the recommendations.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you turn a strength into a recommendation rather than a nice sentence in the summary?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listing the child's strengths from all sources (parent, teacher, child, testing) and drafting one recommendation that uses a strength as the means of intervention.

THEY HOLD — whether the strength is robust enough to build on, or a single observation that should not carry a recommendation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding strengths is part of your assessment. Judging whether one is reliable enough to lean on needs experience of how often apparent strengths hold up.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring your recommendations to supervision with at least one explicitly built on a named strength, and say which evidence shows that strength.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a strength that is generic ('she is a lovely girl') or used only as praise, rather than as the means of intervention.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you say he's good at drawing. How could that be how he plans a story, rather than a reward after it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — at least one recommendation in each report uses a specific, evidenced strength as the route to change.

PASS TEST — Not only compensation for deficit

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the strength-based recommendation in an anonymised report extract. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a strengths paragraph in the findings that is never used again, and ten recommendations that each describe something the child cannot do.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between naming a strength and building on it, cite the strength-based assessment literature, and give two examples of strengths used as intervention routes.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the assessment found few strengths: go back to the parent and child, ask what they enjoy and are proud of, and treat the gap as a gap in your assessment.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
A strengths section in the findings that never reaches the recommendations.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name strengths specifically rather than as preamble' in feedback, and into Formulation — protective factors.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Plan the first three sentences
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The opening sets whether a parent can listen for the rest of the session. Parents often arrive braced for a verdict, and until they know the headline they may hear little else (Reference sheet, 'Structuring the session'). CORU SoP 2.1 is the standard mapped here. An improvised opening drifts into test descriptions and pleasantries, and the parent spends ten minutes waiting for the point.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — your supervisor's exact first three sentences in a feedback session: the welcome, the check on what the parent already knows and wants, and the sign-post of what the session will cover.

WRITE DOWN — those sentences as close to verbatim as you can, straight after, and how the parent's posture changed once the plan was clear.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you script your opening, and does it change when you know the news is hard?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the first three sentences for a supervised feedback session and saying them aloud in supervision beforehand.

THEY HOLD — the session itself, and the decision to adapt the opening if the parent arrives upset, late or with someone unexpected.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the script is preparation you can own. Changing course when the room is not what you planned needs the confidence of someone who has done many sessions.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — open the session yourself, with your supervisor present, using your planned three sentences, then hand to the structure you agreed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — an opening that is all warm-up and no sign-post, or that jumps to test names before asking what the parent wants from today.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before we go on — can I check what you were hoping we'd get to today?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before every feedback session, write and rehearse the first three sentences: welcome, check what they know and want, say what the session will cover and roughly how long.

PASS TEST — You knew how you would open

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your session plan (no identifying details) and a reflective note. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — five minutes about the weather and the test battery, and a parent who interrupts with 'so is it dyslexia or not?'

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the opening matters, what the three sentences need to do, and how to adapt them when the parent arrives angry, tearful or with a question already.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the opening falls flat: pause, name it ('I've started with a lot — can I check what matters most to you today?'), and restart from their answer.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Improvising the opening, so the parent waits through preamble for the point.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask what the parent hopes to hear before starting' and 'Give the overall picture before the detail'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Give the overall picture before the detail
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents sit through explanation waiting for the verdict and hear none of it (Reference sheet, 'Structuring the session'). The same principle — say the headline, then explain — appears in breaking-news protocols in medicine, for example SPIKES (Baile et al., 2000, The Oncologist). CORU SoP 5.27 is the standard mapped here: communication suited to the audience. Leading with scores puts a number between the parent and their child.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when your supervisor gives the headline: which minute of the session, in what words, and whether any number is mentioned before it.

WRITE DOWN — the headline sentence verbatim, and the order in which detail followed — findings, what it means day to day, recommendations.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you boil a twelve-page report into one sentence a parent can repeat at home?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the one- or two-sentence headline for a supervised case and the order of the detail beneath it.

THEY HOLD — delivery of the headline in the session, particularly where it names a diagnosis or a significant difficulty.

WHY THAT SPLIT — distilling the formulation into a sentence tests your understanding and is safe to practise. Delivering significant news for the first time is the moment your supervisor should hold until you have watched it done.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — deliver the headline yourself within the first few minutes, in plain words, then walk through the supporting detail.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a percentile or standard score in the first sentence, and a headline so hedged the parent cannot tell what you found.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'so, in a sentence, what we found is that…' — finishing the headline for you.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — state the overall picture in plain language near the start, before any scores, then give the detail in the order you planned.

PASS TEST — You did not lead with scores

EVIDENCE TO FILE — session plan with headline, and a reflective note. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — twenty minutes of subtest results, then the parent asks 'but what does this mean?' and there is no time left to answer.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why headline-first works, how to write one sentence that is honest and not alarming, and how to translate a percentile into a comparison with other children or with classroom demand.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise mid-session you have buried the headline: stop, say 'let me give you the main point', and state it before continuing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leading with test scores so the parent never hears the overall picture.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Avoid jargon and check understanding repeatedly' and 'Deliver difficult information clearly'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Agree next steps and who does what
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A feedback session that ends in understanding but no action is a conversation, not an intervention. CORU SoP 2.16 is the standard mapped here. Parents often leave feedback meetings with a report and no idea what happens next — who will contact them, when the school plan starts, whether they need to do anything. Agreeing actions in the room is also where you learn which recommendations the family will actually take up.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor closes: whether they summarise actions aloud, name who does each, give dates, and check the parent agrees.

WRITE DOWN — the actions agreed, the person or role holding each, and whether anything was written down for the parent to take away.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when a parent agrees to everything in the room and you suspect none of it will happen?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the action summary during the session and reading it back at the end, with roles and dates.

THEY HOLD — negotiation where parent and school disagree about who should do something, or where the parent wants a referral the service cannot make.

WHY THAT SPLIT — summarising is a skill you can practise safely and is useful to your supervisor. Negotiating between parent and school expectations draws on authority you do not yet hold.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close the session yourself: summarise the agreed actions, name who holds each, check the parent agrees, and say when the written report will arrive.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — every action falling to the school with none for home, or a list of actions with no dates.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'and from your side at home — is there one thing from today you'd like to try?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — end each feedback session with actions agreed aloud, each assigned to a person or role, and confirmed in writing afterwards.

PASS TEST — Someone left with an action

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the post-session note or letter, anonymised. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent rings the school three weeks later asking what is happening, and the school thought the psychologist was following up.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to close a session so that each person leaves with a job, why home actions must be small and specific, and how the written follow-up locks in what was said.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the session ends without agreement: say so honestly, agree the next contact date, and write down what was and was not agreed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Ending the session with a shared understanding but no named actions.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name who delivers' in recommendations, and into Working with Others — home-school links.

WATCH FOR — how your supervisor closes: whether they summarise actions aloud, name who does each, give dates, and check the parent agrees.

micro.name: Avoid jargon and check understanding repeatedly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Terms such as 'working memory', 'standard score' or 'below average range' mean one thing to you and something else, or nothing, to a parent. PSI Code 4.3.1 is the clause mapped here. A single 'does that make sense?' invites a polite yes. Teach-back — asking the person to say it back in their own words — is a well-studied way to check understanding in health communication (Schillinger et al., 2003, Archives of Internal Medicine).

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — every technical term your supervisor uses in a session and whether they explain it the first time; and each point where they check understanding, and how.

WRITE DOWN — the words that needed explaining and the exact phrasing of their checks ('what will you tell your partner when you get home?').

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know when a parent has understood and is not just being polite?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a plain-English version of the key terms for the case, and planning at least two teach-back points in the session.

THEY HOLD — delivery, and reading the parent's response to decide whether to go back over something.

WHY THAT SPLIT — plain-language translation is preparation you can do well now. Reading whether someone has understood, especially through politeness or distress, is learned by watching.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — deliver a section of the feedback, stopping at planned points to ask the parent to say back what they have heard.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — only one check at the end, closed questions ('is that clear?'), and jargon slipping back in when you get nervous.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I just check — when we say working memory, what does that mean for her in the classroom?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain technical terms at first use, and check understanding with open questions at more than one point in the session.

PASS TEST — You checked more than once

EVIDENCE TO FILE — session plan with planned checks marked, and reflective note. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the parent nodded throughout, then tells the class teacher the next day that the psychologist said her son has a low IQ.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain teach-back, give plain-language versions of common assessment terms, and say why 'does that make sense?' is a poor check.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a check reveals a misunderstanding: thank them for saying it, re-explain differently rather than louder, and check again.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Checking understanding once, at the end, with a question that invites a polite yes.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Deliver difficult information clearly', and into report writing for the actual reader.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Name strengths specifically rather than as preamble
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents recognise the formula: two nice sentences, then 'however'. When strengths are generic they are heard as softening, and the parent waits for the bad news. CORU SoP 1.3 is the standard mapped here. Strength-based feedback, as argued by Buckley and Epstein (2004), treats strengths as information about the child as real as the difficulties. A specific strength also tells a parent you have seen their child, not just their scores.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where in the session your supervisor names strengths, how specific they are ('she explained the story's ending better than most children her age' versus 'she's lovely'), and whether strengths reappear later in the recommendations.

WRITE DOWN — each strength named, and the evidence it rested on.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you name a strength so it doesn't sound like the warm-up before the bad news?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting two or three specific strengths for the case, each with the evidence behind it (an observation, a subtest, something the child said).

THEY HOLD — where in the session strengths are placed, which depends on how the parent is likely to receive the main finding.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding and wording evidenced strengths is your assessment work. Positioning them in a hard conversation is a judgement about this parent that your supervisor is better placed to make.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — name the strengths yourself during the session, weaving them into the findings rather than bunching them at the start.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'she's a lovely girl, however…', and strengths so general they could describe any child.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'tell mum what you noticed about how he kept going on that puzzle when it got hard.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name strengths that are specific to this child, evidenced, and connected to the findings or recommendations.

PASS TEST — It does not sound like a formula

EVIDENCE TO FILE — session plan and reflective note. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the parent's face tightens as soon as you start praising, because they know the 'but' is coming.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between strengths as preamble and strengths as findings, and show how one strength can be carried into a recommendation.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent dismisses a strength ('she's only like that with you'): take it seriously, ask where else it shows, and treat the difference as information.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using generic praise as a warm-up before the difficulties.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Build at least one on a strength' in recommendations.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Ask what the parent hopes to hear before starting
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents arrive with a question — is it autism, will she get an SNA, is it my fault — and until it is addressed they may not hear anything else. Asking takes two minutes and reshapes the session (Reference sheet, 'Structuring the session'). CORU SoP 2.14 and PSI Code 1.4.1 are the standards mapped here (read both for their wording before saying what they require). Asking hands the parent some control over a meeting that is otherwise yours.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether and how your supervisor asks the parent what they are hoping for, and how the answer changes what they say next.

WRITE DOWN — the wording of the question, the parent's answer (anonymised), and any part of the plan the supervisor dropped or moved as a result.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when what the parent hopes to hear is not what you are about to tell them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking the question at the start of a supervised session and noting the answer.

THEY HOLD — adjusting the session in response, especially when the parent's hope is for something the findings do not support, such as a diagnosis or a resource.

WHY THAT SPLIT — asking is simple and should be yours early. Responding to a hope you are about to disappoint needs skill you will learn by watching them do it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — ask the question, then adjust your planned order so the parent's main concern is addressed early.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — asking and then ignoring the answer, carrying on with the planned script.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you mentioned you were wondering about secondary school — shall we come to that now?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — open every feedback session by asking what the parent wants to know or hopes to hear, and let the answer shape the order.

PASS TEST — You asked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — reflective note recording that you asked and how it changed the session. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at the end of an hour the parent says 'but you haven't told me whether she can get exemption from Irish', which was the only thing they came to ask.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why asking first matters for power and listening, and how to respond when the hope and the findings do not match.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the parent's question is outside what you can answer (a resource decision, a diagnosis you cannot make): say so early, name who can, and do not let the whole session wait for it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Delivering a prepared script without finding out what the parent came to hear.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Answer the question actually asked' and 'Deliver difficult information clearly'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — whether and how your supervisor asks the parent what they are hoping for, and how the answer changes what they say next.

micro.name: Deliver difficult information clearly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
When the news is hard, the temptation is to soften it until it disappears, and the parent leaves reassured about something that is not reassuring. PSI Code 1.3.4 is the clause mapped here — read it for its exact wording. Clear delivery is kinder in the long run: a parent who hears it later from a school, a CDNT or a report they read alone at the kitchen table loses trust in everyone. SPIKES (Baile et al., 2000) is one structure from medicine worth knowing.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words the hardest sentence: whether they warn first ('I have some news that may be hard to hear'), say it plainly, and then stop.

WRITE DOWN — the exact words used for the difficult finding, and what they did immediately after.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you stop yourself softening it so much that the parent doesn't hear it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the difficult sentence in advance, plainly, and rehearsing it in supervision.

THEY HOLD — delivery of the news itself on your early cases, and the decision about whether a second meeting is needed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing a clear sentence is the preparation. Saying it to a parent for the first time, and handling what follows, is the part to watch done well before you do it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — deliver the difficult finding yourself, with your supervisor present, using your rehearsed words, then pause.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — hedging so heavy ('there may perhaps be some indication of some difficulties') that the parent cannot tell what was found.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'to be clear — what we're saying is that…', restating it plainly.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — deliver a difficult finding in plain words, warn before it, pause after it, and check what the parent heard.

PASS TEST — The parent left knowing

EVIDENCE TO FILE — reflective note and supervision record. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the parent tells the school afterwards that 'the psychologist said he's grand', when the report says he has a significant language difficulty.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain warn–say–pause–check, why softening harms, and the difference between being gentle in manner and being unclear in content.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you learn the parent did not take in the message: contact them, offer a follow-up, and say it again plainly — with your supervisor's agreement.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Softening difficult news until the parent does not know what was found.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Hold silence when someone is upset' and 'Say what you do not know'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words the hardest sentence: whether they warn first ('I have some news that may be hard to hear'), say it plainly, and then stop.

micro.name: Hold silence when someone is upset
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
When a parent cries or goes quiet, the instinct is to fill the silence with more findings, reassurance or recommendations. The Reference sheet names filling a silence after difficult news as a core error. CORU SoP 2.2 is the standard mapped here. Silence gives the parent time to take in what was said and decide what to ask. Filling it tells them the session matters more than their reaction.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does in the seconds after difficult news: whether they speak, how long they wait, whether they offer tissues or water, what their first words are when they do speak.

WRITE DOWN — roughly how long the silence lasted, and the first sentence after it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how long do you wait, and how do you know when to speak?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the rest of the session after your supervisor has delivered difficult news, with the explicit task of not speaking until the parent does.

THEY HOLD — the difficult news itself, and any response to strong emotion such as anger.

WHY THAT SPLIT — holding silence is best practised while someone else carries the main responsibility. Your only job is to tolerate the discomfort without rescuing it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — deliver news yourself and then hold the silence, offering only a brief acknowledgement ('this is hard to hear') if needed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — you rushing on to the recommendations, or filling the gap with reassurance you cannot stand behind ('she'll be absolutely fine').

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a small gesture to wait, or 'take your time — there's no hurry today.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — after difficult information, stop talking, acknowledge briefly if needed, and let the parent speak first.

PASS TEST — You did not fill it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — reflective note. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the parent starts to cry and you begin describing the reading programme, and they hear nothing more that day.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why silence helps, what a brief acknowledgement sounds like, and how to manage your own discomfort in the pause.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent is too upset to continue: offer to stop, agree a second meeting, make sure they are safe to leave, and send the written summary later.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Filling the silence after difficult news with more information.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Answer the question actually asked' and into supervision on the emotional impact of the work.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does in the seconds after difficult news: whether they speak, how long they wait, whether they offer tissues or water, what their first words are when they do speak.

micro.name: Answer the question actually asked
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents often ask a hard question — 'will he ever read?', 'did I cause this?', 'will she go to a mainstream secondary?' — and the easy move is to answer an adjacent, safer one. CORU SoP 2.11 is the standard mapped here. Answering a different question tells the parent the real one cannot be spoken, and they carry it home alone. You may not know the answer, but you can still answer the question.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the questions parents ask in your supervisor's sessions, and whether the answer given addresses that exact question or a related one.

WRITE DOWN — each hard question (anonymised) and the first sentence of the answer.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a parent asks if it's their fault, what do you actually say?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — anticipating the three hardest questions a parent might ask in a supervised case and drafting honest answers.

THEY HOLD — answering those questions in the session on your early cases.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing answers is safe and useful. Answering a parent's fear in the moment, with no time to think, is where you need to have seen it done.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — take the question-and-answer part of the session yourself, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — sliding from 'will he ever read?' to a description of the reading programme, or from 'is it my fault?' to general information about causes.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I think what mum is asking is whether she did something to cause this — is that right?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — when a parent asks a question, check you have understood it, answer that question, and say so if you cannot.

PASS TEST — Not the easier adjacent one

EVIDENCE TO FILE — reflective note. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the parent asks the same question three times in different words, and leaves without an answer.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why we drift to adjacent questions, how to check the question before answering ('is what you're asking…?'), and how to answer honestly when the true answer is 'I don't know'.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise afterwards you answered the wrong question: contact the parent and say 'I don't think I answered what you asked me — can I try now?'

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Answering a safer related question instead of the one the parent asked.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Say what you do not know'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Say what you do not know
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Parents ask about prognosis, cause and the future, and the honest answer is often uncertain. PSI Code 4.1.3 is the clause mapped here — read it for its exact wording. Claiming certainty you do not have leaves the family planning around a guess, and damages trust when it turns out wrong. Saying 'I don't know, and here is how we will find out' is a professional answer, not a failure.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words uncertainty: what they say they do not know, and what they add to it (what would help find out, when it will be clearer).

WRITE DOWN — the phrases they use ('we can't tell yet', 'the research doesn't give a clear answer for a child like her').

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you say you don't know without the parent losing confidence in the assessment?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listing, before the session, what the assessment cannot answer (prognosis, cause, whether a diagnosis would be made by another service) and drafting how to say each.

THEY HOLD — questions about other services' decisions (CDNT, CAMHS, NCSE) where a wrong answer from you would mislead.

WHY THAT SPLIT — knowing the limits of your assessment is your job. Other services' thresholds and waiting times change, and your supervisor is more likely to be current on them.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — answer parent questions yourself, naming uncertainty where it exists and saying how it could be reduced.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — guessing to fill the gap (for example about CDNT waiting times or whether a diagnosis would follow), and over-hedging answers you do know.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that's a fair question, and we honestly don't know yet — what would help us know is…'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — say plainly when you do not know, separate it from what you do know, and say what would reduce the uncertainty.

PASS TEST — Uncertainty admitted

EVIDENCE TO FILE — reflective note, and the limitations section of the report. Log against 3. Intervention and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you tell a parent 'she'll catch up by secondary school' and she doesn't, and the parent later quotes you to the school.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between uncertainty and incompetence, how to express uncertainty with a plan attached, and which questions EPs are and are not in a position to answer.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you gave an answer you should not have: correct it in writing, tell your supervisor, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Guessing at an answer rather than saying you do not know.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Ethical Practice — working within competence — and 'State what you did not assess and what that limits'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Use a named consultation model
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Without a model, consultation becomes a chat that ends in advice. A named model gives you a sequence to return to when the conversation drifts. Problem-solving consultation (Bergan & Kratochwill, 1990, Behavioral Consultation and Therapy), consultation as a framework for EP practice (Wagner, 2000, Educational Psychology in Practice) and solution-focused approaches (Rhodes & Ajmal, 1995, Solution Focused Thinking in Schools) are three. CORU SoP 5.38 is the standard mapped here. The Reference sheet's advice: pick one and use it repeatedly.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which model your supervisor is using, even if they do not name it: do they move through problem identification, analysis, plan, evaluation; or start from exceptions and preferred futures?

WRITE DOWN — the stages you can see in the meeting, and the question that moved it from one stage to the next.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which model were you working from there, and where did you depart from it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing one model, reading its core source, and preparing a one-page prompt sheet of its stages and key questions before a supervised consultation.

THEY HOLD — leading the consultation, while you track the stages on your sheet.

WHY THAT SPLIT — learning a model's structure is reading and preparation. Following it in a live meeting while also listening to a teacher is the harder skill, best learned by tracking someone else first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a consultation using your chosen model, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — skipping from problem statement straight to plan, which is where problem-solving consultation most often fails (Reference sheet; see Gutkin & Curtis, 2009, for the evidence).

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before we talk about what to do — can we get a clearer picture of when this happens?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — use one named model consistently in your consultations and be able to say which stage each part of the meeting was.

PASS TEST — You can say which one

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation record with the model named, anonymised. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — asked in supervision which model you used, you say 'just a general chat, really', and cannot describe how the meeting was structured.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the stages of your chosen model, cite its source, say why problem identification carries so much weight, and compare it briefly with one other model.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the model does not fit a meeting (for example a crisis): name the departure in your record, deal with the immediate need, and return to the model at the next meeting.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Running consultations as unstructured conversations with no model you can name.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Contract at the start', 'Ask questions that open rather than close', and Systemic Change.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Contract at the start
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A teacher who expected an assessment and gets a conversation, or who expected advice and gets questions, will leave frustrated. Contracting — agreeing at the start what the meeting is for, how long it will take and what will come out of it — is part of the consultation process described by Wagner (2000). CORU SoP 5.38 is the standard mapped here. Without it, the teacher's unspoken expectation, usually 'take the child and fix him', governs the meeting.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor opens a consultation: whether they say what the meeting is for, how long it will take, what the teacher will leave with, and what happens with the notes.

WRITE DOWN — the opening words, and any moment later where the contract was referred back to ('we said we'd focus on the mornings').

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when the teacher clearly expected you to take the child out and assess him?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a short contracting script for your service: purpose, time, roles, what is recorded and who sees it, what happens next.

THEY HOLD — the opening itself, especially with teachers or principals who have strong expectations of what an EP visit is.

WHY THAT SPLIT — scripting the contract is preparation. Holding it with a principal who wants something else is authority you are still building.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — open a supervised consultation with your contract, and check the teacher agrees before moving on.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a contract rushed through as a formality, and not noticing when the teacher's expectation is different.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I just check — what were you hoping to get from today?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — begin each consultation by agreeing its purpose, time, roles and output, and check the teacher's own expectation.

PASS TEST — Both parties know what this meeting is for

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation record showing the agreed purpose. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — forty minutes in, the teacher asks 'so when will you be seeing him?', and it is clear she thought this meeting was the preamble to an assessment.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what contracting covers, why it matters in a service where schools expect assessment, and how to renegotiate when the teacher wants something else.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the contract breaks down mid-meeting: stop, name it, re-agree the purpose, and if necessary agree a different meeting for the other need.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Starting a consultation without agreeing what it is for.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask questions that open rather than close' and 'Agree actions with a review point'.

micro.name: Ask questions that open rather than close
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The presenting concern is rarely the workable problem, and questions — not suggestions — get you from 'he's disruptive' to a defined, observable pattern (Reference sheet, 'Problem identification'). 'Have you tried…?' reads as criticism however it is meant. CORU SoP 5.38 and 5.40 are the standards mapped here. A teacher who generates the solution owns it and is more likely to implement it; one handed a solution is less so (Reference sheet, 'Staying out of the expert role').

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the questions your supervisor asks, and how many are open (what, when, how) versus closed or leading ('have you tried a sticker chart?').

WRITE DOWN — the questions that visibly shifted the teacher's thinking — often 'when does it not happen?' or 'what do you think is going on?'

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you stop yourself suggesting something when you can see the answer?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing a bank of opening questions for each stage of your model, and in the meeting asking two or three of them at points your supervisor signals.

THEY HOLD — the flow of the consultation and the decision on when to move to planning.

WHY THAT SPLIT — asking a prepared question is a safe contribution. Knowing when enough has been understood to move on is a judgement that takes many consultations.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the problem-identification and analysis stages with open questions, holding back your own suggestions.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'have you tried…?', questions that are suggestions in disguise, and moving to solutions before the problem is defined.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what do you think is going on for him?' — the question the teacher is rarely asked.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — run a consultation in which your contribution is mainly questions, and the plan comes from the teacher.

PASS TEST — The teacher generated the solution

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation record noting who proposed each action. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you leave with a list of your own strategies, the teacher agreed politely, and at review none has been tried.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why open questions build ownership, give examples at each stage of a problem-solving model, and say why 'have you tried' backfires.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the teacher insists on being told what to do: offer two or three options, ask which fits the class, and let them choose and adapt.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Offering solutions before the problem is defined, or asking 'have you tried…?'

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify who holds the problem and who holds the power' and 'Build capacity rather than doing it for them'.

micro.name: Identify who holds the problem and who holds the power
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The person most worried about a child is not always the person who can change things. A class teacher may carry the problem while the principal controls timetabling and SET deployment; a parent may carry it while the school holds the resource. CORU SoP 5.22 is the standard mapped here. Consulting with someone who has no power over the change produces plans nobody can implement. Schein's work on process consultation (Schein, 1999, Process Consultation Revisited) is one source on reading these relationships.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — who is in the consultation, who is not, who speaks most, and who defers to whom. Notice whether the plan depends on someone who is not present.

WRITE DOWN — for one consultation, who owns the concern, who can change timetabling, staffing or the classroom, and who would have to agree.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide whether the principal needs to be in the room?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — mapping, before the meeting, who holds the concern and who holds each resource the plan might need (class teacher, SET, principal, SNA, parent).

THEY HOLD — the decision to widen the meeting or approach the principal separately.

WHY THAT SPLIT — mapping is analysis you can do from the file. Approaching a principal about who should attend is a relationship move your supervisor makes on behalf of the service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a consultation and, before agreeing actions, check whether those present can carry them out or need someone else's agreement.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a plan that needs the principal's agreement, agreed with a class teacher who cannot give it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is this something you can decide, or does it need to go to the principal first?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before closing a consultation, identify who holds the problem and who holds the power to act, and address the gap.

PASS TEST — You noticed the difference

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation record noting who needs to agree, anonymised. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the class teacher agrees to extra SET input, the principal knows nothing about it, and nothing changes.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between holding a problem and holding the power to change it, and how to map this in any school.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the person with power will not engage: record it, discuss it with your supervisor, and plan within what those present can control.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Agreeing a plan with someone who has no power to carry it out.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Agree actions with a review point', and into Systemic Change.

micro.name: Agree actions with a review point
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Consultations without a written record and a review date evaporate, and the teacher concludes psychology is talk (Reference sheet, 'Closing the loop'). CORU SoP 5.37 is the standard mapped here. Your placement review named record-keeping and consultation write-up as a development area, and this is the habit that addresses it. Sending the record within 24 hours, as the Reference sheet advises, makes the actions visible to everyone.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor closes a consultation: summarising actions, naming who does each, setting a review date, and saying when the record will be sent.

WRITE DOWN — the actions as agreed, the review date, and how soon afterwards the record went out.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you actually send the teacher, and how long does it take you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the consultation record for your supervisor's consultation and sending it to them within 24 hours for checking.

THEY HOLD — the closing summary in the meeting and approval of the record before it goes to the school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the write-up is the named development area and should be yours at once. Your supervisor approves it so you learn what a school needs to see.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close a consultation yourself: summarise actions, roles and a review date aloud, then send the record within 24 hours.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — actions like 'monitor behaviour' with no specifics, and a record that arrives a week later.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'let's read those back — who, what, by when, and when do we meet again?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — close every consultation with specific actions, named roles and a dated review, and send the record within 24 hours.

PASS TEST — Specific and dated

EVIDENCE TO FILE — anonymised consultation record, with the date sent. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at the review, nobody can remember what was agreed and you have no record to check.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what a consultation record needs to contain, why it goes out within a day, and how the review date connects to the Student Support File cycle.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a record has not been sent: send it now, apologise briefly, and confirm the review date is still right.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
No written record and no review date after the consultation.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Set a review date' in recommendations, and into 'Build capacity rather than doing it for them'.

micro.name: Build capacity rather than doing it for them
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
One psychologist cannot see every child, and consultation is how the work reaches more of them (Reference sheet; Gutkin & Curtis, 2009). CORU SoP 5.40 frames this as building capacity. When you solve the problem for the teacher, the next similar child comes back to you. When the teacher understands the process, they can use it again. The pull toward being the expert is strongest when you are a trainee who wants to be useful.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — moments where your supervisor holds back an answer and lets the teacher reach it, and whether they name the process ('what we did there was look for when it doesn't happen').

WRITE DOWN — anything your supervisor did to make the process transferable — a framework handed over, a summary of the steps, a question the teacher can reuse.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know a teacher could do this without you next time?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing a short, practical resource for the teacher based on the consultation process (for example the key questions from problem identification), checked by your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — judgement on how much process to make explicit with this teacher, since some welcome it and some find it patronising.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing resources is safe and useful. Reading a teacher's appetite for learning the process needs experience of many teachers.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a consultation and, at the end, name the process you used and ask the teacher how they might use it with another child.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — you doing the thinking for the teacher, or delivering a lecture on the model the teacher did not ask for.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if another child in your class started doing this next month, what would you do first?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — in each consultation, leave the teacher with a process they can use again, not only a plan for this child.

PASS TEST — They could do it again without you

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation record and any resource left with the teacher. Log against 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the same teacher refers a second child with the same pattern a term later, without having tried anything from the first consultation.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between solving a problem and building capacity, why it matters for a service with limited time, and how to make a process visible without lecturing.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a school relies on you to solve every problem: raise it with your supervisor, and plan a staff session or a series of consultations that hand the process over.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Solving the teacher's problem for them, so they cannot solve the next one.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Systemic Change, and into 'Use a named consultation model' with the next teacher.

Not started

micro.name: Understand how SET hours are allocated
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet sets out the principle: special education teaching (SET) hours come to the school as a block under a profiled model, not per child and not per diagnosis, and the school decides how to deploy them. Parents very often believe that a report or a diagnosis 'gets' their child hours. If you say or imply that, you set up a conflict between the family and the school and then leave. The detail of the profile changes, so for how it is calculated this year check the current Department of Education circular and the NCSE guidance rather than working from memory. CORU SoP 5.13 is the standard mapped here.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor says when a parent or teacher asks 'will the report get him resource hours?' Listen for the exact words: whether they say 'the school has an allocation', whether they explain that the school decides, and how quickly they move on to what the support should be for. Notice how the explanation changes for a principal and for a parent.

WRITE DOWN — the sentence they use with a parent, as close to word for word as you can, plus the terms this school uses ('resource', 'learning support', 'SET') and what each means here.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do parents most often get wrong about hours, and what's the one sentence that puts it right without making the school look bad?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the NCSE guidance on the allocation model and the current Department of Education SET circular (check it has not been replaced), then drafting a five-sentence plain-English explanation for parents. Your supervisor checks it before you use it.

THEY HOLD — the conversation with any parent who is already in dispute with the school about support, or who has been told elsewhere that a report will secure hours.

WHY THAT SPLIT — getting the model right on paper is safe to practise. A parent in conflict with a school needs someone who knows the history, and one wrong sentence from you becomes 'the psychologist said'.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain the allocation model to a parent at a feedback meeting, with your supervisor present, and then move straight on to what the support for their child should look like.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — implying the report or diagnosis unlocks hours; quoting figures or parts of the formula from memory; blaming the school ('they get the hours and decide who gets them'); using 'profiled model' without explaining it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I add something — the school gets its support teaching as one allocation for everyone, so what this report does is help them decide how to use it well for your son.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain in plain words to a parent that SET is allocated to the school and not to the child, that the school decides how it is used through its support planning, and that the report's job is to say what the support should target. Check understanding by asking what they now plan to ask the school.

PASS TEST — You can explain the model to a parent

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a line in the case record noting what was explained; your parent script as a working paper. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent who goes from your meeting to the principal and says 'the psychologist said he's entitled to so many hours a week'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why allocation to schools rather than to children changes how every recommendation must be worded; how SET differs from SNA access and from special class placement; and where to find the current basis of the allocation (the current circular and NCSE guidance, read rather than recalled).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if you realise you told a parent something inaccurate, correct it quickly by phone or in writing, tell your supervisor, and give the school a heads-up so they are not caught off guard at the next meeting.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Telling a parent, or implying in a report, that a diagnosis or assessment will secure a set number of hours for their child.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know how the school deploys what it has', 'Cite the specific circular rather than guidance', and the recommendations section of every report.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

Listen for the exact words: whether they say 'the school has an allocation', whether they explain that the school decides, and how quickly they move on to what the support should be for. Notice how the explanation changes for a principal and for a parent.

micro.name: Cite the specific circular rather than 'guidance'
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: circulars change, so check the current Department circular before you cite anything in a report. CORU SoP 1.13 is mapped here; the Reference sheet reads it as requiring you to be aware of current legislation and to seek out new legislation. 'Department guidance says' cannot be checked and is often out of date. A circular number and title let a principal check what you wrote, and make you check it too. This file does not give circular numbers on purpose: look up the current one each time, because a number you learned last year may have been replaced.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor names circulars in reports and meetings or says 'the guidelines'; where they look them up (the Department of Education circulars search on gov.ie, the NCSE website); and how they confirm a circular is still in force (a later circular that replaces it, the issue date).

WRITE DOWN — the circulars the service cites routinely for SET, SNA access and special class or special school placement, with where you found each one and the date you checked it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you find out when a circular has been replaced, and has an old one ever caught you out in a meeting?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building a one-page reference list of the circulars that currently apply to SET, SNA access and special class/school placement: number, title, issue date, link, and the date you last opened it.

THEY HOLD — confirming that list is current for the service, and deciding which circulars are cited in reports and which are only for background.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding documents is desk research you can do alone. Knowing which ones the service treats as governing, and whether a replacement is expected, is service knowledge you do not yet have.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — draft a report or letter paragraph that refers to allocation, SNA access or placement, citing the circular by number and title; your supervisor reviews it before it goes anywhere.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'as per Department guidance'; a number copied from an old report without opening the current version; paraphrasing a paragraph that has since changed; citing a circular for something it does not say.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'which circular is that from, and when did you last open it? Show me the paragraph.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — whenever you refer in writing to SET allocation, SNA access or placement criteria, name the circular by number and title, having opened the current version on the day you wrote it, and quote only what it actually says.

PASS TEST — You name the circular number

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your dated reference list of circulars; the report paragraph that cites one. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report that cites a replaced circular, and the principal points it out at the review meeting in front of the parents.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to find a circular, how to check it is still in force, why 'guidance' is not a citation, and the difference between a Department circular, NCSE guidance and the Education for Persons with Special Educational Needs (EPSEN) Act 2004. You can also explain why this encyclopedia tells you to check rather than giving a number.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if you cited an outdated circular in a report already issued, tell your supervisor and agree a correction or addendum. Do not quietly fix it in the next version.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'Department guidance states' or copying a circular number from an old report without opening the current version.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Understand how SET hours are allocated', 'Know the SENO route and what the NCSE can do', and 6. Ethical Practice (keeping knowledge current).

micro.name: Know how the school deploys what it has
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Allocation is what arrives at the school; deployment is what the school does with it. The Reference sheet says the principal and SET team deploy the allocation, usually through a support plan review, with the SENCO or SET coordinator holding the overview. It also warns that recommending 'additional SET time' asks the school to take it from another child. A recommendation that ignores how support is actually deployed either asks for something that does not exist or repeats what is already happening. CORU SoP 5.14 is the standard mapped here.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor finds out how support is actually used: in-class or withdrawal, group sizes, who decides which children get what, how often that is reviewed, and whether the timetable matches the plan. Notice the questions they ask the SET coordinator that are not in any form.

WRITE DOWN — for one school, how support is organised this year, who decides, and when it is reviewed. No pupil names in your notes.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you find out how a school really uses its hours, as opposed to what they tell you at the first planning meeting?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking the SET coordinator to walk you through how support is organised this year, and asking to see the SEN policy and, with permission, a Student Support File for a child you are working with.

THEY HOLD — any conversation that questions the school's deployment decisions.

WHY THAT SPLIT — gathering the picture is information-gathering and teaches you the terrain. Questioning deployment is systemic influence, and it depends on a relationship with the principal that your supervisor has built over years and you have not.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for a child you are assessing, find out exactly what support they currently get (who delivers it, how often, group size, in-class or withdrawal, what targets) and write the recommendations around it. Your supervisor reviews them.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'additional SET support' instead of what the support should target; assuming the child gets what the Student Support File says without checking; recommendations the timetable cannot hold.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what is he actually getting now? Then your recommendation is about what that time should be used for.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep allocation and deployment separate in your notes and reports: find out how support is deployed for this child, and write recommendations about how that time is used, not about how much of it there should be.

PASS TEST — Allocation and deployment are different things

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a note of current provision in the case record; the recommendations section of the report. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report recommending 'increased resource hours', which the principal reads as a psychologist who does not know how schools work.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference with an example: the same hours used as withdrawal groups of six on one programme, or as in-class team teaching, with very different results. You can also show how the NEPS Continuum of Support and the Student Support File shape deployment decisions, and why recommendations should name a purpose rather than a quantity.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if the school says your recommendation cannot be delivered, ask what could be done within how support is organised now, and revise it with them rather than defending it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending 'more SET hours' rather than saying what the existing support time should be used for.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Map each Continuum level against provision', 'Identify a gap in the continuum', and the recommendations section of every report.

micro.name: Know the SENO route and what the NCSE can do
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: the Special Educational Needs Organiser (SENO) handles applications for SNA access and for special class or special school placement. That is a different process from SET hours, and trainees routinely mix them up. SNA support is for significant care needs, not learning support. NCSE structures and application routes have changed in recent years, so check the NCSE website for how things work now, including how SNA access is currently decided and how schools reach the local SENO, before you advise anyone. CORU SoP 5.5 is mapped here.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when your supervisor points a school or family to the SENO, what for, and what they say the SENO can and cannot do. Listen for how they separate SNA access (care needs), special class or special school places, and SET (which the school decides).

WRITE DOWN — a simple table: the need, who handles it, and how to make contact. Include the SENO, the principal or SET coordinator, the HSE CDNT, CAMHS, and the NCSE's teacher support services (check current names on the NCSE website).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you usually work with the SENO for these schools, and what do families most often ask them for that isn't theirs to give?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — finding the NCSE's current information on the SENO role, the special class and special school application process and SNA access, and turning it into a contact table for the Cavan schools.

THEY HOLD — direct contact with the SENO about individual children, and anything said to a parent about whether their child is likely to get a special class place.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading the process is safe and quick. Anything a psychologist says about eligibility is heard by parents as a promise, and the working relationship with the SENO belongs to the service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — at a feedback meeting, explain to a parent which route fits their question and who they should contact, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — recommending an SNA for a reading difficulty (the Reference sheet calls this a category error); implying the psychologist decides placement; promising a place; sending a parent to the SENO about SET hours the school decides.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'just to be clear, the SENO deals with applications for places and SNA access. The support teaching is something the school organises, so that's a conversation with the principal.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for any question a school or parent raises about provision, say who decides it and how to contact them, and word recommendations so the right person can act on them. Where you mean an adult nearby for safety, say that and why, rather than writing 'SNA'.

PASS TEST — You know who to contact and for what

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your contact table (roles, not personal names); the case record entry. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a family waiting months on a SENO reply about something the school could have decided in a week.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the difference between SET, SNA access and special class/school placement, who decides each one, why SNA is about care and not teaching, and where the NCSE's role is set out in law (read the EPSEN Act 2004 and the NCSE's own description of its functions rather than summarising from memory).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if a report you drafted sends someone down the wrong route, tell your supervisor, contact the family with the correct route, and correct the report.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending SNA support for a learning difficulty, or sending a parent to the SENO for something the school decides.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Cite the specific circular rather than guidance', 'Visit a range of special education settings', and placement recommendations.

micro.name: Map each Continuum level against provision
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The NEPS Continuum of Support (Classroom Support, School Support, School Support Plus) describes what should happen at each level; the map shows what actually does in this school. The Reference sheet lists what to map: who is on the SEN team, how children are identified, withdrawal versus in-class, group sizes, how plans are written and reviewed, how information moves between the SET and the class teacher, and what happens at transitions. Two schools with the same allocation get very different results, and the difference is organisation. A map built from the policy document alone describes a school that does not exist.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor gets from policy to practice. The Reference sheet's contrast: 'how does it usually work when a teacher is worried about someone?' gets the real process, while 'what is your identification procedure?' gets the policy. Notice who they ask (class teacher, SET, coordinator, principal) and where the accounts differ.

WRITE DOWN — a grid with a row for each Continuum level and columns for: who identifies, what is offered, who delivers, group size, how plans are written and reviewed, and how information returns to the class teacher.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which parts of this map would you check with a second person before trusting them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — filling in the grid from short conversations with a class teacher, a SET and the coordinator, and from the SEN policy.

THEY HOLD — the conversation with the principal about the map, and the decision about which parts are firm enough to use in a report or planning meeting.

WHY THAT SPLIT — collecting the picture teaches you how Irish schools work in practice. Checking it with the principal touches on how the school is led, and needs a relationship you do not yet have.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — build the full map for one Cavan school; your supervisor checks it against what they know of the school.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the SEN policy copied into the grid; a Classroom Support row left empty because nobody thought to describe it; one person's account taken as the whole picture; transitions (class to class, primary to post-primary) missed out.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that's what the policy says. What did the class teacher tell you actually happens when she's worried about a child?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — map all three Continuum levels for a school from at least two sources, mark where accounts differ, and keep it as a working document that informs your formulations for children in that school.

PASS TEST — The map is complete and accurate

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the map as a working paper, with no pupil names; a note of how it was gathered. Log against 4. Systemic Change, not as casework (the Reference sheet names this as why Systemic Change ends up thinly evidenced).

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a map saying School Support Plus plans are reviewed every term, because the policy says so, when none have been reviewed this year.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the three Continuum levels and what each should contain (read the NEPS Continuum of Support guidelines for primary and post-primary for the wording), how to gather practice rather than policy, and why the map belongs in formulation: it tells you whether a difficulty sits in the child or in how support is delivered.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if staff feel checked up on, stop, explain what the map is for (planning support for the children you are seeing), and go back to open, curious questions.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Building the map from the SEN policy and believing it describes what happens.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify a gap in the continuum', 'Present the map back to the school', and the context section of Formulation.
