micro.name: Identify a gap in the continuum
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet's examples: if every child is withdrawn in groups of six for the same programme regardless of need, the organisation is doing the deciding, not the assessment; if plans are written by the SET and never seen by the class teacher, nothing will generalise. These are findings, and they tell you whether a child's difficulty is about the child or about delivery. If it is delivery, an individual intervention will not fix it. CORU SoP 5.35 is mapped here. Naming one gap clearly is worth more than listing everything you noticed.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor notices a delivery-level pattern across cases: several referrals from one class, the same programme for every child, no Classroom Support level before a referral, plans that stop at School Support. Notice how they check it is a pattern and not a single case.

WRITE DOWN — the gap in one sentence, the evidence for it (at least two sources), and which Continuum level it sits at.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell the difference between a gap in the school's system and a gap in one teacher's practice, and why does that difference matter?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — going through your map and your cases in this school and drafting one candidate gap with the evidence for it.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether the gap is real, whether it is worth raising, and whether now is the right time given what else is happening in the school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — spotting patterns is analytical work you can do from the map. Whether and when to raise something depends on the school's current pressures and relationships, which your supervisor knows.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present your candidate gap in supervision with its evidence and say what it means for a child you are working with.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a gap that is really a complaint about a named teacher; a gap based on one source; five gaps where one was asked for; a gap outside the school's control (such as the allocation itself).

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'which of these is the one that, if it changed, would make the most difference to the children you're seeing? Just that one.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name one gap in how support is organised, at a stated Continuum level, backed by more than one source, and link it to what it means for at least one child you are working with.

PASS TEST — You named one

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the gap and its evidence in your map; a line in the relevant formulation showing the link. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a formulation that locates everything in the child when your own map shows the child has had no Classroom Support at all before being referred.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer what a delivery-level factor is, give two examples from the Reference sheet, show how to test whether it is a real pattern, and explain why it belongs in a formulation and not just in your notes (Frederickson & Cline, 2009, on whole-school approaches, is the Reference sheet's reading).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if the gap you named turns out to be wrong once you learn more, say so in supervision, update the map, and remove it from any formulation that relied on it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Naming a gap that is really criticism of one named staff member rather than a feature of how support is organised.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Say what would close the gap', 'Present the map back to the school', and 2. Formulation.

micro.name: Say what would close the gap
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A gap with no suggested change is an observation the school cannot use. The Reference sheet: offer one change, not five, because schools implement one. Fullan (2016, The New Meaning of Educational Change, 5th ed.) argues that change depends on what it means to the people who have to carry it out, so a proposal has to fit the school's existing time, staff and routines. CORU SoP 5.35 is mapped here. A proposal that needs extra resources the school does not have will be nodded at and dropped.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the kind of changes your supervisor suggests: small, specific, within existing resources and routines (a ten-minute handover between SET and class teacher each fortnight; grouping by need rather than year group; a shared one-page plan). Notice how they frame it as the school's idea to build on.

WRITE DOWN — the gap, the proposed change, who would do it, when, and how anyone would know it had worked.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's a change you've suggested that a school actually took up, and what was different about it from the ones they didn't?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting one proposal for the gap you named: who, what, when, with what existing resource, and one sign that it is working.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether the proposal is realistic for this school now, and how it is pitched to the principal.

WHY THAT SPLIT — designing the proposal teaches you to think at school level. Judging what this school can absorb this term depends on its history of change, which your supervisor knows.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — take your proposal through a consultation with the SET coordinator or a class teacher, with your supervisor present, and adjust it based on what they say.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — proposals that need new hours or staff; several changes bundled together; a proposal the school has already tried; telling rather than building the proposal with them.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before we go further — has anything like this been tried here before? What happened?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — propose one concrete change that the school could make within its current resources, agreed with the people who would carry it out, with a named way to check if it has worked.

PASS TEST — You proposed something the school could do

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the proposal and consultation note; any follow-up showing what happened. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a feedback letter ending 'the school may wish to review its model of SEN provision', which nobody can act on.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why one change beats five, what makes a proposal realistic (existing resources, existing routines, someone who owns it), and how to link it to a review point. You can connect this to Fullan (2016) on the meaning of change for those who implement it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if the school agrees but nothing happens, go back at the review point, ask what got in the way without blame, and shrink the change until it fits.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Proposing a change that needs resources the school does not have, or proposing several changes at once.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Present the map back to the school', 'End with three things the school could do this term', and 3. Intervention at school level.

micro.name: Present the map back to the school
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A map filed in your placement folder changes nothing for children. The Reference sheet's approach to feedback: describe rather than judge, for example 'support is currently organised by year group rather than by need, which means one child is working on material above his current level', and offer one change. CORU SoP 5.40 is mapped here, on building capacity among those responsible for delivering interventions. Wagner (2000, Educational Psychology in Practice, 16(1)) describes consultation that works at school and organisational level as well as with individual cases; this is that work.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor gives school-level feedback: who is in the room (principal, coordinator), how they open (what is working first), how they describe the gap in neutral, descriptive terms, and how they end with one agreed action and a date.

WRITE DOWN — the structure of the conversation, the phrases used to describe a gap without blame, and what was agreed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide whether to give this kind of feedback to the principal alone or to the whole SEN team?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing a one-page version of the map and the proposed change, written descriptively, with no names of staff or pupils.

THEY HOLD — leading the feedback meeting with the principal.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing it teaches you descriptive, blame-free wording. The meeting is about how the school is organised, and the principal will expect to hear it from the psychologist who has the ongoing relationship with the school.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present the map and one proposal to the SET coordinator or SEN team, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — judging words ('inadequate', 'failing'); anything that identifies a teacher; presenting it as an inspection finding; leaving without an agreed next step or date.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's been picked up here is a pattern we see in lots of schools — can we talk about which bit of it would be easiest to try first?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — present the map and one proposed change to the school in descriptive terms, agree an action with a named owner and a review date, and follow up at that date.

PASS TEST — It was used, not just submitted

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the one-page summary; a note of what was agreed and what happened at follow-up. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a well-received meeting, a thank-you email, and no change by the time you leave Cavan on 18/12/2026, because nobody owned the next step.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to turn a map into feedback a school will act on: descriptive language, strengths first, one change, a named owner and a date. You can also explain why it is logged as systemic work and what that does for the portfolio.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if a staff member takes the feedback personally, acknowledge it, restate that the pattern is about organisation not individuals, and follow up privately through your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Handing the school a map and leaving without an agreed action, an owner and a follow-up date.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Deliver the good practice presentation', 'Collect and file feedback from the school', and 4. Systemic Change evidence.

micro.name: Arrange visits early in the placement
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
PSI 3.3.6 is NOT yet met. It requires experience in mainstream primary, post-primary AND special education settings; so far there is one post-primary day and no special education at all. The Reference sheet says it plainly: it will not happen unless you ask in week one and get a date. The visits need to be planned into the Cavan Appendix 1 before the placement starts on 05/10/2026, because the placement runs only to 18/12/2026, four days a week, and settings may need several weeks' notice for a visitor. Handbook Table 3 is the standard mapped here. Leave it late and the gap carries into Year 2.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in your first contact with your Cavan supervisor, which special settings the service works with most (special schools, special classes in primary and post-primary, early intervention classes), and who in the service has the link with each one. The Reference sheet's advice: go to the settings the service works with most.

WRITE DOWN — each setting type, the named service contact for it (in your own diary, not this file), and the date you asked.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which of these settings would be most useful to see given the referrals you're expecting this term, and could we go together?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the visits into your draft Appendix 1 before 05/10/2026 as a stated objective tied to PSI 3.3.6, and drafting the request emails to settings for your supervisor to approve.

THEY HOLD — the first approach to each setting's principal, and agreement on which visits go into the placement plan.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the gap is yours to plan for and evidence. The approach goes through the service because settings agree to visitors on the strength of an existing professional relationship, not a trainee's email.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — by the end of week two, have at least two different setting types (for example, a special school and a special class attached to a mainstream school) booked with confirmed dates, with your supervisor checking progress in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — one visit treated as covering the category; dates left as 'sometime in November'; visits squeezed into the last fortnight where there is no time to act on what you learn.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'let's ring them now while we're sitting here and get a date in the diary.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — get visits to a range of special education settings written into the Appendix 1 before the placement begins and booked with confirmed dates in the first weeks of Cavan, with a backup date for each.

PASS TEST — Booked in the first weeks

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the Appendix 1 objective naming PSI 3.3.6; the confirmed booking in your placement diary; the visit days in the Log. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — reaching 18/12/2026 with no special education visit because the first request went out in November and the setting was fully booked.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer what PSI 3.3.6 requires (read the PSI Accreditation Standards, 2022, for the wording), why it must be in the Appendix 1 before the placement starts, which setting types count as different, and how to approach a setting through the service.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if a visit falls through, tell your supervisor the same week, rebook or find an equivalent setting, and tell your university placement tutor early if it looks like PSI 3.3.6 will not be met in Cavan, so it can be planned for Year 2.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving special education visits out of the Appendix 1 and asking for them late in the placement.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Observe structure, staffing and communication supports', 'Log each visit separately in Appendix 5', and PSI 3.3.6.

micro.name: Observe structure, staffing and communication supports
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
You will be asked whether a child needs a special class or a special school, and the Reference sheet says you cannot answer that honestly if you have never been in one. Its list of what to look at: staffing ratios and how adults are deployed; the curriculum in use (L1LP, L2LP or adapted mainstream); communication systems and whether everyone uses them; the sensory environment; what integration looks like in practice; where pupils go afterwards. CORU SoP 5.13 is mapped here. These visits are also how PSI 3.3.6, currently unmet, gets met, so observe the system, not only the children.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how adults are deployed across the day (who leads, who supports, who does personal care); which curriculum framework is actually in use (for L1LP and L2LP read the NCCA material first); which communication system is used and whether every adult uses it the same way; noise, light and the use of quiet spaces.

WRITE DOWN — a structured note under the Reference sheet's headings, with no pupil names or identifying details.

ASK AFTERWARDS — ask a teacher 'what does a child need to be able to do to do well here, and what kind of child finds it hard?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing an observation frame from the Reference sheet's headings before the visit, and completing it during and just after.

THEY HOLD — (if they come) the conversation with the principal about admissions, and interpreting what you saw for placement decisions on current cases.

WHY THAT SPLIT — observing a setting systematically is the learning. Linking it to a live placement question involves individual children and the SENO process, which stay with your supervisor.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead your own observation in a second setting of a different type, and compare it with the first in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — describing the children rather than the system; general impressions ('lovely atmosphere') instead of structure; assuming all special classes work alike; a visit that confirms whatever view you arrived with.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've told me about the children. Tell me how many adults were in the room, what each one was doing, and how the children communicated with them.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for each setting, describe how it works (staffing, curriculum, communication, environment, links with mainstream, where pupils go next) well enough to explain what kind of need it fits, and note how it differs from the other settings you have seen.

PASS TEST — You can describe how the setting works

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the structured observation note (no identifying details); the Appendix 5 entry for that visit. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a later placement recommendation that says 'a special class would be appropriate' without being able to say what that class provides.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer how special schools, special classes and early intervention classes differ, what L1LP and L2LP are (read the NCCA source for the detail), and why the Reference sheet frames placement as fit between need and provision rather than severity.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if you notice your notes are full of judgements rather than descriptions, rewrite them before supervision, and bring your assumptions about special provision to supervision as the Reference sheet suggests (CORU SoP 5.44).

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Observing the children and not the system, so you cannot say what the setting actually offers.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Talk to therapy and SNA staff, not only teachers', placement recommendations framed as fit, and PSI 3.3.6.

micro.name: Talk to therapy and SNA staff, not only teachers
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
In special settings a large part of the day may be delivered by SNAs and, where present, by therapists; a teacher-only account misses how communication systems, personal care and regulation work in practice. CORU SoP 5.39 is mapped here. The Reference sheet asks whether communication systems are used consistently by everyone, and only the people using them can tell you. Speaking to the whole team also helps PSI 3.3.6 evidence: it shows you understood the setting as a system, not a classroom.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — who does what during the visit: which adults support communication, meals, toileting and transitions; who manages distress; whether therapy happens in the classroom or elsewhere, and whether it comes from the HSE CDNT or another arrangement (ask; do not assume).

WRITE DOWN — the roles present, not names, and one thing each role told you about how the setting works.

ASK AFTERWARDS — ask an SNA 'what do you wish psychologists knew about a day here?' and ask a therapist, if present, 'how does your work link with what happens in the classroom?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing two or three short questions for each role before the visit, and asking the teacher or principal at the start whether you may speak briefly with SNAs and therapy staff.

THEY HOLD — any discussion of individual children in the setting, and any agreement about future joint work.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the questions are about how the setting works, which is safe and useful. Individual children are not your cases, and discussing them would need consent the visit does not have.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — hold brief conversations with at least one SNA and, where available, one therapist during a visit, and bring what you learned to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — speaking only to the teacher and principal; treating SNAs as a less reliable source; questions about particular children; taking staff away from pupils at busy moments.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the SNAs are on their break at eleven — that might be a good moment to ask them how the visual timetable is used.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — at every setting visit, speak with the people delivering the day-to-day support, not only the teaching staff, and record what each role contributes to how the setting works.

PASS TEST — You spoke to the people delivering

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the observation note, with a section for each role's account (no names); the Appendix 5 entry. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an account of a special class that describes the teacher's plan in detail and says nothing about how the three adults supporting it actually spend the day.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why SNA and therapy staff hold information teachers do not, how to approach them respectfully and briefly, and how their accounts change what you would write about fit between a child and a setting.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if staff are wary of talking to a psychologist, explain you are there to learn how the setting works, not to assess anyone, and leave it there if they still prefer not to.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking the teacher's or principal's account as the whole picture of how a special setting works.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Log each visit separately in Appendix 5', 'Contribute a psychological perspective', and placement recommendations.

micro.name: Log each visit separately in Appendix 5
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet warns against treating one visit as covering special education: a special school, a special class and an early intervention class are different settings with different pupils. PSI 3.3.6 is currently unmet, and the evidence that it has been met will be your record. If three visits sit in one combined entry, nobody reading the portfolio can tell what range you saw. Handbook Appendix 5 is the standard mapped here; read the Handbook itself for what each entry must contain. The reflection is yours to write — this row gives structure only.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor, or a more senior trainee, records placement activity that counts towards a settings requirement: what they name (setting type, age range, date), and how they separate what happened from what they learned.

WRITE DOWN — for each visit, while fresh: date (DD/MM/YYYY), setting type, age range and UCD Table 3 band, what you observed under each heading, and who you spoke to by role.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when you read a trainee's Appendix 5, what tells you they actually learned something from a visit?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a separate Appendix 5 entry for each visit, in your own words, and logging each visit day on its own row in the Log.

THEY HOLD — reading the entries in supervision and confirming the visits as placement activity.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the reflection must be your own work; nobody, including this file, writes it for you. Your supervisor's role is to confirm what took place and to push your thinking in supervision.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring the entry for your first setting visit to supervision within a week of the visit and use the discussion to strengthen the next one.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — entries that list activities without learning; visits merged into one entry; identifying details of pupils or staff; an entry that does not say what kind of setting it was, so it cannot show range.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this reads as a timetable of the day. What do you now think about special class placement that you didn't think before?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write a separate, dated Appendix 5 entry for every setting visited, naming the setting type and age range, what you observed, and what changed in your thinking, in your own words, with no identifying details.

PASS TEST — Each setting is its own entry

EVIDENCE TO FILE — one Appendix 5 entry per visit; one Log row per visit day. Log against 4. Systemic Change. Prompts to structure your own reflection: what you expected, what you saw, what surprised you, what you would now write differently about fit.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — one paragraph headed 'special education visits' covering three settings, which cannot show PSI 3.3.6 has been met.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why each visit needs its own entry, what makes an entry show learning rather than attendance, and how the entries together show range against PSI 3.3.6. You can offer prompts, but you can also explain why a reflection has to be written by the person who had the experience.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if you find visits were merged or not logged, correct the Log and write the missing entries from your notes now, dated as written, and tell your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Combining several setting visits into one entry, so the range required by PSI 3.3.6 cannot be seen.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into PSI 3.3.6 evidence, 7. Supervision discussion, and the reflective learning essay (which is yours to write).

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor, or a more senior trainee, records placement activity that counts towards a settings requirement: what they name (setting type, age range, date), and how they separate what happened from what they learned.

micro.name: Understand how casework is prioritised here
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: team meetings are where you learn what the service actually is — its priorities, pressures and how decisions are made — and the referral pathway, waiting times and priorities are 'not written down anywhere'. Every service decides differently who is seen first, whether by school prioritisation within allocated time, by clinical urgency, or by other criteria; do not assume Cavan works like Roscommon. CORU SoP 5.5 is mapped here. If you do not know what drives the queue, your recommendations will assume a speed of follow-up the service cannot give.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — at team meetings, how referrals are discussed: who brings them, what makes one urgent (safety, exclusion risk, a transition deadline), who decides, and what happens to cases that wait. Notice what is never said aloud but clearly shapes decisions.

WRITE DOWN — the pathway from referral to closure as a simple flowchart, and the factors that move a case up or down the queue. No child or school names.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'can I ask how a referral like that one usually gets prioritised?' — the Reference sheet's example of a question useful to you and unthreatening to everyone.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the pathway flowchart from what you hear in your first few meetings, and checking it with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — any decision about the priority of your own cases.

WHY THAT SPLIT — mapping the pathway is learning the service. Prioritising cases involves risk and fairness between schools, and those decisions rest with qualified staff and the service's management.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for a case you are working on, explain in supervision where it sits in the queue and why, and what that means for when any follow-up can realistically happen.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — assuming the Roscommon pathway applies; forming opinions on whether the prioritisation is right before you understand it; recommending reviews on timescales the service cannot meet.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've recommended a review in six weeks — given where this school's time sits, is that something we can actually do?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — describe accurately how this service decides what gets seen and when, and use it to set realistic timescales in your own recommendations and to tell schools and families honestly what to expect.

PASS TEST — You know what determines the queue

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your pathway flowchart as a working paper; a note in the team-meeting record of what you learned. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — telling a parent 'we'll see him again before Christmas' when the school has already used its time for the term.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer how this service prioritises, how it differs from another service you know, and why knowing the queue is part of writing realistic recommendations. You can name what drives prioritisation without judging it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if you have promised a timescale the service cannot meet, tell your supervisor, and contact the family or school to correct it before they are left waiting.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Assuming the prioritisation rules from your last placement apply to this service.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Note what the service can and cannot offer', realistic recommendations, and 6. Ethical Practice (honesty about timescales).

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Note what the service can and cannot offer
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet lists, among the things to note in team meetings, caseload sizes, what gets prioritised and which other services are often involved, because this is what makes recommendations realistic. A recommendation for weekly psychologist sessions from a service that works through consultation and time allocated to schools will not happen, and the family will blame the school or the service. CORU SoP 5.5 is mapped here. Knowing the limits also tells you when to signpost to the HSE CDNT, CAMHS or Tusla rather than promise something yourself.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what colleagues say the service does and does not do: individual therapy or not, how often reviews happen, group work, training for schools, which age groups and settings, and what is routinely passed to other services (CDNT, CAMHS, Tusla, primary care psychology).

WRITE DOWN — two lists, 'this service offers' and 'this service refers on for', each with the route.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do schools most often ask this service for that it can't provide, and how do you explain that to them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building the two lists and checking them against any written service description or policy you are given.

THEY HOLD — decisions about whether an exception can be made for a particular case.

WHY THAT SPLIT — knowing the standard offer is basic orientation. Exceptions weigh one school's needs against the service's capacity, which is a management judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — review the recommendations in your own draft reports against the lists, and bring any you are unsure of to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — recommendations the service cannot deliver ('the psychologist will provide weekly sessions'); signposting to services with long waiting lists as if they were quick; not signposting at all.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who would deliver that? If it's us, we don't offer that. If it's the CDNT, what's the route in, and what do we tell the family about the wait?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before finalising any recommendation, check who will deliver it and whether they can, and signpost honestly to other services where this one cannot help.

PASS TEST — You know the limits before recommending

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your service offer and signposting lists as working papers; report recommendations each naming who delivers them. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report whose recommendations assume ongoing psychologist involvement the service has never offered, discovered by the school at the review meeting.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer what this service offers, what it refers on and to whom, and why every recommendation should name who delivers it. You can explain how to tell a family about waiting times honestly without discouraging them.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if an issued report promised something the service cannot give, tell your supervisor, agree how to tell the family and school, and correct the record.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending something that no one in the service, or in any service the child can actually reach, will deliver.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Understand how casework is prioritised here', 'Know the SENO route and what the NCSE can do', and 5. Working with Others.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Prepare something to contribute
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: sitting silently for a term is a wasted term. Team meetings are the one routine place to practise contributing among colleagues rather than in supervision, and CORU SoP 2.16 is mapped here (read the clause for its wording). The advice is to prepare one small, specific thing — a case question, a resource you found, an offer to take something on — because small and specific beats impressive. Logging attendance without logging a contribution leaves you nothing to show for the meetings.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what kinds of contribution land well in this team: brief case questions, sharing a resource, offering to take a task, a short update. Notice how long people speak, how they introduce a case without identifying it unnecessarily, and when in the agenda a newcomer can speak.

WRITE DOWN — two or three contributions from others that were useful, and what made them useful.

ASK AFTERWARDS — ask your supervisor 'is there anything coming up at the next meeting where it would be useful for me to bring something?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing one contribution for each meeting and agreeing it with your supervisor beforehand: a question, a resource, or an offer.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether your contribution fits the agenda, and any presentation of a case that is still active.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing and delivering a small contribution is the practice. Deciding what the team needs to hear about an active case depends on the service's priorities and the case's sensitivity.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make your prepared contribution at the meeting, with your supervisor there, and ask them afterwards how it came across.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — silence; a contribution that runs too long; opinions on how the service should be run (the Reference sheet: save those until you understand why it runs as it does); jargon.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor making a gap for you: 'our trainee found something useful on this last week — do you want to say?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — go into every team meeting with one prepared contribution, make it briefly, and log what you contributed as well as that you attended.

PASS TEST — You spoke

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a Log entry for each meeting with date, meeting type and your contribution; a note in supervision of any feedback. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — ten Log rows reading 'attended team meeting' and nothing else, from a whole term.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why preparing one small thing is better than waiting for the right moment, give examples of useful trainee contributions, and explain the difference between a question and an opinion on service design.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if a contribution falls flat or overreaches, talk it through with your supervisor afterwards, and make the next one smaller and more specific rather than going quiet.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Attending for a whole term without speaking, then logging only attendance.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Contribute a psychological perspective', 'Deliver the good practice presentation', and 5. Working with Others.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — what kinds of contribution land well in this team: brief case questions, sharing a resource, offering to take a task, a short update. Notice how long people speak, how they introduce a case without identifying it unnecessarily, and when in the agenda a newcomer can speak.

micro.name: Contribute a psychological perspective
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: in multi-disciplinary meetings different professions formulate differently and use the same words for different things, and the disagreement is usually about the model, not the facts. Hall (2005, Journal of Interprofessional Care, 19(S1)) describes professional cultures as barriers to teamwork; Frost and Robinson (2007, Child Abuse Review, 16(3)) look at joining up children's services. Your contribution is the psychological formulation, stated plainly and without jargon. CORU SoP 2.11 is mapped here. If you add nothing another discipline would not, the team has lost the reason for having a psychologist there.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor adds a psychological view in a multi-disciplinary meeting: linking behaviour to function or context, pointing to interacting factors rather than one cause, asking what the child's view is, or questioning an assumption. Listen for where people use the same word ('anxiety', 'regulation', 'behaviour') to mean different things.

WRITE DOWN — the contribution and why it was psychological rather than medical, therapeutic or educational.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what did you think the other professions in the room were missing, and how did you decide how to say it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing a short psychological formulation of a case you know, in plain language (three or four sentences), for your supervisor to review before the meeting.

THEY HOLD — speaking for the service in the meeting, and handling any disagreement with another discipline.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing a jargon-free formulation is practice you need. Disagreements between disciplines about an active case have consequences for the child and the working relationships, which your supervisor manages.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — give the psychological formulation of a case in a multi-disciplinary or team meeting, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jargon; repeating what the teacher or therapist already said; arguing with another profession's view rather than adding to it; a formulation too long to be heard.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'to put that another way — the pattern seems to be that it happens when demands go up and the adults nearby change, which gives us something to try.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — in a team or multi-disciplinary meeting, offer a psychological view of a case, in plain language, that adds something the other disciplines did not bring, and notice where your model differs from theirs.

PASS TEST — You added something another discipline would not

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Log entry with meeting type and your contribution; supervision note on how it was received. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a contribution that restated the diagnosis already given, in more technical words, and changed nothing about the plan.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer what a psychological perspective adds in a team (formulation of interacting factors, function, the child's voice, testable hypotheses), how professions use the same words differently, and how to find where a disagreement really lies (Hall, 2005).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if another professional dismisses your view, do not argue it in the room; ask a question that brings out the difference in models, and take it to supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Repeating another discipline's view in psychological jargon instead of adding a distinct perspective.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 2. Formulation, 5. Working with Others, and 'Learn consultation models'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Learn a structured problem-solving model
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet sets out the stages of problem-solving consultation: problem identification, problem analysis, plan design, implementation, evaluation. The model comes from behavioural consultation (Bergan & Kratochwill, 1990, Behavioral Consultation and Therapy). The Reference sheet says the evidence consistently shows problem identification predicts outcome; an early source often cited for this is Bergan and Tombari (1976, Journal of School Psychology) — read it before quoting the finding. Without a model you default to advice-giving, which the Reference sheet calls the least effective form of consultation and the most likely to be politely ignored. CORU SoP 5.38 is mapped here.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in a consultation your supervisor leads, how long they stay on defining the problem before any strategy is mentioned; the questions that turn 'he's disruptive' into something observable ('calls out during whole-class maths, about how often?'); and whether they agree a way to measure change before planning.

WRITE DOWN — the stage-by-stage sequence as it actually happened, and the time spent on each stage.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'at what point did you know you and the teacher agreed on what the problem was, and what did you do when you didn't?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading one source on the model (Bergan & Kratochwill, 1990, or a UK version such as the problem analysis framework of Monsen, Graham, Frederickson and Cameron, 1998, Educational Psychology in Practice), and writing a one-page crib sheet of the stages with example questions for each.

THEY HOLD — leading the consultation itself at first.

WHY THAT SPLIT — learning the stages is desk work. Running them live with a teacher under pressure takes judgement about when to hold back from solutions, which you learn by watching first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a problem-solving consultation with a teacher, using your crib sheet, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jumping to strategies before the problem is defined; accepting a vague problem ('his behaviour'); skipping the agreement on how change will be measured; losing the stages when the teacher goes off track.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before we get to what to try — can we pin down exactly what it looks like, when it happens most, and what you'd see if it were better?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — lead a consultation through each stage in order, name the model in your case note, and record the agreed problem definition, plan and review date.

PASS TEST — You can name and follow its stages

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the consultation record, headed by stage, with the model named; your crib sheet. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a case note that reads 'discussed concerns; advised visual timetable and movement breaks', with no problem definition and no way to tell if anything worked.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the five stages, why problem identification carries the most weight, how to turn a vague concern into an observable definition, and where the model struggles (for example, when the problem is a relationship or a system rather than a behaviour).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if a plan fails, go back to problem identification before designing a new plan; the problem was often defined wrongly in the first place.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Moving to strategies before you and the teacher have agreed exactly what the problem is.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Follow one model explicitly for a set of consultations', 3. Intervention, and 'Identify a gap in the continuum'.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Learn a solution-focused approach
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: solution-focused consultation starts from exceptions and preferred futures rather than causes, using scaling, the miracle question and amplifying what already works. It is quick and suits teachers under time pressure, and it is the framework you already used at Roscommon. The approach comes from solution-focused brief therapy (de Shazer, 1985, Keys to Solution in Brief Therapy); Rhodes and Ajmal (1995, Solution Focused Thinking in Schools) apply it to schools. CORU SoP 5.38 is mapped here. Using the techniques without the stance gives a list of questions with nothing behind them.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor asks exception questions ('when is it a bit better, even slightly?') and scaling questions ('on a scale of 0 to 10, where is it now, and what would one point higher look like?'), and how they follow the answer with 'what's different then?' rather than moving on.

WRITE DOWN — the exact wording of the scaling and exception questions, the teacher's answers, and the small next step agreed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you keep a teacher who wants to talk about everything that's wrong focused on the exceptions, without seeming to dismiss them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing your own scaling and exception questions for an upcoming consultation, adjusted from what you used in Roscommon for this service's settings.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether a solution-focused approach suits this consultation (for example, not where a child protection concern or a serious risk needs a full account of what is happening).

WHY THAT SPLIT — the questions are a skill you already have and can sharpen. Judging when the approach is wrong for the situation needs experience you are still gaining.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead a solution-focused consultation with a teacher using scaling and exception questions, with your supervisor observing.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — asking the scaling question and not following it up; drifting back into problem talk; the stance slipping into advice; brushing aside a teacher's real concern too quickly.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you said it's a four now — what's making it a four and not a two?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — use scaling and exception questions fluently in a consultation, follow each answer up, agree one small step that builds on what already works, and name the approach in your record.

PASS TEST — You can use scaling and exception questions

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation record with the scaling scores and agreed step, with the approach named. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a record showing a scaling question was asked, a number noted, and then a list of your suggestions with no link to the number.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the solution-focused stance (the client has resources; build on exceptions), how scaling and exception questions work and how to follow them up, and where the approach is not enough, such as where a problem needs a full account of cause and risk.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if a teacher says 'it's never better', ask about times it was less bad or about coping, and if that does not open anything, switch to a problem-solving approach and say so.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using scaling and exception questions as a script while still giving advice, so the stance is missing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Follow one model explicitly for a set of consultations', 'Ask your supervisor which model they use', and 3. Intervention.

micro.name: Ask your supervisor which model they use
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet points out that the Irish standards fold consultation into other competencies rather than naming it, so you can get through a placement without ever learning a model. The BPS accreditation standards for UK educational psychology doctoral programmes treat consultation as a core function in its own right (check the current edition and year before citing; read them for the wording). Asking your supervisor which model they use, and whether they were trained in it, tells you what you can learn by watching and where you need other sources. CORU SoP 4.5 is mapped here. A supervisor working from an informal blend is common, and it is worth knowing.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in the consultations you observe, what your supervisor actually does: the sequence, the typical questions, whether they define the problem first or look for exceptions, and whether they name a model to the teacher.

WRITE DOWN — your guess at the model, with the evidence, before you ask them.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which consultation model do you use, were you trained in it formally, and where do you depart from it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking the question in supervision, comparing their answer with what you observed, and noting where they differ.

THEY HOLD — their account of their own practice and training, and any recommendation for what you should read or which model you should adopt this year.

WHY THAT SPLIT — asking is part of your learning. What model they practise, and why, is their professional judgement, and knowing it lets you use supervision well.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — after a consultation you observed, discuss with your supervisor which stages or techniques they used and where the model was adjusted for the setting.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — asking in a way that sounds like a test of them; assuming that a model named on paper is the model in practice; not following up on the training question.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'good question — honestly, I was trained in one approach and I've mixed in bits of another over the years. Let me show you where.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — find out which consultation model your supervisor uses, whether they were trained in it and how, and use that to decide what you can learn from them and what you need to read or seek elsewhere.

PASS TEST — You know whether they were trained in it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a supervision note recording the discussion and what you agreed to learn. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — ending the placement having watched a dozen consultations without being able to say what model your supervisor used.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why asking this question is useful, how to ask it respectfully, and how to learn from a supervisor whose model is informal or mixed while still learning one model properly yourself.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if your supervisor uses a model you have not been taught, ask for a reading, and agree in supervision which model you will follow for your own consultations this placement.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Assuming your supervisor follows a formal model without asking whether they were trained in it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Follow one model explicitly for a set of consultations', 7. Supervision, and the supervision contract.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Follow one model explicitly for a set of consultations
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: learn one model properly this year rather than sampling four; name it in supervision, use it repeatedly, and notice where it fails, because competence comes from repetition with reflection, not from breadth. Never naming the model means it cannot be evidenced. Wagner (2008, in Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle, Frameworks for Practice in Educational Psychology) describes consultation as a framework for practice. CORU SoP 5.38 is mapped here. By the end of Cavan you should be able to say what the model gave you and where it fell short.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — across several consultations your supervisor leads, what stays the same (structure, stance, recording) and what they change for different teachers and problems.

WRITE DOWN — for each consultation you observe, the model's stages and where the supervisor departed from them and why.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when do you decide the model isn't working for this teacher, and what do you do instead?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing one model with your supervisor at the start of Cavan and writing it into the Appendix 1 as a learning objective, with a target number of consultations to be agreed with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — observing and giving feedback on selected consultations, and agreeing when you may move away from the model.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the repeated practice has to be yours. Feedback on whether you are following the model, or only its surface, needs someone who has seen it done well.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — run a series of consultations using the chosen model, naming it in each record, with your supervisor observing some and reviewing all the records.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — drifting away from the model without noticing; using its techniques without its stance; not naming it in the record; not noticing where it fails.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'in this one you skipped straight from problem definition to strategies. What would the analysis stage have added?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — follow one named model for a series of consultations, record it each time, and be able to say what it gave you, where it failed, and what you would use instead in those situations.

PASS TEST — You can say what the model gave you

EVIDENCE TO FILE — consultation records naming the model; supervision notes on what you learned; your Appendix 5 entries (your reflection to write). Log against 4. Systemic Change and 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a set of consultations each run differently, none naming a model, so you cannot evidence that you learned one.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the model you used, what it is good for and poor at, and when you would choose something else — the Reference sheet's grade 5. Prompts for your own reflection: what the model made easier, where it got in the way, what you would do differently. The reflection itself is yours to write.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if the model keeps failing in one kind of situation, that is a finding: bring it to supervision, read about an alternative, and record the switch rather than drifting.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Sampling several models across the placement so none is learned properly or evidenced.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 3. Intervention, 7. Supervision, and consultation evidence for 4. Systemic Change.

micro.name: Cite current peer-reviewed evidence
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: if you say an approach works, cite something. PSI Code 4.2.2 is cited there as requiring you not to misrepresent the effectiveness of what you offer, and a training audience will act on what you tell them, so be as careful about overclaiming in a presentation as in a report. CORU SoP 5.41 is mapped here. A slide saying 'research shows' with no source cannot be checked by the teachers and should not be trusted by you. Evidence reviews such as the EEF's (Education Endowment Foundation) guidance reports are useful starting points, but check that the findings apply to Irish classrooms.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor or experienced colleagues use evidence in training: how many citations appear, how they say the strength of evidence in plain terms ('several good trials', 'promising but early'), and how they deal with popular approaches with weak evidence.

WRITE DOWN — the sources they cite, how they describe the strength of the evidence, and anything they deliberately left out.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you handle it when teachers are already using something the evidence doesn't support?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — searching for current peer-reviewed evidence on your topic (systematic reviews first, then key trials), reading the sources you cite yourself, and listing each claim on your slides with its source.

THEY HOLD — reviewing your claims-and-sources list for overclaiming before the presentation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding and reading evidence is core work for a doctoral trainee. A second reader who knows the field catches the claim that goes further than the study did.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present a draft to your supervisor and defend each effectiveness claim with its source.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'research shows' with no source; citing a book summary rather than the study; old evidence when newer reviews exist; findings from very different settings presented as if they transfer directly; strong words ('proven') for modest evidence.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'where's this claim from? What did the study actually find, and with which pupils?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — make every effectiveness claim traceable to current peer-reviewed evidence you have read, state its strength honestly, and include a short reference list the audience can follow.

PASS TEST — The evidence base is visible

EVIDENCE TO FILE — slides and reference list; your claims-and-sources check. Log against 4. Systemic Change and 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a teacher asks 'where's the evidence for that?' and you cannot name a study.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer how to find and weigh evidence for a training topic, how to describe strength of evidence without jargon, and why overclaiming in training is an ethical issue (the Reference sheet's reading of PSI 4.2.2 — check the Code for the exact wording).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if you realise after the session that you overstated a finding, send a short correction with the handout, and tell your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Saying an approach 'works' or 'research shows' without a source you have read yourself.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Pitch it at teachers rather than examiners', 8. Research, and 6. Ethical Practice.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Pitch it at teachers rather than examiners
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: teachers want something usable on Monday, so every section should end with what to do, not what to know; cut the theory to what makes the practice make sense and put the rest in a handout. CORU SoP 5.40 and 5.8 are mapped here. Your review named delivery of training as a strength, so this is where you build on it. A presentation written for an examiner — citation-heavy, theory first — loses a staffroom in ten minutes, and nothing changes in classrooms.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how experienced presenters turn a study into practice: one sentence on what was found, then 'what this means in your classroom is...'. Notice how much theory they use, where they put the references (often the handout), and how they use examples from Irish classrooms.

WRITE DOWN — two or three translations you thought worked well, from finding to classroom action.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide what to cut when you have twenty minutes at a staff meeting?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — rewriting each evidence slide so that it ends with a classroom action, and moving detail to a one-page handout.

THEY HOLD — feedback on the pitch, and knowledge of this staff's context (what they have already had training on, what they are sceptical of).

WHY THAT SPLIT — translating evidence is the skill you are building. Knowing what this staffroom has already heard, and where the resistance is, is local knowledge your supervisor has.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — rehearse the presentation with your supervisor or a peer acting as a teacher who asks 'so what do I do?' after every slide.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — slides with an author and year but no 'so what'; jargon ('executive functioning', 'effect size') without translation; too many slides; reading from slides.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I'm a second-class teacher with twenty-eight children — what do I do tomorrow morning because of this slide?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — deliver a presentation in which every cited finding is followed by what it means for the audience's practice, in their language, with the theory and full references in a one-page handout.

PASS TEST — Every citation is translated

EVIDENCE TO FILE — slides, handout, and a note of the audience and setting. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — polite applause, no questions, and a staffroom conversation afterwards about how it was 'very academic'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer how to turn a finding into a classroom action, how to decide what goes on a slide and what goes in the handout, and why training that stays at the level of knowledge rarely changes practice (Joyce & Showers, 2002, on the need for follow-up and coaching).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if the audience is disengaged partway through, stop, ask what would be most useful to them now, and skip to the practical part.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Presenting findings with author and year but never saying what the teacher should do differently because of them.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'End with three things the school could do this term', 'Collect and file feedback from the school', and 5. Working with Others.

micro.name: End with three things the school could do this term
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: a one-page summary beats fifty slides, because people keep one page, and every section should end with what to do. Joyce and Showers (2002, Student Achievement Through Staff Development, 3rd ed.) are cited on the Reference sheet for why training alone rarely changes practice without follow-up. Three specific actions the school could take this term, within its own resources, give the training a way to reach classrooms. CORU SoP 5.40 is mapped here. Aspirations ('foster a culture of inclusion') cannot be done, so they won't be.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how presenters close: whether the last slide is a summary of content or a short list of actions; how specific the actions are (who, what, when); whether they link to anything the school already does.

WRITE DOWN — the closing actions from a training session you attend, and whether you could tell who would do each one and by when.

ASK AFTERWARDS — ask a teacher after a training session 'which of those will you actually try?' and note which kind of action they pick.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting three actions, each specific, doable within existing time and staff, and fitting the school's current priorities as far as you know them.

THEY HOLD — checking the actions against what the school is already doing and has capacity for this term.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing concrete actions is the skill. Whether they fit the school's calendar and other demands is local knowledge, and an action that clashes with another initiative will be dropped.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close the presentation with your three actions and ask the staff which one they would start with, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — actions that need extra resources; vague verbs ('promote', 'foster', 'consider'); more than three; actions that are really the psychologist's to do, not the school's.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can we make that second one smaller — what would a teacher do in the first week?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — end the presentation, and the one-page handout, with three concrete actions the school could take this term within its resources, each saying who does what, and link them to the follow-up.

PASS TEST — Actionable, not aspirational

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the final slide and handout; any note of which action the school chose. Log against 4. Systemic Change.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a closing slide that reads 'Key messages: every child is different; relationships matter; inclusion is everyone's responsibility'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the difference between an actionable and an aspirational recommendation, why three is better than ten, and why follow-up matters more than the presentation itself (Joyce & Showers, 2002).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if staff say none of the actions is realistic, ask what would be, and agree one action with them before you leave the room.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Closing with principles or aspirations rather than specific actions the school can take this term.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Collect and file feedback from the school', 'Say what would close the gap', and 3. Intervention at school level.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Collect and file feedback from the school
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet suggests a three-question form at the end: what will you do differently, what was most useful, what was missing. It takes two minutes, gives you evidence for the portfolio, and turns a presentation into a small piece of practice-based research. Kirkpatrick and Kirkpatrick (2006, Evaluating Training Programs, 3rd ed.) separate reaction, learning, behaviour and results; a feedback form measures reaction and intended behaviour, not actual change. CORU SoP 5.40 is mapped here. Without feedback you cannot show the presentation built capacity.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how the service evaluates training: whether forms are used, what they ask, whether they are anonymous, and whether anyone follows up weeks later to see if practice changed.

WRITE DOWN — the questions used, how responses are summarised, and where they are filed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever gone back to a school after training to see if anything changed? What did you find?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — designing a short anonymous form using the Reference sheet's three questions, collecting it at the end, and summarising the responses honestly, including the critical ones.

THEY HOLD — any follow-up contact with the principal to find out whether the agreed actions were taken.

WHY THAT SPLIT — designing and summarising the evaluation is your evidence and research practice. Follow-up with the principal is part of the service's ongoing relationship with the school.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — collect the forms, write a half-page summary, and discuss it in supervision, including what you would change.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — reporting only the positive comments; treating 'enjoyed it' as evidence of change; forms that collect names without need; no follow-up question about actual practice.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what did the people who said something was missing tell you, and what would you change because of it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — collect anonymous feedback at the end, summarise it honestly, and where possible follow up (through your supervisor) to find out whether any of the three actions were taken, stating clearly which Kirkpatrick level each piece of evidence reaches.

PASS TEST — You have evidence it built capacity

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the form, the summary, any follow-up note; Appendix 5 entry (your reflection to write). Log against 4. Systemic Change and 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — no forms, or a folder of forms nobody summarised, and a portfolio that says only 'delivered training to staff'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer the difference between reaction and behaviour change (Kirkpatrick & Kirkpatrick, 2006), how to design a two-minute form that gives usable evidence, and how to write it up honestly as practice-based evaluation. Prompts for your own reflection: what the feedback told you, what surprised you, what you would change. The reflection is yours to write.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — if feedback is poor, report it as it is, take it to supervision, and say what you will change next time; honest poor feedback with a clear response is better evidence than no feedback.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Collecting no feedback, or reporting positive reactions as if they showed practice had changed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 8. Research (practice-based evaluation), 4. Systemic Change evidence, and the portfolio.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Meet the child at their level, literally and in register
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet puts it bluntly: rapport is measurement validity, because an anxious or suspicious child produces scores that underestimate them. Sattler (Assessment of Children: Cognitive Foundations and Applications, 6th ed., 2018) treats establishing rapport and observing test behaviour as part of the assessment itself, not a warm-up. An adult standing over a six-year-old, or talking to a fifteen-year-old as if they were six, starts the session with the child managing you. CORU SoP 2.2 is the standard mapped here. Get it wrong and every score that follows is in question.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor puts their body in the first minute: sitting or crouching to eye level, side-on rather than across a desk, or leaving the child the seat nearest the door. Then listen to register — sentence length, vocabulary, humour — and how it shifts between a Junior Infant and a Leaving Cert student.

WRITE DOWN — the first three sentences they said to the child, word for word, and the child's age band (UCD Table 3).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what did you notice about this child in the corridor that changed how you spoke to them in the room?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — setting up the room before the child arrives (chair heights, table side, materials out of sight until needed) and doing the walk from the classroom, where most of the first impression is made.

THEY HOLD — the introduction and the move into the first task.

WHY THAT SPLIT — room set-up and the corridor walk are low-risk and teach you to read a child before anything is at stake. The introduction sets the tone for scores that will be reported, so it stays with the person accountable for them.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — collect the child, introduce yourself, and settle them into the room, with your supervisor present but not leading.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the two opposite failures: talking down (sing-song voice, over-praise, questions a younger child would be asked) and talking over (adult vocabulary, long sentences, talking about the child to the teacher in front of them).

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor sitting down beside you so you follow suit, or rephrasing one of your sentences more simply without comment.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — adjust position, pace and language to the child in front of you, not to their age on the referral form, and keep adjusting as you learn more about them in the first ten minutes.

PASS TEST — Not talked down to or over

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the behavioural observations section of the report, noting how the child presented and engaged, and a reflective note in Appendix 5 (no identifying details in the Log). Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a teenager who answers in single words for an hour because you opened with 'Hi there, are you having a nice day?', or a young child who never looks up because you talked across a desk.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why register is a validity issue and not just manners, give examples of the same introduction pitched for a five-year-old, a ten-year-old and a sixteen-year-old, and name what to adjust for a child with a language difficulty or a hearing impairment.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you misjudge it: name it lightly ('that was a bit babyish, sorry — you're in fifth class'), recalibrate, and note in the observations section that engagement improved after the adjustment.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Pitching language to the age on the referral form rather than to the child actually in front of you.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Explain what will happen and why', 'Notice and respond to reluctance', and the validity statement in every assessment report.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

Then listen to register — sentence length, vocabulary, humour — and how it shifts between a Junior Infant and a Leaving Cert student.

micro.name: Explain what will happen and why
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet's first three minutes: who you are in a sentence they can repeat, why you are there, what will happen, how long, that some tasks will be too hard for everyone, and what happens to the information. PSI Code 4.3.1 is the clause mapped here. Children often assume they have been sent to a psychologist because they are in trouble or 'stupid'; unless you say otherwise, that belief sits in the room with every item. A child who does not know the tasks get harder will read their first failure as proof.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the exact words your supervisor uses for 'psychologist', 'test' and 'why you are here', and how these change with age. Notice whether they say that the tasks get harder for everyone, and whether they say who will hear about the session.

WRITE DOWN — the explanation near verbatim, then a version for a younger child and one for a teenager in your own words.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do children most often think a psychologist is, and how do you correct it without making it a big deal?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing a scripted explanation for each UCD Table 3 age band you will see in Cavan, and checking it with your supervisor before you use it.

THEY HOLD — the explanation to any child whose referral involves a sensitive reason (bereavement, a child protection history, a recent exclusion).

WHY THAT SPLIT — a script can be tested safely and corrected. Where the reason for referral is itself painful, deciding how much to say needs knowledge of the family and the history that sits with your supervisor.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — give the whole explanation yourself, then ask the child to tell you back what is going to happen, with your supervisor observing.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — explanations that are accurate but too long, jargon ('assessment', 'cognitive'), leaving out what happens to the information, and moving on without waiting for questions.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I add one thing — some of these puzzles get really tricky, and that's the same for everyone who does them.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain purpose, activities, length, the difficulty gradient and who will be told what, in words the child uses, and check it by asking them to say it back rather than asking 'OK?'.

PASS TEST — The child could repeat it back

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a line in the case note recording what was explained and the child's account of it; your age-band scripts as working papers. Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child who asks at the end 'am I in trouble?' or 'will my mam find out?', which means they spent the session not knowing.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a teach-back ('tell me what we're going to do') is a better check than a closed question, why the difficulty-gradient sentence protects effort on later items, and how the explanation links to assent.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child's repeat-back shows a misunderstanding: correct it before starting, not mid-battery, and if the misunderstanding was about confidentiality, redo that part in full.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking 'is that OK?' instead of having the child say back what will happen.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Obtain informed consent and assent', 'Give the child a real choice early', and 'Close so the child leaves feeling competent'.

micro.name: Give the child a real choice early
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A child in an assessment has almost no control: someone else chose the day, the room, the adult and the tasks. Giving them one genuine decision early changes the power in the room and usually increases effort. PSI Code 1.4.1 is the clause mapped here; read the Code for its exact wording. The error is the fake choice — 'shall we start?' when refusal is not an option — which children recognise quickly and which teaches them that your other offers are not real either.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — every point where your supervisor offers the child a decision, and whether each one is real: which seat, pencil or pen, which of two permitted tasks first, when to take the break, whether the door is open or closed.

WRITE DOWN — each choice offered, and whether the child's answer changed anything.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which choices can you give without breaking standardised administration, and where does the manual stop you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listing, for the battery you are using, the decisions that genuinely belong to the child (seating, break timing, order of subtests only where the manual permits it, materials) and checking the list against the administration manual.

THEY HOLD — any decision about altering order or procedure in the testing itself.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding the real choices is a reading task you can do alone. Deciding whether a change to order is permitted affects validity, and the Reference sheet is clear: know exactly what the manual permits before you need it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — offer the child at least one real choice in the first five minutes and honour the answer, with your supervisor observing.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — choices with a correct answer ('would you like to do some puzzles now?'), choices you then override, and choices that break standard procedure.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you asked if she wanted to start — what would you have done if she'd said no? Let's offer her the seat or the break time instead.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — build at least one genuine, permitted decision into the opening of every session, offer it in words the child understands, and act on whatever they choose.

PASS TEST — Something was actually theirs to decide

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a note in the session record of the choice offered and taken; a reflective line in Appendix 5 on how it affected engagement. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a session transcript where every question to the child had only one acceptable answer, or where the child chose and you then did the other thing.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between a real and a rhetorical choice, list the choices that are safe within standardised administration, and link agency to both effort and to the child's right to be heard (UNCRC, 1989, Art. 12).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the child chooses something you cannot allow: say so honestly, explain why in a sentence, and offer a different decision that is genuinely theirs.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Offering a choice the child is not actually allowed to refuse.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Notice and respond to reluctance', 'Ask the child what they think would help', and the voice of the child in Formulation.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
