micro.name: Notice and respond to reluctance
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: refusal is data, and a completed protocol obtained under pressure is worse data than stopping and returning another day. CORU SoP 5.31 is mapped here (read the clause for its wording); adapting and re-evaluating includes writing down what you changed. Reluctance is rarely a single refusal; it is quieter answers, faster guessing, 'I don't know' before the item is finished, and the shift from effort to compliance. Miss it and you report a low score that measures the child's state, not their ability.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the early signs your supervisor reacts to: longer response times, rapid guessing, glancing at the door, slumping, asking how many are left. Notice what they do first — a break, a change of task within permitted limits, a brief acknowledgement — and what they do not do.

WRITE DOWN — the sign, the item or subtest at which it appeared, what preceded it, and the response.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'at what point would you have stopped the session altogether, and how would you have explained that to the school?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping a running behaviour record during the session (time, subtest, sign) while your supervisor administers.

THEY HOLD — the in-the-moment decision to pause, change task or stop.

WHY THAT SPLIT — recording reluctance trains you to see it and gives the report its evidence. Deciding to stop has consequences for validity, for the school's expectations and for the child, and your supervisor is accountable for it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — administer the session and make the call when reluctance appears: pause, acknowledge, offer a break or a permitted change, and record it, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — pushing on to finish the battery because the room is booked or the school expects a report, and encouragement that shades into pressure ('just a few more, come on').

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'let's take a break there' said to the child, then a quiet 'what did you see just now?' to you.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — notice reluctance early, respond by adjusting rather than pushing, record what you saw and did at the moment it happened, and state in the report what it means for how the scores can be read.

PASS TEST — You adjusted rather than pushed on

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the behavioural observations and validity statement in the report; the session record with timings. Log against 5. Working with Others and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a full battery reported as valid when your own notes show the child was guessing from the second half onward.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between fatigue, anxiety, boredom and opposition as causes of reluctance, what the manual permits for each, and why stopping can be the more rigorous choice.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise afterwards that you pushed through: flag it in supervision, weaken or withhold the affected scores in the report, and plan a return visit if needed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Completing the battery through visible reluctance and reporting the scores as valid.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Recognise when standard procedure is not working', 'Re-evaluate whether to continue at all', and 'State the effect on validity in the report'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the early signs your supervisor reacts to: longer response times, rapid guessing, glancing at the door, slumping, asking how many are left. Notice what they do first — a break, a change of task within permitted limits, a brief acknowledgement — and what they do not do.

micro.name: Ask the child what they think would help
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
UNCRC Article 12 (United Nations, 1989) gives a child capable of forming views the right to express them in matters affecting them, with due weight given according to age and maturity. Lundy (British Educational Research Journal, 2007) argues that voice alone is not enough: the child also needs space, an audience and influence. Children often know exactly what helps — sitting near the window, being told the plan for the day, not being picked to read aloud — and no one asks. A report without the child's view is missing a source.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when and how your supervisor asks the child for their view: after rapport is built, not as the first question, and often through an activity rather than directly (drawing, rating scales, sorting cards, a 'best day / worst day').

WRITE DOWN — the questions or tools used, and the child's answers in their own words.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide how much weight a seven-year-old's suggestion gets in the recommendations?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing an age-appropriate way of gathering the child's view for this case, and running that part of the session.

THEY HOLD — deciding which of the child's suggestions go into the report and how they are attributed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — gathering views well is a skill you build by doing. Putting a child's words into a report that the school and family will read needs a judgement about what is safe and fair to the child to include.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — ask the child what makes school harder and what would help, using a method suited to their age and language, with your supervisor observing.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — leading questions ('would it help if your teacher…?'), asking only at the very end when the child is tired, and hearing an answer without following it up.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you said the yard is the worst bit — tell me more about the yard.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — seek the child's view on what would help in every assessment, record it in their words, and show in the report where it shaped a recommendation, or why it did not.

PASS TEST — The child's view was sought

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the 'child's view' section of the report, and the record of the method used. Log against 5. Working with Others (and UNCRC Art. 12 as the mapped standard).

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report whose recommendations came entirely from adults, with the child mentioned only as the subject of test scores.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain Article 12 and Lundy's four elements (space, voice, audience, influence), describe methods for gathering views across the UCD Table 3 age bands and for a child with limited language, and say how due weight is judged.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the child's suggestion conflicts with the adults': report both, explain the reasoning, and tell the child honestly what happened to their idea.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording the child's view in the report but letting it change nothing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the voice of the child in Formulation, recommendations, and 'Include the child's own self-report where age-appropriate'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — when and how your supervisor asks the child for their view: after rapport is built, not as the first question, and often through an activity rather than directly (drawing, rating scales, sorting cards, a 'best day / worst day').

micro.name: Know who does what in this school
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: the principal decides and allocates; the SENCO holds the overview and usually the documentation; the class teacher delivers most of what you recommend; the SNA often knows the child best and is asked least. In Irish schools the SENCO role is usually a special education teacher (SET) or SET co-ordinator, and at post-primary there is often a Student Support Team — titles and roles vary by school. CORU SoP 5.13 is mapped here. Treating 'the school' as one entity is on the Reference sheet's error list.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — who your supervisor asks for what in the first visit to a school: who they book time with, who they ask for the Student Support File, who they ask about the child's day, and who they tell when they leave.

WRITE DOWN — a one-page role map for each school: principal, deputy, SET co-ordinator, class teacher(s), SNA, secretary, and at post-primary year head and guidance counsellor. Names stay in the service record, not your Log.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'in this school, who actually decides whether a recommendation happens?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building and updating the role map for each Cavan school on your caseload, and checking it with the SET co-ordinator.

THEY HOLD — the relationship with the principal, including agreeing the school's priorities for the service's time.

WHY THAT SPLIT — mapping roles is information-gathering you can do from week one. The principal relationship covers the whole service's work in the school, not only your cases, and it is your supervisor's to hold.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make first contact with each role yourself for your own cases: book time through the right person, ask the SNA for their view, and brief the principal at the right point, with your supervisor reviewing who you approached.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — going to the teacher you like rather than the one with the responsibility, and bypassing the SET co-ordinator or the principal on a decision that is theirs.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before you agree that with the class teacher, has the SET co-ordinator seen it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for each request (information, a meeting, a room, a change in provision) identify whose role it is in this particular school and approach them first.

PASS TEST — You approached the right person

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the school role map as a working paper and the case contact log. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a recommendation for extra SET time agreed with the class teacher, who cannot allocate it, and a principal who hears about it from a parent.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the typical division of roles in Irish primary and post-primary schools, how the NEPS Continuum of Support (Classroom Support, School Support, School Support Plus) maps onto who leads at each level, and why the SNA's knowledge is often overlooked.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you went to the wrong person: tell the right person directly, explain what was said, and do not leave the first person holding a commitment they cannot keep.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating 'the school' as one entity and agreeing a change with someone who cannot deliver it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Negotiate a shared referral question', consultation, and implementation of recommendations.

micro.name: Negotiate a shared referral question
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The referral form often carries a request ('assess for dyslexia', 'is it ADHD?') rather than a question the psychologist can usefully answer. Consultation models treat agreeing the question as the first piece of work, not a formality (Wagner, 2000, Consultation: Developing a comprehensive approach to service delivery — read the source itself). CORU SoP 2.13 is mapped here. If school, parent and psychologist hold different questions, the report will satisfy none of them, and the school will read a careful formulation as 'the psychologist didn't give us an answer'.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor turns the school's request into a question: which follow-up questions they ask ('what would be different if this went well?', 'what have you tried?', 'what are you hoping the assessment tells you?'), and whether the parent's question is asked separately.

WRITE DOWN — the original request in the referrer's words, the agreed question, and each step between them.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when the school's question and the parent's question are different?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the referral and the Student Support File beforehand and drafting two or three possible questions to bring to the planning meeting.

THEY HOLD — the planning conversation with the SET co-ordinator and teacher, including any reframing the school may resist.

WHY THAT SPLIT — drafting questions from the file teaches you to see the gap between request and question. Reframing a school's request in the room needs a relationship and credibility you are still building.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the planning conversation for your own case, with your supervisor present, and end it by reading back the agreed question.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — accepting the request unchanged, imposing your own question over the school's, and ending the meeting without saying the question aloud.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I just check we're all agreed what we're trying to find out — would you read it back for us?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — take a school referral, explore the concern behind it with the teacher and SET co-ordinator, agree a question the assessment can answer, check it with the parent, and confirm it in writing.

PASS TEST — Both parties recognise the question

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the agreed question on the case file and in the written summary sent after the planning meeting. Log against 5. Working with Others and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at feedback the teacher says 'but we wanted to know if he needs a special class', and nothing in your file shows that was discussed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between a request and a referral question, show a peer the questions that uncover the concern behind a request, and explain why the parent's question is part of the negotiation, not an afterthought.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the question shifts mid-assessment: go back to the school and parent, renegotiate openly, and record the change rather than quietly answering a different question.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Accepting 'assess for X' as the referral question without finding out what the school needs to know.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask whether the profile answers the referral question', choice of framework in Formulation, and 'Manage disagreement rather than avoiding it'.

Not started

micro.name: Manage disagreement rather than avoiding it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: teachers sometimes disagree with findings, and sometimes they are right, so ask what they see and get to the specific observation behind the position. CORU SoP 2.13 is mapped here. Stone, Patton and Heen (Difficult Conversations, 2010) separate the 'what happened' conversation from the feelings and identity conversations running underneath it, which is useful when a finding implies a teacher's practice is part of the problem. Avoided disagreement does not go away; it resurfaces as recommendations that are politely never implemented.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor responds when a teacher or principal disagrees: whether they defend the finding or ask a question, and how they word a message that implicates provision (describe, don't evaluate; lead with shared purpose; offer one change).

WRITE DOWN — the disagreement in neutral terms, the question your supervisor asked, and what the teacher's specific observation turned out to be.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when did a teacher's disagreement change your view of a case?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing for a likely disagreement: listing the evidence, the teacher's probable view, and a descriptive rather than evaluative way to say the difficult part.

THEY HOLD — the conversation itself where the message implicates provision or the relationship with the school is fragile.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparation is where most of the skill lies and can be done safely. A provision-level message delivered badly can, as the Reference sheet warns, end the relationship, and that relationship belongs to the service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — handle a disagreement yourself in a meeting on your own case, with your supervisor present but letting you lead.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — repeating the finding more firmly, conceding to end the discomfort, and evaluative language ('the differentiation is inadequate') where description would do.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can we hear more about what you're seeing in class? That might be something we didn't capture.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — raise or respond to a disagreement directly: ask what the other person sees, find the specific observation behind their view, say what would change your view, and agree a next step even if you still differ.

PASS TEST — The disagreement was addressed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the meeting note recording both positions and the agreed next step; a reflective entry in Appendix 5 without identifying details. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a meeting that ends with everyone nodding, followed by an email from the principal a week later disputing the report.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why asking 'what do you see?' works better than restating evidence, how to phrase a provision-level message descriptively, and when a disagreement should change your finding versus when it should be recorded as a difference.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a disagreement escalates: pause the meeting, acknowledge the strength of feeling, agree to return with more information, and bring it to supervision the same day.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Defending a finding by restating it instead of asking what the teacher is seeing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Maintain the relationship afterwards', consultation, and 'Identify where sources diverge and say so'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Maintain the relationship afterwards
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: send a short written summary of what was agreed within a day — it prevents misremembering, gives the school something to act from, and evidences record-keeping, which your placement review named as a development area (per the Reference sheet). CORU SoP 2.17 is mapped here. Schools notice psychologists who appear for the assessment and vanish; implementation depends on someone coming back to ask how it is going. Relationships after a disagreement need repair most of all, and they rarely repair themselves.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does after a school meeting: whether a written summary goes out and how quickly, what is in it, and whether they return to the school to review — especially after a difficult conversation.

WRITE DOWN — the structure of their follow-up summary (agreed actions, who, by when, next contact) and when they next contacted the school.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'after a meeting that went badly, what's the first thing you do to repair it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the written summary within one working day of every school meeting on shared cases, for your supervisor to check before it goes.

THEY HOLD — the follow-up call or visit where a relationship has been strained.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the written summary is a discrete, checkable task and the fastest way to build a reputation for reliability. Repair after strain needs the standing your supervisor has with the principal.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — send the summary yourself and make the review contact on your own cases (a call or visit to ask how the recommendations are going), with your supervisor reviewing the summary and your plan.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — summaries that arrive a week late, summaries that record what you said rather than what was agreed, and review contact that never happens because the case felt finished.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'when are you next in contact with that school about this child? Put it in the diary now.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — send a written summary of agreed actions within a day, diarise a review, go back to the school to check implementation, and after any disagreement make a repair contact.

PASS TEST — You went back

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the follow-up summaries and the review contact note on the case file. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a school that, three months later, has not implemented the plan, and a file showing no contact since the feedback meeting. In Cavan (05/10/2026–18/12/2026) plan review dates that fall inside the placement.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why follow-up drives implementation, what a good one-page summary contains, how to plan review within a time-limited placement, and how to hand a school relationship over at the end of placement so it does not lapse.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you missed the follow-up: contact the school, acknowledge the delay without excuses, send the summary, and set the review date.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
No written follow-up, so the school acts on what it remembers rather than what was agreed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into implementation of recommendations, review in Intervention, and record-keeping in Ethical Practice.

micro.name: Prepare the structure before the meeting
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: parents wait through explanation for the verdict and hear almost none of it, so give the headline in the first two minutes, then the detail, then what it means, then what happens next. That order has to be decided before the meeting; under the pressure of a parent's face it will not be improvised. CORU SoP 2.1 is mapped here. Patients forget much of what clinicians tell them (Kessels, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 2003 — check the figures before quoting), which is why a structure matters more than completeness.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor prepares before a feedback meeting: notes on one page, the headline written out, the order of topics, the room and who is attending, and anything they expect to be difficult.

WRITE DOWN — their plan, and afterwards how closely the meeting followed it and where it departed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the one sentence you want the parent to repeat to their partner tonight?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the one-page feedback plan for a case: headline, one evidenced strength, key findings in plain words, what it means, next steps, and the likely questions.

THEY HOLD — the headline wording where the finding is significant or distressing, and the decision on who attends (school staff, the young person).

WHY THAT SPLIT — the plan is the thinking and is fully checkable in advance. How to word a diagnosis-level or distressing headline, and who should be in the room, carry relational risk your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — prepare the plan and lead the feedback meeting for your own case, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a plan that follows the report's section order (test by test) instead of the parent's, and a headline that is buried after ten minutes of background.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — in the pre-meeting: 'read me your first two minutes.' In the meeting: 'maybe it would help to say where we got to overall, and then go through how.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before every feedback meeting, write a one-page plan with the headline, order, plain-language translations, next steps and expected questions, and follow it.

PASS TEST — You knew the order you would take

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the feedback plan as a working paper on the case file. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — forty minutes of subtest-by-subtest explanation and a parent who asks at the door 'so does he have dyslexia or not?'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the headline-first structure works, how to write a headline that is honest without being brutal, and how to adapt the plan when the young person or school staff are in the room.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the meeting departs from the plan (a parent arrives with a different concern, or becomes distressed): follow the parent, then return to the headline before the end so it is not lost.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Walking in without a written headline and working through the report in section order.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Use plain language and check understanding', 'Lead with the child, not the scores', and 'Leave the parent with something concrete'.

micro.name: Use plain language and check understanding
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: plain language is a professional obligation — replace 'percentile' with a comparison to peers, 'working memory' with holding information in mind while doing something with it. If you cannot explain a finding without the term, you do not yet understand it well enough to report it. PSI Code 4.3.1 is mapped here. 'Does that make sense?' is on the Reference sheet's error list because almost everyone says yes. A parent who does not understand the findings cannot advocate for their child.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — every technical term your supervisor avoids or translates in a feedback meeting, and how they check understanding. Notice whether they ask the parent to put it in their own words, and what that reveals.

WRITE DOWN — a glossary: each term (standard score, percentile, processing speed, phonological awareness, working memory) with your supervisor's plain-language version.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a parent says it back, what are the misunderstandings you hear most often?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building your own plain-language glossary for the tests you use and rehearsing the translations with your supervisor before a meeting.

THEY HOLD — the understanding check at the end of the meeting, until you have seen it done several times.

WHY THAT SPLIT — translating terms is preparation you can practise and have corrected. The teach-back check can feel like a test to a parent, and the tone of asking it is learned by watching.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — deliver the findings in plain language and run the understanding check yourself ('when you tell his dad about today, what will you say?'), with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jargon that slips back in under pressure, translations that are accurate but still abstract, and 'does that make sense?' used as the only check.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor asking the parent 'what's your sense of what that means for him in class?' after you use a technical term.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain every finding without jargon, and before the end ask the parent to say back what they will tell someone else; correct anything that did not land.

PASS TEST — You checked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the feedback plan (with your plain-language versions) and a case note recording the parent's summary in their words. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent who tells the school afterwards that the psychologist said their child was 'in the bottom percent for everything', from a profile that said nothing of the kind.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a plain-language explanation for each score type and cognitive term you use, explain why teach-back is more reliable than a closed question, and adapt both for a parent with literacy difficulties or for whom English is an additional language, including when to use an interpreter.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the say-back reveals a major misunderstanding: thank them, re-explain the central point differently, check again, and put the headline in writing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using technical language and checking understanding with 'does that make sense?'.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Leave the parent with something concrete', plain-language report writing, and the parent's own advocacy with the school.

micro.name: Lead with the child, not the scores
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Leading with scores is the first item on the Reference sheet's error list. Parents know their child as a person, and a feedback meeting that opens with numbers tells them the psychologist met a profile, not their son or daughter. CORU SoP 5.27 is mapped here. Starting from something recognisable — how the child approached the tasks, what they said, what they enjoyed — earns the credibility that makes the harder findings believable, and it gives the parent evidence that you actually saw their child.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor opens a feedback meeting: the first thing they say about the child, whether it is a specific observation or a general comment, and how long before any number is mentioned.

WRITE DOWN — the opening description word for word, and the parent's reaction to it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you choose the detail about the child to open with, especially when the session was difficult?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the opening paragraph of the feedback plan: two or three specific observations of how the child engaged, drawn from your session record.

THEY HOLD — the transition from the child to the findings, where the tone shifts.

WHY THAT SPLIT — describing the child from your notes tests how well you observed, and is safe to practise. The move into findings sets the emotional register for the rest of the meeting.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — open the meeting with your description of the child, then move into the findings, keeping the child present throughout ('this is why he found the reading tasks so tiring'), with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a description that could fit any child ('she was lovely to work with'), and findings reported as scores detached from anything the parent recognises.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'do you see that at home — the way she checks everything twice before she answers?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — begin with a specific, evidenced description of the child as you met them, and tie each finding back to something the parent can recognise at home or in school.

PASS TEST — The child is recognisable in your description

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the feedback plan and the report's background and observation sections. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent who says 'that doesn't sound like him' in the first five minutes, after which nothing else you say is trusted.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the child-first opening builds credibility for the findings, how to select observations that are specific and honest, and how to keep linking scores back to everyday behaviour.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the parent does not recognise your description: ask what they see, treat it as information about context (home vs school, one session vs years), and say so in the report.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Opening with scores before the parent has recognised their child in anything you have said.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name strengths specifically', 'Hold distress without rushing past it', and the parent's trust in the findings.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Name strengths specifically
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: lead with a strength, but only one you can evidence from the assessment — invented strengths are heard as consolation and undermine everything else you say. CORU SoP 1.3 is mapped here. 'He's a lovely boy' is not a strength finding; 'his vocabulary is well above what we'd expect for his age, and he used it to explain the picture tasks in real detail' is. Specific strengths also do work: they are what recommendations can build on.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the strengths your supervisor names in feedback and whether each one is tied to evidence (a score, an observation, a teacher report) or is a general compliment.

WRITE DOWN — each strength named and its evidence, and note any that were generic.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when the assessment genuinely didn't show a cognitive strength?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — going through the file and your session record to list every evidenced strength: cognitive, attainment, approach to tasks, social, interests, and what other adults report.

THEY HOLD — deciding which strength leads, especially where the overall picture is of significant difficulty.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding strengths across sources is thorough, checkable work. Choosing the lead strength when the news is hard is a judgement about how the parent will hear it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — name the strengths in the feedback meeting, each with its evidence, and link at least one to a recommendation, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — generic praise, a strength the scores do not support, and strengths mentioned once at the start then dropped.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'and that persistence you saw on the puzzles — that's something the school can really use when they set up the reading programme.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name at least one real strength with the evidence for it, in plain words, and show how it connects to what happens next.

PASS TEST — Not generic praise

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the strengths section of the report and the feedback plan. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'he's a great kid and he tried really hard' as the only positive, followed by twenty minutes of difficulty, and a parent who hears the positive as a cushion.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why specificity is what makes a strength credible, where to look for strengths when test scores are uniformly low (approach to tasks, interests, relationships, adult reports), and how strengths should drive recommendations rather than decorate the report.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent dismisses a strength ('you're just saying that'): give the evidence for it, and do not inflate it to persuade them.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Offering a strength the assessment does not support, so the parent discounts the real findings.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into strengths-based recommendations, Intervention planning, and 'Leave the parent with something concrete'.

micro.name: Hold distress without rushing past it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Feedback can confirm something a parent has feared for years, or tell them something they did not expect; either can bring grief, anger, guilt or relief. Rushing to reassurance or to the recommendations tells them their reaction is in the way. CORU SoP 2.2 is mapped here. Baile and colleagues' SPIKES protocol for breaking bad news in medicine (The Oncologist, 2000) names responding to emotion as a distinct step before moving on; it was written for oncology, so adapt rather than transplant it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does when a parent becomes upset: the pause, the tone, whether they name the feeling, whether they offer tissues or water, how long before they return to the content, and how they check the parent is ready.

WRITE DOWN — what was said at the moment of distress and what brought the meeting back — without identifying details in your Log.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know when a parent is ready to hear the next part?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing for likely distress: which finding is most likely to land hard, what you will say if it does, and making sure there is time, privacy and tissues.

THEY HOLD — responding to the distress in the room.

WHY THAT SPLIT — anticipating distress is planning you can do. Being with a distressed parent without rushing, while holding the professional frame, is learned by watching someone who does it well first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the feedback meeting and respond yourself when the parent becomes upset, with your supervisor present and ready to support.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — filling the silence, premature reassurance ('lots of children have this'), jumping to recommendations, and the opposite: losing the structure so the parent leaves without the key message.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — a hand signal to wait, or 'we don't have to go on right now — take whatever time you need.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — when a parent is distressed, stop, acknowledge it in plain words, allow silence, and return to the content only when they indicate they are ready; offer a second meeting if needed.

PASS TEST — You slowed down

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the case note (including any offer of a follow-up meeting) and a supervision note on the meeting. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent in tears while you talk them through the recommendations, and a complaint afterwards that 'she just kept going'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why pausing is a professional act and not a loss of control, how to name emotion without interpreting it, how cultural context shapes how distress is shown (Tervalon & Murray-García, 1998, on cultural humility), and when to end a meeting and reschedule.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise afterwards that you rushed: contact the parent, acknowledge it, offer another meeting, and take it to supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Rushing to reassurance or recommendations the moment a parent becomes upset.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Leave the parent with something concrete', relationship with the family, and your own wellbeing (Ethical Practice — Manage workload and your own wellbeing).

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Leave the parent with something concrete
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A parent who leaves with a feeling but no plan will ring the school, the GP or you within a week. They need to know what happens next, who does it, by when, and what they can do themselves. CORU SoP 2.16 is mapped here. In the Irish system, next steps usually sit on the NEPS Continuum of Support (Classroom Support, School Support, School Support Plus) or involve onward referral to HSE CDNT or CAMHS; parents rarely know what these mean, or how long waits may be, unless someone tells them.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor ends a feedback meeting: whether they summarise next steps, name who does what, say when the report will arrive, explain any onward referral and its process, and give the parent something written.

WRITE DOWN — the next steps as your supervisor stated them, and what the parent was given to take away.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you tell a parent about a CDNT or CAMHS referral when you don't know how long the wait will be?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing the next-steps section of the feedback plan and a short written summary for the parent: actions, who, when, contacts, and what they can do at home.

THEY HOLD — anything involving onward referral or service commitments, until you know the local pathways and what the service can promise.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a written next-steps summary is concrete and checkable. Referral pathways and waiting times are local knowledge; a wrong promise about a CDNT or CAMHS referral damages trust in the whole service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close the feedback meeting yourself: summarise next steps, check the parent knows what happens next, and hand over the written summary, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — vague endings ('the school will be in touch'), promises about other services' timelines, and next steps that are all for professionals with nothing the parent can do.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'just so you've got it clearly — the three things that happen now are…'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — end every feedback meeting with next steps stated, a named person and timescale for each, when the report will arrive, one thing the parent can do, and a written summary to take away.

PASS TEST — They know what happens next

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the written next-steps summary and the case note. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent phoning the school a week later to ask whether a referral was made, and nobody knowing who was meant to do it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the Continuum of Support levels and the main onward pathways (HSE CDNT, CAMHS, and Tusla where relevant) in plain words, how to talk about waiting lists without guessing, and why a parent needs one action of their own.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a next step does not happen: find out who held it, tell the parent honestly, and make sure it is picked up and recorded.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Ending the meeting without saying who will do what, and by when.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into implementation and review in Intervention, 'Maintain the relationship afterwards', and the parent's advocacy for their child.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor ends a feedback meeting: whether they summarise next steps, name who does what, say when the report will arrive, explain any onward referral and its process, and give the parent something written.

micro.name: Use the service's format and terminology
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Every service records differently: a NEPS team, a CDNT and a CAMHS team each have their own headings, file structure and accepted abbreviations. The note has to be usable by the next person who opens the file, not only by you. CORU SoP 2.10 is the standard mapped here — read the full text on the Reference sheet, Part B. A note in your own format, or in shorthand only you understand, cannot be used once you leave, and in Cavan you leave on 18/12/2026 with cases still open.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the template or headings your supervisor uses for each kind of contact (school visit, consultation, parent phone call, review meeting), where each kind of note sits in the file, and which abbreviations the service accepts. Check even ones that look standard, such as 'SS+' for School Support Plus or 'SSF' for Student Support File.

WRITE DOWN — the headings in order, the document-naming convention, and a list of accepted abbreviations with what they stand for. Ask for the written records policy if the service has one.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if you were off sick tomorrow, what would a colleague need to find in this note to pick up the case?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the note of a visit your supervisor led, on the service template, in the service's terms, and sending it to them the same day.

THEY HOLD — corrections to format and terminology, and the decision on what goes on the formal file and what stays a working paper.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you learn a template by using it, and mistakes cost nothing if they are corrected before filing. What counts as part of the record is a service policy question, and you do not yet know this service's policy.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for your first few weeks in Cavan, write every note on your own cases in the service format and submit it for review before it is filed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — Roscommon habits or university assignment conventions carried into a new service's file; private shorthand; notes filed under the wrong heading or name, so that nobody can find them.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what does "SC re WM" mean here? Would the new principal know, or the psychologist who takes this case after you?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every note is on the service template, filed in the right place, uses only accepted abbreviations, and can be read by a colleague who has never met the child.

PASS TEST — Notes match the service standard

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your supervisor's comment, in the supervision record, on a sample of your notes checked against the template. Do not copy notes into your own Log. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a colleague covering the case cannot tell from the file what was agreed at the last school meeting, because the note is in a format only you use.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a new trainee that format is not bureaucracy. It serves continuity of care, handover, audit and subject access. You can show them where the template lives and walk them through one of your own anonymised notes line by line.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find your early notes used a different format. Do not rewrite or back-date them. If something needs clarifying, add a dated, signed entry marked as a later addition, and use the correct format from then on. Check the service policy on how to amend a record.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Bringing the last service's format and private shorthand into a new service's file.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record consent, contacts and decisions', 'Write the same day', and handover of open cases at the end of the Cavan placement.

micro.name: Store and transfer records lawfully
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Psychological records hold health data, which is special category data under GDPR Article 9. The Data Protection Act 2018 adds further rules in Irish law. The Article 5 principles, including data minimisation and integrity and confidentiality, apply to every note, test protocol and draft report. PSI Code 1.2.6 and 1.2.7 and CORU SoP 1.13 are mapped here. The Reference sheet names records as the area where trainees most often slip through convenience: a draft on a personal laptop, a photo of a record form on a phone, a child's name in an email subject line. Each can be a personal data breach.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor keeps protocols between the school and the office, how they send a report to a school or family (secure email, portal, post, by hand), what goes in an email subject line, and what happens to rough notes once they are typed up.

WRITE DOWN — the service's approved route for storing, sending and destroying each kind of record, and the name of the data protection contact. Do not rely on a remembered retention period — check the service policy for that.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the most common near miss you've seen with records here, and what should I do if I have one?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — carrying and returning protocols by the approved route, sending documents only through service systems, and keeping a simple list of which files you have taken out of the office.

THEY HOLD — any sharing with other agencies (CDNT, CAMHS, Tusla), and any decision on retention or destruction of the formal record.

WHY THAT SPLIT — handling records is a daily routine you must get right from day one. Sharing across agencies needs a lawful basis and a consent decision, and those belong to the service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — manage the records for your own cases from start to finish (storage, sending to school, destroying rough notes as the policy says), with your supervisor spot-checking.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — shortcuts taken for convenience: a draft typed on your own laptop, protocols left in the car overnight, the child's name and school in a subject line, a WhatsApp message to a teacher about a pupil.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'where is that draft saved right now? Is that a service device?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every identifiable record is stored and moved only by approved routes. Nothing goes on a personal phone, laptop, cloud account or messaging app. Rough notes are destroyed as the policy says.

PASS TEST — Nothing identifiable on a personal device

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a line in the supervision record confirming your records practice was reviewed. Your own Log entries contain no identifiers. Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a photo of a record form in your phone's camera roll, syncing to your personal cloud account.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain special category data, the Article 5 principles, why a trainee's own device is outside the service's control, and why 'how long do we keep it?' is answered from the service's retention policy, not from memory.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you send something to the wrong person, or lose a protocol. Tell your supervisor and the data protection contact the same day. Do not try to fix it quietly. The service has to assess it, and may have to notify the Data Protection Commission (GDPR Article 33).

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Working on an identifiable draft report on a personal laptop because the service device was slow.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Learn the records, IT and information governance policy', 'Record consent, contacts and decisions', and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Separate fact from opinion and label opinion
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
'Left his seat four times in twenty minutes' is observation. 'Was not engaged' is inference. The Reference sheet maps PSI Code 1.2.8 as requiring you to avoid conjecture and label opinion clearly; PSI Code 4.2.5 is also mapped — read both clauses in the Code itself. Notes can be disclosed through a subject access request, or read by Tusla or a court. Whoever reads them must be able to tell what you saw, what you were told and by whom, and what you concluded. Inference written as fact cannot be checked by the reader, and you cannot defend it either.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the verbs in your supervisor's notes: 'observed', 'said', 'reported by' against 'appeared', 'in my view', 'suggests'. Notice that every reported statement is attributed to someone: teacher, parent, child or psychologist.

WRITE DOWN — three sentences from an anonymised note, each marked as observed, reported (by whom) or opinion. Note the exact words that give each one away.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you write down a strong clinical impression without it reading as fact?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the observation section of a note as pure description: the behaviour, how often, how long, where, and what came before and after.

THEY HOLD — the interpretive sentence, and how it is worded and labelled.

WHY THAT SPLIT — plain description is the discipline to learn first. Once you can write a paragraph with no inference leaking into it, adding a labelled opinion is safe, because the reader can see what it rests on.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the full note using a visible split, such as 'Observed:', 'Reported by (role):' and 'Psychologist's view:'.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — judgement words ('defiant', 'chaotic home', 'anxious mother') sitting in the factual part, and something a teacher told you written as though you saw it yourself.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — '"Mum is overprotective" — did you see that, did someone tell you, or is it your reading? Then which heading does it go under?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every note separates observed, reported and opinion, names the source of every reported statement, and labels your opinion as yours.

PASS TEST — A reader can tell which is which

EVIDENCE TO FILE — an anonymised extract reviewed in supervision, with the labelling noted in the supervision record. Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'child is anxious about school due to difficulties at home' in a note, with no source and no label, read by the parent after a subject access request.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the three categories (observed, reported by a named person, your labelled opinion) and why a labelled opinion is professional while an unlabelled one is a liability. You can rewrite a peer's sentence to show the difference.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a parent disputes a note. Check whether the disputed line was fact or opinion. Do not alter the original entry. Add a dated correction, marked as later, for a factual error. Record the parent's disagreement beside an opinion. Follow the service's procedure for correction requests.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing an interpretation such as 'disengaged' or 'chaotic home' in the factual part of the note without a source or a label.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Avoid conjecture', into 'Identify where sources converge' in Assessment, and into writing a report the family can read.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the verbs in your supervisor's notes: 'observed', 'said', 'reported by' against 'appeared', 'in my view', 'suggests'. Notice that every reported statement is attributed to someone: teacher, parent, child or psychologist.

micro.name: Avoid conjecture
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Conjecture is a guess written down as if it were evidence: 'probably ADHD', 'likely something going on at home'. It is different from labelled opinion, because it goes beyond anything your evidence supports. PSI Code 1.2.8 is the clause mapped here. A guess about diagnosis in a case note can travel into the school's records, a SENO application or a family's view of their child. It can be disclosed, and it shapes how the next professional reads the child before they have met them.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does with a hunch. Many record it as a question to explore, in the supervision record or a working hypothesis, and never as a conclusion in the case note.

WRITE DOWN — where hypotheses are kept in this service (case note, working paper, supervision record) and the exact wording used for a hypothesis that has not been tested yet.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'where do you write down a hypothesis you haven't tested yet, and what words do you use?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing notes that stop at the evidence, and bringing your hunches to supervision to talk through.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether a hypothesis is strong enough to go on the file as a labelled question for further assessment, and how it is worded.

WHY THAT SPLIT — hunches are useful and should be discussed. The risk is in where they are written down, and your supervisor knows what this service's file can safely carry.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write notes on your own cases, then reread each one before filing and take out any sentence that goes beyond what you saw, heard or were told.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — diagnostic labels you are not in a position to give ('presents as autistic'), guesses about family life, and words like 'probably', 'likely' and 'seems to be due to'.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what in this visit would let you write "likely dyslexic"? If nothing, where does that sentence belong?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — reread every note for conjecture before filing. A hypothesis goes to supervision, or onto the file as a clearly labelled question for further assessment. It never goes in as a finding.

PASS TEST — You did not speculate in the record

EVIDENCE TO FILE — an anonymised before-and-after rewrite discussed in supervision, noted in the supervision record. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'possible ASD?' in a note after a single classroom visit, which the school then repeats in a letter home.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer the difference between observation, labelled opinion that rests on evidence, and conjecture. You can rewrite a guess as a question for assessment, e.g. 'attention across settings to be explored through teacher rating scales and a second observation'.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find a guess on the file. Do not delete it. Add a dated, signed entry marked as a later addition, saying the comment was a hypothesis and not a finding. Tell your supervisor, and follow the service policy on amending records.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing a possible diagnosis into a case note after one visit.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Separate fact from opinion and label opinion', into Formulation (hypotheses tested, not assumed), and into 'Include a limitations paragraph'.

micro.name: Write the same day
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Contemporaneous notes carry weight because they are written at or near the time, before memory starts filling gaps. CORU SoP 2.8 is the standard mapped here. The Reference sheet records that record keeping and the write-up of observations and consultations were named in your review. It says this one habit addresses that more than anything else in the skill. A note written on the day takes minutes. A note rebuilt a week later takes far longer, loses detail, and reads as rebuilt.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — when and where your supervisor writes notes: in the car, in the staffroom, in the last slot of the day. Notice roughly how long each one takes, and how they plan a school day to leave room for it.

WRITE DOWN — the gap between contact and note for every note you see written, and the method (typed, dictated, handwritten then typed).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's your rule when a day runs over and you can't write up before you leave?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing your own note of every meeting you attend jointly, before you leave the school, and sending it to your supervisor that day.

THEY HOLD — the official note on their cases, and a comparison of your note with theirs.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you build the habit when little rides on it. Comparing the two notes while memory is still fresh shows you exactly what you missed and what you added.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — same-day notes on all your own cases, with your supervisor checking the dates of notes against the dates of contact.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a Friday batch of the week's notes, and notes dated the day of contact but written later, which misrepresents the record.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this note is for Tuesday. When did you actually write it? Then that's the date that goes on it.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — plan every school day with a writing slot after each contact. The Reference sheet suggests eight minutes in the car before you drive off. If same-day truly fails, write it the next working day and record both the contact date and the date written.

PASS TEST — Notes are contemporaneous

EVIDENCE TO FILE — dates on the file, checked by your supervisor, plus a weekly tally in your Log of notes written the same day and later (numbers only, no identifiers). Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — five school visits written up from memory on a Sunday evening, each dated as if written on the day.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why contemporaneity matters, both legally and for accuracy, and show a peer how to fit writing time into a rural school-visit day with long drives between schools.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you have a backlog. Write the oldest notes first, each with the true date of writing. Tell your supervisor. If the backlog comes from the workload rather than from habit, raise it as a workload issue.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing up a week's notes in one batch and dating them as though they were written on the day.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record consent, contacts and decisions', 'Raise workload before it becomes a problem', and the review development area on record keeping.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — when and where your supervisor writes notes: in the car, in the staffroom, in the last slot of the day. Notice roughly how long each one takes, and how they plan a school day to leave room for it.

micro.name: Record consent, contacts and decisions
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The file should let anyone rebuild what you did, with whom, when, on what consent, and what was decided. CORU SoP 1.15 is the standard mapped here. The Reference sheet lists 'recording what was discussed but not what was decided' as a common error. In a complaint or review, a file that holds the conversation but not the decision, who owns it and the date leaves the service unable to show what was agreed. It also leaves the school unable to show it did what was agreed.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor keeps a contact log (date, who, how, why) apart from the narrative notes, and how they end every meeting note: the action, who owns it, and the date.

WRITE DOWN — the closing structure they use, e.g. 'Agreed: … / By whom: … / By when: … / Review: …', and how phone calls and emails are logged.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a school says "we never agreed that", what does the file need to show?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping the contact log for a shared case, and drafting the decisions section of each meeting note.

THEY HOLD — confirming decisions with the school and parents, and settling any disagreement about what was agreed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — logging contacts is mechanical and teaches you the rhythm of a case. Confirming decisions with other people is consultation, and a mistake there affects the relationship with the school.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — on your own cases: a consent note of what was explained, every contact logged (phone calls and emails included), and every meeting closed by reading back the decisions, owners and dates to the group before it ends.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — phone calls with parents that never reach the file, and 'discussed next steps' with no step named.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who is running the reading intervention, from when, and when do we check it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the file shows consent and what was explained, every contact, and every decision with an owner, a date and a review point.

PASS TEST — The file shows what you did and when

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the contact log and meeting notes on the case file, and an anonymised count of contacts in your Log. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the file shows three school visits but not the phone call in which the parent withdrew consent for a classroom observation.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can set out the minimum a file needs: consent and what was explained, every contact, and each decision with owner, date and review. You can explain why reading decisions back at the end of a meeting prevents most later disputes.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find a contact that was never recorded. Add it now, dated today and marked as a later entry, giving the date of the original contact and why it was missed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording what was discussed at a meeting but not what was decided, by whom, or by when.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record what was explained, not just that consent was given', 'Write recommendations a teacher could act on Monday', and review meetings on the Continuum of Support.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Know the countersigning standard before drafting
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Countersigning means your supervisor puts their name to your report. The Reference sheet calls that a higher bar than 'accurate', because they are staking their registration on your reasoning. Each supervisor and service has a standard: template version, section order, how scores are reported, what goes in an appendix, what is sent with the draft, and turnaround. CORU SoP 2.10 is mapped here. The Reference sheet points to NEPS templates and house style. Ask for the current version rather than reusing Roscommon's. Finding the standard out from a returned draft wastes a draft and a week.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — ask for two or three recent anonymised reports your supervisor wrote or countersigned. Look at section order, length, how scores and confidence intervals are shown, whether raw scores appear, and how recommendations are laid out.

WRITE DOWN — a one-page house-standard checklist: template version, headings, score conventions, what goes with the draft (raw data, scoring), and the expected turnaround.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what makes you send a trainee's draft back unread, rather than edit it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the house-standard checklist and bringing it to supervision in the first week in Cavan.

THEY HOLD — the standard itself, and any exceptions for particular cases, referrers or report types.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you can only aim at a standard you can see. Writing it down makes your supervisor's unspoken expectations explicit, and gives you both something to point to when a draft comes back.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — before each draft, say the standard back to your supervisor: template, length, main reader, due date, and what you will send with it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — assuming the Roscommon template or a university assignment format applies, and starting to draft before asking.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'before you start: what is this one for, who reads it first, and when do I get it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — ask for the standard at the start of every placement and with every new supervisor, keep the checklist, and draft to it.

PASS TEST — You asked at the start

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the checklist (no identifiers) with the Placement Plan, and the supervision record of the conversation. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a first draft in the wrong template, with scores reported differently from the service's convention, returned before the reasoning was even read.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why countersigning is a higher bar than accuracy, and give a new trainee the questions to ask a supervisor in week one.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — two psychologists you work with hold different standards. Name it in supervision and agree which applies to which case. Do not blend the two into a report that meets neither.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Drafting the first report of a placement in the previous service's template without asking.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Proofread against the service template', every other report micro-skill, and the Cavan Placement Plan.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Proofread against the service template
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Most errors a supervisor catches are not reasoning errors. They are another child's name left over from a previous report, a score copied wrongly from the record form, a percentile that does not match the standard score, the wrong pronoun, or the wrong age at testing. A parent who spots one stops trusting the whole report, and a wrong score can change what a school or SENO does. CORU SoP 2.8 is the standard mapped here. Proofreading is a method, not a final skim.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor checks a report before it leaves: whether they check every score against the protocol, check names and dates in a separate pass, or read it aloud.

WRITE DOWN — their checking sequence as a numbered list, and which classification descriptors the service uses for each test.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the worst error you've seen reach a family, and how was it caught?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — a score-by-score check of one of your supervisor's draft reports against the record forms and scoring output, before they send it.

THEY HOLD — sign-off, and the decision on any discrepancy you find.

WHY THAT SPLIT — checking someone else's report trains your eye. You are not blind to text you did not write, the way every author is to their own.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — proofread your own draft in separate passes: (1) names, pronouns, date of birth, age at testing, school, class; (2) every score, confidence interval, percentile and descriptor against the protocol; (3) template headings and order; (4) read aloud for sense.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a previous report reused as a starting point (the usual source of wrong names), and descriptors taken from a different test's classification system.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'your text says "average" but the table says 78. Which test's descriptors are you using?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every draft goes to your supervisor already checked in separate passes against the protocols and the template, with raw data and scoring attached.

PASS TEST — No score or name errors

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your supervisor's feedback on the draft, and your proofreading checklist. Log against 5. Working with Others and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report reaches a family with another child's first name in paragraph four.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer the multi-pass method, and explain why scores are checked against the protocol, not against your own earlier table, which may already hold the error.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — an error is found after the report is issued. Tell your supervisor at once. Issue a corrected version marked as corrected, dated, with the reason, as the service policy says. If personal data went to the wrong person, treat it as a possible data breach.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Building a new report from an old one and leaving the previous child's name in the text.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Score the phonological composites correctly', 'Store and transfer records lawfully', and requiring only house-style edits (Reference sheet grade 5).

micro.name: Include a tool rationale
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The reader needs to know why these tools were chosen for this referral question, not only which were used. A rationale shows the assessment was planned from the question rather than run as a default battery. It also lets a later psychologist judge what the results can and cannot answer. CORU SoP 3.2 is the standard mapped here. Without a rationale, a report that used a cognitive battery for a question about peer relationships has no defence.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor's reports explain why each tool was chosen, and how: one line per tool, or a paragraph linking tools to hypotheses.

WRITE DOWN — the chain they use: referral question → hypothesis → tool → what the result could tell us. Note also where they explain choosing not to use a tool.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when do you decide not to do a cognitive assessment, and how do you explain that to the school?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting a rationale table for a shared case: each tool, the question or hypothesis it addresses, whether its age norms fit, and any limitation for this child (language, sensory, cultural).

THEY HOLD — the choice of tools, and whether each is within your agreed competence.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the rationale shows whether you understand why the tools were chosen. The choice itself has consequences, and competence levels, that you do not yet carry.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — choose the tools for your own case, write the rationale before you administer anything, and defend it in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a rationale written after the fact to justify a default battery; tools named with no link to the question; norms that may not fit the child. Check the manual's norm sample rather than assuming.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'which hypothesis does this subtest test? What would you conclude if it came out average?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the report states, for every tool, why it was used for this question, plus any reason its results should be read with caution for this child.

PASS TEST — It is there

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the rationale section of the report, named in your Appendix 5 entry. Log against 5. Working with Others and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an 'assessments administered' list of five tools with no reason given for any, one of them normed on an age range that does not include the child.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the hypothesis-testing logic of choosing tools (Sattler, 2018, report-writing chapters; read the source for detail) and show a peer how one referral question leads to a short battery.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you realise after administering that a tool was the wrong fit. Say so in the rationale and the limitations, give its results less weight, and do not build conclusions on them.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Listing the tools administered with no reason linking any of them to the referral question.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know your publisher competence level for every tool', 'Include a limitations paragraph', and 'Judge which source to weight and why'.

micro.name: Include an integration section
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet puts it plainly. The findings section can be organised by source, but the formulation cannot. It must name where sources agree, where they conflict, and what you make of the conflict, and this is the biggest single difference between a grade 3 and a grade 5 report. Report-writing texts agree: organise the synthesis by theme or question, not by instrument (Lichtenberger, Mather, Kaufman & Kaufman, 2004). CORU SoP 5.27 and 5.32 are mapped here. Without integration, your supervisor cannot see your reasoning, so cannot countersign it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in your supervisor's reports, where the findings end and the integration begins, and whether each integration paragraph draws on more than one source.

WRITE DOWN — the paragraph pattern: a claim about the child → evidence from two or more sources → any conflict named → what it means for the referral question.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when your test results and the teacher's account point opposite ways, how do you write that so the family doesn't feel disbelieved?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the integration section of a shared case, working from the source-by-domain grid you built in Assessment.

THEY HOLD — the conclusions, and the wording of any conflict between a parent's account and a teacher's.

WHY THAT SPLIT — drafting integration is where you find out whether you understood the case. Wording conflict between people the family knows has consequences for relationships your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the integration section for your own case. Your supervisor reads it on its own, without the findings, to see if it stands.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the findings repeated in the order collected, joined by 'furthermore'; conflicting evidence quietly dropped; paragraphs that open with a test name.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'cover the findings section. Does this still tell me what you think is going on, and why?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the report has an integration section organised by question or theme, where each paragraph makes a claim, cites more than one source, and names any conflict.

PASS TEST — Not a list of tests

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report, with the integration section named in your Appendix 5 entry. Log against 5. Working with Others and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a section headed 'Integration' that repeats the index scores in the order the subtests were given.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between findings and integration, and take a peer's test-by-test summary through a rewrite into claim-first paragraphs.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the sources will not integrate. Say so. Name the competing readings, say which evidence supports each, and state what further information would decide between them.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
An integration section that lists findings in the order they were collected.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name the framework in the formulation', 'Write recommendations a teacher could act on Monday', and 'Identify where sources diverge and say so'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Name the framework in the formulation
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A formulation without a named framework is the author's intuition, and the reader cannot check it. Naming the framework tells the reader how the evidence was organised and what kind of explanation to expect. The Reference sheet's reading for this macro is the problem-analysis framework (Monsen & Frederickson, 2008, 'The Monsen et al. problem-solving model ten years on', in Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle (Eds.), Frameworks for Practice in Educational Psychology; the original is Monsen, Graham, Frederickson & Cameron, 1998, Educational Psychology in Practice). CORU SoP 5.29 is mapped here. Grade 4 on the Reference sheet requires a named framework.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor names a framework in the formulation, where it appears (a heading, the first sentence, a citation), and whether the paragraphs follow its structure.

WRITE DOWN — the framework used in each report you read, the citation, and one sentence on why it fitted that case.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you name the framework even in a short report? Do schools and parents notice?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — proposing a framework for a shared case with one line of reasoning, and drafting the formulation under its headings.

THEY HOLD — whether the framework fits, and the final formulation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — proposing and drafting show whether you can use a framework or can only name it. Whether it truly fits the case is a judgement your supervisor models first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — choose, name and cite the framework in your own report, and write the formulation using its steps.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a framework named in the first sentence and then ignored, so the paragraphs still follow the order of the tests, or a citation copied from someone else's report without being read.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've named problem analysis. Show me where in this section the problem is defined and the hypotheses are tested.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the formulation names a framework, cites it in APA style in the text and the reference list, and follows its structure.

PASS TEST — Named and cited

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the formulation section of the report, named in your Appendix 5 entry. Log against 5. Working with Others and 2. Formulation.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'using an interactive factors approach' in one line, with no citation and nothing afterwards that follows the approach.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what naming a framework gives the reader, and show a peer how the same evidence reads differently under two frameworks (check which frameworks the UCD Handbook names — read it for the wording).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — halfway through, the framework does not fit the case. Say so in supervision, switch deliberately, and name the change rather than blending two frameworks without saying so.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Naming a framework in the formulation and then writing a formulation that does not follow it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name and cite it in the report' and 'Use the framework's own structure' in Formulation, and into 'Include a limitations paragraph'.
