micro.name: Include a limitations paragraph
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet is blunt: a report with no limitations section is not at countersigning standard. The limitations must be specific. Not 'all assessment has limitations', but, for example, that a test was given in the child's second language, so the verbal index is likely to underestimate their reasoning. PSI Code 2.3.1 is the clause mapped here. Specific limitations show competence. A generic paragraph shows a template, and a supervisor putting their name to the report will notice.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the limitations paragraph in each of your supervisor's reports: its position, its length, and whether each point is tied to this child and this assessment.

WRITE DOWN — every limitation named across three reports, sorted into types: language, attention or fatigue on the day, a missing informant, norms, a single observation, a tool adapted from standard procedure.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which limitation do you most often see missed in trainee reports?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the limitations paragraph for a shared case from your session notes, the adaptation record and your list of sources not reached.

THEY HOLD — the final wording, and how strongly each limitation should qualify the conclusions.

WHY THAT SPLIT — collecting limitations is systematic work you can do. Judging how much each one weakens a conclusion is a skill your supervisor demonstrates first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the limitations paragraph for your own report and link each limitation to the conclusion it affects.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a paragraph copied from the last report, and limitations stated but never linked to the conclusions they weaken.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you say the teacher form wasn't returned. Which conclusion does that make less certain?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every report has a limitations paragraph, specific to this child and this assessment, with each limitation linked to the conclusion it affects.

PASS TEST — Every report, no exceptions

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the reports, and a running tally in your Log of reports with a specific limitations paragraph (numbers only). Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'the results should be interpreted with caution' as the whole paragraph, word for word as in your last three reports.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can take the Reference sheet's second-language example and show a peer how to turn a generic caution into a specific one, and why that specific version is what makes the conclusions trustworthy.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a limitation comes to light after the report is issued. Discuss it with your supervisor and issue a dated addendum if it changes how a conclusion should be read.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Pasting the same generic caution into every report instead of naming this child's specific limitations.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Include a limitations paragraph in every report' in Ethical Practice, 'State what you did not assess and what that limits', and 'State the effect on validity in the report'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Write recommendations a teacher could act on Monday
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The class teacher's question is 'what do I do on Monday?' (Reference sheet). Recommendations are the part most readers turn to first. The Reference sheet requires them to be addressed to roles and set at a level of the NEPS Continuum of Support (Classroom Support, School Support, School Support Plus). CORU SoP 5.34 is mapped here. A recommendation such as 'provide a structured literacy programme' gives nobody a task, a time or a resource, so it is unlikely to happen, and there is nothing to review.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor words recommendations: whether each one names who does it, what exactly, how often, with what resource, from when, and how it will be reviewed. Notice how they link it to the school's Student Support File.

WRITE DOWN — two or three recommendations you think work, and the parts that make them usable.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you know if a school can actually deliver what you recommend before you write it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting recommendations for a shared case, grouped by Continuum level and by role (class teacher, special education teacher, parent, child).

THEY HOLD — checking that the school can realistically resource each one, and the final list.

WHY THAT SPLIT — drafting shows whether your recommendations flow from the formulation. Knowing what a particular school can deliver comes from a relationship with that school that your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the recommendations for your own report and test them: give them to the class teacher or a non-psychologist and ask what they would do first.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jargon, recommendations that do not follow from the formulation, and wish lists no school could resource.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who does this, how often, starting when, and what does it look like on a Tuesday morning in third class?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every recommendation names a role, a specific action, frequency, a resource the school has or can get, a start date and a review point, set at a Continuum level.

PASS TEST — Specific, resourced, dated

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the recommendations section, and a note of the readability test you ran. Log against 5. Working with Others and 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'the school should consider social skills support' in a report, and at review no one can say who was meant to deliver it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can take a vague recommendation and rebuild it with role, action, frequency, resource, date and review, and explain why the Continuum level matters for the school's planning.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — at review, a recommendation was not carried out. Find out why (resource, clarity, buy-in) before recommending it again, and rewrite it so it can be delivered.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommendations with no named role, no Continuum level and no date, so nobody owns them and nothing can be reviewed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Link the profile to what the school can deliver', Intervention planning, and 'Judge who will read this and what they need'.

micro.name: Quote the child's own words
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Children have the right to express their views in matters affecting them, and to have those views given due weight (UNCRC Article 12). Lundy (2007, British Educational Research Journal) argues that voice alone is not enough: the view needs an audience and has to have influence. A report that describes a child only through scores and adult accounts is about the child without the child being in it. Quoting their own words, with their knowledge, puts the child in the report as a person, and often gives the recommendation that matters most.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor gathers the child's views (a conversation, a drawing, scaling, a sort of what helps and what is hard) and where those words appear in the report.

WRITE DOWN — the methods used at different ages, and how quotations are introduced and placed near the recommendations they inform.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you tell the child their words will be in the report? What do you leave out, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — gathering the child's views in a session, recording their exact words at the time, and proposing which quotations belong in the report.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether any quotation could expose or embarrass the child if read by peers, parents or staff, and the final choice.

WHY THAT SPLIT — recording the child's words accurately is yours from the start. Judging how a quotation will land with each reader is a risk judgement your supervisor models first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — include the child's own words in your report, with the child told beforehand that what they say may be written down and who will read it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a token quotation at the end with no link to the recommendations, words paraphrased into adult language, and quotations that reveal more than the child agreed to.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'she said "I hate reading out loud". Which recommendation answers that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the report quotes the child's own words, with their knowledge, in a section on their views, and at least one recommendation responds to what they said.

PASS TEST — The child appears as a person

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the child's-views section of the report, named in your Appendix 5 entry. Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a twelve-page report on a ten-year-old in which the only mention of the child's view is 'X was cooperative throughout'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain Article 12 and Lundy's model, and show age-appropriate ways to get views from a child who is non-speaking, very young or reluctant (visual scales, choices, AAC, observation of preferences).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a parent objects to a quotation, or the child regrets saying something. Talk it through with your supervisor, and weigh removing or rewording it against the child's right to be heard.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Describing the child only through test scores and adult reports, with no trace of their own view.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Include the child's own self-report where age-appropriate', 'Include the child's construction of the problem', and 'Check the young person could read what is written about them'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor gathers the child's views (a conversation, a drawing, scaling, a sort of what helps and what is hard) and where those words appear in the report.

micro.name: Judge who will read this and what they need
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The same findings must reach a parent, a class teacher, a SENCO, a SENO and sometimes another professional, and each reads for a different question (Reference sheet). A parent asks what it means for their child and what happens now. A teacher asks what to do on Monday. A SENO asks what is being applied for and what evidence supports it. Another professional asks what you found and how confident you are. CORU SoP 5.27 is mapped here. Writing without deciding who the primary reader is produces a document that serves nobody fully.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor decides who a document is for before writing: a report, a letter to a family, a referral to a CDNT or CAMHS, a note to a principal. Notice what changes in each: length, vocabulary, what comes first.

WRITE DOWN — for each document you see, the primary reader, the question that reader brings, and where in the document it is answered.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a report goes to the family and the school, who do you write it for first?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — before drafting any shared document, writing one line at the top: primary reader, their question, and other readers.

THEY HOLD — the call when readers' needs conflict, e.g. a parent who will read a sentence the SENO needs for an application.

WHY THAT SPLIT — naming the reader is a habit you can build at once. Balancing readers with competing needs involves relationships and service processes your supervisor knows.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for your own documents, name the primary reader in supervision before drafting, and show where their question is answered in the first page.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — writing for your supervisor or your university marker rather than the actual reader, and forgetting that the family will read everything.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who reads this first, and what do they want to know by the end of page one?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every document you write has a named primary reader, their question answered early, and other readers accounted for.

PASS TEST — You can name the primary reader

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the reader line on your drafts (kept with working papers) and supervision discussion. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a referral letter to a CDNT written like a parent summary, missing the developmental and assessment detail the receiving team needs to accept it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can set out the Reference sheet's reader-by-reader questions and show a peer how the same finding is placed differently for each.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a reader says the document did not help them. Ask what question they came with, and fix the layering (summary, body, recommendations) rather than adding more text.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing every document for your supervisor or marker rather than for the person who will act on it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Change register between family and professional audiences' and 'Write recommendations a teacher could act on Monday'.

micro.name: Change register between family and professional audiences
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A single register cannot serve a parent and a consultant at once (Reference sheet). CORU SoP 2.2 and 5.25 are mapped here (read both for their wording). A family letter full of index names and percentiles leaves a parent unsure what it means for their child. A referral to CAMHS written in a warm, informal register can be read as lacking the detail needed to triage it. Harvey (2006, Journal of Clinical Psychology) examined what makes psychological reports clear to readers — read it for the specific variables.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — two documents your supervisor wrote about the same child, one to a family and one to another professional. Compare sentence length, technical terms, how scores are described, and what is said first.

WRITE DOWN — pairs of sentences that say the same thing in the two registers, e.g. a standard score with confidence interval against 'within the range we would expect for his age'.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you leave out of the family letter that must go in the professional one, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the family version of a document your supervisor wrote for professionals, or the other way round.

THEY HOLD — checking that the meaning did not shift between versions, and that nothing in the family version is softened into inaccuracy.

WHY THAT SPLIT — rewriting is the exercise that builds the skill. The check matters because the commonest failure is a family version that is kinder but no longer true.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write both versions for your own case and bring them side by side to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a family version that is the professional version with a glossary added; a professional version that has lost precision; the two versions contradicting each other.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'read me the first paragraph of each. If the parent later read the professional one, would it feel like the same child?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — produce family and professional versions that read differently in register, but say the same thing in substance, with no contradiction between them.

PASS TEST — Two versions read differently

EVIDENCE TO FILE — both versions on the case file, and an anonymised pair of sentences in your supervision notes. Log against 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a family letter reading 'FSIQ 82 (12th percentile), VCI relative weakness', with no explanation of what that means for the child.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to translate a finding between registers without changing its meaning, and why the family can read the professional version too, so it must also be respectful.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the family reads the professional version and is upset by a phrase. Look at what the phrase implied. Change the wording if it was disrespectful or unclear, not if it was accurate and simply unwelcome, and talk it through with them.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Sending a family the professional report with a glossary attached and calling it the family version.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Produce an accessible or plain-language version' and feedback meetings with families.

micro.name: Produce an accessible or plain-language version
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Some readers need more than a change of register: a parent with literacy difficulties, a parent reading in a second language or through an interpreter, a parent with an intellectual disability, or a young person. The Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 prohibit discrimination in providing services, including on grounds of disability and race — read the Acts for the exact duty on reasonable accommodation. NALA's plain English guidance is a practical standard. A report issued in a family's home language is strong evidence of this skill.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor finds out a family's reading and language needs before writing (a question at intake, the school's knowledge, the parent's own request), and what they produce: a plain-language summary, a translated report, easy-read, or a feedback meeting with a written summary to follow.

WRITE DOWN — the service's arrangements for interpreters and translation, and any accessible templates it uses.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you ask a parent about their reading without embarrassing them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the plain-language version: short sentences, common words, no idiom, one idea per sentence, headings that are questions the parent would ask.

THEY HOLD — arranging and paying for translation or interpreters, and checking the plain version still says what the full report says.

WHY THAT SPLIT — plain-language drafting is a writing skill you can practise now. Translation involves service budgets and approved providers.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — produce the accessible version for your own case, and state in the report that it was prepared with the reader's needs in mind (Reference sheet).

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — idiom that will not survive an interpreter ('on the right track', 'a bit all over the place'), long sentences, and a plain version that drops the key finding.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'read that sentence as if it were going through an interpreter. What comes out the other side?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — where a reader needs it, produce a plain-language or accessible version, and record in the report and case file that you did and why.

PASS TEST — It exists where it is needed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the accessible version on the case file and the sentence in the report recording the adaptation. Log each translated or accessible report you produce, with no identifying details. Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent who reads little English receives a twelve-page report and signs off on recommendations they could not read.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain plain-language principles (NALA guidance), the difference between plain language, easy-read and translation, and why the adaptation is recorded in the report.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you learn after issue that the parent could not read the report. Offer a meeting, with an interpreter if needed, go through it verbally, follow up with an accessible written summary, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using idiom and long sentences in a report that will be read through an interpreter.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Check the young person could read what is written about them', 'Obtain assent from the child in their own language', and feedback with families.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Check the young person could read what is written about them
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The young person is a reader of their own report, now or later. They may read it at home, see it at a review meeting or request their records. They have a right of access to their personal data under GDPR Article 15, and the service will have a policy on requests made by or for a child — check it. UNCRC Article 12 is mapped here. A teenager who reads that they are 'low functioning' or 'oppositional' learns how adults see them. Writing as though they will read it is both respectful and good practice.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor writes with the young person in mind as a reader: how they describe difficulties, whether strengths come first, whether the young person is addressed directly or talked about.

WRITE DOWN — phrases they avoid and what they use instead, e.g. 'finds reading effortful' rather than 'poor reader'.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever gone through a report with a teenager? What did they react to?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — rereading a shared draft as the young person, marking every phrase that would hurt, confuse or label them, and suggesting alternatives.

THEY HOLD — deciding what stays because it must be said, and whether to share the report or a version of it directly with the young person.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading as the young person is a skill of perspective you can practise now. Whether and how to share with a minor involves consent, guardians and service policy.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for your own report, reread it as the young person before sending, and where it fits, prepare a short version for them in their own terms.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — deficit labels, third-person language about a young person in the room, and difficulties described without strengths or context.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if Aoife read this sentence at fifteen, what would she take from it about herself?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every report is reread from the young person's point of view before issue, with the language adjusted so it is accurate and respectful. Where appropriate, a version for the young person is prepared.

PASS TEST — You considered them as a reader

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the version for the young person, if made, and a note of the reread in supervision. Log against 5. Working with Others and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a post-primary student reads 'significant cognitive deficits' about themselves in a report left on the school's shared drive.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a young person is a reader of their own report (Article 12; right of access), show strengths-based wording that is still accurate, and show a peer how to make a one-page version for a young person.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a young person is upset by what they read. Meet them with your supervisor, listen, explain what was meant, and change wording that was unnecessarily hurtful, recording the change as a dated amendment.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing a report about a teenager in language you would not be willing to read out to them.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Quote the child's own words', 'Obtain assent from the child in their own language', and Working with Others with young people and families.

micro.name: Submit vetting early enough to clear before day one
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Under the National Vetting Bureau (Children and Vulnerable Persons) Acts 2012–2016, a relevant organisation must not let a person do relevant work with children until it has received a vetting disclosure for that person. That is a legal bar, not a formality. You apply through the organisation's liaison person, usually by e-vetting, and processing time varies with demand, so no fixed figure is given here. Check with the placement. Arrive with vetting pending and you cannot see children, and the lost days come off your placement.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how the placement handles vetting for you: who their liaison person is, whether they accept a disclosure from UCD or need their own, and what proof they want on day one.

WRITE DOWN — the liaison person's name, the date you submitted, the date of the disclosure, and which organisation it was issued to.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'does a vetting disclosure from another organisation cover me here, or do I need yours?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — completing the forms, supplying ID and addresses accurately, and chasing progress.

THEY HOLD — the organisation's decision that you are cleared to start relevant work.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the application is yours and mistakes in it cause most of the delay. The legal decision to let you work with children belongs to the organisation.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — submit vetting for the next placement without being reminded, as soon as the placement is confirmed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — leaving it until the month before, and assuming last year's disclosure transfers.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — the placement co-ordinator asking, 'where are you with vetting for Cavan?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for every placement, confirm what vetting that organisation needs, apply early, and hold the disclosure before your first day.

PASS TEST — Cleared, not pending

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the disclosure (or the organisation's confirmation) on your placement file. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — Cavan starts on 05/10/2026 and you spend the first week unable to see a child.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a new trainee what the Vetting Acts require, why it is the organisation's disclosure that counts, and how to plan the timing.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when vetting has not cleared by day one: tell the placement and the university at once, and agree non-contact work (induction, file reading, policy) so no one is put in a position where you see children uncleared.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Starting a placement on the assumption that vetting from an earlier placement carries over.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Complete service induction' and into every direct-contact skill in the file.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Complete Children First training and file the certificate
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Children First Act 2015 and the Children First National Guidance (DCYA, 2017) set out how anyone working with children recognises and reports concerns. Tusla provides a free e-learning module, 'Introduction to Children First', which issues a certificate. Placements and universities expect it before you start. More importantly, it is the minimum grounding for the child protection skills below. Check with UCD whether it needs refreshing each year or other training on top.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which child protection training your supervisor and the service require, and whether the service adds its own policy training.

WRITE DOWN — the course, provider, date completed, and any renewal requirement.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'is there anything in this service's child safeguarding statement that the Tusla module doesn't cover?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — completing the module properly (not clicking through) and filing the certificate.

THEY HOLD — confirming that your training meets the service's requirement.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the training is yours. Whether it is enough for this service is their call, because services often have extra requirements.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — complete and file the training before each placement, and read the service's Child Safeguarding Statement in the first week.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a certificate that exists but whose content you cannot recall when a concern comes up.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what would you do if a child told you something in a session this afternoon?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep a current certificate, dated before the placement starts, on file, and know where the service's safeguarding statement is.

PASS TEST — Certificate dated before placement

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the certificate on the placement file and in your portfolio. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a certificate dated after your first day of child contact, found at placement audit.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what the Children First training covers, how it relates to the Act and the Guidance, and what each service adds through its own safeguarding statement.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find your training is out of date mid-placement: tell your supervisor, complete it at once, and take their direction on contact in the meantime.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Completing the module after child contact has already begun.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know the Tusla reporting thresholds' and 'Recognise and act on child protection concerns'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Know the Tusla reporting thresholds
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Children First Act 2015 defines harm as assault, ill-treatment, neglect or sexual abuse. For mandated persons it sets thresholds: for most categories the child's health, development or welfare must have been, or be at risk of being, seriously affected; for sexual abuse there is no 'serious' qualifier. Separately, the Guidance asks anyone with reasonable grounds for concern to report to Tusla. Read the thresholds in Children First National Guidance (2017) chapter 3 in full — they include specific provisions, such as for 16–17-year-olds, that are not summarised here.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks through a concern: whether it is 'reasonable grounds for concern' (report) or at the mandated threshold (report as a mandated person), and how they use the Guidance.

WRITE DOWN — the four categories of harm and the threshold wording for each, from the Guidance, not from memory.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the hardest threshold call you've made, and what tipped it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the Guidance thresholds and testing yourself on anonymised case examples, then checking your answers with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — live threshold judgements until you have shown you can make them. The legal duty to report is still yours if you are a mandated person.

WHY THAT SPLIT — threshold knowledge can be rehearsed safely. Real calls need practised judgement, but the duty itself is never delegated.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for a live concern, state your threshold judgement and your reasoning to your supervisor the same day.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — waiting for certainty before reporting. The test is reasonable grounds, not proof.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've described it as not serious enough. Which threshold wording are you using?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — state the category of harm and whether it meets the threshold, citing the Guidance wording, and act on it.

PASS TEST — You can state what reaches the threshold

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision record of threshold discussions. Log against 6. Ethical Practice. Do not record identifiable case details in your personal log.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a concern at threshold not reported because you were waiting to be sure.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the four categories, the mandated thresholds, the 'reasonable grounds' standard for everyone, and the specific provisions — citing the Guidance chapter, not paraphrasing from memory.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you are unsure: consult the DLP or Tusla (Tusla will discuss a concern informally), and when in doubt, report.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Waiting for proof when the test is reasonable grounds for concern.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know you are a mandated person and what that means' and 'Recognise a concern against the threshold'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Know you are a mandated person and what that means
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Schedule 2 of the Children First Act 2015 lists the classes of mandated persons, including psychologists. A mandated person who knows, believes or has reasonable grounds to suspect harm at threshold must report it to Tusla as soon as practicable. Telling the DLP does not discharge that duty, though a joint report with the DLP is allowed. Whether a trainee on placement is a mandated person in their own right depends on the Schedule 2 wording. Confirm it in writing with UCD and the placement, and act as if you are until told otherwise.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor describes their own duty, and how the service handles joint reports with the DLP.

WRITE DOWN — the exact Schedule 2 wording that covers psychologists, and UCD's written position on whether it covers trainees.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if you and the DLP disagreed about whether to report, what would you do?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — getting UCD's written position on your status, and reading section 14 of the Act (the duty to report) yourself.

THEY HOLD — nothing in the duty itself. If you are a mandated person, the duty is yours. What your supervisor holds is support and advice.

WHY THAT SPLIT — this is the one place in the file where the usual split does not apply. The law makes the duty personal.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — when a concern arises, you decide whether your duty is engaged and make or join the report, with your supervisor supporting.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — handing it to the DLP and assuming that is the end of your part.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'have you confirmed the report went in, and is your name on it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — make, or confirm you are named on, a report to Tusla for any concern at threshold, as soon as practicable, and keep your record.

PASS TEST — The duty is personal, not delegable

EVIDENCE TO FILE — UCD's written confirmation of your status on file; your own record of any report. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the DLP decides not to report, you do nothing more, and the concern was at threshold.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain Schedule 2, section 14, joint reporting, and the difference between the DLP's role and the mandated person's own duty.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the DLP will not report and you believe the threshold is met: report to Tusla yourself, tell your supervisor, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Believing that telling the DLP discharges your own duty as a mandated person.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Act the same day without waiting for supervision' and 'Report to the DLP and record the time'.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Complete health and safety and lone working induction
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Educational psychologists work alone in schools, homes and cars. The service's lone working procedure exists so someone knows where you are, when you are due back, and what to do if you are not. CORU SoP 3.13 and 3.14 place safe practice on you as well as the employer. Home visits carry particular risk: an unknown environment, other adults present, pets, and no colleague nearby. Skipping induction means you will not know the procedure on the day you need it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does before a home visit: who they tell, the check-in time, what they take, where they park, and the code word or exit plan if the service has one.

WRITE DOWN — the service's lone working procedure step by step: sign-out, check-in, escalation if you miss a check-in.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever left a visit early? What made you go?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — following the sign-out and check-in procedure for joint visits yourself.

THEY HOLD — the risk assessment for the visit and the decision on whether it goes ahead.

WHY THAT SPLIT — following the procedure builds the habit while someone is with you. Assessing risk from a referral needs knowledge of the area and the family that you do not yet have.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — do the pre-visit risk check yourself and present it to your supervisor before a visit you lead.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — skipping sign-out for a 'quick' visit, and not reading the file for risk information.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is there anything on file about other adults in the house?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — follow the lone working procedure for every visit, and read the file for risk information before you go.

PASS TEST — You know the procedure for a home visit

EVIDENCE TO FILE — induction checklist signed. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you are at a home visit that becomes unsafe and nobody knows where you are.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can walk a new trainee through the procedure, explain why each step exists, and describe the warning signs that should end a visit early.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a visit feels unsafe: leave, without explaining in detail if need be, contact your check-in person, and record and report it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Doing a 'quick' home visit without signing out because it was only twenty minutes.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Identify the DLP by name in week one' and into Working with Others — home-based work.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Identify the DLP by name in week one
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Children First National Guidance (2017) says organisations providing services to children should appoint a Designated Liaison Person (DLP) for child protection. Schools must appoint a DLP and a deputy DLP under the Department of Education's Child Protection Procedures for Primary and Post-Primary Schools 2017 (revised 2023); the DLP is normally the principal. Your placement service will also have its own DLP. When a concern arises you have minutes, not days, to act. Having to find out who the DLP is at that moment costs time and adds stress. The UCD Handbook §6.2 expects you to know this — read that section for the exact requirement.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — who your supervisor names as DLP for the service, and how they find the DLP for each school they visit.

WRITE DOWN — the service DLP and deputy, with phone numbers, and the DLP for every school on your caseload.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if a school's DLP isn't available, who do you go to?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building the DLP list for your schools, confirming each name with the school office.

THEY HOLD — the service-level contact and any escalation.

WHY THAT SPLIT — building the list is a simple task that should be yours from day one. The escalation routes are the service's to set.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — keep the DLP list current and check the DLP when you first visit each new school.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a list made once and never updated when schools change principal.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who's the DLP at the school you're going to this morning?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — have the DLP and deputy for the service and every school written down, where you can reach them without a laptop, by the end of week one.

PASS TEST — Written down, not looked up later

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the DLP list, kept securely. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a child discloses and you spend twenty minutes finding out who to tell.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the DLP role, how it differs from your own duty as a mandated person, and why the list must exist before it is needed.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when neither DLP can be reached: your own duty to report to Tusla still stands, so report directly and tell the DLP afterwards.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Not knowing the school's DLP when you are on site with a concern.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Report to the DLP and record the time' and into 'Act the same day without waiting for supervision'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Learn the referral and risk pathways
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
You will meet needs you cannot meet: self-harm, suicidal thinking, mental illness, disability, family crisis. Each has a route, such as CAMHS, primary care psychology, the Children's Disability Network Team, Tusla, the GP or emergency services, and each route has criteria, a way in and a waiting time. Knowing that a pathway exists is not enough. You need to know what happens after you refer, or you cannot tell the family what to expect or judge whether the referral is the right one.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor decides where to refer, and what they tell the family about what happens next.

WRITE DOWN — for each main pathway: who can refer, how, the criteria, what happens next, the likely wait, and what to do in an emergency.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which referral route do trainees most often misunderstand here?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building a one-page pathway map for the service and checking it with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — referral decisions for your cases, and any urgent risk response.

WHY THAT SPLIT — mapping is research you can do alone. Referral decisions and risk responses carry consequences you need to have seen handled first.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — propose the referral route for your case and explain to your supervisor what will happen after it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — referring to a service whose criteria the child does not meet, and not knowing the emergency route for suicide risk.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what does CAMHS need to see in the referral to accept it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — refer by the right route, and tell the family accurately what will happen next and how long it may take.

PASS TEST — You know what happens after you refer

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the pathway map and referral records. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a referral rejected weeks later for not meeting criteria, and a family left waiting for nothing.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the local pathways, their criteria and what to expect, and the emergency route for risk.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a referral is rejected: find out why, tell the family, and find another route rather than closing the case.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Referring without knowing the service's criteria, so the referral bounces and the family waits for nothing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Refer on and maintain responsibility until contact is made' and into Working with Others.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor decides where to refer, and what they tell the family about what happens next.

micro.name: Learn the records, IT and information governance policy
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Psychological records are special category personal data under the GDPR (Article 9) and the Data Protection Act 2018. You need to know where records are kept, who can see them, how long they are kept, how they are destroyed, and what to do if data is lost. Retention periods are set by the service's policy, and HSE and Department of Education services differ, so check rather than assume. A lost notebook or an email to the wrong address is a reportable data breach.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor keeps notes, protocols and reports; what they carry out of the office; how they send reports; and what they never email.

WRITE DOWN — the service's rules on storage, transport, email, retention and breach reporting, and the Data Protection Officer's contact.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the most common data mistake you see from new staff?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — following the policy for your own notes and protocols from the first day.

THEY HOLD — decisions on sharing information with other agencies.

WHY THAT SPLIT — handling your own records is a daily habit. Sharing across agencies has legal conditions that need someone who knows them.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — manage your caseload records to policy; your supervisor spot-checks.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — protocols in the car overnight, notes on a personal device, identifiable details in your own learning log.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'where are the protocols from this morning right now?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — store, transport, send and retain records to policy, and know what to do if something is lost.

PASS TEST — You know where records live and for how long

EVIDENCE TO FILE — induction checklist signed. Log against 6. Ethical Practice. Keep identifiers out of your own log.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report emailed to the wrong parent, and you do not know who to tell.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why psychological records are special category data, the service's retention and transport rules, and the breach procedure.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when data is lost or misdirected: tell your supervisor and the Data Protection Officer at once, because the controller has 72 hours to notify the Data Protection Commission where required (GDPR Art. 33).

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Keeping identifiable case details in your own learning log or on a personal device.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into record-keeping throughout — 'Record what was explained', 'Record verbatim what was said or seen, at the time'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Ask which tools you may administer independently here
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Test publishers restrict who may buy and use their instruments, and services add their own rules about what trainees may do unsupervised. PSI Code 3.3.6 is the standard mapped here — not to be confused with PSI accreditation criterion 3.3.6 on placement settings; read the Code clause itself before citing it. If this is not agreed in writing, a trainee can end up giving a test they are not permitted to use alone, and the scores may not be usable. The Placement Plan is where this belongs, agreed at the start.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which tools your supervisor uses, which they would let a trainee administer, and which they would not.

WRITE DOWN — every tool you might use, with the publisher's qualification level and the service's rule for trainees.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'is there a tool here that you'd never let a trainee give alone, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the list of tools and your proposed level of independence for each.

THEY HOLD — agreeing the list and signing the Placement Plan.

WHY THAT SPLIT — drafting shows your knowledge of the tools. The decision rests on their responsibility for your work.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise the tools list in the first placement planning meeting and get it agreed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — assuming that because you gave a test at the last placement you can give it alone here.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is that in the Placement Plan yet?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — have the list of tools, and the level of independence for each, written into the Placement Plan in the first two weeks.

PASS TEST — Agreed in writing in the Placement Plan

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the signed Placement Plan. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you administer a test alone and your supervisor says afterwards that you were not cleared for it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain publisher qualification levels, how services add their own rules, and why agreeing this in writing protects the child, the trainee and the supervisor.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you are asked to give a tool not on the agreed list: say so, and ask for it to be added or supervised.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Assuming last placement's tool clearances carry over to this one.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know your publisher competence level for every tool' and into Assessment administration skills.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Explain purpose, process and who will see the report
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Consent is only informed if the person knows what they are agreeing to: why you are involved, what you will do, how long it will take, what will be written, and who will read it. PSI Code 1.3.5 is the clause mapped here. Parents often assume the report stays with them, or that the school sees everything, or nothing. Someone who finds out afterwards who read the report has not given informed consent, and trust is hard to rebuild.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor explains involvement at the first meeting: the words they use, the order, and what they check the parent understood.

WRITE DOWN — the explanation as near verbatim as you can, and especially how they describe who receives the report.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do parents most often misunderstand about who sees the report?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the explanation of process and timing, from a script you have checked with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — questions about sharing with other agencies, and any hesitation from the parent.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the process explanation can be scripted. Questions about information-sharing need someone who knows the service policy exactly.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — give the whole explanation and take the consent, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jargon, rushing, and consent taken before the explanation has finished.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I just check — did you follow who'll get a copy?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain purpose, process and who will see the report in plain words, check understanding, and only then take consent.

PASS TEST — In plain words, before anything begins

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the consent form and a note of what was explained. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent upset at the feedback meeting because they did not know the school would get the report.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the elements of informed consent, why each matters, and how to check understanding without making the parent feel tested.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a parent realises later they did not understand: stop, re-explain, and let them re-consent or withdraw.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking a signature before explaining who will see the report.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State the right to stop or withdraw', 'Record what was explained, not just that consent was given', and Working with Others.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: State the right to stop or withdraw
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Consent is ongoing. A parent, young person or child can stop a session or withdraw from involvement at any point, and must be told so at the start (PSI Code 1.3.5). Families often feel they cannot say no to a psychologist the school has brought in, especially where they fear it will affect support. Unless the right to withdraw is stated, consent is not truly voluntary. Families who know they can stop are, in practice, more likely to stay.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether and how your supervisor tells families and children they can stop, and whether they repeat it later.

WRITE DOWN — the words they use for adults and the words they use for children.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'has anyone ever withdrawn? How did you handle what the school expected?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — saying the right-to-withdraw sentence to the parent and the child, from a script checked by your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — what happens if someone does withdraw, including the conversation with the school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the statement is short and can be practised word for word. Handling a withdrawal involves the school relationship and service consequences.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — state the right to stop, to parent and child, at the start and again before any demanding task.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — mentioning it so quickly, or so formally, that nobody could act on it.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor adding, to the child, 'and you can say stop to us too.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — tell every parent and child, in words they understand, that they can stop or withdraw at any time without it affecting the help they get, and record that you said it.

PASS TEST — It was mentioned

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the note of consent discussion. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a parent who wanted to stop but did not know they could, and complains afterwards.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the right to withdraw is part of valid consent, how to say it so it is heard, and how to adapt it for a young child.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when someone withdraws: accept it without pressure, record it, tell the referrer only what the family agrees to, and leave the door open.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Stating the right to withdraw so briefly that no one could act on it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Recognise and respond to non-verbal withdrawal' and 'Re-evaluate whether to continue at all'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: State the limits of confidentiality before disclosure
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Confidentiality has limits: risk of serious harm to the person or others, child protection concerns, and legal requirements such as a court order. Those limits must be explained before someone discloses, not after (PSI Code 1.2.9; CORU SoP 1.12). A young person who tells you something and then learns you have to pass it on may feel betrayed, and may not tell another adult again. Explaining the limits first lets them choose what to say, knowing what will happen.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor explains the limits to a parent, to a teenager and to a young child. Notice how the words change with age.

WRITE DOWN — the limits they list, and the child-friendly version.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you explain limits without making a child think you expect them to disclose something?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — explaining the limits to a young person from a script checked with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — responding to anything disclosed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the explanation can be practised. Responding to a disclosure needs the child protection skills below, which you build next.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — explain the limits yourself at the start of every session with a child or young person, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — leaving it out with young children, and 'everything's confidential' said as reassurance.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor adding the limits if you forgot.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — explain the limits at the start, in age-appropriate words, before any conversation that could lead to disclosure.

PASS TEST — First, not after

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the note of the explanation. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a teenager tells you about self-harm after you said everything was confidential, and now you have to break that.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the limits, the reason for stating them first, and how to phrase them for different ages.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a disclosure comes before you explained the limits: do not promise secrecy, explain honestly now what you must do, and tell them what happens next.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Promising a child that 'everything you say stays in this room'.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Do not investigate or question further' and 'Recognise a concern against the threshold'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Establish who holds guardianship before contact
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The person bringing the child is not always the person who can consent. Under the Guardianship of Infants Act 1964, as amended by the Children and Family Relationships Act 2015, a mother is automatically a guardian, as is a father married to her. An unmarried father may or may not be: he becomes a guardian automatically only if he has lived with the mother for 12 consecutive months after 18/01/2016, including at least 3 months with the mother and child after the birth; otherwise only by statutory declaration with the mother or by court order. For a child in care, Tusla may hold consent rights depending on the type of order. The exact rules have conditions not set out here, so check with the service rather than relying on this summary.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor checks guardianship at referral: what they ask, what they record, and what they do when parents are separated.

WRITE DOWN — the questions they ask and where the answer is recorded.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you do when one guardian consents and the other objects?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — checking the referral form and file for guardianship, and flagging anything unclear.

THEY HOLD — decisions where guardianship is disputed or where a child is in care.

WHY THAT SPLIT — checking the file is routine. Disputed guardianship and care orders need legal knowledge and service policy.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — confirm guardianship yourself before first contact, with your supervisor checking.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — assuming the parent who made contact is the only guardian, and not asking about a child in care.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the form says parents separated. Have you checked with dad?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — confirm and record who holds guardianship, and whose consent is needed, before any contact with the child.

PASS TEST — You checked rather than assumed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the guardianship note on the case file. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a complaint from a guardian who did not know their child had been assessed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the basic rules on guardianship, the common complications (separation, unmarried fathers, care orders) and where to get authoritative advice.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you discover mid-involvement that a guardian was not consulted: stop, tell your supervisor, and contact the guardian before continuing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Assuming the parent who phoned the school is the only person whose consent is needed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Explain purpose, process and who will see the report' and 'Record what was explained'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Use supported decision-making where capacity is in question
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, commenced on 26/04/2023, applies to adults. It is relevant to young adults on your caseload (UCD Table 3). It presumes capacity, requires all practicable steps to help a person decide before concluding they cannot, and says an unwise decision is not proof of incapacity (section 8). Capacity is judged decision by decision: can the person understand, retain, use and weigh the information, and communicate a decision (section 3)? PSI Code 1.3.10 is the clause mapped here. Assuming incapacity takes away a right.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does to help a young adult with an intellectual disability or communication need to understand and decide: easy-read materials, time, a trusted person present, visual supports.

WRITE DOWN — each support used and how the young person showed their decision.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell the difference between someone who can't decide and someone who needs more help to?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing accessible materials (easy-read, visuals) for the consent conversation.

THEY HOLD — any judgement about capacity, and any involvement of decision supporters.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing materials is concrete and checkable. A capacity judgement has legal weight.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the consent conversation using supports, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — speaking to the carer instead of the young person, and taking the carer's view as consent.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor redirecting: 'let's ask Seán what he thinks.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — presume capacity, use every practicable support, and record how you supported the decision.

PASS TEST — How, not just that

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the note recording supports used and how the decision was expressed. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'consent obtained from mother' for a nineteen-year-old who was never asked.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the ADMCA 2015 principles, the functional test, and the practical supports that help someone decide — citing sections and the Decision Support Service guidance.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when, even with support, the young person cannot decide: record the steps taken, involve your supervisor, and follow the Act's framework rather than defaulting to a carer's say-so.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking a carer's consent for an adult who was never supported to decide for themselves.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Obtain assent from the child in their own language' and into Working with Others — young adults and families.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Recognise and respond to non-verbal withdrawal
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Many children will not say 'stop'. They withdraw assent by turning away, going quiet, putting their head down, fidgeting, looking at the door, or saying 'I don't know' to everything. Younger children and children with communication needs may have no other way to tell you. PSI Code 1.4.3 is the clause mapped here. Carrying on past these signs overrides the child's wishes and produces data that is not valid.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the non-verbal signs your supervisor responds to, and what they do: pause, check in, offer a choice, stop.

WRITE DOWN — the sign, what your supervisor did, and how the child responded.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which signs do you treat as a no, and which just as needing a break?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — watching for signs during your supervisor's session and telling them what you saw afterwards.

THEY HOLD — responding in the session.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you learn the signs fastest when you are not also administering. Responding in the moment is the next step.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — watch for signs in your own session and respond — pause, name what you notice, offer a choice — with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — reading withdrawal as 'being difficult' or 'avoidance of hard items' and pressing on, because the subtest is nearly finished.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I think she might want a rest. Shall we check?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — respond to non-verbal withdrawal by checking in and, if it continues, stopping — and record what you saw.

PASS TEST — You stopped

EVIDENCE TO FILE — protocol annotation and case note. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a completed protocol from a child who had clearly withdrawn, with no note that they had.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can describe the common non-verbal signs of withdrawal, how they vary with age and need, and how to check in without pressure.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise afterwards that you missed withdrawal: note it, reconsider the validity of the data, and tell your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating a child's silence and turning away as defiance to work through.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Re-evaluate whether to continue at all' and 'Recognise when standard procedure is not working'.

micro.name: Obtain assent from the child in their own language
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Children have the right to express views in matters affecting them (UNCRC Article 12). Assent is their agreement, given in terms they understand, alongside the consent of guardians. 'Their own language' means literally their home language, or Irish, or sign language or AAC, and also words pitched at their age and understanding. Assent sought in words the child did not understand is not assent. A child who was never asked has been done to, not worked with.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor asks a child for assent: the words, visual supports, how they check understanding, and what they do if the child hesitates.

WRITE DOWN — the phrasing for different ages, and any supports for language or communication.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you worked with an interpreter for a child? What did you need to do differently?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing child-friendly explanations and visual supports for assent, checked with your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — arranging interpreters, and decisions where a child says no but guardians have consented.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing materials is concrete. A conflict between the child's no and the parents' yes needs judgement and relationship.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — ask the child for assent yourself, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — asking in adult language, and not asking at all because the parent has consented.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can you tell me back what we're going to do today?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — ask every child for assent in words and a language or mode they understand, check their understanding, and record their answer.

PASS TEST — The child was asked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — note of the child's assent in the case record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the child tells a teacher later that they did not know what the psychologist was doing with them.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain assent versus consent, Article 12, and how to adapt for age, language, and communication needs.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a child refuses despite parental consent: respect it for now, explore why, and plan with the family, rather than overriding it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Taking the parent's consent as enough and not asking the child.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record what was explained, not just that consent was given' and into 'Include the child's own self-report where age-appropriate'.

micro.name: Record what was explained, not just that consent was given
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A tick box saying 'consent obtained' proves nothing about whether consent was informed. If a complaint arises, the question is what the person was told. CORU SoP 1.15 is the standard mapped here. A good consent note records what was explained (purpose, process, who sees the report, limits of confidentiality, right to withdraw), who was present, questions asked, and the answer given. That note protects the family, the child and you.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor writes in the file after a consent conversation, and how long after the conversation they write it.

WRITE DOWN — the headings they use (explained, present, questions, answer), and anything they add beyond the signed form.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever needed a consent note to answer a complaint? What did it need to show?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the consent note after a conversation your supervisor led.

THEY HOLD — checking the note, and adding anything you missed.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the note after watching tests whether you noticed what was said. Their check shows you what you missed.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — take consent and write the note yourself; your supervisor reviews it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a note that records the outcome (consent given) and not the content.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if the mother complained next year, would this note show what she was told?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — after every consent conversation, write a note that records the content: what was explained, who was present, questions, and the answer.

PASS TEST — The note shows the content

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the consent note in the case record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a file that says 'consent given' and nothing else, when the parent says they were never told the school would see the report.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why content matters more than the tick, and show a peer a short template for a good consent note.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find a thin consent note on your own file: add a dated addendum with what you remember, clearly marked as written later.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording 'consent obtained' with no record of what was explained.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into record-keeping throughout, and into 'Keep notes at each stage' in ethical decision-making.

Not started

micro.name: Recognise a concern against the threshold
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Concerns rarely arrive as clear disclosures. They come as an injury with a vague explanation, a child who flinches, hunger, a comment in a drawing, a change in behaviour, or something a parent says. Children First National Guidance (2017) lists signs for each category of harm. Read that list, not a summary. The skill is noticing, then holding what you noticed against the threshold for 'reasonable grounds for concern'. Missing it leaves a child unprotected; noticing and not acting is worse.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor notices in a session or a file that makes them pause, and what they do next.

WRITE DOWN — the observation, and which category of harm and which threshold they considered (without identifying details in your own log).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the smallest thing that has ever led you to a report?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — noticing and naming anything that concerns you, to your supervisor, the same day.

THEY HOLD — the threshold judgement, while you are learning it. Your own duty to report stands regardless.

WHY THAT SPLIT — noticing is something you can do from day one. Threshold judgement needs practice, but never at the cost of not acting.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make the threshold judgement yourself and state it to your supervisor with your reasons.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — explaining signs away ('he's always clumsy') and waiting for more before saying anything.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if you're wondering, that's the concern. What category is it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — notice, name the category of harm, judge it against the threshold, and act — the same day.

PASS TEST — You knew it when you saw it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your contemporaneous record and the report record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice. No identifiers in your own log.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you noted something in a session, thought about it for a week, and then it was too late to report as soon as practicable.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the categories, signs and thresholds from the Guidance, and why 'reasonable grounds' is a lower bar than certainty.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise later that something you saw was a concern: act now, record why it was delayed, and tell your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Explaining away a sign because the family seemed nice.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Do not investigate or question further', 'Record verbatim what was said or seen, at the time', and 'Act the same day'.

Not started

micro.name: Do not investigate or question further
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
When a child discloses, your role is to listen, reassure, and pass it on — not to investigate. Investigation belongs to Tusla and An Garda Síochána. Leading or repeated questions can contaminate the child's account and harm a later investigation or prosecution. They can also distress the child. Children First National Guidance (2017) sets out how to respond: listen, do not ask leading questions, do not promise confidentiality, tell the child what happens next.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor would respond to a disclosure. You are unlikely to see one, so role-play it or talk it through.

WRITE DOWN — the words your supervisor would use: acknowledging, not leading, not promising, and explaining what happens next.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the question you most want to ask in that moment, and why shouldn't you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — rehearsing a disclosure response in role play with your supervisor playing the child, including a child who stops mid-sentence.

THEY HOLD — feedback on every question you asked and every promise you made.

WHY THAT SPLIT — this is a skill you must do alone the first time it happens, with no one to hand it to, so rehearsal is the main way to learn it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — role-play your response to different disclosures (partial, retracted, about a sibling), with your supervisor coaching.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'did he hurt you?', 'where did he touch you?', 'are you sure?' — any question that leads or tests.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'stop there. What did that question just put in her head?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — if a child discloses: listen, use open prompts only if needed ('tell me more'), do not promise secrecy, tell them what happens next, and do not interview.

PASS TEST — You did not interview the child

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your contemporaneous record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a record full of your questions, so the child's account can no longer be separated from your prompting.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why leading questions contaminate a child's account and how to respond using open prompts only.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you asked a leading question: record exactly what you asked and what the child said, and tell the DLP and Tusla so they know.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking 'did he hurt you?' in an effort to be sure before reporting.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record verbatim what was said or seen, at the time' and 'Report to the DLP and record the time'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Record verbatim what was said or seen, at the time
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Your record may be read by Tusla, An Garda Síochána or a court. A record made at the time, in the child's own words, with what you saw described factually, carries weight. A paraphrase written days later does not. CORU SoP 2.8 and 3.12 are the standards mapped here. The record must separate fact (what was said, what was seen) from your opinion, and be dated, timed and signed.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what a good child protection record looks like. Ask your supervisor to show you an anonymised example or the service template.

WRITE DOWN — the headings: date, time, place, who was present, the child's exact words, what you saw, what you said, who you told and when.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what makes a record useless to Tusla?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing practice records from role-played disclosures, and having your supervisor critique them.

THEY HOLD — feedback on factual accuracy and separation of fact and opinion.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the record is a skill that can be practised to standard before you need it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write the record after a role-played or real concern, straight away, and have it checked.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — interpretation in place of description ('she seemed scared of her dad'), and paraphrase in place of the child's words.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is that what she said, or what you think she meant?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — record the child's exact words, what you saw, and what you said, as soon as possible — dated, timed and signed, with fact and opinion separate.

PASS TEST — Contemporaneous and factual

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the record on the case file, per service policy. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a record written two days later: 'child indicated possible abuse at home'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what makes a child protection record usable, and why exact words and the separation of fact from opinion matter.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you could not record at the time: record as soon as possible, and note when the record was written and why it was delayed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Paraphrasing the child's words into your own summary.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Report to the DLP and record the time' and into record-keeping throughout.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started
