micro.name: Act the same day without waiting for supervision
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Children First Act 2015 requires a mandated person to report to Tusla 'as soon as practicable'. Your next supervision may be days away. Waiting for it can leave a child at risk overnight, and delay is a common way to fall short of the duty. Supervision is for support and learning after you act, not permission before. If your supervisor is available the same day, talk to them — but the timing is set by the concern, not by the diary.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how quickly your supervisor acts on a concern, and whether anything waits until the end of the day or week.

WRITE DOWN — the timeline: when the concern arose, when the DLP was told, when Tusla was contacted.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what would you do if this came up at 4pm on a Friday?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — telling your supervisor and the DLP straight away, and being part of the report.

THEY HOLD — support and advice. If you are a mandated person, the duty to report is still yours.

WHY THAT SPLIT — acting straight away is the non-negotiable part, and it is yours from the start.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the same-day response, contacting your supervisor if available but not waiting if they are not.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'I'll bring it to supervision on Thursday.'

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'don't wait for me. Ring the DLP now and we'll talk after.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — act the same day: DLP, and a report to Tusla if at threshold, whether or not your supervisor is reachable.

PASS TEST — The duty does not wait

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the record with times, and the report. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a concern held until supervision three days later.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain 'as soon as practicable', why supervision follows action rather than preceding it, and what to do out of hours (Tusla out-of-hours service, or An Garda Síochána if a child is in immediate danger).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise you have delayed: act now, record the delay honestly, and tell your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Holding a concern until the next supervision session.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Report to the DLP and record the time' and 'Bring it to supervision afterwards, not instead'.

micro.name: Report to the DLP and record the time
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The DLP makes sure the organisation responds consistently, and makes or joins reports to Tusla. Telling them is part of the procedure in every school and service (Children First National Guidance, 2017). If you are a mandated person, telling the DLP does not replace your own duty, but a joint report can meet both. The record of who you told, and when, is what shows the duty was met. Tusla accepts reports through its online portal or by the standard report form — check the current route.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor reports to a DLP: in person or by phone, what they say, and what they write down afterwards.

WRITE DOWN — the elements: whom you told, when, what you said, what they said they would do, and whether a Tusla report was made and by whom.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you follow up to know the report went in?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — making the call to the DLP, with your supervisor there, and writing the record.

THEY HOLD — support in the conversation, and escalation if the DLP does not act.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the call and the record are the core actions and should be yours. Escalating over a DLP needs confidence and knowledge of the service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — report to the DLP yourself and record it, with your supervisor informed the same day.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — no time on the record, and no check that a Tusla report was made.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what time did you speak to her, and is she reporting today?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — report to the DLP, record who and when, and confirm a Tusla report has been made (jointly or by you).

PASS TEST — The file shows who and when

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the record on the case file, and the report reference if you have one. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the file says 'discussed with principal' with no date, time, or outcome.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the DLP's role, joint reporting, and exactly what a report record must contain.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you cannot confirm the Tusla report was made: make it yourself, and record that you did.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Telling the DLP and not recording when, or whether a report followed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Bring it to supervision afterwards, not instead'.

micro.name: Bring it to supervision afterwards, not instead
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Child protection work is distressing and the decisions are rarely clean. Supervision afterwards is where you check your judgement, process what you heard, and learn for the next time. The UCD Handbook §6.2 is the reference mapped here — read it for the programme's exact expectation. The order is what matters. Supervision instead of action is a breach. Action with no supervision after leaves you carrying it alone and learning nothing from it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor uses their own supervision after a child protection case.

WRITE DOWN — what they bring: the decision, the reasoning, the emotional impact.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you still carry from cases like this, and what helps?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — bringing the case to supervision: what happened, what you did and when, how it affected you.

THEY HOLD — review of your decision-making, and support.

WHY THAT SPLIT — naming the impact is yours. Reviewing the decision is how they help you calibrate.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the supervision discussion: timeline, threshold, action, what you would do differently.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a factual account with no mention of impact on you, or a discussion that re-opens whether to act when action has already been taken.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'and how was it for you?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — after any child protection action, put it on the next supervision agenda, with the record, and reflect on both judgement and impact.

PASS TEST — Supervision follows the action

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the supervision record. Consider an Appendix 8 entry if a dilemma arose. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — no mention of the case in supervision, and a trainee who carries it alone.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why supervision comes after action, and what good supervision of a child protection case covers.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a case stays with you: raise it again in supervision, and use the employee assistance or occupational health service.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Using supervision as the place to decide whether to act.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Seek supervision when stressed, not only when stuck' and into Supervision.

micro.name: Identify the issue and all affected parties
micro.code: PSI Code Appendix A step 1 · Appendix B
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The PSI Code of Professional Ethics sets out an ethical decision-making procedure in Appendix A. Its first step is to identify the issue and everyone affected by it; the sheet maps Appendix B here too — read both in the Code itself. Dilemmas are usually framed around the obvious parties: the child and the parent. Missing a party — a sibling, a teacher, the service, the wider public, or you — means their interests are never weighed. Most poor decisions are poor at this first step.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor frames a dilemma when they first raise it, and who they name.

WRITE DOWN — the dilemma in one sentence, and every party affected, including those your supervisor adds.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'who's the party people usually forget in a dilemma like this?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the issue and listing all affected parties for a dilemma your supervisor is working.

THEY HOLD — the decision.

WHY THAT SPLIT — listing parties is where trainees learn to look wider, and it is safe to practise on a live case your supervisor holds.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — frame a dilemma in your own case and present the issue and all the parties in supervision before discussing what to do.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — stopping at the child and the parent, and leaving out siblings, the teacher, the service, other children in the class, and yourself.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'who else is affected by what you decide — including you?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for any dilemma, write the issue in one sentence and list every affected party, including the less obvious ones.

PASS TEST — Including ones you would otherwise miss

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 dilemma entry. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a decision that protected the child and parent and harmed a sibling nobody had thought about.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can walk a peer through step 1 on a worked case, and show the prompts that surface hidden parties: who else lives there, who else is in the room, who pays, who is responsible if it goes wrong.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a party emerges late: add them, and go back through the later steps rather than bolting them on.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Framing a dilemma around the child and parent only.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Scan the Code for the clauses that apply' and 'Evaluate each party's rights and responsibilities'.

micro.name: Scan the Code for the clauses that apply
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Step 2 of the PSI Code Appendix A procedure is to check the Code for the clauses relevant to the issue. The Code is organised under four ethical principles — respect for the rights and dignity of the person, competence, responsibility, and integrity — each with numbered clauses. Citing clause numbers makes your reasoning checkable and shows it is grounded in the Code, not personal values. Dilemmas often turn on two clauses in tension, and you only see the tension once both are written down.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor opens the Code itself when a dilemma arises, or works from memory, and how fast they find the relevant principle.

WRITE DOWN — the clause numbers they cite, what each says, and where two clauses pull against each other.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which clauses come up most often in EP work, and which are most often misread?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — searching the Code for relevant clauses for a live dilemma, and listing them with numbers.

THEY HOLD — interpretation of how the clauses apply.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding clauses builds your familiarity with the Code. Weighing them against each other is judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present the relevant clauses and the tension between them in supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — citing one clause that supports what you wanted to do anyway.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what clause would someone arguing the other side cite?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — cite every relevant Code clause by number, including those that pull against your preferred option.

PASS TEST — You cite clause numbers

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 dilemma entry with clauses. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'this would breach confidentiality' with no clause, and no mention of the clause that pulls the other way.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the four principles, find clauses quickly, and show how two clauses can conflict.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the Code does not answer the question: say so, and move to the rights and consequences analysis in the next steps.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Citing only the clause that supports the option you had already chosen.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Evaluate each party's rights and responsibilities'.

micro.name: Evaluate each party's rights and responsibilities
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Step 3 of the Appendix A procedure is to consider the rights, responsibilities and welfare of each affected party. Taking each party separately stops the loudest voice setting the frame, and shows where interests truly conflict and where they only seem to. A child's right to privacy, a parent's right to information, a school's duty of care, and your own professional responsibility can all be real at once.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor weighs parties, and whether they give the child's interests explicit weight.

WRITE DOWN — a table of parties, with each one's rights, responsibilities and interests.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a child's view and the parent's rights conflict, how do you weigh them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building the table for a live dilemma: one row per party, columns for rights, responsibilities, interests and welfare, with the source for each right (the Code, UNCRC, statute).

THEY HOLD — the weighting between rows.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the table is analysis you can practise and have checked. Weighing competing rights needs experience of how such conflicts usually resolve.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present the table and your view on which rights carry most weight, and why.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — treating adults' rights as automatically outweighing the child's.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what does the child have a right to here?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — consider each party separately — rights, responsibilities, welfare — and write it down.

PASS TEST — Each considered separately

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 dilemma entry. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a decision where the child's view was never considered as a separate interest.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can walk a peer through a rights-and-responsibilities table, drawing on the UNCRC and the Code.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when rights cannot be reconciled: be explicit about whose rights are being limited and why, and record it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating the parent's view as the child's.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Generate as many alternative courses as possible'.

micro.name: Generate as many alternative courses as possible
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Step 4 of Appendix A is to generate alternatives. Under pressure, dilemmas collapse into two options: tell or do not tell, continue or stop. The best choice is often a third one nobody considered: tell with the young person's involvement, delay briefly to prepare, share part of the information, consult first. Generating alternatives is the step that most often turns a dilemma into a manageable decision.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how many options your supervisor considers, and whether they generate them before judging any. Judging too early is what shrinks the list to two.

WRITE DOWN — every option they name, including the ones they reject quickly, and the unobvious ones: timing, partial sharing, involving the young person.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the option you didn't think of until later?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — brainstorming options for a live dilemma, on paper, before any are evaluated, aiming for at least five including some you would not choose.

THEY HOLD — adding options from their experience and choosing between them.

WHY THAT SPLIT — generating options is creative and safe to practise. Choosing carries the consequence, so it stays with them for now.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring at least four options to supervision, written down, before discussing which is best.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — two options, one obviously right, so the 'dilemma' was never really one — or options that are the same thing reworded.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's a third way? What if you did it later, or with her, or only in part?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — list more than two options, including the unobvious ones, before evaluating any.

PASS TEST — More than two

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 dilemma entry. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a forced choice between two bad options when a better one existed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show how to widen options: involving the person, timing, partial sharing, consultation, and doing nothing yet.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when every option is bad: choose the least harmful, and record why.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Framing every dilemma as a choice between two options.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Evaluate the likely outcome of each'.

micro.name: Evaluate the likely outcome of each
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Step 5 of Appendix A is to evaluate the likely consequences of each option for each party. This is where the earlier steps pay off: parties, rights and options meet. Thinking consequences through — short and long term, for each person — often shows that the option that feels most ethical in the moment has costs you had not seen, or the reverse.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor tests each option: 'what happens next if we do this — and then what?' Notice whether they think past the first reaction.

WRITE DOWN — the consequences they name for each option, for whom, and over what time frame.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which consequence do trainees most often miss?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the consequences of each option for each party, in a grid, short and long term.

THEY HOLD — correcting your predictions from what they have seen happen in similar cases.

WHY THAT SPLIT — predicting consequences improves with experience, so theirs corrects yours. The grid makes your predictions visible so they can be corrected.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present the consequence grid and your recommendation in supervision, and defend it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — short-term thinking (what calms today's meeting), and consequences for the child left out because the adults were louder.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'and six months from now? What does the child experience?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for each option, think through short and long-term consequences for each party, and write them down.

PASS TEST — Consequences thought through

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 dilemma entry. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a decision that solved the immediate problem and damaged the relationship with the family for the rest of the involvement.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show how to lay out a consequence grid — options by parties by time frame — and how to test predictions against experience.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when consequences cannot be predicted: choose the most reversible option, set a date to review, and record that uncertainty was part of the decision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Choosing the option that relieves your discomfort now rather than the one with the best consequences.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Decide and record the decision'.

Not started

micro.name: Decide and record the decision
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Step 6 of Appendix A is to make the decision. Recording it — what was decided, why, and which options were rejected — lets you, your supervisor, or a reviewer see that the decision was reasoned. It also makes it defensible if challenged. A decision reached in conversation and never written down is, for any later purpose, a decision nobody can show was made.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how and where your supervisor records an ethical decision: the case file, their supervision record, or both — and whether they record options they rejected.

WRITE DOWN — what the record contains: decision, reasoning, Code clauses, options rejected, who was consulted, date.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever needed to show your reasoning afterwards?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing up the decision for a dilemma your supervisor decided, including the reasons for rejecting the other options.

THEY HOLD — the decision itself, and checking your write-up is accurate.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing up someone else's decision tests whether you followed the reasoning, without you carrying the consequence.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make the decision on your own case and write it up, with your supervisor agreeing it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — recording the decision and not the reasoning.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'would someone reading this know why you didn't choose option two?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — decide, and record the decision, the reasoning and the options rejected, on the day.

PASS TEST — Written down

EVIDENCE TO FILE — case record and Appendix 8 dilemma entry. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a challenge months later and no record of why you did what you did.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain what a decision record needs and why the rejected options matter: they show the decision was a choice, not a default.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you did not record at the time: write it now, dated, clearly marked as written later, and say so if asked.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording what was decided but not why.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Take responsibility for the consequences' and 'Keep notes at each stage'.

micro.name: Take responsibility for the consequences
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Step 7 of Appendix A is to take responsibility for the decision and its consequences, and to act to correct them where they are harmful. A decision made through a good procedure can still go badly. What matters then is honesty: saying so, correcting what can be corrected, and learning from it. Defending a bad outcome because the procedure was followed misses the point of having a procedure.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about a decision that went badly: whether they own it, explain it away, or blame the system.

WRITE DOWN — what they did afterwards: who they told, what they corrected, what they changed in their practice.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'tell me about a decision you'd make differently now, and what you did once you knew.'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reviewing the outcome of a decision, and naming anything that went wrong.

THEY HOLD — deciding on corrective action.

WHY THAT SPLIT — naming what went wrong is the habit. What to do about it may involve the family, the school or the service.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — review your own decision's outcome in supervision, name what went wrong, and propose corrective action.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — defensiveness, blaming the procedure or the family, and treating 'I followed the steps' as the end of the matter.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'setting aside what others did, what's yours in this?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — review the outcome, own the part that was yours, and act to correct harm.

PASS TEST — Including where it went wrong

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 follow-up and supervision record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a harmful outcome explained away as the right decision on the information available, with nothing done about it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain step 7, and model owning a decision that went wrong.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the consequence is serious: tell your supervisor at once, follow service procedure, and consider whether it needs to be reported.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Defending a bad outcome because the procedure was followed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Keep notes at each stage' and into Supervision.

micro.name: Keep notes at each stage
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The pass test for this micro-skill records that the PSI Code strongly recommends keeping notes throughout the decision-making procedure. Read the Appendix A wording yourself. Notes at each stage show the reasoning as it developed, not as reconstructed after the outcome is known. They protect you if challenged, and they are the raw material for your Appendix 8 dilemma entries.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor keeps notes as a dilemma unfolds, or only records the outcome once it is settled.

WRITE DOWN — the headings they use, and where the notes are kept (case file, supervision record, or a separate log).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'where do you keep these notes, and who can see them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping dated, stage-by-stage notes for a dilemma your supervisor is working through, one heading per step of Appendix A.

THEY HOLD — the decision and the case record.

WHY THAT SPLIT — note-keeping is a habit you can build on someone else's decision first, so it is automatic by the time the decision is yours.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — keep your own stage-by-stage notes on a dilemma in your case, and bring them to supervision at each step rather than at the end.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — notes written all at once, after the event, which read as if you knew the answer from the start.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'when did you write this part?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep dated notes at each of the seven steps as you go.

PASS TEST — The Code strongly recommends it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 dilemma entry. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an Appendix 8 entry written from memory weeks later, which reads as if you knew the answer from the start.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer a simple seven-step note template, and explain why contemporaneous notes carry weight.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when notes are missing for a stage: write what you remember, dated and marked as later.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing the whole dilemma record after the outcome is known.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Appendix 8 and into Supervision.

micro.name: Know your publisher competence level for every tool
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Publishers restrict each instrument to users with particular qualifications, and label them by level in their catalogues. The level systems differ between publishers and between the UK/Ireland and US catalogues, so check each tool rather than assuming. PSI Code 3.3.6 is the clause mapped here — not to be confused with PSI accreditation criterion 3.3.6 on placement settings; read the Code clause itself before citing it. As a trainee you usually use restricted tools under supervision, and the qualification rests with your supervisor. If you cannot say which tools need which level, you cannot tell when you are working beyond what you are entitled to do.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about restricted tools: which ones they say a trainee can give under supervision, and which they reserve.

WRITE DOWN — every tool in the service's cupboard, with the publisher and the qualification level printed in that publisher's catalogue.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which tools here would you never let a trainee give without you in the room, and is that the publisher's rule or yours?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — building a table of tools, publisher levels, and your status for each (not trained, trained and supervised, cleared by placement).

THEY HOLD — confirming the table, and the service's own rules on top.

WHY THAT SPLIT — looking up levels is research you can do accurately yourself. Placement clearance is their decision under their qualification.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — keep the table current and consult it before offering to use any tool.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'I've done a WISC before' used as if it answered the question for another test or another setting.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what level is that one, and who holds it for your use here?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — for any tool, state the publisher's level, who holds the qualification for your use, and what supervision is agreed.

PASS TEST — You can state it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the tools table alongside the Placement Plan. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — administering a restricted instrument with no agreed supervision, so the scores may not be defensible and the service is exposed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how publisher levels work, why they exist, and how trainee use sits under a qualified supervisor.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find you used a tool beyond your agreed level: tell your supervisor, and decide together whether the scores can be reported and how.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating experience with one tool as clearance for a different tool.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask which tools you may administer independently here' and 'Say early what you are not yet competent to do'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Say early what you are not yet competent to do
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Supervisors allocate work based on what they think you can do. If you do not tell them where you are not yet competent, they will assume you can, and the gap shows up in front of a family or school. CORU SoP 1.2 and PSI Code 2.2.2 are the clauses mapped here. Saying it early, at allocation or in the Placement Plan, is professional. Saying it after the work has gone wrong is too late, and no one can fix the problem in time.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about what they do not do: referrals they pass on, tools they have not used, areas they consult on.

WRITE DOWN — the words they use to say it, without apologising or over-explaining.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you wish trainees told you earlier?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing your own list of areas where you are not yet competent: tools, age bands, presenting problems, types of meeting.

THEY HOLD — how the work is allocated around that list.

WHY THAT SPLIT — honest self-assessment is yours. Allocation is theirs, and they can only do it well with your list.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise competence gaps at allocation, before accepting work, with your supervisor responding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — accepting everything to look capable, and flagging gaps only once work is under way.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is there anything in this case you haven't done before?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — state competence gaps at allocation, without being asked, and propose how the gap will be covered (co-working, supervision, training).

PASS TEST — Before being asked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision record and Placement Plan. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you lead a feedback meeting on a presentation you have never worked with, and cannot answer the parent's questions.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why early disclosure of gaps is a professional strength, and how to phrase it with a plan attached.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you find a gap mid-case: say so straight away, and agree with your supervisor how to cover it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Accepting work beyond your competence to avoid looking less capable.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Decline work that exceeds you' and into Supervision.

micro.name: Decline work that exceeds you
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Sometimes flagging a gap is not enough, and the right answer is no. A request might be far beyond your training — a complex risk assessment, a court report, a presentation you have no grounding in — or no adequate supervision may be available. PSI Code 2.2.3 is the clause mapped here. Declining protects the child from work that is not good enough. A trainee who says yes to everything is a risk to the people they work with.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor declines work: to a school, a colleague, a manager. Notice the words and whether they offer an alternative.

WRITE DOWN — a phrase you could use yourself.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when did you last say no to a piece of work, and how did it land?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — identifying requests that exceed you, and saying so to your supervisor.

THEY HOLD — declining on your behalf to the school or service, while you are learning how.

WHY THAT SPLIT — recognising the limit is yours. Saying no to a principal on a live placement involves relationships your supervisor manages.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — decline work yourself, to the person asking, with an alternative, and your supervisor informed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — saying yes and then quietly struggling, or declining without offering any alternative.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'would it help to say you can do the observation but not the report?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — decline work that exceeds you, clearly and courteously, with an alternative where possible, and record it.

PASS TEST — You declined

EVIDENCE TO FILE — case note or email, and supervision record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report written beyond your competence, which then has to be withdrawn or corrected.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain when declining is required rather than optional, and how to do it while keeping the relationship.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you are pressured to accept: repeat the limit, explain the risk to the child, and escalate to your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Saying yes to work beyond you because the school needs it done.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Refer on and maintain responsibility until contact is made'.

micro.name: Refer on and maintain responsibility until contact is made
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Referral is a handover, not an exit. Until the receiving service has made contact, the child is still yours to hold in mind. Referrals get lost, rejected, or sit on waiting lists while risk changes. PSI Code 3.4.3 is the clause mapped here. A trainee who closes the file the day the referral letter goes has left the child in a gap between services. That gap is exactly where harm can go unnoticed.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does after sending a referral: whether they diarise a follow-up, and what they tell the family and school in the meantime.

WRITE DOWN — the steps from referral sent to referral accepted and contact made.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you had a referral go missing? How did you find out?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the referral, confirming it was received, and diarising a follow-up date to check contact has been made.

THEY HOLD — the decision to refer and when to close.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the referral and tracking it are practical. Closing the case carries responsibility for what happens after.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make the referral, follow it up, and keep the family informed, with your supervisor overseeing.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — closing the file when the letter goes, and no follow-up date.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'has CAMHS acknowledged it yet? When will you check?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — refer, confirm receipt, follow up until the receiving service has made contact, and only then hand over.

PASS TEST — You did not drop it at referral

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the referral, acknowledgement and follow-up notes. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a family who waited months for a service that never received the referral.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why responsibility continues after referral and show a simple tracking method.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a referral is lost or rejected: tell the family, re-refer or find another route, and record the gap.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Closing the case the day the referral letter is posted.

micro.name: Include a limitations paragraph in every report
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A limitations paragraph is where you state the limits of your own competence and your evidence in writing. CORU SoP 1.2 is the standard mapped here. It sits in Ethical Practice as well as Assessment because it is the public form of knowing your limits. Every report has some. A report that states none is either unusually complete or not being honest, and readers cannot tell which. This micro-skill is about consistency — every report, not only the difficult ones.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether every report your supervisor writes has a limitations paragraph, including the straightforward ones.

WRITE DOWN — the limitations stated in three of their reports, and how each is specific to that case.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'do you ever write a report without one?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the limitations paragraph for every report you contribute to.

THEY HOLD — the final wording.

WHY THAT SPLIT — making it a habit on every draft is what builds consistency. Wording that the family will read is still theirs to approve.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — write limitations for each of your own reports, and have your supervisor check them for specificity.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — the same paragraph pasted into every report.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this is the same wording as your last report. What's specific to this child?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every report has a specific limitations paragraph, including your own competence limits where relevant.

PASS TEST — Every one

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the reports. Keep a tally in your Log. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 1. Assessment.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — one report in five without a limitations paragraph, and that is the one that gets challenged.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a limitations paragraph is an ethical requirement, not just an assessment convention, and show what makes one specific.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a report went out without one: issue an addendum if the missing limits matter to the conclusions.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Pasting the same generic limitations paragraph into every report.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State what you did not assess and what that limits' and into report quality throughout.

micro.name: Track your actual caseload and travel load
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Educational psychology in rural Ireland involves long drives between schools. A caseload that looks manageable on paper can be unmanageable once travel, report-writing and meetings are counted. CORU SoP 1.18 is the standard mapped here. Without the numbers you cannot raise workload credibly — 'I'm overwhelmed' is easier to dismiss than 'I have twelve open cases, eleven hours' driving a week, and six reports due'. The Cavan placement (05/10/2026–18/12/2026, four days a week) is where to start counting.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor tracks their own workload: a spreadsheet, a diary, a whiteboard. Notice whether they count travel and writing time.

WRITE DOWN — the categories they track.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's a realistic caseload for a trainee here, and how would you know I was over it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping a weekly record: open cases, sessions, meetings, reports due, travel hours, and hours worked.

THEY HOLD — deciding what is a reasonable load.

WHY THAT SPLIT — keeping the numbers is yours. Judging what is reasonable needs knowledge of the service and of trainee norms.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring your numbers to supervision each week, with a one-line summary of how the load is.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — numbers kept but not looked at, and travel and writing time left out.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've got four reports due next week and two days in schools. When are you writing?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep a weekly workload record that includes travel and writing, and know your numbers without looking.

PASS TEST — You know the numbers

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the weekly record, which can sit in the Log. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you realise in week nine that four reports are overdue and you did not see it coming.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer a simple workload tracker and explain why travel and writing time are where caseloads hide.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the numbers show you are over capacity: take them to supervision and ask for re-prioritisation, not more effort.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Counting cases but not travel or report-writing time.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Raise workload before it becomes a problem'.

micro.name: Recognise your own warning signs
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Burnout is described as emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment (Maslach & Jackson, Journal of Occupational Behaviour, 1981). It builds slowly, and the person inside it is often the last to see it. Everyone's early signs are different: sleep, irritability, dread before work, cynicism about families, cutting corners on records. CORU SoP 5.45 is the standard mapped here. Knowing your own signs is what lets you act before your judgement is affected.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about their own stress, if they do, and what they do to manage it.

WRITE DOWN — for yourself, privately, what you notice in yourself when stretched: body, mood, thinking, behaviour.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what are your early signs, and what do you do when you notice them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — naming your warning signs, privately, and deciding which you will share in supervision.

THEY HOLD — noticing if they see signs you have not mentioned.

WHY THAT SPLIT — your signs are yours to know. A supervisor is a second pair of eyes, not a monitor.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — check your signs weekly, and raise it in supervision when they appear.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a trainee who says they are fine while their records slip and their language about families turns cynical.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you seem stretched. How are you actually doing?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name your warning signs, check them regularly, and act on them.

PASS TEST — You can name them

EVIDENCE TO FILE — nothing personal needs filing. A supervision note that wellbeing was discussed is enough. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you notice at the end of placement that you were running on empty for weeks, and your later reports show it.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain burnout and its early signs, citing sources, and help a peer identify their own.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the signs are there and not easing: tell your supervisor, use the employee assistance or university counselling service, and see your GP.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Noticing your signs and deciding to push through until the placement ends.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Seek supervision when stressed, not only when stuck' and 'Refrain from practice where judgement is seriously impaired'.

micro.name: Raise workload before it becomes a problem
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Workload raised early can be solved by re-prioritising, deferring or re-allocating. Workload raised after deadlines are missed becomes a performance conversation, and families and schools have already been let down. CORU SoP 1.18 is the standard mapped here. Trainees often hold back because they fear looking less capable than their peers. Supervisors consistently prefer to hear early.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor raises workload with their own manager: what they bring and what they ask for.

WRITE DOWN — the structure: the numbers, the pinch point, the specific ask.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the earliest point you'd want me to tell you I was stretched?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — spotting the pinch point in your workload record and naming it.

THEY HOLD — the decision about what to defer or re-allocate.

WHY THAT SPLIT — spotting the problem is yours. Re-prioritising involves other people's work and service commitments.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise a workload issue before a deadline is at risk, with the numbers and a proposal.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — waiting until you are already behind, and raising it as a general complaint with no proposal.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what would you take off your list if you could?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — raise workload as soon as your numbers show a pinch point ahead, with a specific proposal.

PASS TEST — Before, not after

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision record. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you raise it the day after a report deadline was missed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why early is better, and how to raise workload with numbers and a proposal.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when raising it did not change anything: raise it again, in writing, and involve the university placement tutor if needed.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Raising workload only after a deadline has been missed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Seek supervision when stressed, not only when stuck' and into Supervision.

micro.name: Seek supervision when stressed, not only when stuck
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Supervision is not only for case problems. PSI Code 4.1.2 is the clause mapped here, and the pass test records that seeking support is required, not merely permitted. Stress affects judgement, record-keeping and how you relate to families, so it is a practice issue, not only a personal one. Trainees often bring cases to supervision and keep stress to themselves. That leaves the supervisor managing risks they cannot see.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor's supervision sessions have space for wellbeing, and how it is raised.

WRITE DOWN — how the agenda is set, and whether wellbeing is a standing item.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you use your own supervision when you're stressed?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — adding wellbeing to your supervision agenda as a standing item, and saying one honest sentence under it each week, even when it is 'steady'.

THEY HOLD — creating space for it, and responding.

WHY THAT SPLIT — raising it is yours; the supervisor cannot respond to what they do not know, and a standing item makes it ordinary rather than an alarm.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise stress in supervision when it is there, and link it to its effect on your practice.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'fine' every week, and stress raised only as an excuse after something has gone wrong.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you said fine. On a scale of one to ten?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — bring stress to supervision when it is present, not only case problems.

PASS TEST — It is required, not permitted

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision record noting wellbeing discussed. Log against 6. Ethical Practice and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — your supervisor learns you were struggling from your placement evaluation, not from you.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why stress is a practice issue and how to raise it in supervision without it becoming therapy.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when supervision is not a safe place to raise it: use the university placement tutor or another route.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Bringing only case problems to supervision and keeping stress to yourself.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Refrain from practice where judgement is seriously impaired' and into Supervision.

micro.name: Know the seven-day notification duty
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The UCD Handbook §5 sets out a seven-day notification duty. Its exact triggers and route were not in the sources used to write this row, so do not act on a summary. Read §5 and write down, in your own words, what triggers it, who you notify, how, and within what time. Duties like this usually cover changes in circumstances that bear on fitness to practise. Missing the deadline can become a professional issue in itself, whatever the underlying matter was.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor or placement tutor mentions notification duties at induction.

WRITE DOWN — the exact wording of Handbook §5: what triggers it, who is notified, how, and the time limit.

ASK AFTERWARDS — ask your placement tutor, 'can you give me an example of something that would trigger the seven-day duty?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading §5 and summarising it in your own words on one page.

THEY HOLD — (placement tutor) confirming your summary is correct.

WHY THAT SPLIT — reading the rule is yours. Confirming your reading avoids acting on a misunderstanding when it matters.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — keep your summary where you can find it, and check a hypothetical scenario against it with your tutor.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — assuming the duty only covers serious matters, and not knowing how to notify.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if that happened on a Friday, when would the seven days end?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — know the trigger, the recipient, the method and the deadline, and act within it if needed.

PASS TEST — You could act on it if needed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your one-page summary of §5, kept in your portfolio. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — something triggers the duty and you learn about the deadline after it has passed.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the duty to a new trainee from the Handbook text, not from memory.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you missed the deadline: notify at once, explain the delay honestly, and tell your placement tutor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Not reading §5 until something triggers it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Refrain from practice where judgement is seriously impaired'.

micro.name: Refrain from practice where judgement is seriously impaired
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Illness, bereavement, exhaustion, medication, alcohol, or a crisis at home can all seriously impair judgement. PSI Code 2.5.1 is the clause mapped here: a psychologist whose judgement is seriously impaired should refrain from practice. The difficulty is that impairment affects the judgement you would use to notice it. So the skill is knowing your signs in advance, having an agreed plan, and accepting a supervisor's view when they see it before you do.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how the service handles a psychologist who is unwell or in crisis: cover arrangements, how cases are protected, and whether it is treated as normal.

WRITE DOWN — who you would tell, and how your cases would be covered.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever stepped back from work? How did you know it was time?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — agreeing in advance with your supervisor what would lead you to step back, and who covers.

THEY HOLD — the decision if you are not able to make it yourself.

WHY THAT SPLIT — a plan made while well is the only reliable one, because impaired judgement is poor at judging itself.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — if impaired, say so, step back from direct work, and hand over cases per the plan.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — pushing on because of placement days or deadlines, and seeing families while unwell.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I think you need to go home. I'll cover this afternoon.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — recognise serious impairment, stop direct practice, tell your supervisor and tutor, and follow any notification duty.

PASS TEST — You would know and would act

EVIDENCE TO FILE — nothing personal needs filing. Supervision record of the plan. Log against 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a feedback meeting led while seriously unwell, with a family given confused or inaccurate information.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the duty, why a pre-agreed plan matters, and why stepping back is professional rather than a failure.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you realise afterwards that you practised while impaired: tell your supervisor, review the affected work, and correct anything that needs it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Continuing to see families while seriously unwell because placement days are needed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Supervision, and into 'Know the seven-day notification duty'.

micro.name: Know the 30 minutes per placement day entitlement
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet summarises PSI Accreditation Standards (2022) 3.3.9 as requiring thirty minutes of supervision per placement day; read 3.3.9 itself so you quote the standard's words rather than a paraphrase. At four Cavan days a week that is two hours weekly — the formal hour plus an hour of informal contact. A trainee who does not know the figure cannot notice a shortfall, and one who cannot state it turns a requirement into a favour she has to ask for.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor talks about supervision time in the first meeting: as a fixed commitment with a figure attached, or as 'whenever we get a chance'. Notice whether they count informal contact (a call after a visit, a drive to a school) as supervision or treat only the booked hour as real.

WRITE DOWN — the figure, the 3.3.9 reference, and the weekly total it produces for four days a week.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how have you tracked supervision time with previous trainees, and what counted?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 in full before week one (the text is on the Reference sheet, Part B), doing the arithmetic for the Cavan pattern, and bringing both to the contract conversation.

THEY HOLD — the decision about how the time is split between formal and informal contact, within the standard.

WHY THAT SPLIT — knowing the entitlement is your job and no one else will do it for you. How the time is delivered depends on the supervisor's diary and service, so the shape is agreed, not dictated.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — state the entitlement yourself in the contract meeting, citing 3.3.9, and propose how the two weekly hours will be made up, with your supervisor responding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — apologetic framing ('I know you're busy, but…') that makes the standard sound optional, or the opposite — reading it out like a grievance before any problem exists.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you're right, that's the figure — let's write down what counts as the informal hour so neither of us has to guess later.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — carry the figure and the source in your head, apply it to whatever days-per-week pattern you are on, and use it calmly the first time the hour moves, without needing to look it up.

PASS TEST — You can state it if the hour slips

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the signed contract recording the entitlement and how it will be met; running totals on the supervision records. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — reaching December unable to say whether the standard was met, because you never knew the figure and never counted.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a first-year peer where the figure comes from, how to convert it for a three-, four- or five-day pattern, why informal contact counts only if it is recorded, and why quoting a standard is less awkward than making a request.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the total falls short: raise it with the figure and the dates in hand, propose a make-up plan, and if it persists, use the UCD route for placement concerns — read the Handbook for the route itself.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating supervision time as whatever the supervisor can spare rather than as a stated, countable standard.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record day, time, duration and format', 'Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively', and 'Raise it if it slips twice'.

Notice whether they count informal contact (a call after a visit, a drive to a school) as supervision or treat only the booked hour as real.

micro.name: Know the four components expected
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Supervision is not one thing. The pass test names four components — educative, supportive, evaluative and safeguarding — mapped here to Handbook §6.1; read that section yourself for UCD's exact wording. They echo Proctor's (1986) formative, restorative and normative functions and Kadushin's (1976) educational, supportive and administrative ones. A trainee who knows only the educative strand accepts sessions that never check her wellbeing, never give her a judgement of her standard, and never look at risk.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which component each part of a session is actually doing: teaching you something (educative), attending to how you are coping (supportive), telling you where your work stands (evaluative), or checking that clients and you are safe (safeguarding). Notice which your supervisor defaults to and which rarely appears.

WRITE DOWN — one example of each from the first sessions, with the component label.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which of the four do you find hardest to fit into an hour, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the four components into the draft contract with one line each on what they will look like in practice, and noting Proctor's (1986) three functions alongside as the underlying model.

THEY HOLD — the evaluative component — the judgement of your competence that feeds the mid-placement review and written feedback.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you can name and ask for all four. Evaluation is the one that is genuinely theirs: it is the gatekeeping part of the role, and a trainee cannot evaluate herself on the supervisor's behalf.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — in the contract meeting, walk through the four components and agree how each will be met over the placement, with your supervisor adding or amending.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — reciting labels without being able to say what each looks like in an EP service, and folding safeguarding into 'supportive' when it is about the child, not about you.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'give me an example of what safeguarding in supervision would look like for a school visit next month.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — name the four components without prompting, give a practice example of each, and use them to notice when supervision has run on one strand for weeks.

PASS TEST — Educative, supportive, evaluative, safeguarding

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the contract listing the four components; component tags on each supervision record. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a run of records that are all educative case discussion, no evaluative feedback until the mid-placement review surprises you, and no safeguarding item logged in a term of school visits.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the four components, map them roughly onto Proctor (1986) and Kadushin (1976) — noting the mapping is approximate, not one-to-one — and show why safeguarding and evaluation protect clients and the profession, not just the trainee.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when one component is missing: name it on the next agenda ('I'd like some evaluative feedback on my report writing'), rather than waiting for the review.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Knowing only the teaching function of supervision, so the evaluative and safeguarding components go missing unnoticed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Tag which of the four components the session covered', 'Take the weekly supervision hour', and 7. Supervision competency evidence.

micro.name: Bring a draft to week one
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet's point: signing in week one is the only moment when asking for something feels normal rather than like a complaint. Arriving with a draft means the conversation is about your terms rather than a template you skim and sign. Scaife (2019, Supervision in Clinical Practice, 3rd ed.) and Page and Wosket (Supervising the Counsellor and Psychotherapist, 3rd ed., 2015) both treat contracting as the first stage of supervision, not an administrative extra. With nothing prepared, the default fills the gap.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor responds to a trainee who arrives with a draft versus one who arrives empty-handed: which items they accept without discussion, which they amend, and which they add that you did not think of (usually cover arrangements and out-of-hours contact).

WRITE DOWN — every item they added or changed, and the reason given.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do trainees usually leave out of a first contract that causes trouble in the second month?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting it before week one: entitlement (3.3.9), four components, day and time, cancellations, out-of-session contact, leave cover, disagreement, records and who holds them, observation dates, any adjustments you want in writing.

THEY HOLD — service-specific items you cannot know: cover within the Cavan team, local protocols, diary constraints.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the draft shows you know the standard; the service detail is theirs, and a contract that ignores it will not survive the term.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the week-one meeting from your draft, item by item, and agree amendments on the page, with your supervisor responding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a draft so rigid it reads as distrust, or so thin it is a template with names added. Also watch for leaving out the Table 3 Early Years and Young Adult bands and PSI 3.3.6 special-setting visits, which belong in the Appendix 1 conversation at the same meeting.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this is good — can we leave the observation dates until I've seen the diary, but agree a week for each now?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — produce a first draft for any new placement without being asked, tailored to that service, and use it to structure the first supervision meeting.

PASS TEST — You arrived with something

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the draft (dated) and the signed final version, so the changes are visible; a supervision record for the contracting session. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — signing the service's standard form in week three, after casework has started, with 'weekly' as the only commitment and no observation dates.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why contracting comes first in the supervision literature (Scaife, 2019; Page & Wosket, 2015), which items prevent the common breakdowns, and why a new supervisor means a new contract — the Roscommon arrangement does not carry over.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do if week one passes without a contract: raise it at the next meeting, bring the draft, and do not start new casework on an unwritten arrangement if you can avoid it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Arriving in week one with nothing and signing whatever template the service uses.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record day, time, duration and format', 'Agree how cancellations are handled', and 'Arrange it in the first weeks' (observation).

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor responds to a trainee who arrives with a draft versus one who arrives empty-handed: which items they accept without discussion, which they amend, and which they add that you did not think of (usually cover arrangements and out-of-hours contact).

micro.name: Record day, time, duration and format
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
'Weekly' is not a commitment; 'Tuesday 10:00–11:00, in person, at the service base' is. The Reference sheet lists writing 'weekly' as a named error: an unspecified hour is the first thing to move when the caseload grows, and there is nothing to point to when it does. Carroll (2014, Effective Supervision for the Helping Professions, 2nd ed.) places responsibility for the structure of supervision partly on the supervisee. Vague terms protect neither of you.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor's week is actually shaped: which days they are in schools, which are admin or team days, and when they are least likely to be called away. Notice whether they propose a slot that is realistic or one that is ideal.

WRITE DOWN — the proposed day, start and end time, whether it is in person, online or phone, and the location.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which slot in your week has survived best with other trainees, and which has always been eaten?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — proposing two or three specific slots that fit your placement days, avoiding the last hour of the day, and writing the agreed one into the contract in full.

THEY HOLD — the final choice, since their diary carries more constraints than yours.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you bring options so the decision is quick and specific. They choose because a slot they cannot protect will fail, however well you have drafted it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — put the specifics into the contract yourself, read them back, and set the recurring calendar invitation from your side the same day, with your supervisor confirming.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'as arranged', 'weekly', or 'Tuesdays' with no time; a slot at the end of a school day; online by default when in person is available and better for the difficult items.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'let's not put it at four — that's when the phone calls come. Can you do Tuesday morning?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — write every supervision arrangement with day, time, duration, format and location, and put it in both calendars as a recurring appointment before you leave the room.

PASS TEST — Specific, not 'as arranged'

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the signed contract; a recurring calendar entry; supervision records showing the agreed slot was used. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a contract that says 'weekly supervision as arranged', and by November you cannot say when the last formal hour was.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why specificity is what makes the hour defensible, why the end-of-day slot fails, and why format matters (in-person sessions tend to be where the harder items get raised — your experience, not a research claim).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the agreed slot proves unworkable: renegotiate a new specific slot and amend the contract, rather than drifting into 'whenever suits'.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'weekly' or 'as arranged' instead of a named day, time, duration and format.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Protect the hour', 'Agree how cancellations are handled', and 'Send it the day before'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor's week is actually shaped: which days they are in schools, which are admin or team days, and when they are least likely to be called away. Notice whether they propose a slot that is realistic or one that is ideal.

micro.name: Agree how cancellations are handled
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Supervision is rarely lost in one decision; the Reference sheet describes it going gradually — moved once, shortened, merged into a car journey. A cancellation clause stops that drift by deciding in advance who rearranges and by when. PSI Supervision Guidelines (2024) are mapped here; read them for the wording. The Reference sheet's rule is that a missed hour is rescheduled within the same week, not dropped. Without that, each cancellation is negotiated from scratch, and the trainee usually concedes.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what actually happens when your supervisor's day is disrupted: do they rebook the hour on the spot, leave it to you, or let it lapse? Notice whether trainee-initiated and supervisor-initiated cancellations are treated the same.

WRITE DOWN — the rule you agree: who rearranges, the deadline for the replacement, and what happens if it cannot be found.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when you've had to cancel before, what made it easy or hard to put the hour back?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting a clause naming who rebooks (whoever cancels, or always you), the window (same week), and the fallback (a phone session rather than nothing).

THEY HOLD — agreement on what counts as a legitimate reason to move it, and on cover when they are on leave.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the mechanics are yours to propose. Cover arrangements depend on the team, and only the supervisor can commit a colleague.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise cancellations as a contract item, propose your clause, and agree it in writing, with your supervisor amending.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a clause that only binds the supervisor (which reads as mistrust), or one with no deadline ('we'll rearrange') that permits drift.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'whoever cancels books the replacement before the end of the same day — does that work for you?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — apply the clause every time without it becoming a confrontation: when the hour is cancelled, reply the same day with two replacement slots in the same week, and log the change.

PASS TEST — Who rearranges, and by when

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the clause in the signed contract; supervision records noting rescheduled sessions with original and new dates (DD/MM/YYYY). Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — three cancelled hours in a term, none replaced, and no record that they were ever due.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why the cancellation clause is the part of the contract that does most work, how to draft one that binds both people, and how the record of rescheduled sessions becomes evidence of the 3.3.9 total.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the clause is ignored: name it at the next session with dates, and if it continues, follow 'Raise it if it slips twice'.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Agreeing 'we'll rearrange' with no named person and no deadline.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Protect the hour', 'Raise it if it slips twice', and 'Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — what actually happens when your supervisor's day is disrupted: do they rebook the hour on the spot, leave it to you, or let it lapse? Notice whether trainee-initiated and supervisor-initiated cancellations are treated the same.

micro.name: Both sign and date it
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
An unsigned contract is a draft, and a draft carries no weight when you need to point to it. The row maps this to Handbook Appendix 8; check which form UCD expects the signed contract on. Signing and dating makes the agreement visible to UCD if a problem arises later. The Reference sheet's Appendix 4 lesson applies directly: an 84-day log still waiting for countersignature is the position a same-day signature avoids.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor treats signing as a formality at the end or as the moment the agreement becomes real, and whether they keep a copy themselves.

WRITE DOWN — the date signed, where each copy is held, and whether UCD needs a copy and by when (check the Handbook; do not assume).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'have you ever had to go back to a signed contract with a trainee, and what did it settle?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing the final version with all agreed amendments incorporated, bringing two copies (or a signable digital version), and filing yours the same day.

THEY HOLD — their signature and their copy, and any service-level sign-off their line manager requires.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the administration is yours because you carry the consequence if it is missing. Any internal service approval is outside your reach.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close the contracting meeting by reading back the final terms, signing and dating it together, and confirming where the copies go, with your supervisor present.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'I'll sign it later' left open, undated signatures, a signed version that differs from what was agreed, and no copy kept.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'print it now and we'll both sign before you go — otherwise it'll sit in my inbox.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — ensure every placement contract is signed and dated by both of you in the first week, in DD/MM/YYYY, with a copy filed where you and UCD can find it.

PASS TEST — It is signed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the signed and dated contract in your placement folder; a supervision record for the session in which it was signed. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an unsigned Word document in your email drafts in March, when you need it to show what was agreed about the hour or the observations.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why signature and date matter (evidence, accountability, a fixed point for review), why the same-day habit applies to Appendix 4 and every other countersigned form, and why the contract should be revisited at the mid-placement review.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do if it was never signed: get it signed now with the actual date, not backdated, and note in the record that it was signed late.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving the contract unsigned 'for later', so it cannot be relied on when it is needed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Get them co-signed', 'Protect the hour', and the mid-placement review.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Protect the hour
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet calls the weekly hour the single most protective thing in the placement and the first to disappear. It is where you find out what you did not know you did not know. PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 is mapped here. The hour goes by small erosions, and each one feels reasonable; a trainee who does not guard it structurally will find in December that it has not been happening and nobody said so.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor does to keep the hour intact: phone off, door closed, not taking calls, starting on time. Notice what they treat as a legitimate reason to interrupt it (a child protection matter) and what they defer.

WRITE DOWN — for each week, whether the hour happened, its actual length, and anything that cut into it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the thing that most often takes supervision time away from you, and how do you stop it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping the recurring calendar entry, confirming the room, arriving on time with the agenda sent, and rebooking at once when it moves.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether a genuine emergency overrides the hour on the day.

WHY THAT SPLIT — most of protecting the hour is logistics, and a trainee who manages them removes most of the reasons it slips. Judging a service emergency requires authority and information you do not have.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — manage the weekly hour yourself: calendar, room, agenda, start and finish, with your supervisor attending.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — accepting moves without rebooking, letting it become the last slot of the day, and filling it with updates that could have been an email so it feels dispensable.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'we've moved this three times — let's find a slot we can both actually keep.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep the hour happening weekly across the placement, rebook within the week when it moves, and keep it for supervision rather than case management.

PASS TEST — It happened

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a supervision record for every session held, with date and duration; rescheduled sessions noted. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — records for six sessions in an eleven-week placement, with no note of why the others did not happen.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how the hour erodes (moved, shortened, merged into a journey), the structural protections that stop it, and why keeping it is part of ethical practice rather than a personal preference.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when it has lapsed: count the missed sessions with dates, raise it functionally at the next contact, and agree a make-up plan in writing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Letting the hour move, shrink or merge into other contact without rebooking it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Raise it if it slips twice', 'Complete a record for every session', and 'Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
