micro.name: Raise it if it slips twice
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet's rule: cancelled twice in a row is a pattern, and you name it at the next session. PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 makes supervision a requirement of the programme, not a courtesy; read the standard so you can say so accurately. Supervision can be insufficient without anyone behaving badly — a stretched service, a supervisor across too many schools. Trainees often decide the shortfall is their fault for needing too much and wait until the end, when nothing can be fixed.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor responds when a pattern is named: whether they treat it as information to act on or as criticism. Notice how they talk about supervision shortfalls in their own work, if they do.

WRITE DOWN — dates of the sessions that did not happen, the reason if given, and what was agreed when you raised it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if supervision started slipping with a trainee, how would you want them to tell you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping the count, and raising it yourself in functional terms at the next contact: 'we've had two of the last four sessions — can we look at how to protect it?'

THEY HOLD — the fix inside the service, and any conversation with their manager about capacity.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you are the person who notices first and whose placement depends on it. The remedy often sits with workload and staffing, which only the supervisor can address.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise the slippage at the start of the next session, with dates, and propose a remedy, with your supervisor responding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — apologising for raising it, framing it as a complaint about them rather than a problem to solve together, or not naming the standard at all.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'thanks for saying it — you're right, and it's a requirement. Let's book the next four now.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — raise any second consecutive miss at the next contact, calmly, with dates and the standard; if it does not change, contact UCD placement staff through the route the Handbook sets out (read §6.4.3 for the route yourself).

PASS TEST — It is a requirement, not a courtesy

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision records noting the missed dates and the conversation; any email to UCD kept. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — telling your tutor at the end-of-placement review that supervision 'hadn't really happened since November'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the second miss is the trigger, how to raise it without blame, why using the UCD route is not disloyalty (the Reference sheet's point), and why waiting harms the children on your caseload as well as you.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when raising it changes nothing: document, contact UCD, and keep practising safely — which may mean holding back from new complex work until supervision is back.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Deciding a supervision shortfall is your fault for needing too much, and saying nothing until the end.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively', 6. Ethical Practice (working within competence), and the mid-placement review.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

micro.name: Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet summarises PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 as thirty minutes per placement day; read the standard itself. At four days a week that is two hours weekly: the formal hour plus an hour of informal contact — corridor conversations, a call after a difficult visit, a joint drive to a school. The informal hour is real supervision but only counts if it is logged. At the end of placement the log is the evidence the standard was met.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the informal supervision that happens around the formal hour: advice in the car, a phone call after a feedback meeting, a quick check before a consultation. Notice how much of your learning happens there.

WRITE DOWN — each informal contact the same day: date, minutes, format, topic in a line.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'would you count that conversation in the car as supervision? What would make it count?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping a running cumulative total: placement days to date × 30 minutes against minutes logged, formal and informal, updated weekly.

THEY HOLD — agreement that a given informal contact was supervision, confirmed by their countersignature on the records.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the arithmetic is yours and takes a minute a week. Only the supervisor can confirm that a conversation was supervision rather than chat, which is why records need their signature.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring the running total to supervision monthly and state where it stands, with your supervisor checking it against their own recollection.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — counting every conversation generously, or the opposite — logging only the formal hour and showing a shortfall that did not exist.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that phone call was ten minutes of logistics, not supervision — don't count it. The drive to the school was, though.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep a cumulative total from day one, know at any point whether you are ahead or behind, and act before the gap is too big to close.

PASS TEST — You track the total

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision records for formal and informal contact with minutes; a running total you can show on request. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an end-of-placement claim that the standard was met, with records showing only the formal hours and no way to evidence the rest.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to calculate the requirement for any days-per-week pattern, what informal contact legitimately counts, and why the record rather than the memory is what evidences the standard.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do if the total falls behind: show the figures, propose added sessions, and raise it early through 'Raise it if it slips twice' rather than at the final review.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Not logging the informal contact, then being unable to show the standard was met.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Complete a record for every session', 'Get them co-signed', and the end-of-placement review.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the informal supervision that happens around the formal hour: advice in the car, a phone call after a feedback meeting, a quick check before a consultation. Notice how much of your learning happens there.

micro.name: Send it the day before
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
An agenda sent the day before means your supervisor arrives having thought about your questions, and the hour starts at the substance. Sending it as you walk in removes the only benefit, as the Reference sheet notes. It also leaves a dated, searchable record of what you raised and when, which matters if a concern later turns out to have been raised early. Handbook §6.2 is mapped here; read it for UCD's expectation. Carroll (2014) places this responsibility with the supervisee.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor uses an agenda that arrives in advance: do they come with a view, a resource, or a question back? Compare a session where they had it the day before with one where they saw it on arrival.

WRITE DOWN — when you sent it, whether they had read it, and what difference it made to the first ten minutes.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'is the day before enough notice for you, or would another time work better for you to think about it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing and sending the agenda by email at a fixed time the day before, every week, as a fifteen-minute habit.

THEY HOLD — adding their own items, and deciding whether anything on yours needs to move earlier (a risk item should not wait for Tuesday).

WHY THAT SPLIT — the habit is entirely yours. The supervisor may know that an item needs action sooner than the hour, and advance notice gives them the chance to say so.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — send the agenda the day before each session for several weeks, with your supervisor responding by email or at the start of the session.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — agendas that drift to the morning of the session, then to arrival; and urgent items (a safeguarding concern) held for the agenda when they needed action that day.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'item two shouldn't have waited for supervision — ring me the same day next time.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — send an agenda the day before every supervision session, at a regular time, by email so it is timestamped, and act on anything urgent immediately rather than parking it.

PASS TEST — In advance, not on arrival

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the sent agendas in a dedicated email folder; agenda items reflected in the supervision record. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an agenda typed on your phone in the car park, which your supervisor reads for the first time while you wait.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why advance notice changes the quality of the hour, why email beats a verbal list (timestamp, record), and where the line sits between an agenda item and something that needs action now.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do in a week you miss it: send a short agenda as early as you can, and never hold a child protection concern for supervision — report to Tusla as soon as practicable, then bring it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Sending the agenda as you walk in, which removes the only benefit.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Keep it to three items', 'Update on actions agreed last time', and 'Record topics, actions and who does what'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Keep it to three items
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: an hour holds roughly three substantive items, not eight. Ten items turn supervision into a list read aloud and push the difficult item off the end. Good items share a shape — you have already thought about them and got stuck — and priority order means that if time runs out, you lose the least important thing. Handbook §6.2 is mapped here. Case updates that could be an email should be an email.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how long a single substantive item actually takes in your supervisor's sessions, and what happens to the items at the bottom of a long list.

WRITE DOWN — for each session, how many items were covered in depth, and which were rushed or dropped.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when a trainee brings a long list, which items do you wish they'd sent by email instead?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing three items the day before: one case you are stuck on, one thing you did that you are unsure about, one forward-looking item — each a line, in priority order, with updates moved to email.

THEY HOLD — the right to reorder or swap an item if something more pressing needs the time.

WHY THAT SPLIT — selection is the skill you are building. The supervisor may see a risk or priority you cannot, which is a reason to let them move items, not to add more.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring a three-item agenda each week and keep the session to it, with your supervisor following your lead.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — items that are status updates ('case update'), items with no thinking behind them, and a list that quietly grows back to six.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's the actual question on item one? Tell me the two options you're stuck between.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — produce a focused agenda every week: three items, each showing your prior thinking and the question you want answered, updates handled elsewhere.

PASS TEST — Focused

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the sent agendas; supervision records showing each item discussed in depth, with cases identified by reference number only. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an eight-item agenda where item eight, the one you were worried about, is 'if we have time' and never happens.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the three-item shape, how to turn 'case update' into a real question ('two competing formulations — which does the data support?'), and why the limit is what protects the difficult item.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when more than three things genuinely need supervision: prioritise, email the rest, and ask for extra time rather than squeezing.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Bringing a long list of status updates so the hour becomes a list read aloud.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT

micro.name: Update on actions agreed last time
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: end the agenda with last week's actions and their status, in two lines. It makes the sessions cumulative rather than a series of unconnected hours, and it produces the record of change that your reflections and the reflective essay draw on. Handbook §6.2 is mapped here. Without the loop, actions agreed in supervision quietly lapse, and the same problem returns three weeks later as if new.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor refers back to what was agreed last time, and how they respond when an action was not done — curiosity about why, or moving on.

WRITE DOWN — the actions from each session in a running list with owner and due date, and their status the following week.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when an action from supervision doesn't get done, what does that usually tell you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping the running action list, and adding a short 'Last time' section to each agenda: action, owner, done / partly / not, and one line on why.

THEY HOLD — their own actions (a resource, a phone call, a decision) and accountability for those.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the tracking is yours because it is your development being recorded. The supervisor's actions stay theirs, but listing them keeps both sides honest.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — open or close each session with the action update, spending no more than a few minutes on it, with your supervisor listening.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — actions marked 'done' that were half done, undone actions carried forward week after week without comment, and actions too vague to judge.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'that's been on the list three weeks — what's actually in the way?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — carry every action from one session into the next agenda, report its status honestly, and treat a repeatedly undone action as an item worth discussing.

PASS TEST — You closed the loop

EVIDENCE TO FILE — agendas with a 'Last time' section; supervision records whose actions match the next agenda. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a term of records with actions that are never mentioned again, so no one can tell what changed as a result of supervision.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why closing the loop makes supervision cumulative, how a run of action updates becomes evidence of development over the placement, and why a stuck action is information rather than failure.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when actions keep slipping: check whether they were too big, too vague, or the wrong action, and redesign them in the session.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Never referring back to last week's actions, so nothing accumulates.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record topics, actions and who does what', the reflective essay (hers to write), and the mid-placement review.

micro.name: Include at least one thing that went badly
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: the item you are avoiding is almost always the highest-value item. CORU SoP 4.3 and PSI Code 4.1.2 are mapped here — read both for their exact wording. Ladany, Hill, Corbett and Nutt (1996, Journal of Counseling Psychology) found supervisees commonly withhold material from supervisors, including clinical mistakes; read the paper for the figures. Unwritten, the difficult item will not survive the first twenty minutes.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor responds when you or another trainee brings a mistake: whether they get curious, reassure too fast, or move straight to fixing. Notice whether they ever describe something of their own that went badly.

WRITE DOWN — what made it easier or harder to raise, in your own notes only.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's something that went badly early in your career that supervision helped you with?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — putting one thing that went badly on the agenda in writing each week — a subtest mis-administered, a feedback meeting that landed badly, a decision you are unsure of — stated plainly without self-criticism.

THEY HOLD — deciding whether it needs action beyond supervision (correcting a report, contacting a family, reporting).

WHY THAT SPLIT — naming it is your responsibility and the core of reflective practice. Whether it has consequences for a client is a professional judgement the supervisor is accountable for.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — raise the difficult item yourself, early in the session rather than at the end, with your supervisor responding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — leaving it until the last five minutes, softening it until it is not recognisable, or only ever bringing minor errors while the real one stays off the list.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'let's take that one first — tell me exactly what happened, not what you should have done.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — include at least one thing that went badly on every agenda, raise it without being prompted, and follow through on whatever it needs.

PASS TEST — Not only successes

EVIDENCE TO FILE — agendas showing the item; supervision records noting what was discussed and decided; your reflection on it (yours to write — prompts only here). Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a term of agendas that read like a success log, and a mid-placement review that raises a problem you never brought.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why non-disclosure undermines supervision (Ladany et al., 1996 — check the details in the source), why a written item is more likely to be raised, and how naming mistakes protects clients.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do if something serious went badly — a missed safeguarding concern — act first (Tusla as soon as practicable; the DLP does not discharge your duty), then bring it; supervision follows action, never replaces it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Omitting the difficult item from the agenda and then not raising it.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record any ethical dilemma using the seven steps', 6. Ethical Practice, and the reflective essay (hers to write).

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Complete a record for every session
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet treats the supervision record (Appendix 8) as both assessed and the only proof that the supervision standard was met. Written on the day it takes about ten minutes; reconstructed in June it is visibly reconstructed. The pass test's figure — nineteen for a 75-day placement — is roughly one per week of a four-day pattern; count your own placement weeks rather than assuming. Missing records leave no evidence that supervision happened.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor keeps their own note of sessions, what they record, and how quickly after the session they write it.

WRITE DOWN — a list of all expected sessions for the placement (one per placement week), ticked off as each record is completed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's in your supervision notes that isn't in mine, and should it be?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing every record within the day: date (DD/MM/YYYY), duration, format, who was present, items discussed, decisions, actions.

THEY HOLD — checking the record is accurate, correcting anything they would put differently, and countersigning.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the record is yours because it is your evidence and your learning. The supervisor's check is what makes it a shared account rather than one person's memory.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — complete the record after each session and send or show it to your supervisor within the week, with them reading and correcting.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — records that slip to Friday, then to 'batch them later'; records so brief they could describe any session; and informal contact never recorded.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I haven't seen last week's or the week before — let's do them now before we start.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep a complete, same-day set of records for every formal session and logged informal contact across the placement, so the count matches the weeks.

PASS TEST — 19 for a 75-day placement

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the full set of records in date order on the supervision record form (Appendix 8). Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — eleven records for a nineteen-week placement, several in identical wording, written the same week in June.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to calculate the expected number for any placement length and pattern, why same-day records are more accurate and more credible, and how the sequence becomes evidence of development.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when records are missing: write them now from agendas and emails, marked honestly as written late with the date written, and never present them as contemporaneous.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing records up in bulk at the end of placement, so they are visibly reconstructed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Get them co-signed', 'Keep to 30 minutes per placement day cumulatively', and the reflective essay (hers to write).

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor keeps their own note of sessions, what they record, and how quickly after the session they write it.

micro.name: Record topics, actions and who does what
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet's error: recording what was discussed but not what was decided. A record of topics shows supervision happened; a record of decisions and named actions shows it changed something. Handbook §6.1 is mapped here. Vague actions ('think about the case') cannot be checked the following week, and a disputed recollection of who agreed to do what is exactly what a specific record prevents. Cases are identified by reference number, never by name.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor closes each item: do they summarise the decision and who does what, or does the conversation move on without one?

WRITE DOWN — for each item: the question, the decision, who does what, and by when (DD/MM/YYYY).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'can we agree the actions out loud at the end, so we both write the same thing?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading back the actions in the last five minutes and writing them into the record with owner and date; asking for a short email of agreed actions if that helps you (a reasonable workflow request, as the Reference sheet puts it).

THEY HOLD — decisions that are theirs to make (case allocation, whether to contact a family, risk) and their own actions.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing it down is yours. Who decides is part of the record: a supervisor's decision recorded as yours, or vice versa, causes problems later.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — close each session by reading the actions back and write the record the same day, with your supervisor confirming.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — actions with no owner, no date, or no verb you can check ('consider', 'reflect on'); children named instead of referenced; third-party detail that belongs in the case file.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — ''look into it' isn't an action — what will you actually do, and by when?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — produce records where every item has a decision or an explicit 'no decision yet', and every action has an owner, a checkable verb and a date.

PASS TEST — Actions are specific

EVIDENCE TO FILE — supervision records (Appendix 8) with an actions section; the next agenda's 'Last time' update. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a record reading 'discussed case, discussed report, discussed wellbeing' with nothing decided and nothing to follow up.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between a topic record and a decision record, what makes an action specific, and what must not go into supervision records (names, third-party detail, personal health detail — PSI Code 1.2.6 and 1.2.8 as mapped on the Reference sheet).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you and your supervisor remember a decision differently: go back to the record, correct it together, and agree to read back actions in future.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording what was discussed but not what was decided, or by whom.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Update on actions agreed last time', 'Get them co-signed', and 7. Supervision evidence.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor closes each item: do they summarise the decision and who does what, or does the conversation move on without one?

micro.name: Get them co-signed
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A record signed by both people is evidence; one written only by the trainee is a claim. The Reference sheet's advice is to get records signed periodically rather than all at the end: a signature each month is administration, a run of unsigned records in June is a problem. The row maps this to Handbook Appendix 8. The Appendix 4 lesson applies — an 84-day log still awaiting countersignature is exactly the position to avoid repeating.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor handles paperwork: do they sign on the spot, take things away, or need reminders? Notice what they check before signing.

WRITE DOWN — the date each record was signed, and which records are outstanding.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'would it be easier for you to sign records monthly at the end of a session, or as I send them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping a signature tracker, bringing unsigned records to supervision at a fixed interval (monthly works), and making signing take two minutes.

THEY HOLD — the signature, and any corrections before they sign.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you carry the consequence if signatures are missing, so the administration is yours. The signature is theirs because it confirms the account is accurate — they should not sign what they have not read.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — set a monthly signing point in the contract or diary and bring the records, with your supervisor reading and signing in the session.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — waiting to be asked, bringing a large bundle at once, or records the supervisor disagrees with presented for signature without discussion.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'leave these with me' — and you agreeing a date by which you'll collect them.

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — keep every record countersigned within about a month of the session, with no backlog at the end of placement, and chase outstanding signatures without awkwardness.

PASS TEST — Signed, not just written

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the countersigned supervision records (Appendix 8); your signature tracker. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the last week of placement with twelve unsigned records and a supervisor on leave.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why countersignature matters (shared accountability, evidential weight), why monthly beats final-week, and how the same habit applies to Appendix 4 and Appendix 7.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when signatures are outstanding at the end: list them, agree a date with your supervisor, tell UCD if they cannot be obtained, and do not sign on anyone's behalf.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving all countersignature to the final week.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Complete a record for every session', the end-of-placement submission, and the Appendix 4 countersignature habit.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Tag which of the four components the session covered
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The pass test's shorthand — E, S, Ev, Sg — tags each record as educative, supportive, evaluative or safeguarding (Handbook §6.1 is mapped here; check its wording). Tagging costs nothing at the time and means that in December you can see by filtering whether you ever had evaluative feedback or safeguarding discussion. The Reference sheet makes the same point for competency tags: supervision is evidence, not just support. Untagged, a gap stays invisible.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which components each session actually covered, as opposed to what the agenda intended. A session about a report can be educative and evaluative; one after a difficult visit can be supportive and safeguarding.

WRITE DOWN — the tags on each record, and the competency tags (1–8) alongside.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'looking at this month's tags, which component have we under-done?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — tagging each record with the components and the competencies it touched, and reviewing the pattern monthly.

THEY HOLD — confirming or amending the tags when they countersign, particularly Ev, since that is their judgement.

WHY THAT SPLIT — tagging is a quick self-audit you can do alone. The supervisor's check stops you tagging a session as evaluative when no evaluation of your standard was actually given.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — tag each record and bring a monthly tally to supervision, with your supervisor reviewing the balance.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — every session tagged with all four (which means the tags mean nothing), or a month with no Sg tag in a caseload of school visits.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I wouldn't call that session evaluative — I didn't give you a view on your standard. Let's do that next time.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — tag every record accurately, notice when a component has been absent for several weeks, and put it on the next agenda.

PASS TEST — E, S, Ev, Sg

EVIDENCE TO FILE — tagged supervision records (Appendix 8); a monthly tally. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — records with no tags, or all four on every record, and no way to show what kind of supervision you received.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the four components, how they relate to Proctor's (1986) normative, formative and restorative functions (approximately), and how tagging turns records into an audit of the supervision itself.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the tally shows a gap: name the missing component on the next agenda with a specific request.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Tagging every session with all four components so the tags show nothing.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know the four components expected', 'Prepare and send an agenda in advance', and 7. Supervision evidence.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Record any ethical dilemma using the seven steps
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
PSI Code of Professional Ethics (2025) Appendix A sets out a seven-step ethical decision-making procedure, and the Reference sheet maps PSI 3.6.1 as requiring a systematic procedure; copy the step wording from the Code (reproduced on the Reference sheet), not from memory. The Reference sheet's point: a single well-written dilemma entry is worth more than twenty routine records, and Ethical Practice is hard to evidence any other way. A dilemma recorded as 'discussed a tricky case' shows no reasoning.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor reasons through a dilemma aloud: do they identify who is affected, name the clauses in tension, generate more than one option? Notice which Appendix A steps they do intuitively and which they skip.

WRITE DOWN — the dilemma in one sentence without identifying details, then each step as it is discussed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which step do you think trainees most often skip, and what does it cost?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the dilemma entry using all seven Appendix A step headings, filling in your reasoning at each, cases by reference number only.

THEY HOLD — the decision where the case is theirs, and any action that must happen outside supervision.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the structured reasoning is yours to practise and evidence. Where a dilemma involves child protection, the action is not a supervision matter: report to Tusla as soon as practicable, and telling the DLP does not discharge your duty. Supervision follows action.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — bring a dilemma to supervision, work it through the seven steps yourself, and write the entry, with your supervisor challenging each step.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — jumping from the problem to the decision, only one option generated, clauses named without saying what they require, and no record of the outcome.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've told me what you did. What else could you have done, and which clause would each option have honoured?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — recognise a dilemma when it arises, record it through all seven steps, and complete the entry once the outcome is known.

PASS TEST — All seven, from PSI Appendix A

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a dilemma entry in the supervision records (Appendix 8), countersigned; any reflection on it is yours to write. Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an entry that states the problem and what you decided, with steps three to six missing and no Code clause named.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can walk a peer through the Appendix A steps using an anonymised example, explain why generating options matters more than the decision, and explain why a safeguarding concern is acted on first and recorded after.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a dilemma entry reveals a poor decision: record it honestly, note what you would do differently, and discuss any remedial action with your supervisor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording a dilemma as a problem and a decision with none of the reasoning steps between them.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 6. Ethical Practice evidence, 'Include at least one thing that went badly', and the reflective essay (hers to write).

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor reasons through a dilemma aloud: do they identify who is affected, name the clauses in tension, generate more than one option? Notice which Appendix A steps they do intuitively and which they skip.

micro.name: Arrange it in the first weeks
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet summarises PSI Accreditation 3.3.9 as requiring observation in both directions; trainees routinely complete being observed and skip observing. Handbook §6.2 is mapped here. Asking vaguely ('could I observe you sometime?') produces agreement and no date. Family consent must be arranged by your supervisor, so it needs time. Left to the end of the Cavan placement (to 18/12/2026), it will not happen.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which parts of your supervisor's diary in the first weeks offer good observation opportunities: a feedback meeting, a consultation, a first meeting with a wary parent, a session in a special setting.

WRITE DOWN — two or three candidate events with dates, and what you would learn from each.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which kind of meeting do you think I'd learn most from watching you in at this stage?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — asking in week one for a specific kind of event, writing agreed dates into the contract, and linking one where possible to a special-education setting to help with PSI 3.3.6.

THEY HOLD — choosing the case, seeking family and school consent, and deciding whether your presence is appropriate.

WHY THAT SPLIT — asking early and specifically is yours. Consent and suitability are the supervisor's professional responsibility to the family.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — make the request in the contracting meeting with specific events in mind, and follow up until a date is in the diary, with your supervisor arranging consent.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — vague requests, waiting to be offered, and leaving it until the final month.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I've a feedback meeting on the third week — I'll ask the family this week, put it in your diary.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — arrange observations of your supervisor in the first weeks of every placement, with dates agreed and consent in hand before the caseload builds.

PASS TEST — Front-loaded, as the handbook expects

EVIDENCE TO FILE — observation dates in the signed contract; the Appendix 7 forms for each observation. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the last week of placement, no observation of your supervisor done, and one of the 3.3.9 requirements unmet.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why observation is front-loaded (you need the learning before you face the situation), how to ask specifically, and how to use observations to widen setting experience.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when a planned observation falls through: ask for the next similar event immediately, and if none arises, raise it as a requirement, not a favour.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking vaguely to observe 'sometime' and never getting a date.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Agree a focus before observing', PSI 3.3.6 setting coverage, and Appendix 7.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — which parts of your supervisor's diary in the first weeks offer good observation opportunities: a feedback meeting, a consultation, a first meeting with a wary parent, a session in a special setting.

micro.name: Agree a focus before observing
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: watch for process, not content. You already know what a standardised administration looks like; what you do not know is how they manage the room, the interruption, the run of wrong answers. CORU SoP 5.8 is mapped here — read it for its wording. Bandura's (1977, Social Learning Theory) account of observational learning puts attention first: without a focus, you watch everything and learn little.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moments linked to your agreed focus: how they open with a wary parent, what they say when a child refuses, how they decline to give a score on the day, how they close a meeting that has gone badly.

WRITE DOWN — the focus agreed beforehand, and every moment that relates to it, with verbatim phrases where possible.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'was that a typical example of how you handle that, or did something about this case change it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing a focus from your own development needs (supervision records and agendas will show them) and proposing it before the observation.

THEY HOLD — refining it to fit the event, and telling you if the case makes the focus inappropriate or unlikely to arise.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the focus should come from your learning needs, which you know. The supervisor knows the case and whether the moment you want to see is likely to happen.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — agree the focus with your supervisor before the observation, observe against it, and debrief against it, with them adjusting where needed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a focus so broad it is not a focus ('how you do assessments'), or one on content you already know rather than process.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you know the WISC — watch what I do when the parent starts to cry, if she does.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — set a specific, process-focused aim for every observation, tied to your development needs, and record against it.

PASS TEST — You knew what you were watching for

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the focus written on the Appendix 7 form before the observation; notes against it. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an Appendix 7 form that says 'observed an assessment, very useful' with nothing specific learned.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a focus matters (Bandura, 1977, on attention in observational learning), the difference between process and content, and how to choose a focus from your own records.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when the moment you wanted to see does not arise: observe what did happen, and ask your supervisor to talk you through how they would have handled the moment.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Watching the content you already know rather than the process you do not.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record what they did that you would not have' and 'Ask afterwards why they did it that way'.

WATCH FOR — the moments linked to your agreed focus: how they open with a wary parent, what they say when a child refuses, how they decline to give a score on the day, how they close a meeting that has gone badly.

micro.name: Record what they did that you would not have
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The value of observation lies in the gap between what you would have done and what an experienced practitioner did. General admiration ('she was very good with the parent') records nothing you can use. CORU SoP 4.3 is mapped here (read the clause for its wording). The Reference sheet advises writing verbatim phrases: the actual words someone uses to decline to give a score on the day are more useful than a principle about managing expectations.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moments where your supervisor made a choice you would not have: waited instead of speaking, sat beside rather than opposite, named a feeling, changed plan, stopped a task.

WRITE DOWN — the moment, what they did (verbatim phrases where possible), and what you would have done instead.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'I'd have kept going at that point — what made you stop?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the notes during or immediately after the observation, and completing your section of the Appendix 7 form on the day.

THEY HOLD — checking you have not recorded identifying detail about the family or child, and confirming your account of what happened.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the reflection is yours; no one else can say what you would have done. The supervisor protects the family's information, which your notes must respect.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — after the observation, write two or three specific differences between their practice and yours, and share them in the debrief, with your supervisor responding.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — notes that praise rather than analyse, notes that summarise the case, and identifying details in your record.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — ''good rapport' isn't a note — what exactly did I do in the first two minutes?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — record specific moments, verbatim where possible, where your supervisor's practice differed from what you would have done, and name what you will adopt.

PASS TEST — Specific, not general admiration

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your section of the Appendix 7 form, completed on the day (yours to write; prompts only here). Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an Appendix 7 section left blank until June, or completed with 'very informative, excellent rapport'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between admiration and analysis, why verbatim phrases are useful, and how to turn an observation into a technique you then use.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when you disagree with something you observed: note it, raise it respectfully in the debrief, and treat the answer as learning either way.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording general admiration instead of specific moments you would have handled differently.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Ask afterwards why they did it that way', Appendix 7, and the reflective essay (hers to write).

micro.name: Ask afterwards why they did it that way
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet: experienced practitioners make moves automatically and often have not put them into words until asked. Polanyi (1966, The Tacit Dimension) — 'we can know more than we can tell' — and Schön (1983, The Reflective Practitioner) on reflection-in-action describe the same gap. CORU SoP 4.5 is mapped here. If you do not ask, you copy the surface of what they did without the reasoning that makes it transferable.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the decision points: a change of tack, a pause before speaking, a question not asked, a task abandoned. These are the moments with reasoning behind them.

WRITE DOWN — two or three decision points, each as a question you want to ask ('you changed tack when she mentioned the older brother — what were you thinking?').

ASK AFTERWARDS — the questions you wrote down, starting with the one you are least sure about.

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — preparing the questions, booking ten minutes for the debrief the same day, and writing up the answers.

THEY HOLD — deciding how much of their reasoning about the case can be shared, particularly where it involves confidential family information.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the curiosity is yours. Some reasoning rests on information you are not party to, and the supervisor decides what can be said.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — lead the debrief with your questions, listen, and ask follow-ups, with your supervisor explaining.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — questions about content ('what score did he get?') instead of decisions, questions framed as criticism, and debriefs postponed until the detail has faded.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'good question — and what would you have done if I'd kept going?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — debrief every observation on the same day with specific questions about decisions, and record the reasoning you were given.

PASS TEST — You asked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the debrief notes on the Appendix 7 form; a supervision record if the debrief used supervision time. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an observation with no debrief, so you can describe what they did but not why.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the question is where the learning is (Polanyi, 1966; Schön, 1983), how to phrase it so it invites reasoning rather than defence, and how to use the answer.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you can say what to do when your supervisor cannot articulate why: ask what they noticed first, or what would have made them do it differently.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Not asking about the decisions you noticed, so you learn the what and not the why.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record what they did that you would not have', 7. Supervision, and your own practice in 5. Working with Others.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the decision points: a change of tack, a pause before speaking, a question not asked, a task abandoned. These are the moments with reasoning behind them.

micro.name: Arrange both observations early
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Observation is the only point at which your supervisor sees what you actually do rather than your account of it; every other supervision conversation passes through your own report. The UCD Handbook §6.2 is the reference mapped here — read it for the exact number and timing the programme sets rather than relying on this row. An observation in the last fortnight produces feedback you have no time left to act on, and the Appendix 7 form then records a comment with no follow-through.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor slots observations into the diary: which kinds of visit they think suit it (a consultation, a parent meeting, part of an assessment), and how much notice the school and family need so that consent for a second adult in the room is sought properly.

WRITE DOWN — the dates proposed, the activity, who has to agree to the observer being present, and where the Appendix 7 form will be kept.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when in a placement have you found observation most useful to a trainee, and why then?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — raising observation at the first supervision session, proposing two or more dates in the first month, and choosing an ordinary piece of work rather than a showcase.

THEY HOLD — the final choice of session, checking that consent for their presence is in place, and completing their half of Appendix 7.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the timing is your responsibility because an early observation serves your learning. Whether a given family or school can accommodate an observer is a service judgement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — book the first observation in the opening weeks of the Cavan placement (05/10/2026 onwards) and the second with enough weeks left to act on what comes out of it; put both in the supervision record.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — dates that keep sliding because 'the right case' has not come up, or an over-prepared session chosen to look polished.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the parent meeting on Tuesday is ordinary enough — shall I just come to that one?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — within the first month the first observation is booked and dated, the second is scheduled with time to act on it, and consent for the observer is arranged through the usual service route.

PASS TEST — Booked in the first month

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the dated booking in the supervision record, then the completed Appendix 7 forms. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — both observations crammed into the last fortnight in December, with no time to show any change in practice before the placement ends on 18/12/2026.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a newer trainee why the minimum is not a target, why early observation is worth more than polished observation, and how to ask for it in week one without it sounding like a request for approval.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — an observation is cancelled (child absent, school closure). Rebook at the same session, not 'when things settle'. Record the cancellation and new date in the supervision record so the gap is explained.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Waiting for the ideal case, so that both observations fall at the end of placement.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Request a focus you find hard', 'Act on the feedback and say so next time', and the Appendix 7 trainee section.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

WATCH FOR — how your supervisor slots observations into the diary: which kinds of visit they think suit it (a consultation, a parent meeting, part of an assessment), and how much notice the school and family need so that consent for a second adult in the room is sought properly.

micro.name: Request a focus you find hard
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Feedback is only as useful as the question it answers: 'any feedback welcome' tends to produce reassurance, while 'watch how I handle a parent who disagrees' produces something you can use. CORU SoP 4.5 is the standard mapped here — read its full text on the Reference sheet. Choosing a focus you find hard is also evidence that you are directing your own development. Being observed only on administration, where you are already fluent, wastes the one chance to have someone see your weak spot.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which parts of practice your supervisor finds hardest to teach by telling: managing a disagreement, pacing a feedback meeting, engaging a reluctant adolescent, handling silence. These are the areas where observation adds most.

WRITE DOWN — a short list of your own candidate focuses, ranked by how uncomfortable they make you, with one concrete behaviour for each that an observer could watch.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which part of my work do you think you'd learn most from seeing?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — naming the focus in writing before the session, as a behaviour an observer can see (for example 'how I respond when a parent rejects a recommendation').

THEY HOLD — agreeing whether the chosen session will actually show that behaviour, and adding a second focus if they have noticed something you have not.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the focus is yours because self-direction is what is being assessed. Your supervisor may see a blind spot you cannot name, and their addition is part of the learning.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — pick the session that exposes the hard skill, send the focus to your supervisor a few days before, and resist the urge to swap to an easier activity nearer the date.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a focus so broad it cannot be observed ('my rapport'), or a quiet switch back to standardised administration because it feels safer.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — '"rapport" is too wide for me to watch. Which moment in the meeting do you actually dread?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each observation has a written focus, chosen by you, on something you find hard and that the observer can see happen.

PASS TEST — Not administration, which is easiest

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the stated focus written at the top of your Appendix 7 section and in the supervision record. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — two observations of a cognitive assessment you have given many times, and feedback that says 'well administered, good rapport' and nothing you can change.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between a focus and a topic, and show a peer how to turn 'my feedback meetings' into 'how I explain a low score to a parent without softening it into meaninglessness'.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the hard moment does not arise (the parent agrees with everything). Say so in your section of the form, take what feedback there is, and ask to keep the same focus for the next observation.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asking to be observed on the activity you are best at and inviting general feedback.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Receive critical feedback without defending' and into the targets you set in Appendix 6.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Receive critical feedback without defending
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Defending and collapsing cost you the same thing: the information. Stone and Heen (Thanks for the Feedback, 2014) describe how people reject feedback by arguing with the giver or the accuracy rather than hearing what is being said. CORU SoP 4.3 and PSI Code 3.5.2 are mapped here — read both in full. A trainee who argues each point in the room teaches their supervisor to give less feedback, and supervisors are likely to read defensiveness as a problem with using supervision.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor gives difficult feedback: whether they lead with the observation, the effect on the child or parent, or a question. Notice your own body and the first sentence that forms in your head.

WRITE DOWN — the feedback word for word as it is said, before you interpret it. Mark anything you disagree with privately, for later, not now.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'is there anything you held back today because you weren't sure how I'd take it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listening, writing it down, and asking only clarifying questions ('what did you see that made you think that?'). No explanation of why you did it.

THEY HOLD — the content and framing of the feedback, and the pace at which it is given.

WHY THAT SPLIT — your job in the room is to receive, not to respond on substance. The response comes the following week, once you have had time to think, which is when you can disagree properly if you still do.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — after an observation, take the feedback, summarise it back in one or two sentences, and say when you will return to it. Stop there.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'yes, but the child was tired', a justification after every point, or the opposite: agreeing with everything, apologising, and taking nothing specific away.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you don't need to explain it now. Write down what I said and tell me next week what you make of it.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — take critical feedback without arguing or apologising, record it accurately, ask one clarifying question, and return to it at the next session.

PASS TEST — You listened

EVIDENCE TO FILE — your verbatim note of the feedback in your Appendix 7 section and the supervision record. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the supervision record shows a discussion of why the feedback was unfair, and nothing about what you will try.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why 'receive now, respond later' protects the information, name the common ways feedback gets deflected (Stone & Heen, 2014), and model a clarifying question that is not a defence in disguise.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you catch yourself defending mid-sentence. Stop, say 'sorry, I'll take that away', and write it down. If you still disagree a week later, bring your reasoning to supervision calmly, with evidence.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Explaining why you did it before you have finished hearing what was seen.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Act on the feedback and say so next time' and into CORU SoP 4.3 evidence in Appendix 6.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor gives difficult feedback: whether they lead with the observation, the effect on the child or parent, or a question. Notice your own body and the first sentence that forms in your head.

micro.name: Act on the feedback and say so next time
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The return is what gets noticed: coming back the following week with what you tried is the difference between receiving feedback and using it. CORU SoP 4.3 is mapped here. The Reference sheet sets the top grade as a specific change in practice that followed an observation. A trainee who nods, fills in the form and changes nothing leaves no trace of learning in the record, and the next observation finds the same thing.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor follows up on feedback they have given earlier: do they ask, or wait for you to raise it? Notice which changes they consider meaningful and which they treat as cosmetic.

WRITE DOWN — one change you will try, where you will try it (the next similar session), and how you will know whether it made a difference.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what would you need to see next time to know I've taken this on?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing the change, trying it in the next comparable session, and opening the following supervision with what happened.

THEY HOLD — judging whether the change addresses what they saw, and deciding whether to observe the same skill again.

WHY THAT SPLIT — acting on feedback is the trainee's half of the contract. Only the observer can say whether the change reached what they were pointing at.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — put the observation feedback as the first item on the next supervision agenda, report what you did differently and what you noticed, and record it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a change that is a restatement of the feedback ('I'll be more aware of pace') rather than something done; or the feedback silently dropped.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you said you'd pause after giving the scores. Did you, in the Thursday meeting? What happened?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — within a week or two of each observation, you try a specific change, tell your supervisor unprompted, and the record shows the before and after.

PASS TEST — Something changed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the supervision record entry reporting the change, cross-referenced to the Appendix 7 form. This is also raw material for the reflective essay. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the second observation's feedback repeats the first almost word for word.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to turn a feedback comment into one behaviour, one setting and one sign of success, and explain why reporting back unprompted matters more than getting it right first time.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the change did not work, or made things worse. Report that too: it is still acting on feedback. Ask in supervision what else to try, and record both attempts.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Completing the form and never mentioning the feedback again.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Trace a change in practice to a specific reflection' in the reflective essay and 'Rate again at the end and compare' in Appendix 6.

Not started

micro.name: Know what counts as immediate here
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Trainees rarely fail to raise a crisis because they missed it; more often they did not want to interrupt or were unsure it was serious enough. The UCD Handbook §6.2 is the reference mapped here — read its wording for the programme's requirement. The Reference sheet's test is deliberately low: if you are asking whether it is serious enough to interrupt someone, it is. The cost of an unnecessary call is minutes; the cost of waiting can be a child's safety.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which situations your supervisor treats as needing a same-day call: a child protection or welfare concern, a disclosure, a child indicating intent to harm self or others, an escalating parent or school conflict, an error you have made with consequences.

WRITE DOWN — the service's own list, if it has one, and any categories it adds for this area (for example contact with CAMHS or Tusla already open on a case).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's something a trainee sat on that you wish they'd rung you about?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — learning the categories (crisis, welfare concern, ethical dilemma) and, when in doubt, making the call rather than deciding alone that it can wait.

THEY HOLD — the judgement on anything borderline once you have raised it, and the decision about further escalation within the service.

WHY THAT SPLIT — your part is not to under-call. Grading severity is where experience matters, and you only get that experience by bringing borderline cases forward.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for the first weeks in Cavan, raise any borderline concern with your supervisor the same day and say which category you think it falls into and why.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — concerns held to the weekly session because they 'weren't really child protection', and ethical dilemmas (a school asking you to alter a report, a consent problem) not recognised as urgent.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you were right to ring. Next time something like this, don't wait until Friday.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you can name the three kinds of concern that cannot wait, recognise them in the moment, and raise them the same day without talking yourself out of it.

PASS TEST — Crisis, welfare concern, ethical dilemma

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a supervision record note that the categories and service protocol were reviewed at induction. Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an unexplained injury noted during an observation and first mentioned at supervision four days later.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the low threshold for interrupting, why trainees under-call, and the difference between 'immediate' (same day) and 'important' (next session).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you realise you held something that should have been raised. Raise it now, act on any duty that still applies, and record honestly when you became aware and when you raised it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Deciding alone that a concern was not serious enough to interrupt your supervisor.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Know how to reach your supervisor out of session', 'Act first where the duty is yours', and 6. Ethical Practice.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Know how to reach your supervisor out of session
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A concern that has to be raised the same day needs a route that works when your supervisor is in another school, on leave or in a meeting. The UCD Handbook §6.2 is mapped here. The Reference sheet notes that the supervision contract should say who covers; if it does not, find out before you need it. Discovering on the day that you only have an office email address wastes time a child may not have.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor is reached when out of the office, who covers when they are on leave, and whether the service has a senior psychologist or duty line for urgent queries.

WRITE DOWN — mobile number, a named deputy and their number, the DLP for each school you visit, and the Tusla contact route for the area, kept on paper and on your service phone.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if I can't get you and it can't wait, who exactly do I ring next?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — collecting the numbers in week one, keeping them with you in every school, and checking them against your diary so you know who covers on any given day.

THEY HOLD — writing the cover arrangement into the supervision contract and telling you when it changes (leave, courses).

WHY THAT SPLIT — carrying the route is yours because you are the one who will need it. Cover depends on service rotas that only your supervisor can arrange.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — at the start of each week, check who covers on each day you are in a school and confirm the DLP name for each visit.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a contact list that lives only in an email, a deputy never named, and no DLP name for a school you are visiting for the first time.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I'm at a course on Wednesday. Who are you ringing if something comes up at the school that afternoon?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — before every school day you have your supervisor's number, the named cover, the school DLP's name and the Tusla route, and you know which to use first.

PASS TEST — You have the number

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the supervision contract clause on out-of-session contact and cover. Do not log personal phone numbers in your own Log. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a disclosure at 2.30pm, your supervisor unreachable, and nobody else's number on you.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the route has to be set up before the day, what goes on a contact card, and why not reaching your supervisor never suspends a Children First duty.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you cannot reach anyone. Act on any duty that is yours (DLP, and Tusla if at threshold; An Garda Síochána if a child is in immediate danger), record every attempt at contact with times, and tell your supervisor as soon as you reach them.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Having only an office email address for your supervisor and no named cover.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Act first where the duty is yours' and 'Record the contact and what was agreed'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor is reached when out of the office, who covers when they are on leave, and whether the service has a senior psychologist or duty line for urgent queries.

micro.name: Act first where the duty is yours
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Under the Children First Act 2015 a mandated person must report to Tusla as soon as practicable; telling the DLP does not discharge that duty, though a joint report can meet it. CORU SoP 1.17 is also mapped — read its full text. Supervision informs what you do and supports you afterwards; it does not replace the report or grant permission to make it. Waiting to consult first is the commonest way a trainee falls short of the duty.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the order in which your supervisor acts on a concern: stop, record, DLP, Tusla, then supervision. Notice that the conversation with their own supervisor comes after the report, not before.

WRITE DOWN — the sequence as this service practises it, and whether you are a mandated person in this role (check with UCD and the service rather than assuming).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when did you last act before you could talk it through, and how did you know that was right?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — the actions that are your duty: stopping the activity, not questioning further, recording, telling the DLP, and reporting to Tusla or joining a joint report.

THEY HOLD — advice on the process, escalation if the DLP does not act, and review afterwards.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the legal duty sits with the person who holds the concern. A supervisor can guide you, but cannot take the duty off you, and cannot make it wait.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — in a live or role-played concern, follow the sequence to the end yourself, ringing your supervisor if reachable but not holding any step for them.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — 'I'll run it past you first', continuing the assessment after a disclosure, or asking the child more questions to be sure.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'don't wait for me. Go to the DLP now, make sure a report goes in today, and we'll talk after.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — where a concern meets the threshold you act the same day (DLP and Tusla report, jointly or yourself) and inform your supervisor, whether or not they were reachable beforehand.

PASS TEST — Supervision informs, it does not replace

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the timed record on the case file and the report reference, per service policy. Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a concern held overnight because your supervisor was at a course and you wanted their view first.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain 'as soon as practicable', why the DLP route does not discharge a mandated person's duty, and why supervision follows action. Point peers to Children First National Guidance (DCYA, 2017) rather than your summary.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you realise you waited. Act now, record the delay and the reason honestly, and bring it to supervision as a learning event rather than hiding it.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Waiting to consult your supervisor before making a report that is yours to make.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record the contact and what was agreed', 'Bring it to supervision afterwards, not instead', and 6. Ethical Practice.

Not started

micro.name: Record the contact and what was agreed
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The record of who you told, when and what was agreed is what shows the duty was met and the concern was handled; without it, a well-handled concern looks like an unhandled one. Handbook Appendix 8 is mapped here — check the form itself for its headings. The Reference sheet also advises writing a dilemma entry afterwards. A managed concern that exists only as a line in the day log is lost as evidence for Ethical Practice and Supervision.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what your supervisor writes after an urgent contact: time of each call, who was spoken to, what was said, what each person agreed to do, and when they followed up.

WRITE DOWN — the elements of a usable record, and where each part goes: the case file (per service policy), the supervision record, and an Appendix 8 dilemma entry.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'if this record were read in a year by someone who wasn't there, what would they need?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the timed record of each contact and agreement the same day, and drafting your own Appendix 8 entry.

THEY HOLD — reviewing the record for completeness, adding their own note of the out-of-session contact, and countersigning where the form requires it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the person who made the calls holds the facts. Your supervisor checks that the record would stand up and that the agreed actions were completed.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — after any out-of-session contact, record it the same day and bring it to the next formal session even though the matter is resolved.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — no times, 'discussed with supervisor' with no content, agreed actions with no owner, and no Appendix 8 entry.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what time did you ring me, and what did we agree you'd do next? Put that in, and who was doing each part.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every urgent contact has a record with time, person, content and agreed actions, and any dilemma is written up in Appendix 8 with your own reflection.

PASS TEST — Time and content

EVIDENCE TO FILE — case file record (per service policy), supervision record, Appendix 8 dilemma entry. The Appendix 8 reflection is yours to write. Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a managed disclosure that appears only as 'CP concern — DLP informed' in the day log.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer what a complete contact record contains and explain why a resolved concern still goes to formal supervision and Appendix 8.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find a past concern was never written up properly. Write it now from your contemporaneous notes, date it as written today, and state that it was written later. Do not back-date.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recording that you raised a concern but not when, with whom, or what was agreed.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Appendix 8 dilemma entries, 'Work an ethical dilemma through a decision procedure', and the reflective learning essay.

micro.name: Attend consistently
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Peer supervision is the first thing dropped when placement gets busy, usually by everyone at once, after which the group stops existing. PSI Accreditation Standards 3.3.9 is the standard mapped here — read the clause itself for what the programme must provide. Attendance is most of the contribution. It also only counts if it can be evidenced: sessions not recorded cannot be counted toward supervision requirements later.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how established peer or group supervision in the service or cohort runs: who convenes, how often, how cancellations are handled, and whether practising psychologists attend their own group.

WRITE DOWN — the schedule, format (in person, online), convenor, and the ground rules agreed at the first meeting.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what has kept your peer group going, and what made previous ones stop?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — putting every session in the diary as a fixed appointment, protecting it from school visits, and logging attendance the same day.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) agreeing that the time is protected within placement days, and counting it toward supervision where the programme allows.

WHY THAT SPLIT — attending is entirely in your control. Whether peer time counts toward requirements is a programme and service decision you should confirm, not assume.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — attend every scheduled session across the Cavan placement, and if a clash is unavoidable, send apologies in advance and rearrange the clash, not the group.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — sessions quietly skipped for report writing, and a log that shows none of them.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'I see the peer group isn't in your diary this week. What's it been displaced by?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you attend peer supervision as a fixed commitment and each session is logged with date, format, and a brief note of what was discussed (anonymised).

PASS TEST — Attendance is recorded

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 entry for each session, per the Reference sheet guidance; check the form for its headings. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you attended six sessions but logged none, and cannot evidence peer supervision at the end-of-year review.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why groups fail by gradual attrition, why logging is part of attending, and how to rescue a group that has lapsed (propose one date, one case, one convenor).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the group stops meeting. Offer to convene the next session yourself, and tell your supervisor, so the gap is visible and can be addressed rather than silently lost.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Attending but not logging, so the sessions cannot be evidenced.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Present a case at least once a trimester' and the supervision evidence in Appendix 8.
