micro.name: Present a case at least once a trimester
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Presenting is where you practise explaining a case to people who are not obliged to be kind about it, which later becomes multidisciplinary team work. CORU SoP 4.5 is mapped here (read the clause for its wording). Listening to other people's cases is useful but does not evidence that you sought review of your own work. A case you have already solved wastes the group's time and your own.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how experienced presenters structure a case: referral question, what was done, formulation and the framework behind it, where they are stuck, and the specific question for the group.

WRITE DOWN — that structure as a one-page template, and how much anonymisation each presenter used (no names, no school, no identifying detail).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what question did you want the group to answer, and did they answer it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing a case you are stuck on, preparing a structured, anonymised presentation, and ending with one clear question.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) a check beforehand that the case is anonymised enough and that sharing it fits service policy.

WHY THAT SPLIT — preparing and presenting is the skill. What may be shared outside the service is a governance question that your supervisor should confirm.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — present at least once each trimester, allow time for preparation, bring the stuck part rather than the resolved part, and note what the group raised.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a narrative of everything you did with no question at the end, identifying detail, or a case chosen because it went well.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's the one thing you want them to help you with? Start with that.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each trimester you present an anonymised case with a structured account and a specific question, and record what you took away.

PASS TEST — Listening does not evidence it

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 entry naming the date, that you presented, the question, and what changed in the case as a result. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a year of regular attendance and no record of ever presenting your own work.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can give a newer trainee the presentation structure, explain why the stuck part is the valuable part, and show how to anonymise a case properly.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the group does not answer your question, or you realise mid-presentation that you have identified the school. Stop, ask the group not to record or repeat it, and tell your supervisor the same day.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Presenting a case you have already resolved, so the group has nothing to work on.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Bring a case from an under-covered age band', 5. Working with Others, and multidisciplinary case discussion.

micro.name: Bring a case from an under-covered age band
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
UCD Table 3 age bands are the frame for breadth across the programme, and your own coverage record shows Early Years and Young Adult unevidenced so far. A case from a thin age band brought to peer supervision earns both a presentation and breadth evidence, and exposes you to reasoning you have had less practice with. Breadth cannot be added retrospectively, so this has to be planned: the case only exists if the Appendix 1 plan put you in contact with that age group.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which age bands the other trainees' cases come from, and which questions come up in each (for example transition to school, or transition from post-primary). Notice whose reasoning is least familiar to you.

WRITE DOWN — your own coverage against the Table 3 bands from your Log, and which band is thinnest.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what do you think about differently with a case at that age that I wouldn't think of?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — mapping your coverage, flagging the thinnest band at your first Cavan supervision, and choosing a case from it to present when one arises.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) allocating work in that band where the service can, and confirming it is planned in Appendix 1.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you know your gaps; the service controls the caseload. Coverage only happens if both sides plan for it at the start.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — once you hold a case from the under-covered band, present it to the peer group with the age-specific question you are unsure about.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a case chosen from a thin band but presented as though age made no difference, or an identifying detail slipping through because the setting is small.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what's different about this because of the child's age? Ask the group that.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you track your age-band coverage, bring at least one case from a thin band to peer supervision, and log it as both a presentation and breadth evidence.

PASS TEST — It doubles as breadth evidence

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 8 entry for the presentation; Log row tagged with the age band and 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — every case you present is primary-age, and the end-of-year review finds the same gaps as the start.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain Table 3 breadth, why it cannot be evidenced after the fact, and how peer supervision can be used to deepen learning in a thin band once contact exists.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — no case in the thin band arises. Record that it was planned and did not happen, raise it in supervision, and carry it forward into the next Appendix 1 rather than inventing coverage.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Presenting only from the age band you already know best.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into Table 3 breadth, 'Carry the targets into the next Placement Plan', and PSI 3.3.6 setting coverage planning.

micro.name: Offer something useful to someone else's case
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The useful contribution is usually a question, not a suggestion: 'what did the child say about it?' opens a case, while 'have you tried X?' tends to close it. CORU SoP 5.8 is mapped here (read the clause for its wording). Proctor (Group supervision, 2nd ed., 2008) and Hawkins and McMahon (Supervision in the helping professions, 2020) discuss group process in supervision. A group that converges too quickly on one explanation stops thinking, and someone has to say so.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which contributions change how a presenter sees their case, and which are ignored. Notice the ratio of questions to advice, and the moment a group settles on one explanation.

WRITE DOWN — two or three questions that opened a case up, word for word, to reuse. Nothing identifying about other people's cases.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (of a presenter) 'which comment was actually useful to you, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — listening to the whole presentation, then offering one question that tests the formulation, or naming a hypothesis the group has not considered.

THEY HOLD — (the presenter) the decision on what to take away; (the convenor) managing time and turn-taking.

WHY THAT SPLIT — your role is to widen someone else's thinking, not to take the case over. The presenter owns the case and the choice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — in each session, contribute at least once to someone else's case, and at least once in a while name the group process ('we've all agreed quite quickly — what would make us wrong?').

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — advice given before the question has been asked, a contribution that retells your own case, or silence all session.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can you turn that suggestion into a question for her?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you contribute to others' cases with questions that open them up, and you notice and name premature agreement in the group.

PASS TEST — You contributed

EVIDENCE TO FILE — a brief line in your Appendix 8 peer entry noting your contribution in general terms (no case details). Log against 7. Supervision and 5. Working with Others.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you attend every session and say nothing, or say 'have you tried a reward chart?' before the presenter has finished.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why questions help more than solutions, give examples of opening questions, and describe how a group can converge too early.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a contribution lands badly and the presenter becomes defensive. Acknowledge it, rephrase as a question, and check with them afterwards. If group dynamics are persistently unhelpful, raise it with the convenor.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Offering a solution before understanding the case, which closes the discussion down.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 5. Working with Others, consultation skills, and CORU SoP 5.8.

micro.name: Rate all eight before day one, dated
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The before-and-after structure is the point of the self-evaluation: the comparison is the evidence of development, and it only works if the first rating was genuinely made first. The UCD Handbook §4.5a is mapped here — read its wording, and the form itself, for exactly what is rated. A rating written after the placement has started is visibly retrospective and forfeits the comparison. This row is a scaffold: the ratings are yours to make and write.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how the form is laid out: which competencies it lists, what the rating descriptors actually say, and where the date goes. The Reference sheet cautions that the Handbook describes a range without explicitly setting out a five-point scale, so read the descriptors rather than assuming one.

WRITE DOWN — the exact descriptor wording and any questions to ask the programme about the scale.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (your supervisor) 'how do you read a before-rating when it arrives on your desk?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — completing and dating the before ratings for every competency listed, yourself, before the first Cavan placement day (05/10/2026) or at the very latest in week one.

THEY HOLD — reading the ratings at the first supervision session and discussing them; not writing them for you.

WHY THAT SPLIT — self-evaluation is only evidence if it is your own judgement. Your supervisor's role is to see it and use it to plan, which also makes the date credible.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — sit down with your Roscommon Log, supervision records and end-of-year feedback, rate each competency against the form's own descriptors, date the document, and share it at the first supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a form still blank at week three, one competency skipped because it felt hard to judge, or a date that does not match when it was actually written.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'can I see your before-ratings this week? We'll use them to plan the Appendix 1.'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every competency on the form is rated by you, the document is dated before or in the first week of placement, and it has been seen by your supervisor.

PASS TEST — Before, genuinely

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the dated Appendix 6 (before), with the supervision record noting it was discussed. Your ratings and wording are your own. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the before and after versions are both written in the same week in December.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a peer why the date matters more than the number, why the form's descriptors should be quoted rather than paraphrased, and why you ask the programme about the scale instead of assuming it.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you missed the start. Complete it now, date it truthfully, and say in the document that it was completed late and when. Do not back-date.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Completing the 'before' rating after the placement has started and dating it as though it had not.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Rate honestly, including low', 'Name two or three priority targets', and 'Rate again at the end and compare'.

micro.name: Rate honestly, including low
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A low rating at the start feels like an admission, but it is what makes development visible; a trainee who rates high at the start has nothing to show at the end. CORU SoP 4.3 and PSI Code 4.1.3 are mapped here — read both in full. The Reference sheet notes that supervisors can read an inflated first rating as poor self-awareness, which is itself assessed. Boud, Keogh and Walker (1985) treat returning honestly to experience as the start of learning from it. The judgement is yours; this row only offers prompts.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the gap between what you have done and what you have done independently. Notice where you have only observed, or done a task with close support, compared with where you have done it alone.

WRITE DOWN — for each competency, one piece of evidence from your Log or supervision records that supports the rating you are considering, and one thing you have not yet done at all.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (your supervisor) 'where do you think I'm over- or under-rating myself?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — rating each competency against the form's descriptors and your evidence, including low ratings where you have little or no experience.

THEY HOLD — a view on whether your ratings match what they have seen, offered for discussion rather than as a correction to your form.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the rating is a measure of your self-awareness, so it has to be yours. Their view is calibration, and the discussion itself can be recorded in supervision.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — rate each competency with one evidence point beside it, then check the whole set for consistency: are the ratings where you have least evidence also the lowest?

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — uniform middling ratings that avoid any judgement, high ratings on areas you have barely touched (for example organisational or systemic work), and ratings justified by effort rather than evidence.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what have you actually done in this area on your own? Does the rating match that?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each rating reflects your evidence, low where experience is thin, and you can defend any rating with a specific example.

PASS TEST — An honest low start shows trajectory

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 6 (before), in your own words, and a supervision record note that ratings were discussed. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — every competency rated near the top at the start of Year 1, so the end rating cannot show movement and the self-evaluation reads as unaware.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why an honest low rating is a strength in this document, how to anchor each rating to evidence, and why the descriptors must be read in the Handbook's own words.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — your supervisor thinks a rating is inflated or too harsh. Discuss the evidence, then decide yourself whether to revise. If you keep your rating, note the discussion in the supervision record.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Rating yourself high at the start because a low rating feels like failure.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Name two or three priority targets' and 'Rate again at the end and compare'.

micro.name: Name two or three priority targets
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A target is only useful if you can tell at the end whether you met it: 'improve at formulation' cannot be evidenced, whereas a target with a named framework, a number of cases and a visible product can. CORU SoP 4.3 is mapped here. The Reference sheet suggests drawing targets from the development areas identified at your end-of-year review. Too many targets dilute effort; two or three priorities give a comparison that writes itself. The targets are yours to set and word.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor frames development goals for themselves or other trainees: whether each has an action, a setting, an amount and a product you could point to.

WRITE DOWN — your development areas from the end-of-year review, the lowest before-ratings, and which of these the Cavan placement can realistically support.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which of these could this placement actually give me the work to meet?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing two or three targets and wording each so that it names what you will do, how often or in which cases, and what evidence will show it.

THEY HOLD — a judgement on whether the service can provide the opportunities each target needs, and agreement to plan for them.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the priorities come from your self-evaluation, so they are yours. Whether a target is achievable here depends on caseload and settings the service controls.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — draft the targets, test each with the question 'how will I know in December?', and bring them to the first supervision session for discussion.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — targets that are traits ('be more confident'), targets that need work this placement cannot offer, or six targets where two would do.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what would I see in your file in December that shows you met this one?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you set two or three targets, each specific, linked to a low rating or a named development area, and achievable in this placement.

PASS TEST — Specific and achievable

EVIDENCE TO FILE — targets in your own words in Appendix 6, agreed in the supervision record. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'develop my formulation skills' as the only target, with nothing at the end that shows whether it happened.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can show a peer how to turn a vague aim into an evidenceable target, and why fewer targets make a better comparison.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — mid-placement, a target becomes impossible (no cases of that kind arrive). Record why in supervision, adjust the target with your supervisor, and explain the change in the end comparison rather than dropping it silently.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing targets that cannot be evidenced, such as 'improve at formulation'.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Carry the targets into the next Placement Plan' and 'Rate again at the end and compare'.

micro.name: Carry the targets into the next Placement Plan
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Targets that live only in Appendix 6 do not shape what work you are given; targets in the Placement Plan do. Handbook Appendix 1 is mapped here — read the form for where targets and settings go. This matters especially for PSI 3.3.6, which is not yet met: it requires mainstream primary, post-primary and special education, and special-setting visits must be written into the Appendix 1 before the placement starts, not added afterwards.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor turns a trainee's development needs into caseload decisions: which schools, which referrals, which settings (including special schools or special classes) are allocated and why.

WRITE DOWN — each Appendix 6 target alongside the specific opportunity in Cavan that could meet it, and the outstanding breadth needs (special education setting, further post-primary contact, thin age bands).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which of these can we write into the plan now, and which depend on referrals we don't have yet?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — bringing your Appendix 6 targets and outstanding breadth needs to the planning meeting, and drafting how each appears in Appendix 1.

THEY HOLD — deciding what the service can commit to, arranging access to settings such as special schools, and signing the plan.

WHY THAT SPLIT — you know your gaps and targets. The service controls allocation and access, so the plan has to be a joint document signed before work begins.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — before the placement begins, check that every priority target and the special-setting visits needed for PSI 3.3.6 appear in Appendix 1 with a named opportunity.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — an Appendix 1 that repeats generic programme aims, no special education setting named, and targets that appear nowhere in the plan.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'your target on consultation isn't in here. Which school could that happen in?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each Appendix 6 target has a matching line in Appendix 1, and required settings (including special education for PSI 3.3.6) are planned in before day one.

PASS TEST — They appear in Appendix 1

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the signed Appendix 1, cross-referenced to Appendix 6. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — December arrives with the targets met in name only, and no special education contact because it was never in the plan.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the Placement Plan, not the self-evaluation, is what drives allocation, and why breadth and setting requirements cannot be evidenced retrospectively.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a planned opportunity falls through. Record it in supervision, agree an alternative, and amend the plan in writing with your supervisor rather than letting the target lapse.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Setting targets in Appendix 6 that never appear in the Appendix 1 Placement Plan.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into PSI 3.3.6 setting coverage, Table 3 breadth, and 'Rate again at the end and compare'.

micro.name: Rate again at the end and compare
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The end comparison is where development is either shown or merely claimed. The UCD Handbook §4.5a is mapped here. The Reference sheet advises accounting for every change, including ratings that did not move: an unchanged rating explained by lack of opportunity, with a forward plan, is strong; an unexplained identical rating looks like disengagement. This row is a scaffold for structuring the comparison; the ratings and explanations are yours to write.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor reads change: what they count as evidence of movement (a dated product, observed practice, feedback) and what they discount (confidence, effort).

WRITE DOWN — a two-column comparison: before rating and after rating for each competency, with a space for the evidence and reason beside each, and a separate list of competencies that did not move.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'where have you seen me change this term, and where haven't you?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — re-rating each competency in the final weeks, before reading your before-ratings again, then comparing and writing the explanation for each change or non-change.

THEY HOLD — their own view of your progress, given in the end-of-placement review, and discussion of any large disagreement.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the comparison is your self-evaluation. Their perspective checks it but does not replace it.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each competency, prompt yourself: what moved, what shows it (dated Log entry, report, observation feedback), what did not move and why, and what that means for the next placement.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — every rating raised by one point with no evidence, unchanged ratings left unexplained, and a claim of change contradicted by the supervision record.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this one hasn't moved. Why not, and what would move it next time?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you complete the after-ratings, place them beside the before-ratings, and account for each change and non-change with evidence and a forward plan.

PASS TEST — Movement is visible

EVIDENCE TO FILE — Appendix 6 (after), in your own words, and the supervision record of the end-of-placement review. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — before and after forms that differ by a point here and there, with no explanation of why anything changed or stayed the same.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why unchanged ratings need a reason, how to anchor change to dated evidence, and how the comparison feeds the next Placement Plan.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find a rating went down. That can be honest: you now understand the competency better. Say so plainly, give the evidence, and set it as a target for the next placement.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving unchanged ratings unexplained, so the comparison reads as disengagement.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into the reflective learning essay, the next Appendix 1, and CORU SoP 4.3.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)

micro.name: Cover placement, college sessions and independent study
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The essay is where the portfolio either becomes a coherent account of the year or stays a pile of forms. The UCD Handbook §4.5b is mapped here; read it yourself and list its requirements before writing, because the Reference sheet notes that Appendix 6 does two jobs and you need to check whether you are writing one document or two. Writing only about placement and omitting college sessions and independent study means writing the wrong thing well. The essay is yours to write; this row gives structure only.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in §4.5b and any marking guidance the programme provides, the exact strands required, the word limit, and whether it is submitted within Appendix 6 or separately.

WRITE DOWN — a planning table with a row per strand (placement, college sessions, independent study) and columns for a dated example, what it changed in your practice, and the source record you will draw on.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (programme tutor) 'is this one document with the self-evaluation, or two?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the requirements yourself, building the planning table, and drafting the essay in your own words.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor or tutor) clarification of what the programme requires; they do not read drafts for content unless the programme allows it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the essay is assessed as your own reflection. Clarifying requirements is fair; shaping the content for you is not.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each strand, find at least one dated example and ask: what did I learn, where did I use it, what changed? Link college teaching to a placement moment where you applied (or failed to apply) it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — an essay that is all placement, reading lists named without saying what they changed, and college sessions described as a timetable.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'where did something from a lecture actually turn up in your practice?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — your essay addresses each required strand with dated examples, linked to changes in practice, in your own words.

PASS TEST — All three strands

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the essay (yours to write) in Appendix 6 or as the programme directs, with the planning table kept privately. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a strong placement narrative that never mentions college teaching or independent reading, so a required strand is missing.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain how to read §4.5b into a checklist, how a planning table stops a strand being forgotten, and why reading only counts when you can say what it changed.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you realise late that a strand is thin. Go back to your Log and supervision records for dated material, and write honestly about what that strand contributed, even if it was less than the others.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing only about placement and leaving out college sessions and independent study.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Trace a change in practice to a specific reflection' and the completed Appendix 6.

micro.name: Name what was hard and what it cost
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
An account with no difficulty in it is not credible, and markers tend to read it as performance. The UCD Handbook §4.5b and CORU SoP 5.45 (recognising personal emotional responses and developing self-care) are mapped here. The unit of analysis is your practice, not your private life: you are not required to disclose anything personal you do not wish to. This row offers structure and prompts; the reflection is yours to write.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in your own supervision records and Log, the moments you found hard: a feedback meeting that went badly, a disclosure, a case you felt out of your depth on, a workload peak. Notice which ones changed how you practise.

WRITE DOWN — for two or three moments: what happened (briefly), what you noticed in yourself, what it cost (time, sleep, confidence, a relationship with a school), and what you did about it.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (yourself) 'which difficulty do I most want to leave out, and why?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing which difficulties to write about, and how much of your personal response to include.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) nothing in the essay itself; they may have discussed the same moments in supervision, which you can draw on.

WHY THAT SPLIT — disclosure is your choice. The essay needs honesty about practice, not about your private life, and you set that boundary.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — use a structure to move from event to learning: for example Gibbs's (1988) reflective cycle (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan) as a scaffold, not a set of headings to copy into the essay.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — difficulty written as a confession with no link to practice, or difficulty minimised so it reads as a success story.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — (your own check) 'have I said what it cost and what I did about it, or only that it was hard?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the essay names real challenges, what they cost, and how you responded, in your own words, while keeping the focus on practice.

PASS TEST — Challenges are expected

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the essay (yours to write); supporting supervision records stay on file. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — an essay in which everything went well, or one that discloses personal material at length without any link to practice.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between reflection and confession, how a model like Gibbs (1988) can scaffold thinking, and why honest difficulty strengthens the essay.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — writing about a hard moment stirs up more than expected. Stop, take it to supervision or the university counselling service, and choose a different example if that one is not ready to be written about.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving out every difficulty, so the essay reads as a performance.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Reflect on your own culture, values and biases' and 'Name a self-care strategy and evidence it works'.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — in your own supervision records and Log, the moments you found hard: a feedback meeting that went badly, a disclosure, a case you felt out of your depth on, a workload peak. Notice which ones changed how you practise.

micro.name: Reflect on your own culture, values and biases
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 5.44 asks you to reflect critically on the 'self' and the impact of your own culture, values, experiences, beliefs and biases, using supervision to assist the process. The Reference sheet treats this and 5.45 as the essay's real brief. Schön (1983) distinguishes reflection-in-action from reflection-on-action; the essay is largely the latter, but noting moments you adjusted in the room shows both. The reflection is yours to write; this row gives prompts only.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — moments when your own assumptions shaped a judgement: what you expected of a family, a school, a child's language or background, and where that expectation was wrong or had to be checked.

WRITE DOWN — two or three such moments (anonymised), what you assumed, where the assumption came from, and what happened when it was tested.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (in supervision) 'where do you think my own background has shaped how I've read a case?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — identifying your own values and assumptions, and choosing which examples to write about and how.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) questions in supervision that help you see what you might have missed; the supervision record of those discussions is source material.

WHY THAT SPLIT — CORU 5.44 names supervision as an aid to this reflection, but the insight and the writing must be yours.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each example, prompt yourself: what did I assume, what did it lead me to do, how did I find out, what do I do differently now? Quote your supervision record where a question changed your view.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a general statement ('I am aware of my biases') with no example, or a list of identity characteristics with no link to a decision you made.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — (your own check) 'can I point to a specific moment where this assumption changed something I did?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the essay names at least one specific way your culture, values or assumptions affected your practice, how you noticed, and what changed, in your own words.

PASS TEST — This is where CORU 5.44 lands

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the essay (yours to write), with the supervision record entries you drew on. Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a paragraph asserting awareness of bias without a single example from practice.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain CORU 5.44, Schön's (1983) distinction as a way into it, and how supervision records provide evidence that the reflection is real rather than reconstructed.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you cannot find an example. Look at cases where you and a parent or teacher disagreed, or where your first hypothesis was wrong, and take that question to supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Stating awareness of bias without a specific example of it affecting practice.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 6. Ethical Practice, culturally responsive assessment, and CORU SoP 5.44.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — moments when your own assumptions shaped a judgement: what you expected of a family, a school, a child's language or background, and where that expectation was wrong or had to be checked.

micro.name: Trace a change in practice to a specific reflection
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
'I have developed in confidence' is an assertion; a dated sequence showing what you did before, what you reflected on, and what you did afterwards is evidence. CORU SoP 4.3 is mapped here. The Reference sheet suggests a ten-minute weekly habit — one dated paragraph about what you noticed — so the essay becomes an editing task rather than writing from memory. The essay is yours to write; this row suggests how to find and structure the evidence.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — in your Log's development column, supervision records and Appendix 7 feedback, a chain: a moment you noticed something, a reflection or piece of feedback, and a later dated occasion where you did it differently.

WRITE DOWN — two or three such chains, each with dates (DD/MM/YYYY), the source record, and what specifically changed.

ASK AFTERWARDS — (yourself) 'what would someone reading my file see that shows this change, without my telling them?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — finding the chains in your own records and writing them up in your own words, with dates and sources.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) the supervision records and observation feedback that corroborate the change.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the change and its account are yours. Records held jointly show the reflection was real, which is why quoting them strengthens the essay.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — keep a weekly dated paragraph through the Cavan placement; when drafting, pick the chains with the clearest before and after, and quote the supervision record at the turning point.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — change asserted without dates, a before and after with no reflection between them, or examples that are all descriptions of what happened.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — (your own check) 'where exactly is the reflection in this example, and when did the practice change?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the essay traces at least one change in practice back to a specific, dated reflection or piece of feedback, in your own words.

PASS TEST — Reflection that changed something

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the essay (yours to write), cross-referenced to the Log, supervision record and Appendix 7. Log against 7. Supervision.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'I grew in confidence over the year' with no example, no date and no source.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between asserting and evidencing change, how a weekly dated habit produces material, and how to use supervision records as source material.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you reach the essay with no weekly notes. Reconstruct from dated records you already hold (Log, supervision notes, Appendix 7), say plainly where memory is filling gaps, and start the weekly habit now.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Asserting development instead of evidencing it with dated examples.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Rate again at the end and compare' and the completed portfolio.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — in your Log's development column, supervision records and Appendix 7 feedback, a chain: a moment you noticed something, a reflection or piece of feedback, and a later dated occasion where you did it differently.

micro.name: Name a self-care strategy and evidence it works
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
CORU SoP 5.45 asks you to recognise personal emotional responses and develop effective self-care; PSI Code 4.1.1 is also mapped — read both in full. Burnout builds over time — Maslach and Jackson (1981) describe it as emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment — and an intention ('I will look after myself') is not a strategy. The essay needs a specific activity you actually did, and some evidence that it helped. What you disclose is your choice; this row gives prompts, and the text is yours to write.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — what you actually did when the work was heavy: a boundary on evening emails, a walk between schools, raising workload in supervision, using the employee assistance or university counselling service.

WRITE DOWN — one or two strategies, when you used them (dated), what prompted them, and what you noticed afterwards (sleep, backlog, mood, quality of records).

ASK AFTERWARDS — (in supervision) 'have you noticed any difference in how I've been working since I started doing this?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — choosing and using a strategy, noting its effect, and deciding how much to say about it in the essay.

THEY HOLD — (your supervisor) noticing and naming signs of strain, and space in supervision to talk about wellbeing; nothing private needs to go on file.

WHY THAT SPLIT — self-care is yours. Supervision is one place it can be supported, and a brief record that wellbeing was discussed is enough evidence.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — use the strategy consistently for several weeks, note briefly when you did and what changed, and raise it in supervision at least once.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a strategy that exists only in the essay, a general list ('exercise, sleep, friends') with no evidence of use, or over-disclosure that moves the essay away from practice.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — (your own check) 'can I show when I did this and what difference it made?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — the essay names a specific self-care activity you carried out, when, and what evidence shows it helped, in your own words.

PASS TEST — An activity, not an intention

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the essay (yours to write); a supervision record line that wellbeing was discussed. Log against 7. Supervision and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — 'I will prioritise self-care next year' as the only statement on the subject.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain CORU 5.45, why an intention is not evidence, and how to record a strategy's effect without over-disclosing.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the strategy stops working, or strain continues. Raise it in supervision, use the employee assistance or university counselling service, see your GP, and write honestly about what you learned from it not working.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing a self-care intention with no evidence it was ever carried out.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Manage workload and your own wellbeing' in 6. Ethical Practice and CORU SoP 5.45.

micro.name: Frame an answerable question from a real referral
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A referral arrives as a worry ('he can't read', 'she won't come in'), not as a question you can search. The Reference sheet maps CORU SoP 5.42 here. Evidence-based medicine made the structured question its first step (Richardson, Wilson, Nishikawa & Hayward, 1995, the 'well-built clinical question'; Sackett et al., 1996, BMJ), and the Reference sheet uses the same population–intervention–comparison–outcome shape. Search on the worry and you get thousands of hits and no answer; search on a framed question and twenty minutes is enough.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the moment in a planning conversation where your supervisor turns 'what can we do about his reading?' into something narrower: which age, which difficulty (decoding, fluency or comprehension), which kind of help, delivered by whom, measured how.

WRITE DOWN — the referral worry in the school's own words, then the question your supervisor would actually look up, set out as population, intervention, comparison, outcome.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what did you already know about this child that made you narrow the question that way?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the structured question from an anonymised referral form before the planning meeting, in one sentence, with each of the four parts named.

THEY HOLD — whether the question is the right one. Often the referral question is not the real question, and that is a formulation judgement.

WHY THAT SPLIT — writing the four parts is a technical skill you can practise at once. Deciding that the school asked about behaviour but the real issue is language is case judgement, and that stays with your supervisor until your formulations are trusted.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each new Cavan referral, write the answerable question in the case note before you search anything, and bring it to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a question too broad to search ('interventions for anxiety'), a question that assumes the answer ('does a weighted blanket help'), or one with no outcome anyone could measure.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if you found the perfect paper, what age would the children be, what would they be compared with, and what would have changed?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every case where you intend to recommend something has a written question naming the population (age band and difficulty), the intervention, the comparison and a measurable outcome.

PASS TEST — Specific enough to search

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the question as the first line of your search note, and the same question at the head of the Appendix 5 research entry. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you type 'dyslexia interventions' into a database, get several thousand records, read the first three abstracts and stop.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can take a peer's vague referral and, out loud, turn it into a four-part question, explaining why each part narrows the search and why the outcome must be something a school could observe. You can show why 'what works for autism?' has no answer and 'what helps a nine-year-old autistic child tolerate transitions between lessons?' might.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the search returns nothing. Widen one part at a time, usually the population first (age band, then diagnosis), and note each change so you know what the evidence is actually about.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Searching on the referral worry instead of a framed question, so the search is unbounded and the answer is whatever came up first.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Search a database rather than a search engine', 'Judge applicability to this child in this context', and 2. Formulation.

Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the moment in a planning conversation where your supervisor turns 'what can we do about his reading?' into something narrower: which age, which difficulty (decoding, fluency or comprehension), which kind of help, delivered by whom, measured how.

micro.name: Search a database rather than a search engine
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
The Reference sheet's order is syntheses first (Cochrane, Campbell Collaboration, the EEF Teaching and Learning Toolkit, What Works Clearinghouse), then PsycINFO or ERIC with a structured question, with Google Scholar kept for chasing a known paper. CORU SoP 5.41 is mapped here. A general search engine ranks by popularity and advertising, not by study quality, so the first page is full of commercial programme sites and testimonials — exactly the weak evidence the Reference sheet warns is sold to schools.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — where your supervisor goes first when a school asks 'is this programme any good?': a synthesis, a database, a NEPS good practice guide, or a colleague. Notice whether they check the EEF Toolkit or a Cochrane or Campbell review before looking at single studies.

WRITE DOWN — the databases the service or UCD gives you access to, how to reach them through the UCD library proxy, and any NEPS or Department guidance your supervisor treats as the starting point.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when you have only twenty minutes, what is your search order?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — running the search: synthesis sources first, then PsycINFO and ERIC with your four-part question turned into search terms, with limits set for age and date.

THEY HOLD — which synthesis or guidance the service treats as authoritative, and what counts as good enough to put in front of a school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the mechanics of database searching are yours from your UCD training. What a service is prepared to recommend on the strength of a search is a professional standard your supervisor sets.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each case, search at least one synthesis source and one bibliographic database before recommending anything, and bring a one-page summary to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a search that began and ended in Google or Google Scholar, a programme's own website cited as evidence, or a single hit treated as the literature.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'is there a systematic review on this? Did you check the Toolkit or Campbell before you went to single studies?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you search syntheses first, then at least one of PsycINFO or ERIC, using subject headings as well as free text, and you use Google Scholar only to find the full text of a paper you already know about.

PASS TEST — PsycINFO, ERIC, not Google

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the search note (databases, date searched, terms, number of hits) attached to the Appendix 5 research entry. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a school report recommends a programme on the strength of its publisher's website and a blog post.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why a database indexes peer-reviewed work by subject and a search engine does not, why a synthesis beats a single study, and how to use thesaurus terms (PsycINFO's index terms, ERIC descriptors) as well as keywords. You can demonstrate a twenty-minute search on a peer's question.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the proxy fails or you are in a school with no access. Note the question, search later, and do not recommend from memory in the meantime; tell the school the recommendation will follow once you have checked the evidence.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Treating the first page of a general search engine as the literature, and ending up citing a publisher's own website.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Record the search terms and databases used', 'Appraise quality rather than accepting the first result', and 'Cite evidence for recommendations'.

WATCH FOR — where your supervisor goes first when a school asks 'is this programme any good?': a synthesis, a database, a NEPS good practice guide, or a colleague. Notice whether they check the EEF Toolkit or a Cochrane or Campbell review before looking at single studies.

micro.name: Record the search terms and databases used
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A search you cannot repeat is a search nobody can check, including you in six months. CORU SoP 5.43 is mapped here. Systematic review reporting standards (PRISMA 2020, Page et al., 2021, BMJ) ask for the full search to be reported so others can reproduce it; a placement search does not need that rigour, but it needs the same principle. The Reference sheet's advice is a note per topic — question, what you searched, what you found, what you concluded — because you will be asked the same questions across a career.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — whether your supervisor keeps any record of past searches or reading on common referral topics (a folder, a shared drive, a reading list), and how they decide a previous search is still current.

WRITE DOWN — a template for your own search note: question, date, databases, exact search string, limits applied, number of hits, number read in full, what you concluded.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'which questions do you get asked so often that you wish you'd kept a note the first time?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — keeping the search note for every search you run on a case, completed on the day you search.

THEY HOLD — any shared resource the service keeps, and whether your note is good enough to add to it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the record of your own search is plainly your job. Adding to a service's shared reading is a decision about what the whole team will rely on, which is not yours to make alone on placement.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — keep a search log across the Cavan placement, one entry per search, and bring it to supervision when a recommendation depends on it.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — notes that say 'searched PsycINFO for social skills' with no terms, date or limits, so the search cannot be rerun and the gaps cannot be seen.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'if I ran your search tomorrow, would I get the same papers? Which terms, which years, which age limit?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every search behind a recommendation has a note someone else could rerun: databases, date, exact string with Boolean operators, limits, hits, and which papers you read in full.

PASS TEST — Reproducible

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the search note, kept with no child identifiers, attached to or summarised in the Appendix 5 research entry. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a supervisor asks why you did not find a well-known review, and you cannot say what you searched, so nobody can tell whether the gap was in the literature or in your search.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why the exact string matters (a missing synonym or truncation symbol changes the results), why the date matters (the literature moves), and why a search note with no identifiers can be reused across cases and shared.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you realise a past recommendation rested on a search you did not record. Rerun it now, record it properly, and check whether the answer still holds; if it does not, raise it in supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Keeping no record of what was searched, so the search cannot be checked, repeated or reused.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Log the search as an Appendix 5 research entry', 'Cite current sources rather than the familiar ones', and 8. Research.

micro.name: Appraise quality rather than accepting the first result
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Most of what a search returns will not stand up. The Reference sheet gives five questions: design, sample, comparison, effect size, and who funded it and who developed the programme. CORU SoP 5.41 and 5.3 are mapped here. The CASP checklists give a free, design-specific version of the same discipline. Evaluations run or commissioned by a programme's developer have been reported to show larger effects than independent ones (for education, see Wolf, Morrison, Inns, Slavin & Risman, 2020 — read the paper before quoting a figure). Accept the first result and you may recommend something that technically works and practically does not.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor reacts to a programme a school is already using or has been sold: what they ask first, whether they look at who ran the evaluation, and whether they ask about effect size or only 'is there research on it'.

WRITE DOWN — the five Reference sheet questions, and the CASP checklist that fits each design you meet (randomised trial, systematic review, qualitative study, cohort).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's the most common weak evidence schools show you, and how do you tell them without offending anyone?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — reading the full paper, not the abstract, and completing the relevant CASP checklist or the five questions for each study a recommendation rests on.

THEY HOLD — the overall judgement about how confident the evidence lets the service be, and how that is said to a school.

WHY THAT SPLIT — appraising a single paper is a skill your UCD training has given you. Weighing a body of evidence and putting it in words a principal will accept is judgement built over years of practice.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each recommendation, appraise the two or three key studies behind it and give your supervisor a short note: design, sample, comparison, effect size, funder or developer, and your verdict.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — statistical significance treated as practical importance; a pre-post design with no control accepted as proof; outcome measures built by the programme's own developer; a small sample making large claims.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'compared with what? And who wrote the evaluation?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you read the method section, name the design, check sample and comparison, look for an effect size, check who developed and funded the work, and reject what does not stand up. For effect-size benchmarks, Cohen's (1988) small, medium and large are a rough guide only; check the current EEF Toolkit entry rather than quoting a figure from memory.

PASS TEST — You judged the study, not the abstract

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the completed appraisal note with the Appendix 5 research entry. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — you recommend a programme because an abstract said 'significant improvement', and the study turns out to be twelve children with no control group, evaluated by the author.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a teacher, without jargon, why 'significant' does not mean 'big', why a comparison group matters, and why a developer's own evaluation is a starting point and not a verdict. You can walk a peer through one CASP checklist on a real paper.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find the evidence for something already in a report is weaker than you said. Raise it in supervision, agree how to correct it with the school, and adjust the evaluation line so the school can see whether it is working for this child.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Reading the abstract, seeing 'significant', and never checking design, comparison, effect size or who ran the evaluation.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Judge applicability to this child in this context', 'Say where the evidence is thin', and 'Cite evidence for recommendations'.

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Judge applicability to this child in this context
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A well-run trial tells you what worked on average, for those participants, delivered by those staff. It does not tell you it will work for this child in this school. Cartwright and Hardie (2012, Evidence-based policy, Oxford University Press) set out this gap between 'it worked there' and 'it will work here'. CORU SoP 5.4 is mapped here (read the clause for its wording). Ignore applicability and you recommend a programme built for groups of eight with a trained tutor to a two-teacher rural school with one SET and no one to run it.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the questions your supervisor asks about a school before recommending anything: who would deliver it, how often, with what training, in what room, alongside what else the child already gets under the Continuum of Support.

WRITE DOWN — the gap between the study and this case: the sample's age, language, difficulty and setting, set against the child's; and the delivery the study used, set against what this school can realistically provide.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when do you recommend something with good evidence that the school can only half deliver, and when do you choose something weaker that they'll actually do?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the comparison between the study conditions and this child's situation: age band, needs, co-occurring difficulties, school size, staffing, and the level of the Continuum the child is at.

THEY HOLD — the trade-off between strength of evidence and feasibility, and the conversation with the principal about capacity.

WHY THAT SPLIT — setting out the differences is careful reading you can do now. Deciding what a school can carry depends on knowing the school, its history with the service, and what has been tried before.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — for each evidence-based recommendation, add two or three lines to your working notes: how this child and school differ from the study, and what adaptation, if any, is needed.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a programme recommended at a dose or group size the school cannot provide; evidence from a different age band or population applied without comment; adaptations that remove the part that made it work.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'the trial ran three sessions a week with trained staff. Who is going to do that here?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — you check the study sample against the child (age, needs, language, setting) and the delivery against the school's capacity, and your recommendation says what has been adapted and why.

PASS TEST — Transferability considered

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the transferability lines in your working notes, and a sentence in the report recommendation where adaptation matters. Log against 8. Research and 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — the report recommends a well-evidenced programme, the school cannot resource it, it is delivered at a fraction of the dose, and at review everyone concludes the child 'did not respond'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between whether something works (efficacy in a trial) and whether it will work here (fit, fidelity and capacity), and why fidelity to the active ingredients matters more than fidelity to every detail. Fixsen et al. (2005, implementation research synthesis) is a useful starting point for the implementation side.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — the school has adapted a programme beyond recognition. Find out what they kept, agree which parts are essential, and build the review so you can tell whether the reduced version is doing anything.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Recommending the best-evidenced option without asking whether this school, with this staffing, can deliver it as it was tested.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Say where the evidence is thin', 'State how a recommendation would be evaluated', and 3. Intervention.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP

micro.name: Log the search as an Appendix 5 research entry
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A search that is done but not recorded does not count towards the Research competency, and on placement the Research competency is mostly evidenced through this kind of practice-based work rather than a separate project. The Reference sheet maps 'Handbook Appendix 5' here — check the current UCD Placement Handbook for the exact headings and expectations of an Appendix 5 entry before writing one; do not rely on memory or on this row. The entry is yours to write: this row gives structure and prompts, not text to submit.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor links a piece of reading to a case decision when they talk it through, and what they think a good research entry shows: the question, the search, the appraisal, and what changed as a result.

WRITE DOWN — the Appendix 5 headings from the current Handbook, and one example (from your Roscommon entries or a peer's, anonymised, with permission) of an entry your supervisor thought was strong.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'when you read a trainee's research entry, what tells you they actually used the evidence and didn't just find it?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — writing the entry: the question, how you searched, what you found, how you appraised it, what you concluded, and how it shaped what you recommended. The wording is yours.

THEY HOLD — feedback on whether the entry shows applied research competence, and the countersignature where the Handbook requires it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the entry is your own evidence of learning and must be in your own words. Your supervisor judges it; they do not write it, and neither does this workbook.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — aim for at least one research entry tied to a real Cavan case in the first half of the placement, completed within a week of the search while it is fresh, and bring it to supervision.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — an entry that is a literature summary with no case link; child identifiers; a search with no record; a conclusion that never says what you then did differently.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'what did you recommend because of this reading that you wouldn't have otherwise?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each entry names the question, the search (reproducibly), the appraisal, the conclusion and the effect on your practice, with no child or school identifiers, in your own words, under the Handbook headings.

PASS TEST — It is recorded

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the Appendix 5 entry itself, with the search note behind it kept on your own file. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — at the end of Cavan you have run several good searches and none of them is in Appendix 5, so the Research competency looks unevidenced.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain to a new trainee why a research entry is about using evidence rather than listing it, and show the chain from question to search to appraisal to recommendation to review, using an anonymised example of your own.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you reach the end of a block with no entries. Go back through your search log, choose the search that most changed a recommendation, and write it up now while you can still reconstruct it. Do not write up a search you cannot evidence, and do not use generated text for the entry.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Doing the searching but never writing it up, so the Research competency has no evidence at the end of the placement.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 8. Research, 'Cite evidence for recommendations', and the Research evidence reviewed at end-of-placement evaluation.

Not started

micro.name: Attach a source to every substantial recommendation
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
A cited recommendation tells the reader the claim is not only your opinion and lets them check it; the Reference sheet names this as one of the features that moves a report from a 3 to a 5. CORU SoP 5.4 is mapped here. The Reference sheet's rule is to cite the intervention, the framework and any claim about what typically works, at synthesis level, and not to pad: two or three well-chosen citations in a school report, not fifteen. An uncited recommendation invites the question 'says who?', and you may not be in the room when it is asked.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — which recommendations in your supervisor's reports carry a citation and which do not. Usually the intervention and the framework do; routine classroom strategies and test scores do not.

WRITE DOWN — where the citation sits (in the sentence, in a footnote, in a short reference list at the end), how many a typical school report carries, and which sources your supervisor cites often.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you decide which recommendation is substantial enough to need a source?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — adding the citation to each substantial recommendation in your draft, drawn from your own search note, and building the reference list.

THEY HOLD — whether the service's report template carries references at all, and how many are appropriate for this reader.

WHY THAT SPLIT — finding and attaching the source is your research work. Some services keep school reports reference-light for readability, and that is a house style your supervisor knows and you do not yet.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — draft every Cavan report with a source attached to each intervention and framework recommendation, and a short reference list.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — a report with no citations, or the opposite: a reference list padded with test manuals and single trials so it looks scholarly and reads like a literature review.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this recommends a structured phonics programme. Where would the teacher go to check that's well supported? And do we need the other twelve references?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each intervention, framework and 'what typically works' claim carries a synthesis-level source; routine strategies do not; the reference list is short and complete.

PASS TEST — There is a reference list

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report recommendations and reference list, named in the Appendix 5 entry. Log against 8. Research and 3. Intervention.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a principal asks why the report recommends a particular approach over the one the school already uses, and the report gives no basis beyond your say-so.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between citing to support a claim and citing to impress, why the synthesis is usually the right level for a school reader (for example, citing a review such as Snowling & Hulme, 2011, rather than one trial), and why test manuals are not cited for every score.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you realise a report has gone out with a key recommendation unsupported. Note the source in the case file and add it at the next review or addendum; if the recommendation cannot be supported, raise it in supervision.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Leaving the main intervention recommendation uncited, or padding the report with references that do no work.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Cite current sources rather than the familiar ones', 'Use APA 7th consistently', and 'Say where the evidence is thin'.

micro.name: Cite current sources rather than the familiar ones
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
Everyone has sources they learned in first year and have cited ever since. Evidence moves: syntheses are updated, recommendations change and programmes are re-evaluated. The EEF Toolkit, for instance, is revised over time, so any rating you quote may have changed — check the current toolkit entry. PSI Code 2.4.1 is the clause mapped here; read it in the Code itself. Citing an outdated source can mean recommending something the evidence has since moved away from, and an examiner notices a reference list with nothing from the last decade.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how your supervisor keeps up to date: journals they read, NEPS or Department guidance updates, PSI Division of Educational, Child and Adolescent Psychology events, and how they check whether a source they have used for years is still current.

WRITE DOWN — the date of each synthesis you rely on, whether a newer version or update exists, and any guidance document the service treats as current.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'what's something you used to recommend that you've stopped recommending because the evidence changed?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — checking the date and currency of every source you cite: looking for a newer version of a review, checking the current EEF Toolkit entry, and noting when a classic is cited for a concept rather than for current evidence.

THEY HOLD — the service's view on which guidance is current, and when an older source is still the right one.

WHY THAT SPLIT — checking dates is mechanical and yours. Knowing that a newer paper has not displaced an older one, or that a guidance document is under revision, often comes from experience in the field.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — before each report goes to your supervisor, check each reference: is there a newer synthesis, update or edition? Note the check in your search log.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — every citation a decade old or more; a superseded edition; a Toolkit rating quoted from memory; a classic used as though it were current evidence of effectiveness.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this review is quite old. Has it been updated? What does the Toolkit say now?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each source is the most recent adequate synthesis you could find, older sources are there for a reason you could state, and figures from living resources such as the EEF Toolkit are checked on the day.

PASS TEST — Recency checked

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the recency check noted in your search log, and the reference list in the report. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report quotes a Toolkit rating that has since been revised, and a teacher who checked the website points it out at the review meeting.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the difference between a foundational source cited for an idea (Vygotsky for the zone of proximal development, for example) and a source cited as evidence that something works, which should be current. You can show a peer how to check for updates to a review.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you find a newer review that changes the picture after the report has gone. Raise it in supervision, decide with your supervisor whether the school needs to be told, and update your search note so it is not repeated.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Citing the source you have always cited without checking whether it has been updated or superseded.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Say where the evidence is thin', 'Record the search terms and databases used', and 8. Research.

micro.name: Use APA 7th consistently
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
APA 7th (American Psychological Association, 2020, Publication manual, 7th ed.) is the convention your reports and your thesis use. The Reference sheet maps the UCD Academic Integrity Policy here: accurate referencing is part of how you show whose ideas are whose. Inconsistent or wrong referencing reads as careless thinking to an examiner, and a citation that does not match its reference list entry cannot be checked.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — how references appear in the service's reports: whether they follow APA 7th strictly, whether the house style changes anything, and how guidance documents from NEPS, the Department or the HSE are referenced (corporate author, year, title, URL).

WRITE DOWN — model references for the source types you cite most: journal article with DOI, book, chapter, government or agency report, webpage such as the EEF Toolkit, and test manual.

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'does the service follow APA exactly in reports to schools, or is there a house variation I should use?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — every in-text citation and reference list entry in your drafts, checked against the manual or the UCD library APA guide.

THEY HOLD — the service's house style, where it differs from APA, and the final sign-off on the report.

WHY THAT SPLIT — formatting is entirely checkable and entirely yours. A service may deliberately simplify referencing for parents, and that is its decision.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — format every reference in your Cavan reports and Appendix entries yourself, using a reference manager if you have one, and check the final list by hand before submission.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — in-text citations with no matching entry; 'et al.' used wrongly; missing DOIs; a mix of styles pasted from different sources; agency reports with no author or year.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'this cites Hulme 2011 in the text, but the list has Snowling and Hulme. Which is it?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — every in-text citation matches a list entry and every entry is cited; format follows APA 7th throughout, including DOIs and agency authors.

PASS TEST — Formatting is correct

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report reference list and your Appendix 5 entries. Log against 8. Research.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report reference list with three styles, a missing year and a citation to a paper that is not in the list, returned by your supervisor with the note 'please tidy before this goes out'.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain the main APA 7th rules for the source types EPs use most, how to reference a living webpage (with a retrieval date only where the manual requires one — check), and how a reference manager helps and where it gets things wrong.

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — a report goes out with referencing errors. Correct the master copy on the file, fix your template, and do a final check of the list against the text before every future report.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Letting in-text citations and the reference list drift apart, so a reader cannot find the source.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'Attach a source to every substantial recommendation', written report quality, and the thesis.

micro.name: Say where the evidence is thin
micro.text:
WHY THIS MICRO-SKILL MATTERS
PSI Code 4.2.6 is mapped here, and the Reference sheet reads it as requiring you not to suppress disconfirming evidence; it also cites 4.2.2 on not exaggerating effectiveness — read both clauses in the Code itself before quoting them. The Reference sheet's position is that 'evidence for Y is mixed, and it is recommended here because of [case-specific reason]' is more impressive than pretending certainty. Overstate the evidence and a school invests a term in something that was never likely to deliver, and trusts the next report less.

1 · WATCH
WATCH FOR — the words your supervisor uses for strength of evidence: 'strong', 'promising', 'mixed', 'limited', 'no trials, but'. Notice how they recommend something with a thin base without apologising for it.

WRITE DOWN — a short scale of phrases matched to evidence strength, and the phrases your supervisor avoids ('proven', 'guaranteed', 'research shows' with no qualifier).

ASK AFTERWARDS — 'how do you tell a school the evidence is mixed without them hearing "don't bother"?'

2 · DO ALONGSIDE
YOU TAKE — drafting the sentence that states the strength of the evidence for each recommendation, based on your appraisal note.

THEY HOLD — how that is framed for this school and family, particularly when a family is committed to an approach with little evidence behind it.

WHY THAT SPLIT — the evidence judgement follows from your appraisal. Telling parents that something they value has a thin base is a relationship conversation that your supervisor has had many times.

3 · LEAD, SUPERVISOR IN ROOM
YOU RUN IT — in each Cavan report, give every substantial recommendation one of: strong evidence, mixed or limited evidence with a case-specific reason, or no trial base with reasoning and an evaluation plan.

WHAT THEY ARE WATCHING FOR — certainty the evidence does not support; a single trial presented as settled; disconfirming findings left out; a no-evidence recommendation with no evaluation line.

STEPPING IN LOOKS LIKE — 'you've written "research shows". Does it? How strongly, and in children like this one?'

4 · LEAD, DISCUSS AFTER
YOU DO IT ALONE — each recommendation states how strong its evidence is, mixed or absent evidence is named honestly, and any recommendation with no trial base carries its reasoning and a plan to evaluate it for this child.

PASS TEST — Honest about the base

EVIDENCE TO FILE — the report recommendations, cross-referenced to your appraisal note in the Appendix 5 entry. Log against 8. Research and 6. Ethical Practice.

WHAT FAILURE LOOKS LIKE — a report says an approach 'has been shown to be effective' when your own appraisal found one small uncontrolled study.

5 · LEAD AND TEACH
YOU CAN TEACH IT — you can explain why stating uncertainty is an ethical requirement and a mark of competence, not a weakness, and why an honest 'no trials, but here is the reasoning and here is how we will know' is evidence-informed practice (CORU SoP 5.4).

WHEN IT GOES WRONG — you overstated the evidence in a report that has gone out. Raise it in supervision, agree a correction for the school, and make sure the evaluation line will show whether the recommendation is working for this child.

THE ERROR THAT COSTS MARKS
Writing 'research shows' when the evidence is mixed or thin, and leaving out what did not support the recommendation.

WHAT IT FEEDS INTO NEXT
→ Feeds into 'State how a recommendation would be evaluated', 6. Ethical Practice, and 3. Intervention.

WHERE I AM NOW (as at build — update in Skill progression)
Not started

THE SINGLE NEXT STEP
WATCH FOR — the words your supervisor uses for strength of evidence: 'strong', 'promising', 'mixed', 'limited', 'no trials, but'. Notice how they recommend something with a thin base without apologising for it.
