▸  Consider what else raises scores: bullying, bereavement, family stress, autism (social anxiety items overlap with social communication difficulty), and a pupil telling you what they think you want to hear. The RCADS has no validity scale; your observations are the check.

▸  Write the plan at the right Continuum level: Classroom Support (predictable routines, a named adult, planned check-ins), School Support (a small-group or individual CBT-informed programme, where the school has trained staff), School Support Plus (EP casework, referral). Re-administer after intervention to track change.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Letting a young person leave before you have read the depression items.

▸  Writing 'meets criteria for generalised anxiety disorder' from a questionnaire.

▸  Reporting only the total score and losing the subscale shape.

▸  Treating a low self-report as reassurance when the parent and teacher describe marked anxiety.

▸  Reading items aloud without recording that you did.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Chorpita, B. F., Yim, L., Moffitt, C., Umemoto, L. A., & Francis, S. E. (2000). Assessment of symptoms of DSM-IV anxiety and depression in children: A revised child anxiety and depression scale. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 38(8), 835–855. — plus the current RCADS user's guide from the authors.

▸  Ebesutani, C., Bernstein, A., Nakamura, B. J., Chorpita, B. F., & Weisz, J. R. (2010). A psychometric analysis of the Revised Child Anxiety and Depression Scale—Parent Version in a clinical sample. Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology, 38(2), 249–260.

▸  De Los Reyes, A., & Kazdin, A. E. (2005). Informant discrepancies in the assessment of childhood psychopathology. Psychological Bulletin, 131(4), 483–509.

▸  Department of Children and

tool.name: BASC-3
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know the family of forms (Reynolds & Kamphaus, 2015): Teacher Rating Scales (TRS) and Parent Rating Scales (PRS) at preschool, child and adolescent levels; Self-Report of Personality (SRP) at child, adolescent and college levels, with an interview version for younger children; plus the Structured Developmental History and the Student Observation System. The catalogue's 'BASC-3 SRP' is part of this entry. Check the exact age bands for each form in the manual before you choose.

▸  Decide why you want it. The BASC-3 is broad — externalising, internalising, school problems and adaptive skills in one instrument. That breadth suits a referral where you do not yet know what is driving the behaviour; for a narrow question (attention only, anxiety only) a focused measure is quicker and the Reference sheet (Part A, 'Behavioural and emotional rating scales') suggests the SDQ as a general first screen.

▸  Get at least a parent and a teacher form; at post-primary add the SRP and more than one subject teacher (Reference Part D, Adolescent). Is it all classes or some? That question often matters more than the scores.

▸  Norms are US. There are general and clinical norm groups, and combined-sex and sex-specific options — decide which you will use before scoring and state it in the report.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  It is a rating scale, so administration is instruction: the time frame (recent months — check the form wording), rate what you see rather than what you think causes it, answer every item. Raters who have known the child only a few weeks are rating a stranger.

▸  For the SRP, stay with the young person, check reading level, read items aloud if needed and record it. Tell them in advance who will see it.

▸  Check the form for omissions before the rater leaves; too many omitted items invalidate a scale, and the threshold is in the manual.

▸  Look at critical items on the SRP and PRS the same day. Some items concern self-harm, hopelessness or feeling unsafe; an endorsement goes to the risk route that day, not to the report next week.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score through Q-global or by hand with the manual. Scores are T-scores with percentiles; clinical and adaptive scales run in opposite directions (high is concerning on clinical scales, low on adaptive scales). Check the classification bands in the manual before you label anything 'at risk' or 'clinically significant'.

▸  Check the validity indexes first — they flag inconsistent, overly negative or overly positive responding (the SRP has additional indexes). A 'caution' or 'extreme caution' flag changes how much weight you put on everything else.

▸  Report composites and the scales beneath them, rater by rater, in a table that lets the reader compare home, school and self side by side.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  It describes the pattern and leaves the formulation to you (tool catalogue). 'Elevated hyperactivity at school but not at home' is a finding; why is your hypothesis, to be tested with observation and interview.

▸  Treat rater differences as information about settings and demands, not as someone being wrong (De Los Reyes & Kazdin, 2005). Lay them out and ask each rater what the child is like when it goes well.

▸  Adaptive scales matter for planning: social skills, functional communication and study skills are what you build the intervention on. Do not leave them out because the clinical scales are more dramatic.

▸  Elevated attention, anxiety or depression scales are reasons to refer or investigate, not diagnoses. ADHD goes to CAMHS or paediatrics; persistent low mood with impairment goes via the GP. You describe and recommend (PSI 2.2.2).

▸  Pitch recommendations at the Continuum level: a whole-class behaviour approach at Classroom Support, a targeted plan with a named adult at School Support, a functional behaviour assessment and multi-agency plan at School Support Plus.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Skipping the validity indexes.

▸  Reading high adaptive scores as a problem, or low clinical scores as reassurance, because the directions were confused.

▸  Finding a critical item on the SRP after the young person has gone home.

▸  Writing 'has ADHD' or 'is depressed' from rating-scale elevations.

▸  Not stating that the norms are US and which norm group was used.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Reynolds, C. R., & Kamphaus, R. W. (2015). BASC-3: Behavior Assessment System for Children (3rd ed.) manual. Pearson. — the chapters on validity indexes and interpretation.

▸  De Los Reyes, A., & Kazdin, A. E. (2005). Informant discrepancies in the assessment of childhood psychopathology. Psychological Bulletin, 131(4), 483–509.

▸  Achenbach, T. M., McConaughy, S. H., & Howell, C. T. (1987). Child/adolescent behavioral and emotional problems: Implications of cross-informant correlations for situational specificity. Psychological Bulletin, 101(2), 213–232.

tool.name: ADOS-2
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it is: the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (Lord et al., 2012) is a standardised, semi-structured observation of social communication, play and restricted/repetitive behaviour. There is a Toddler Module and Modules 1–4, chosen by expressive language level and age, not age alone — pre-verbal or single words (Toddler, Module 1), phrase speech (Module 2), fluent speech in children and younger adolescents (Module 3), fluent speech in older adolescents and adults (Module 4). The catalogue's 'ADOS-2 Toddler / Module 1', 'Module 2/3' and 'Module 3/4' are all this entry.

▸  Know who administers it. The ADOS-2 requires specific training — a recognised clinical training course and supervised practice — and is normally used within a multidisciplinary diagnostic process. In Ireland that is usually the HSE CDNT, CAMHS or a specialist assessment service (including Assessment of Need pathways under the Disability Act 2005), or a private diagnostic team. Check the publisher's and your service's current training requirement; a trainee EP on a school placement will almost never administer it.

▸  What the EP does with an ADOS-2 report: read it for what the child did in that structured hour — eye contact, gesture, reciprocal conversation, play, sensory interests — and set it beside what you see in class and yard. Use the observations (not the classification) to plan: where the child needs visual structure, explicit social teaching, predictable transitions, and adaptations to language demands.

▸  What the EP must not do: administer it without the training; re-score or re-run the algorithm from a report; tell a parent or school 'the ADOS shows autism' or 'the ADOS rules out autism'; treat a classification as the diagnosis; or use it as a school screening tool. Diagnosis is made by the team against DSM-5-TR or ICD-11 criteria, integrating history (e.g. ADI-R), observation and other information (NICE, 2011/2017).

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  If you are not trained, you do not administer it — say so plainly if a school or parent asks. What you can contribute to the diagnostic team is the school picture: structured classroom and yard observation, teacher information, SRS-2 or SCQ where appropriate, and your own account of the child across settings (Reference Part D).

▸  If you observe a trained colleague, watch how the activities create 'presses' for social communication — a pause for the child to initiate, an unexpected event, a request for help — and how the examiner keeps them standard while keeping the child engaged. The skill is in the presses, not the materials.

▸  Ask what the session was like for the child: new room, strangers, time of day, medication, anxiety. One hour in a clinic is a small sample; school observation over several settings complements it.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Coding and the algorithm (Social Affect and Restricted and Repetitive Behaviour domains, with a module-specific classification) are done by the trained examiner. Calibrated severity scores are available for some modules (Gotham et al., 2009) — check the report for what was used.

▸  When quoting a report, quote the author's name, role and date and the narrative observations, not only the classification. If something in the report looks inconsistent, contact the author rather than reinterpreting it.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  An ADOS-2 classification is one piece of evidence. Masking, anxiety, a good day, or a very structured examiner can lower scores in a verbally able child — often a girl — while language disorder, severe anxiety, attachment difficulty or low cognitive level can raise them. That is why it is team-used, not stand-alone (tool catalogue).

▸  If the ADOS-2 report and school observations disagree, the difference is information about setting and demand. Raise it with the CDNT keyworker or the diagnostic team in writing, not by contradicting their conclusion in your report.

▸  Translate for the school: each observation becomes a practical adjustment and a Continuum level — visual timetable and explicit transition warnings at Classroom Support; social communication teaching and a key adult at School Support; individual plan, NCSE/SENO involvement or special class consideration at School Support Plus.

▸  Your report says, for example: 'The CDNT assessment (ADOS-2 among other measures) noted…; in school I observed…; this suggests…' It does not restate or revise a diagnosis.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Administering or scoring the ADOS-2 without the required training.

▸  Writing 'the ADOS-2 confirmed autism' as if the observation made the diagnosis.

▸  Treating a non-spectrum classification as a rule-out in a masking child.

▸  Quoting the classification and ignoring the narrative observations that actually guide teaching.

▸  Contradicting a team diagnosis in an EP report instead of raising the discrepancy with the team.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Lord, C., Rutter, M., DiLavore, P. C., Risi, S., Gotham, K., & Bishop, S. L. (2012). Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, Second Edition (ADOS-2) manual. Western Psychological Services. — the introduction and the interpretation chapter.

▸  National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. (2011, updated 2017). Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s: Recognition, referral and diagnosis (CG128). NICE.

▸  Gotham, K., Pickles, A., & Lord, C. (2009). Standardizing ADOS scores for a measure of severity in autism spectrum disorders. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 39(5), 693–705.

▸  Current HSE and PSI guidance on autism assessment in Ireland (Reference Part A cites PSI Autism Guidelines, 2022) — check title and version before citing.

tool.name: SCQ (Social Communication Questionnaire)
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know where it comes from: the SCQ (Rutter et al., 2003; developed by Berument et al., 1999) is a short parent-completed yes/no questionnaire built from ADI-R items. It is for children aged 4 and over with a mental age above about 2 (tool catalogue). It is a screen — its job is to say 'worth a fuller look' or 'probably not', not to diagnose.

▸  Choose the form. The Lifetime form asks about the child's whole developmental history and is the one used for screening and referral; the Current form asks about the recent period and is more useful for describing present functioning and planning. Check the manual for the exact time frames.

▸  Know its weak spots before you rely on it: it depends on parental recall and knowledge of development; it is less sensitive in younger children and in verbally able children, particularly girls who mask (tool catalogue); and it is parent-report only, so it cannot tell you about school.

▸  Pair it with something from school — observation, teacher consultation, SRS-2 teacher form (Reference Part D, School Age) — and with a developmental history taken in conversation.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Explain to the parent what it is for, that it is a questionnaire not a test of the child, and that you will talk it through with them. Offer to read it with them if literacy, language or time is a barrier, and record that you did.

▸  Several items ask about behaviour at a specific earlier age. Parents often struggle with these; tell them to answer as best they can and note which items they were unsure about.

▸  Go through it together afterwards. 'You said yes to this one — can you tell me what that looked like?' turns a tick into history and catches misreadings.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score according to the manual — items are scored so that a higher total means more autism-related features, and some items are reverse-keyed. Check the scoring key rather than counting 'yes' answers.

▸  Compare the total with the manual's screening threshold. Check the manual for the figure and its basis before you quote it; do not quote a cut-off from memory in a report.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  A score above the threshold means refer for a full assessment — to the CDNT or through the Assessment of Need route, or via the GP — not 'likely autistic'. Say so in those words.

▸  A score below the threshold does not rule out autism, particularly in a verbally able child or a child whose parent has little comparison (tool catalogue; Chandler et al., 2007). If school or parent concern persists, the concern stands.

▸  Consider what else raises SCQ scores: language disorder, intellectual disability, significant anxiety, attachment difficulties and hearing impairment. Name the alternatives you considered in the report.

▸  Use the item content for planning even without a diagnosis — social communication needs described by the parent can go into a School Support plan now, while referral proceeds.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Writing 'the SCQ indicates autism'.

▸  Treating a below-threshold score as a rule-out.

▸  Using the Current form for a screening decision that needs the Lifetime form.

▸  Handing the form over without discussing the answers with the parent.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Rutter, M., Bailey, A., & Lord, C. (2003). The Social Communication Questionnaire manual. Western Psychological Services.

▸  Berument, S. K., Rutter, M., Lord, C., Pickles, A., & Bailey, A. (1999). Autism screening questionnaire: Diagnostic validity. British Journal of Psychiatry, 175(5), 444–451.

▸  Chandler, S., Charman, T., Baird, G., Simonoff, E., Loucas, T., Meldrum, D., Scott, M., & Pickles, A. (2007). Validation of the Social Communication Questionnaire in a population cohort study of autism spectrum disorders. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry, 46(10), 1324–1332.

tool.name: Vineland-3
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Like the ABAS-3, it measures what the person usually does, not what they can do when asked. The Vineland-3 (Sparrow et al., 2016) covers Communication, Daily Living Skills and Socialization, with optional Motor Skills (younger ages — check the manual) and Maladaptive Behavior sections, summarised as an Adaptive Behavior Composite.

▸  Choose the format: the Interview Form (a semi-structured interview with a parent or caregiver), the Parent/Caregiver Form (a rating form) and the Teacher Form, each in comprehensive and shorter domain-level versions. The age range runs from birth into late adulthood (tool catalogue: birth–90; 'Vineland-3 adult' is this entry) but the Teacher Form covers school ages only — check the ranges.

▸  The Interview Form is the Vineland's strength and needs practice: you ask open questions about the area and score the items from what you hear, rather than reading items aloud. Rehearse it with your supervisor before using it with a family.

▸  If intellectual disability is in question you need both an adaptive and a cognitive measure (Reference Part D, School Age; AAIDD definition). In special settings it is often more useful than an IQ score for planning (Reference Part D, Special Setting).

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  For the interview, start broad ('Tell me about how she gets dressed in the morning'), then narrow to the items you still need. Record what the parent said as well as your score — it is the evidence behind the rating.

▸  Keep the distinction between 'can' and 'does' in front of the parent: 'Does he usually do it without being reminded?' A skill done only with prompting scores differently from one done independently; check the scoring rules.

▸  For rating forms, sit with the rater or at least explain the response options, and check for 'don't know' or estimated items before they leave.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score with the manual or Q-global. Domain and composite standard scores, subdomain v-scale scores, and age equivalents are available; basal and ceiling rules apply on the comprehensive interview — check them.

▸  Look at subdomains, not just the composite. A flat profile and a spiky one (e.g. strong daily living, weak interpersonal relationships) lead to different plans.

▸  Norms are US; state that in the report.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Compare with the cognitive profile. Adaptive scores well below cognitive may mean lack of opportunity, anxiety or over-support; adaptive above cognitive may mean good scaffolding or an underestimate on the cognitive test.

▸  Watch for adult support suppressing independence — an item 'usually done' may mean usually done by the SNA. Ask who does it.

▸  Home and school ratings often differ; the difference tells you where skills generalise and where they do not.

▸  For young adults and school leavers, use it for transition planning and adult-services referral (tool catalogue 'Vineland-3 adult'): travel, money, self-care and community skills are what the next placement needs to know.

▸  Maladaptive behaviour items are descriptive; they do not diagnose. Use them to prioritise and refer.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Reading interview items aloud instead of conducting a semi-structured interview.

▸  Scoring what the child can do in the clinic rather than what they usually do.

▸  Reporting the composite without the subdomain profile.

▸  Using the Vineland alone to suggest intellectual disability.

▸  Missing that 'usually does' means 'an adult does it with him'.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Sparrow, S. S., Cicchetti, D. V., & Saulnier, C. A. (2016). Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Third Edition (Vineland-3) manual. Pearson. — the interview-technique chapter first.

▸  Tassé, M. J., Schalock, R. L., Balboni, G., Bersani, H., Borthwick-Duffy, S. A., Spreat, S., Thissen, D., Widaman, K. F., & Zhang, D. (2012). The construct of adaptive behavior: Its conceptualization, measurement, and use in the field of intellectual disability. American Journal on Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities, 117(4), 291–303.

tool.name: TEA-Ch2
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it measures: the Test of Everyday Attention for Children, Second Edition (Manly et al., 2016) is a performance-based battery of attention — sustained, selective and switching attention and related executive control — using game-like tasks. There are junior and older versions by age; check which covers the child (catalogue: 5:0–15:11).

▸  Know what it is not: it measures attention on standardised tasks in a quiet room with an adult present, which is the setting where many children with attentional difficulties do best. It cannot tell you about everyday functioning — pair it with BRIEF-2 or Conners and classroom observation (tool catalogue; Reference Part D, School Age).

▸  Check the kit and equipment before the session: some tasks are timed, some use audio or computer delivery. Test the laptop, audio and response devices; a failed audio track invalidates the task.

▸  Plan the order and breaks. Fatigue affects sustained attention scores directly; do not put it at the end of a long cognitive session.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Follow the practice items and scripted instructions exactly. Many tasks depend on the child understanding the rule before the scored trial; the manual says when you may repeat practice.

▸  Observe how the child performs as well as the score: drifting partway through, impulsive responding, self-talk, needing to restart. These are often what makes the result useful to a teacher.

▸  Record anything that interferes — noise, interruptions, the child needing the toilet. On timed attention tasks an interruption is not a minor note.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Convert raw scores using the manual or scoring software for the child's age; many tasks yield scaled scores and some yield separate speed and accuracy scores. Check which scores the manual recommends interpreting for each task.

▸  Look at speed–accuracy trade-offs; a fast, error-prone child and a slow, accurate child can have similar totals and different needs.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Interpret the pattern across types of attention: difficulty sustaining attention on a dull task is different from difficulty switching between rules, and the recommendations differ (chunked tasks and movement breaks vs explicit transition cues).

▸  Normal-range scores do not rule out attentional difficulty in class — the test setting is structured and one-to-one (Manly et al., 2001 discuss the value and limits of the test context). Weight rater and observation data accordingly.

▸  Consider alternative explanations for low scores: anxiety, fatigue, low mood, language comprehension of instructions, hearing, motivation.

▸  It does not diagnose ADHD. It can describe an attention profile and support a referral to CAMHS or paediatrics, and it can inform School Support level recommendations now (PSI 2.2.2).

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Concluding 'no attention difficulty' from normal-range test scores despite classroom concern.

▸  Running it at the end of a long session.

▸  Not checking audio or computer equipment before starting.

▸  Presenting TEA-Ch2 findings as evidence for or against ADHD.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Manly, T., Anderson, V., Crawford, J., George, M., Underbjerg, M., & Robertson, I. H. (2016). Test of Everyday Attention for Children, Second Edition (TEA-Ch2) manual. Pearson.

▸  Manly, T., Anderson, V., Nimmo-Smith, I., Turner, A., Watson, P., & Robertson, I. H. (2001). The differential assessment of children's attention: The Test of Everyday Attention for Children (TEA-Ch), normative sample and ADHD performance. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 42(8), 1065–1081.

tool.name: Leiter-3
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know why you would choose it. The Leiter-3 (Roid et al., 2013) assesses non-verbal cognitive ability and attention/memory with instructions given by gesture and demonstration, not speech. It is the option when language disorder, hearing impairment, autism with limited speech or very recent arrival with EAL would make a verbal battery invalid (tool catalogue; Reference Part D, Special Setting).

▸  Know what it cannot tell you: verbal reasoning, which for many children is the area of concern. Use it alongside other information, not instead of understanding the child's language (tool catalogue).

▸  Practise the gestural administration until it is natural. Pantomimed instruction is a skill; awkward or inconsistent gestures are a source of error the norms do not account for.

▸  Norms are US. For children with EAL, a non-verbal test reduces but does not remove cultural loading — familiarity with test materials and the idea of timed puzzles also differ. Record the child's language and schooling history (Cummins, 2000).

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Keep speech to the minimum the manual allows. If you start explaining in words, you have changed the test; note any verbal support you gave.

▸  Watch how the child approaches the tasks — trial and error vs planning, attention to detail, response to getting items wrong. This is especially informative when you cannot rely on talk.

▸  Check the rules for each subtest (start, stop and timing) in the manual before the session. Some attention and memory subtests have specific timing requirements.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score with the manual or scoring software: subtest scaled scores and a Nonverbal IQ, plus attention/memory composites if those subtests were given. Check which subtests feed which composite.

▸  Report confidence intervals and percentiles, and state that the score is a non-verbal estimate.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Report it for what it is: 'non-verbal reasoning, measured without spoken instructions'. Do not present a Nonverbal IQ as a general IQ.

▸  Where the Leiter-3 is in the average range and language is weak, the finding is important: it points toward a language-specific need and toward SLT, not toward a general learning difficulty.

▸  Where it is low, consider attention, motivation, visual processing and unfamiliarity with the task before concluding low ability. Intellectual disability needs an adaptive measure too (Reference Part D).

▸  In a special setting, link findings to the curriculum the child is following (L1LP/L2LP) rather than to mainstream norms.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Reporting the Nonverbal IQ as if it were a full-scale IQ.

▸  Giving spoken explanations and not recording it.

▸  Choosing it for an EAL pupil without recording language and schooling history.

▸  Concluding intellectual disability from a non-verbal score alone.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Roid, G. H., Miller, L. J., Pomplun, M., & Koch, C. (2013). Leiter International Performance Scale, Third Edition (Leiter-3) manual. Stoelting.

▸  Cummins, J. (2000). Language, power and pedagogy: Bilingual children in the crossfire. Multilingual Matters.

tool.name: WNV (Wechsler Non-Verbal)
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know the instrument: the Wechsler Nonverbal Scale of Ability (Wechsler & Naglieri, 2006) for ages 4:0–21:11 uses pictorial directions and brief standard instructions, with minimal language demand (tool catalogue). Subtests differ between the younger and older age batteries, and there are shorter and longer versions — check the manual for which subtests each uses.

▸  Choose it for a reason and write the reason in the report: EAL, language disorder, hearing impairment or a child for whom a verbal battery would measure language rather than reasoning (tool catalogue: 'state why a non-verbal measure was chosen').

▸  Check the norms and instruction languages your kit supports. The WNV was designed with translated instructions for several languages; check whether the child's language is among them and whether an interpreter is needed.

▸  Like any non-verbal measure, it cannot tell you about verbal reasoning (tool catalogue).

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Use the pictorial directions as designed and the standard verbal instructions only as the manual permits. Practise the pictorial demonstrations beforehand; they should be as fluent as a spoken script.

▸  Some subtests are timed and some involve memory; follow the timing and discontinue rules exactly.

▸  Observe the child's approach and record it: planning, persistence, response to difficulty, use of trial and error.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Convert raw scores using the manual for the child's age. The WNV yields T-scores for subtests and a full-scale score; check the manual for the score metrics and which subtests feed it.

▸  Report the full-scale score with its confidence interval and percentile, and describe the subtests in plain language.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Frame the result as non-verbal ability. It is not a full picture of cognitive ability and should not be presented as one.

▸  Put it beside what you know about language: an average WNV with weak English or weak language may point to EAL or DLD rather than a general learning difficulty; seek SLT and EAL information before drawing conclusions (Cummins, 2000).

▸  Consider the child's educational history, culture and familiarity with tests; non-verbal does not mean culture-free.

▸  Recommendations should build on the strength — visual supports, modelling and demonstration — at the right Continuum level.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Not stating why a non-verbal measure was used.

▸  Describing the result as the child's IQ.

▸  Using English instructions with a child who needed the translated or pictorial version.

▸  Concluding general learning difficulty without language and schooling history.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Wechsler, D., & Naglieri, J. A. (2006). Wechsler Nonverbal Scale of Ability (WNV) administration and scoring manual, and technical and interpretive manual. Harcourt Assessment / Pearson.

▸  Cummins, J. (2000). Language, power and pedagogy: Bilingual children in the crossfire. Multilingual Matters.

tool.name: BAS-3
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know the instrument: the British Ability Scales, Third Edition (Elliott & Smith, 2011, GL Assessment) is a UK-normed cognitive battery for 3:0–17:11 with an Early Years battery and a School Age battery. Core scales give a General Conceptual Ability (GCA) and cluster scores; diagnostic scales assess memory, processing speed and related skills; and there are attainment scales. Check the manual for which subtests belong to each cluster and battery.

▸  Check which edition and norms your service holds (tool catalogue). Some services still hold BAS-II kits; do not mix record forms or norm tables across editions.

▸  Choose it for a reason. The BAS-3's UK norms and flexible item sets are useful for younger children and for children who find a long Wechsler battery hard; write why you chose it over WISC-V UK or WPPSI-IV UK.

▸  As with any cognitive battery, rule out vision, hearing, language and emotional confounds first and write the referral question down.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  The BAS-3 uses item sets with decision points rather than simple start and stop rules: the child is given a block of items suited to their level, and you decide whether to continue, stop or go back based on the number passed. Learn the decision rules for each subtest before the session.

▸  Follow the scripted instructions and teaching items exactly; record responses verbatim where required.

▸  Record behaviour as you go — approach, persistence, language, attention — just as you would for WISC-V.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Raw scores convert to ability scores (because different item sets are given to different children) and then to T-scores and standard scores. Check the conversion steps in the manual; this is where scoring errors happen.

▸  Report GCA and cluster scores with confidence intervals and percentiles; check whether differences between clusters are statistically significant and unusual using the manual's tables.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Interpret clusters and subtest patterns with the same caution as any battery — a GCA can hide very different profiles (Watkins, 2000 on profile analysis).

▸  Use the attainment scales for a quick check, but for a full literacy or numeracy picture you need a dedicated attainment test (e.g. WIAT-III UK).

▸  Link findings to classroom demands and recommendations at the right Continuum level: e.g. a weak memory or processing-speed cluster becomes chunked instructions, written backup and extra time at Classroom Support, and a targeted plan at School Support.

▸  State the edition and norms used, and any adaptations. UK norms are closer than US norms to Irish pupils but are not Irish norms; say so.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Misapplying the item-set decision rules.

▸  Converting raw scores straight to T-scores without the ability-score step.

▸  Mixing BAS-II and BAS-3 materials or norms.

▸  Reporting a GCA when clusters differ significantly without comment.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Elliott, C. D., & Smith, P. (2011). British Ability Scales, Third Edition (BAS3) administration and scoring manual, and technical manual. GL Assessment.

▸  Watkins, M. W. (2000). Cognitive profile analysis: A shared professional myth. School Psychology Quarterly, 15(4), 465–479.

tool.name: Beery VMI
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it measures: the Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration (Beery et al., 2010) asks the child to copy a sequence of increasingly complex geometric forms. It measures the integration of visual perception and fine motor control — relevant to handwriting and copying (Reference Part D, DCD and handwriting).

▸  Know what it cannot tell you alone: whether a low score is visual, motor or integrative. For that you need the supplementary Visual Perception and Motor Coordination tests (tool catalogue).

▸  Check the edition and form (full form vs shorter form for younger children) and the norms; the age range extends from early childhood into adulthood (tool catalogue: 2:0–100).

▸  It is often used by OTs; where an OT is involved, coordinate so the child is not tested twice.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Follow the manual: the child copies each form in the booklet without erasing or rotating the booklet; stop according to the discontinue rule. Check the rules before the session.

▸  Observe grip, posture, pressure, speed and hand dominance — often as informative as the score for OT referral and classroom advice.

▸  Give the supplementary tests in the order and conditions the manual specifies if you need to separate visual from motor difficulty.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score each copied form against the manual's specific criteria; do not score by impression. Scoring the forms is where trainee error is common — have your first protocols checked.

▸  Convert to standard scores and percentiles for the child's age using the manual.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  A low VMI with a normal Visual Perception score points toward motor involvement; the reverse points toward perception. Both low suggests broader difficulty — interpret with care and in context.

▸  Link to classroom demands: copying from the board, handwriting speed (DASH), worksheet layout. Recommendations include reducing copying, providing notes, and access to keyboarding, with RACE applications where relevant at post-primary.

▸  It does not diagnose DCD. That is made by OT/paediatrics with motor assessment (e.g. Movement ABC-2) and history (DCD-Q). You describe and refer.

▸  Consider vision (ophthalmology check) and attention before concluding a visual-motor difficulty.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Scoring forms by impression rather than the criteria.

▸  Reporting a low VMI as a diagnosis of DCD.

▸  Not giving the supplementary tests when the question is visual vs motor.

▸  Ignoring vision as a possible factor.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Beery, K. E., Buktenica, N. A., & Beery, N. A. (2010). The Beery-Buktenica Developmental Test of Visual-Motor Integration (6th ed.) manual. Pearson.

▸  Feder, K. P., & Majnemer, A. (2007). Handwriting development, competency, and intervention. Developmental Medicine and Child Neurology, 49(4), 312–317.

tool.name: Preschool Language Scales-5 (PLS-5)
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know whose test it usually is. The PLS-5 (Zimmerman, Steiner & Pond, 2011; UK edition published by Pearson — check the year on your copy) is in Irish practice a speech and language therapist's instrument, administered by Primary Care or CDNT SLTs. Check the publisher's user qualification level and your service's policy before you consider administering it yourself; in most cases you will not.

▸  What you will usually do is read an SLT report that contains it. Know the structure so you can read it: two scales — Auditory Comprehension and Expressive Communication — combining into a Total Language score, reported as standard scores with percentile ranks. Check the report for confidence intervals and the edition (US or UK norms).

▸  Age range birth–7:11 (tool catalogue). Beyond early primary the SLT will usually move to the CELF-5 UK; if the report you are reading is a PLS-5 on a child over about 6, ask why — it may have been chosen deliberately for a child with significant language needs.

▸  Establish home language exposure first (tool catalogue, 'CANNOT TELL YOU'). A child learning English as an additional language will score low on an English-normed test; that describes their English, not a disorder. Ask what languages are spoken at home, by whom, and since when, and whether the SLT assessed in the home language.

▸  Check hearing before any language referral — a history of glue ear or a missed newborn/school hearing follow-up changes the picture. Ask when audiology last saw the child.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  If you are ever asked to administer it, follow the script exactly: verbal stimuli are the test, and toy manipulation tasks for the youngest ages have specified materials and prompts. Record verbatim.

▸  Your usual role is complementary: observe the child in the preschool or classroom (following group instructions, joining play, how peers understand them), gather parent and practitioner report, and bring the child's functional communication to the joint discussion. The PLS-5 is a structured one-to-one sample; you see the child in the noisy room.

▸  Contribute the developmental and early years context the SLT may not have: AIM (Access and Inclusion Model) supports in the preschool, PHN developmental checks, and how the child copes with routine and transitions (Reference Part D, Early Years).

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Scoring is from manual tables by exact age; the scores that matter are the two scale scores and Total Language with confidence intervals. Do not quote cut-offs or severity bands from memory — check the manual or quote the SLT.

▸  When you cite an SLT's PLS-5 results in your report, give the author, date, scale scores and percentiles, and keep their wording for any diagnostic statement (for example DLD). Do not restate it as your conclusion.

▸  Look at the gap between the two scales. A receptive score well below expressive is easily missed in class, because the child talks and so is assumed to understand.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Language diagnosis (DLD, or language disorder associated with another condition) is made by the SLT, using the CATALISE framework of functional impact and persistence, not a single score (Bishop et al., 2017). The EP does not diagnose it.

▸  Read the PLS-5 alongside cognitive and adaptive information. Low language in the context of broadly low development points to a different formulation and different supports from low language in an otherwise typically developing child — but this is a hypothesis to discuss with the SLT, not a conclusion from one report.

▸  Translate the SLT's findings into what the setting does: simplified and chunked instructions, visual supports, modelling and expanding the child's utterances, checking comprehension rather than compliance. Name the SLT's own programme and who will run it.

▸  In early years, remember the Continuum of Support is a school framework; in preschool the equivalent structures are AIM and the setting's own planning. Say which applies and check local arrangements.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Administering it without checking user qualification and service policy.

▸  Interpreting a low score in an EAL child without establishing home language exposure.

▸  Restating an SLT's diagnostic conclusion as your own finding.

▸  Missing a receptive–expressive split because the child is chatty.

▸  Referring to SLT without first checking hearing and existing assessments.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Zimmerman, I. L., Steiner, V. G., & Pond, R. E. (2011). Preschool Language Scales (5th ed.): Examiner's manual. Pearson. — and the UK edition's supplement; check which your SLT colleagues use.

▸  Bishop, D. V. M., Snowling, M. J., Thompson, P. A., Greenhalgh, T., & the CATALISE-2 consortium. (2017). Phase 2 of CATALISE: A multinational and multidisciplinary Delphi consensus study of problems with language development: Terminology. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 58(10), 1068–1080.

tool.name: Schedule of Growing Skills II
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it is: a developmental screening and profiling tool for 0–5 (tool catalogue), by Bellman, Lingam and Aukett (1996). It places a child's skills against developmental expectations across nine skill areas; it is not a cognitive assessment and does not give an IQ-type score.

▸  The nine areas, as set out in the manual, cover posture and locomotion, manipulation, vision, hearing and language, speech and language, interactive social and self-care social skills — check the exact area names in your kit and use them as printed in the report.

▸  Know where it sits in the Irish early years pathway. Part D lists it with developmental history, PHN records and Griffiths III via CDNT; NEPS involvement at this age is usually consultation, not assessment (Reference Part D, Early Years). Before using it, ask whether a PHN, CDNT or paediatric assessment already exists — duplicate testing is burdensome for families.

▸  Check the norms and edition. The standardisation is from the 1990s and UK-based; check the manual for the sample and treat it as a profiling tool, not a precise normative comparison.

▸  Plan the setting: the child's own preschool or home, a parent present, familiar toys available. A young child's performance in a strange room with a stranger underestimates them.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Combine direct observation, structured play items and parent report, as the manual specifies. For many items the parent is the best informant; record which items were observed and which were reported.

▸  Follow the child's lead within the structure: present items in the order that keeps the child engaged rather than rigidly, if the manual permits — check. Note state, attention, interest in people versus objects, and how the child responds to the parent.

▸  Time: 20–30 minutes (tool catalogue). Stop and rearrange if the child is tired, hungry or distressed; a partial profile with a note is better than a complete one obtained under distress.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  The output is a developmental profile — the level reached in each skill area, charted — rather than a standard score. Check the manual for how levels are assigned and how to chart them.

▸  Score immediately and chart the profile. The shape — even across areas, or one area standing apart — is what you will talk to parents and CDNT about.

▸  Record the child's age corrected for prematurity if relevant and if the manual advises it; check the manual's guidance and state what you did.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  It tells you where a child is, not why (tool catalogue). A delay in speech and language could reflect hearing, language exposure, a language disorder, social communication difference or global delay — the profile is a reason to ask, not an answer.

▸  An uneven profile is the key finding: language and social areas behind motor and self-care suggests a different referral from a profile that is behind evenly. Say which referrals follow — audiology, SLT, CDNT, paediatrics — and why.

▸  A screening tool at this age has limited predictive value; development in the preschool years is variable. Write a review point, not a prognosis.

▸  Frame recommendations for the preschool: AIM supports, practitioner strategies for language and play, and what the setting should watch for over the next term. Check current AIM levels and eligibility with the local service before naming them.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Presenting the profile as a diagnosis or an IQ equivalent.

▸  Assessing a child already assessed by the CDNT or PHN without checking first.

▸  Not recording which items were observed and which reported by the parent.

▸  Ignoring hearing and language exposure when speech and language is the low area.

▸  Writing a prognosis from a single preschool screen.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Bellman, M., Lingam, S., & Aukett, A. (1996). Schedule of Growing Skills II: User's guide. NFER-Nelson. — check the publisher and edition on your kit (later distributed by GL Assessment).

▸  Frederickson, N., & Cline, T. (2015). Special educational needs, inclusion and diversity (3rd ed.). Open University Press. — the chapters on early identification.

tool.name: Renfrew Action Picture Test
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know whose test it usually is. The Renfrew Action Picture Test (RAPT; Renfrew, first published 1966, revised editions since — check the edition on your copy) is widely used by SLTs. It is quick and simple, which is exactly why it is misused. Check your service's policy on EP use; most often you will read it in an SLT report.

▸  Know what it measures: the information content and grammar of the child's spoken responses to a set of action pictures (tool catalogue: 'Information and grammar in spoken narrative'). It does not measure receptive language (tool catalogue).

▸  About 10 minutes (tool catalogue). The catalogue gives 3:0–8:11, but the 5th edition (2019, re-standardised) gives age norms only to about 8:5 — check the upper limit in your edition before using it with an older child. Older editions give age equivalents from a dated UK sample. Know which edition you or the SLT used before quoting any score.

▸  Establish home language and hearing first, as for any English-language test. An EAL child's grammar in English is not a measure of their language ability.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Use the exact question for each picture as printed. The question shapes the response — a leading question produces a fuller sentence and a higher grammar score.

▸  Record the child's response verbatim, as it is said, including errors and omissions. Scoring depends on the exact words. If your service permits, audio-record with consent; you cannot reconstruct grammar from notes afterwards.

▸  If you are not administering it, your role is to observe the child's spoken language in class and play — length and complexity of sentences, whether others understand them, how they retell a story — and bring that to the discussion with the SLT.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Two scores: Information (content words conveyed) and Grammar (the structures used), each scored against the manual's criteria and converted to age equivalents or scores depending on the edition. Use the scoring examples in the manual; do not score on impression.

▸  Age equivalents are the weakest kind of score — they are not equal-interval and exaggerate small differences. Report them cautiously and say so; check whether your edition gives standard scores.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Compare Information and Grammar. Good information with weak grammar looks different from weak information with adequate grammar — the first often reflects expressive language structure, the second can reflect word-finding, vocabulary or attention to the picture.

▸  One ten-minute picture task is a narrow sample. Put it beside the SLT's broader assessment (for example CELF-5 UK or PLS-5), classroom observation and parent report before drawing any conclusion.

▸  Language diagnosis stays with the SLT (Bishop et al., 2017). The EP contribution is how the child's expressive language affects learning and participation, and what the class teacher does: modelling and recasting, sentence frames, time to respond, and accepting non-verbal ways of showing knowledge.

▸  Say what it cannot tell you in the report: receptive language, pragmatics and written language are not measured.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Rephrasing the question to 'help' the child.

▸  Scoring from memory or notes instead of a verbatim record.

▸  Quoting age equivalents as though they were precise.

▸  Treating good expressive language as evidence of good understanding.

▸  Drawing a language conclusion from the Renfrew alone.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Renfrew, C. (2019). Action Picture Test (5th ed.). Speechmark/Routledge. — earlier editions (e.g. 1997) have older norms; check the edition on your copy.

▸  Bishop, D. V. M., Snowling, M. J., Thompson, P. A., Greenhalgh, T., & the CATALISE-2 consortium. (2017). Phase 2 of CATALISE: A multinational and multidisciplinary Delphi consensus study of problems with language development: Terminology. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 58(10), 1068–1080.

tool.name: YARC (York Assessment of Reading for Comprehension)
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know the parts. The YARC (Snowling et al., 2009; later editions — check yours) has an Early Reading set for the youngest children, a Passage Reading set for primary, and a separate Secondary version (Stothard et al., 2010). The catalogue range is 4:0–16:0; confirm which booklet covers your child's age.

▸  Know the question it answers: reading accuracy, reading rate and reading comprehension from connected text (tool catalogue). It is built around the Simple View of Reading (Gough & Tunmer, 1986) — decoding and language comprehension can fail separately — which is why it is useful for separating a decoding problem from a comprehension problem.

▸  Pair it with a phonological measure (tool catalogue, 'CANNOT TELL YOU') such as PhAB2 or CTOPP-2 if decoding is weak, and with oral language information (SLT report, BPVS-3) if comprehension is weak.

▸  Find out what the school already has: Micra-T or Drumcondra standardised results, and the special education teacher's own records (Reference Part D, School Age). The YARC adds most when it separates components that a group test merges.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Choose the starting passage as the manual directs (usually from a single-word reading test or reading level), not by age alone. A child started too high is timed struggling with a text and the rate and comprehension scores are contaminated.

▸  Mark errors live while timing; know the error categories and the rules on prompting before the session. Practise on a colleague — as with WIAT-III Oral Reading Fluency, a reading-aloud task cannot be re-scored from memory.

▸  Follow the manual on whether the child may look back at the text when answering, and on which passages count towards which score. Check this every time; it is where trainees drift.

▸  Record reading behaviour: finger-tracking, self-correction, guessing from the first letter, reading for meaning versus word-by-word, and the child's response to not knowing a word.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Accuracy, rate and comprehension each convert to standard scores by age; check the manual for which passages must be completed for each score to be valid, and whether the rate score applies to all passages.

▸  Score the same day and double-check the age calculation and table. Report each component separately with its percentile; a single 'reading age' hides exactly the split the test was chosen to find.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Read the three components as a profile. Accurate and slow is a fluency problem. Accurate and fluent with weak comprehension is a language or vocabulary problem — the 'poor comprehender' profile described by Nation and Snowling. Inaccurate decoding is phonological. Each leads to different recommendations.

▸  For a poor comprehender, look for oral language weakness before recommending reading comprehension strategies alone; oral vocabulary and language work is the evidence-based target (Clarke, Snowling, Truelove & Hulme, 2010).

▸  Always ask what has been taught and for how long. A low accuracy score after two years of structured phonics is a different finding from one with no systematic teaching.

▸  Link to the Continuum of Support and to what the school can deliver: the finding names the target, and the recommendation names who, how often, for how long and how progress will be measured (Skill progression, 'Link the profile to what the school can deliver').

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Starting at the wrong passage.

▸  Reporting a single reading score instead of the accuracy/rate/comprehension profile.

▸  Treating weak comprehension as a reading problem without checking oral language.

▸  Not pairing weak decoding with a phonological measure.

▸  Concluding a difficulty without establishing instructional history.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Snowling, M. J., Stothard, S. E., Clarke, P., Bowyer-Crane, C., Harrington, A., Truelove, E., Nation, K., & Hulme, C. (2009). York Assessment of Reading for Comprehension: Passage Reading. GL Assessment. — the manual; check the edition and author list on your copy.

▸  Clarke, P. J., Snowling, M. J., Truelove, E., & Hulme, C. (2010). Ameliorating children's reading-comprehension difficulties: A randomized controlled trial. Psychological Science, 21(8), 1106–1116.

▸  Gough, P. B., & Tunmer, W. E. (1986). Decoding, reading, and reading disability. Remedial and Special Education, 7(1), 6–10.

tool.name: Neale Analysis of Reading Ability
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know the edition. In Ireland and the UK the version in most cupboards is the NARA II (Neale, 1997, second revised British edition). Its UK standardisation dates from the 1990s — check the year in your manual and say in the report that the norms are dated.

▸  Know what it measures: accuracy, comprehension and rate from graded narrative passages read aloud (tool catalogue), age 6:0–12:11. It does not measure spelling or written expression (tool catalogue).

▸  It has parallel forms, so it can be used to measure progress without repeating the same passages. Check which form the child had last and when, if they have been assessed before.

▸  Decide between the Neale and the YARC. Both give accuracy, rate and comprehension; the YARC has more recent norms and was designed around the Simple View of Reading. Know why you chose the one you used, and say so if asked.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  The examiner supplies words the child cannot read, within the manual's rules, so that comprehension is less contaminated by decoding. This is the Neale's distinctive feature — learn the prompting rule and the time allowed before you supply a word.

▸  Mark errors live using the manual's error categories (for example mispronunciations, substitutions, refusals, additions, omissions, reversals) and time each passage. Check the category list and the discontinue rule in your manual before the session.

▸  Ask the comprehension questions exactly as printed after each passage. Follow the manual on whether the passage stays in view.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Raw scores convert to reading ages, percentiles and standard scores for accuracy, comprehension and rate — check the manual tables for your form. Score the same day.

▸  Report standard scores and percentiles in preference to reading ages; reading ages are unequal-interval and tempt readers to over-interpret a few months' difference.

▸  The error analysis is often more useful than the score: tally the error types and note whether errors preserve meaning.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Compare accuracy with comprehension. Because the examiner supplies unknown words, comprehension can hold up despite weak accuracy — that pattern points to decoding as the barrier and to good language comprehension to build on.

▸  Weak comprehension with adequate accuracy needs an oral language explanation checked before a reading one (see YARC). Weak rate with adequate accuracy points to fluency work.

▸  Put the result beside the school's standardised tests (Micra-T, Drumcondra), a phonological measure and instructional history. The Neale on its own does not establish dyslexia (Rose, 2009).

▸  Say in the report that the norms are dated and that this limits the precision of the standard score.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Using it outside 6:0–12:11.

▸  Not supplying words as the manual requires, or supplying them too soon.

▸  Reporting reading ages as the headline result.

▸  Re-testing with the same form within a short interval.

▸  Not stating the age of the norms in the report.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Neale, M. D. (1997). Neale Analysis of Reading Ability: Second revised British edition — manual. NFER-Nelson.

▸  Rose, J. (2009). Identifying and teaching children and young people with dyslexia and literacy difficulties. Department for Children, Schools and Families.

tool.name: Phonological Assessment Battery (PhAB2)
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know its lineage. The original PhAB was developed by Frederickson, Frith and Reason (1997); PhAB2 Primary (Gibbs & Bodman, 2014, GL Assessment) is the updated edition for 5–11 years; there is no PhAB2 secondary edition, and for older pupils the original PhAB (6–14 years) is still the GL version (GL Assessment product information). The catalogue's 5:0–14:11 merges the two — check which kit you hold and its age range.

▸  Know what it measures: phonological awareness, rapid naming and phonological memory (tool catalogue). It does not measure reading comprehension or vocabulary (tool catalogue).

▸  Choose it when decoding is the concern — for example when the YARC or Neale shows inaccurate reading — and have the reading results and instructional history in front of you. A phonological battery without a reading measure answers half a question.

▸  It is UK-normed, which is an advantage over US-normed batteries such as CTOPP-2 for Irish children. Check whether the Irish-medium context (Gaelscoil, Gaeltacht) or EAL affects the child's performance on English phonological tasks.

▸  Practise clean phoneme production before the session — no added vowel ('buh' for /b/) — and have the stopwatch ready for the naming tasks (Skill progression, 'Administer phonological awareness subtests to standard').

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Follow the script, practice items and discontinue rules for each subtest. Oral stimuli mean your voice is the test: pace, stress and repetition rules all matter.

▸  Rapid naming tasks are timed: start the timer on the child's first response, not your instruction, and record errors and self-corrections as you go (Skill progression, RAN micro-skill; Wolf & Bowers, 1999).

▸  Note behaviour that affects scores: hearing or attention lapses, stammer, word-finding difficulty, anxiety about being timed.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Raw scores convert to standard scores by age from the manual tables. Check the age calculation, the table and every transcription twice.

▸  Report each subtest and any composites with percentiles; check the manual for which subtests are grouped and whether a composite is provided.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Phonological processing difficulty is the best-supported account of why decoding fails (Stanovich, 1988). A weak phonological profile is consistent with a dyslexic-type difficulty; it does not confirm dyslexia on its own (Rose, 2009).

▸  Separate the strands. Weak phonological awareness points to explicit phonological and phonics teaching; weak rapid naming with adequate awareness points to fluency difficulty (the double-deficit view, Wolf & Bowers, 1999) and to fluency practice and time accommodations.

▸  Set the profile beside oral language, cognitive profile, attendance and teaching history before calling the difficulty specific (Skill progression, 'Distinguish a specific difficulty from a general one').

▸  Write what it does and does not establish, and recommend at the right Continuum level with what, who, how often and how progress will be measured.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Adding a vowel to isolated consonants.

▸  Starting the naming timer on your instruction.

▸  Writing that the scores 'confirm' dyslexia.

▸  Administering it without a reading measure alongside.

▸  Ignoring Irish-medium schooling or EAL when interpreting English phonological tasks.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Gibbs, S., & Bodman, S. (2014). Phonological Assessment Battery Primary (PhAB2 Primary): Manual. GL Assessment. — administration and interpretation chapters. Original: Frederickson, N., Frith, U., & Reason, R. (1997). Phonological Assessment Battery. NFER-Nelson.

▸  Wolf, M., & Bowers, P. G. (1999). The double-deficit hypothesis for the developmental dyslexias. Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(3), 415–438.

▸  Rose, J. (2009). Identifying and teaching children and young people with dyslexia and literacy difficulties. Department for Children, Schools and Families.

tool.name: CTOPP-2
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it is: the Comprehensive Test of Phonological Processing, second edition (Wagner, Torgesen, Rashotte & Pearson, 2013), published by Pro-Ed. It is the battery named in the Skill progression phonological micro-skills ('CTOPP-2 or equivalent — timing, error recording, scoring the composites'). It is not in the tool catalogue — note it as 'CTOPP-2 — MEASURES: phonological awareness, phonological memory, rapid naming' if you add it to a band list.

▸  Know the norms: CTOPP-2 is US-normed. For an Irish child that is a real limitation — accent, dialect and curriculum differ — and the report should say so. A UK-normed battery (PhAB2) may be the better first choice; check what your service holds and prefers.

▸  Check the age range and version in the manual: there are separate subtest sets for younger and older children, and which subtests feed which composite changes with age band (Skill progression, 'Score the phonological composites correctly').

▸  Some subtests use recorded audio so the stimulus is standard; check which ones in your edition and test the audio device before the child arrives (Skill progression, 'Administer phonological awareness subtests to standard').

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Use the audio where the manual requires it, and deliver live items cleanly — no added schwa, no stress on the target sound, no repeats the manual forbids. An inaccurate administration cannot be rescued at scoring.

▸  Rapid naming subtests: start the timer on the child's first response, stop on the last, record errors and self-corrections live. Note anything that affected speed.

▸  Follow the ceiling (discontinue) rule for each subtest exactly; continuing past it or stopping short makes the scaled score uninterpretable. If you break a rule, note it on the form at that point and check with the manual whether the subtest is still scoreable.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Subtests give scaled scores (mean 10, SD 3) and composites give index scores (mean 100, SD 15) (Wagner et al., 2013; Skill progression). Each conversion uses the child's exact age on the day.

▸  Calculate age twice, borrowing correctly across months and days; check the sum of scaled scores before looking up a composite; check the subtest-to-composite mapping for this age band. Score independently and have your supervisor check before reporting.

▸  Report composites with confidence intervals and percentiles. A composite is more reliable than any single subtest; report subtests where they diverge within a composite.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  A low phonological composite shows the child did poorly on these tasks, on this day, compared with a US norm sample. It does not by itself establish dyslexia, explain every reading problem, or predict which intervention will work (Skill progression, 'Interpret a phonological profile in context').

▸  Separate phonological awareness, phonological memory and rapid naming, as for PhAB2. Weak phonological memory alone also raises questions about verbal working memory and language — check against the WISC-V and SLT information.

▸  Put the scores beside reading accuracy, fluency and comprehension, oral language, teaching history and the child's own account; use 'consistent with', not 'confirms'.

▸  State the US-norm limitation in the report and in feedback to parents.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Not stating that the norms are US-based.

▸  Skipping the audio where the manual requires it.

▸  Using the wrong age-band composite mapping.

▸  Starting the rapid naming timer on your instruction.

▸  Writing that the profile 'confirms' dyslexia.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Wagner, R. K., Torgesen, J. K., Rashotte, C. A., & Pearson, N. A. (2013). Comprehensive Test of Phonological Processing (2nd ed.): Examiner's manual. Pro-Ed.

▸  Stanovich, K. E. (1988). Explaining the differences between the dyslexic and the garden-variety poor reader: The phonological-core variable-difference model. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 21(10), 590–604.

▸  Wolf, M., & Bowers, P. G. (1999). The double-deficit hypothesis for the developmental dyslexias. Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(3), 415–438.

tool.name: Sandwell Early Numeracy Test
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it is: an individually administered test of early number concepts, developed in Sandwell's inclusion support service and published by GL Assessment in two versions: SENT-R for 4–8 years and SENT KS2–KS3 for 8–14 years (GL Assessment product information) — check the authors, edition and year on your copy.

▸  Know what it measures: early number concepts across five strands (tool catalogue), which cover areas such as identifying numbers, oral counting, value, object counting and number language — check the strand names in your manual and use them as printed. It does not measure formal procedural knowledge at upper primary level (tool catalogue).

▸  Age range in the catalogue is 4:0–14:0, which covers both versions: use SENT-R up to 8 and SENT KS2–KS3 from 8 — check you have the right version before quoting a standard score for an older child. It is most informative for younger children and older pupils working at an early number level (for example in a special class).

▸  Ask what the school already knows: Sigma-T or Drumcondra maths results, the class teacher's observations, and what maths programme and manipulatives the child has been taught with. Maths difficulty that follows long absence or a change of school is an instructional question first.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Use the materials specified (cards, counters) and the exact wording. Number language items depend on the words used; paraphrasing changes the item.

▸  Watch how the child gets the answer, not only whether it is right: counting all versus counting on, finger use, subitising small quantities, reliance on rote sequences, and whether they check.

▸  Note maths anxiety — freezing, guessing to end the item, distress at being wrong. It lowers performance and is itself a finding.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score each strand and convert as the manual directs; check whether your edition gives standard scores, age equivalents or both, and report the strand profile, not only a total.

▸  Use the strand profile to find the lowest secure point — the foundation the teaching should start from.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Early number sense (quantity, counting principles, number language) underpins later arithmetic. A child weak in object counting or value needs concrete work at that level before procedures (Dowker, 2004).

▸  Consider the alternatives: general learning difficulty, language difficulty affecting number vocabulary, attention, maths anxiety and missed teaching can all lower scores. Check the cognitive and language profile before calling a difficulty specific.

▸  The test describes current skills; it does not diagnose dyscalculia. If a specific number-sense difficulty is suspected, a screener such as the Dyscalculia Screener adds timing information — still not a diagnosis.

▸  Recommend small-step, concrete-pictorial-abstract teaching at the level the profile shows, at the right Continuum level, and repeat the test (parallel form if available) to measure progress.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Reporting only a total, not the strand profile.

▸  Paraphrasing number-language items.

▸  Ignoring how the child reached answers.

▸  Calling it a dyscalculia assessment.

▸  Not checking instructional history and attendance.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Sandwell Early Numeracy Test — Revised (SENT-R): manual. GL Assessment. — check authors and year on your copy.

▸  Dowker, A. (2004). What works for children with mathematical difficulties? (Research Report RR554). Department for Education and Skills.

tool.name: Dyscalculia Screener / DysCalculiUM
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know that these are two different tools. The Dyscalculia Screener (Butterworth, 2003) is a computer-based screener for school-age children; DysCalculiUM (Beacham & Trott — check the year and publisher) is a screener for older students and adults, developed for further and higher education. Catalogue age: 6:0+ / 15+.

▸  Know what the Dyscalculia Screener measures: basic number sense, using timed tasks such as dot enumeration and number comparison, alongside an arithmetic achievement measure (tool catalogue: 'Number sense and dot enumeration timing'). The theory behind it is Butterworth's account of dyscalculia as a core deficit in representing numerosity (Butterworth, Varma & Laurillard, 2011).

▸  Know what it cannot tell you: it does not diagnose, and it does not separate anxiety from difficulty (tool catalogue). A slow, anxious child can screen positive.

▸  Check the computer set-up before the session: working keyboard or response keys, no distractions, and a child who can use the response format. Timing is the measure, so hardware lag or an unfamiliar keyboard matters.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Follow the on-screen instructions and practice items; do not coach during timed items. Stay with the child and note behaviour: guessing, hesitation, distress, attention drifting.

▸  Afterwards, ask the child how it felt and what they did — counting dots one by one versus seeing the number at a glance is a useful observation to set beside the timing data.

▸  For DysCalculiUM with an older student, consider it alongside their own account of maths history and current course demands; it is a screen, not an assessment for exam or college accommodations on its own.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Scoring is automated; check how the software reports results (for example whether it gives a descriptive outcome as well as scores) and read the manual's guidance on what a positive screen means. Do not quote a cut-off from memory.

▸  Print or save the report and record the date, the version and any problems during the session.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  A positive screen is a reason to investigate further, not a conclusion. Say that in the report in those words.

▸  Separate number sense (slow or inaccurate on dot enumeration and comparison) from arithmetic (weak on calculation with adequate number sense). The first suggests a core number difficulty; the second more often reflects teaching, memory for facts or anxiety.

▸  Consider maths anxiety explicitly — it lowers speed and accuracy and is common. Use the child's account, observation and, if appropriate, a brief anxiety measure; name what you considered.

▸  Recommend targeted number-sense work with regular review, and say whether the question of a specific mathematical difficulty should be revisited after a period of intervention.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Reporting a positive screen as dyscalculia.

▸  Ignoring maths anxiety as an explanation.

▸  Confusing the Dyscalculia Screener with DysCalculiUM.

▸  Not checking the computer set-up before a timed test.

▸  Using a screen alone to support exam or college accommodations.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Butterworth, B. (2003). Dyscalculia Screener: Manual. NFER-Nelson.

▸  Butterworth, B., Varma, S., & Laurillard, D. (2011). Dyscalculia: From brain to education. Science, 332(6033), 1049–1053.

▸  Dowker, A. (2004). What works for children with mathematical difficulties? (Research Report RR554). Department for Education and Skills.

tool.name: Piers-Harris 3
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know what it is: the Piers-Harris Self-Concept Scale, third edition (Piers, Shemmassian & Herzberg, 2018), published by WPS. A self-report questionnaire of how children see themselves across six domains (tool catalogue). The catalogue gives 7–18, the Piers-Harris 2 range; the third edition extended the age range — check your manual before using it at either end.

▸  Know the domains before you use it; check the exact names in your manual. They cover behaviour, anxiety, happiness, intellectual and school status, physical appearance and social acceptance. Know which items sit in which domain so you can follow up specific answers.

▸  Know what it cannot tell you: whether low self-concept is cause or consequence — usually it is consequence (tool catalogue). It is not a depression or anxiety measure and does not assess risk.

▸  It is US-normed. Some items and the norm comparison are culturally loaded; say so in the report. Check reading level: read items aloud for a child with literacy difficulty, and record that you did.

▸  Plan for what an answer might open. Items touch on unhappiness and worry; decide before the session how you will follow up, and know the same-day risk and child protection route in case a child discloses self-harm, suicidal thoughts or abuse.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Explain the purpose honestly, tell the child there are no right answers, and check they understand the response format. For younger children or weak readers, read each item aloud.

▸  Watch as they answer: hesitation, changed answers, items that provoke a comment. Afterwards, go back to two or three striking responses and ask about them — the conversation is often worth more than the score.

▸  If a response or comment raises concern about self-harm, suicidal ideation, abuse or neglect, follow the same-day risk and child protection route: act, report to Tusla as soon as practicable (telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty), then take it to supervision.

3 · SCORING IT
▸  Score by hand or software as the manual directs: a total score and domain scores as T-scores, plus response-validity indicators (inconsistent responding and response bias) — check the manual for the exact indices and their interpretation, and do not quote cut-offs from memory.

▸  Check the validity indicators before interpreting anything. A child answering 'yes' to everything, or giving the answers they think adults want, produces a profile that looks meaningful and is not.

4 · INTERPRETING IT
▸  Read the domain profile, not only the total. Low intellectual and school status with adequate social acceptance tells a different story from the reverse — and often points to the learning difficulty behind the referral.

▸  Treat low self-concept as usually a consequence (tool catalogue): of repeated failure, peer difficulty or adversity. The formulation should ask what is producing it, and the recommendations should act on that, not only on 'self-esteem'.

▸  Triangulate with the child's own account (solution-focused interview, 'My Thoughts About School'), teacher and parent report (Reference Part D, School Age and Adolescent). In adolescents, watch for low mood underneath a low score and refer to CAMHS or Primary Care Psychology where warranted — the EP does not diagnose.

▸  Report findings to the child in a way that does not confirm a negative self-view; lead with what they said was going well.

5 · THE ERRORS THAT COST MARKS
▸  Interpreting the profile without checking the validity indicators.

▸  Treating it as a measure of depression or risk.

▸  Using it without a plan for following up a worrying answer.

▸  Reporting only the total score.

▸  Recommending 'self-esteem work' without addressing the cause.

6 · WHAT TO READ
▸  Piers, E. V., Shemmassian, S. K., & Herzberg, D. S. (2018). Piers-Harris Self-Concept Scale (3rd ed.): Manual. Western Psychological Services.

▸  Harter, S. (2012). The construction of the self: Developmental and sociocultural foundations (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

▸  Department of Children and Youth Affairs. (2017). Children First: National guidance for the protection and welfare of children. Government of Ireland. — check for updates.

tool.name: WAIS-IV UK
tool.text:
1 · BEFORE YOU OPEN THE KIT
▸  Know where it sits. WAIS-IV UK covers 16:0–90:11 (Wechsler, 2010, UK adaptation of the 2008 US edition); WISC-V UK runs to 16:11, so at 16:0–16:11 either is defensible (tool catalogue). As a rule of thumb, a 16-year-old still in school with a question about learning is often better served by WISC-V (child-oriented items, comparison with school-age peers); a school leaver or a question about third-level or adult services points to WAIS-IV. Whichever you choose, say why in the report.

▸  Check the edition in the cupboard. WAIS-5 was published in the US in 2024 — check whether a UK-normed edition is available to your service and which one current good practice expects you to use. Norms age, and an older standardisation can inflate scores; if you use WAIS-IV, know when its UK norms were collected (check the technical manual).

▸  Write the referral question first. In Irish EP practice the WAIS-IV usually answers questions about a young person at post-primary, in Youthreach or preparing for further/higher education (e.g. evidence for DARE or college disability supports), or about eligibility for adult disability services (Reference Part D, Adolescent and Young Adult). None of these is answered by an IQ alone — plan the attainment, adaptive and functional measures that go beside it.

▸  Rule out the confounds before the session: vision and hearing, first language and years of English-medium schooling, medication, sleep, substance use, current mental state, and whether they have had a Wechsler battery in the past year (practice effects). A young adult who is exhausted, low in mood or has been up all night gives you a result about today, not about their ability.

▸  Know the structure: four indices — Verbal Comprehension, Perceptual Reasoning, Working Memory, Processing Speed — plus FSIQ and GAI, built from ten core subtests with supplementary subtests available. Some supplementary subtests are only normed for part of the age range; check which composites need which subtests in the manual before you pack the kit.

2 · ADMINISTERING IT
▸  Follow the script verbatim, including the adult start points, reversal and discontinue rules — they differ from WISC-V, and trainees who learned WISC-V first carry WISC habits across. Build a separate one-page crib for WAIS-IV.
