▸  IRELAND — CHRONIC ABSENCE (all causes, not EBSA): Tusla's annual attendance report for 2022/23, as reported by the Department of Education (19/05/2025), recorded over 110,000 primary and 65,000 post-primary pupils missing 20 or more days. This is total absence, not EBSA — never quote it as an EBSA rate. Check the latest Tusla report.

▸  IRELAND — EBSA SPECIFICALLY: no national EBSA rate is published — rate not stated here, check before quoting. Local CYPSC and NEPS data may exist.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: separation-based reluctance at school entry is common and usually transient. Compulsory attendance under the Education (Welfare) Act 2000 begins at 6.

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: peaks around school entry and again at 10–11 (Kearney, 2008 — check). Somatic complaints and separation themes dominate.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: the peak in most accounts, especially at the move to post-primary. Social-evaluative and academic pressures dominate; co-occurring low mood is more common.

▸  SEX RATIO: studies generally report no strong sex difference (Kearney, 2008) — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Transient relu

condition.name: Separation Anxiety Disorder
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Separation Anxiety Disorder (F93.0) · ICD-11 6B05
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.2 Anxiety) — and 3.6 School attendance where it drives non-attendance

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Education (Welfare) Act 2000 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  An anxiety disorder defined by DEVELOPMENTALLY INAPPROPRIATE and EXCESSIVE fear or anxiety about separation from attachment figures (American Psychiatric Association, 2022, DSM-5-TR).

▸  Criteria require at least three of eight features — e.g. excessive distress when separation occurs or is anticipated; persistent worry that harm will befall an attachment figure or that an event (getting lost, kidnapped) will cause separation; reluctance or refusal to go to school or elsewhere; reluctance to sleep away from the attachment figure; nightmares of separation; physical complaints when separation is anticipated (APA, 2022). Check the full list before relying on it.

▸  DURATION: at least 4 weeks in children and adolescents; typically 6 months or more in adults (APA, 2022). Significant distress or impairment, and not better explained by another condition (e.g. autism-related resistance to change).

▸  Since DSM-5 (2013) it sits in the anxiety disorders chapter and can be diagnosed in adults; the earlier requirement of onset before 18 was removed.

▸  THE KEY WORD IS 'DEVELOPMENTALLY'. Separation distress is normal from around 8 months to preschool (Bowlby, 1969/1982). The disorder is the same fear, out of proportion for age and persisting.

▸  MAINTAINED BY ACCOMMODATION. Well-meant parental accommodation — staying with the child, avoiding separations, answering calls from school — reduces distress now and maintains the fear (Lebowitz et al., 2013). This is the lever parent-led treatments pull.

▸  NOT an attachment disorder. Children with separation anxiety usually have strong, selective attachments; the fear is about losing them. Reactive attachment disorder is a different, much rarer condition linked to severe early neglect.

▸  NOT caused by 'overprotective parenting' in any simple sense. Temperament, genetics, life events and parental anxiety interact; accommodation maintains the fear but rarely created it. Say so plainly to parents.

▸  NOT normal clinginess. Most young children protest at separation and settle quickly. The disorder is persistent, excessive for age and impairing.

▸  NOT only a young-child problem. It can persist into or begin in adolescence and adulthood (APA, 2022), and in adolescence is often hidden behind 'I feel sick' or refusal to go on school trips.

▸  NOT treated by keeping the child close until they grow out of it. Avoidance maintains anxiety; CBT with graded exposure and parent involvement is the best-supported treatment for childhood anxiety (James et al., 2020).

▸  NOT the same as EBSA, though often its driver in younger children. A child can have separation anxiety and attend school, and many children with EBSA do not have separation anxiety.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL (CHILDREN): 6–12-month prevalence around 4% (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR). Commonly described as the most prevalent anxiety disorder in children under 12 (APA, 2022) — check the current text.

▸  ADOLESCENTS: 12-month prevalence around 1.6% in US data (APA, 2022).

▸  ADULTS: 12-month prevalence around 0.9–1.9% (APA, 2022).

▸  IRELAND: no national prevalence figure identified — rate not stated here, check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: diagnosis is difficult because separation distress is developmentally expected; identification rises at school entry.

▸  SEX RATIO: community samples suggest it is somewhat more common in girls; clinic samples are more even (APA, 2022) — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Diagnosis is less common because distress is expected — rate not stated here, check.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Most often identified at school entry and in the early primary years, when daily separation becomes compulsory and prolonged. Also after life events — a move, a bereavement, a parent's illness — at any age. Adolescent and adult presentations are recognised (APA, 2022).

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: Primary Care Psychology (mild to moderate) or CAMHS (severe, complex, or with mood or risk concerns), usually via GP referral. Private clinical psychologists and psychiatrists also diagnose. The EP does not diagnose.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS psychiatrist or psychologist. Primary Care psychologist. Private clinical psychologist. An SDQ or RCADS completed in school is a screen, not a diagnosis.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   GP → Primary Care Psychology for mild to moderate; CAMHS for severe or complex, or where mood or risk is present. Tusla if the fear points to a welfare concern. NEPS consultation for the school plan.

▸ 'SHOULD WE HAVE COME SOONER?'
   'It's genuinely hard to tell normal settling-in from something more at the start — most children do settle. That it's lasted this long is what tells us it needs a plan, and now there is one.'

WHAT YOU SEE AT THIS AGE
▸  Crying and clinging at preschool or junior infants drop-off, refusing to let go, distress lasting long after the parent has left, sleep refusal without the parent. Most children settle within minutes; the concern is the child who does not, or whose distress is escalating after the first term. Parent and staff report only — no self-report.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Crying and clinging at preschool or junior infants drop-off, refusing to let go, distress lasting long after the parent has left, sleep refusal without the parent. Most children settle within minutes; the concern is the child who does not, or whose

condition.name: Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Social Anxiety Disorder (F40.10) · ICD-11 6B04
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.2 Anxiety) — and 4. SOCIAL (4.1 Friendships and social skills) · 3.6 School attendance where it drives non-attendance

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  An anxiety disorder defined by marked fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in which the person may be scrutinised by others — conversations, meeting new people, being observed eating or drinking, performing or speaking in front of others (American Psychiatric Association, 2022, DSM-5-TR).

▸  The core fear is of NEGATIVE EVALUATION — acting in a way, or showing anxiety symptoms (blushing, shaking), that will be humiliating or lead to rejection. Situations are avoided or endured with intense fear, out of proportion to the actual threat, typically for 6 months or more (APA, 2022).

▸  IN CHILDREN, the anxiety must occur in PEER settings, not only with adults, and may be expressed as crying, tantrums, freezing, clinging, shrinking or failing to speak (APA, 2022). A 'performance only' specifier applies where the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public.

▸  THE BEST-SUPPORTED MODEL is cognitive: Clark & Wells (1995) describe self-focused attention, a distorted internal image of how one appears, SAFETY BEHAVIOURS (avoiding eye contact, rehearsing sentences, hiding the face) and anticipatory and post-event rumination. Safety behaviours prevent disconfirmation and make the person look more awkward. Leigh & Clark (2018) apply the model to adolescents.

▸  TEMPERAMENT MATTERS. Behavioural inhibition — a tendency to withdraw from the unfamiliar, identifiable in toddlers (Kagan et al., 1984) — substantially raises risk (Clauss & Blackford, 2012 — check the effect size before quoting).

▸  Onset is typically in late childhood to adolescence. DSM-5 reported a median age of onset in the US of 13, with most onsets between 8 and 15 (APA, 2013; check DSM-5-TR text).

▸  NOT shyness. Shyness is a common, normal temperament; social anxiety disorder is marked, persistent and impairing. Many shy children never develop it.

▸  NOT autism. Autistic young people may avoid social situations because of social communication difference, sensory load or the effort of masking; in social anxiety the social understanding is typically intact and the driver is fear of evaluation. They can co-occur, and both must be assessed separately.

▸  NOT a lack of interest in people. Socially anxious young people usually want friendships and feel the loss keenly. 'He prefers his own company' can be a misreading.

▸  NOT fixed by 'just throwing them in'. Unplanned exposure with safety behaviours intact rarely helps; planned, graded exposure with safety behaviours dropped is what the evidence supports (Clark & Wells, 1995; NICE, 2013).

▸  NOT a phase that will pass unaided. Untreated, it tends to be chronic and is associated with later depression and substance use (NICE, 2013) — check the specific figures before quoting.

▸  NOT selective mutism, although they are closely related. Selective mutism is its own DSM-5-TR anxiety disorder, in which the child consistently does not speak in specific settings; social anxiety is commonly present alongside it.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: 12-month prevalence in the US around 7%, with much lower estimates in many other countries using the same instruments (APA, 2013/2022) — check the DSM-5-TR text before quoting any European or international figure.

▸  IRELAND: no national figure identified — rate not stated here, check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: rarely diagnosed. Behavioural inhibition and selective mutism are the related presentations at this age.

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: emerging, particularly in the later primary years.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: the main onset window (APA, 2013 — median onset 13 in US data).

▸  SEX RATIO: more common in females in community samples, with the difference more pronounced in adolescents (APA, 2022) — check the ratio before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Rarely diagnosed at this age — rate not stated here, check.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Usually late primary to mid-adolescence (US median onset 13; APA, 2013 — check). Social-evaluative demands rise sharply at the move to post-primary, and peer judgement becomes developmentally central, so the fear becomes both more intense and more visible.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: Primary Care Psychology (mild to moderate), CAMHS (severe, complex, or with mood or risk concerns), usually via the GP. Private clinical psychologists and psychiatrists. The EP does not diagnose.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS psychiatrist or psychologist. Primary Care psychologist. Private clinical psychologist. Jigsaw may provide a summary of brief intervention rather than a diagnosis.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   GP → Primary Care Psychology or CAMHS depending on severity. Jigsaw (12–25) for milder adolescent need. SLT where language may be contributing. CDNT where autism is a question.

▸ 'SHOULD WE HAVE COME SOONER?'
   'Social anxiety is one of the easiest difficulties to miss — quiet, compliant young people don't cause problems in class. That she's been noticed now is good, and it responds well to help.'

WHAT YOU SEE AT THIS AGE
▸  A child who is very slow to warm up, watches rather than joins, freezes when addressed by unfamiliar adults and may not speak in the setting. Much of this is temperament and settles with warmth and time. Consistent non-speaking in the setting while speaking at home points toward selective mutism and an SLT and Primary Care referral.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: A

condition.name: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), including Complex PTSD
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (with preschool subtype, 6 years and under) · ICD-11 6B40 PTSD · ICD-11 6B41 Complex PTSD (ICD-11 only — NOT a DSM-5-TR diagnosis) — check codes before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.5 Trauma, attachment and loss)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 1.2 · 1.12 · 3.1 · 3.2 · 3.10 · 5.28 · 5.31 · 5.32 · 5.45

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 1.2.5 · 1.3.14 · 3.3.2 · 3.3.4 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Children First: National Guidance (2017) · Child Protection Procedures for Primary and Post-Primary Schools (Department of Education — check current revision) · EPSEN Act 2004 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A trauma- and stressor-related disorder that can follow exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence — experienced directly, witnessed, or learned about happening to someone close (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR). The EVENT is a requirement; distress without a qualifying event is not PTSD.

▸  DSM-5-TR groups symptoms in four clusters: INTRUSION (memories, nightmares, flashbacks, distress at reminders), AVOIDANCE of reminders, NEGATIVE CHANGES IN THINKING AND MOOD (blame, shame, detachment, loss of interest), and ALTERED AROUSAL (hypervigilance, startle, irritability, sleep and concentration difficulty). Duration more than one month, with clear impairment.

▸  PRESCHOOL SUBTYPE (6 years and under) in DSM-5-TR: fewer symptoms required, and symptoms may show as play — repetitive play re-enacting themes, frightening dreams without recognisable content, regression, new fears (APA, 2022; building on Scheeringa's work with young children).

▸  ICD-11 (WHO, 2019/2022) defines PTSD more narrowly around three core elements: RE-EXPERIENCING IN THE PRESENT (vivid intrusions, flashbacks, nightmares — not simply remembering), AVOIDANCE, and a PERSISTENT SENSE OF CURRENT THREAT (hypervigilance, startle) (Brewin et al., 2017).

▸  COMPLEX PTSD is an ICD-11 diagnosis (6B41) and does NOT exist in DSM-5-TR. It requires the PTSD core PLUS 'disturbances in self-organisation': affect dysregulation, a persistently negative self-concept (worthless, defeated, ashamed), and difficulty sustaining relationships. It typically follows prolonged or repeated trauma from which escape was difficult — e.g. ongoing abuse or domestic violence (WHO, 2019/2022; Brewin et al., 2017). Evidence on applying it to children is still developing — check before relying on it.

▸  The best-supported psychological account (Ehlers & Clark, 2000) is that the trauma memory is poorly processed — stored as fragments that intrude, feel current, and are triggered by cues — while the person's appraisals ('I'm not safe', 'it was my fault') keep the sense of threat alive. This is why avoidance maintains it, and why trauma-focused therapy works.

▸  It is TREATABLE. Trauma-focused CBT for children and young people has the strongest evidence base and is the NICE first-line recommendation (NICE, 2018, NG116 — check for updates). Treatment is delivered by clinical services (CAMHS, Primary Care Psychology), not by the school EP.

▸  NOT the inevitable result of a frightening event. Alisic et al. (2014), meta-analysing trauma-exposed children and adolescents, found around 16% developed PTSD; most did not. Distress in the first weeks is expected and usually settles.

▸  NOT the same as 'trauma', 'complex trauma', 'developmental trauma' or ACEs. Those are descriptive terms (Part D lists them as NOT a DSM diagnosis). 'Developmental trauma disorder' was proposed (van der Kolk, 2005) and not adopted in DSM-5. Complex PTSD is a specific ICD-11 diagnosis, not a synonym for 'had a hard childhood'.

▸  NOT something an ACE score can identify. The ACE score was built for population epidemiology (Felitti et al., 1998); its originators warn against using it to screen or predict for individuals (Anda et al., 2020).

▸  NOT helped by getting the child to talk it all through straight away. NICE (2018, NG116) advises against psychologically-focused debriefing to prevent PTSD. Immediate support is practical safety, calm, connection and routine (Hobfoll et al., 2007) — the NEPS critical incident approach follows the same logic.

▸  NOT always visible as fear. In children it often looks like irritability, anger, poor concentration, 'daydreaming' (dissociation), sleep loss and falling attainment — and is routinely misread as ADHD, conduct difficulty or laziness.

▸  NOT permanent damage. 'Traumatised for life' framing is inaccurate and harmful; recovery is common and effective treatment exists. Equally NOT 'children are resilient, they'll forget' — untreated PTSD can persist for years.

▸  NOT a reason to drop expectations. Trauma-informed practice means predictability, safety and relationship WITH clear, calm boundaries — not the absence of structure.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  AFTER EXPOSURE: about 15.9% of trauma-exposed children and adolescents developed PTSD in Alisic et al.'s (2014) meta-analysis. Rates were higher after interpersonal trauma (assault, abuse) than non-interpersonal (accidents, disasters), and higher in girls.

▸  BY AGE 18 (UK cohort): Lewis et al. (2019), E-Risk cohort in England and Wales, reported that 31.1% had experienced trauma and 7.8% met criteria for PTSD at some point by 18; only 20.6% of those with PTSD had received help from mental health professionals.

▸  IRELAND: no national child PTSD prevalence figure is stated here — check before quoting. Do not transfer UK or US figures to an Irish caseload as if local.

▸  COMPLEX PTSD IN CHILDREN: rate not stated here — the ICD-11 diagnosis is recent and child prevalence studies are limited. Check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: rate not stated here. Diagnosis at this age is specialist-only and uses the preschool subtype.

▸  SCHOOL AGE AND ADOLESCENT: most identification happens here, after a known event (road traffic accident, assault, sudden death witnessed, medical trauma, domestic violence) or when a child protection concern emerges.

▸  SEX RATIO: higher rates in girls in Alisic et al. (2014) — 32.9% for girls after interpersonal trauma vs 8.4% for boy

condition.name: Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Reactive Attachment Disorder (Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders) · ICD-11 6B44 — check code before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.5 Trauma, attachment and loss) — and 4. SOCIAL (4.2 Relationships with adults)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 1.2 · 1.12 · 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.32 · 5.39

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 1.2.8 · 3.3.2 · 3.3.4 · 1.3.11

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Child Care Act 1991 · Children First: National Guidance (2017) · EPSEN Act 2004 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A RARE disorder of the child's attachment behaviour toward caregivers, arising from SEVERELY INSUFFICIENT CARE in early childhood (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR). It sits in the Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders chapter, not with neurodevelopmental conditions.

▸  CORE PICTURE: a consistent pattern of INHIBITED, emotionally WITHDRAWN behaviour toward adult caregivers — the child rarely seeks comfort when distressed and rarely responds to comfort when offered — plus social and emotional disturbance: minimal responsiveness to others, limited positive affect, and unexplained irritability, sadness or fearfulness even during non-threatening interactions with caregivers.

▸  REQUIRES a history of extremes of insufficient care: social neglect or deprivation, repeated changes of primary caregiver, or rearing in settings that severely limit the chance to form selective attachments (e.g. some institutional care). The care is presumed responsible for the behaviour.

▸  Further DSM-5-TR requirements: evident before age 5; developmental age of at least 9 months; criteria for autism NOT met. ICD-11 (WHO, 2019/2022) describes the same core picture.

▸  The underlying idea (Zeanah & Gleason, 2015) is that the child has had no consistent adult to form a selective attachment WITH — it is the ABSENCE or severe distortion of attachment, not an unusual attachment style.

▸  Features often REDUCE substantially once the child is placed in sensitive, stable care (Zeanah & Gleason, 2015 — check), which is itself diagnostically informative and hopeful.

▸  Diagnosis is specialist and multi-source: history of care, observation with caregivers and strangers, and ruling out autism, intellectual disability and depression. It is not made from school observation, from a questionnaire, or from a care history alone.

▸  NOT the same as 'attachment difficulties' or 'attachment issues' as used loosely in schools. Most children described that way do NOT have RAD. Woolgar and Baldock (2015) found attachment problems were over-identified in looked-after and adopted children by community services, while more common and treatable problems (ADHD, conduct, anxiety) were missed.

▸  NOT an insecure attachment pattern. Avoidant, ambivalent and disorganised patterns from the Strange Situation are research classifications of a relationship, not diagnoses; insecure patterns are common in the general population. Granqvist et al. (2017) warn specifically against using disorganised attachment as a diagnostic or child protection marker.

▸  NOT caused by ordinary parenting stress, working parents, crèche or a parent's depression alone. RAD requires EXTREMES of insufficient care.

▸  NOT autism. Both can look socially withdrawn, but RAD requires the care history and resolves substantially with good care; autism is neurodevelopmental, present regardless of care quality, and includes restricted and repetitive behaviour. DSM-5-TR excludes RAD if autism criteria are met (Davidson et al., 2015 on telling them apart).

▸  NOT a label for a child who is 'controlling', 'manipulative' or aggressive. Those words describe behaviour with many possible causes and do not make a RAD diagnosis.

▸  NOT treated by 'holding therapy', 'rebirthing' or coercive 'attachment therapy'. These are harmful, have caused deaths, and are rejected by NICE (2015, NG26 — check wording) and by an APSAC task force (Chaffin et al., 2006).

▸  NOT a reason to exclude other explanations. Children with this history also have high rates of language difficulty, ADHD and — where there was prenatal alcohol exposure — FASD. Assess these.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: uncommon, and population data are scarce. Minnis et al. (2013) screened all 1,646 children aged 6–8 in a deprived urban UK area and estimated RAD prevalence at 1.40% (95% CI 0.94–2.10) — the authors concluded that in this deprived population RAD 'was not rare'. The rate in less deprived populations is not established — check before quoting.

▸  HIGHER in children with histories of institutional care, severe neglect or multiple placements; the Bucharest Early Intervention Project (Zeanah et al., 2005) found signs of RAD more common in institutionalised children. Rate not stated here — check.

▸  IRELAND: no national figure stated here — check before quoting. Children in care of Tusla are the group where the question most often arises.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: the age at which it is defined and diagnosed (evident before age 5).

▸  SCHOOL AGE AND OLDER: RAD can be present at 6–8 (Minnis et al., 2013), so it is not only an early-years question; but what schools see is more often a descriptive attachment-related difficulty, ADHD, conduct difficulty, DLD or trauma.

▸  SEX RATIO: rate not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Rate for this age band not stated here — check before quoting. (Minnis et al., 2013, 1.4%, is for 6–8-year-olds — see School Age.)

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Defined before age 5 (DSM-5-TR) and usually identified in early childhood, often soon after a child comes into care or is adopted, when the contrast with a new, sensitive carer makes the pattern visible. A first diagnosis at school age or later is uncommon and needs the early history.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CAMHS or a specialist infant/child mental health service, usually with input from the Tusla social worker and

condition.name: Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (DSED)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder (Trauma- and Stressor-Related Disorders) · ICD-11 6B45 — check code before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 4. SOCIAL (4.2 Relationships with adults) — and 3. EMOTIONAL (3.5 Trauma, attachment and loss)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 1.2 · 1.12 · 3.1 · 3.2 · 3.10 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 1.2.8 · 3.3.2 · 3.3.4 · 1.3.11

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Child Care Act 1991 · Children First: National Guidance (2017) · EPSEN Act 2004 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A RARE disorder in which a child ACTIVELY APPROACHES AND INTERACTS WITH UNFAMILIAR ADULTS without the normal wariness, following SEVERELY INSUFFICIENT CARE in early childhood (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR). Previously part of 'RAD, disinhibited type' in DSM-IV; separated in DSM-5 (2013).

▸  DSM-5-TR features (at least two): reduced or absent reticence with unfamiliar adults; overly familiar verbal or physical behaviour; diminished or absent checking back with the caregiver in unfamiliar settings; willingness to go off with an unfamiliar adult with little or no hesitation.

▸  The behaviour is NOT simply impulsivity (as in ADHD) — it is socially disinhibited. Same care-history requirement as RAD: social neglect, repeated changes of caregiver, or rearing in severely limiting settings. Developmental age at least 9 months.

▸  Unlike RAD, DSED can occur in a child who HAS formed an attachment to a caregiver; it is about indiscriminate engagement with strangers, not the absence of attachment (Zeanah & Gleason, 2015).

▸  DSED tends to be MORE PERSISTENT than RAD after placement in good care (Zeanah & Gleason, 2015 — check). In the English and Romanian Adoptees study, disinhibited social engagement persisted into young adulthood in some who had experienced prolonged early institutional deprivation (Sonuga-Barke et al., 2017).

▸  In the ERA study, it was one of several 'deprivation-specific' patterns — alongside inattention/overactivity, cognitive impairment and quasi-autistic features — linked mainly to deprivation lasting beyond about six months (Kumsta et al., 2010).

▸  The main practical risk is SAFETY: a child who will go off with anyone, and an adolescent who over-trusts strangers online or offline.

▸  NOT a friendly, sociable or confident child. Many children are outgoing; DSED is marked, cross-context disinhibition with strangers PLUS the care history. Do not pathologise extroversion.

▸  NOT ADHD — though the two often co-occur. ADHD impulsivity is general; DSED is specifically social and specifically toward unfamiliar adults. Assess both.

▸  NOT autism. Some autistic children approach strangers without typical social caution, but autism includes the restricted/repetitive domain and is present regardless of care history.

▸  NOT Williams syndrome — a genetic condition in which marked sociability with strangers is characteristic. Where there are also medical, cognitive or facial features, the question is medical; refer via GP/paediatrics.

▸  NOT a sign that the child is 'well attached' because they are affectionate with everyone. Indiscriminate affection is the concern, not reassurance.

▸  NOT the result of ordinary parenting or day care. It requires extremes of insufficient care.

▸  NOT solved by attachment 'therapies' involving coercion — these are rejected (NICE, 2015, NG26; Chaffin et al., 2006).

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: RARE in the general population — rate not stated here, check before quoting.

▸  HIGHER in children with histories of institutional care or severe neglect; BEIP and ERA samples show it most clearly (Zeanah & Gleason, 2015; Sonuga-Barke et al., 2017). Rates vary by sample — check before quoting.

▸  IRELAND: no national figure stated here — check. Children adopted internationally from institutional settings and children in care of Tusla are the groups where it most often arises.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: when it is most often first recognised, often soon after adoption or entry to care.

▸  SCHOOL AGE AND ADOLESCENT: persists in a proportion; the concern shifts to boundaries, peer relationships and vulnerability.

▸  SEX RATIO: rate not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Rare; higher in children with institutional or severely neglectful early care — rate not stated here, check.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Usually recognised in early childhood, often soon after adoption or entry to care, when carers and preschool staff notice the child going to any adult. Unlike RAD there is no 'before age 5' requirement in DSM-5-TR, and it can persist into adolescence and beyond.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CAMHS or a specialist infant/child mental health service, with Tusla social worker and carer input; some adoption or fostering specialist services. Not the school EP.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS psychiatrist or clinical psychologist; a specialist attachment or infant mental health clinician; a private clinical psychologist in care or adoption work. Older reports may say 'disinhibited attachment' or 'RAD, disinhibited type' (DSM-IV).

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   CAMHS (via GP, or via Tusla for children in care); SLT; paediatrics for development, FASD and genetic questions; the Tusla social worker for care planning. Tusla, the DLP and An Garda Síochána (if immediate danger) for any safety concern.

▸ 'SHOULD WE HAVE COME SOONER?'
   'This pattern often only shows once a child is settled and people can see how they are with strangers compared with family. Coming now, while we can build safety habits before adolescence, is good timing.'

WHAT YOU SEE AT THIS AGE
▸  A toddler or preschooler who goes readily to strangers, climbs onto unfamiliar laps, does not check back with the carer or key worker, and would leave with an unknown adult. Observe in the setting; carer and key-worker report. Safety plan and refer — do not s

condition.name: English as an Additional Language and bilingual development (DLD vs EAL)
condition.code: Not a DSM diagnosis · language difference, not disorder
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Education Act 1998 · Children First Act 2015 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  NOT A DISORDER. A child with English as an Additional Language (EAL) is learning English on top of one or more home languages. Being bilingual or multilingual is a normal developmental route, not a clinical category. This entry exists because the EP's real question is DIFFERENCE versus DISORDER: is this a child still acquiring English, a child with a genuine language disorder (DLD) who is also bilingual, or both?

▸  SEQUENTIAL vs SIMULTANEOUS. Simultaneous bilinguals meet both languages from birth; sequential learners start English later, often at preschool or school entry. Sequential learners are expected to lag monolingual English peers on English measures for years — that lag is the expected course, not a finding (Paradis, Genesee & Crago, 2011).

▸  BICS and CALP. Cummins (1979, 1981) distinguished conversational, context-embedded language (Basic Interpersonal Communicative Skills) from the decontextualised academic language of the classroom (Cognitive Academic Language Proficiency). The timescales commonly cited from his work are roughly 1–2 years for conversational fluency and around 5–7 years to approach age norms in academic English — treat these as broad estimates from specific samples, not rules. The trap: a child who chats fluently in the yard is assumed to have 'enough English', so classroom difficulty is read as a learning or language disorder.

▸  DISTRIBUTED KNOWLEDGE. A bilingual child's vocabulary is split across languages — words for home life in one, school words in the other. Testing in one language alone underestimates what the child knows (Bedore & Peña, 2008; Kohnert, 2010).

▸  WHAT DLD LOOKS LIKE IN A BILINGUAL CHILD. DLD is a disorder of the language-learning system, so it shows in ALL the child's languages, not only in English. CATALISE (Bishop et al., 2017) is clear that a child learning EAL should not be identified with DLD on the basis of English alone; evidence of difficulty in the home language is needed.

▸  THE BEST SINGLE SIGNAL is RATE OF PROGRESS compared with peers of similar language background and similar length of exposure to English — and the parent's account of first-language development. A child who is slow in both languages, slower than similar peers, and whose parents were worried before English arrived, is a different child from one who is simply newer to English (Paradis et al., 2011).

▸  IRISH CONTEXT. EAL pupils are in most Irish schools, including children arriving under temporary protection or international protection, and children from long-settled migrant families. Irish-medium schools add a further layer — many pupils are learning Irish as an additional language too. Local data on numbers vary; check the school's own figures.

▸  NOT a cause of language disorder. Growing up with two languages does not cause DLD or delay language overall; bilingual children with DLD have DLD, not 'too many languages' (Kohnert, 2010; Paradis et al., 2011).

▸  NOT a reason to stop the home language. Advice to parents to 'speak only English at home' is not supported by evidence and can harm the parent–child relationship, the child's identity and the first language that later English builds on (Cummins' interdependence hypothesis, 1979). Do not give it; correct it when you hear it.

▸  NOT a learning difficulty because English literacy lags. Early English reading may lag while decoding in English is being learned; persistent decoding difficulty that does not respond to teaching, especially if the home-language literacy is also weak, needs a separate look.

▸  NOT 'fine' because conversational English is fluent. Yard English (BICS) is not classroom English (CALP). Fluent chat and poor written comprehension is the expected pattern for several years (Cummins, 1981).

▸  NOT selective mutism when the child is quiet in the first months. Many sequential learners go through a non-verbal or 'silent' period while listening and absorbing (Tabors, 2008). It is time-limited and typically context-general in English; the child talks freely in the home language. Selective mutism is persistent and context-specific — see differential.

▸  NOT measured by an English-normed verbal test. A low Verbal Comprehension Index or BPVS-3 score in a child with EAL measures English exposure, not verbal reasoning. Reporting it as 'low verbal ability' is a serious and common error.

▸  NOT solved by translating a test. Translating a standardised test on the spot invalidates its norms; items differ in difficulty across languages. What you get is qualitative information, not a score.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: EAL is not a disorder, so there is no prevalence in the clinical sense. The relevant figures are how many pupils speak another language at home — check the latest CSO Census and Department of Education data before quoting any Irish figure.

▸  IRELAND: the proportion of pupils with a home language other than English or Irish has risen sharply since the 2000s and again with recent arrivals under temporary protection. Rate not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  DLD IN BILINGUAL CHILDREN: there is no evidence that DLD is more or less common in bilingual than monolingual children; the difficulty is identification, not incidence. Norbury et al. (2016) estimated DLD at around 7% in a UK school-entry population — check before quoting for a bilingual subgroup.

▸  MIS-IDENTIFICATION: both over-identification (EAL read as disorder) and under-identification (a real disorder dismissed as 'just EAL') are documented (Bedore & Peña, 2008). Patterns of disproportionality by language and ethnicity in special educational need

condition.name: Major Depressive Disorder
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Major Depressive Disorder · ICD-11 6A70 (single episode depressive disorder) / 6A71 (recurrent depressive disorder) — check codes before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.4 Mood) — and 3.7 Risk and safeguarding

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A mood disorder defined by one or more MAJOR DEPRESSIVE EPISODES: at least two weeks of depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), plus further symptoms, together making five or more of nine, with clear distress or impairment (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR).

▸  IN CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS the mood can be IRRITABLE rather than sad — DSM-5-TR allows this explicitly. The young person described as 'snappy, rude and fed up with everything' may be depressed.

▸  The nine symptom areas: depressed or irritable mood; loss of interest or pleasure; change in weight or appetite (in children, failure to make expected gains); sleep disturbance; psychomotor agitation or slowing; fatigue; worthlessness or excessive guilt; poor concentration or indecisiveness; recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation, plan or attempt.

▸  It is EPISODIC. Episodes can be single or recurrent, and are specified by severity (mild, moderate, severe) and features. It must not be better explained by a substance, medical condition or a bipolar disorder.

▸  Onset rises sharply in adolescence, and adolescent-onset depression often recurs (Thapar, Collishaw, Pine & Thapar, 2012). Early identification and support matter.

▸  Best understood in a biopsychosocial frame: genetic and family risk, cognitive style (Beck, 1967), loss of reinforcement and withdrawal (behavioural accounts), and life events such as loss, bullying, family conflict and abuse. School is both a source of stress and a key place for protection.

▸  For the EP the job is: RECOGNISE, ASK ABOUT RISK, REFER and SUPPORT the school to adapt — not to diagnose. Diagnosis is made by CAMHS, Primary Care Psychology, GP or psychiatry.

▸  NOT ordinary sadness. Sadness after a loss or disappointment is normal. Depression is pervasive, persistent (at least two weeks, most of the day, nearly every day) and impairs functioning.

▸  NOT 'just teenage moods'. Irritability, withdrawal and loss of interest are too often put down to adolescence. Persistent change from the young person's own baseline needs asking about.

▸  NOT always visible as sadness. In young people it can present as irritability, anger, boredom, school refusal, falling grades, somatic complaints or dropping out of sport and friends.

▸  NOT made worse by asking about suicide. Asking directly about suicidal thoughts does not increase suicidal ideation (Dazzi, Gribble, Wessely & Fear, 2014). Not asking is the risk.

▸  NOT laziness or a behaviour problem. Poor concentration, slowness and missing work are symptoms. Sanctions for incomplete homework can deepen worthlessness.

▸  NOT something the EP treats with medication advice. Antidepressants for young people are a specialist medical decision (NICE NG134, 2019); the EP does not advise on them (PSI 2.2.2).

▸  NOT always 'depression' when mood is low. Bereavement, adjustment to a life event, bipolar disorder, trauma, substance use and medical causes (e.g., thyroid, anaemia) can look similar and need a medical view.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: a meta-analysis by Costello, Erkanli and Angold (2006) estimated depression at roughly 3% in children under 13 and nearer 6% in adolescents 13–18 — check before quoting; estimates vary by method and year.

▸  IRELAND: the My World Survey (Dooley & Fitzgerald, 2012; My World Survey 2, Dooley et al., 2019) reports substantial rates of depressive symptoms in Irish adolescents and young adults. Specific rates not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: less common before puberty; presentation more often irritability, somatic complaints and withdrawal.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: marked rise across adolescence (Thapar et al., 2012). This is the main age band for EP concern.

▸  SEX RATIO: roughly equal before puberty; after puberty depression is more common in girls, often reported as about 2:1 (Thapar et al., 2012) — check before quoting.

▸  HIGHER RISK GROUPS: young people with a parent with depression, with chronic illness or disability, autistic young people, LGBTI+ young people, young people in care and those who have experienced abuse, bullying or bereavement — rates not stated here, check.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Low and uncertain at this age — rate not stated here, check.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Can occur in childhood but rises steeply from early to mid-adolescence (Thapar et al., 2012). In schools, concern typically surfaces in the senior primary years and across post-primary, often via attendance, falling grades, withdrawal or a disclosure — the difficulty is that it is often internalised and noticed late.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CAMHS (consultant psychiatrist and multidisciplinary team) for moderate to severe presentations or where there is risk; Primary Care Psychology for mild to moderate; GP as gateway. Private psychiatrists and clinical psychologists also. Medication is prescribed only by a doctor, usually a psychiatrist for under-18s.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS psychiatrist or psychologist; Primary Care psychologist; GP letter; Jigsaw clinician (note: Jigsaw typically supports rather than diagnoses — check); private clinician. A school-completed SDQ, MFQ or RCADS is a screen, not a diagnosis.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   GP first in most areas (urgently if risk); CAMHS for moderate to severe or risk; Primary Care Psychology for mild to moderate; Jigsaw for early support (12–25, check area); Emergency Department or emergency services

condition.name: Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Persistent Depressive Disorder · ICD-11 6A72 Dysthymic disorder — check codes before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.4 Mood) — and 3.7 Risk and safeguarding

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A CHRONIC depressive disorder: depressed mood for most of the day, on more days than not, for at least TWO YEARS in adults — and at least ONE YEAR in children and adolescents, where the mood can be IRRITABLE (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR).

▸  At least two further symptoms are present: poor appetite or overeating; sleep difficulty or oversleeping; low energy or fatigue; low self-esteem; poor concentration or difficulty making decisions; feelings of hopelessness. The person is not free of symptoms for more than two months at a time.

▸  DSM-5 (2013) brought together what were previously 'dysthymic disorder' and 'chronic major depressive disorder' under one label. ICD-11 retains 'dysthymic disorder'. Older reports may use either term.

▸  It is often LOWER-GRADE than a major depressive episode, but because it is long-lasting it can be as impairing — shaping self-concept, friendships and learning over years.

▸  Major depressive episodes can occur on top of it — sometimes called 'double depression' (Keller & Shapiro, 1982). Childhood-onset dysthymia has been followed prospectively and found to be long-lasting and to carry a high risk of later major depression (Kovacs, Akiskal, Gatsonis & Parrone, 1994).

▸  Because it has lasted so long, the young person and those around them may see it as personality — 'he's always been a bit negative'. That is the central identification problem.

▸  As with MDD, the EP recognises, asks about risk, refers and supports the school. Diagnosis is by CAMHS, Primary Care Psychology, GP or psychiatry.

▸  NOT personality or temperament. 'She's just a glass-half-empty child' may describe years of untreated depressive symptoms. Chronicity is the feature, not the explanation.

▸  NOT 'mild so it doesn't matter'. Being less intense than a major depressive episode does not mean less impairing; the length of time is what does the damage (Kovacs et al., 1994).

▸  NOT free of risk. Suicidal ideation can occur, particularly when major depressive episodes are superimposed. Ask about risk as you would with MDD.

▸  NOT only sadness. In young people, persistent irritability, low self-esteem and hopelessness may be the most visible features.

▸  NOT a reaction to a single event. If the low mood began with a clear stressor and is resolving, think adjustment or bereavement instead.

▸  NOT something the EP diagnoses or treats with medication advice (PSI 2.2.2).

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: less well studied in young people than MDD. Rate not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  IRELAND: no Irish-specific figure for dysthymia in young people identified here — check before quoting.

▸  SCHOOL AGE AND ADOLESCENT: childhood onset is recognised and is associated with long episodes and later MDD (Kovacs et al., 1994).

▸  SEX RATIO: rate not stated here — check.

▸  IDENTIFICATION: likely under-identified because it is chronic and lower-grade, and because it can be read as personality or as 'always been like that'.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Not established at this age — rate not stated here, check.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Can begin in childhood or adolescence; by definition the young person has had symptoms for at least a year before it can be identified. Often recognised late — in senior primary or post-primary — because it has been read as temperament, or only when a major depressive episode sits on top of it.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CAMHS or Primary Care Psychology depending on severity and risk; GP as gateway; private psychiatrist or clinical psychologist. Medication decisions sit with a doctor, usually a psychiatrist for under-18s.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS psychiatrist or psychologist; Primary Care psychologist; private clinician. Older reports may say 'dysthymia' or 'dysthymic disorder'. School screening measures (SDQ, MFQ, RCADS) are screens, not diagnoses.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   GP first (urgently if risk), who refers to CAMHS or Primary Care Psychology; Jigsaw (12–25, check area) for early support; ED or emergency services if risk is imminent; Tusla where abuse or neglect is suspected.

▸ 'SHOULD WE HAVE COME SOONER?'
   'Long-standing low mood is one of the hardest things to spot, because it becomes part of how everyone sees the child — including the child. You've noticed now, and that's what counts.'

WHAT YOU SEE AT THIS AGE
▸  Persistent flatness, irritability or loss of pleasure in a young child would prompt concern about the child's circumstances and relationships rather than this diagnosis. Parent report and referral via GP or Primary Care.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Persistent flatness, irritability or loss of pleasure in a young child would prompt concern about the child's circumstances and relationships rather than this diagnosis. Parent report and referral via GP or Primary Care.

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: A child who has been irritable, flat or down on themselves for a year or more, with tiredness, poor concentration and low self-esteem — often described as 'always like that'. Parent and teacher report on duration, pupil interview, MFQ or RCADS, and a direct, age-appropriate risk question.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: Long-standing low mood, hopelessness and low self-worth, with falling engagement, possible substance use and a risk of superimposed major depression. Self-report is primary; always ask about risk.

▸  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: Long-standing low mood affecting college or work transitions; the person may say they 'have

condition.name: Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ICD-10-CM F91.3) · ICD-11 6C90 Oppositional defiant disorder (qualifier: with / without chronic irritability-anger — check subcodes before quoting)
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class · 2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school) — and 3. EMOTIONAL (3.4 Mood) where irritability dominates

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 3.4 · 3.10 · 3.12 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32 · 5.34

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8 · 1.1.4

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Children First National Guidance (2017) · EPSEN Act 2004 · Education Act 1998 (s.29 appeals) · Education (Welfare) Act 2000 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · Children Act 2001 · GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A DSM-5-TR diagnosis in the 'Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorders' chapter: a frequent, persistent pattern of ANGRY/IRRITABLE MOOD, ARGUMENTATIVE/DEFIANT BEHAVIOUR, or VINDICTIVENESS lasting at least six months (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022).

▸  Criteria require at least four of eight listed symptoms across the three groupings, shown with at least one person who is not a sibling. Frequency guide: under 5 years, most days; 5 and over, at least once a week — unless otherwise stated in the criterion (APA, 2022). Verify wording against the DSM-5-TR text before quoting any criterion.

▸  SEVERITY is defined by SETTINGS, not intensity: mild = one setting; moderate = some symptoms in at least two settings; severe = some symptoms in three or more settings (APA, 2022). An 'ODD — mild' report may describe a child who is only oppositional at home.

▸  Stringaris and Goodman (2009) showed the symptoms split into IRRITABLE, HEADSTRONG and HURTFUL dimensions. The irritable dimension predicts later anxiety and depression; the headstrong and hurtful dimensions predict later conduct problems. ICD-11 builds this in with a 'chronic irritability-anger' qualifier.

▸  It is a DESCRIPTION of a pattern in relationships, not an explanation of it. The diagnosis tells you what is happening between the child and adults; it does not tell you why. That is the formulation — and that is the EP's job.

▸  The pattern is INTERACTIONAL. Patterson's (1982) coercion model: demand → escalation → adult withdraws the demand → escalation is reinforced for the child, and withdrawal is reinforced for the adult. Both sides learn. This is why parenting programmes work and why 'fixing the child' alone does not.

▸  DSM-5-TR states ODD should not be diagnosed where criteria for Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder are met (DMDD takes precedence), and that symptoms must not occur exclusively during a psychotic, substance use, depressive or bipolar disorder (APA, 2022).

▸  NOT a character judgement. 'Oppositional' and 'defiant' are clinical labels for a pattern; in a school report they read as moral verdicts. PSI 1.2.8 requires discretion so information is not used to a child's detriment — describe behaviour and context instead.

▸  NOT a sufficient explanation. Behaviour that looks like defiance is very often an unmet need: Hollo, Wehby and Oliver (2014) meta-analysed studies of children with emotional and behavioural disorders and found that a large majority had language deficits that had never been identified. 'Won't' is frequently 'can't understand' or 'can't do'.

▸  NOT the same as ADHD, though they often co-occur. In ADHD, non-compliance is typically forgetting, losing track or acting before thinking; in ODD the pattern is directed at adults and has an angry or vindictive quality. Untreated ADHD plus years of correction commonly produces an oppositional pattern on top.

▸  NOT a trauma response mislabelled — but it can be. Hypervigilance, controlling behaviour and rapid threat-based escalation after adversity can meet ODD criteria on paper. Ask about adversity before accepting a behavioural formulation.

▸  NOT anxiety-free. Refusal is one of the commonest faces of anxiety — the child who refuses to read aloud or go into the hall may be avoiding fear, not authority. The irritable dimension of ODD is itself linked to later emotional disorder (Stringaris & Goodman, 2009).

▸  NOT 'Pathological Demand Avoidance'. PDA is a profile described by Newson, Le Maréchal and David (2003); it is not a diagnosis in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11. Some families and clinicians use it to describe an anxiety-driven, extreme avoidance of everyday demands, often in autistic children; the evidence base and its status are debated. Record the term if a family uses it, describe the behaviour, and do not confirm or dismiss it.

▸  NOT a life sentence. Many children with an ODD diagnosis do not go on to conduct disorder; the headstrong/hurtful dimension, early onset, and adversity raise that risk (Stringaris & Goodman, 2009; Burke et al., 2002).

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: Polanczyk et al. (2015) pooled worldwide prevalence of ODD in children and adolescents at about 3.6% (disruptive behaviour disorders overall about 5.7%). DSM-5-TR reports prevalence estimates ranging roughly 1–11% depending on sample and method — check the text before quoting a single figure.

▸  IRELAND: no national ODD prevalence figure is stated here — check before quoting. Growing Up in Ireland reports SDQ conduct-problem data, which is a screening measure, not a diagnostic rate.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: oppositional behaviour is developmentally normal in toddlers; DSM-5-TR sets a higher frequency threshold under 5 (most days) for that reason. Diagnosis at this age should be rare and cautious.

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: typical period of first identification in school; symptoms usually first appear in the preschool years and rarely begin after early adolescence (APA, 2022).

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: some continuity; a subgroup progresses to conduct disorder, and the irritable subgroup to anxiety or depression.

▸  SEX RATIO: DSM-5-TR reports a modest male predominance before adolescence (about 1.4:1), not consistently found in adolescence or adulthood (APA, 2022) — check current text before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS

condition.name: Conduct Disorder (CD)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Conduct Disorder (ICD-10-CM F91.1 childhood-onset · F91.2 adolescent-onset · F91.9 unspecified onset) · ICD-11 6C91 Conduct-dissocial disorder (childhood / adolescent onset; limited prosocial emotions qualifier — check subcodes before quoting)
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class · 2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school) — and 3. EMOTIONAL (3.5 Trauma, attachment and loss · 3.7 Risk and safeguarding) where relevant

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 3.4 · 3.10 · 3.12 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32 · 5.34

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8 · 1.1.4

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Children First National Guidance (2017) · EPSEN Act 2004 · Education Act 1998 (s.29 appeals) · Education (Welfare) Act 2000 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · Children Act 2001 · GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A DSM-5-TR diagnosis: a repetitive and persistent pattern of behaviour that violates the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms or rules (APA, 2022).

▸  Criteria require at least three of fifteen behaviours in the past 12 months, at least one in the past 6 months, across four groups: AGGRESSION to people and animals; DESTRUCTION OF PROPERTY; DECEITFULNESS OR THEFT; SERIOUS VIOLATIONS OF RULES (e.g. truancy beginning before age 13). Verify the full list against DSM-5-TR before quoting.

▸  ONSET SPECIFIERS: childhood-onset (at least one symptom before age 10), adolescent-onset (none before 10), unspecified (APA, 2022). The distinction matters because the outcomes differ.

▸  Moffitt's (1993) developmental taxonomy: a small LIFE-COURSE-PERSISTENT group, with early onset and neurodevelopmental and family adversity, and a larger ADOLESCENCE-LIMITED group whose antisocial behaviour is more social and more often desists. Later follow-ups have complicated this, but it remains the most useful frame for a school conversation.

▸  'WITH LIMITED PROSOCIAL EMOTIONS' specifier: at least two of lack of remorse or guilt; callous lack of empathy; unconcern about performance; shallow or deficient affect — persistently, over 12 months, across relationships and settings (APA, 2022). This maps to research on callous-unemotional traits (Frick et al., 2014). It is a small subgroup and must never be inferred from a single incident.

▸  Severity (mild / moderate / severe) is based on the number of problems and the harm caused (APA, 2022).

▸  It is heavily shaped by CONTEXT: poverty, harsh or inconsistent parenting, abuse and neglect, peer groups, school exclusion. The behaviour is real and harmful; the causes are rarely in the child alone.

▸  NOT 'a bad kid'. The diagnosis describes behaviour over 12 months; it is not a prediction of adult criminality. Most young people with conduct problems do not go on to antisocial personality disorder (Moffitt, 1993; APA, 2022).

▸  NOT the same as delinquency or offending. Offending is a legal category; CD is a clinical description of a pattern with impairment. A single serious incident does not make a diagnosis.

▸  NOT 'psychopathy'. Callous-unemotional traits are a narrow, research-defined dimension (Frick et al., 2014). Do not use 'psychopath', 'no conscience' or similar in any report or conversation.

▸  NOT separate from harm done to the child. Many children with conduct problems have experienced abuse, neglect, domestic violence, or exploitation. Cruelty to animals, fire-setting and sexualised aggression can be indicators of the child's own victimisation.

▸  NOT untreatable. NICE CG158 (2013, updated 2017) recommends parent training for younger children, child-focused social and cognitive problem-solving programmes for older children, and multimodal interventions (e.g. multisystemic therapy) for adolescents — check for updates.

▸  NOT solved by exclusion. Removing a young person from school removes structure, adult relationships and supervision, and exposes them to peers and exploitation. Exclusion is a risk factor, not an intervention.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: Polanczyk et al. (2015) pooled worldwide prevalence of CD in children and adolescents at about 2.1%. DSM-5 reports one-year population prevalence estimates from about 2% to over 10%, median about 4% — check the DSM-5-TR text before quoting.

▸  IRELAND: no national CD prevalence figure is stated here — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not meaningfully diagnosed; aggression at this age is common and developmental.

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: childhood-onset cases are identified here; this is the group Moffitt (1993) links to persistent difficulty.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: prevalence rises; most new cases are adolescent-onset (APA, 2022).

▸  SEX RATIO: more common in males in DSM-5-TR; DSM-5-TR notes females are more likely than males to show lying, truancy, running away and substance use rather than physical aggression (APA, 2022) — check current text before quoting a ratio.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Not meaningfully estimated at this age — check before quoting.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Childhood-onset CD is identified in the primary years, often after a history of ODD and ADHD. Adolescent-onset CD appears from about 13 onwards, when peer influence, independence and unsupervised time increase. Identification often follows a crisis — a serious incident, suspension, or Garda contact.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CAMHS psychiatrist or clinical psychologist, or a private psychiatrist or clinical psychologist. Some young people are assessed through youth justice routes (e.g. assessment linked to Oberstown Children Detention Campus or court reports). The EP does not diagnose it.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS; a private clinical psychologist or psychiatrist; a forensic or court-ordered assessment; occasionally Tusla-commissioned assessment for a child in care. Check whether the report was written for a clinical, legal or care purpose — it shapes what it says.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   CAMHS via GP where ther

condition.name: Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (DMDD)
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (ICD-10-CM F34.81), in the Depressive Disorders chapter · ICD-11: no equivalent category — nearest is 6C90.0 ODD with chronic irritability-anger (check before quoting)
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.4 Mood) — and 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class · 2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 3.4 · 3.10 · 3.12 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32 · 5.34

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8 · 1.1.4

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · Children First National Guidance (2017) · EPSEN Act 2004 · Education Act 1998 (s.29 appeals) · Education (Welfare) Act 2000 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · Children Act 2001 · GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  A DSM-5 diagnosis introduced in 2013 and retained in DSM-5-TR, placed in the DEPRESSIVE DISORDERS chapter — not with the behaviour disorders (APA, 2022). It is a MOOD diagnosis whose most visible sign is behaviour.

▸  Core features: severe, recurrent TEMPER OUTBURSTS (verbal and/or behavioural) grossly out of proportion to the situation and inconsistent with developmental level, on average three or more times a week; PLUS persistently IRRITABLE OR ANGRY MOOD between outbursts, most of the day, nearly every day, observable by others (APA, 2022).

▸  Duration and settings: present for 12 months or more without a break of three or more consecutive months; present in at least two of three settings (home, school, peers) and severe in at least one (APA, 2022).

▸  AGE RULES (verify wording against DSM-5-TR before quoting): the diagnosis should not be made for the first time before age 6 or after age 18; by history or observation, onset of the criteria is before age 10 (APA, 2022). So DMDD is a school-age-onset diagnosis — onset is before 10, first diagnosis between 6 and 18.

▸  Why it exists: to address the rise in bipolar disorder diagnoses in children in the United States, many of whom had chronic, non-episodic irritability rather than distinct manic episodes. Research on 'severe mood dysregulation' showed these children tended to develop depression and anxiety, not bipolar disorder (Leibenluft, 2011).

▸  Exclusions: it cannot co-exist with ODD, Intermittent Explosive Disorder or bipolar disorder; if DMDD criteria are met, ODD is not diagnosed. There must never have been a distinct period of more than one day meeting criteria for mania or hypomania (APA, 2022).

▸  It is DSM-only. ICD-11 chose not to include it and instead added a 'with chronic irritability-anger' qualifier to ODD. A child could be described differently depending on which system the clinician used.

▸  NOT 'tantrums'. Tantrums are normal and episodic. DMDD requires frequent, severe outbursts PLUS an irritable mood that persists between them, for a year, across settings.

▸  NOT childhood bipolar disorder. The irritability is chronic, not episodic; there are no distinct manic episodes. Leibenluft (2011) summarises the evidence that these young people are more likely to develop depression and anxiety than bipolar disorder.

▸  NOT ODD with a new name. It sits in the depressive disorders chapter because the underlying problem is mood. Recommendations should address emotional regulation and wellbeing, not only compliance.

▸  NOT a diagnosis for under-6s. Irritability in preschoolers can be significant and deserve support, but DSM-5-TR says DMDD is not diagnosed for the first time before 6.

▸  NOT uncontroversial. Critics have questioned its distinctiveness from severe ODD and its stability over time; ICD-11 did not adopt it (Stringaris et al., 2018 review the debate). Hold it lightly and focus on the child's actual pattern.

▸  NOT explained by the diagnosis alone. As with ODD, test for unmet learning and language need, ADHD, anxiety, autism, sleep difficulty and adversity — all of which can drive chronic irritability.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: the original DSM-5 text (2013) estimated 6-month to 1-year prevalence among children and adolescents at probably about 2–5%, and expected higher rates in males and school-age children than in females and adolescents. That estimate predates the community studies below, and the DSM-5-TR (APA, 2022) prevalence section may differ — check the current text before quoting any figure.

▸  Copeland et al. (2013) applied DMDD criteria retrospectively to three US community samples (ages 2–17) and found 3-month rates of roughly 0.8–3.3%, the HIGHEST in the preschool sample (with the age-of-onset rule set aside), and very high co-occurrence with other disorders — check figures before quoting.

▸  IRELAND: no Irish figure stated here — check before quoting. DMDD is used less often in Irish and UK services than in the US; many Irish reports will describe the same child as ODD, ADHD with emotional dysregulation, or anxiety.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not diagnosed (APA, 2022).

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the band where onset must occur (before 10) and where most first diagnoses are made.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: can be first diagnosed up to 18; outbursts may lessen while irritability and risk of depression and anxiety continue (Stringaris et al., 2018).

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Not applicable as a diagnosis at this age (APA, 2022).

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Onset of the criteria must be before age 10, and the diagnosis is not made for the first time before 6 or after 18 (APA, 2022 — verify wording). In practice it is usually named between 6 and 12, after a year or more of daily irritability and frequent outbursts across home and school.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CAMHS psychiatrist or clinical psychologist, or a private psychiatrist. It is used less often in Irish services than in the US; the same child may be described as ODD (with chronic irritability-anger under ICD-11), ADHD with emotional dysregulation, or anxiety. The EP does not diagnose it.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CAMHS; a private psychia

condition.name: Selective Mutism
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Selective Mutism (anxiety disorders chapter; ICD-10-CM F94.0) · ICD-11 6B06 Selective mutism — verify in the ICD-11 browser before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.2 Anxiety) — and 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Disability Act 2005 (Assessment of Need) · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  An ANXIETY disorder: consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected (usually school), despite speaking in other situations (usually home) (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR). DSM-5 (2013) moved it into the anxiety disorders chapter; ICD-11 also places it among anxiety and fear-related disorders.

▸  Criteria in outline: lasts at least ONE MONTH and is not limited to the first month of school; interferes with educational achievement or social communication; is NOT attributable to lack of knowledge of, or comfort with, the spoken language required; is not better explained by a communication disorder and does not occur exclusively during autism or a psychotic disorder (APA, 2022). Read the full criteria before quoting.

▸  The child CAN speak. Speech is blocked by anxiety at the EXPECTATION of speaking — often strongest with particular people, in particular places, or when others can hear. Johnson & Wintgens (2016) describe it as a fear of speaking to certain people, maintained like any phobia.

▸  MAINTAINING CYCLE: expectation to speak → anxiety rises → silence (or an adult answering for the child) → relief. The relief reinforces the silence (negative reinforcement). Well-meaning adults maintain it from both directions — by pressing for speech and by rescuing.

▸  Onset is usually BEFORE AGE 5, but it is often first noticed at school entry, because that is where sustained speaking to non-family adults is first expected (APA, 2022).

▸  Wide range of severity: some children whisper to one friend, nod, point or write; others freeze, avoid eye contact, and cannot eat, laugh, cough or use the toilet in school. Muris & Ollendick (2015) review the strong link with behavioural inhibition and social anxiety.

▸  The evidence-based approaches are BEHAVIOURAL and graded: stimulus fading ('sliding-in'), shaping and graded exposure, delivered in the real setting, with the pressure to speak removed (Cohan et al., 2006; Johnson & Wintgens, 2016). SLT involvement is standard practice in Ireland and the UK.

▸  NOT defiance or control. The older term 'elective mutism' implied a choice; DSM-IV (1994) renamed it 'selective' to remove that implication. Treating the silence as oppositional raises anxiety and entrenches it.

▸  NOT shyness that will pass by itself. Shy children warm up and speak when they need to; in SM the pattern persists and becomes more habitual the longer it continues (Johnson & Wintgens, 2016). 'Wait and see' is not a plan.

▸  NOT the EAL silent period. Children new to a language commonly go through a non-verbal period in that language while receptive understanding builds (Tabors, 2008). DSM-5-TR excludes mutism explained by lack of knowledge of or comfort with the language. SM is more likely where the child is ALSO silent in the home language in school (e.g., with a same-language peer or adult), or silence persists well after receptive English is established (Toppelberg et al., 2005) — check the paper for their duration guidance before quoting.

▸  NOT a language disorder — but speech and language difficulties co-occur in a substantial proportion (Kristensen, 2000), and embarrassment about speech can feed the mutism. SLT assessment still matters, often using home recordings.

▸  NOT usually caused by trauma or abuse. Reviews do not support assuming a traumatic cause (Viana et al., 2009). Do not create suspicion without basis — and do not ignore indicators either. Sudden-onset mutism is a different picture (see red flags).

▸  NOT fixed by pressure, bribes, tricks or 'I'll wait until you say it'. Pressure raises anxiety; the evidence-based approaches reduce pressure while graduating exposure (Cohan et al., 2006).

▸  NOT autism — though the two can co-occur. The question is whether silence is context-specific and fear-linked (SM) or part of a social communication difference present across settings, including home.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: DSM-5-TR reports point prevalence from clinic and school samples of roughly 0.03%–1% (APA, 2022). Bergman, Piacentini & McCracken (2002) found about 0.7% in a US early-primary school sample. Check the current DSM-5-TR text before quoting.

▸  IRELAND: no Irish prevalence figure stated here — check before quoting. Expect most schools to meet a child with SM only occasionally, so staff experience will usually be low.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: onset usually here; identification most often in preschool or junior/senior infants (APA, 2022).

▸  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: main window for referral and intervention.

▸  ADOLESCENT 13–16: new onset is uncommon; long-standing SM is harder to shift, and residual social anxiety is common (Muris & Ollendick, 2015) — rate not stated here, check.

▸  SEX RATIO: more girls than boys in many clinical samples (Viana et al., 2009), but the DSM-5 text states prevalence does not seem to vary by sex (check the DSM-5-TR wording) — do not quote a ratio.

▸  BILINGUAL / MIGRANT CHILDREN: higher rates are reported (reviewed by Toppelberg et al., 2005) — and this is exactly where over-identification from the silent period is most likely. Hold both.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Most cases begin here; band-specific rate not stated — check (DSM-5-TR range roughly 0.03–1% across samples).

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Onset is usually before age 5 (APA, 2022), but identification typically happens at school entry (junior infants) or at a transition,

condition.name: Specific Phobia
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Specific Phobia (ICD-10-CM F40.2xx — subtype codes, check before quoting) · ICD-11 6B03 Specific phobia — verify in the ICD-11 browser
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 3. EMOTIONAL (3.2 Anxiety)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.2.4 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Children First Act 2015 · EPSEN Act 2004 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · Education (Welfare) Act 2000 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  Marked fear or anxiety about a SPECIFIC object or situation that almost always provokes immediate fear, is actively avoided or endured with intense distress, is out of proportion to the actual danger, typically lasts 6 months or more, and causes significant distress or impairment (APA, 2022, DSM-5-TR).

▸  In children the fear may show as crying, tantrums, freezing or clinging (APA, 2022). Children do not need to describe it as fear or recognise it as excessive.

▸  Five specifiers (APA, 2022): ANIMAL; NATURAL ENVIRONMENT (heights, storms, water); BLOOD-INJECTION-INJURY; SITUATIONAL (lifts, planes, enclosed spaces); OTHER — in children often choking, vomiting (emetophobia), loud sounds or costumed characters.

▸  BLOOD-INJECTION-INJURY phobia is physiologically different: a rise then sudden drop in heart rate and blood pressure can cause fainting (vasovagal response). Applied tension was developed for this (Öst & Sterner, 1987). Relevant to school vaccination sessions.

▸  MAINTAINED BY AVOIDANCE. Each avoidance brings relief and prevents the child learning that the feared outcome does not happen or can be coped with. Exposure works by creating new, competing learning — the inhibitory learning account (Craske et al., 2014).

▸  EVIDENCE-BASED TREATMENT is CBT with graded exposure (James et al., 2020). Intensive one-session treatment has RCT support in young people (Ollendick et al., 2009). In Ireland this is delivered by Primary Care Psychology or CAMHS. The EP's role is formulation, school adjustments and supporting a clinician's plan.

▸  Normal fears follow a developmental sequence — separation and strangers in infancy; animals, dark and imaginary creatures in early childhood; injury and natural events in middle childhood; social and evaluative fears in adolescence (Gullone, 2000). A phobia is persistence, disproportion and impairment beyond this.

▸  NOT ordinary childhood fear. Most children fear the dark, dogs or monsters at some stage (Gullone, 2000). Diagnosis needs persistence, disproportion and impairment. Do not pathologise a developmentally normal fear.

▸  NOT helped by reassurance and avoidance alone. Both bring short-term relief and keep the fear alive. Family accommodation of anxiety is associated with greater symptom severity (Lebowitz et al., 2013).

▸  NOT exposure if it is forced. Making a child pat a dog without their agreement, or surprising them with the feared thing, is not exposure therapy — it can sensitise the child and damages trust. Exposure is graded, planned, agreed and repeated.

▸  NOT always what it looks like. Emetophobia can look like an eating difficulty or school refusal during winter bugs; choking phobia can look like food refusal; fear of hand dryers can look like a toileting problem. Always ask what the child fears will HAPPEN.

▸  NOT the same as sensory aversion in autism — though the two can sit together. A child who covers their ears at the hand dryer may be in sensory pain rather than fear. Both need a response; they need different responses.

▸  NOT usually the EP's to treat. CBT with exposure is delivered by Primary Care Psychology or CAMHS. Some EP services offer brief CBT-informed work under supervision — check your service model and your own competence (PSI 2.2.4).

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: DSM-5-TR reports approximately 5% in children and approximately 16% in 13–17-year-olds, with 12-month prevalence around 7–9% in US adult community samples (APA, 2022). Check the current text before quoting.
