▸  AUTISM-RELATED CATATONIA (hedged): a slower, progressive deterioration described mainly in autistic adolescents and young adults — increased slowness, freezing mid-movement, needing physical or verbal prompts to start or finish actions, reduced speech, loss of previously established skills, sometimes episodes of agitation (Wing & Shah, 2000; Breen & Hare, 2017). How best to define and measure this, and how common it is, remain debated.

▸  It is TREATABLE. Medical treatment is available and often effective, and delay can lead to serious complications (Benarous et al., 2018; Cornic et al., 2009). Decisions about treatment sit entirely with the medical team — the EP does not advise on medication or treatment (PSI 2.2.2).

▸  THE EP ROLE: RECOGNISE a change from the child's own baseline, DOCUMENT it precisely, and REFER urgently through the medical route. Nothing else in this row outranks that.

▸  NOT 'just part of the autism'. A new loss of skills or new slowing in an autistic young person is a CHANGE and needs medical assessment — diagnostic overshadowing is the key risk (Breen & Hare, 2017).

▸  NOT only a feature of schizophrenia. That was the historical view; DSM-5 (2013) made catatonia a specifier across many conditions and a condition in its own right because it occurs with mood disorders, neurodevelopmental conditions and medical illness (APA, 2022).

▸  NOT defiance or 'refusing'. Negativism and mutism in catatonia are not chosen; pushing harder or applying consequences is inappropriate.

▸  NOT selective mutism. Selective mutism is consistent silence in specific social contexts with normal movement; catatonic mutism comes with motor signs and a change from baseline.

▸  NOT ordinary shyness, low mood or teenage withdrawal — although severe depression can progress to catatonia, which is why a marked slowing needs a doctor.

▸  NOT something to wait and see about. Where features are new or worsening, the route is medical and prompt.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  CHILDREN AND ADOLESCENTS: rare; community prevalence not stated here — check before quoting. Most paediatric literature is case series from specialist centres (Benarous et al., 2018).

▸  AUTISM: Wing & Shah (2000), in a clinic-referred sample, reported catatonic features in around 17% of those aged 15 and over — a referred sample, not a population estimate; check before quoting.

▸  AGE: onset in autism-related catatonia described mostly in adolescence and early adulthood (Wing & Shah, 2000; Breen & Hare, 2017) — check.

▸  IRELAND: no figure stated here — check before quoting.

▸  SEX RATIO: not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Rate not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Can occur at any age but is rare in young children; most paediatric cases are adolescents. Autism-related catatonia is described mostly from adolescence into early adulthood. Identification is usually prompted by a change noticed at home or school.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: medical teams — paediatrics (including neurology for medical causes), CAMHS psychiatry, adult psychiatry from 18; in hospital, liaison psychiatry. For autistic or ID young people, CDNT or MHID colleagues may raise it but diagnosis and treatment are medical. The EP does not diagnose.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   Paediatrician or paediatric neurologist; CAMHS or liaison psychiatrist; hospital discharge summary. A CDNT report may describe skill loss without naming catatonia — check.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   Urgent GP → paediatrics and/or CAMHS. Emergency Department or emergency services if not eating/drinking, feverish, rigid or deteriorating. Inform the CDNT keyworker where one exists. Tusla if any protection concern.

▸ 'SHOULD WE HAVE COME SOONER?'
   'Changes like this often creep up slowly, and it's very hard to see them day to day. You've noticed it and acted — that's what matters now.'

WHAT YOU SEE AT THIS AGE
▸  Loss of skills in a young child (speech, walking, play) is a medical and developmental red flag in its own right, whatever the cause. Refer urgently vi

condition.name: Other specified / unspecified neurodevelopmental disorder
condition.code: DSM-5-TR Other Specified Neurodevelopmental Disorder (F88) · Unspecified Neurodevelopmental Disorder (F89) · ICD-11 6A0Y Other specified neurodevelopmental disorders · 6A0Z Neurodevelopmental disorders, unspecified — check codes before quoting
condition.text:
WHERE THIS SITS
▸  NEPS referral form category: 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability) — and whichever NEPS area the individual profile points to (language, attention, social, motor)

▸  UCD competency: 1. Assessment

▸  CORU: 3.1 · 3.2 · 5.28 · 5.29 · 5.30 · 5.31 · 5.32

▸  PSI: 2.2.2 · 2.3.1 · 1.3.1 · 1.2.8

▸  Law and policy: Disability Act 2005 (Assessment of Need) · EPSEN Act 2004 · Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 · Children First Act 2015 · GDPR

WHAT IT IS, AND WHAT IT IS NOT
▸  Two RESIDUAL categories in the DSM-5-TR neurodevelopmental chapter, used when a child has neurodevelopmental symptoms causing clinically significant impairment that do not meet full criteria for any specific neurodevelopmental disorder (APA, 2022).

▸  OTHER SPECIFIED: the clinician states WHY criteria are not met or what the presentation is. DSM-5-TR's example is 'neurodevelopmental disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure' (ND-PAE), which is also proposed in DSM-5-TR Section III as a condition for further study (APA, 2022).

▸  UNSPECIFIED: the clinician chooses NOT to state the reason — including when there is insufficient information to be more specific, for example early assessment, emergency settings, or a child too young or unwell to assess fully (APA, 2022).

▸  ICD-11 has parallel residual codes (6A0Y, 6A0Z) (WHO, 2019/2022). The Reference sheet lists 6A0Z; check the browser before quoting.

▸  WHEN IT IS LEGITIMATELY USED: a child with clear, impairing difficulties across several areas (e.g. attention, social communication, motor, learning) that fall just short of each specific diagnosis; a provisional label before a fuller assessment; FASD-type presentations where a clinic uses ND-PAE; a genetic syndrome with a neurodevelopmental profile that does not fit a single category.

▸  WHY IT EXISTS: neurodevelopmental difficulties are dimensional and overlap heavily. Gillberg's ESSENCE concept (2010) and the 'transdiagnostic' research agenda (Astle et al., 2022) both argue that many children present with mixed profiles that single categories fit poorly.

▸  WHAT IT DOES NOT DO: the label tells you almost nothing about the child's needs. Two children with this code can have entirely different profiles. For the EP, the job is to DESCRIBE THE PROFILE — strengths, needs, impact, and what helps — rather than lean on the code.

▸  NOT a 'mild' diagnosis. It means criteria for a named disorder were not met or not specified — impairment still has to be clinically significant.

▸  NOT a diagnosis of 'autistic traits' or 'ADHD traits'. Clinicians sometimes use it that way informally; if so, the report should say which traits and what impact — check with the author.

▸  NOT a gateway to specific placements. Many specialist placements (e.g. an autism special class) are tied to a specific diagnosis; a residual code usually will not meet those criteria — check current NCSE criteria before advising a family.

▸  NOT needed for school support. Mainstream support under the Continuum of Support is allocated on NEED, not diagnosis (Department of Education, Circular 0013/2017 on the Special Education Teaching allocation model — check for updates).

▸  NOT permanent. Unspecified categories, especially in young children, are often provisional; review is expected.

▸  NOT a substitute for an EP formulation. An educational report that says 'has other specified neurodevelopmental disorder' and stops has told the teacher nothing.

HOW COMMON AT THIS AGE
▸  OVERALL: rate not stated here — check before quoting. Residual categories are inconsistently recorded across services.

▸  IRELAND: no national figure stated here — check before quoting. Use of the residual codes may vary between CDNTs, CAMHS and private clinicians.

▸  EARLY YEARS: more often used provisionally when a full picture cannot yet be established (APA, 2022).

▸  ND-PAE / FASD: prevalence figures vary widely by method and country; no Irish figure stated here — check before quoting.

▸  SEX RATIO: not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Rate not stated here — check before quoting.

▸  AT OTHER AGES (for context): SCHOOL AGE 6–12 · ADOLESCENT 13–16 · YOUNG ADULT 17–26 · SPECIAL SETTING

THE PATHWAY AND THE TIMELINE
▸ TYPICAL AGE OF IDENTIFICATION, AND WHY THEN
   Most often given in Early Years or early School Age, when a child has clear multi-area difficulties but the picture is not yet clear enough — or does not fit — for a specific diagnosis. Sometimes given later after a CDNT or private assessment that does not reach threshold for autism or ADHD.

▸ WHO DIAGNOSES IT
   Ireland: CDNT team (psychologist, often with SLT/OT); CAMHS psychiatrist; paediatrician; private clinical psychologist or psychiatrist. The EP does not diagnose.

▸ WHO COULD HAVE WRITTEN THE REPORT IN FRONT OF YOU
   CDNT multidisciplinary report; an Assessment of Need report (Disability Act 2005 — check what it says about diagnosis); paediatric letter; private clinician. It may appear as 'NDD NOS' or 'unspecified NDD'.

▸ WHO YOU REFER TO
   CDNT for complex multi-area needs (check local referral routes); Primary Care SLT/OT for specific areas; GP/paediatrics for medical, genetic or FASD questions; review by the original diagnosing service at a stated interval.

▸ 'SHOULD WE HAVE COME SOONER?'
   'Mixed profiles are genuinely harder to pin down, and many families hear "wait and see" at first. You've got a clear description of his needs now — that's what we build on.'

WHAT YOU SEE AT THIS AGE
▸  Mixed delays across language, play, motor and attention that do not yet fit a specific diagnosis. Describe development across domains; review expected. Global Developmental Delay may be used instead for under-5s with delays across several areas (see its own row).

▸  EARLY YEARS 0–5: Mixed delays across language, play, motor and attention that do not yet fit a specific diagnosis. Describe development across domains; review expected. Global Developmental Delay may be

presentation.name: Working memory difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty HOLDING and WORKING ON information in mind for a few seconds while doing something else with it — keeping a sentence in mind while writing it, carrying a number in mental arithmetic, remembering step three while doing step one.

•  Baddeley and Hitch (1974) framed working memory as a limited-capacity system (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive); Baddeley (2000) added the episodic buffer. The classroom question is which of these is overloaded, not whether the child 'has' it.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis. Part D lists it as 'Executive function profile, not a diagnosis' — nobody diagnoses it, and it needs no diagnosis to be acted on.

•  Gathercole and Alloway (2008) describe the classroom signature: losing track mid-task, partial instruction-following, place-keeping errors, abandoning tasks — often misread as inattention or not listening.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT poor long-term memory. A child may remember every detail of a match from last year and still lose a three-step instruction in ten seconds — they are different systems.

•  NOT the same as ADHD. Weak working memory is common in ADHD and also occurs on its own, and in DLD and dyslexia. Do not let a low Working Memory Index carry a diagnostic implication in your report.

•  NOT fixed by computerised training. Melby-Lervåg and Hulme (2013) found training improves the trained task but with no convincing transfer to reading, maths or attention; do not recommend it as a classroom intervention.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: forgets the second half of an instruction; wanders off mid-task in play. Capacity is developmentally small at this age — describe against peers in the same room, and do not score.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the peak referral window. Copying, multi-step maths, sentence writing and following oral instructions break down; the child often looks 'dreamy' or starts and stops.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: note-taking, multi-part exam questions, mental arithmetic in science, and following a subject teacher who talks while writing. Many subject teachers in one day means many sets of instructions to hold.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: lecture note-taking, reading dense text, workplace instructions given verbally. Self-report and strategy use become the main evidence.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: interpret against what the setting routinely scaffolds — a child who manages with a visual timetable may be showing that the scaffold works, not that capacity is adequate.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  DLD

•  Dyslexia

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Acquired brain injury

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  WISC-V UK Working Memory Index (Digit Span, Picture Span; Letter-Number Sequencing as secondary) — look at the verbal versus visual split and at forward versus backward span; check the manual for interpretation rules.

•  BRIEF-2 Working Memory scale, parent and teacher (self-report at adolescence) — describes everyday perception, not capacity itself.

•  Classroom observation during an instruction-heavy task: count instructions given, steps retained, and what the child does when they lose track (copies a peer, asks, stops).

•  Work-sample analysis: place-keeping errors, missed words in copied sentences, incomplete multi-step answers.

•  Rule out hearing (audiology), language comprehension (DLD) and anxiety — each lowers span scores for a different reason.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  REDUCE THE LOAD, DON'T TRAIN THE CAPACITY: one instruction at a time, or instructions written and left visible. Gathercole and Alloway (2008) recommend reducing the amount to be held, increasing meaningfulness, and repeating.

•  EXTERNAL MEMORY AIDS the child is taught to use: task checklists on the desk, word banks, number lines, worked examples left on the board, a written homework record the teacher checks.

•  CHECK BACK, not 'do you understand?': ask the child to say what they will do first. Build this into routine so it is not singling out.

•  BREAK WRITING into plan / say / write: oral rehearsal of the sentence before writing it; scribe or dictation for longer pieces where content is the target.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support in most cases; School Support where a targeted plan in the Student Support File is needed. Review after 6–8 weeks with a named measure (e.g., steps completed independently).

•  DO NOT recommend commercial working memory training as an intervention for attainment (Melby-Lervåg & Hulme, 2013; Melby-Lervåg et al., 2016). REFER to audiology or SLT where hearing or language comprehension is in question.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Working memory is the mental notepad we hold things on for a few seconds while we use them. Hers is smaller than most children her age, so when there's a lot to hold, some of it falls off.'

•  'This isn't a diagnosis and nobody diagnoses it. It is a description of how she learns, and it tells us exactly what to change — fewer things to hold at once, and more written down.'

•  'At home: one instruction at a time, and ask her to tell you back what she's going to do. It's not about checking up — it's about giving her a second go at holding it.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When he stops mid-task it's usually because the instruction has fallen out, not because he's switched off. Written steps on the desk fix most of it.'

•  'Count the steps in your instructions for a morning. Three or more in one breath is where he loses the thread.'

•  'Don't ask "do you understand?" — he'll say yes. Ask "what are you going to do first?"'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your brain has a little whiteboard for remembering things for a short time. Yours fills up quickly, so we'll write things down to help it.'

•  OLDER: 'Working memory is like RAM on a phone — too many apps open and it slows down. It's not about being clever. Writing things down

presentation.name: Inhibition difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty STOPPING or HOLDING BACK a response — the answer shouted out, the hand that reaches before the thought, the comment said before it is checked. Diamond (2013) groups inhibitory control (self-control and interference control) as one of three core executive functions.

•  Barkley (1997) places behavioural inhibition at the centre of his account of self-regulation: without the pause, the other executive functions do not get a chance to operate.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). It is described, formulated and supported; nobody diagnoses it.

•  It shows in two forms: MOTOR/BEHAVIOURAL (blurting, touching, grabbing, leaving the seat) and COGNITIVE/INTERFERENCE (being pulled by a distractor, giving the habitual answer rather than the correct one).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT defiance. Defiance is a choice against a known rule; poor inhibition is acting before the rule is retrieved. Ask the child afterwards — they usually know the rule and are as surprised as the adult.

•  NOT a character flaw or poor parenting. It is developmental: inhibitory control improves steadily through childhood (Diamond, 2013), and some children are on a slower curve.

•  NOT fixed by consequences alone. Sanctions after the event do not supply the pause before it; structure and cues that arrive BEFORE the moment of response do.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: grabbing toys, difficulty waiting a turn, running off. Much of this is typical at this age — describe against same-age peers in the same setting.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: calling out, interrupting, rushing work and missing the instruction, reacting physically in the yard. Peer relationships start to suffer.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: impulsive comments to staff, risk-taking, online impulsivity, careless exam errors. The social cost rises and so does the disciplinary record.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: impulsive spending, driving, workplace comments, submitting before checking.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: interpret against the setting's baseline and check whether the behaviour is communicative (e.g., in a child with limited speech, grabbing may be requesting).

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Acquired brain injury

•  Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder

•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Structured classroom observation with a comparison peer: frequency of calling out or out-of-seat per interval, and — crucially — what happens in the second before (trigger) and after (payoff).

•  BRIEF-2 Inhibit scale (parent, teacher; self-report in adolescence) and Conners-4 impulsivity content — perception across settings; disagreement between raters is data.

•  TEA-Ch2 subtests tapping response inhibition (check the manual for which subtests and age range).

•  Pupil interview after an incident: 'What did you notice first? When did you know?' — tells you whether the rule was known and when it arrived.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PUT THE PAUSE OUTSIDE THE CHILD: 'think time' before hands up, mini-whiteboards so everyone answers at once, a sticky note to write the thought down rather than say it.

•  PRE-CORRECT, don't only correct: a quiet reminder of the rule immediately before the known hot spot (lining up, yard, transitions).

•  REINFORCE THE WAIT, not only the outcome: specific praise within seconds of a successful hold-back ('you waited — thank you').

•  PLAN THE HOT SPOTS in the Student Support File: which times, which settings, which adult is nearby. Supervised transitions often matter more than in-class strategies.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support to School Support; School Support Plus where safety or exclusion risk is involved and outside agencies are engaged.

•  DO NOT recommend reduced timetables as a behaviour strategy without a planned return and review; REFER to CAMHS or Primary Care if the pattern is pervasive across settings and a diagnostic question is raised.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Most of us have a split-second brake between wanting to do something and doing it. His brake is slower to engage. He knows the rules — the brake just arrives late.'

•  'That's why punishment afterwards doesn't change much. What helps is reminders just before the tricky moment, and noticing when he does manage to wait.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Ask him afterwards and he'll tell you the rule. The problem isn't knowing it, it's retrieving it in time.'

•  'Pre-correction at transitions and a whole-class answer method (whiteboards, think-pair-share) remove most of the call-outs without singling him out.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your brain has brakes, like a bike. Yours are a bit slow sometimes. We're going to practise a stop-and-think so the brakes catch up.'

•  OLDER: 'Your mouth sometimes gets there before your brain has checked it. That's a speed thing, not a you-being-bad thing. Let's figure out the moments it happens most.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — impulsive self-endangering behaviour (running onto roads, climbing heights, impulsive self-harm in adolescence): follow the school's risk and safeguarding procedure the same day.

•  BOUNDARY — do not describe the child as 'ADHD-like' in reports; describe the behaviour and its frequency. Diagnosis is for CAMHS/Primary Care/paediatrics.

•  WATCH — a new onset of disinhibition in an adolescent: may reflect substance use, mood change or neurological change; refer via GP.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'He knows he shouldn't do it — so why does he?' A: 'Knowing and stopping are two different skills. His knowing is fine; his stopping is slow.'

•  Q: 'Should he be sanctioned?' A: 'The school's code of behaviour applies to him as to anyone, and consequences are fine. They just won't be enough on their own — the change comes from what we put in place before the moment.'

•  Q: 'Is it ADHD?' A: 'Inhibition difficulty is central to ADHD but it also

presentation.name: Cognitive flexibility difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty SHIFTING — between tasks, rules, perspectives or strategies. Diamond (2013) names cognitive flexibility as the third core executive function, building on inhibition and working memory.

•  In class it looks like: stuck on one method when it isn't working, distress when the timetable changes, difficulty seeing another person's view in a dispute, repeating an error after being shown the fix.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it; you describe the situations where shifting breaks down.

•  Zelazo's Dimensional Change Card Sort (Zelazo, 2006) shows the developmental shape: younger children know the new rule and still sort by the old one — knowing and switching dissociate.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT stubbornness or oppositionality. The child is usually not choosing to resist; they cannot find the other route quickly enough. Treating it as defiance escalates it.

•  NOT only an autism feature. It is prominent in autism and also appears in ADHD, anxiety, OCD and after brain injury. Do not use it as evidence for any single diagnosis.

•  NOT removed by insisting on change. Unplanned change increases load; planned, previewed change builds tolerance.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: distress at transitions (tidy-up time, leaving a preferred activity), rigid play scripts. Much is typical — describe relative to peers.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: difficulty with open-ended tasks, with a substitute teacher, with a changed routine; perseverating on a wrong method in maths.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: moving between subject teachers with different rules, reinterpreting a question in an exam, compromise in friendships. Rigid black-and-white thinking may overlap with anxiety.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: changes in course structure, workplace role change, group work. Strain shows as withdrawal or conflict.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: distinguish flexibility difficulty from sensory overwhelm and from communication difficulty — a child who cannot understand the change cannot adapt to it.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

•  Generalised Anxiety Disorder

•  Acquired brain injury

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  BRIEF-2 Shift scale (parent, teacher, self-report) — note that Shift sits in the Emotion Regulation Index (with Emotional Control), not the Behaviour or Cognitive Regulation Index; compare Shift with Emotional Control to see whether rigidity travels with emotional reactivity.

•  Observation across a planned transition and an unplanned one: latency to engage, what the child says, what helps.

•  Work-sample analysis: repeated use of one strategy across different problem types; difficulty with 'explain another way' questions.

•  Parent and pupil interview about change at home and school: which changes are tolerable and which are not — the difference is the formulation.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PREVIEW CHANGE: visual timetable with changes marked in advance; a named 'change card' or signal. Tell the child about a substitute teacher the day before where possible.

•  TEACH FLEXIBILITY EXPLICITLY using shared vocabulary — 'Plan A / Plan B', 'big deal / little deal'. Unstuck and On Target (Cannon et al., 2011) is a school-based curriculum with trial evidence in autistic children (Kenworthy et al., 2014).

•  MODEL SHIFTING aloud: 'This isn't working, so I'm going to try a different way.' Make the switch visible and normal.

•  OFFER BOUNDED CHOICE rather than open-ended tasks: two or three options for how to start.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support to School Support; plan transitions (class to class, primary to post-primary) explicitly in the Student Support File.

•  DO NOT frame the child's rigidity as defiance in behaviour records. REFER to CDNT or CAMHS if rigidity is accompanied by distress, rituals or social-communication differences that raise a diagnostic question.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Some brains find it harder to change tracks. When the plan changes, she has to stop, let go of the old plan and build a new one — and that takes her longer than most children.'

•  'Warning her ahead of time and having a Plan B ready makes a big difference. It isn't spoiling her; it's giving her the time her brain needs to switch.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When he digs in, he's usually stuck rather than refusing. Give him a way out — a choice of two ways to start — rather than repeating the instruction louder.'

•  'Changes to the day are the flashpoints. A heads-up in the morning is worth more than any strategy in the moment.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Sometimes your brain gets stuck on one track like a train. We'll practise having a Plan B so the train can switch.'

•  OLDER: 'You like knowing how things will go, and it's hard when they change. That's a real thing. Let's work out what helps you shift when you get stuck.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — rigid rituals that cause the child distress or take up significant time, or intrusive worries: consider referral via GP to CAMHS for assessment of anxiety or OCD.

•  WATCH — meltdowns at transitions escalating in frequency or intensity: plan with the school, and check for sensory load, sleep and communication difficulty.

•  BOUNDARY — do not suggest autism in writing on the basis of rigidity alone; describe and, if warranted, recommend referral.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should we just make him cope with change?' A: 'Tolerance grows from planned, small, previewed changes — not from surprise ones. We build it step by step.'

•  Q: 'Does this mean she's autistic?' A: 'Finding change hard is common in autism and also in many children who aren't autistic. On its own it isn't enough to say. If there's more to the picture, we can talk about a referral.'

•  Q: 'Why can he do it at home but not in school?' A: 'Home often has fewer unexpected changes. The difference tel

presentation.name: Planning and organisation difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty working out the STEPS to a goal, putting them in ORDER and managing TIME — planning an essay, sequencing a science practical, breaking a project into weeks.

•  Dawson and Guare (2018) treat planning/prioritisation, organisation and time management as distinct executive skills; separating them tells you which support to write.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Distinct from 'Organisation of materials' (physical belongings), which is its own presentation.

•  Load rises sharply when tasks become longer, less structured and more self-directed — typically late primary and the move to post-primary.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT laziness. The child often wants to start and cannot see where to begin; that reads as avoidance from the outside.

•  NOT solved by 'try harder' or 'be more organised'. If the child could generate the plan, they would. The plan must be taught, modelled and then faded.

•  NOT only an ADHD feature. It is common in ADHD and appears in DCD, autism, after brain injury, and in many children with no diagnosis.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: difficulty sequencing a simple activity (getting dressed, setting up play). Mostly developmental — describe, do not score.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: stories without a structure, projects left to the last night, difficulty with multi-step maths. Visible from about 3rd–4th class when independent tasks lengthen.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: Junior Cycle classroom-based assessments and projects, homework across subjects, revision planning. Often the first time the difficulty becomes visible.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: Leaving Certificate study, third-level assignments, self-directed deadlines. Supports through the college disability service may apply — check locally.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: the setting may already plan for the pupil; ask what the pupil does independently vs what adults do.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  DCD

•  Autism

•  Acquired brain injury

•  Dyslexia

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  BRIEF-2 Plan/Organise scale (parent, teacher; self-report in adolescence) — check self-report scale names in the manual.

•  Task analysis on a real piece of work: ask the child to plan a short piece aloud and note where the plan breaks (no goal, no steps, no order, no time).

•  Work-sample analysis: structure of extended writing, completion of multi-part assignments.

•  Pupil interview on homework and projects: 'Walk me through last week's project — when did you start, what happened next?'

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PROVIDE THE PLAN, THEN FADE IT: writing frames, project checklists with dates, graphic organisers — then remove steps as the pupil takes them over (Dawson & Guare, 2018).

•  BREAK LONG TASKS into dated chunks with check-ins: an adult checks step 1 before step 2 is due.

•  TEACH A PLANNING ROUTINE explicitly: 'Goal – Plan – Do – Review' or similar; practise it on low-stakes tasks first.

•  USE VISIBLE TIME: timers, backward-planning calendars, a wall planner at home for older pupils.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for frames and checklists; School Support where a targeted adult check-in is needed. Organisational skills programmes (e.g., Abikoff et al., 2013) have trial evidence in ADHD samples.

•  DO NOT recommend reduced curriculum as the first response; the target is the planning skill, not the content.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He can do each step — what's hard is working out the steps in the first place and putting them in order. That's a planning skill, and it can be taught.'

•  'For now, adults need to give him the plan. The aim is to hand it over bit by bit, not to do it for him forever.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Give her the skeleton — a writing frame or a checklist with dates — and you'll see what she actually knows about the topic.'

•  'Check in at the first step, not at the deadline. By the deadline it's too late to help.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Big jobs are like a big sandwich — you can't eat it in one bite. We'll cut it into bites together.'

•  OLDER: 'You know the stuff. The hard part is working out what to do first and when. We'll use a plan sheet until you can make your own.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — a sharp deterioration after transition to post-primary: check for mood, sleep, bullying and school avoidance, not just organisation.

•  WATCH — acquired change after illness or head injury: GP/neurology route.

•  BOUNDARY — organisation difficulty is not in itself evidence for a diagnosis; describe it and consider it in the full formulation.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should I just do the planning for her?' A: 'At first, yes — do it with her, out loud. Then let her do more of it each time. The goal is her holding the plan by the end of the year.'

•  Q: 'He was fine in primary — why now?' A: 'Post-primary asks for far more self-planning: more teachers, more subjects, longer tasks. The difficulty was always there; the demand is new.'

•  Q: 'Is there an app for this?' A: 'Some pupils do well with digital planners; some don't. Whatever tool, it only works if someone checks it with them at first.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case where planning difficulty was the stated concern — did your assessment separate planning from working memory, attention and literacy?

•  Discuss how to write a fading plan so the support has an end point and a review date.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Abikoff, H., Gallagher, R., Wells, K. C., Murray, D. W., Huang, L., Lu, F., & Petkova, E. (2013). Remediating organizational functioning in children with ADHD: Immediate and long-term effects from a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 81(1), 113–128.

→ Dawson, P., & Guare, R. (2018). Executive skills in children and adolescents: A practical guide to assessment and intervention (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

→ Diamond, A. (2013). Executive f

presentation.name: Task initiation difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty GETTING STARTED on a task at the point it is set, even when the child has the skill to do it. Dawson and Guare (2018) list task initiation as a distinct executive skill.

•  Classroom signature: sharpening pencils, looking around, asking to go to the toilet, sitting with a blank page after everyone else has begun.

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Several different mechanisms produce the same blank page: not knowing where to start (planning), not having held the instruction (working memory), fear of getting it wrong (anxiety), low energy (mood or sleep), or finding the task unreadable (literacy).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as not being able to do the work. Many children finish quickly once started — the start is the problem.

•  NOT always executive. Perfectionism and fear of failure are common causes of delay; so is an unidentified literacy difficulty. Formulate the mechanism before recommending.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: needs adult to begin every activity; waits to be shown. Common and developmental.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: slow to start independent work, especially writing; completes well with an adult beside them.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: homework and study left until late; procrastination. Steel (2007) links procrastination to task aversiveness, impulsiveness and low expectancy of success.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: assignments and applications delayed; associated with anxiety and low mood in some — ask.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: distinguish initiation from not understanding the request; use first-then boards and visual start cues.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Generalised Anxiety Disorder

•  Major Depressive Disorder

•  Autism

•  Dyslexia

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation: measure latency — time from instruction to first productive action — with a comparison peer. It is a cleaner measure than 'on-task %'.

•  BRIEF-2 Initiate scale (parent and teacher forms only; the self-report form has Task Completion instead — check the manual).

•  Test the mechanism: give the same task with (a) a written first step, (b) an adult reading it aloud, (c) a lowered stakes 'draft' framing. Whichever reduces latency tells you the cause.

•  Pupil interview: 'What goes through your head when the teacher says "start now"?' — often reveals worry or confusion.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  GIVE THE FIRST STEP, CONCRETELY: 'Write the date and the title' or 'do question 1' — start the task with the child if needed and walk away after the first line.

•  IMPLEMENTATION INTENTIONS for older pupils: 'When I get home and have eaten, I will open my maths copy at the kitchen table.' Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006) found if–then plans increase goal attainment.

•  LOWER THE STAKES of starting: draft copies, 'just get three ideas down', timers for 5 minutes of work.

•  ADDRESS THE MECHANISM: if anxiety or perfectionism is driving delay, the support is different — see anxiety-focused approaches rather than more prompting.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support where a daily check-in adult is planned.

•  DO NOT rely on repeated verbal prompts ('get started') — they rarely help and build dependence.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Starting is its own skill. She can do the work — it's the launching that's hard. We're going to make the first step so small and clear she can't miss it.'

•  'If she's worried about getting it wrong, that can look exactly the same. It's worth noticing which it is at home.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Stand beside him, get the first line down with him, and walk away. Measure how long until he starts — if that shortens, it's working.'

•  'If a blank page is common, check he can read the task. An unreadable worksheet produces the same delay.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Starting is like pushing a swing — the first push is the hardest. I'll give you the first push.'

•  OLDER: 'Loads of people find starting the hardest bit. Let's make the first step tiny — like, just write the title. Then see what happens.'

•  ASK: 'Is it more that you don't know where to start, or that you're worried it'll be wrong?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — initiation difficulty with flat mood, withdrawal or loss of interest in things previously enjoyed: consider low mood; ask about sleep, appetite, self-harm; follow the school's risk procedure if indicated.

•  WATCH — worsening avoidance that extends to attending school: consider emotionally based school avoidance and plan early.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Isn't he just being lazy?' A: 'Children who are genuinely not bothered don't usually look worried at a blank page. Something is getting in the way of starting; the task is finding out what.'

•  Q: 'How long should we prompt her before stepping in?' A: 'Give the first step clearly once, then help her start. Repeated prompting doesn't add much and can become a battle.'

•  Q: 'Will she always need someone to start her?' A: 'Not if we fade it. The aim is for her to use the written first step on her own within a few weeks.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case where you recorded 'slow to start' — how did you test which mechanism was driving it?

•  Discuss the line between executive initiation difficulty and anxiety-driven avoidance, and what changes in your recommendations.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Dawson, P., & Guare, R. (2018). Executive skills in children and adolescents: A practical guide to assessment and intervention (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

→ Gollwitzer, P. M., & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 38, 69–119.

→ Steel, P. (2007). The nature of procrastination: A meta-analytic and theoretical review of quintessential self-regulatory failure. Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65–94.

presentation.name: Self-monitoring difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty CHECKING one's own work, behaviour and effect on others while it is happening or afterwards — not noticing errors, not noticing that a peer is annoyed, handing in work unchecked.

•  Draws on metacognition — thinking about one's own thinking (Flavell, 1979). BRIEF-2 separates Self-Monitor (awareness of own behaviour and its effect) from Task-Monitor (checking work).

•  An executive function profile, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Often explains the 'careless error' pattern: the child can find and fix the error when asked, but did not look.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT carelessness as an attitude. The child usually cares about the result and is surprised by the errors.

•  NOT lack of empathy when it is social. Not noticing the effect of a comment is different from not caring about it.

•  NOT fixed by 'check your work' as an instruction. Without a concrete routine for HOW to check, the child re-reads what they meant, not what they wrote.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: little awareness of own errors is typical — describe, do not interpret.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: careless errors in maths, unchecked spelling, not noticing when talking too long. Self-monitoring grows through this period.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: exam errors from misreading, unawareness of social impact, overestimating how well work went.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: poor calibration of own performance at college or work; unexpected feedback causes distress.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: use visual self-check prompts matched to the pupil's communication level.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Acquired brain injury

•  Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  BRIEF-2 Self-Monitor (parent, teacher, self-report) and Task-Monitor (parent and teacher only) scales — check the manual.

•  Error analysis: ask the child to check a piece of work; count errors found unprompted vs with a prompt ('there are three errors in line 2').

•  Calibration question: 'How well do you think you did?' before marking — the gap between prediction and result is the measure.

•  Observation of peer interaction: does the child notice and repair when a peer shows annoyance?

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SELF-MONITORING CHECKLISTS for work: 3–4 items specific to the child's errors (capital letter, units, re-read the question), ticked before hand-in.

•  SELF-MONITORING OF BEHAVIOUR with a tally or rating card the pupil completes, then compares with an adult rating. Reid, Trout and Schartz (2005) reviewed self-regulation interventions in ADHD and found positive effects.

•  BUILD IN A PAUSE: 'finished? read it once, point to each word' — a routine for all pupils so it isn't singling out.

•  SOCIAL MONITORING: teach cues explicitly (body language, turn-length) through social stories or role-play where social impact is the concern.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for checklists; School Support where an individual self-monitoring programme with review is planned.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He does know how to do it right. What's hard is stopping to check. That checking can be taught with a simple list.'

•  'When he says a test went well and it didn't, he's not lying — he genuinely didn't notice. That's the skill we're working on.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Give her a three-item personalised checklist based on her actual errors. Generic checklists don't help much.'

•  'Ask her to predict her score before you mark. The gap tells you whether self-monitoring is improving.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Let's be detectives on your own work — find the three sneaky mistakes!'

•  OLDER: 'Your brain moves fast and doesn't always look back. This checklist is the look back.'

•  ASK: 'Which mistakes do you make most? Let's put those on your list.' Pupils who choose the items use the list more.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — marked lack of awareness of danger or of social consequences that places the child at risk (online, with older peers): consider safeguarding and discuss with the DLP; where there is reasonable concern, report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  BOUNDARY — do not infer autism from poor social self-monitoring alone; describe and refer if a broader pattern exists.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Why doesn't he just check his work?' A: 'Checking has to be triggered, and for him it isn't automatic yet. The checklist is the trigger.'

•  Q: 'She says she did really well and then fails — is she in denial?' A: 'Usually not. She doesn't yet have a good internal gauge. We build it by predicting and comparing.'

•  Q: 'How long before we see a change?' A: 'We'll measure errors found without a prompt over a half-term and review then.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a report where you wrote 'careless errors' — rewrite it as a self-monitoring description with a measurable target.

•  Discuss where social self-monitoring difficulty becomes a question for CDNT or SLT (pragmatics).

13 · CITATIONS
→ Flavell, J. H. (1979). Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: A new area of cognitive–developmental inquiry. American Psychologist, 34(10), 906–911.

→ Reid, R., Trout, A. L., & Schartz, M. (2005). Self-regulation interventions for children with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Exceptional Children, 71(4), 361–377.

→ Dawson, P., & Guare, R. (2018). Executive skills in children and adolescents: A practical guide to assessment and intervention (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

presentation.name: Motivation and engagement with work
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of how much the pupil INVESTS in school tasks — behaviourally (does the work), emotionally (cares about it) and cognitively (thinks hard about it). Fredricks, Blumenfeld and Paris (2004) set out these three dimensions of engagement.

•  Motivation is not a fixed trait: Self-Determination Theory (Ryan & Deci, 2000) links it to autonomy, competence and relatedness; expectancy-value theory (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002) to 'can I do it?' and 'is it worth it?'.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D lists it as 'Added — not in the conditions index'). Nobody diagnoses low motivation.

•  It is almost always the END of a chain — repeated failure, an unidentified learning difficulty, a relationship breakdown, low mood — rather than the start.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT an explanation. 'He isn't motivated' describes the behaviour; the formulation must say WHY. Weiner's (1985) attribution theory is useful: children who attribute failure to fixed ability stop trying.

•  NOT the same everywhere. A pupil disengaged in Irish and maths but engaged in PE and woodwork is telling you something specific about competence.

•  NOT fixed by rewards alone. External rewards can support starting; for tasks already of interest they can reduce intrinsic motivation (Ryan & Deci, 2000).

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: engagement in play is the measure; low engagement at this age is a flag for development, communication or wellbeing, not motivation.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: task avoidance, rushing to 'be finished', clowning. Often first appears around the time literacy demands outstrip skill.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: disengagement by subject, disinterest in exams, 'what's the point'. Relationships with teachers and peers carry heavy weight.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: disengagement from course; ask about mood, fit of course, finances and substance use.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: engagement is often the primary outcome; describe what the pupil engages with and build from it.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Major Depressive Disorder

•  Dyslexia

•  Emotionally Based School Avoidance (EBSA)

•  Borderline Intellectual Functioning

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Subject-by-subject and task-by-task comparison: where is engagement high, and what do those tasks have in common?

•  Pupil interview using a solution-focused or scaling approach: 'On a scale of 1–10 how much do you want to do well in X? What makes it a 4 and not a 2?'

•  Attainment assessment — always. Rule out a literacy or maths difficulty before interpreting disengagement.

•  Mood screen where appropriate (e.g., RCADS or MFQ at adolescence) — low mood commonly presents first as disengagement.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  BUILD COMPETENCE FIRST: tasks pitched so the pupil succeeds most of the time; visible progress (a graph of words read, marks gained).

•  OFFER REAL CHOICE (autonomy) within the task: order, topic, method of recording.

•  A NAMED ADULT with a short regular check-in (relatedness). This is often the single most effective change.

•  PRAISE STRATEGY AND EFFORT specifically, not ability. Hattie and Timperley (2007) found feedback about the task and process is more useful than praise directed at the self.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support where a mentoring or check-in arrangement is planned; School Support Plus if low mood or school avoidance is involved and outside services engaged.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When a child stops trying, it's usually because trying stopped working for them. Our job is to find out where, and make success possible again.'

•  'We checked his reading and maths as part of this, because a hidden difficulty is one of the commonest reasons children switch off.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Look at where she IS engaged — what's different about those tasks? That's the recipe.'

•  'A two-minute check-in with the same adult each morning can do more than any reward chart.'

•  'Make progress visible — a simple graph of what he got right this week versus last. Children re-engage when they can see they are getting better.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Which bits of school do you like best? What makes them good?'

•  OLDER: 'I'm not here to tell you to try harder. I want to know what's got in the way. What's the most pointless-feeling subject, and why?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — hopelessness, loss of interest in everything, talk of death or self-harm: follow the same-day risk procedure; do not leave the pupil alone; inform the DLP and parents per protocol; where the threshold is met, report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  WATCH — sudden disengagement after a period of coping: ask about events at home, bullying, relationships and substance use.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'He could do it if he wanted to — why won't he?' A: 'Sometimes that's true, and even then "wanting to" is shaped by whether it's worked before. Let's look at what's changed.'

•  Q: 'Should we use a reward chart?' A: 'For getting started on things he doesn't enjoy, a short-term reward can help. It won't fix the underlying reason on its own.'

•  Q: 'Is she depressed?' A: 'Losing interest can be part of low mood, and I'll ask about it. If there are signs, the GP is the right next step.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a referral that says 'unmotivated' — what hypotheses did you generate and how did you test them?

•  Discuss how to write about motivation in a report without it reading as a judgement of the child's character.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Eccles, J. S., & Wigfield, A. (2002). Motivational beliefs, values, and goals. Annual Review of Psychology, 53, 109–132.

→ Fredricks, J. A., Blumenfeld, P. C., & Paris, A. H. (2004). School engagement: Potential of the concept, state of the evidence. Review of

presentation.name: Work rate and pace of output
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The pupil produces LESS work, or takes MUCH LONGER, than peers of similar ability — unfinished copies, unfinished tests, homework taking hours.

•  Slow output is a final common pathway: processing speed, handwriting speed, spelling retrieval, reading speed, attention, perfectionism and fatigue all produce it. The assessment task is to find which.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses slow work rate.

•  Processing speed develops through childhood and adolescence (Kail, 1991); a WISC-V Processing Speed Index describes speed on simple visual tasks, which is not the same as classroom output speed.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as low ability. A pupil can reason well and produce slowly — the Processing Speed Index is often the lowest index in otherwise even profiles.

•  NOT dawdling or laziness until shown otherwise. Timed copying and free-writing samples usually show a genuine ceiling.

•  NOT only handwriting. Slow typing, slow reading of the question, and re-checking from anxiety all look identical in the finished copy.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: slow to complete play tasks and self-care; describe motor and attention factors; do not score speed.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: unfinished written work, copying from the board not done, slow in timed tables. Parent reports homework taking far longer than intended.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: unfinished exam papers — the point at which it affects results. RACE (SEC) evidence may be sought; check the current scheme and criteria.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: timed exams at third level, workplace volume. College disability services may provide accommodations — check locally.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: set expectations by output quality and independence, not volume against mainstream peers.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DCD

•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (dysgraphia)

•  Generalised Anxiety Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  WISC-V UK Processing Speed Index (Coding, Symbol Search) — check whether low speed is motor-driven (Coding) or visual scanning (Symbol Search) using the manual's guidance.

•  DASH (Barnett et al., 2007) or DASH-17+ for handwriting speed; compare copying (motor) with free-writing (motor plus composition).

•  Reading speed: timed reading measure or WIAT-III UK reading fluency tasks.

•  Observation of a timed task: does the child start late, write slowly, stop to re-check, or drift off? Each points somewhere different.

•  Rule out vision and motor difficulties (ophthalmology/OT) where copying or handwriting is the bottleneck.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  REDUCE VOLUME, KEEP CHALLENGE: 'show me the five hardest questions' rather than all twenty; the learning target stays the same.

•  PROVIDE PRINTED NOTES and cloze worksheets so time goes on thinking, not copying.

•  TEACH KEYBOARDING where handwriting is the bottleneck, and check typing is actually faster before relying on it.

•  NEGOTIATE HOMEWORK by time, not by quantity: 'stop at 30 minutes and note where you got to'.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support for keyboarding programme or targeted handwriting support; consider RACE evidence at post-primary (check current SEC criteria).

•  DO NOT recommend extra time or a reader/scribe for State exams without checking the SEC's current RACE criteria — schools apply to the SEC, and eligibility rules change.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She understands the work. It's getting it onto the page that takes her longer — her hand, her eyes and her brain are working at a slower pace than her thinking.'

•  'Homework should be time-limited. If she's still working after the agreed time, stop, write a note, and let the teacher know. That's information for us, not failure.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Mark what he got to, not what he didn't. Unfinished is information about pace, not effort.'

•  'Print the notes. Copying from the board is using his whole lesson on transcription.'

•  'If you want to know what he can do, give him the five hardest questions rather than the whole page — you'll see his thinking without the volume.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your thinking is quick, and your hand is a bit slower. We'll find ways so your hand doesn't slow your thinking down.'

•  OLDER: 'Being slower at getting it down isn't the same as being slower at thinking. We'll get the teachers to judge your thinking.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — slowing that is NEW, or accompanied by fatigue, headaches, clumsiness or loss of skills: GP review — possible medical, neurological or visual cause.

•  WATCH — slowness from excessive checking, erasing and rewriting: may be perfectionism or OCD; ask gently about worries.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Will she get extra time in the Leaving Cert?' A: 'That depends on the SEC's current RACE scheme and its criteria, and the school makes the application. I can describe her needs; I can't promise an outcome.'

•  Q: 'Should he use a laptop?' A: 'Only if typing is faster for him — we'll measure both. A laptop that's slower than handwriting doesn't help.'

•  Q: 'Her Processing Speed score is low — is that a disability?' A: 'It's a description of how quickly she does simple visual tasks. It helps explain why work takes longer. It isn't a diagnosis.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a profile with a low PSI — how did you separate motor, visual and attentional contributions before writing recommendations?

•  Discuss how to word slow pace in reports so it does not cap expectations of the pupil's thinking.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Barnett, A., Henderson, S. E., Scheib, B., & Schulz, J. (2007). Detailed Assessment of Speed of Handwriting (DASH). Pearson.

→ Kail, R. (1991). Developmental change in speed of processing during childhood and adolescence. Psychological Bulletin, 109(3), 490–501.

→ Wechsler, D. (2016). We

presentation.name: Homework completion and follow-through
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Homework not recorded, not brought home, not started, not finished or not handed in — each a DIFFERENT failure point in a chain that runs from the classroom to the kitchen table and back.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Cooper, Robinson and Patall (2006) found the homework–achievement association stronger at secondary than at primary; at primary, the bigger risk is homework becoming a nightly conflict that damages the parent–child relationship.

•  Langberg et al. (2012) developed the HOPS programme for middle-school pupils with ADHD, targeting homework recording, materials and planning — the chain, not the attitude.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a reliable measure of effort. It is heavily shaped by home circumstances — space, time, caring responsibilities, parent literacy, shift work.

•  NOT solved by sanctions for missing homework. If the break is at 'recording', detention doesn't reach it.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not applicable in the usual sense; home learning activities depend on the adult.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: homework journal not filled in, parent unaware, battles at home; tasks taking far longer than intended.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: many subjects and teachers, online platforms, longer assignments. Recording and planning fail first.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: self-directed study; follow-through becomes a question of planning, mood and competing demands (work, care).

•  SPECIAL SETTING: homework often individualised or not set; check that home tasks match what the family can realistically support.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Dyslexia

•  DCD

•  Generalised Anxiety Disorder

•  Emotionally Based School Avoidance (EBSA)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  MAP THE CHAIN with the pupil and parent: recorded? brought home? started? finished? returned? — find the first link that breaks.

•  Time diary for one week: how long does homework actually take versus what the school intends?

•  Ask about home context sensitively: space, time, siblings, caring roles, device/internet access, language of home.

•  Check attainment: homework that cannot be read cannot be done.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  FIX THE BROKEN LINK: if recording — teacher checks the journal or the task is posted online; if bringing home — a checklist at the locker; if starting — a set time and place.

•  SET A TIME LIMIT agreed between school and home; beyond it, stop and note it.

•  OFFER HOMEWORK CLUB or supervised study where home circumstances make homework unrealistic — check what the school or local services provide.

•  REDUCE VOLUME before increasing support; quality over quantity.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (routine checks); School Support (individual plan, check-in adult); School Support Plus where family support services are involved.

•  DO NOT recommend homework that relies on parental teaching the family cannot provide — it widens gaps.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Homework has five steps — writing it down, bringing it home, starting, finishing, handing it in. We're going to find which step is breaking and fix that one.'

•  'If it's taking over the evening, that's too much. We'll agree a time limit with the school so it stops being a fight.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Can you check his journal before he leaves for the next four weeks? That's where it's breaking.'

•  'Accept a note from home saying "worked 30 minutes, got to here" as done. It keeps the home–school relationship working.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Homework goes on a journey — from school to home and back. Let's find where it's getting lost.'

•  OLDER: 'Where does it go wrong — writing it down, remembering it, starting, or finishing? Be honest; there's no wrong answer.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — homework never possible because the pupil is caring for others, has no food, or disclosures suggest neglect or harm: child protection procedure; inform the DLP; report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  WATCH — homework distress with tears, sleep loss or refusal to go to school: consider anxiety and EBSA.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should we just stop homework?' A: 'At primary, the evidence for homework is weaker, and the relationship matters more. A reduced, time-limited amount is a reasonable plan to agree with the school.'

•  Q: 'He says there's no homework every day.' A: 'Then recording is the broken link. The school can check or post it so you're not relying on his memory.'

•  Q: 'Is it the school's job or ours?' A: 'Both. The school fixes what happens in class; you fix the time and place at home. We'll write down who does what.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case where homework was the presenting concern — did you ask about home circumstances, and how did you do it without judgement?

•  Discuss how to recommend reduced homework without undermining a teacher's authority.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Cooper, H., Robinson, J. C., & Patall, E. A. (2006). Does homework improve academic achievement? A synthesis of research, 1987–2003. Review of Educational Research, 76(1), 1–62.

→ Langberg, J. M., Epstein, J. N., Becker, S. P., Girio-Herrera, E., & Vaughn, A. J. (2012). Evaluation of the Homework, Organization, and Planning Skills (HOPS) intervention for middle school students with ADHD as implemented by school mental health providers. School Psychology Review, 41(3), 342–364.

→ Dawson, P., & Guare, R. (2018). Executive skills in children and adolescents: A practical guide to assessment and intervention (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

presentation.name: Organisation of materials, books and equipment
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty KEEPING TRACK of physical belongings: wrong books, lost copies, no pencil, overflowing bag and locker, crumpled notes, PE gear forgotten.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). BRIEF-2 has a separate Organisation of Materials scale on the parent and teacher forms; check the manual.

•  Distinct from planning (organising steps and time). A pupil can plan an essay well and still arrive without the copy it's in.

•  Abikoff et al. (2013) targeted materials management alongside time and planning in Organizational Skills Training and found improvements in ADHD samples.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT carelessness about school. Most pupils are embarrassed by it, and repeated sanctions for missing equipment are a common route to disengagement.

•  NOT only an ADHD feature — common in DCD (motor planning of packing), in dyslexia (reading the timetable), and after transition to post-primary for many pupils.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: adults manage belongings; describe independence in routines (coat, bag) against peers.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: messy tray, missing homework copies, lost letters home.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: the peak — many subjects, lockers, timetables that change by day, digital and paper materials. Often the most visible first-year difficulty.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: digital file management, bringing documents to appointments, managing course materials.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: adults often hold materials; build independence in small steps if it is a goal.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  DCD

•  Autism

•  Dyslexia

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Bag, locker and desk check with the pupil (with their consent): what's there, what's missing, what system exists?

•  BRIEF-2 Organisation of Materials (parent, teacher).

•  Teacher survey across subjects at post-primary: how often does the pupil arrive without materials, and in which subjects?

•  Check reading of the timetable and whether the pupil can use it — a literacy issue can look like disorganisation.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  COLOUR-CODE by subject: copy, book and folder the same colour; timetable in the same colours.

•  A PACKING ROUTINE at a fixed time (evening before), with a laminated checklist for each day, checked by an adult at first.

•  SPARE SET IN SCHOOL for high-frequency losses (pencil case, calculator) — removes the daily sanction cycle.

•  WEEKLY BAG CLEAR-OUT with a named adult for the first half-term, then fade.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support where a key adult and a fading plan are written into the Student Support File.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Keeping track of things is a real skill, and his is behind. We'll give him a system — colours and a checklist — and check it with him until it becomes habit.'

•  'It's not about him not caring. Most children in this position are fed up with being in trouble for it.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Keep a spare pencil case in the room. It costs a euro and saves ten minutes of conflict a week.'

•  'Sanctions for forgotten equipment don't teach the system — the checklist does. Check it with her for a few weeks.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Let's make your bag a colour game — green for maths, blue for English.'

•  OLDER: 'Loads of people lose stuff. The ones who don't usually have a system, not a better brain. Let's build yours.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — belongings repeatedly missing, damaged or taken: consider bullying.

•  WATCH — no materials because the family cannot afford them: sensitively link with school supports (e.g., book rental schemes — check what the school provides).

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should we just pack his bag for him?' A: 'Pack it WITH him, using the checklist, and hand more of it over each week.'

•  Q: 'Will a locker help?' A: 'Only if there's a system for it. A locker can make things worse if nothing tells him what to take when.'

•  Q: 'Is this ADHD?' A: 'It's common in ADHD, and also common without it. On its own it isn't enough to say.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring the case where materials were the main teacher complaint — was the sanction cycle itself maintaining the problem?

•  Discuss how to frame a 'spare set' recommendation for staff who see it as rewarding forgetfulness.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Abikoff, H., Gallagher, R., Wells, K. C., Murray, D. W., Huang, L., Lu, F., & Petkova, E. (2013). Remediating organizational functioning in children with ADHD: Immediate and long-term effects from a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 81(1), 113–128.

→ Gioia, G. A., Isquith, P. K., Guy, S. C., & Kenworthy, L. (2015). BRIEF-2: Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (2nd ed.). PAR.

→ Dawson, P., & Guare, R. (2018). Executive skills in children and adolescents: A practical guide to assessment and intervention (3rd ed.). Guilford Press.

presentation.name: Sustained attention in whole-class vs one-to-one
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A pupil who ATTENDS WELL one-to-one (with you, with the SET) but drifts, fidgets or disengages in whole-class teaching. The gap itself is the finding.

•  One-to-one gives constant adult proximity, immediate feedback, controlled pace, one voice and low noise; whole-class removes all of these at once. The question is which one matters for this pupil.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  It is a well-recognised limitation of assessment: the testing room is close to ideal conditions, so test attention can overestimate classroom attention (Barkley, 2015, discusses this for clinic assessment).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT evidence that there is 'nothing wrong' because the child attended in your assessment. That is the expected result, not a disconfirmation.

•  NOT necessarily attention. Whole-class failure may be language comprehension (DLD), hearing in noise, anxiety about being asked, or a visually busy room (Fisher, Godwin & Seltman, 2014).

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: attends in small group or with an adult, drifts at circle time. Circle-time attention is developmentally short — compare with peers.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: fine at the SET table, lost during teacher-led lessons, especially long oral input.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: variation by subject teacher is large; lecture-style classes hardest.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: lectures vs tutorials; recorded lectures may help.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: smaller groups already; compare 1:1 with the class group and note sensory factors.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  DLD

•  Hearing impairment

•  Generalised Anxiety Disorder

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observe BOTH: a whole-class lesson and a one-to-one/small-group session, same pupil, same week. Use momentary time sampling with a comparison peer in class.

•  Kofler, Rapport and Alderson (2008) meta-analysed classroom inattention in ADHD — note variability as well as average; record how on-task changes across a lesson.

•  Check hearing (audiology) and language comprehension; ask where the pupil sits relative to the teacher and noise sources.

•  TEA-Ch2 as a structured measure — interpreted knowing it is a one-to-one condition.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  BRING THE ONE-TO-ONE FEATURES INTO CLASS: seating near the teacher, a check-in after the instruction, shorter input with active response (whiteboards).

•  CHUNK ORAL INPUT: 5–10 minutes of teacher talk then a task; visual support alongside speech.

•  REDUCE NOISE AND VISUAL CLUTTER near the pupil's seat where feasible.

•  A PRIVATE CUE agreed with the pupil to re-engage without public correction.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support where in-class support rather than withdrawal is planned — withdrawal alone can hide the difficulty.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When I worked with her on her own, she concentrated really well. That's good news and it's also the clue: it's the busy classroom that's hard, and we can change parts of that.'

•  'It doesn't mean she's fine and the school is wrong — both are true.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'He did well with me one-to-one, which tells us what works: closeness, short bursts, quick feedback. Let's see which of those we can bring to your room.'

•  'Check he's heard and understood the instruction before he starts — whole-class input is where he loses it.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'You listened brilliantly with me. What's different in the big class?'

•  OLDER: 'You can clearly focus — you did with me. What makes it harder in class? Noise, where you sit, the teacher talking a long time?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — staring spells with no response in class: consider absence seizures; GP/paediatric referral.

•  WATCH — pupil avoids whole-class settings out of fear of being asked: consider anxiety or selective mutism.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'She concentrated with you — so why do you say she has a difficulty?' A: 'Because it's the classroom that we need her to learn in. The difference between the two tells us what to change.'

•  Q: 'Should he be taken out for one-to-one more?' A: 'Some withdrawal can help, but the bigger gain is making the classroom work for him. Otherwise we move the problem rather than solve it.'

•  Q: 'Could it be his hearing?' A: 'It's worth ruling out, especially if he struggles in noise. The GP can refer for audiology.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring an assessment where the pupil attended well with you — did your report say so without implying the teacher's concern was unfounded?

•  Discuss how to plan paired observations efficiently within a limited school time allocation.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Barkley, R. A. (Ed.). (2015). Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: A handbook for diagnosis and treatment (4th ed.). Guilford Press.

→ Fisher, A. V., Godwin, K. E., & Seltman, H. (2014). Visual environment, attention allocation, and learning in young children: When too much of a good thing may be bad. Psychological Science, 25(7), 1362–1370.

→ Kofler, M. J., Rapport, M. D., & Alderson, R. M. (2008). Quantifying ADHD classroom inattentiveness, its moderators, and variability: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 49(1), 59–69.

presentation.name: Note-taking and recording from the board
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty getting information from the board, screen or teacher's speech into a copy accurately and in time. It stacks several demands: look up, find place, hold a chunk in working memory, look down, spell, write, look up again.

•  Far-point copying (board) is harder than near-point copying (from a sheet on the desk) because of the repeated shift in gaze and place-finding.

•  Note-taking from speech adds listening, selecting and summarising in real time. Kiewra (1985) found the benefit of notes comes from both encoding and later review.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT simply laziness or messiness — the load is real and each sub-skill can be tested.

•  NOT fixed by switching to laptops automatically. Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014) reported longhand note-takers did better on conceptual questions; a later replication (Morehead, Dunlosky & Rawson, 2019) found smaller and less consistent effects. Choose by the pupil's speed and accuracy.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not applicable — pre-writing.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: copying homework and spellings from the board — errors, missed lines, running out of time.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: copying notes from slides and taking notes from teacher talk across many subjects; revision notes then incomplete.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: lecture notes; recordings and slides often available — check the college policy.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: adapted recording methods (photos, symbols) — check the goal is learning, not copying.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  DCD

•  Visual impairment

•  ADHD

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (dysgraphia)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Compare near-point and far-point copying of the same passage: words per minute and errors.

•  DASH (copying tasks) for handwriting speed; spelling assessment (WIAT-III UK) for spelling load.

•  Vision: ask about recent eye tests; refer via GP/school vision screening to optometry/ophthalmology if in doubt.

•  Check seating: distance and angle to the board, glare on screens.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PROVIDE PRINTED NOTES or slides in advance — the pupil annotates rather than copies.

•  HOMEWORK ON A SLIP or posted online, not copied from the board.

•  SEATING with a direct, near view of the board.

•  TEACH NOTE-TAKING explicitly at post-primary: headings, key words, abbreviations, Cornell-style layout; practise on short clips.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (printed notes, seating); School Support for keyboarding or note-taking skills teaching; consider assistive technology through the relevant scheme — check current NCSE/Department arrangements.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Copying from the board means looking up and down, holding the words in mind, and spelling them — all at once. For him, doing all those at speed is too much, so notes come home incomplete.'

•  'The fix is simple: give him the notes on paper so his effort goes on understanding them.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
