•  'Printed notes free her to listen. Copying uses up the attention she needs for the content.'

•  'Please don't rely on her copying the homework from the board — a slip or the online post means you know she has it.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Copying from the board is a hard job — look, remember, write. We'll give you a sheet so you can skip the hard bit.'

•  OLDER: 'Notes are for learning from later. If copying takes all your time, you're not learning in class. Let's get you the notes and teach you how to add to them.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — squinting, headaches, holding work close, or copying errors only from far distance: vision check.

•  WATCH — sudden deterioration in handwriting or copying, or new clumsiness: GP review for a medical or neurological cause.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Won't printed notes make him lazy?' A: 'He'll still need to read, highlight and add to them. What we remove is the transcription, not the thinking.'

•  Q: 'Should she type her notes?' A: 'If she types faster and more accurately than she writes, yes. We'll measure both first.'

•  Q: 'Is this dyslexia?' A: 'Copying difficulty is common with dyslexia but isn't evidence of it on its own. We look at reading and spelling separately.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring the case where copying was the concern — did you separate vision, motor, spelling and working memory load?

•  Discuss how assistive technology applications are made locally and who the SENO involvement is — check current practice.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Kiewra, K. A. (1985). Investigating notetaking and review: A depth of processing alternative. Educational Psychologist, 20(1), 23–32.

→ Morehead, K., Dunlosky, J., & Rawson, K. A. (2019). How much mightier is the pen than the keyboard for note-taking? A replication and extension of Mueller and Oppenheimer (2014). Educational Psychology Review, 31(3), 753–780.

→ Mueller, P. A., & Oppenheimer, D. M. (2014). The pen is mightier than the keyboard: Advantages of longhand over laptop note taking. Psychological Science, 25(6), 1159–1168.

→ Barnett, A., Henderson, S. E., Scheib, B., & Schulz, J. (2007). Detailed Assessment of Speed of Handwriting (DASH). Pearson.

presentation.name: Study skills and revision strategy
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The pupil works hard but studies INEFFICIENTLY — re-reading, highlighting and copying notes — and results do not reflect the time spent.

•  Dunlosky et al. (2013) reviewed ten learning techniques: practice testing and distributed practice were rated HIGH utility; highlighting, re-reading and summarisation LOW. Most pupils use the low-utility ones.

•  Roediger and Karpicke (2006) showed retrieval practice (testing yourself) produced better long-term retention than restudying, even though restudying felt more effective.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a character issue. Study strategy is rarely taught explicitly, and effective strategies feel harder, so pupils choose the ones that feel productive.

•  NOT only an issue for pupils with SEN, though executive, literacy and anxiety difficulties make it worse.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not applicable.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: spelling tests and tables — rehearsal by copying out; can teach 'look, cover, write, check' and self-quizzing early.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: Junior Cycle and into senior cycle; revision timetables, past papers, managing volume. The main window for teaching strategy.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: Leaving Certificate and third level; self-directed study; exam anxiety common.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: overlearning, repetition with retrieval, and consistent formats — principles still apply.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Dyslexia

•  Generalised Anxiety Disorder

•  DLD

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Study-skills interview: 'Show me how you revised for your last test' — ask to see the actual materials.

•  Check reading speed and comprehension; a pupil who cannot read notes efficiently cannot revise from them.

•  BRIEF-2 self-report (planning, working memory) and an anxiety measure where exam stress is raised (e.g., RCADS self-report).

•  Look at results versus reported effort: large effort / low result suggests strategy; low effort / low result suggests something else.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  TEACH RETRIEVAL PRACTICE: flashcards, self-quizzing, past-paper questions, 'brain dump' then check.

•  SPACE IT OUT: short sessions across weeks rather than long ones the night before (distributed practice — Cepeda et al., 2006).

•  TURN NOTES INTO QUESTIONS: every heading becomes a question to answer from memory.

•  PLAN THE WEEK: a simple revision timetable with subjects spaced and a review slot — adult check-in at first.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (whole-class teaching of study skills benefits all); School Support where an individual study-skills programme or mentoring is planned.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She's putting in the hours, but re-reading and highlighting feel productive without sticking. Testing herself works better, even though it feels harder.'

•  'Short, regular sessions beat long ones the night before.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'A five-minute low-stakes quiz at the start of class is one of the most effective things you can do for retention — for everyone.'

•  'Model how to turn notes into questions. Most pupils have never been shown.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  OLDER: 'Re-reading your notes feels like studying, but your brain is recognising, not remembering. Testing yourself is harder — that's why it works.'

•  OLDER: 'Show me how you studied for the last test and we'll find one thing to change.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — exam stress with panic, sleep loss, not eating, or hopelessness: consider anxiety or low mood; follow risk procedures if self-harm is raised.

•  WATCH — studying for many hours with little retention: check for underlying literacy or language difficulty.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'He studies all the time — why is he failing?' A: 'How he studies matters more than how long. We'll teach him the strategies with the best evidence.'

•  Q: 'Should she do grinds?' A: 'Grinds can help content. They won't necessarily teach her how to revise, which is the gap here.'

•  Q: 'What about mind maps?' A: 'Fine for organising, but they're a starting point — she then needs to test herself on them.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a post-primary case — did your recommendations target strategy, or only volume and time?

•  Discuss how to support exam anxiety within the EP role and when to refer to Primary Care or CAMHS.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380.

→ Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

→ Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.

presentation.name: Help-seeking
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Whether the pupil knows WHEN they need help, WHO to ask and HOW to ask — and does so. Part D lists it under 1.1 as 'knowing when and how to ask'; help-seeking from adults in relationships sits separately under 4.2.

•  Nelson-Le Gall (1981) framed help-seeking as a problem-solving skill; Newman (2002) distinguishes ADAPTIVE help-seeking (asking for hints to solve it yourself) from EXECUTIVE help-seeking (asking for the answer).

•  Ryan, Pintrich and Midgley (2001) found pupils who most need help are often least likely to ask, with avoidance linked to perceived threat to competence.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT independence. A pupil who never asks may be sitting silently lost; a pupil who always asks may be over-reliant. Both are help-seeking difficulties.

•  NOT only a confidence issue. Not knowing that one doesn't understand (self-monitoring) and not having the language to ask (DLD) produce the same silence.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: seeks help from familiar adults through gesture and proximity; describe pattern with familiar vs unfamiliar adults.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: silent when stuck, or hand constantly up; relies on peers or SNA.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: peer visibility makes asking costly; many will not ask in front of the class.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: not using college supports, disability services or tutors until crisis.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: teach functional requests (help card, AAC symbol) as a core skill.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia)

•  Selective Mutism

•  Autism

•  DLD

•  ADHD

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation: when the pupil is stuck, what happens? Count stuck episodes and what the pupil did (asked teacher / peer / waited / guessed / gave up).

•  Pupil interview: 'When you don't know what to do, what do you do? Who would you ask? What would make it easier?'

•  Check self-monitoring (do they know they're stuck?) and language (can they phrase the question?).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PROVIDE A LOW-VISIBILITY WAY TO ASK: help card on the desk, traffic-light cups, a sticky note, an agreed quiet signal.

•  TEACH THE SCRIPT: 'I've tried __, I'm stuck at __.' Practise with low stakes.

•  ASK THREE BEFORE ME (resources, peer, then adult) for over-reliant pupils, with explicit teaching of what the three are.

•  PRAISE ASKING specifically: 'Good question — that's exactly when to ask.'

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support where a specific programme or an SNA fading plan is written in.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He often sits stuck rather than asking. We're going to give him a quiet way to ask so he doesn't have to put his hand up in front of everyone.'

•  'At home, praise the asking itself — that's the habit we're building.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'She doesn't ask because it feels too visible. A card on her desk she can turn over means you'll know.'

•  'For him it's the opposite — he asks before trying. Teach him the "three before me" steps and praise him when he uses them.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'When you're stuck, you can turn your card to red and I'll come. That's a clever thing to do.'

•  OLDER: 'Asking isn't a sign you're behind — it's what people who do well do. What would make it easier to ask?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — a pupil who will not seek help from any adult when hurt, frightened or unwell: consider whether they are unsafe or have learned not to ask; discuss with the DLP and consider child protection procedures; if there is reasonable concern, report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  WATCH — no speech with some adults in school but speech at home: consider selective mutism and refer via SLT/CAMHS routes.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Why doesn't he just put his hand up?' A: 'For some children, being seen to not know is a big risk. We make asking less visible first, then build up.'

•  Q: 'She asks the SNA for everything — is that a problem?' A: 'It can become one. We'll build her independence in steps, so she knows when to try first and when to ask.'

•  Q: 'Is it anxiety?' A: 'It can be. It can also be not knowing she's stuck, or not having the words. We'll look at which.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring the case where help-seeking was raised — did you distinguish under-asking from over-asking, and their causes?

•  Discuss the safeguarding angle: a child who doesn't ask adults for help at all.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Nelson-Le Gall, S. (1981). Help-seeking: An understudied problem-solving skill in children. Developmental Review, 1(3), 224–246.

→ Newman, R. S. (2002). How self-regulated learners cope with academic difficulty: The role of adaptive help seeking. Theory Into Practice, 41(2), 132–138.

→ Ryan, A. M., Pintrich, P. R., & Midgley, C. (2001). Avoiding seeking help in the classroom: Who and why? Educational Psychology Review, 13(2), 93–114.

presentation.name: Fatigue, sleep and time-of-day effects on attention
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.1 Attention, concentration and work skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Attention, behaviour or work rate that VARIES by time of day, day of week or across a term in a way that tracks tiredness, sleep, hunger or (for some pupils) medication timing.

•  Astill et al. (2012) meta-analysed a century of research on sleep in school-age children and found shorter sleep associated with poorer cognitive performance and more behavioural problems.

•  Paruthi et al. (2016, American Academy of Sleep Medicine consensus) recommend 9–12 hours for children aged 6–12 and 8–10 hours for adolescents aged 13–18 per 24 hours.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it — sleep disorders themselves are a medical question.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a separate problem from attention — a tired child screens positive on attention and behaviour ratings. Always ask about sleep before interpreting any attention measure.

•  NOT only a home issue. School factors (timetable load, afternoon PE, lunch timing) contribute and can be changed.

•  NOT an EP matter to treat medically — snoring, sleep apnoea, medication timing and suspected sleep disorders go to the GP.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: afternoon dysregulation, dropped naps; describe daily rhythm with parents.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: good mornings, poor afternoons (or the reverse); Mondays worse after irregular weekends.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: circadian shift toward later sleep (Carskadon, 2011) colliding with early school start; screens and phones in the bedroom; first-period classes hardest.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: irregular sleep, part-time work, late-night study; ask about substances and mood.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: sleep difficulties are common in some neurodevelopmental and genetic conditions — ask parents directly; seizures and medications may affect alertness.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Sleep disorders

•  Major Depressive Disorder

•  Epilepsy

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Ask the parent about bedtime, wake time, snoring, night waking, screens, and weekend vs weekday — a one-week sleep diary is simple and informative.

•  Teacher rating by time of day: rate attention for the same pupil in morning and afternoon for two weeks.

•  Observation scheduled at two points in the day, not one.

•  The Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (Owens et al., 2000) is a research and clinical screen — check whether it is available and appropriate in your service before using it.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SCHEDULE DEMANDING WORK for the pupil's best time of day where the timetable allows.

•  MOVEMENT BREAKS and a snack/water check in the known low period.

•  SHARE SLEEP HYGIENE INFORMATION with families neutrally (regular times, screens out of the bedroom, wind-down routine).

•  REFER VIA GP where snoring, gasping, very restless sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness or suspected sleep disorder is reported.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for timetable and breaks; School Support where a plan is shared with home; School Support Plus if medical input is involved.

•  DO NOT advise on medication timing or melatonin — refer to the prescriber or GP (PSI 2.2.2).

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Tiredness looks exactly like attention difficulty. Before we decide anything, it's worth checking how he's sleeping.'

•  'If he snores loudly or stops breathing for a moment in his sleep, mention it to the GP — it can affect concentration during the day.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Rate her attention in the morning and afternoon for two weeks — if there's a big difference, that shapes the plan.'

•  'Put the hardest tasks at her best time of day, and a movement break before the slump.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'When is your brain most awake — morning or after lunch?'

•  OLDER: 'Teenagers' body clocks shift later — that's biology, not laziness. What time do you actually get to sleep? Is your phone in your room?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — a child consistently exhausted because of circumstances at home (no bedtime supervision, caring for others, unsafe night-time environment): child protection concern; inform the DLP; report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  WATCH — excessive sleepiness, staring spells or unusual episodes: GP/paediatric referral (sleep disorder, seizures).

•  WATCH — sleep change with low mood or withdrawal in adolescence: ask about mood and self-harm; follow risk procedures.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Could his attention problems just be sleep?' A: 'Sometimes a large part is. That's why we check sleep first — and if sleep improves and attention doesn't, that's useful information too.'

•  Q: 'Should she take melatonin?' A: 'That's a medical question for the GP or consultant. I can tell you what we see in school at different times of day.'

•  Q: 'He's worse after lunch — is it his medication wearing off?' A: 'It could be one explanation, and the prescriber is the right person to ask. Our time-of-day ratings will help them.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring an assessment where you didn't ask about sleep — how might it change your interpretation of attention ratings?

•  Discuss how to share time-of-day information with a prescriber without straying into medication advice.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Astill, R. G., Van der Heijden, K. B., Van IJzendoorn, M. H., & Van Someren, E. J. W. (2012). Sleep, cognition, and behavioral problems in school-age children: A century of research meta-analyzed. Psychological Bulletin, 138(6), 1109–1138.

→ Carskadon, M. A. (2011). Sleep in adolescents: The perfect storm. Pediatric Clinics of North America, 58(3), 637–647.

→ Owens, J. A., Spirito, A., & McGuinn, M. (2000). The Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ): Psychometric properties of a survey instrument for school-aged children. Sleep, 23(8), 1043–1051.

→ Paruthi, S.,

presentation.name: AAC and communication access
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) is any method that supplements or replaces speech: unaided (sign, gesture — including Lámh, the Irish key word sign system) and aided (symbols, communication books, PODD, PECS, speech-generating devices).

•  Beukelman and Light (2020) define the aim as communicative competence across partners and settings, not use of a device for its own sake.

•  Part D: 'Not a DSM diagnosis.' It describes how a pupil accesses communication — and therefore access to assessment, learning and consent.

•  Communication ACCESS includes the partners: whether adults model the system, whether it is available all day, and whether vocabulary covers what the pupil wants to say (not only requests).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a barrier to speech. Millar, Light and Schlosser (2006) found AAC did not hinder speech development and was associated with gains in some cases; Romski and Sevcik (2005) addressed this and related myths directly.

•  NOT something a child must 'earn' through prerequisites (e.g., cognitive level, eye contact). Current practice rejects readiness criteria (Romski & Sevcik, 2005).

•  NOT the SLT's responsibility alone. A device used only in SLT sessions is not communication access.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: early introduction alongside speech; key word sign and symbols in preschool; parent coaching.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: consistent use across class, yard and home; vocabulary for curriculum and for social talk; literacy access.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: age-appropriate vocabulary (including humour, complaint, relationships, sexuality education content), self-advocacy, device ownership.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: transition to adult services — device, support and training continuity; consent and decision-making supports.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: often where AAC is most used; check consistency across staff and whether the system is actually available all day.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Autism

•  Cerebral palsy

•  Genetic syndromes (Down, Fragile X, 22q11.2, Williams, Prader-Willi, Angelman, Rett)

•  Global Developmental Delay

•  Speech Sound Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Communication Matrix / AAC review — describe the pupil's current forms and functions of communication.

•  Observe across partners and settings: who models the system, how often, and what happens when the pupil initiates?

•  Liaise with the SLT (CDNT or Primary Care) for the AAC assessment and system; the EP does not select devices.

•  Adapt cognitive and adaptive assessment: non-verbal measures (e.g., Leiter-3), adaptive measures (Vineland-3/ABAS-3) — and state clearly what cannot be concluded from verbal-dependent tests.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  AIDED LANGUAGE MODELLING by all adults: point to symbols while speaking — the pupil needs to see the system used to learn it.

•  SYSTEM AVAILABLE ALL DAY, including yard, lunch, transport and home; a named person responsible for charging and updating.

•  VOCABULARY BEYOND REQUESTS: comment, refuse, ask, joke, complain.

•  PLAN ASSESSMENT ACCESS: consent and pupil voice gathered through the pupil's system, with the time it needs.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support Plus — AAC typically involves SLT from the CDNT or Primary Care; assistive technology applications through the relevant Department/NCSE scheme with the SENO (check current scheme and criteria).

•  DO NOT withhold AAC while waiting for speech to develop, and do not describe a pupil as 'non-verbal' in reports as if that meant 'no communication'.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Using pictures or a device doesn't stop her talking. The research says it can help speech, and it gives her a voice now.'

•  'The biggest help is if you use it with her — point to the symbols as you talk. That's how she learns it, like any language.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'If the device is in his bag, he has no voice. It needs to be out and charged all day.'

•  'Model on it as you talk. You don't need to be an expert — just use it.'

•  'Give him time to answer on it — a device reply takes longer than speech. If you move on, he learns there's no point.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  Use the pupil's system to explain who you are and why you're there; allow time and accept all responses.

•  YOUNGER / LIMITED SYSTEM: offer a small set of choices on symbols ('like / don't like', 'help / stop') and check yes/no reliability first.

•  OLDER: 'I want to know what YOU think. Take your time — I'll wait.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — pupils without reliable speech are at higher risk of abuse and less able to disclose; ensure they have vocabulary to report harm (body parts, 'stop', 'hurt'); on any concern follow child protection procedures and report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  WATCH — behaviour escalating when the system is unavailable: behaviour may be communication; do not treat as misbehaviour.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Will a device make him lazy about talking?' A: 'No — the research doesn't show that, and some children talk more once they have another way to communicate.'

•  Q: 'Who pays for the device?' A: 'That depends on the scheme — school assistive technology through the Department/NCSE with the SENO, or health-funded through the CDNT. It's worth checking the current rules with both.'

•  Q: 'How do you assess her if she can't speak?' A: 'Using her own communication system, non-verbal tasks and what the people who know her report. I'll be clear in the report about what we can and can't conclude.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring an assessment where you adapted procedures for an AAC user — how did you record the adaptation and its effect on interpretation?

•  Discuss how you gathered the child's voice and consent through AAC, and what 'good enough' looked like.

13

presentation.name: English as an Additional Language (EAL)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A pupil whose home or first language is not English, learning English (and often Irish) in school. Part D: 'Not a disorder — can mimic language disorder, rule out.'

•  Cummins distinguished conversational fluency (BICS) from academic language proficiency (CALP); the latter is widely cited as taking several years longer to develop (Cummins, 2008). Fluent playground English does not mean the pupil can access a textbook.

•  Newly arrived pupils may go through a non-verbal or 'silent' period (Tabors, 2008) — normal, not a sign of difficulty.

•  The key question for an EP is whether a difficulty exists IN BOTH (or all) languages — a true language disorder does; an EAL learning stage does not.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a special educational need in itself, and NOT a language disorder. Most EAL learners are typically developing learners of a new language.

•  NOT a reason to stop using the home language. Advising families to switch to English is not supported by evidence and may harm the parent–child relationship and the home language (Paradis et al., 2021).

•  NOT assessable with English-normed tests as if the pupil were a monolingual English speaker — standard scores are not valid for this purpose.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: silent period, mixing languages; describe development in home language through parents (with interpreter).

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: conversational English fast, academic language slower; literacy decoding may be fine while comprehension lags.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject-specific vocabulary across many subjects; late arrivals face exam pressure; check current criteria for exemption from Irish.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: third-level access, language support; prior education and qualifications may not transfer.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: interpreters and home-language input are still needed; avoid assuming the pupil's needs are purely language-related or purely SEN-related.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  English as an Additional Language and bilingual development (DLD vs EAL)

•  DLD

•  Hearing impairment

•  Selective Mutism

•  Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (including Complex PTSD)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Language history with parents through a professional interpreter (NEPS interpreter request form per Part D — check your service's current procedure) — first words, home-language development, prior schooling, languages spoken by whom.

•  Ask: is the pupil developing at a similar rate to other EAL peers with similar exposure? Comparison with EAL peers, not monolingual peers.

•  Use non-verbal measures (e.g., Leiter-3, WNV) cautiously and dynamic assessment (test–teach–retest) to see learning rate.

•  Rule out hearing and vision; consider trauma and interrupted schooling in refugee and displaced pupils.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  LANGUAGE SUPPORT through the school's special education / EAL support allocation, following NCCA (2006) guidance — check current Department circulars for how EAL support is allocated.

•  VISUAL SUPPORTS, key vocabulary pre-taught, bilingual glossaries and peer buddies.

•  VALUE THE HOME LANGUAGE: encourage families to keep using it; allow pupils to plan or explain in it where possible.

•  MONITOR PROGRESS over time and compare with EAL peers; if progress is markedly slower in BOTH languages, consider SLT referral.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support for targeted EAL support; School Support Plus if a possible language disorder or trauma needs outside services.

•  DO NOT report standard scores from English-normed language tests as if valid; describe performance and state the limitation.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Learning a new language for school takes years, and chatting with friends comes much faster than the language of books. What we're seeing is normal for a child learning English.'

•  'Please keep speaking your own language at home. It helps her English, not hurts it — a strong first language gives her something to build on.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'He sounds fluent, but that's playground English. Classroom and textbook language takes longer — pre-teach the key words and use visuals.'

•  'Compare him with other EAL pupils who arrived at the same time. That's the fair comparison.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  Use an interpreter where needed. 'You're learning a whole new language — that's a big thing to do. Which language do you think in?'

•  OLDER: 'What's hardest — understanding the teacher, reading, or writing? Is it easier in your own language?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — difficulty in the home language as well, reported by parents: consider possible language disorder or hearing impairment; SLT referral.

•  WATCH — pupils who have experienced displacement, war or trauma: consider trauma-informed approaches and referral routes (Primary Care, CAMHS, specialist services).

•  RED FLAG — any safeguarding concern (including trafficking or exploitation indicators): follow child protection procedures; report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should we only speak English at home?' A: 'No. The evidence supports keeping the home language — it helps rather than hinders English.'

•  Q: 'Could it be dyslexia or a language disorder?' A: 'It's possible, but we need to know if the difficulty shows in her first language too. That's why we ask about home language development.'

•  Q: 'How long before he catches up?' A: 'Conversational English often comes quickly; academic English takes considerably longer. We'll look at his progress over time rather than a snapshot.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case involving an interpreter — how did you brief them, and what could not be translated?

•  Discuss how you reported test results for an EAL pupil, and whether any score could be misr

presentation.name: Bilingual language development
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Typical development of two (or more) languages — simultaneously from birth or sequentially. In Ireland this includes Irish-medium education (Gaelscoileanna, Gaeltacht schools) as well as home languages other than English.

•  Grosjean (1989): 'the bilingual is not two monolinguals in one person'. Vocabulary is distributed across languages; Pearson, Fernández and Oller (1993) found bilingual toddlers' total conceptual vocabulary comparable to monolinguals' when both languages were counted.

•  Hoff et al. (2012) found that language skill in each language tracks the amount of exposure to it — a lower score in one language often reflects less exposure, not difficulty.

•  Part D: 'Not a disorder.' Code-switching (mixing languages) is a normal feature of bilingual speech.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a cause of language disorder or delay. Bilingual children with DLD have difficulties in both languages; bilingualism does not cause them (Kohnert, 2010).

•  NOT a cognitive advantage to promise parents. The 'bilingual advantage' in executive function is contested (Paap & Greenberg, 2013). The case for bilingualism rests on communication, family and culture — which is strong enough.

•  NOT confusing for children with SEN. Children with DLD or intellectual disability can become bilingual; dropping a home language is not recommended on these grounds (Paradis et al., 2021).

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: mixing languages, possible slightly later milestones in each language separately; total vocabulary is the fairer measure.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: language of schooling may overtake home language; Irish-medium pupils may show a temporary lag in English literacy that is expected and usually resolves — check the Irish-medium guidance.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: language identity, choice of language by context; home language may weaken without support.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: bilingualism as asset for study and work; formal recognition of home-language qualifications varies.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: support both languages where possible; keep the family language in the plan.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  English as an Additional Language and bilingual development (DLD vs EAL)

•  DLD

•  Speech Sound Disorder

•  Selective Mutism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Detailed language history: which language, with whom, since when, how much (percentage estimates across the day).

•  Sample both languages if at all possible — through parents, an interpreter, or an SLT with the relevant language.

•  Interpret English-normed tests cautiously; for Irish-medium pupils, consider which language the test is administered in and whether norms apply.

•  Look for difficulty in BOTH languages and for slow learning even with good input — the markers of disorder rather than difference.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  KEEP BOTH LANGUAGES: advise families to use the language they are most fluent and comfortable in with their child.

•  COUNT BOTH LANGUAGES when describing vocabulary and expressive language in reports.

•  SUPPORT LITERACY TRANSFER: phonics and reading skills learned in one language support the other; explicitly link them.

•  REFER TO SLT where difficulty is present across both languages, persists despite good exposure, or parents report concerns in the home language.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support; School Support where a targeted language plan is needed.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Children can learn two languages well. Sometimes each language looks a little behind on its own, but together his words add up to about the same as other children's.'

•  'Speak to him in the language you're most comfortable in. That gives him the richest language model.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Mixing languages is normal. It's not confusion — it's using everything she has.'

•  'If you're worried about his language, the question is whether he struggles in his home language too. Ask the parents.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'You know two languages — that's brilliant. Which one do you use with your granny?'

•  OLDER: 'Some things are easier to say in one language than the other. That's normal for people who speak more than one.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — limited progress in both languages despite good exposure, or parent concern in home language: SLT referral.

•  WATCH — pupil speaking at home but not in school: consider selective mutism (as distinct from a silent period) — refer via SLT/CAMHS route.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should we stop speaking Polish so he catches up in English?' A: 'No. Keeping his home language supports his English, and it's his family language.'

•  Q: 'Will Irish-medium school hold back her English reading?' A: 'Some temporary lag in English is common in immersion and usually resolves. If it doesn't, we look further.'

•  Q: 'Does being bilingual make children smarter?' A: 'The research is mixed on that. The real benefits are being able to talk with family and belong to two cultures.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case where a bilingual pupil's scores were low — did you count both languages and describe exposure?

•  Discuss Irish-medium assessment: which language, which norms, and how you stated limitations.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Grosjean, F. (1989). Neurolinguists, beware! The bilingual is not two monolinguals in one person. Brain and Language, 36(1), 3–15.

→ Hoff, E., Core, C., Place, S., Rumiche, R., Señor, M., & Parra, M. (2012). Dual language exposure and early bilingual development. Journal of Child Language, 39(1), 1–27.

→ Kohnert, K. (2010). Bilingual children with primary language impairment: Issues, evidence and implications for clinical actions. Journal of Communication Disorders, 43(6), 456–473.

→ Paap, K. R., & Greenberg, Z. I. (2013). There is no coherent evidence for a bilingual advantage in executive processing. Cognitive Psychology, 66(2), 232–258.

→ Pearson, B. Z

presentation.name: Vocabulary gap from limited exposure
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Vocabulary below age expectations because of LESS OPPORTUNITY — fewer conversations, fewer books, interrupted schooling, EAL — rather than a difficulty learning words.

•  Hart and Risley (1995) reported large differences in words heard by children in different socioeconomic groups; Sperry, Sperry and Miller (2019) challenged the size and generality of that 'word gap'. Romeo et al. (2018) found conversational turns, not just words heard, related to language and brain measures.

•  Stanovich (1986) described 'Matthew effects': children with more vocabulary read more and gain more vocabulary, widening gaps over time.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). The key distinction is from DLD: the child with a vocabulary gap learns new words quickly when taught.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a judgement on families. Exposure varies for many reasons; the recommendation is about what school can add.

•  NOT DLD — unless the child is also slow to learn new words with good teaching, and has difficulties in grammar and other language areas. Dynamic assessment distinguishes the two.

•  NOT fixed by word lists alone; words need repeated, meaningful encounters in context.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: limited vocabulary on entry; responds quickly to rich language environments.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: reading comprehension limited by vocabulary even when decoding is fine.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject-specific and academic vocabulary across subjects; exam questions misunderstood.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: academic vocabulary at third level; workplace terminology.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: consider whether the setting itself offers rich enough language input.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  English as an Additional Language and bilingual development (DLD vs EAL)

•  Hearing impairment

•  Borderline Intellectual Functioning

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  BPVS-3 (receptive vocabulary) — useful as a snapshot; note that it measures single-word receptive vocabulary only.

•  Dynamic assessment: teach 5 new words, check retention after a week. Fast learners suggest exposure; slow learners suggest need for SLT input.

•  Language history and literacy environment through parent conversation, sensitively.

•  Reading comprehension vs decoding comparison (e.g., YARC).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  ROBUST VOCABULARY INSTRUCTION: explicitly teach Tier 2 words (useful across subjects) with multiple exposures (Beck et al., 2013).

•  PRE-TEACH key words before a topic; word walls; subject glossaries.

•  INCREASE CONVERSATIONAL TURNS: back-and-forth talk, not just talk at the child (Romeo et al., 2018).

•  SHARED READING at school and signposting to library schemes for families — check local services.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for whole-class vocabulary teaching; School Support for targeted small-group vocabulary programmes.

•  REFER to SLT if progress is slow despite teaching, or if other language areas are affected.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He hasn't had as many chances to hear and use some of these words yet — and he learns them quickly when we teach them. That's a good sign.'

•  'Talking together — about anything — really helps. It's the back and forth that matters.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Pre-teach the five key words before the topic. She'll get so much more out of the lesson.'

•  'Choose useful words, not just topic words — "compare", "describe", "evidence" come up everywhere.'

•  'Teach a new word, then use it again tomorrow and next week. One encounter is rarely enough.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Let's be word collectors — find new words and see if you can use them!'

•  OLDER: 'Some words you just haven't come across yet. That's fine — we'll build your word bank, especially the ones that come up in every subject.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — slow word learning even with good teaching, or difficulties in grammar and understanding: consider DLD; SLT referral.

•  WATCH — very limited language with signs of neglect or deprivation: consider child protection; discuss with the DLP; where the threshold is met, report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is this a language disorder?' A: 'We checked how quickly she learns new words — she learns them well. That points to needing more exposure rather than a disorder.'

•  Q: 'What can we do at home?' A: 'Talk together — about dinner, the news, what you see. Read together if you can. Back-and-forth conversation matters more than which words.'

•  Q: 'Will he catch up?' A: 'With targeted teaching, many children close a lot of the gap. We'll track his progress and review it.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case where low vocabulary was attributed to home — did you check learning rate before drawing that conclusion?

•  Discuss how to write about language exposure in a report without judging the family.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Beck, I. L., McKeown, M. G., & Kucan, L. (2013). Bringing words to life: Robust vocabulary instruction (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.

→ Hart, B., & Risley, T. R. (1995). Meaningful differences in the everyday experience of young American children. Brookes.

→ Romeo, R. R., Leonard, J. A., Robinson, S. T., West, M. R., Mackey, A. P., Rowe, M. L., & Gabrieli, J. D. E. (2018). Beyond the 30-million-word gap: Children's conversational exposure is associated with language-related brain function. Psychological Science, 29(5), 700–710.

→ Sperry, D. E., Sperry, L. L., & Miller, P. J. (2019). Reexamining the verbal environments of children from different socioeconomic backgrounds. Child Development, 90(4), 1303–1318.

→ Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading: Some consequences of individual differences in the acquisition of literacy. Reading Research Quarterly, 21(4), 360–4

presentation.name: Participation in oral work and classroom talk
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  How much and how well the pupil contributes to spoken classroom activity — answering questions, discussion, group work, presentations. Part D notes this is Form 2 wording.

•  Oral participation is a learning tool, not just a behaviour: dialogic teaching approaches (Alexander, 2020; Mercer & Littleton, 2007) show talk is how pupils develop and test their thinking.

•  A referral description, not a diagnosis (Part D). Nobody diagnoses it.

•  Low participation is a common final pathway for language difficulty, anxiety, stammering, EAL, hearing loss, autism and cultural expectations about talking to adults.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT shyness by default. A pupil who does not talk in class may have a language difficulty, anxiety or selective mutism — each needs a different response.

•  NOT fixed by 'cold-calling' or pressure to speak. Pressure increases avoidance in anxious pupils and in selective mutism (Johnson & Wintgens, 2016).

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: talks with family, not with staff; limited speech in group time. Silent periods in EAL are normal.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: rarely volunteers answers; one-word responses; avoids reading aloud.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: oral exams (e.g., language orals), presentations and group work become assessed; anxiety about peer judgement rises.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: seminars, interviews and workplace communication.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: support participation through AAC and structured turn-taking.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Selective Mutism

•  Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia)

•  Childhood-Onset Fluency Disorder (stuttering)

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation: count spontaneous vs prompted contributions, length of utterance, and context (whole class, small group, pair, one-to-one).

•  Check language (BPVS-3, CELF-5 via SLT), hearing (audiology), and fluency (SLT).

•  Pupil interview: 'When do you find it easy to talk in school? When is it hard?' — use drawing or scaling for younger or anxious pupils.

•  Parent interview: does the pupil speak freely at home? If yes, and not at school at all, consider selective mutism.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  WAIT TIME: pause 3+ seconds after a question before taking answers; Rowe (1986) found longer wait time increased the length and number of responses.

•  THINK–PAIR–SHARE and talk partners: rehearse in a pair before speaking to the class.

•  GRADED PARTICIPATION: non-verbal responses (whiteboards, thumbs), then pair talk, then small group, then whole class.

•  DO NOT force speech; for suspected selective mutism, remove pressure to speak and seek SLT/CAMHS advice — follow a structured approach (Johnson & Wintgens, 2016).

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for whole-class approaches; School Support for individual plans; School Support Plus where SLT or CAMHS is involved.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She talks freely at home but not much in class. We want to understand why — it could be confidence, language, or worry — and then make talking easier for her.'

•  'Please don't push her to talk in school. Pressure usually makes it harder.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Give him time to think before you take answers — even a few seconds makes a difference.'

•  'Let her rehearse with a partner first. It's much easier to say something twice.'

•  'Count her contributions in pair work versus whole class for a week — that tells us where to start building.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Some children find it easier to talk to one friend than the whole class. What's easiest for you?'

•  OLDER: 'Talking in class can feel like everyone's watching. What would make it easier — writing first, talking to a partner, or something else?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — no speech in school at all but normal speech at home: consider selective mutism; SLT/CAMHS referral via GP.

•  WATCH — increasing avoidance, distress or refusal to attend school: consider social anxiety and EBSA; plan early.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is he just shy?' A: 'Maybe, and shyness is fine. But we check language, hearing and worry first, because the support is different for each.'

•  Q: 'Should the teacher call on her more to build confidence?' A: 'Not without warning. Pair talk first, then small groups, then whole class — building up step by step.'

•  Q: 'Will she lose marks for not speaking?' A: 'Where oral work is assessed, the school can look at reasonable adjustments — for State exams that's the SEC's RACE scheme; check the current criteria.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case of low participation — did you ask whether the pupil talks at home, and did that change your formulation?

•  Discuss how to advise teachers who believe pressure to speak builds confidence.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Alexander, R. (2020). A dialogic teaching companion. Routledge.

→ Johnson, M., & Wintgens, A. (2016). The selective mutism resource manual (2nd ed.). Speechmark.

→ Mercer, N., & Littleton, K. (2007). Dialogue and the development of children's thinking: A sociocultural approach. Routledge.

→ Rowe, M. B. (1986). Wait time: Slowing down may be a way of speeding up! Journal of Teacher Education, 37(1), 43–50.

presentation.name: Following multi-step verbal instructions
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of what the child does when an adult gives a spoken instruction with more than one step: they carry out the first or last part, stall, copy peers, or ask again. It is a behaviour seen in the classroom, not a diagnosis.

•  Following a spoken instruction draws on at least four things at once: HEARING it, UNDERSTANDING the words and grammar (especially 'before', 'after', 'unless', 'except'), HOLDING it in working memory, and ORGANISING the action. The presentation is the same whichever link breaks — the assessment is about finding which one.

•  Gathercole and colleagues showed in laboratory analogues of classroom tasks that children with low working memory lose instructions as length increases (Gathercole et al., 2008; Jaroslawska et al., 2016).

•  Receptive language difficulty is the other common route: a child with DLD may hold all the words but misread the order or the conditional (Bishop et al., 2017, CATALISE). These are different problems with different recommendations.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT defiance or 'not listening' by default. Hollo, Wehby and Oliver (2014) found a large proportion of children identified with behavioural difficulties had unidentified language difficulties — rate varies by study, check before quoting. Ask whether the child understood before asking why they did not comply.

•  NOT explained by 'he can follow instructions at home'. Home instructions are usually short, routine, contextualised and repeated; classroom instructions are longer, novel, delivered to a group and often at speed.

•  NOT proof of ADHD. Attention is one route, but a child who loses instructions only when language is complex, and holds them fine when they are visual, is pointing you at language rather than attention.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: two-step, then three-step, instructions emerge through the preschool years; a child copying peers rather than responding to the words is the classic sign. Frame it as developmental and involve SLT early.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the main referral window — instructions lengthen in 1st to 3rd class and move from routine to novel ('Put your maths copy away, take out your reader, and turn to the page we finished on Tuesday'). Check hearing first.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: at post-primary the load moves to subject teachers giving multi-part homework and practical instructions (science, home economics, woodwork). A student who never has the homework written down may be losing it at the point of instruction.

•  YOUNG ADULT / SPECIAL SETTING: in special settings, compare the length and complexity of instructions staff give against the pupil's receptive level on the SLT or EP assessment — mismatch is common and easy to fix.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  ADHD

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Hearing impairment

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ASK HEARING FIRST: when was hearing last checked, any history of glue ear or grommets? A fluctuating conductive loss produces exactly this presentation. REFER to audiology via GP if not recently checked.

•  OBSERVE with a comparison peer: note the instruction given (write it down verbatim), how many steps, whether it was visual-supported, and what the child did. Five logged instructions tell you more than a rating scale.

•  SEPARATE LANGUAGE FROM MEMORY: compare WISC-V UK Working Memory Index with Verbal Comprehension; ask SLT for CELF-5 UK (Following Directions and, at younger ages, Linguistic Concepts are the relevant subtests — check the age ranges in the manual). If memory is low and language intact, the recommendation is different from the reverse.

•  TRY THE ADJUSTMENT IN THE SESSION: give the same instruction chunked, with a gesture or picture, and note the difference. A dynamic test of what helps is the most usable finding for the teacher.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: give instructions in the order they are to be done, one step at a time, with the key word stressed; avoid 'before you do X, do Y' constructions, which reverse the order.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: back every multi-step instruction with a visual — written steps on the board, a numbered checklist, or a picture sequence for younger children — so the child is not relying on memory alone (Gathercole & Alloway, 2008).

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: teach the child a script for asking again — 'Can you say the second bit again?' — and make it acceptable to use. Children with language difficulty often stop asking because it draws attention.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: if receptive language is implicated, a targeted plan with SLT input on concept vocabulary (before/after, first/last, unless/except), reviewed after a term with a specific measure (e.g. number of three-step instructions completed unaided out of five).

•  REFER: SLT via HSE Primary Care where receptive language is the concern; CDNT where needs are complex and multiple; audiology via GP where hearing has not been checked.

•  DO NOT recommend 'improve listening skills' without saying what, how, and who — it is unmeasurable and locates the problem in effort.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When a teacher gives a long instruction, she loses part of it. That can happen because the words are hard to understand, because it's hard to hold them in mind, or because of hearing — and we're finding out which, because each needs a different fix.'

•  'It isn't that she's not listening or doesn't care. At home your instructions are shorter and she knows the routine, which is why it looks different there.'

•  SIGNPOST: ask the GP for a hearing check if one has not been done recently; HSE Primary Care SLT for a language assessment.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Count the steps. If it's three or more, give it one step at a time or put it on the board. That single change usually shows you whether it's memory or understanding.'

•  'Watch for him copying the child beside him — that's a sign he didn't get the words, not t

presentation.name: Narrative and sequencing in spoken account
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of how the child tells a story or recounts an event: whether there is a beginning, middle and end, whether events come in order, whether the listener can follow who did what, and whether causes and feelings are included.

•  Narrative is a demanding language task — it requires vocabulary, grammar, sequencing, perspective-taking and holding the whole story in mind. Story grammar models (Stein & Glenn, 1979) break it into setting, initiating event, internal response, attempt, consequence and reaction, which gives you a checklist for what is missing.

•  Narrative is a sensitive indicator of language difficulty in school-age children, often more so than single-word vocabulary tests (Botting, 2002). A child can score adequately on a vocabulary test and still be unable to give a coherent account.

•  It matters beyond English class: a child who cannot sequence a spoken account cannot tell a teacher what happened in the yard, cannot give a clear account in a behaviour incident, and may not be able to disclose.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as imagination or creativity. A child may have rich ideas and still struggle to organise them in language; judge structure separately from content.

•  NOT 'rambling' or 'lying' when the account keeps changing. Inconsistent retelling is a recognised feature of narrative difficulty and must be considered before an account is judged unreliable — especially in behaviour or safeguarding contexts.

•  NOT only a speech and language issue. Autistic children may give a sequenced account that omits other people's intentions and feelings; the gap there is perspective rather than order.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: early narratives are 'heaps' and chains of events; a basic sequence with a problem and a resolution develops through the early school years. Renfrew Action Picture Test and the Bus Story (Renfrew, 1997) are typical SLT tools here.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: expect increasingly complete story grammar — goals, attempts, consequences — and use of connectives ('because', 'so', 'then', 'after that'). Difficulty shows in news time, oral reports, and in written composition, which inherits the oral structure.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: narrative moves into explanation, argument and recount across subjects (history essays, science write-ups). A student who cannot sequence orally usually struggles to structure extended writing too.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: use personally relevant recount (what did you do at the weekend, with photos) rather than a fictional story; it separates memory for events from the language to express them.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Intellectual Disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ELICIT TWO KINDS: a retell (story you have just told them, with pictures) and a personal recount (something that happened to them). Retell tests comprehension and memory; recount tests generation. Record verbatim.

•  SCORE AGAINST STORY GRAMMAR: tick setting, initiating event, feeling, attempt, consequence, ending; count connectives. This gives a plain-language description the teacher can use without a standard score.

•  USE STANDARDISED MEASURES via SLT where available — Renfrew Bus Story, ERRNI (Bishop, 2004) — rather than improvising norms. Renfrew Action Picture Test covers information and grammar up to about age 8 (see Part G).

•  CROSS-CHECK WITH WRITING: look at a sample of the child's written stories. If written and oral structure are both weak, the difficulty is language organisation; if only written, look at spelling and handwriting load.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: use a visual story frame (who, where, when, what happened, how they felt, how it ended) for news time and oral work; fade it as structure becomes internal.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: teach sequencing and cause words explicitly — first, next, then, because, so, in the end — and model them in the teacher's own recounts.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a small-group narrative intervention planned with SLT input, with a baseline and review (e.g. number of story grammar elements in a retell, before and after a set period). Narrative-based intervention has a supportive evidence base (Petersen, 2011).

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: in behaviour incidents, get the child's account with visual supports — a drawn comic strip or sequence of boxes — rather than an unstructured verbal interview, and record that this was done.

•  REFER: SLT via HSE Primary Care, or CDNT where needs are complex, for full language assessment if narrative weakness sits within broader language difficulty.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Telling a story in order is one of the hardest things we do with language. She has lots to say, and the difficulty is putting it in order so the listener can follow.'

•  'You can help at home by asking about her day in steps: what happened first, then what, and how did it end — and by using photos from the day as prompts.'

•  SIGNPOST: HSE Primary Care SLT; the school's own support plan.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When he tells you what happened, his account jumps around. That's a language organisation difficulty, not evasiveness. A story frame or a quick drawn sequence will get you a clearer account.'

•  'His written stories have the same shape as his spoken ones. Work on the oral structure first and the writing usually follows.'

•  'Model the connectives you want: first, then, because, so. Say them out loud when you recount things yourself.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Stories are like a train — each carriage is one bit and they go in order. Let's build your train.' Use boxes or cards the child can move.

•  OLDER: 'You've got the ideas. The tricky bit is putting them in order so someone else can follow. A plan with boxes makes that easier, in speaking and in writing.'

•  ASK: 'When you tell someone what happened, do they understand you?' and 'What makes it easier?'

10

presentation.name: Word-finding difficulty
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A difficulty retrieving a word the child knows, at the moment it is needed. The child understands the word and may use it at other times, but in conversation or on demand it will not come.

•  It shows as long pauses, fillers ('um', 'the thing'), circumlocution ('the thing you cut with' for scissors), substituting a related word ('knife'), gesture, or giving up. Tip-of-the-tongue states are the everyday version.

•  Messer and Dockrell (2006) describe competing accounts: weak semantic representations (the word is only partly known) versus a retrieval or phonological access problem (the word is known but hard to reach). Which one applies shapes the intervention.

•  It is common in children with DLD and is associated with slow rapid naming in children with reading difficulty (German, 2000). It affects oral answers, class discussion and timed tasks disproportionately.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a vocabulary gap. If the child does not know the word at all (fails to recognise it on a receptive test), that is exposure or vocabulary, not word-finding.

•  NOT not knowing the answer. A child who says 'I know it, I just can't say it' is often right; offer a multiple-choice or a first-sound cue and see.

•  NOT stuttering, although the two can co-occur and pauses can look similar. Stuttering involves repetitions, prolongations and blocks on sounds; word-finding involves the word itself not arriving.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: hard to separate from ordinary vocabulary growth; note frequent 'that thing' and heavy gesture in a child whose understanding is good.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: noticeable in oral answers, news time, and quick-fire questioning; the child may stop volunteering. Rapid naming tasks (PhAB2) are often slow alongside.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject-specific vocabulary multiplies the load; students may avoid oral presentations, orals in Irish and modern languages, and class discussion. Anxiety about being put on the spot is common and understandable.

•  YOUNG ADULT: may affect interviews and oral exams; adjustment requests should be evidence-based and specific.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  Stuttering

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  COMPARE RECEPTIVE WITH EXPRESSIVE: BPVS-3 (receptive) against an expressive naming measure such as EVT-3 or an SLT naming test. Good receptive with weaker expressive naming for the same words is the signature.

•  TEST WITH CUES: when naming fails, give a semantic cue ('you use it to cut paper') then a phonological cue ('it starts with sc-'). Which cue helps tells you which account fits (Messer & Dockrell, 2006).

•  OBSERVE TIMED vs UNTIMED: note whether answers improve with wait time. Record pause length in class discussion informally.

•  RAPID NAMING: PhAB2 rapid naming subtests (see Part G) where literacy is also a concern.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: allow wait time before taking an answer, and warn the pupil in advance of the question they will be asked, so retrieval is not happening under an audience.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: accept alternative responses — pointing, choosing from options, writing, or describing — where the aim is to check understanding rather than naming.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: pre-teach topic vocabulary with rich semantic and phonological information (meaning, category, first sound, number of syllables, rhymes) — word-web or 'word map' approaches, planned with SLT.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: teach the pupil self-cueing strategies — describe it, think of the category, think of the first sound — and practise them explicitly; review use after a set period.

•  REFER: SLT via HSE Primary Care where word-finding sits within wider language difficulty. For oral exams at post-primary, check the current State Examinations Commission (RACE) criteria — do not promise an accommodation.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He knows the words — you can see it when he picks the right picture. The difficulty is getting the word out when he needs it, like when a name is on the tip of your tongue, but more often.'

•  'Waiting, and not finishing his sentences for him, helps. If he's stuck, ask what it's used for or what it starts with.'

•  SIGNPOST: HSE Primary Care SLT.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When she goes quiet in answer to a question, it's often the word not arriving rather than not knowing. Give her ten seconds, or a choice of two.'

•  'Tell her the question before you ask it in front of the class. That one change reduces both the pause and the anxiety.'

•  'Pre-teaching the key words for a topic — meaning, first sound, syllables — gives the words better hooks to be pulled out by.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Words live in a big cupboard in your head. Sometimes the right word is at the back and it's hard to reach. We can learn tricks to find it.'

•  OLDER: 'You know the word — it's the retrieval that's slow, like a file that takes ages to load. Describing it, or thinking what it starts with, can help it load.'

•  ASK: 'What happens when you're asked a question in class and the word won't come?' and 'What would help?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — new-onset word-finding difficulty, or loss of words previously used, in a child or young person: medical until proven otherwise. Refer to GP promptly.

•  WATCH — a student withdrawing from all oral participation because of word-finding: anxiety is secondary but real, and needs addressing in its own right.

•  BOUNDARY — describe the pattern; SLT assesses and diagnoses language disorder.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'She knows it — why won't she just say it?' A: 'Knowing a word and getting it out quickly are two different systems. She has the first; the second is slow for her.'

•  Q: 'Is it a memory problem?' A: 'It's a specific kind — retrieving words — rather than general memory. She may remember events and facts well.'

•  Q: 'Will she get extra

presentation.name: Interpreter need and how it changes the assessment
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.2 Language skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Not a difficulty in the child — a condition of the assessment. Where the child, the parents, or both do not share a language with the EP well enough for informed consent, history-taking or feedback, a professional interpreter is needed, and the assessment itself changes.

•  It changes CONSENT (consent must be informed in a language the parent understands — PSI Code of Ethics; GDPR transparency), HISTORY (developmental history in the home language is often the best evidence of whether a difficulty exists in both languages), and TESTING (standardised verbal tests lose their norms when translated or interpreted).

•  Part D lists the NEPS interpreter request form as the route; check your service's current procedure and budget before booking.

•  HSE guidance on interpreting (HSE, 2009, 'On Speaking Terms') and BPS guidance for psychologists (BPS, 2017) both say: use trained interpreters, brief them, and avoid using family members — and never children — to interpret.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT something a sibling, the child themselves, or a bilingual teacher can do instead. They cannot be neutral, may soften or omit, and it places an improper burden on a child. A parent's choice to bring a family member should be discussed and recorded.

•  NOT a way to make a verbal IQ test valid. A WISC-V verbal subtest interpreted live is no longer the standardised test; its norms do not apply and standard scores should not be reported as if they did.

•  NOT needed only for the parent meeting. The child's own proficiency in English must be judged separately — a child can be conversationally fluent and still need home-language support for academic language (Cummins, 1984).

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: developmental history and play observation carry the assessment; the interpreter mainly serves the parent. Ask about language development in the home language specifically.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the child may be the family's informal interpreter at home; do not use them in that role here. Consider non-verbal measures (WNV, Leiter-3) and dynamic assessment for the child.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: the young person may prefer to speak English and not use the interpreter for their own part — ask them, and record the choice. Keep the interpreter for the parent.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: check whether AAC systems exist in the home language, and whether the family's understanding of the placement was ever gained in their language.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Bilingual language development

•  EAL

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  PLAN AHEAD: book a professional interpreter for the specific language and dialect; confirm the interpreter does not know the family (small communities); allow roughly double the time for meetings.

•  BRIEF AND DEBRIEF: before, explain the purpose, confidentiality, that you need word-for-word rendering, and any technical terms; after, ask about cultural meanings you may have missed and check the interpreter is all right if content was distressing.

•  CHOOSE MEASURES THAT SURVIVE: WNV or Leiter-3 for non-verbal reasoning; dynamic assessment (test–teach–retest) to see learning rate; home-language history; school work samples. State in the report exactly which procedures were modified and why.

•  RECORD IT: the interpreter's name/agency, language, and which parts of the assessment were interpreted, in the file and the report.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  IN THE REPORT: state that an interpreter was used, for which parts, and how this limits interpretation of any scores. Do not report translated verbal subtests as standard scores.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: where the child is still acquiring English, recommend language-rich teaching, visual support and home-language use where possible, rather than special educational provision for a presumed disability.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: where there is concern about a difficulty in BOTH languages (by history and observation), plan a targeted intervention with a baseline and review — slow response to good teaching is itself evidence.

•  FEEDBACK: give feedback through the interpreter, in plain language, and provide a written summary translated where the service allows. Check understanding with teach-back ('Can you tell me what you'll say to the school?').

•  REFER: SLT (Primary Care) where language difficulty is suspected in both languages; ask whether a bilingual SLT or home-language assessment is available — often it is not, so check locally.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'I've asked for an interpreter so that you can say everything in your own language and understand everything I say. The interpreter is here for you, keeps everything confidential, and isn't part of the school.'

•  'Some of the tests I use only work properly in English. So I'll use ones that don't depend on English, and I'll rely a lot on what you tell me about how he speaks at home.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's EAL supports; local intercultural or migrant support organisations — check current services locally.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Please don't ask her older brother to translate for the parents at meetings. It isn't fair on him and we lose information. The service can book an interpreter.'

•  'Before we think about a learning difficulty, the question is: does she have this difficulty in her home language too? Her parents are the best source on that.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'This person is here to help your mam/dad and me understand each other. You don't have to do any translating today.'

•  OLDER: 'You can talk to me in English or in [language] — whichever is easier for you. Which would you like?' Respect the answer.

•  ASK: 'Which language do you think in when you're doing maths? When you're telling a story?' — useful and often revealing.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — any child protection concern arising in an interpreted meeting: follow the same-day procedure; the

presentation.name: Cognitive profile differences (verbal, fluid, working memory, processing speed)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of unevenness across the indexes of a cognitive battery — typically WISC-V UK Verbal Comprehension, Visual Spatial, Fluid Reasoning, Working Memory and Processing Speed — where some areas are clearly stronger than others. It is a pattern in scores, not a condition.

•  Uneven profiles are common in the general population: a meaningful discrepancy between some pair of indexes is the norm rather than the exception. Check the base-rate tables in the WISC-V UK manual before calling any difference 'unusual'.

•  Its practical value is in explaining the child's experience of school — e.g. a child with strong verbal reasoning and slow processing speed who understands everything and finishes nothing — and in deciding whether the Full Scale IQ is a fair summary or whether the General Ability Index should be reported (follow the manual's guidance and say why in the report).

•  Profile analysis — reading diagnostic meaning into specific patterns of index or subtest scores — has weak evidence for predicting diagnosis or response to intervention (Watkins, 2000; McGill, Dombrowski & Canivez, 2018).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a diagnostic signature. There is no 'dyslexia profile' or 'ADHD profile' on the WISC-V that identifies the condition; low working memory and processing speed are found across many groups and in many children with no diagnosis.

•  NOT evidence of a 'hidden high IQ' being held down. A high index in one area does not mean the child's 'true' ability is that number.

•  NOT a reason to discard FSIQ automatically. Where indexes are uneven, say so and explain which summary you rely on and why — that is a judgement to justify, not a rule to apply silently.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: WPPSI-IV UK profiles are less stable over time; describe strengths and needs cautiously and plan to review rather than to label.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the WISC-V UK is the usual tool. The practical question is whether a slow processing speed or low working memory is limiting output — check this against classroom work samples, not just the scores.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: profiles feed into RACE and subject-choice decisions. Processing speed evidence may be relevant to access arrangements — check current SEC criteria, which the EP does not set.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: WAIS-IV UK; profile may support DARE (Disability Access Route to Education) or college disability service applications — check current evidence requirements with the institution.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Intellectual Disability

•  Borderline Intellectual Functioning

•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  DLD

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  INTERPRET FROM THE TOP: overall ability, then index scores, then only cautiously subtests. State confidence intervals, not single numbers.

•  TRIANGULATE every notable index with a classroom observation: if Processing Speed is low, is written output slow in class? If Working Memory is low, are instructions lost? A score without a classroom correlate is a weak finding.

•  CHECK THE CONDITIONS: fatigue, anxiety, medication timing, language status (EAL), visual or motor difficulty all depress specific indexes. Record testing conditions and your behavioural observations.

•  USE BASE RATES: report whether a discrepancy is common in the standardisation sample, not only whether it is statistically significant.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  WRITE TO THE PROFILE, NOT THE LABEL: e.g. for slow processing speed — reduce copying, give printed notes, mark for content not volume; for low working memory — chunked instructions and visual checklists (Gathercole & Alloway, 2008).

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: use the relative strength as a route in — strong verbal reasoning supports oral explanation and discussion; strong visual-spatial supports diagrams and graphic organisers.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: where a weakness is limiting access to the curriculum, set a specific, measurable target tied to the classroom behaviour (e.g. proportion of written task completed), not to the index score.

•  IN THE REPORT: explain in one plain sentence what each important index means for this child's day, and state explicitly that the profile is not itself a diagnosis.

•  DO NOT recommend cognitive 'brain training' to raise an index score as an educational intervention: gains on trained tasks have not been shown to transfer reliably to attainment (Melby-Lervåg & Hulme, 2013).

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Everyone has things their mind does quickly and things it does more slowly. Her reasoning with words is a real strength; the speed at which she gets things down on paper is slower. That's why she knows more than her copybook shows.'

•  'This pattern is common, and it isn't a diagnosis. What it gives us is a plan for how to teach her.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's support plan; if a diagnosis is being asked about, the relevant route (CAMHS, CDNT, SLT) — say which, and why.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Her processing speed is the bottleneck, not her understanding. If you mark her work for the quality of what's there rather than how much, you'll see her real level.'

•  'Don't read the profile as a label. Use it to decide where to lighten the load and where to lean on her strengths.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your brain is really good at [strength]. [Weakness] takes it longer. That's how brains are — everybody's is a different shape.'

•  OLDER: 'You understand things well — the scores show that. Getting it all down quickly is harder for you. That's why the tests feel unfair sometimes, and it's why extra time or typed work might help.'
