•  ASK: 'Which kinds of school work feel easy, and which feel slow?' — the answer often matches the profile, and it is their evidence too.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — a very low Processing Speed alongside motor slowness or clumsiness: consider DCD and OT referral rather than assuming a cognitive explanation.

•  WATCH — a pr

presentation.name: Underachievement not meeting SLD criteria
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose attainment is lower than expected — from their age, their ability, their earlier progress, or their classmates — but whose difficulty does not meet criteria for a Specific Learning Disorder (DSM-5-TR) because it is not severe enough, not persistent despite targeted help, or better explained by something else.

•  The comparison matters and must be named: below AGE norms (low attainment), below what ABILITY predicts (underachievement in the classic sense), or below the child's OWN earlier trajectory (a falling-away). Each points to different causes.

•  IQ–achievement discrepancy on its own does not reliably distinguish children who need different teaching (Stuebing et al., 2002; Fletcher et al., 2019). The field has moved to looking at response to good teaching over time — NEPS Continuum of Support is built on that logic.

•  It is one of the most common referral pictures and the one where formulation matters most: the causes are usually multiple — instruction, attendance, motivation, anxiety, language, home circumstances — rather than one.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT 'no problem'. Not meeting SLD criteria means the label does not fit, not that the child's difficulty is unreal or undeserving of support. Support under the Continuum does not require a diagnosis.

•  NOT laziness. 'Could do better if he tried' is an interpretation; describe the behaviour and look for what sits beneath it (Interactive Factors Framework — Frederickson & Cline, 2015).

•  NOT settled by a single test session. A one-off attainment score below expectation is a hypothesis; trajectory over time and response to targeted teaching are the evidence.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: rarely described as underachievement; frame as developmental progress and learning opportunity.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: often surfaces at standardised testing (Drumcondra, Micra-T, Sigma-T) or when a gap to peers widens in the senior classes. Check attendance, instruction history and language first.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: transition to post-primary often exposes it — more subjects, more independent work, less monitoring. Consider motivation, peer context, mood and executive demands alongside attainment.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: may present as failure to progress at third level; distinguish from a newly exposed learning difficulty, mental health difficulty, or change of circumstances.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  Dyscalculia

•  ADHD

•  Anxiety

•  Intellectual Disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  BUILD THE TRAJECTORY: collect standardised test results across years, school reports, and work samples. A flat low line, a steady decline and a sudden drop mean different things.

•  INSTRUCTION AND ATTENDANCE: what has actually been taught, and was the child present? Ask for attendance records and intervention history (see 'Instruction history').

•  ATTAINMENT AND ABILITY: WIAT-III UK against WISC-V UK where warranted — report both with confidence intervals and describe the gap in plain language rather than as a discrepancy 'diagnosis'.

•  THE CHILD'S ACCOUNT: pupil interview on effort, confidence, what school feels like, and what gets in the way. Anxiety and low self-concept often appear here first.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a targeted intervention in the specific area of weakness, with a baseline, a defined period, and a named review measure. The response is itself the next piece of assessment.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: differentiated tasks that are pitched to be achievable with effort, and feedback that names the strategy used, not the ability.

•  ADDRESS THE MAINTAINING FACTORS named in the formulation — attendance (Tusla Education Support Service where relevant), anxiety, sleep, peer context — not only the skill gap.

•  IN THE REPORT: state plainly that the difficulty does not currently meet criteria for SLD, what it DOES look like, and what would change that view (e.g. persistence despite well-delivered intervention over time).

•  REVIEW: set a date. If progress with good intervention is minimal, escalate to School Support Plus and reconsider the formulation.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He is behind where we would expect, and that's real. It doesn't fit the definition of dyslexia at the moment, which means we don't think there's one specific cause — it looks more like a few things adding up.'

•  'He doesn't need a label to get help. The school can put support in now and we'll see how he responds — that tells us a lot.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's support plan; Tusla Education Support Service if attendance is a factor.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'She doesn't meet SLD criteria, but she does need targeted support. Let's agree one specific target, measure it now, and look again in eight to ten weeks.'

•  'The formulation has several parts. Can we look at [attendance / confidence / language] alongside the literacy?'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Some things in school feel hard right now. That doesn't mean you can't do them — it means we need to find the right way to help.'

•  OLDER: 'You're not where you'd like to be in [subject], and I don't think it's because you're not able. Let's work out together what's getting in the way.'

•  ASK: 'When did school start to feel harder?' and 'What's one thing that would make a difference?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — a sharp fall in attainment with withdrawal, mood change or unexplained absence: consider mental health, bullying, or something happening at home. Follow risk or child protection procedures where indicated.

•  WATCH — a child long described as 'lazy' whose difficulty has never been assessed: check hearing, vision and language before anything else.

•  BOUNDARY — you can describe that SLD criteria are not currently met; frame it as a present judgement that may change, not a permanent ruling.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q

presentation.name: Giftedness / exceptional ability
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose ability or performance in one or more areas is well above that of their peers. There is no single agreed definition: some models use high general ability, others domain-specific talent, others the interaction of ability, creativity and commitment (Renzulli, 1978).

•  Gagné's model distinguishes GIFTS (natural aptitudes) from TALENTS (developed achievement), with the environment and the child's own motivation as the catalysts between them (Gagné, 2004). This is useful because it makes the school's job — development — explicit.

•  In Ireland the Education Act 1998 (s.2), as enacted, included 'the educational needs of exceptionally able students' in its definition of special educational needs; the EPSEN Act 2004 definition is framed around disability and EPSEN s.52 amended the 1998 definitions — check the current consolidated text before quoting. There is no dedicated funded category. The NCCA's draft guidelines (NCCA, 2007) address exceptionally able students in mainstream classrooms; the Centre for Talented Youth Ireland (CTYI, DCU) runs programmes and assessments — check current offerings.

•  The EP's role is usually to describe the child's profile and needs, advise on differentiation and wellbeing, and consider whether anything else is also present.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a guarantee of high achievement. Many able children underachieve, particularly if work is consistently too easy, or where the child hides ability to fit in.

•  NOT a special educational need under the EPSEN Act 2004 definition, which is framed around disability (check the current legal position). This limits formal resourcing, but does not remove the school's responsibility to differentiate.

•  NOT inherently linked to emotional fragility. Evidence does not support a general view that gifted children are more anxious or socially troubled; problems, where present, often relate to fit between child and environment (Subotnik, Olszewski-Kubilius & Worrell, 2011).

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: early reading, advanced vocabulary or number interest; asynchrony (advanced cognition, age-typical emotions) is common. Avoid early labelling; provide rich opportunity.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: boredom, perfectionism or behaviour problems when work is well below level; or a quiet child doing just enough. Parents often identify before school does.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject choice, acceleration questions, and peer identity become central. Some young people downplay ability to fit in.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: early entry or advanced programmes; the challenge may be first real difficulty after years of ease.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Twice exceptional

•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Anxiety

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ASK THE QUESTION BEHIND THE REFERRAL: is it confirmation of ability, behaviour, boredom, social fit, or suspected additional need? The answer shapes whether a cognitive battery is needed at all.

•  COGNITIVE AND ATTAINMENT: WISC-V UK and WIAT-III UK where it will change the plan. Note ceiling effects at the top of the range and report confidence intervals.

•  WORK SAMPLES AND CURRICULUM LEVEL: is the child working at, above or below their level? Compare classroom output with test performance — a large gap may suggest disengagement or an additional need.

•  CHILD VOICE: what does the child find interesting, easy, frustrating? Talk about mistakes and challenge — perfectionism shows here.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: differentiate by depth and complexity, not by more of the same work. Compacting (skip what is already mastered) and extension tasks with genuine challenge (NCCA, 2007).

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: teach productive struggle — name effort and strategy in feedback, allow the child to experience difficulty in a safe way.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: where needs are marked, a plan agreed with parents that may include subject acceleration, enrichment, or mentoring. Acceleration decisions should consider social and emotional readiness and be reviewed.

•  SIGNPOST: CTYI (DCU) programmes; local enrichment. Check costs and eligibility before recommending.

•  DO NOT recommend grade skipping without a structured decision process and school agreement; it is not the EP's decision alone.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She is very able, particularly in [area]. What she needs is work that makes her think, not just more of the same.'

•  'Being able doesn't mean everything will be easy. Learning how to handle getting things wrong is part of what she needs now.'

•  SIGNPOST: CTYI; the NCCA guidelines; the school's differentiation plan.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'He isn't bored because he's difficult — he's bored because the work doesn't stretch him. Let him skip what he's already mastered and go deeper instead.'

•  'Watch for the child who never makes mistakes and never takes a risk. That's perfectionism, and it needs challenge that feels safe.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'You learn some things really quickly. Your teacher and I want to find you work that's just tricky enough to be fun.'

•  OLDER: 'You find a lot of school easy. That means you haven't had much practice at being stuck, and being stuck is how people get really good at things.'

•  ASK: 'What's the most interesting thing you've learned this year? What's something you'd like to learn that school doesn't teach?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — high ability masking an additional need (see 'Twice exceptional'): a child performing at age level while testing very highly may be compensating.

•  RED FLAG — anxiety, withdrawal, or self-harm in a high-achieving young person: ability does not protect. Follow the risk protocol.

•  BOUNDARY — you describe ability and needs; you do not make acceleration or placement decisions.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is he gifted?' A: 'His reasoning is well above his age, particularly i

presentation.name: Twice exceptional (high ability plus SLD, ADHD or ASD)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child who has both high ability and a learning difficulty or developmental condition — commonly dyslexia, ADHD, autism or DCD. Reis, Baum and Burke (2014) give an operational definition: high potential in one or more areas alongside one or more disabilities.

•  The core issue is MASKING in both directions: ability can compensate for the difficulty (so attainment looks age-appropriate and nothing is flagged), and the difficulty can hide the ability (so the child is seen only for what they cannot do).

•  The result is often a child whose output looks average, whose teachers see no problem, and whose parents see a child who is frustrated, exhausted or anxious — a mismatch that is itself a clue.

•  It is a descriptive term, widely used in the literature (Foley-Nicpon et al., 2011), not a diagnosis.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a way to dismiss a difficulty ('he's too bright to be dyslexic') or ability ('she has ADHD so she can't be gifted'). Both can coexist.

•  NOT identified by a single discrepancy between index scores. A large spread on the WISC-V is common and not a marker by itself; the evidence is ability, a specific difficulty, and the functional consequences together.

•  NOT necessarily a problem at school. Some twice-exceptional children do well; the concern is where compensation is costing them wellbeing or potential.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: rarely identified. Advanced language with motor or social difficulty may be early signs.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: typical profile — strong verbal reasoning and weak spelling or output, reading at age level but far below reasoning; or advanced interests with social or attentional difficulty. Exhaustion after school is common.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: compensation often breaks down as volume and independence demands increase at post-primary; referral often comes first here.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: may be first identified at third level where support services assess; retrospective history is important.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  DCD

•  Giftedness / exceptional ability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  LOOK AT BOTH SIDES: cognitive (WISC-V UK) and attainment (WIAT-III UK) together, with the specific skill assessment for the suspected difficulty (e.g. phonological processing via PhAB2, DASH for handwriting speed).

•  COMPARE AGAINST THE CHILD'S OWN ABILITY as well as age norms — and be clear in the report which comparison you are making and why.

•  HISTORY AND WELLBEING: ask about effort, fatigue, anxiety, and self-concept; a child working twice as hard to stay average is a key finding.

•  REFER for diagnostic assessment of ADHD or autism via CAMHS or CDNT where warranted; the EP describes and formulates.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: provide challenge in the area of strength and accommodation in the area of difficulty at the same time — e.g. advanced reading content with text-to-speech; complex maths with reduced copying.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: reduce the output bottleneck — typed work, oral responses, scribe for extended tasks where appropriate.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a plan that names both the strength and the need, so neither gets lost; include a wellbeing element.

•  REFER where the difficulty may meet diagnostic criteria (CAMHS, CDNT, SLT, OT) and say so in the report.

•  DO NOT recommend removing enrichment or extension to 'focus on the weaknesses'; this tends to reduce engagement and self-concept.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He is very able, and he also has a genuine difficulty with [area]. Because he's clever, he's been covering it up — that's why the school hasn't seen it, and why he's so tired at home.'

•  'He needs both things: challenge where he's strong, and support where he's not. One doesn't cancel the other.'

•  SIGNPOST: relevant support organisations for the difficulty (e.g. Dyslexia Ireland, ADHD Ireland, AsIAm); CTYI for enrichment — check current provision.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Her work looks average, but her reasoning is well above average. The gap is the difficulty — she's using her ability to hide it.'

•  'Give her harder content with easier output — let her show understanding orally or typed.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your brain is super at [strength] and finds [difficulty] harder. That's not weird — lots of clever people are like that.'

•  OLDER: 'You're very able and you have [difficulty]. Both are true. You've probably been working really hard to keep up, and that's why you're tired.'

•  ASK: 'What's the most frustrating part of school for you?' and 'When do you feel smart?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — marked anxiety, school avoidance or low mood in a child described as 'bright but underachieving': the strain of compensation can be significant. Follow the risk protocol where needed.

•  WATCH — a school reluctant to put support in place 'because she's doing fine': gather evidence of the cost to the child.

•  BOUNDARY — you do not diagnose ADHD or autism; describe and refer.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'How can he be gifted and dyslexic?' A: 'They're about different things. Dyslexia affects how words are decoded and spelled; it doesn't affect reasoning. Lots of people have both.'

•  Q: 'Why didn't the school see this?' A: 'Because she was compensating well enough to look average. That's very common for children like her.'

•  Q: 'Will she get support if she's not behind?' A: 'Support under the Continuum is based on need. Her need is real even if her attainment isn't low; I'll describe it so the school can plan.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a case where you nearly missed either the ability or the difficulty, and discuss what finally showed it.

•  Ask how to write about a child who is 'average' on attainment but well below their own reasoning level, without over-reaching.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Reis, S. M., Baum,

presentation.name: Understanding and responding to adult direction
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description, in referral-form wording, of how a child responds when an adult tells them what to do — whether they understand the direction, whether they act on it, how quickly, and what happens when they do not. It sits under general ability and comprehension in Part D because the first question is whether the child UNDERSTOOD.

•  Three quite different things produce the same observation of 'doesn't do what he's told': the child did not understand (language, general ability, hearing); the child understood but could not organise or start the action (attention, executive function); or the child understood and chose not to (motivation, relationship, anxiety, escape).

•  Children with unidentified language difficulties are over-represented among those referred for behaviour (Hollo, Wehby & Oliver, 2014). Checking comprehension first is both good practice and a matter of fairness.

•  Responding also depends on the RELATIONSHIP with the adult and the SETTING. A child who responds to one teacher and not another is telling you something about the interaction, not only about themselves.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as 'compliance' or 'defiance'. Those words describe an interpretation of intent; this presentation describes what happens. Keep reports at the level of the behaviour (PSI 1.2.8 — distinguish fact from opinion).

•  NOT explained by the child 'understanding perfectly well' because they respond to routine directions. Routine directions are supported by context; novel ones depend on language.

•  NOT a diagnosis of ODD. ODD is diagnosed by others and requires a persistent pattern lasting at least six months (DSM-5-TR; symptoms may be confined to one setting, which is then rated mild); a few weeks in one class is not that.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: responding to simple directions develops across the preschool years; watch for a child who follows gestures and routine but not words alone — a language flag.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: classroom directions increase in length and abstraction; distinguish 'did not understand' from 'did not start' from 'refused' through observation and a quick in-session check.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: autonomy and peer audience make public direction more loaded; a student may refuse to save face. Private, respectful directions work better.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: calibrate the language of staff directions to the pupil's comprehension level; many apparent refusals are misunderstandings.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Hearing impairment

•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  OBSERVE AND LOG: write down several directions verbatim, the child's response, and what the adult did next. Note whether a visual or gesture accompanied the direction.

•  CHECK COMPREHENSION DIRECTLY: in a calm one-to-one setting, give a range of directions of increasing complexity; compare with CELF-5 UK or BPVS-3 via SLT where available, and WISC-V UK Verbal Comprehension.

•  FUNCTIONAL VIEW: where refusal seems to be the issue, an ABC record (antecedent–behaviour–consequence) can show what the behaviour achieves (e.g. escape from a hard task).

•  ASK THE CHILD: 'When the teacher tells you to do something, what happens?' — the answer may reveal confusion, anxiety or a relationship issue.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: give directions in short, concrete language, one at a time, after gaining attention (name first), paired with a visual or gesture; check understanding by asking the child to say what they will do.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: use private, calm directions rather than public ones; give a brief wait time before repeating; repeat in the same words.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: if comprehension is weak, a targeted language plan with SLT input; if refusal is functional, a behaviour support plan based on the function identified, not on escalating sanctions.

•  REFER: SLT (Primary Care) for receptive language; audiology via GP if hearing is unclear; CAMHS or Primary Care Psychology where emotional or behavioural difficulty is significant and persistent across settings.

•  DO NOT recommend increasing sanctions for non-compliance before comprehension has been checked.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When a child doesn't do what they're asked, it can be because they didn't understand, couldn't get started, or didn't want to. We're working out which, because the help is different for each.'

•  'At home you probably give directions he knows well. At school they're often new and longer.'

•  SIGNPOST: GP for a hearing check; HSE Primary Care for SLT.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Before we treat this as behaviour, let's check he's understood. Say his name, one short direction, and ask him to tell you what he'll do.'

•  'Keep it private and give him a few seconds. Repeating it louder or faster usually makes it worse.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Sometimes grown-ups say things and it's hard to know what they mean. It's OK to say "I don't get it."'

•  OLDER: 'I want to understand what happens when teachers tell you to do things. Is it that it's not clear, or that it feels unfair, or something else?'

•  ASK: 'Which teachers are easiest to understand? What do they do differently?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — a child who is frightened of adult direction, freezes, or reacts with intense distress: consider trauma and ask carefully about safety. Follow child protection procedures where indicated; report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  WATCH — escalating sanctions, reduced timetables or exclusion for non-compliance in a child with a language or learning difficulty. Raise it promptly.

•  BOUNDARY — do not describe the child as 'oppositional' or 'defiant' in a report; describe what happens.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE A

presentation.name: Curriculum access at the current level
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of whether the child can meaningfully access the curriculum being taught in their class — not just attend, but understand, participate and progress. It is a question about FIT between the child and what is being offered.

•  It is often the real question behind referrals framed as 'is he in the right placement?', 'does she need a special class?', or 'why isn't he learning?'. Part D places it under general ability because it is most often raised where cognitive or adaptive functioning is well below age.

•  In Ireland the answer can involve differentiation within the mainstream class, withdrawal or in-class support from the Special Education Teacher, a special class, a special school, or at post-primary Level 1 or Level 2 Learning Programmes at Junior Cycle (NCCA) — check current guidance for which applies.

•  The EP describes the child's current level, what they can access with support, and what support would be needed; placement decisions are made by parents with the school and NCSE/SENO, not by the EP.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a judgement that the child 'belongs' elsewhere. Inclusion is the default under the EPSEN Act 2004; the question is what support makes access possible.

•  NOT the same as attainment. A child can be well below age level and still access the curriculum with good differentiation, and a child near age level may not access it because of anxiety or sensory need.

•  NOT settled by IQ alone. Adaptive functioning, language, social participation and the child's own experience matter as much.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: often framed as school readiness. The AIM programme (Access and Inclusion Model) supports preschool access — check current provision.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the gap between the child's level and the class level widens in the senior classes; differentiation that worked in 1st class may not stretch far enough by 5th.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject-based teaching and exam focus make access harder; L1LP and L2LP options at Junior Cycle, and reduced subject load, are relevant — check current NCCA guidance.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: the question may be the reverse — whether the child is sufficiently challenged, or could access more mainstream curriculum.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Intellectual Disability

•  Borderline Intellectual Functioning

•  DLD

•  Autism

•  Global Developmental Delay

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  CURRENT LEVEL: attainment (WIAT-III UK or school-based measures) and cognitive profile (WISC-V UK or WNV where language is a barrier), with adaptive functioning (ABAS-3 or Vineland-3) where intellectual disability is in question.

•  OBSERVE A LESSON: how much of what is taught does the child understand? What do they do during whole-class teaching? Is the differentiation meaningful or cosmetic?

•  WORK SAMPLES: compare the child's work with class work — is it the same task, a modified task, or unrelated?

•  CHILD AND PARENT VOICE: what does the child say school is like? What do the parents want — which may differ from the school's view.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: describe differentiation at a practical level — which lesson elements the child can join, what the modified task looks like, and which adult does what (Tomlinson, 2014).

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT / SCHOOL SUPPORT PLUS: an individual plan with specific curriculum targets at the child's level, reviewed termly, drawing on the NCCA guidelines for students with general learning disabilities where relevant.

•  IN THE REPORT: describe the child's current level and needs precisely enough that the school, parents and SENO can consider options — without recommending a specific placement unless the service's policy permits it.

•  SIGNPOST: SENO for discussion of placement options; check current NCSE processes and timelines.

•  DO NOT imply that a special class or school is the solution before the mainstream supports have been properly described and tried.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She's working at a level quite a bit below her class at the moment. The question for all of us is how to make sure she's learning, not just present.'

•  'There are different ways to do that — more support in her class, some small-group work, or other options. The SENO can talk you through them. It's your decision with the school; I'll give you the information to help.'

•  SIGNPOST: SENO; NCSE parent information.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'He can join the discussion and the practical parts of the lesson. The written task needs to be a different one, pitched at his level, on the same topic.'

•  'Let's name exactly what "access" looks like for him in maths and English, so we can see if it's working.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'I want to find out which parts of school feel OK and which parts feel too hard, so the grown-ups can help.'

•  OLDER: 'Some of the work in class might feel like it's going too fast. Let's work out which bits make sense and which bits don't.'

•  ASK: use a visual rating (smiley scale or traffic lights) for different lessons — it gives a clear picture quickly.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — a child on a reduced timetable or spending most of the day outside the classroom without a clear plan: check the school's rationale and review arrangements against current Department guidance.

•  WATCH — a child who has 'plateaued' in mainstream without any change to their programme: needs review, not more of the same.

•  BOUNDARY — the EP informs placement decisions; parents, schools and NCSE/SENO make them.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Should she be in a special class?' A: 'That's something you'd decide with the school and the SENO. What I can tell you is what she needs to learn well, and we can see where that's best provided.'

•  Q: 'Is he just going to fall further behind?' A: 'The gap may widen in some areas, and that's why the programme should be built

presentation.name: Interrupted or missed schooling
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.3 Comprehension and general ability)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose education has been disrupted — by poor attendance, prolonged illness, frequent moves, homelessness, care placements, migration or conflict, pandemic closures, or school refusal. It sits under general ability in Part D because it is the key thing to rule out before concluding a child's attainment reflects their ability.

•  Missed schooling produces gaps in taught content, not necessarily in learning capacity. Engzell, Frey and Verhagen (2021) found measurable learning loss after relatively short school closures, larger in disadvantaged groups.

•  Irish law requires the principal to inform the Educational Welfare Officer (Tusla Education Support Service, TESS) where a student has been absent for an aggregate of not less than 20 school days in a school year (Education (Welfare) Act 2000, s.21(4)) — check the current Tusla guidance on how to report.

•  Children arriving under international or temporary protection may have had interrupted schooling, schooling in another language, or schooling with a different curriculum. Their attainment in English-medium tests may reflect this rather than ability.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a learning difficulty. Low attainment after missed schooling may resolve with teaching; assess response to teaching before concluding a disorder.

•  NOT simply a parent responsibility or a 'behaviour' problem. Attendance difficulty often has causes — anxiety, illness, bullying, family stress — that need understanding.

•  NOT a reason to delay assessment indefinitely. Where difficulty persists despite good teaching after return, it may reflect a learning need alongside the gap.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: disrupted preschool attendance mainly affects language exposure and social experience; describe opportunity rather than delay where possible.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: gaps in foundational literacy and numeracy compound quickly; a child who missed early phonics teaching may appear to have a reading difficulty.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: missed schooling may reflect school avoidance, mental health, caring roles, or exclusion; transitions are high-risk points for disengagement.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: early school leaving; Youthreach and further education routes may be relevant — check current options.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Emotionally Based School Avoidance

•  Trauma

•  Anxiety

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Chronic illness

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ATTENDANCE AND HISTORY: get attendance records for each year, schools attended, and the reasons for absences or moves. Ask what was taught in each setting.

•  ATTAINMENT AND LEARNING RATE: attainment tests show the gap; dynamic assessment (teach–test–retest) or progress under targeted teaching shows learning capacity.

•  WELLBEING: ask about anxiety, peer relationships, experiences in previous schools and, where relevant, trauma — using trauma-informed questioning and within your competence.

•  LANGUAGE: where schooling was in another language, assess in a way that does not confuse language acquisition with learning difficulty (see 'Interpreter need').

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: identify the specific content gaps (e.g. phonics, place value) and teach them directly, rather than assuming the child needs a general 'catch-up'.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a targeted plan with a baseline and review; the rate of progress is the key evidence for whether there is also an underlying learning need.

•  ATTENDANCE: where attendance is the ongoing issue, a plan with the family and, where required, TESS/Educational Welfare Officer; address underlying causes such as anxiety or bullying.

•  WELLBEING: a key adult and a planned re-entry for children returning after long absence; for children with trauma histories, predictable routines and a relational approach.

•  IN THE REPORT: state clearly how the interrupted schooling limits interpretation of attainment and cognitive scores.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She's missed quite a bit of teaching, so some of what she finds hard is simply things she hasn't been taught yet. That's fixable. We'll see how she responds to teaching before we think about anything else.'

•  'Being in school regularly is the biggest thing that will help. If something is making that hard, let's talk about it.'

•  SIGNPOST: TESS/Educational Welfare Officer where relevant; school Home School Community Liaison where available.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'He isn't slow — he's missed a lot. Find out which specific skills are missing, teach those directly, and measure the progress. That tells us if there's anything else.'

•  'Coming back after a long absence is hard. A named adult and a clear plan for the first weeks matter.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'You've missed some school, so some things are new for you. That's not your fault. We'll help you learn them.'

•  OLDER: 'Some of the work feels hard because you missed when it was taught. That's a gap, not a limit. What would make coming to school easier?'

•  ASK: 'What was school like before? What's it like now?' — listen for bullying, anxiety or practical barriers.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — unexplained or escalating absence, especially with signs of neglect, caring responsibilities, or risk: follow child protection procedures and report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty; bring it to supervision after acting.

•  RED FLAG — a child out of school entirely without a plan: raise with the school and TESS.

•  BOUNDARY — do not diagnose trauma or mental health difficulties; describe, and refer to CAMHS, Primary Care Psychology or Tusla supports as appropriate.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Does she have a learning difficulty or is it just the missed school?' A: 'That's the right question. The best way to tell is to teach her what she's miss

presentation.name: Auditory processing concerns
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of concern that a child has difficulty making sense of what they hear — particularly speech in noise, rapid speech, or similar-sounding words — despite normal hearing on a standard test. It is listed in Part D as 'not a DSM diagnosis'.

•  Auditory Processing Disorder (APD) is diagnosed by audiologists, not psychologists. The British Society of Audiology describes APD as difficulty in the perception of speech and non-speech sounds, and recommends a structured audiological assessment (BSA, 2018 — check for updates).

•  The construct is contested. Dawes and Bishop (2009) reviewed APD in relation to language, attention and literacy difficulties and highlighted overlap and the risk of attributing language or attention problems to auditory processing.

•  Availability of APD assessment in the Irish public system is limited and varies — check locally before recommending it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a hearing loss. Standard hearing must be checked first; APD concern is only meaningful once peripheral hearing is known to be normal.

•  NOT a diagnosis the EP can make or confirm from cognitive testing. A low working memory or verbal score does not indicate APD.

•  NOT a reason to stop looking. Where concerns are about listening, language, attention and literacy all need exploring alongside.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: concern usually presents as speech or language delay; hearing and SLT assessment come first. APD is not usually assessed at this age.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: typical report — 'hears but doesn't understand', struggles in noisy classrooms, mishears words, difficulty with phonics. Hearing check and SLT come first.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: difficulty in large classes, practical rooms, and oral language exams; self-report becomes more useful.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: lectures, open-plan workplaces; students may seek support through third-level disability services.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  Hearing impairment

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  HEARING FIRST: confirm a recent audiology assessment. If none, REFER via GP. Ask about glue ear history.

•  LANGUAGE: SLT assessment (CELF-5 UK) to check receptive language — a very common explanation for 'listening' concerns.

•  ATTENTION AND MEMORY: WISC-V UK Working Memory, observation, and rating scales where attention is also raised.

•  CLASSROOM LISTENING ENVIRONMENT: observe noise levels, where the child sits, and whether they do better with visual support or in quiet.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: reduce background noise, seat the child near the teacher and away from noise sources, face the child when speaking, and give key information visually too.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: check understanding after instructions; pre-teach key vocabulary; provide written notes.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: if phonological or literacy difficulty is present, a targeted literacy intervention; if language difficulty is found, an SLT-informed plan.

•  REFER: audiology via GP for hearing; SLT via Primary Care for language. Where an APD assessment is requested, check local availability and explain the limits of the construct honestly.

•  DO NOT recommend commercial auditory training programmes as a solution for literacy or language difficulty without good evidence.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He can hear, but it sounds like making sense of what he hears — especially when it's noisy — is harder for him. There are a few reasons that can happen, and we want to check them all.'

•  'The first step is a full hearing test. Then language. Auditory processing assessment is done by audiologists, and it's not widely available here, so let's not wait on it for classroom changes.'

•  SIGNPOST: GP for audiology referral; HSE Primary Care SLT.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'She finds it hard to follow speech when it's noisy. Seat her near you, face her when you talk, and put key points on the board.'

•  'It's worth checking she understood. Ask her to tell you what she's going to do.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Sometimes it's hard to hear what the teacher says when the room is noisy. Let's find the best seat for you.'

•  OLDER: 'You can hear fine, but your brain has to work harder to pick out speech in noise. That's why you get tired or miss things.'

•  ASK: 'Where in school is it hardest to listen? Where is it easiest?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — a child who has never had a hearing check, or has a history of recurrent ear infections: refer to audiology before any other conclusion.

•  RED FLAG — sudden change in hearing or listening: medical, refer to GP urgently.

•  BOUNDARY — APD is diagnosed by audiologists; the EP describes and refers.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Could it be auditory processing disorder?' A: 'It's possible, and it's diagnosed by audiologists, not psychologists. It overlaps a lot with language and attention difficulties, so we check those too.'

•  Q: 'Where can we get an APD test?' A: 'Availability in Ireland is limited — ask your GP about audiology. I'd not wait for it to make classroom changes.'

•  Q: 'Will an auditory training programme help?' A: 'The evidence for those programmes improving reading or language is limited. Classroom changes and targeted teaching are more reliable.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Ask your supervisor how they respond to parents who have been told privately that their child has APD, and how that fits with the EP's assessment.

•  Discuss the local audiology route and what the service realistically offers.

13 · CITATIONS
→ British Society of Audiology. (2018). Position statement and practice guidance: Auditory processing disorder (APD). BSA. (Check for updates.)

→ Dawes, P., & Bishop, D. V. M. (2009). Auditory processing disorder in relation to developmental disorders of language, communication and attention: A review and critique. Interna

presentation.name: Literacy difficulty not meeting SLD criteria
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose reading, writing or spelling is below expected level, but whose profile does not meet criteria for Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in reading or written expression (DSM-5-TR) — because the difficulty is mild, recent, not persistent despite targeted teaching, or better explained by other factors.

•  Reading difficulty exists on a continuum; there is no natural cut-off between 'dyslexic' and 'poor reader' (Snowling & Hulme, 2012; Elliott & Grigorenko, 2014). Where the line falls depends on the definition used.

•  In Ireland, the Task Force on Dyslexia (DES, 2001) defined dyslexia broadly and emphasised a continuum of need. NEPS practice focuses on need and response to intervention rather than on labels — check the current NEPS guidance.

•  What matters for the child is the specific skill profile: decoding, fluency, comprehension, spelling and writing each need describing, because the intervention follows the profile.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT 'no problem'. A child below expected levels needs targeted teaching whether or not a diagnostic label applies.

•  NOT dyslexia 'in waiting'. Some children will go on to meet criteria; many will respond to good teaching. Use the language of current need.

•  NOT explained by 'lack of reading at home' without evidence. Ask about instruction, attendance, language and hearing before attributing cause.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: phonological awareness and letter knowledge are the foundations; describe these rather than 'literacy difficulty'.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the main identification window; standardised tests (Micra-T, Drumcondra) and teacher concern trigger referral. Response to intervention over time is key evidence.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: reading demands across subjects rise; comprehension and fluency may matter more than decoding. Access arrangements need specific evidence — check RACE criteria.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: literacy difficulty can limit further education access; supports may not require an SLD diagnosis.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  DLD

•  ADHD

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Hearing impairment

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  PROFILE THE SKILLS: WIAT-III UK (word reading, pseudoword decoding, reading comprehension, spelling, written expression), YARC or Neale for passage reading, and PhAB2 for phonological processing.

•  INSTRUCTION AND RESPONSE: what has been taught, for how long, and what progress was made? Response to well-delivered intervention is central evidence (Fletcher et al., 2019).

•  RULE OUT: hearing, vision, language (SLT), attendance, EAL.

•  CHILD'S VIEW: attitude to reading, avoidance, confidence — often more predictive of engagement than the scores.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a targeted intervention matched to the profile — systematic phonics for decoding, repeated reading for fluency, explicit comprehension strategies for comprehension — with baseline and review after a defined period (Brooks, 2016, lists evaluated schemes).

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: access to texts at an appropriate level, pre-teaching vocabulary, and alternative ways to show understanding.

•  REVIEW: if progress is limited despite well-delivered intervention, move to School Support Plus and reconsider the formulation.

•  IN THE REPORT: describe the specific literacy profile and state that SLD criteria are not currently met, with the evidence and what would change that view.

•  DO NOT recommend coloured overlays, vision therapy, or other interventions lacking robust evidence as treatments for reading difficulty.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Her reading is behind where we'd expect, and she needs extra help. It doesn't fit dyslexia at the moment, which is actually good news — it often means she'll respond well to the right teaching.'

•  'Reading difficulties are on a scale; there isn't a sharp line. What matters is what she needs now.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's support plan; Dyslexia Ireland for general information.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'His decoding is the weak point; comprehension is fine when text is read to him. Focus the intervention on decoding and fluency, and let him access content orally meanwhile.'

•  'Let's set a clear measure now and review in eight to ten weeks. If he doesn't respond, that's important information.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Reading is tricky for you right now. We're going to find the best way to help you get better at it.'

•  OLDER: 'Your reading is slower than you'd like. That's not about being clever. The right practice can make a big difference.'

•  ASK: 'What's the hardest bit about reading? What helps?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — a child whose literacy difficulty has been 'watched' for years without targeted intervention: escalate.

•  RED FLAG — reading avoidance combined with distress, school avoidance or low mood: address wellbeing alongside literacy.

•  BOUNDARY — describe the profile; avoid labelling dyslexia or 'not dyslexia' as a permanent verdict.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is she dyslexic or not?' A: 'At the moment her profile doesn't meet the criteria. She has a real reading difficulty and needs help. We'll look again if she doesn't respond to good teaching.'

•  Q: 'Will she get a reader in exams?' A: 'That depends on the State Examinations Commission's criteria, which have specific evidence requirements. We'll look at it closer to the time.'

•  Q: 'Should we try coloured glasses?' A: 'The evidence doesn't support them for reading difficulty. Structured reading teaching has much better evidence.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Discuss how your supervisor writes a literacy report where SLD criteria are not met, and the exact words used.

•  Bring a case where parents strongly wanted a dyslexia label, and how it was handled.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Department of Education and Science. (2001). Report of th

presentation.name: Reading stamina and avoidance of reading aloud
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of two related behaviours: a child who tires quickly or stops reading after short periods (stamina), and a child who avoids or becomes distressed when asked to read aloud in front of others (avoidance).

•  Low reading stamina usually reflects effortful, non-automatic reading — when decoding takes conscious effort, reading is exhausting. Fluency research (Kuhn & Stahl, 2003) links automaticity to reading endurance and comprehension.

•  Avoidance of reading aloud often reflects anxiety about public performance and fear of exposure. Stanovich (1986) described 'Matthew effects': poor readers read less, so fall further behind — avoidance feeds this cycle.

•  Both behaviours are observable and need no diagnosis to address; both can hide an underlying decoding or fluency difficulty.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT laziness or lack of interest. A child who avoids reading has usually found it effortful or humiliating.

•  NOT only a reading issue. Anxiety, stuttering, or visual difficulty can underlie avoidance of reading aloud; ask and observe.

•  NOT solved by insisting on reading aloud in class 'for practice'. Public reading under anxiety tends to reinforce avoidance.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not typically relevant; watch for avoidance of book activities combined with speech or language difficulty.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: round-robin reading in class exposes struggling readers; avoidance may show as toilet requests, behaviour or illness at reading time.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: volume of reading across subjects rises; low stamina limits homework and study. Public reading in class is more socially loaded.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: dense academic reading; text-to-speech and audio texts become important supports.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  Anxiety

•  ADHD

•  Visual impairment

•  Stuttering

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  FLUENCY: YARC or Neale for reading rate and accuracy on passages; note how performance changes across a longer passage.

•  OBSERVE: a reading lesson — what happens when reading aloud is expected? Note avoidance behaviours and their timing.

•  ASK THE CHILD: how reading makes them feel, especially aloud; use a scaling question.

•  RULE OUT VISION: ask when eyes were last checked; refer to optometry/ophthalmology if not recent or if there are signs of visual strain.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: never require unprepared reading aloud in front of the class; offer the chance to rehearse a passage in advance or read to one adult.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: break reading into shorter sections with breaks; provide audio versions or text-to-speech for long texts where content, not decoding, is the aim.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a fluency intervention — repeated reading, paired reading — with baseline and review (Rasinski, 2003).

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: address anxiety directly where present — graded exposure to reading aloud in safe settings, and teaching the child to request an alternative.

•  DO NOT recommend round-robin reading as practice for this child.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Reading takes him a lot of effort, so he tires quickly. And reading aloud in front of others is stressful for him — that's why he avoids it.'

•  'At home, short reading times, reading together, and audiobooks for enjoyment are all good. It's about keeping reading positive.'

•  SIGNPOST: local library audiobook services; the school's support plan.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Reading aloud is a big source of anxiety for her. Give her the passage in advance, or let her read to you alone.'

•  'Her reading slows down a lot after a page or two. Break the text up and give her audio support for longer pieces.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Reading can make you tired, like running a race. We'll make the race shorter and take breaks.'

•  OLDER: 'Reading takes more effort for you, so it's tiring. And reading out loud is stressful — lots of people feel that. You can ask to practise first.'

•  ASK: 'How do you feel when you're asked to read out loud? What would make it easier?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — marked distress, somatic complaints or school avoidance linked to reading: address anxiety and consider EBSA; follow risk procedures where indicated.

•  WATCH — headaches, rubbing eyes, losing place: refer for vision check.

•  BOUNDARY — describe the pattern; do not diagnose anxiety or visual problems.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Shouldn't he practise reading aloud to get better?' A: 'Yes, but in a safe setting. Reading to one adult or rehearsing first helps; reading cold in front of the class tends to make avoidance worse.'

•  Q: 'Is listening to audiobooks cheating?' A: 'No. It builds vocabulary and knowledge, and keeps him enjoying stories while his reading develops.'

•  Q: 'Why does she read well for a bit and then fall apart?' A: 'Because reading takes a lot of effort for her, and effort runs out. Shorter sections help.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Discuss how to raise the issue of round-robin reading with a teacher tactfully.

•  Bring a case where reading avoidance turned out to be mainly anxiety, and one where it was mainly skill.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading: Some consequences of individual differences in the acquisition of literacy. Reading Research Quarterly, 21(4), 360–407.

→ Kuhn, M. R., & Stahl, S. A. (2003). Fluency: A review of developmental and remedial practices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(1), 3–21.

→ Rasinski, T. V. (2003). The fluent reader: Oral reading strategies for building word recognition, fluency, and comprehension. Scholastic.

presentation.name: Handwriting speed and legibility under time pressure
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose handwriting is slow, illegible, or both — particularly when time is limited, such as in tests, dictation and copying. The difficulty may be motor, orthographic (spelling and letter formation memory), or linked to planning and language.

•  Handwriting fluency constrains composition: when transcription takes effort, less capacity is available for ideas and structure (Graham et al., 1997). A child may have good ideas but produce very little writing.

•  The DASH (Barnett et al., 2007) assesses handwriting speed for ages 9–16; the DASH-17+ extends this. Part D notes it cannot tell you legibility or the reason for slowness — that needs observation and further assessment.

•  It matters for access arrangements: State Examinations Commission RACE arrangements may consider handwriting speed evidence — check current criteria each year, as they change.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT laziness or carelessness. Slow or messy writing is often effortful writing.

•  NOT always motor. Poor spelling, weak letter-form memory, or difficulty planning sentences can all slow handwriting.

•  NOT a diagnosis of DCD or dysgraphia. The EP describes the pattern; OT assesses motor coordination.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: pencil grip, drawing and early letter formation; OT involvement if fine motor delay is marked.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: copying from the board and writing stories show the gap; legibility decreases as speed is pushed.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: note-taking, extended answers and exams make speed critical; keyboarding becomes important.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: exams at third level; typed exams and extra time may be available through disability services.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DCD

•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (dysgraphia)

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  DASH (9–16) or DASH-17+ for handwriting speed; compare copy tasks with free writing to separate motor from composition load.

•  WORK SAMPLES: compare untimed and timed writing for legibility; note letter formation, spacing and fatigue.

•  OBSERVE: grip, posture, pressure, and fatigue during a writing task.

•  REFER: OT via Primary Care or CDNT where motor coordination difficulty is suspected (Movement ABC-2 and DCD-Q are OT-led or supporting tools).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: reduce copying — provide printed notes, allow photos of the board, and mark work for content rather than neatness.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: allow extra time or reduced volume for written tasks; teach keyboarding skills and allow typed work.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a targeted handwriting programme if motor or letter-formation issues are present, planned with OT input where available; review progress (Feder & Majnemer, 2007).

•  ACCESS ARRANGEMENTS: where relevant, gather evidence for RACE according to current SEC criteria — describe the difficulty accurately; do not promise an outcome.

•  DO NOT recommend repeated copying or handwriting practice alone as a solution for slow writing if the difficulty is spelling or planning.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Writing takes her a lot of effort. When she has to write quickly, her writing gets harder to read and she runs out of time. It's not carelessness.'

•  'Typing and printed notes can help her show what she knows. An OT can look at the motor side if needed.'

•  SIGNPOST: GP or Primary Care for OT referral; school for access arrangement information.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'His handwriting slows down and becomes less legible under time pressure. Reduce copying and mark for content.'

•  'Let him type longer pieces. The quality of his ideas is much better than what he gets on paper.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Writing is hard work for your hand. We'll find ways to make it easier.'

•  OLDER: 'Your writing slows you down, especially in tests. That's not about your ideas. Typing or extra time can help you show what you know.'

•  ASK: 'Does your hand get tired when you write? When is writing easiest?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — pain, marked fatigue, or deterioration in handwriting: refer for OT or medical review.

•  WATCH — a young person avoiding written work or exams because of handwriting: address the barrier and wellbeing together.

•  BOUNDARY — do not diagnose DCD or dysgraphia; describe and refer.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Will she get extra time in the Leaving Cert?' A: 'That depends on the State Examinations Commission's criteria, which change. I can describe her handwriting speed and difficulty; the decision is theirs.'

•  Q: 'Should he just practise more?' A: 'Practice helps if the issue is motor. If it's spelling or planning, practice alone won't fix it. Let's find out which.'

•  Q: 'Can he use a laptop?' A: 'Keyboarding is a good option for many students with slow handwriting. The school can plan for it.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Ask how the service contributes to RACE evidence at post-primary — who gathers it, what the EP's role is, and what the school's own assessment covers — so you do not duplicate or overstep.

•  Ask about the local OT route (Primary Care versus CDNT) and realistic waiting times before you write 'refer to OT' in a report.

•  Bring a DASH profile where copy speed was adequate but free-writing speed was slow, and talk through whether the bottleneck is motor, spelling or composition.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Barnett, A., Henderson, S. E., Scheib, B., & Schulz, J. (2007). Detailed Assessment of Speed of Handwriting (DASH). Pearson.

→ Graham, S., Berninger, V. W., Abbott, R. D., Abbott, S. P., & Whitaker, D. (1997). Role of mechanics in composing of elementary school students: A new methodological approach. Journal of Educational Psychology, 89(1), 170–182.

→ Feder, K. P., & Majnemer, A. (2007). Handwriting development, competency, and intervention. Developmental M

presentation.name: Spelling as a barrier to written output
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose written output is limited because spelling is effortful or insecure — they avoid words they cannot spell, write short simple sentences, or spend so long on spelling that ideas are lost.

•  Spelling draws on phonological knowledge, orthographic memory (letter patterns), and morphology (word parts). A child may spell phonetically but inaccurately ('sed' for 'said'), or struggle to represent sounds at all.

•  Spelling instruction improves spelling and also supports reading and writing (Graham & Santangelo, 2014). Teaching spelling and composition together benefits written output (Berninger et al., 2002).

•  The barrier is often invisible: teachers see short, simple writing and may conclude limited ideas, when the child's oral language is much richer.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a reflection of vocabulary or ideas. Compare oral and written expression; the gap is the evidence.

•  NOT fixed by weekly spelling tests alone. Memorised lists often do not transfer to free writing.

•  NOT necessarily dyslexia. Spelling difficulty is part of dyslexia but also occurs alone or with language difficulty.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: emergent spelling; phonological awareness and letter-sound knowledge are the foundations.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: difficulty shows in free writing and dictation; the child may copy well but spell poorly independently.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject vocabulary and exam writing expose the gap; spell-checkers and assistive technology become key.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: written assignments at third level; assistive technology and proofreading supports.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  DLD

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (dysgraphia)

•  ADHD

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  WIAT-III UK Spelling and Written Expression; compare with Oral Expression to show the gap.

•  ERROR ANALYSIS: classify spelling errors — phonetic, non-phonetic, morphological, visual — to guide intervention.

•  WORK SAMPLES: compare free writing, dictation and copied work; note word choice avoidance.

•  PhAB2 for phonological processing where phonological errors dominate.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: separate composing from spelling — let the child draft freely, then edit spelling; provide word banks for topic vocabulary.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: mark for content and ideas first; correct a small number of high-frequency words rather than every error.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: structured, explicit spelling teaching based on the error analysis — phonics, morphology, common patterns — with review (Graham & Santangelo, 2014).

•  ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY: spell-checkers, word prediction or speech-to-text for longer pieces (see 'Assistive technology not yet trialled').

•  DO NOT reduce the child's writing to what they can spell; this narrows vocabulary and ideas.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'His ideas are much better than his writing shows. Spelling takes up so much effort that he keeps it short and simple.'

•  'Let him get his ideas down first, then look at spelling. Word prediction on a device can help too.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's support plan; Dyslexia Ireland for resources.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'She uses "big" instead of "enormous" because she can't spell "enormous". Give her a word bank and let her draft freely.'

•  'Look at the kind of errors she makes — that tells you what to teach. "Sed" for "said" is a memory-for-patterns issue; "sd" means she is not hearing all the sounds yet, which is a phonics issue.'

•  'Ten spellings learned for Friday rarely carry into her stories. Fewer words, chosen from her own writing, practised in sentences, transfer better.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'You have great ideas. Spelling is tricky for you, so let's get the ideas down first and fix spelling after.'

•  OLDER: 'Your ideas are good. Spelling slows you down. Tools like word prediction can help you write what you actually want to say.'

•  ASK: 'Do you ever use a different word because you can't spell the one you want?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — refusal to write or distress around writing tasks: address confidence and anxiety.

•  WATCH — spelling difficulty with reading difficulty, persisting despite teaching: consider fuller literacy assessment.

•  BOUNDARY — describe; SLD identification requires the full picture over time.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Why can he get 10/10 in the spelling test and then spell the same words wrong in his story?' A: 'Learning a list for a test is different from recalling spellings while thinking about ideas. Spelling needs to become automatic for it to hold in free writing.'

•  Q: 'Is using spellcheck cheating?' A: 'No — it helps him show what he knows, while spelling teaching continues alongside.'

•  Q: 'Is it dyslexia?' A: 'Spelling difficulty is part of dyslexia, but it also happens without it. We'll look at reading and his response to teaching too.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a spelling error analysis from a real work sample (anonymised) and check that your categories — phonological, orthographic, morphological — match your supervisor's reading.

•  Discuss how to present an oral–written gap in a report so the teacher reads it as 'ideas are there, transcription is the barrier' rather than as a comment on effort.

•  Ask what spelling programmes local schools actually use, so your recommendation fits what is available.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Graham, S., & Santangelo, T. (2014). Does spelling instruction make students better spellers, readers, and writers? A meta-analytic review. Reading and Writing, 27(9), 1703–1743.

→ Berninger, V. W., Vaughan, K., Abbott, R. D., Begay, K., Coleman, K. B., Curtin, G., Hawkins, J. M., & Graham, S. (2002). Teaching spelling and composition alone and together: Implications for the simple view of writing. Journal of Educational Psycho

presentation.name: Assistive technology not yet trialled
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a gap in support: a child with a literacy or output difficulty for whom assistive technology (AT) — text-to-speech, speech-to-text, word prediction, spell-checkers, keyboarding, audio books, digital note-taking — has not yet been tried. Part D lists it because it is a common omission and a practical recommendation.

•  AT can compensate for a barrier while skills continue to be taught. Text-to-speech has shown a small-to-moderate benefit for reading comprehension in students with reading disabilities (Wood et al., 2018); word processing and related tools can support writing (MacArthur, 2009).

•  In Ireland, the Department of Education scheme for assistive technology is for pupils with physical or communicative disabilities, applied for through the SENO — check the current circular and criteria. Many free or built-in tools (operating system dictation and read-aloud) need no funding.

•  The key word is TRIALLED: the recommendation is a structured trial with a measure, not simply 'give her a laptop'.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a replacement for teaching reading and writing skills. AT is used alongside intervention, not instead of it.

•  NOT a 'cheat'. It provides access to the content; the learning is the thinking.

•  NOT automatically effective. Without training, set-up and practice, AT is often abandoned.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: rarely relevant for literacy; AAC is a separate question (see 'AAC and communication access').

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: keyboarding skills and audio books can start; text-to-speech for reading content beyond decoding level.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: AT becomes central for volume of reading and writing; exam use must follow SEC RACE rules — check current guidance.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: third-level disability services often provide AT training; the habit should already be established.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (dysgraphia)

•  DCD

•  Visual impairment

•  Physical disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ASK what has been tried, for how long, and with what training. Often a device was provided but never set up or taught.

•  PROFILE THE BARRIER: decoding (text-to-speech), spelling (word prediction, spell-check), handwriting (keyboarding, speech-to-text), organisation (digital planners).

•  TRIAL IN SESSION: compare the child's output with and without a tool on a short task; note the difference and the child's reaction.

•  CHILD'S VIEW: some young people resist AT because it marks them out; ask directly.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a structured AT trial — name the tool, the task it supports, who will train the pupil, how long the trial lasts, and how success will be measured (e.g. words written in 10 minutes; comprehension scores with and without text-to-speech).

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: allow AT use in class routinely, not only in support sessions, so the child builds fluency with the tools.

•  TRAINING: include teacher and parent in the set-up; teach keyboarding explicitly where needed.

•  FUNDING: where specialist equipment is needed, the school can apply via the SENO under the current Department scheme — check eligibility. Consider free, built-in tools first.

•  DO NOT recommend a device without a plan for training and review.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'There are tools that read text aloud or type what she says. They don't replace learning to read and spell, but they let her get at the same content as her classmates now.'

•  'Many are free and already on phones and laptops. The school can help set them up and teach her to use them.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's SET; SENO for specialist equipment; Dyslexia Ireland for AT information.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Let's trial text-to-speech for his history reading for six weeks. Before we start, give him two short passages with questions — one read by him, one read by the tool — and repeat that at the end. That's our measure.'

•  'AT works best if it's used in class every day, not only in support sessions. If he only uses it in the SET room, he won't be fluent with it when it matters.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'This app can read the words to you so you can enjoy the story. You'll keep learning to read too.'

•  OLDER: 'Text-to-speech or dictation can help you work faster and show what you know. Want to try it and see if it helps?'

•  ASK: 'Would you feel OK using this in class? What would make it easier?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — AT provided but unused: check training, set-up and the young person's feelings about it.

•  WATCH — AT used instead of any literacy teaching: skills teaching should continue.

•  BOUNDARY — EP recommends AT trials; funding decisions sit with the Department/SENO.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Won't this stop her learning to read?' A: 'No. She'll keep being taught to read. The technology lets her access her textbooks at her thinking level while that happens.'

•  Q: 'Can he use it in exams?' A: 'The State Examinations Commission has specific rules about assistive technology. Check the current year's guidance with the school.'

•  Q: 'Who pays for it?' A: 'Many tools are free. For specialist equipment, the school can apply to the SENO under a Department scheme; eligibility criteria apply.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring a draft AT recommendation and ask your supervisor to test it: does it name the tool, the task, the trainer, the trial length and the measure?

•  Ask about the current Department AT scheme criteria, which pupils it does and does not cover, and how the service links with SENOs on applications.

•  Discuss how to respond when a young person refuses AT because it marks them out — and whether the recommendation should change.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Wood, S. G., Moxley, J. H., Tighe, E. L., & Wagner, R. K. (2018). Does use of text-to-speech

presentation.name: Instruction history
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.4 Literacy — reading (fluency / comprehension), writing and spelling)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D wording: 'Instruction history — what has actually been taught — rule out before concluding disorder'. A description of what literacy (and numeracy) teaching the child has actually received: content, method, intensity, duration and consistency.

•  DSM-5-TR requires that learning difficulties persist despite targeted intervention, and that they are not better explained by inadequate instruction. Instruction history is therefore not optional context — it is part of the criteria.

•  Vellutino et al. (1996) found that many poor readers made good progress with daily one-to-one tutoring, suggesting that instructional experience accounts for much early reading difficulty.

•  Response to intervention models (Fuchs & Fuchs, 2006) and the NEPS Continuum of Support both rely on documented instruction and response to it as core assessment evidence.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a judgement on the teacher or school. It is a factual account of what has been taught, which is essential for interpreting attainment.

•  NOT answered by 'he's had learning support'. The detail matters — what programme, how often, for how long, with what progress.

•  NOT only about literacy. The same logic applies to numeracy and to any skill that depends on teaching.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: early language and literacy experiences; preschool attendance.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: phonics programmes, intervention records, class size and staffing changes, time in support.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: primary school history matters as much as current teaching; records may need to be sought.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: retrospective; ask about schooling and any support received.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in written expression (dysgraphia)

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Interrupted or missed schooling

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ASK SPECIFIC QUESTIONS: which phonics programme; how many sessions a week, for how long; group size; who delivered it; what measures were taken before and after.

•  LOOK AT RECORDS: Student Support File, support plans, progress data, standardised scores across years.

•  CONSIDER CONTINUITY: changes of school, teacher absence, missed schooling (see 'Interrupted or missed schooling').

•  LINK TO RESPONSE: interpret current attainment against the instruction received — poor progress despite good instruction is more significant than low attainment without it.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  IN THE REPORT: include a concise instruction history, and state how it affects interpretation of attainment scores and any conclusions about SLD.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: where instruction has been limited or inconsistent, recommend a well-specified, evidence-based intervention with clear dosage, delivery and progress measures before drawing conclusions (Castles, Rastle & Nation, 2018).

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT PLUS: where good instruction has been delivered with limited response, this strengthens the case for further assessment and more intensive support.

•  RECORD-KEEPING: recommend that intervention records include programme, frequency, duration and progress data, so future assessment can use them.

•  DO NOT conclude SLD where instruction history is unknown or clearly inadequate.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Before we decide whether there's a learning difficulty, we need to know what she's been taught and how she responded. That's standard practice.'

•  'If she hasn't had the right teaching yet, the best test is to give it to her and see what happens.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Can you tell me exactly what reading intervention he's had — which programme, how often, and what progress was measured? It makes a big difference to how I interpret the scores.'

•  'This isn't about blame. It's about knowing whether the difficulty is instructional or something more.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Can you tell me about how you learn to read in school? Who helps you?'

•  OLDER: 'What help have you had with reading or maths over the years? What worked and what didn't?'

•  ASK: the child is often the best source on what actually happened in support sessions.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — no records of intervention despite long-standing concern: raise as a gap and recommend clear planning.

•  WATCH — a label of SLD in a previous report with no documented instruction history: interpret with caution.

•  BOUNDARY — describe instruction history factually; avoid evaluative comments about individual teachers.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Why does it matter what she was taught?' A: 'Because a child can't read words she hasn't been taught to decode. We need to know whether the difficulty remains after good teaching.'

•  Q: 'He's had learning support for years — isn't that enough?' A: 'It helps to know what that support involved and how he responded. That tells us what to try next.'
