•  Q: 'Are you saying the school didn't teach him?' A: 'No. I'm gathering the facts so the conclusions are fair to him.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Ask your supervisor for the exact questions they use to get instruction history from a SET, and how they phrase them so the school does not feel judged.

•  Bring a case where instruction history changed your conclusion — e.g. a 'dyslexia' referral where systematic phonics had never been delivered.

•  Discuss how to handle a previous private report that concluded SLD without any account of instruction received.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Vellutino, F. R., Scanlon, D. M., Sipay, E. R., Small, S. G., Pratt, A., Chen, R., & Denckla, M. B. (1996). Cognitive profiles of difficult-to-remediate and readily remediated poor readers: Early intervention as a vehicle for distinguishing between cognitive and experiential deficits as basic causes of specific reading disability. Journal of Educational Psychology, 88(4), 601

presentation.name: Numeracy difficulty not meeting SLD criteria
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.5 Maths skills — concepts and computation)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a child whose maths attainment is below expected level but who does not meet criteria for Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (DSM-5-TR) — because the difficulty is mild, recent, not persistent despite targeted teaching, or better explained by other factors.

•  Maths difficulty is heterogeneous: number sense, fact retrieval, procedural knowledge, word problems, working memory and anxiety each contribute differently (Dowker, 2009). Two children with the same low score may need very different teaching.

•  Geary (2004) described different subtypes — procedural, semantic memory (fact retrieval), and visuospatial — useful for describing profiles without diagnosis.

•  Part D lists related presentations: number sense, fact recall versus procedure, word problems as a reading barrier, and working memory load in multi-step calculation. Describe which apply.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT dyscalculia 'lite'. Many children with maths difficulties have no core number sense deficit; the difficulty may be instructional, anxiety-related, or language-related.

•  NOT 'just not a maths person'. This belief is common and can become self-fulfilling; maths skills respond to teaching.

•  NOT settled by a single test score. Error analysis and response to teaching matter more.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: counting, subitising, comparing quantities; the Sandwell Early Numeracy Test covers early number concepts.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: difficulty with number facts, place value, and word problems; Sigma-T and school tests often trigger referral.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: algebra and multi-step problems add load; anxiety often increases. Junior Cycle maths level choices matter.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: everyday numeracy (money, time) may be the functional focus.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Maths anxiety

•  ADHD

•  DLD

•  Intellectual Disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  WIAT-III UK Numerical Operations and Maths Problem Solving; Sandwell Early Numeracy Test for younger or lower-attaining pupils.

•  ERROR ANALYSIS on actual classwork: procedural errors, fact errors, place value errors, reading errors in word problems.

•  SEPARATE THE LOADS: read the problem aloud to test whether reading is the barrier; reduce working memory demands to see if performance improves.

•  ANXIETY: ask about feelings about maths; consider a maths anxiety measure (see 'Maths anxiety').

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: a targeted maths intervention matched to the error profile, with baseline and review (Dowker, 2009, reviews evaluated interventions).

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: concrete–pictorial–abstract progression; visual aids (number lines, hundred squares); reduce working memory load with written steps.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: read word problems aloud or provide them at the child's reading level so maths is being assessed.

•  ADDRESS ANXIETY where present — see 'Maths anxiety'.

•  IN THE REPORT: describe the maths profile and state that SLD criteria are not currently met, with the evidence and what would change that view.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He finds maths hard, particularly [specific area]. It doesn't fit dyscalculia at the moment — it looks more like [specific gaps / anxiety / language in word problems].'

•  'Maths builds on itself, so filling the specific gaps makes a big difference.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's support plan.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Her errors are mostly place value. Targeted work on that will help more than general practice.'

•  'Try reading the word problems to him — if he can do them then, reading is the barrier, not maths.'

•  'He counts on his fingers for 7 + 8 because the fact isn't stored yet. Let him use a number line for now so the new work isn't blocked by the old gap, and practise the facts separately.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Some parts of maths are tricky for you. We'll use blocks and pictures to make them easier.'

•  OLDER: 'Maths is harder for you in some areas. That's not because you can't do maths — it's specific bits we can work on.'

•  ASK: 'What bit of maths do you find hardest? What bit is OK?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — persistent difficulty with basic number sense despite good teaching: consider further assessment for dyscalculia.

•  WATCH — strong avoidance or distress around maths: address anxiety.

•  BOUNDARY — describe the profile; avoid permanent labels.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is it dyscalculia?' A: 'Her profile doesn't meet the criteria at the moment. She does have real difficulties in [area], and they can be taught.'

•  Q: 'I was bad at maths too — is it genetic?' A: 'Some aspects of maths ability are heritable, but teaching and confidence make a big difference. Let's focus on what helps.'

•  Q: 'Should he drop to Foundation Level?' A: 'That's a decision for later, with the school. For now, let's target the gaps and see how he responds.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Bring an error analysis from a real (anonymised) maths copy and check your reading of it — which errors are procedural, which are fact retrieval, which are place value.

•  Discuss how to describe a maths difficulty in a report without over-reaching to dyscalculia, and what evidence would change your view.

•  Ask which maths interventions local schools actually run, so recommendations are realistic.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Dowker, A. (2009). What works for children with mathematical difficulties? The effectiveness of intervention schemes. Department for Children, Schools and Families.

→ Geary, D. C. (2004). Mathematics and learning disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 37(1), 4–15.

→ Gersten, R., Chard, D. J., Jayanthi, M., Baker, S. K., Morphy, P., & Flojo, J. (2009). Mathematics instruction for students with learning disabilities: A meta-analysis

presentation.name: Maths anxiety
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.5 Maths skills — concepts and computation)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of feelings of tension, fear or dread that interfere with doing maths — in class, in tests, or in everyday situations involving numbers. It is not a DSM diagnosis.

•  Ashcraft (2002) describes maths anxiety as disrupting working memory: worry uses up capacity needed for calculation, so anxious children perform below their actual skill level (Ashcraft & Kirk, 2001).

•  The relationship with performance is bidirectional: poor performance can cause anxiety, and anxiety can cause poor performance (Carey et al., 2016). Both need addressing.

•  Adult anxiety about maths can transmit to children — Beilock et al. (2010) found that female teachers' maths anxiety was associated with girls' maths achievement in early primary. Parents' and teachers' attitudes matter.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as a maths learning difficulty. Children with good maths skills can be very anxious; children with difficulties may not be.

•  NOT general anxiety. Maths anxiety can be specific; but check for broader anxiety too.

•  NOT fixed by more timed tests or 'toughening up'. Timed pressure often increases anxiety.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: rarely apparent as anxiety; early number play and adult attitudes ('I was never good at maths') lay the foundations.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: can appear early in primary; timed tables tests, 'around the world' games and public answering at the board are common triggers. Look for stomach aches on maths days.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: often increases; affects subject level choices and exam performance.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: may limit course choice and career options.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Anxiety

•  ADHD

•  Numeracy difficulty not meeting SLD criteria

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ASK DIRECTLY: 'How do you feel when you're doing maths?' Use a scaling question; ask about specific situations (tests, answering in class, homework).

•  MEASURE: the modified Abbreviated Math Anxiety Scale (mAMAS; Carey et al., 2017) is designed for children — check norms and availability before use.

•  COMPARE PERFORMANCE: timed versus untimed tasks; public versus private answering. A large gap suggests anxiety is affecting performance.

•  CHECK SKILLS: WIAT-III UK maths subtests and error analysis, so you know whether a skills gap sits alongside the anxiety.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: reduce timed pressure and public answering; allow private or written responses.

•  CLASSROOM SUPPORT: normalise mistakes as part of learning; praise strategy and effort rather than speed.

•  SCHOOL SUPPORT: targeted maths teaching for any skills gaps alongside anxiety support — e.g. teaching a simple worry-writing or calming routine before tests (Ramirez & Beilock, 2011).

•  INVOLVE ADULTS: share information with parents and teachers about how their attitudes to maths can influence children; encourage positive language about maths.

•  REFER: where anxiety is broader or severe, consider Primary Care Psychology or CAMHS.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'She gets very anxious about maths, and when she's anxious, her brain has less room to do the maths. So she does worse than she actually can.'

•  'Try to avoid saying things like "I was never good at maths" in front of her. It can make her feel it's inevitable.'

•  SIGNPOST: the school's support plan; Primary Care Psychology if anxiety is broader.

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'His anxiety is reducing his performance. He does much better untimed and in private. Can we reduce the timed and public elements?'

•  'Praise his strategies rather than his speed — "you checked it with a number line, that was smart" rather than "well done, quick".'

•  'A two-minute worry-writing slot before a test has some evidence behind it (Ramirez & Beilock, 2011) and costs nothing to try.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Sometimes maths makes you feel worried. When we're worried, our brain gets busy with the worry. We can learn ways to calm it down.'

•  OLDER: 'Anxiety about maths takes up space in your head that you need for the sums. That's why you go blank in tests. There are things that can help.'

•  ASK: 'When is maths OK? When is it scary?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — severe anxiety, panic, or school avoidance linked to maths: address wellbeing; follow risk procedures where needed.

•  WATCH — anxiety spreading beyond maths to general school or social anxiety: consider referral.

•  BOUNDARY — do not diagnose anxiety disorder; describe and refer.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is she bad at maths or just anxious?' A: 'Often both, and each makes the other worse. She did better when the pressure was off, so anxiety is a big part of it.'

•  Q: 'Should we do more timed practice so she gets used to it?' A: 'Timed practice usually increases anxiety for children like her. Build confidence first, then gradually increase challenge.'

•  Q: 'I'm terrible at maths myself — what can I do?' A: 'Try to keep your language positive about maths. Show her that making mistakes is normal and how you work things out.'

12 · BRING TO SUPERVISION
•  Discuss how to assess maths anxiety alongside maths skills in one session without the assessment itself becoming the anxious event — e.g. untimed tasks first, then timed.

•  Ask about local routes for anxiety support where it is broader than maths (Primary Care Psychology, CAMHS thresholds).

•  Reflect with your supervisor on your own relationship with maths, and whether it shows in how you talk about it with children.

13 · CITATIONS
→ Ashcraft, M. H. (2002). Math anxiety: Personal, educational, and cognitive consequences. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 11(5), 181–185.

→ Ashcraft, M. H., & Kirk, E. P. (2001). The relationships among working memory, math anxiety, and performance. Journal of Experimental Psychol

presentation.name: Number sense and estimation
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.5 Maths skills — concepts and computation)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  An intuitive feel for QUANTITY — knowing without counting that 7 is more than 4, that 48 is close to 50, that 3 × 19 cannot be 570. Dehaene (2011) describes an 'approximate number system' that we share with infants and other species, on which exact symbolic number is later built.

•  The classroom signs: counting all objects one by one where peers subitise (see 'three' at a glance); no sense of whether an answer is reasonable; cannot place 50 on a 0–100 line; treats digits as labels with no size attached.

•  Jordan et al. (2009) found kindergarten number competence (counting, number comparison, simple number combinations) predicted mathematics achievement years later — early number sense is a foundation, not an optional extra.

•  Estimation is a separate, teachable skill that develops with experience: Siegler and Booth (2004) showed young children's number-line estimates move from a compressed (logarithmic-like) to a linear pattern with age, and linearity relates to maths achievement.

•  A descriptive learning profile, not a diagnosis (Part D, 1.5 Maths skills). It is the core weakness in many accounts of dyscalculia (Butterworth, 2005), but the presentation also occurs with low instruction, language difficulty or general learning difficulty.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same as weak arithmetic. A child may compute accurately by laborious counting and still have poor number sense — the giveaway is slowness and an inability to say whether an answer is roughly right.

•  NOT proof of dyscalculia. Halberda et al. (2008) found approximate-number acuity correlates with maths achievement, but the link is modest and contested; a weak dot-comparison score on its own does not establish a Specific Learning Disorder.

•  NOT fixed. Ramani and Siegler (2008) showed that playing a linear number board game for a handful of short sessions improved preschool children's number-line estimation and magnitude comparison — number sense responds to the right experience.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: subitising small sets, one-to-one correspondence, 'which has more?', rote counting that is not yet tied to quantity. Part D: observe during play — no standardised maths measure at this age.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: finger counting persisting beyond peers, counting on from 1 rather than from the larger number, no sense of place value (writes 'one hundred and six' as 1006), wildly unreasonable answers accepted without comment.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: fractions, decimals, percentages and negative numbers are the stress points — a pupil who thinks 0.25 is bigger than 0.5 'because 25 is bigger'. Estimation in science and money is weak; calculator answers are not sense-checked.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: budgeting, timekeeping, measurement in trades and apprenticeships, reading data in course work. Self-report of 'I have no feel for numbers' is common and worth taking seriously.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: work from the functional level — does the young person know 'more/less', 'enough', 'too much' in real contexts (money, time, cooking)? Number sense taught through daily routines transfers better than worksheets.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Intellectual Disability

•  ADHD

•  DLD

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Informal probes you can run in ten minutes: dot subitising (flash 1–5 dots), 'which is bigger?' with digits, a 0–100 (or 0–1000) number-line estimation task (after Siegler & Booth, 2004), counting on from a given number, and 'is this answer about right?' items.

•  Sandwell Early Numeracy Test (early and primary) or the Dyscalculia Screener / DysCalculiUM (Part D tools) — screens of number sense; they cannot give you a diagnosis and do not separate anxiety from difficulty.

•  WIAT-III UK maths subtests for attainment in context; then error-analyse the actual items — which errors are number-sense errors (unreasonable magnitude) and which are procedural slips?

•  Ask the class teacher what number sense teaching the child has had, and look at the Continuum of Support record — a gap that closes quickly with targeted teaching is a different finding from one that persists.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  TEACH QUANTITY WITH CONCRETE AND VISUAL MODELS before symbols: tens frames, bead strings, Numicon-type shapes, place-value counters — moving to pictures and then digits (concrete–pictorial–abstract). Name the materials in the plan so staff use them consistently.

•  LINEAR NUMBER GAMES: short, frequent sessions with a linear board game or number-line activities; Ramani and Siegler (2008) is the evidence to cite. Parents can do this at home with a board game and no worksheets.

•  ESTIMATE FIRST, CALCULATE SECOND: build 'about how much?' into every calculation task and ask the pupil to compare the answer with the estimate. Praise good estimates, not only exact answers.

•  TARGETED SMALL-GROUP INTERVENTION at School Support: a structured numeracy programme delivered by a trained teacher (e.g., Maths Recovery-based approaches, Wright et al., 2006; Catch Up Numeracy, Holmes & Dowker, 2013) — check what the school is trained in and what the local evidence is.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for most; School Support where a Student Support Plan with a named programme is needed; School Support Plus where progress is minimal after a well-delivered intervention and a question of dyscalculia or general learning difficulty is being considered.

•  REVIEW with a named measure after 6–10 weeks (e.g., number-line estimation accuracy, counting-on from a given number). DO NOT set timed tables tests as the main response — they test retrieval, not number sense.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Number sense is the feel for how big numbers are — knowing 48 is nearly 50 without working it out. At the moment he counts everything one by one, which is slow and tiring, and he doesn't notice when an answer is way o

presentation.name: Recall of number facts vs procedural method
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.5 Maths skills — concepts and computation)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of WHERE in calculation the pupil breaks down: (a) RETRIEVING basic facts (6 + 7, 8 × 4) quickly from memory, (b) carrying out a PROCEDURE (column subtraction, long division), or (c) UNDERSTANDING why the procedure works. These separate, and the recommendation depends on which one fails.

•  Geary (1993) distinguished a semantic-memory pattern (persistent difficulty retrieving facts, with frequent retrieval errors) from a procedural pattern (immature procedures, frequent procedural errors) in children with mathematical difficulties — a useful framework for error analysis.

•  Fact retrieval normally develops from counting strategies, through derived-fact strategies ('6 + 7 is double 6 plus 1'), to direct retrieval (Baroody, 2006). A pupil who still counts on fingers for single-digit facts in senior primary has not made that shift.

•  Poor fact recall is reported as common in dyslexia as well as dyscalculia — verbal-code retrieval is involved — so a literacy-affected pupil may present here without any number-sense weakness. Rate not stated here — check before quoting.

•  A descriptive learning profile, not a diagnosis (Part D, 1.5 Maths skills).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT 'not trying to learn tables'. Some pupils rehearse repeatedly and still cannot retrieve reliably; more rote drill without a strategy rarely closes that gap (Baroody, 2006).

•  NOT a reason to hold a pupil back from higher-level maths. A pupil with weak fact recall can reason well about fractions or algebra if given a facts reference — conceptual work should not wait for fact fluency.

•  NOT the same pattern in every pupil. Accurate but slow (counting strategies) and fast but wrong (guessing, confused retrieval) need different responses — record speed AND accuracy.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not yet applicable as fact recall; counting-all and counting-on strategies are the typical and expected ones.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: persistent finger-counting for addition facts; tables recited from the start ('7, 14, 21...') to find 7 × 6; column methods followed but with regrouping errors, or facts correct but procedure muddled.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: fact-recall gaps slow every multi-step problem in algebra and science; pupils may hide finger counting under the desk. Procedural errors in fractions and equations show whether understanding or recall is the barrier.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: reliance on the calculator for simple facts; mental arithmetic under time pressure (shop work, trades) is the functional issue. Calculator use is usually the right accommodation, not remediation of facts.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: functional facts (money totals, time) matter more than full tables; calculators and number lines are appropriate life tools.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Dyslexia

•  ADHD

•  DLD

•  Intellectual Disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  WIAT-III UK maths subtests: compare Math Fluency (speeded facts) with Numerical Operations (untimed written calculation) — check the manual for which fluency subtests apply at each age. A split between them is the key finding.

•  Strategy interview: give ten facts and ask 'how did you work that out?' after each. Record whether the answer was retrieved, derived or counted — this is more informative than the score.

•  Error analysis on classroom work: classify every error as fact error, procedural error (wrong step, wrong order, regrouping) or conceptual error (e.g., subtracting smaller from larger in each column regardless of position).

•  Check literacy and phonological memory if fact recall is the only weakness — a verbal retrieval difficulty may be shared with reading.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  IF RECALL IS THE BARRIER: teach derived-fact strategies explicitly (doubles, near doubles, bridging through 10, commutativity) rather than more rote drill (Baroody, 2006); provide a tables square or number facts sheet during work where the target is the procedure or the reasoning.

•  IF PROCEDURE IS THE BARRIER: a written step-by-step model card for each method, worked examples alongside practice (Sweller & Cooper, 1985), and one method taught consistently across classes — agree it at school level.

•  IF UNDERSTANDING IS THE BARRIER: return to concrete and pictorial models of the procedure (place-value counters for regrouping) before the written algorithm.

•  SHORT, LOW-STAKES FACT PRACTICE: a few minutes daily on a small set of target facts, tracked on the pupil's own chart. Avoid public timed tests for pupils who find them distressing.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (reference aids, method cards); School Support where a targeted fact-strategy programme is timetabled. At post-primary, note calculator access and check the current State Examinations Commission rules before promising any exam arrangement.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He understands how to do the sums — the method is fine. What's slow is pulling out the basic facts like 7 times 8. Every time he has to work one out, he loses his place in the bigger problem.'

•  'Drilling tables over and over hasn't worked, and that's common. We're going to teach him shortcuts — like 7 × 8 is double 7 × 4 — and let him use a tables square when the real task is something else.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'If you look at her errors, most are in the facts, not the method. Give her a tables square during problem-solving — you'll see what she can actually reason out.'

•  'For him it's the other way round: he knows his facts but the steps in long division get shuffled. A method card on the desk with the steps numbered is the quickest fix.'

•  'When you're checking progress, time the facts separately from the procedure — otherwise you won't know which one is improving.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Some sums your brain just knows, and some it has to work out. We're

presentation.name: Word problems
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.5 Maths skills — concepts and computation)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D's fuller wording is the point: 'Word problems — reading as the barrier, not the maths'. A pupil who can calculate 23 − 8 but cannot solve 'Sam had 23 stickers and gave 8 away...' may be failing at READING (decoding), LANGUAGE (vocabulary and sentence structure), BUILDING A MENTAL MODEL of the situation, or at the MATHS itself.

•  Riley, Greeno and Heller (1983) classified simple word problems into change, combine and compare types; compare problems ('Anna has 5 more than Ben...') are consistently harder, largely because of the language of comparison.

•  Fuchs et al. (2006) found that word-problem skill draws on language and reasoning abilities partly distinct from those predicting computation — so word problems are a separate skill to assess, not a harder version of arithmetic.

•  Maths vocabulary carries meanings that differ from everyday use ('difference', 'product', 'left', 'fewer', 'altogether'), and EAL learners and pupils with DLD are especially exposed to this.

•  A descriptive learning profile, not a diagnosis (Part D, 1.5 Maths skills).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT solved by key-word strategies ('altogether means add'). Verschaffel, Greer and De Corte (2000) document how key-word and surface strategies lead pupils to compute without understanding; 'left' can mean subtract, or not.

•  NOT evidence of weak maths ability if the pupil succeeds when the problem is read aloud. That result tells you the barrier is reading, and the recommendation is about access, not maths teaching.

•  NOT always reading. Some pupils decode fluently and still cannot build the situation model — the difficulty is language comprehension or reasoning, and read-aloud will not help.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: oral story problems in play ('three teddies, one more comes') — comprehension of the situation is the task; not a presenting concern at this age.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the typical referral — 'good at sums, can't do problems'. Compare problems, two-step problems and problems with irrelevant information are where errors cluster.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: long-context questions across maths, science and business; state-exam style questions with heavy text. Reading load in maths papers becomes an exam-access question.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: workplace and course problems embedded in documents (quotes, invoices, dosage). Self-report of 'I freeze when it's written out' is common.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: problems presented through real objects and real situations (shop, cooking) remove most of the reading barrier; check comprehension of question words ('how many', 'how much more').

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Dyslexia

•  DLD

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  ADHD

•  Autism

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  THE KEY COMPARISON: give matched problems in three conditions — pupil reads independently; adult reads aloud; same maths as a bare calculation. The pattern across conditions is the finding (reading barrier vs language/reasoning barrier vs maths barrier).

•  WIAT-III UK Math Problem Solving alongside Numerical Operations and the reading subtests — check the administration manual for how items are presented, so you know how much reading the subtest actually demands.

•  Ask the pupil to retell the problem in their own words or draw it before solving — failure to retell indicates comprehension; correct retell with wrong operation indicates the mathematical model.

•  Check decoding (e.g., WIAT-III reading subtests or YARC) and receptive vocabulary/grammar (e.g., CELF-5 UK subtests if language is in question, or refer to SLT).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  IF READING IS THE BARRIER: problems read aloud (adult, peer or text-to-speech) in class and in class tests; reduced text; key maths vocabulary pre-taught. At post-primary, gather evidence early for Reasonable Accommodations in State Examinations (RACE) — check current SEC criteria before advising.

•  IF LANGUAGE/SITUATION MODEL IS THE BARRIER: teach pupils to represent the problem — draw it, act it out, use a bar model — before choosing an operation. Schema-based instruction, which teaches problem types explicitly, has supporting evidence for pupils with learning difficulties (Jitendra & Star, 2011).

•  RETIRE KEY-WORD LISTS: replace them with 'What is happening in this story? What do we know? What are we finding?'

•  TEACH MATHS VOCABULARY explicitly as subject vocabulary, with everyday-versus-maths meanings contrasted ('difference', 'volume', 'table').

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support in most cases; School Support where a targeted problem-solving programme or reading intervention is timetabled. REFER to SLT where language comprehension is in question.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Her maths is fine — when I read the problems to her she got most of them. It's the reading that's getting in the way, so we're going to make sure she has the problems read to her in maths, and keep working on reading separately.'

•  'At home, try telling him a maths story out loud and asking him to draw it. Drawing the story before doing the sum is the skill he needs.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Can you try reading the next few problems aloud to him? If he gets them, we know the barrier is reading, not maths — and that changes where your effort goes.'

•  'The key-word lists on the wall are sending her wrong. "Left" doesn't always mean take away. Ask her to draw what's happening first.'

•  'Compare problems are the hardest type for nearly everyone — expect errors there and teach them directly.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'The sums aren't the tricky part for you — it's the words. We're going to read them together and draw a picture of the story.'

•  OLDER: 'You're good at maths. When the question is a paragraph long, the reading uses up your energy before you get to the maths. There are ways round that.'

•  ASK: 'Tell me what's happen

presentation.name: Working memory load in multi-step calculation
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.5 Maths skills — concepts and computation)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A pupil who can do each step of a calculation but loses track when the steps have to be HELD and COMBINED — forgetting the carried digit, losing the partial answer in long multiplication, dropping a step in a two-step problem, or doing mental arithmetic that collapses beyond one operation.

•  Raghubar, Barnes and Hecht (2010) review evidence that working memory contributes to mathematics performance across ages, with the specific components involved varying by age and task.

•  Sweller's (1988) cognitive load theory explains the mechanism: when a task imposes more elements to hold than working memory allows, performance and learning both drop. Multi-step calculation is a high-load task by design.

•  Ashcraft and Kirk (2001) showed that maths anxiety consumes working memory and disrupts performance most on high-load calculations (e.g., carrying) — anxiety and load interact.

•  A descriptive learning profile, not a diagnosis (Part D, 1.5 Maths skills). The maths-specific version of the working memory difficulty described under 1.1.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT carelessness. Errors that cluster at the point of carrying, borrowing or holding a partial result are load errors; carelessness is scattered.

•  NOT a gap in the method. If the pupil completes the same calculation correctly with jottings or a place-value grid, the method is known — the barrier is holding it in mind.

•  NOT fixed by working memory training. Melby-Lervåg and Hulme (2013) found no convincing transfer from working memory training to arithmetic; reduce the load instead.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not a presenting concern; small-number reasoning in play with objects present (no load to hold).

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: mental maths beyond one step; column addition and subtraction with regrouping; long multiplication; two-step word problems. Copying a sum from the board adds a transcription load before the maths starts.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: multi-step algebra, rearranging formulae, long calculations in science and accounting. Teachers who model on the board while talking add simultaneous load.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: practical calculation in work or course contexts (quotes, measurements, dosages) where written working is not usual — the pupil should be taught to write it anyway.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: keep calculations to one step with visible materials; use calculators and structured recording sheets as routine rather than as an exception.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  DLD

•  Dyslexia

•  Acquired brain injury

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Error analysis on 10–20 multi-step items: mark where each error occurs. Load errors cluster at carries, borrows and intermediate results.

•  Load contrast: give the same calculation (a) mentally, (b) with free jottings, (c) with a structured place-value grid. Improvement from (a) to (c) is the evidence of a load barrier.

•  WISC-V UK Working Memory Index and Arithmetic subtest (where administered) alongside WIAT-III UK Numerical Operations — interpret together, not in isolation; check the manual for what Arithmetic draws on.

•  Ask about anxiety: 'What happens in your head when a long sum comes up?' — a pupil who 'goes blank' may be losing working memory to worry.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  EXTERNALISE THE STEPS: jottings expected and praised; place-value grids and squared paper; a numbered step card for each written method on the desk (Gathercole & Alloway, 2008, on reducing load).

•  WORKED EXAMPLES next to practice items (Sweller & Cooper, 1985); fade them gradually, one step at a time.

•  REMOVE TRANSCRIPTION LOAD: give the sums printed on the sheet rather than copied from the board.

•  SEPARATE THE TARGET: when the lesson target is the reasoning, allow a calculator for sub-steps; when the target is the method, keep numbers small so the method, not the arithmetic, is being practised.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (aids, printed sums, worked examples); School Support if a targeted plan is needed, with review after 6–8 weeks on independent completion of a named multi-step calculation type.

•  ADDRESS ANXIETY alongside load where present — low-stakes practice, no public timing.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He knows how to do each step. The trouble is holding the carried number and the partial answer in his head at the same time — it falls out. Writing it down fixes most of it.'

•  'When you help at home, encourage him to write every step, even ones he thinks he can do in his head. It's not babyish — it's how mathematicians work.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'His errors are all at the carry. Give him a place-value grid and they'll largely disappear — that tells us it's load, not understanding.'

•  'Can the sums be printed on the sheet? Copying them from the board uses up the working memory he needs for the maths.'

•  'When you model a method, stop talking while you write — talking and writing at once is two streams for him to hold.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your brain is juggling too many balls in long sums. When you write them down, you put some balls on the table.'

•  OLDER: 'You know the method. Your head just has limited desk space. Writing working out is using a bigger desk.'

•  ASK: 'At which point do you lose track — at the start, the middle or the end?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — anxiety building around maths (avoidance, illness on test days): the load problem is being compounded; address both.

•  WATCH — a sudden change in capacity: consider health, sleep, head injury or mood before assuming a learning profile.

•  BOUNDARY — a low working memory score does not imply ADHD; describe what happens in maths.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Shouldn't she be able to do it in her head by now?' A: 'Mental maths is the highest-load way to calculate. Writing it down is

presentation.name: Fine motor difficulty (handwriting, pencil grip)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty with small, precise hand movements — pencil grip, letter formation, spacing, speed and legibility of handwriting, and related tasks such as cutting, buttons, rulers and opening containers.

•  Handwriting is not only motor: Feder and Majnemer (2007) describe it as depending on fine motor control, visual-motor integration, motor planning, kinaesthesia and attention, plus teaching and practice. The assessment question is which of these is failing.

•  Why it matters: Graham, Harris and Fink (2000) showed that extra handwriting instruction for young writers with weak handwriting improved not only handwriting fluency but also compositional fluency — slow transcription limits what a child can put on the page.

•  Part D lists it as 'Not a DSM diagnosis'. It is often part of Developmental Coordination Disorder (DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 6A04), but it can also occur alone, with hypermobility, or with poor instruction. Diagnosis of DCD is an OT/CDNT/paediatric decision, not the EP's.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT laziness or untidiness. A child who writes slowly, presses hard and complains of a sore hand is usually working harder than peers, not less.

•  NOT dyslexia by default. Poor spelling and poor letter formation often co-occur, but they have different causes; a child can spell well orally and still produce illegible script.

•  NOT fixed by a pencil grip alone. Grip aids and sloped boards are widely used; the evidence for them as stand-alone interventions is limited — check current OT reviews — and they work best inside a plan that includes practice and, where needed, keyboarding.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: immature grasp, avoidance of drawing and colouring, difficulty with scissors, beads, construction toys. Part D: Movement ABC-2 (3+) and parent report on dressing and feeding; OT is usually the pathway, not NEPS assessment.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: letter formation, reversals persisting beyond peers, slow copying, fatigue, poor spacing and alignment. Part D: DCD-Q, Movement ABC-2, Beery VMI, DASH and observation of posture and grip; OT for diagnosis.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: volume of writing rises sharply; speed becomes the functional problem, and exam access (word processor, scribe) is the live question. Part D: DASH, Beery VMI, self-report on social impact, RACE.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: note-taking, handwritten exams, practical course demands; DASH-17+ and functional demands (Part D).

•  SPECIAL SETTING: check whether OT recommendations (seating, equipment, adapted tools) are actually in place and used before adding new ones (Part D).

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Hypermobility spectrum disorder

•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Dyslexia

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  DASH (9–16) or DASH-17+ for handwriting speed across copying and free-writing tasks — compare copying with free writing to separate motor speed from composition.

•  Beery VMI with the Visual Perception and Motor Coordination supplements — without the supplements you cannot tell whether the breakdown is visual, motor or integrative (Part D).

•  DCD-Q (parent questionnaire) and Movement ABC-2 where a wider motor question is raised — these inform an OT referral; they do not give you a diagnosis.

•  Observation while writing: grip, posture, paper position, pressure (look at the back of the page), fatigue over 10 minutes, and whether quality drops as speed increases.

•  Work sample across subjects and across the year; check vision (optometry/ophthalmology) where copying from the board is the main difficulty.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  EXPLICIT HANDWRITING PRACTICE: short, frequent, taught letter formation with a consistent script. Santangelo and Graham (2016) meta-analysis supports explicit handwriting instruction for legibility and fluency.

•  REDUCE THE WRITING LOAD WHERE WRITING IS NOT THE TARGET: printed worksheets, fill-in notes, photographs of the board, oral answers, scribing for longer pieces.

•  TEACH KEYBOARDING early (touch-typing programme) for pupils whose handwriting will stay slow — begin in primary so it is fluent by post-primary exam years.

•  ENVIRONMENT: chair and table height so feet are flat and forearms rest on the desk; paper angled; grip or sloped board if an OT recommends it.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (reduced load, keyboarding access); School Support where a handwriting programme is timetabled. REFER to OT (HSE Primary Care for a single-area need; CDNT where needs are complex — check local access criteria). At post-primary, begin gathering RACE evidence early; check current SEC criteria.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'His ideas are good — you can hear it when he talks. Getting them onto paper is slow and tiring for his hand, so what he writes is much shorter than what he knows.'

•  'This isn't a diagnosis on its own. An occupational therapist is the right person to look at whether it's part of a wider coordination difficulty, and I'll help you with the referral.'

•  'Typing is a real skill for him to learn now, not a shortcut. Ten minutes of a typing programme a few times a week makes a difference over a year.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Mark his content separately from his handwriting — otherwise we're penalising him twice for the same thing.'

•  'Check the back of his page — pressing that hard is exhausting. Short writing bursts with a break work better than one long piece.'

•  'Where copying isn't the point, give him the text printed. Save his writing energy for the parts that matter.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your hand muscles are still learning to work together. We're going to practise and find some tools that make writing less tiring.'

•  OLDER: 'Your brain is quicker than your hand. That's why we'll get you typing — so your writing can keep up with your thinking.'

•  ASK: 'Does your hand hurt when you write? Where? After how long?' — pain a

presentation.name: Gross motor difficulty (PE, balance, ball skills)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty with whole-body movement: balance, running, hopping, catching and kicking, climbing, riding a bike, navigating a crowded space, and learning new sequences of movement in PE or sport.

•  Part D lists it as 'Not a DSM diagnosis'. It is central to Developmental Coordination Disorder (DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 6A04), which Blank et al. (2019) define by motor performance substantially below age expectations, interfering with daily life and not explained by another condition — that is a diagnosis for OT, physiotherapy, paediatrics or the CDNT.

•  The school cost is often social: yard games, team selection and PE are public. Cairney et al. (2005) found children with DCD had lower self-efficacy toward physical activity and participated less in organised and free play.

•  It may reflect hypermobility (joint laxity, fatigue, pain), low muscle tone, lack of opportunity, or a medical condition — the description is where you start, not where you finish.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT 'not sporty'. Many children are uninterested in sport; this presentation is about difficulty that persists with practice and affects daily function (stairs, playground, carrying a tray).

•  NOT something children reliably grow out of. Blank et al. (2019) note motor difficulties in DCD commonly persist into adolescence and adulthood — do not advise 'wait and see' without a referral.

•  NOT a reason to exclude from PE. Exclusion removes the practice the child most needs; adaptation keeps participation.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: late or unusual motor milestones, frequent falls, difficulty with stairs, tricycles, climbing frames. Part D: Movement ABC-2 (3+), parent report, preschool observation; OT/physio is the pathway.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: last to be picked, avoids yard games, bumps into peers, slow to change for PE, poor ball skills. Part D: DCD-Q, Movement ABC-2, classroom and yard observation; OT for diagnosis.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: PE avoidance, forged notes, embarrassment in changing rooms; practical subjects (science, technology, home economics) with equipment. Part D: self-report on PE avoidance and social impact.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: driving, workplace and practical course requirements; fatigue and pain may be the main complaint (Part D).

•  SPECIAL SETTING: physical access, seating, equipment and whether physiotherapy/OT programmes are carried out in the school day (Part D).

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Hypermobility spectrum disorder

•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Cerebral palsy / neuromuscular conditions (medical)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  DCD-Q (parent) and Movement ABC-2 (Part D tools) to describe the difficulty and support the referral — they inform an OT or physio assessment; they do not diagnose.

•  Observation in PE and yard, not only the classroom: balance, catching, running gait, spatial awareness, how the child manages the social side (hanging back, clowning).

•  Developmental history with parents: milestones, falls, toileting and dressing, pain, fatigue, family history of joint hypermobility.

•  Pupil voice on PE — 'What's the worst bit of PE for you?' — and a self-esteem or self-perception measure where appropriate (e.g., Piers-Harris 3).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  ADAPT, DON'T EXCLUDE: larger or softer balls, reduced distances, stations rather than competitive team selection, individual targets, extra time to learn sequences. Teacher selects teams, not captains picking in public.

•  TASK-ORIENTED PRACTICE: Blank et al. (2019) recommend task-oriented approaches (e.g., CO-OP, Polatajko & Mandich, 2004) that practise the actual skill the child wants to do, rather than generic process-based training.

•  BUILD ACTIVITY OUTSIDE PE: find a movement activity the child enjoys (swimming, cycling, dance) to protect fitness and confidence — low participation has its own health consequences (Cairney et al., 2005).

•  PRACTICAL LOGISTICS: extra time and a private space for changing; velcro or elastic laces on PE days; seat near the door for movement between rooms.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (PE adaptation) to School Support (Student Support Plan including PE teacher and SNA role where relevant). REFER to OT/physiotherapy via HSE Primary Care or CDNT — check local access criteria.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Her body finds it harder than most to learn and plan movements — catching, balancing, running round others. It isn't about effort.'

•  'The right person to look at this properly is an occupational therapist or physiotherapist. In the meantime, we can make PE work for her rather than against her.'

•  'Find one active thing she enjoys and keep her doing it. Confidence in her body matters as much as the skills.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'He isn't avoiding effort — he's avoiding being seen to fail in front of the class. Stations and individual targets remove most of that.'

•  'Please don't let captains pick teams. It's the single moment he dreads most.'

•  'Give him a head start on changing — he's slow with buttons and laces, and being last every time is what the others notice.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Some bodies learn movements quickly, some need more practice. Yours needs a bit more, and that's fine — we'll practise the things you want to get better at.'

•  OLDER: 'Coordination is a skill that some people's brains find harder. It's got nothing to do with how clever or strong you are. What sport or movement would you actually like to be able to do?'

•  ASK: 'What would make PE better for you?' — the answer often points straight to the adaptation.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — loss of motor skills, increasing falls, new weakness, difficulty rising from the floor or climbing stairs, or pain: prompt GP or paediatric review — this may be medical, not developmental.

•  WATCH — bullying in PE or the yard, and forged notes or chronic PE avoida

presentation.name: Sensory modulation difficulties (over- or under-responsive)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty GRADING the response to sensory input so it matches the situation: OVER-RESPONSIVE (hand dryers, fire drills, labels, lunch-hall noise feel intolerable), UNDER-RESPONSIVE (does not notice being called, a cut, being messy), or SENSORY SEEKING (constant movement, touching, chewing, crashing).

•  Miller et al. (2007) proposed a nosology in which sensory modulation difficulties sit alongside sensory discrimination and sensory-based motor difficulties — the three presentations Part D lists separately. It is an occupational therapy framework, not a DSM or ICD diagnosis ('Not a DSM diagnosis', Part D).

•  Dunn's (1997) model crosses neurological threshold (high/low) with response style (passive/active), giving four patterns — low registration, sensation seeking, sensory sensitivity and sensation avoiding — which the Sensory Profile 2 (Dunn, 2014) measures.

•  DSM-5-TR includes hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input as one possible restricted/repetitive feature of autism, and sensory modulation differences are well documented in autistic children (Ben-Sasson et al., 2009). They also occur in children without autism.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a diagnosis — and 'Sensory Processing Disorder' is not in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11. The American Academy of Pediatrics (Zimmer et al., 2012) advised against using it as a stand-alone diagnosis; describe the behaviour and its impact.

•  NOT a reason to stop looking. A child who covers their ears in the hall may be over-responsive — or anxious, or in pain from an ear condition (audiology), or escaping a demand. Sensory explanations are hypotheses to test.

•  NOT reliably fixed by generic 'sensory diets'. Evidence for many sensory-based strategies (weighted vests, brushing) is weak or mixed; Ayres Sensory Integration delivered by trained OTs has some trial evidence in autism (Schaaf et al., 2014). Check current reviews before recommending specific strategies.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: distress at haircuts, nail cutting, textures of food and clothing; unusually high pain tolerance; constant crashing and climbing. Separate from typical toddler preferences by intensity and impact on daily life.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: meltdowns in the lunch hall or at assemblies, refusal to wear the uniform, avoidance of messy art or PE changing, chewing sleeves, seeking movement in class.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: noise and crowding in corridors and at class changeover; deodorant, food smells in home economics; the young person may manage by withdrawing, skipping school or using headphones.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: open-plan offices, lecture halls, public transport. Self-knowledge and self-advocacy become the main supports.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: the sensory environment is often the biggest single factor in behaviour — audit it (noise, light, crowding) before attributing behaviour to the child.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Anxiety disorders

•  Fragile X syndrome

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation across contrasting environments (quiet room, busy hall, yard) with an ABC record — does the behaviour follow the sensory event, or the demand that comes with it?

•  Parent and teacher report on everyday sensory responses; the Sensory Profile 2 (Dunn, 2014) and the Sensory Processing Measure are questionnaires most often used and interpreted by OTs (check the publisher's user qualifications) — know what they measure and read the OT report rather than administering them yourself unless trained.

•  Environmental audit of the classroom: noise, lighting, seating position, visual clutter, crowding at transitions.

•  Rule out hearing (audiology), vision, pain and anxiety — each can mimic over-responsivity.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CHANGE THE ENVIRONMENT FIRST: quieter seating position, early or late entry to the lunch hall, warning before bells and fire drills where possible, a planned quiet space the child can go to — framed as regulation, not exclusion.

•  FOR SEEKING: build movement into the day (jobs, standing options, movement breaks) rather than relying on sanctions for fidgeting.

•  ALLOW REASONABLE ADJUSTMENTS: ear defenders in specific situations, uniform adjustments (seamless socks, soft fabric), alternatives to messy tasks initially with graded exposure.

•  TEACH SELF-KNOWLEDGE: help the child name their sensory triggers and choose a strategy — the aim is self-regulation, not adult-managed rescue.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for most adjustments; School Support where a plan includes planned breaks and a quiet space. REFER to OT (Primary Care or CDNT) for sensory assessment; DO NOT prescribe specific sensory diets or equipment yourself.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Her brain turns the volume up very high on some sensations — the hand dryer, the hall at lunchtime. What's a background noise to us feels like an alarm to her.'

•  'This isn't a diagnosis in itself. An OT can look at it in more detail. For now, we're changing a few things in her day so she isn't overwhelmed before lessons even start.'

•  'You probably know her triggers better than anyone. Can we make a list together?'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Watch the minutes before the incidents — lining up in a noisy corridor or the lunch hall. That's where we can make the biggest difference with the least effort.'

•  'For him, moving isn't misbehaving — it's how he keeps himself alert. Give him a job that involves moving and see if the fidgeting settles.'

•  'A quiet space works if it's planned and he chooses it — not if it's where he's sent after trouble.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Everyone's body has a volume control for noises and touches. Yours is turned up high for some things. We're going to find ways to help when it's too loud.'

•  OLDER: 'Some people notice sounds, textures and smells much more than others. It's not weird — i

presentation.name: Sensory discrimination difficulties
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty INTERPRETING the qualities of sensory information — telling apart similar sounds, shapes or textures, judging where the body is and how much force to use, or where one is being touched. The child registers the input but reads it imprecisely.

•  Miller et al. (2007) place sensory discrimination as a separate pattern from modulation (how strongly one responds) and sensory-based motor difficulties (how movement is organised). Part D lists it as 'Not a DSM diagnosis'.

•  In class it looks like: pressing too hard and breaking pencil leads (proprioception), being rough with peers without meaning to, not finding an object in a bag by touch (tactile), confusing similar-looking letters or shapes beyond the expected age (visual), or mishearing similar words despite normal hearing (auditory).

•  Much of what gets called 'discrimination' in school overlaps with established constructs — visual perception, phonological awareness, auditory processing — assessed by other professionals. Use the most specific accurate description.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a hearing or vision impairment — those must be ruled out first by audiology and optometry/ophthalmology. A child who 'mishears' may have fluctuating glue ear.

•  NOT the same as phonological awareness difficulty in dyslexia, though they can look alike. Difficulty distinguishing similar speech sounds is assessed through language and literacy assessment and SLT, not through a sensory framework.

•  NOT a diagnosis or a reason to delay literacy or maths teaching; it is a description that should shape how things are taught.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: messy handling of objects, unusual force in play, difficulty with shape sorters and puzzles, confusing similar objects by feel. Observe, describe and refer to OT; do not score.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: letter and number reversals persisting beyond peers, heavy-handed writing, clumsy handling of equipment, peers complaining of rough play, difficulty with fastenings out of sight (back buttons).

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: fine judgement in practical subjects (measuring, handling equipment in science, woodwork), sport, and social touch (too-hard back slaps). Self-consciousness rises.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: practical course and workplace tasks requiring fine sensory judgement; self-knowledge and adapted methods are the main support.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: interpret with the child's wider profile; discrimination difficulties commonly sit alongside modulation and motor difficulties and need an OT-led plan.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Autism

•  Dyslexia

•  DLD

•  Hearing impairment / visual impairment (medical)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Beery VMI Visual Perception supplement (Part D tool) — separates visual discrimination from motor coordination; interpret alongside the main VMI.

•  Observation: pressure on the page, handling of objects out of sight, force in play and in writing, response to touch cues.

•  Rule-outs: recent hearing test (audiology) and vision check (optometry/ophthalmology) before any other interpretation; phonological assessment (e.g., PhAB2) where speech-sound discrimination is in question.

•  Read any OT report carefully: OT tools such as the Sensory Integration and Praxis Tests (Ayres, 1989) assess discrimination directly; these are not EP tools.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PAIR THE WEAK CHANNEL WITH A STRONGER ONE: add visual cues to spoken instructions, verbal labels to visual discrimination tasks, and let the child look while doing fastenings or tasks they cannot feel precisely.

•  TEACH FORCE GRADING EXPLICITLY for writing and handling: pencils that show pressure, 'light / medium / heavy' practice, soft writing surfaces — ideally set by an OT.

•  FOR LETTER AND NUMBER CONFUSION: consistent explicit teaching with multisensory cues and one letter of a confusable pair at a time; a reference strip on the desk.

•  SOCIAL COACHING for rough play: name the problem as force, not intent, and practise gentle touch explicitly with peers' understanding.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support in most cases. REFER to OT (Primary Care or CDNT) for sensory and motor assessment; audiology or optometry first where hearing or vision is uncertain.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'His body doesn't give him clear information about how hard he's pressing or pushing. So he breaks pencils and his hugs are too strong — it's not that he means to be rough.'

•  'Before anything else, can we make sure his hearing and eyesight have been checked recently? Those need to be ruled out first.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When she can see what she's doing she's much more accurate — so let her look, and give visual backup to spoken instructions.'

•  'He isn't being aggressive with the others; he misjudges force. It's worth saying that to the class in a general way and practising.'

•  'Keep a letter strip on her desk. The b/d confusion is about telling similar shapes apart, not carelessness.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your hands and body are still learning to tell how hard they're pushing. We're going to play games to practise gentle and strong.'

•  OLDER: 'Some people's bodies give them fuzzy signals about pressure or touch. Using your eyes to check is a smart way round it.'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — possible hearing loss (fluctuating response, speech unclear, ear infections): audiology referral via GP before any sensory explanation.

•  WATCH — injuries the child does not notice or report: may indicate under-responsiveness; ensure first-aid checks are proactive.

•  BOUNDARY — sensory discrimination assessment belongs to OT; describe what you observe and refer rather than interpreting OT tools.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Is this why she reverses her letters?' A: 'It might be part of it. Reversals are common in early writers; when they p

presentation.name: Motor-based sensory difficulties
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Miller et al. (2007) use 'sensory-based motor' difficulties for two patterns: POSTURAL difficulties (poor core stability and balance, slumping, tiring quickly when sitting upright, leaning on the desk or propping the head on a hand) and DYSPRAXIA in Ayres' sense — difficulty with praxis: having the idea for a movement, planning it and sequencing it.

•  Ayres (1972) framed praxis as ideation → motor planning → execution. A child who can copy a movement but cannot generate one ('What could you do with this box?') has a different difficulty from one who knows what to do but cannot sequence it.

•  Part D lists it as 'Not a DSM diagnosis'. The DSM-5-TR / ICD-11 diagnosis that overlaps is Developmental Coordination Disorder; in Ireland 'dyspraxia' is widely used as an everyday synonym for DCD. Use the diagnostic term only when a qualified professional has made the diagnosis.

•  The classroom picture: fatigue by mid-morning, sitting on the edge of the seat or wrapping legs round chair legs, W-sitting on the floor, slowness learning new routines (a new PE sequence, a new way of setting out a page), and disorganised movement around the room.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT poor attitude or slouching by choice. Postural fatigue looks like disengagement; correcting it with 'sit up straight' treats a stamina issue as a behaviour issue.

•  NOT the same as low intelligence. Praxis difficulties can make a bright child look disorganised and slow in practical tasks — keep reasoning and motor planning separate in your report.

•  NOT a diagnosis in its own right. The framework is used by OTs to plan intervention; it does not replace a DCD diagnosis and it is not a label for school records.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: slow to learn new play movements (climbing sequences, pedalling), limited play ideas with novel toys, tiring quickly, frequent falls. Observe and refer to OT — no scoring.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: slumping, leaning, fidgeting to stay upright, poor organisation of body and materials, slow to learn dance or PE routines, struggles with dressing sequences.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: fatigue across a long timetable, difficulty with new practical procedures (lab equipment, woodwork), awkward in crowded corridors; embarrassment drives avoidance.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: learning new motor routines at work or in training (driving, catering, trades); energy management across the day.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: seating and positioning are often the first question — is the child physically supported enough to attend and learn? (Part D: equipment and seating in place.)

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Hypermobility spectrum disorder

•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Cerebral palsy (medical)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation across a morning: posture at start vs after 45 minutes; how the child sits on the floor; how they approach a novel physical task (ideas, sequencing, execution).

•  Movement ABC-2 and DCD-Q (Part D tools) to describe motor performance and support an OT referral.

•  Developmental history: milestones, hypermobility, fatigue, pain, sleep. Where pain or fatigue is prominent, GP review (hypermobility spectrum disorder is a medical question).

•  Check existing OT or physio reports and whether recommended seating, equipment or programmes are actually in place (Part D, Special Setting).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SEATING FIRST: chair and table height so feet are flat and hips and knees are roughly at right angles; a footrest if needed; seat back used. Consider OT advice on seating supports rather than purchasing equipment unassessed.

•  PLAN FOR FATIGUE: alternate seated and active tasks; allow standing work; schedule demanding writing earlier in the day if energy drops later.

•  TEACH NEW MOTOR SEQUENCES EXPLICITLY: break into steps, demonstrate, verbalise ('first..., then...'), practise with feedback; allow extra repetitions before public performance. CO-OP-style verbal self-guidance supports this (Polatajko & Mandich, 2004).

•  ORGANISATION SUPPORTS: visual sequences for dressing and setting up materials; consistent layout of the classroom and the desk.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support (seating, pacing, explicit teaching); School Support where a plan coordinates OT/physio recommendations. REFER to OT or physiotherapy (Primary Care or CDNT — check local criteria).

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Holding herself upright takes more effort for her than for most children, so she tires and slumps — it's her body, not her attitude.'

•  'Learning a new movement — a dance, tying laces, a PE routine — needs to be broken down and practised more. Once she has it, she keeps it.'

•  'An OT is the right person to look at this. In school we'll start with her chair and table, which is simple and often makes a real difference.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When he props his head on his hand, he's not bored — he's tired from holding himself up. Swap to a standing task and see if he re-engages.'

•  'Show and say the steps of a new routine, one at a time, and give him a practice before he has to do it in front of everyone.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your body muscles get tired more quickly than some people's. We'll make your chair just right and take moving breaks.'

•  OLDER: 'Learning new movements takes your brain a few more practices than other people. Once it's learnt, it's learnt. It's nothing to do with how smart you are.'

•  ASK: 'When in the day do you feel most tired?' — useful for timetabling demanding tasks.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — pain, joint dislocation or subluxation, or marked fatigue: GP review; hypermobility-related conditions are medical and need medical assessment.

•  WATCH — loss of skills or progressive weakness: prompt GP or paediatric review.

•  BOUNDARY — do not write 'has dyspraxia' in reports without a diagnosis; describe the postural and planning

presentation.name: Presentation and care of written work
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The appearance and organisation of written work across copies and books: layout on the page, legibility, headings and dates, margins, crossings-out, torn or lost pages, work that starts and stops. Part D notes this is 'Form 2 wording' — the phrase teachers are likely to use when referring, so expect it on referral paperwork (check the current form in your service).

•  It is a DESCRIPTION WITH MANY POSSIBLE CAUSES: motor (handwriting control and speed), visual-spatial organisation, executive function (planning, organisation of materials), spelling uncertainty (constant crossing out), perfectionism or anxiety (rubbing out until the page tears), low motivation, or home circumstances.

•  It matters because presentation affects how work is judged: Graham, Harris and Hebert (2011) found that less legible versions of the same text receive lower quality ratings — the pupil's content is marked down for its handwriting.

•  A descriptive presentation under 1.6 Co-ordination (Part D), not a diagnosis. Your job is to find which of the causes above is operating.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a measure of effort or of care about school. Some of the most anxious, conscientious pupils produce the worst-looking pages because they erase repeatedly.

•  NOT a single-cause problem. A plan that only addresses neatness (e.g., rewriting untidy work) usually fails and damages motivation.

•  NOT a reason to mark content down. Presentation and content should be assessed separately so the pupil's knowledge is visible.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not applicable as written work; observe drawing, colouring within spaces and use of paper.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: messy copies, work not starting at the margin, letters drifting off the line, torn pages, missing dates and headings, books lost or left at home. Compare copies across subjects.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: many teachers, many copies and folders; organisation of materials across subjects and legibility under exam time pressure are the live issues. Links with RACE evidence where legibility affects exam access.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: handwritten exams and notes; most work shifts to typing, which usually resolves presentation but not organisation.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: adapted recording formats (worksheets, photographs, symbol-supported writing, typing) are often more appropriate than handwritten copies.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  ADHD

•  Dyslexia

•  Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder

•  Visual impairment (medical)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Work sampling across subjects and across the year: is it consistent (suggests a skill difficulty) or variable by subject, time or teacher (suggests motivation, anxiety or teaching match)? Look at the first and last pages of a copy.

•  Compare copied work with composed work, and timed with untimed: DASH gives a structured comparison of speed across tasks.

•  Watch the pupil write: grip and posture, erasing behaviour, time spent on first line, whether they plan the page.

•  Brief pupil interview: 'What do you think of how your copy looks? What makes it hard?' — perfectionism and embarrassment show up quickly.

•  Rule out vision (copying from board), and consider BRIEF-2 Organisation of Materials if organisation across the day is the pattern.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  SEPARATE CONTENT FROM PRESENTATION in marking and feedback; agree across teachers which pieces of work are presentation targets and which are not.

•  SCAFFOLD THE PAGE: ruled margins, squared paper for maths, a model page at the front of the copy, pre-printed headings or date stamps, writing frames for longer pieces.

•  ONE-LINE CROSSING OUT, NOT ERASING: teach and permit a single neat line through errors — reduces tearing and time lost, and helps perfectionistic pupils.

•  TYPING FOR EXTENDED WORK where handwriting speed or legibility is the barrier; keep short handwritten tasks for practice.

•  ORGANISATION ROUTINES: colour-coded copies and folders by subject, a weekly bag check with a named adult, photographs of a correctly packed bag.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support in most cases; School Support where handwriting or organisation needs a targeted plan. REFER to OT where motor factors dominate.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Her copies look messy, but when I looked closely, most of the mess is rubbing out — she wants it perfect and keeps erasing. That's a different problem from not caring.'

•  'We're going to separate what he knows from how it looks when we mark his work, so he gets credit for the content.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Compare his maths copy with his English copy — if one is much tidier, the problem isn't only motor. What's different about the two lessons?'

•  'Let her cross out with a single line. The erasing is costing her time and tearing pages, and the anxiety behind it grows every time.'

•  'A model page stuck inside the cover shows him exactly where the date, the title and the margin go. It takes one minute to make.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Your ideas are what matter most. We'll make some lines and boxes on your page to help your writing find its place.'

•  OLDER: 'Teachers sometimes mark how work looks without meaning to. Typing longer pieces and using a model page is about making sure they see what you actually know.'

•  ASK: 'What bothers you most about your copies?' — the answer separates embarrassment, perfectionism and motor difficulty.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — excessive rewriting, erasing through the page, distress at small mistakes: consider anxiety or obsessive-compulsive features; talk with parents about GP or CAMHS routes if it is spreading beyond schoolwork.

•  WATCH — sudden deterioration in presentation: mood, sleep, home events, bullying or health (including vision) before assuming a learning difficulty.

•  WATCH — books repeatedly damaged, lost or never brought, al

presentation.name: Self-care and independence skills at school
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 1. LEARNING (1.6 Co-ordination — fine motor / handwriting, gross motor / PE skills)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The practical skills a pupil needs to get through the school day without adult help: dressing and undressing for PE, fastenings and shoelaces, toileting and hand-washing, opening lunch containers and eating, managing belongings, moving between rooms, and — for older pupils — managing their own timetable and any medical routines.

•  These are adaptive skills. Adaptive behaviour measures such as the ABAS-3 (Harrison & Oakland, 2015) and Vineland-3 (Sparrow et al., 2016) include self-care and daily living domains, and adaptive functioning is part of how intellectual disability is defined in DSM-5-TR.

•  Summers, Larkin and Dewey (2008) found children with DCD had difficulty with dressing, personal hygiene and eating skills and took longer to master them — self-care difficulty is often motor as well as cognitive.

•  Independence is shaped by the SUPPORT AROUND the child as well as their skills: Giangreco et al. (1997) described how close, constant adult proximity can reduce independence and peer interaction. Part D lists this as an added descriptive presentation under 1.6.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT the same at home and at school. A child who dresses independently at home with unlimited time may not manage in a crowded changing room in five minutes — check both settings before concluding.

•  NOT solved by more adult help. Doing the task for the child is quicker today and builds dependence over the year; the goal is planned fading.

•  NOT only a special-education issue. Mainstream pupils with DCD, autism or hypermobility commonly have self-care needs that are invisible until PE, lunch or a school trip.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: toileting, coat and shoes, eating, tidying — the core of preschool independence. Wide normal variation; describe relative to the setting and involve parents in shared targets.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: PE changing, laces and buttons, lunch boxes, bringing the right books, managing the toilet independently, following the day's routine without prompts.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: lockers, timetables, moving between rooms, managing money in the canteen, personal hygiene and menstrual care, self-management of medical needs.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: travel, cooking, money, self-advocacy; transition planning to further education, training or work — adaptive measures at adult level (ABAS-3 adult form, Vineland-3 adult) inform this.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: independence targets are central to the curriculum; check whether skills taught in school are practised at home and vice versa.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Autism

•  Hypermobility spectrum disorder

•  Physical disability (e.g., cerebral palsy, spina bifida — medical)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation at the points of greatest demand — PE changing, lunch, home time, moving between rooms — timing the task and noting what prompts are given and by whom.

•  ABAS-3 or Vineland-3 (parent and teacher) where a broader adaptive profile is needed, e.g., when intellectual disability or transition planning is in question.

•  Task analysis of the specific skill: which steps the child does alone, with a prompt, or not at all — this is the baseline for teaching.

•  Map adult support: how much help the SNA or teacher gives, whether it has faded over time, and what the child does when the adult is not there.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  TEACH ONE SKILL AT A TIME USING TASK ANALYSIS: break it into steps; use backward chaining (the adult does all but the last step, the child completes it, then the last two...) so the child always finishes successfully.

•  VISUAL SEQUENCES: photographs or symbols of each step at the point of use (changing area, toilet, locker).

•  PLANNED PROMPT FADING: move from physical to gestural to verbal to no prompt; write the fading plan into the Student Support Plan with dates. Review the SNA role against independence goals — access to the SNA scheme is for care needs (check the current Department of Education circular and NCSE guidance).
