•  ADAPT THE TASK: velcro or elastic laces, uniform with easier fastenings, lunch in easy-open containers, extra time or an earlier start for changing.

•  HOME–SCHOOL LINK: agree the same method and cue words at home, and practise at weekends when time pressure is low.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support to School Support; School Support Plus where OT, CDNT or physiotherapy are involved. REFER to OT (Primary Care or CDNT) for motor-based self-care difficulty.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He can do more than he's getting a chance to show — the adults around him have been helping to save time. We're going to plan how to step back gradually.'

•  'We'll teach one skill at a time, starting at the end — you do all of the zip except pulling it to the top, and he does that. Then a bit more each week.'

•  'Using the same words and the same order at home and school makes it much faster.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'She dresses herself at home — just slowly. Give her a five-minute head start before PE and see what she can do alone.'

•  'Can we write down what help the SNA gives for toileting and lunch, and plan to reduce it one step at a time? Otherwise it never reduces.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'You're getting bigger and able to do more things yourself. Let's pick one thing to practise — which one would you like?'

•  OLDER: 'The goal is for you to be able to do this without anyone hovering. What would you like to be able to do on your own by the summer?'

•  ASK: 'Is there anything at school you'd like help with, or would like less help with?' — older pupils often want less adult help than they receive.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — new wetting or soiling after being continent, or regression in self-care: GP review, and consider emotional causes; in some cases this can be an indicator of distress or abuse — foll

presentation.name: Behaviour that challenges
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  An umbrella description for behaviour that puts the pupil or others at risk, or seriously limits their learning or access to ordinary settings. Emerson (1995) defined challenging behaviour as culturally abnormal behaviour of such intensity, frequency or duration that physical safety is likely to be placed in jeopardy, or that is likely to seriously limit use of, or result in denial of access to, ordinary community facilities.

•  The term was chosen deliberately: the behaviour CHALLENGES THE SERVICE to respond, rather than the child being 'challenging' (Royal College of Psychiatrists, British Psychological Society & Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists, 2007). Keep that emphasis in your language.

•  Part D lists it as 'Not a DSM diagnosis'. It sits beside diagnoses such as ODD, DMDD and Intermittent Explosive Disorder in 2.1 Behaviour in class, but most pupils referred with it have no such diagnosis — and do not need one to be helped.

•  NEPS's Behavioural, Emotional and Social Difficulties continuum guidance (NEPS, 2010) frames the response through the Continuum of Support: whole-class approaches first, then targeted and individualised plans informed by assessment of what the behaviour achieves for the pupil.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a description of the child's character. 'He is challenging' closes down thinking; 'he hits out when asked to write in front of peers' opens it up. Describe behaviour operationally.

•  NOT explained until you know its function. The same behaviour (e.g., throwing a book) may be escape from a task, bid for adult attention, or an overwhelmed response to noise — each needs a different plan.

•  NOT solved by escalating sanctions alone. Punishment-only approaches may suppress behaviour briefly without teaching an alternative; Positive Behaviour Support (Carr et al., 2002) combines prevention, skill teaching and consistent response.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: tantrums, biting, hitting — often developmental and communicative. Part D: ABC recording by preschool staff, structured observation, SDQ (2–4 version); frame it as developmental.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: refusal, disruption, aggression to peers or staff, running out of class. Part D: ABC grid across a week, time sampling with a peer comparison, SDQ or BASC-3, functional behaviour assessment, Continuum level check.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: defiance with staff, walking out, verbal aggression, damage; suspension and reduced timetable risk rises. Part D: BASC-3 including self-report, subject-teacher survey (all classes or some?), pupil's own account, discipline record.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: conduct expectations in courses or work; less often a NEPS referral (Part D). Self-report and functional analysis.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: behaviour against the setting's baseline, staff consistency, and whether the environment is generating the behaviour (Part D). NICE (2015) guidance on challenging behaviour and learning disabilities is relevant here.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder

•  Intermittent Explosive Disorder

•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Intellectual Disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  OPERATIONAL DEFINITION first: what exactly the pupil does, how often, how intensely, for how long — agreed with staff so everyone records the same thing.

•  ABC recording over at least a week and a scatterplot by time and lesson (Touchette et al., 1985) to find patterns; functional behaviour assessment interview with staff (O'Neill et al., 2015).

•  SDQ or BASC-3 (teacher and parent; BASC-3 SRP self-report at adolescence) for a broader picture across settings — note where reports disagree.

•  Check the learning side: literacy, language and attention screen — always test whether an unmet learning need is driving the behaviour (see 'Behaviour as communication of an unmet learning need').

•  Check the Continuum record: what has been tried, for how long, with what fidelity. 'Nothing works' often means nothing has been implemented consistently.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  A BEHAVIOUR SUPPORT PLAN in the Student Support File with four parts: PREVENT (change triggers and setting events), TEACH (a replacement behaviour that meets the same need), RESPOND (what adults do when the behaviour happens — consistent, brief, calm) and SAFETY (a crisis plan if risk is present).

•  FUNCTION-BASED STRATEGIES: match the plan to what the behaviour achieves (escape, attention, access, sensory) — see 'Behaviour function'.

•  WHOLE-SCHOOL FIT: check the plan is consistent with the school's code of behaviour (Education (Welfare) Act 2000, s.23; NEWB, 2008) and that all staff who meet the pupil know it.

•  RESTRICTIVE PRACTICES only as a last resort, only as set out in school policy and the Department of Education's Understanding Behaviours of Concern and Responding to Crisis Situations: Guidelines for Schools in Supporting Students (published 12/12/2024) — physical intervention only as the last part of a planned positive approach. Record and report every use as the Guidelines require; check for later update circulars.

•  REDUCED TIMETABLES only within Circular 0047/2021, Guidelines for the Use of Reduced School Days (in effect from 01/01/2022): parental consent, a plan to return to full time, a time limit, and notification to Tusla Education Support Service (TESS). Check for any later revision.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support for an individual plan; School Support Plus when risk is present or external agencies are involved (CAMHS for moderate–severe; Primary Care for mild–moderate — Part D). REFER to Tusla if the behaviour raises child-protection concerns.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'We're not looking for someone to blame. We're trying to understand what his behaviour is doing for him — what it gets him out of or into — so we can teach him a better way to get the same thing.'

•  'You know him outside sch

presentation.name: Behaviour function (ABC analysis, trigger-behaviour-consequence)
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A way of understanding behaviour by what it ACHIEVES for the person, not what it looks like. Part D: 'Formulation approach, not a diagnosis'. The ABC model records the Antecedent (what happened before), the Behaviour (exactly what the pupil did) and the Consequence (what happened after).

•  Iwata et al. (1982/1994) developed experimental functional analysis and showed that the same behaviour could be maintained by different consequences in different people. The four functions most commonly described are: ESCAPE/AVOIDANCE (of a task, demand or situation), ATTENTION (adult or peer), TANGIBLE (access to an item or activity), and AUTOMATIC/SENSORY (the behaviour itself feels good or relieves discomfort) — Durand and Crimmins (1988) built the Motivation Assessment Scale around these.

•  SETTING EVENTS (slow triggers) matter as much as immediate triggers: poor sleep, hunger, a bad morning at home, a change of teacher, pain. They make a trigger more potent on some days than others (O'Neill et al., 2015).

•  In schools the EP uses DESCRIPTIVE functional assessment (interviews, ABC records, scatterplots) rather than experimental functional analysis, which deliberately manipulates conditions and requires specialist setting and ethical safeguards.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a way of saying the child is 'manipulative' or 'attention-seeking'. Every behaviour meets a need; 'attention-seeking' should be read as 'attention-needing' — and the response is to give attention in a better way, not withhold it entirely.

•  NOT a single fixed answer. A behaviour can serve more than one function, and functions change over time and across settings. Hold your hypothesis tentatively and test it.

•  NOT a diagnostic tool. ABC data describe what maintains a behaviour; they say nothing about whether the pupil has ADHD, autism or any other condition.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: most behaviour serves communication — getting, avoiding, or telling you something is wrong. Part D: ABC recording by preschool staff is the core method.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: escape from literacy and maths tasks, peer attention in class and adult attention in the corridor are common functions. Part D: ABC grid across a week, time sampling, functional behaviour assessment.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: peer attention and status, escape from exposure (being seen to fail), and avoidance of specific teachers or subjects; the young person's own account is essential data (Part D: pupil interview).

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: self-report and functional analysis (Part D); the person can often identify their own triggers and payoffs with support.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: sensory/automatic and communicative functions are more common in pupils with limited speech; pair function-based planning with communication (AAC) review. Part D lists 'Functional behaviour assessment (ABC)' as the tool here.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  Autism

•  Intellectual Disability

•  ADHD

•  DLD

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  ABC recording by the adults present, over at least a week and across settings; train them to write what they saw, not what they concluded ('threw pencil case' not 'had a tantrum').

•  Scatterplot by time and lesson (Touchette et al., 1985) to find when behaviour does and does not happen — the 'does not' is as important as the 'does'.

•  Functional assessment interview with staff and parents (O'Neill et al., 2015) and the pupil's own account: 'What happens after you do that? What do you get? What do you avoid?'

•  State the hypothesis in one sentence: 'When [setting event] and [trigger], [pupil] does [behaviour], in order to [function].' Then check whether the data support it.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  PREVENT: change the antecedent — adjust task difficulty, give a choice, pre-correct, alter seating, address setting events (breakfast, a calm arrival routine).

•  TEACH A REPLACEMENT that serves the SAME function more efficiently: e.g., a break card for escape, a 'check-in' routine for attention. Functional Communication Training (Carr & Durand, 1985) is the classic evidence base.

•  CHANGE THE PAYOFF: make sure the problem behaviour no longer gets the pupil what it used to (e.g., the task is still there after the outburst), while the replacement behaviour gets it quickly.

•  REVIEW WITH DATA: repeat ABC or frequency recording after 4–6 weeks; if the behaviour has not changed, revisit the hypothesis rather than intensifying the same plan.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support for an individual function-based plan; School Support Plus when external agencies are involved. Share the hypothesis with all staff who work with the pupil.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When she tears up her work, she ends up out of the room and away from the writing. We think that is what keeps the behaviour going — so we're going to give her a better way to say "this is too hard" and make the writing more doable.'

•  'We're looking for patterns, not blame. The records help us see when things go wrong and, just as importantly, when they don't.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Write what you saw, not why you think he did it. "Threw the pencil case" rather than "had a tantrum" — we'll work out the why from the pattern.'

•  'If he's sent out every time he refuses, the refusal is working for him. Let's keep him in with a doable version of the task instead.'

•  'A break card only works if he actually gets the break quickly when he uses it — otherwise he'll go back to what worked before.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'When you do that, what happens next? Is there a better way to show me you need a break?'

•  OLDER: 'Everything we do has a reason. I'm trying to figure out what this is doing for you, so we can find a way that gets you the same thing with less trouble.'

•  ASK: 'What would you rather happen instead?' — the answer often names the function.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH

presentation.name: Emotion regulation in the classroom
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  How a pupil notices, tolerates and manages strong feelings during the school day — frustration at a hard task, disappointment at losing, anxiety before a test, anger in a peer dispute — well enough to keep learning and keep relationships intact.

•  Gross (1998) described emotion regulation as a process with points of intervention: situation selection and modification, attentional deployment, cognitive change (reappraisal), and response modulation. Classroom support can act at each point, not only on the final outburst.

•  Regulation develops from CO-REGULATION (an adult calms the child) to SELF-REGULATION. Eisenberg, Spinrad and Eggum (2010) link weaker emotion-related self-regulation to both externalising and internalising difficulties. Children who have had less consistent co-regulation — including after trauma — may need more of it for longer.

•  Siegel's (1999) 'window of tolerance' is a helpful shared image for staff: within it, the child can think and learn; outside it (hyper-aroused or shut down), teaching and reasoning do not land.

•  A descriptive presentation, not a diagnosis (Part D, 2.1). It sits beside DMDD and Intermittent Explosive Disorder in Part D, but most pupils with regulation difficulty do not have these diagnoses.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT only anger. Shut-down, tearfulness, withdrawal and silent refusal are regulation difficulties too, and are more easily missed.

•  NOT a choice in the moment. A pupil outside their window of tolerance cannot use strategies they know when calm; the teaching happens before and after, not at the peak.

•  NOT solved by a feelings chart alone. Programmes such as the Zones of Regulation (Kuypers, 2011) are widely used, but the evidence base for specific branded programmes varies — check before claiming effectiveness. The adult's own regulation and relationship are the active ingredients.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: tantrums are developmentally normal; the question is intensity, frequency and recovery time. Co-regulation by a familiar adult is the intervention.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: outbursts at transitions, losing games, hard tasks or perceived unfairness; slow recovery; anxiety showing as refusal or stomach aches. Emotion vocabulary is still developing.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: irritability, withdrawal, rapid escalation with staff, masking in class and releasing at home. Consider mood and anxiety carefully; self-report becomes central (Part D: RCADS self-report, MFQ, Beck Youth Inventories-2, BASC-3 SRP).

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: self-management in course and workplace settings; self-awareness and help-seeking are the main supports.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: interpret against the setting baseline, communication level and sensory environment; many regulation difficulties are triggered by sensory overload or communication breakdown.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder

•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Anxiety disorders

•  Post-traumatic stress disorder / trauma-related presentations

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation and ABC records focused on the BUILD-UP: what the pupil's early signs are, how long from first sign to peak, and what helped recovery.

•  SDQ (emotional and conduct subscales) or BASC-3; at adolescence add self-report (RCADS self-report, MFQ, Beck Youth Inventories-2) where anxiety or low mood is in question.

•  Pupil interview with a visual scale (e.g., a 1–5 feelings thermometer): 'What does a 2 look like for you? A 4? What helps at a 3?'

•  Parent interview on home patterns, sleep, recent events, and any history of adversity — asked sensitively and without probing for trauma details.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CO-REGULATE FIRST: a named, trusted adult; calm, low-word responses at the peak; a planned calm space the pupil can use before the peak, not only after it.

•  TEACH EMOTIONAL LITERACY AND STRATEGIES WHEN CALM: naming feelings, noticing body signals, practising two or three strategies (breathing, movement, asking for a break). Emotion Coaching (Gus et al., 2015) gives staff a simple script: empathise and validate, then set limits, then problem-solve.

•  ADJUST THE TRIGGERS: preview hard tasks, reduce public failure, plan transitions, build in movement.

•  WHOLE-CLASS SEL: social and emotional learning programmes improve social-emotional skills and behaviour (Durlak et al., 2011). Check what the school already runs (e.g., SPHE, Weaving Well-being) and build on it.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support to School Support (individual regulation plan); School Support Plus with CAMHS or Primary Care where anxiety, mood or DMDD-type presentations are in question (CAMHS for moderate–severe, Primary Care for mild–moderate — Part D).

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When his feelings get big, the thinking part of his brain goes offline for a while. That's why talking to him at that moment doesn't work — it's after he's calm that he can learn.'

•  'We're going to help him notice the early signs and practise a couple of things that help, so he can catch it sooner.'

•  'What helps him calm down at home? We'd like to use the same approach in school.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'At the peak, fewer words and a calm voice. The talking and the consequences come later, once she's back.'

•  'Can we notice her early signs together? Jaw tight, pencil tapping, going quiet — that's when a break helps, before it becomes an outburst.'

•  'Look after yourself in these moments too. Our own calm is the most powerful tool we have.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Feelings are like weather — sometimes sunny, sometimes stormy. When it's stormy inside, we have some things that help the storm pass.'

•  OLDER: 'Everybody has a point where feelings take over and thinking switches off. Let's work out your early warning signs so you can do something before you get there.'

•  ASK: 'What does your body feel like just before you lose i

presentation.name: Response to correction and repair after an incident
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Two linked moments: (1) how the pupil responds when an adult corrects them — a reminder, a reprimand, feedback on work — and (2) whether and how they can REPAIR afterwards: acknowledge, make amends, and re-enter the relationship and the class.

•  Common difficult patterns: escalation on any correction (arguing, walking out), denial even when seen, collapse into 'I'm stupid / everyone hates me', or apparent indifference. Each points to something different.

•  Shame versus guilt matters: Tangney and Dearing (2002) distinguish guilt ('I did a bad thing' — linked to repair) from shame ('I am bad' — linked to hiding, denial and anger). Public or harsh correction pushes pupils toward shame, which makes repair less likely.

•  Some pupils are especially sensitive to perceived rejection (Downey & Feldman, 1996): they anticipate it, perceive it readily and react strongly — correction is heard as rejection.

•  A descriptive presentation, not a diagnosis (Part D, 2.1). Part D lists it as an added presentation.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT simply defiance or lack of remorse. Denial and anger after correction often protect against shame; an apparently indifferent pupil may be shut down, not uncaring.

•  NOT a skill every pupil already has. Repair — saying sorry meaningfully, putting something right — needs language, perspective-taking and emotional recovery, which some pupils (e.g., with DLD or autism) find hard and must be taught.

•  NOT 'Pathological Demand Avoidance'. PDA is not a diagnosis in DSM-5-TR or ICD-11; if strong reactions to demands are part of the picture, describe them and consider the wider assessment rather than using the label.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: tantrums or hiding after being told no; 'sorry' is learned as a word before it is understood. Adults model repair ('I'll help you fix the tower').

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: arguing back, crying, tearing work after a correction; reluctance to return to class after an incident; peers keep the story going.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: loss of face in front of peers is the strongest driver; public correction escalates, private correction often lands. Repair with a subject teacher may matter more than with the year head.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: response to feedback in courses and work; supervisors' style and the young person's self-appraisal shape the outcome.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: check that correction is understood (language level, visual support) and that repair is modelled concretely; consistency across staff is essential.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  DLD

•  Anxiety disorders

•  Reactive Attachment Disorder / attachment difficulties

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observation of correction episodes: how correction is given (public/private, tone, words), the pupil's immediate response, and time to recovery. Compare staff whose corrections work with those whose do not.

•  Pupil interview after a calm period: 'What was going on for you when Ms X said that? What did you think she thought of you?' — reveals shame and rejection sensitivity.

•  Language check (receptive and expressive): can the pupil understand the correction and put their view into words? Refer to SLT if not.

•  Background: history of harsh correction, adversity or disrupted attachments — asked sensitively through parents and relevant professionals, not by probing the child.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CORRECT PRIVATELY AND BRIEFLY: least-intrusive first (a look, proximity, a quiet word), with take-up time rather than standing over the pupil (Rogers, 2015). Focus on the behaviour, not the person.

•  SEPARATE THE INCIDENT FROM THE RELATIONSHIP: an explicit 'fresh start' message ('Tomorrow is a new day — I'm glad you're here') after each incident.

•  RESTORATIVE REPAIR when calm, not in the heat of the moment: structured questions such as 'What happened? What were you thinking? Who has been affected? What needs to happen to put it right?' (Hopkins, 2004). Scaffold with visuals or a script for pupils with language needs.

•  FEEDBACK ON WORK that focuses on the task and next steps rather than the self (Hattie & Timperley, 2007).

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for most (staff approach); School Support where a named adult leads repair and re-entry routines. Consider CAMHS or Primary Care if low self-worth, anxiety or mood are prominent.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'When he's corrected, he seems to hear "you're a bad person" rather than "that was the wrong thing to do". So he gets defensive. We're going to change how we correct him and help him learn how to put things right.'

•  'At home, try to separate the behaviour from him: "that was unkind" rather than "you're so unkind" — and always follow up with a fresh start.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Quiet and private works much better with her than in front of the class. Say it, walk away, give her a minute.'

•  'Once he's calm, do the repair conversation — short, with the four questions. And make sure there is a clear fresh start after.'

•  'He's not unrepentant; he's ashamed. The denial is protection.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Everyone makes mistakes. When we make one, we can fix it. Let's think about how you could fix this.'

•  OLDER: 'Getting told off in front of people is horrible — most people get defensive. Doing something wrong doesn't make you a bad person. What would help you put this right?'

•  ASK: 'When a teacher tells you off, what goes through your head?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — extreme self-criticism after correction ('I should die', 'I hate myself'): treat as a risk indicator; follow the same-day risk procedure.

•  WATCH — fear responses to correction (flinching, panic, freezing) that may indicate harsh treatment at home or elsewhere: consider child protection; inform the DLP and, as a mandated person, report to Tusla as soon as practicable where the thres

presentation.name: Transitions between activities and between classes
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Difficulty with the many MICRO-TRANSITIONS of a school day: stopping a preferred activity, moving from yard to class, changing subject, lining up, moving between rooms at post-primary, and adjusting to unplanned change (substitute teacher, cancelled PE).

•  Transitions combine several demands at once: stopping (inhibition), shifting (flexibility), understanding what comes next (language and predictability), organising materials and body (motor and executive function), and coping with noise and crowding (sensory).

•  Hume et al. (2014) describe transition as a frequent source of difficulty for autistic pupils and outline visual and structured supports; structured teaching approaches (Mesibov et al., 2004) rely heavily on making 'what comes next' visible.

•  A descriptive presentation, not a diagnosis (Part D, 2.1 — added). Distinct from major educational transitions (preschool to primary, primary to post-primary), which Part D covers elsewhere under transition planning.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT defiance. A pupil who refuses to stop drawing may be unable to disengage or unsure what happens next. Ask which demand is failing.

•  NOT an autism-only issue. ADHD (disengaging and organising), anxiety (uncertainty), DLD (not understanding the instruction) and DCD (organising materials and body) all produce transition difficulties.

•  NOT only in-class. Corridors, stairs and lines are often the least supervised and most crowded parts of the day — much transition behaviour happens there.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: distress at tidy-up time, leaving the yard, going home; typical at this age, but intensity and recovery time are the markers.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: slow to settle after yard, difficulty with lining up, meltdowns at unexpected changes; the minutes after break are often the most difficult.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: moving between rooms and teachers multiple times a day, lockers, bells, crowds; late arrival or avoidance of certain corridors.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: timetabled changes in college or work; self-management with planners and phone reminders.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: visual schedules and transition objects are routine — check whether they are actually used and updated.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Anxiety disorders

•  DLD

•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Scatterplot of incidents by time of day (Touchette et al., 1985) — transition-linked difficulty shows as clusters at the start of lessons, after break and at changeover times.

•  Observation of two or three transitions: what warning was given, how the instruction was delivered, where the pupil went and what they did.

•  Pupil interview: 'Which change in the day is hardest? What would help?' — older pupils can often identify specific corridors, times or teachers.

•  Check language comprehension of transition instructions and any sensory load (corridor noise, crowding).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  MAKE 'WHAT COMES NEXT' VISIBLE: visual timetable with changes marked in advance; 'first–then' boards for younger pupils; a personal timetable card at post-primary.

•  WARN BEFORE THE CHANGE: a countdown (verbal, visual timer) before stopping a preferred activity; tell the pupil about unplanned changes as early as possible.

•  GIVE THE PUPIL A ROLE: messenger, equipment carrier, first or last in line — reduces waiting time and crowd exposure.

•  STRUCTURE THE START OF LESSONS: a consistent settling task on the desk ('do now' task) so the transition ends quickly in predictable work.

•  AT POST-PRIMARY: leave class a few minutes early to avoid crowds, a quieter route, a locker in an accessible spot, a named adult to check in with at the start of the day.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support for most; School Support where an individual transition plan is needed.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'He does well once he's settled into something. It's the changing — stopping one thing and starting another — that's hard. We're going to make the changes more predictable.'

•  'A countdown works at home too: "five more minutes, then dinner" with a timer he can see.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Most of her incidents happen in the first ten minutes after break. A settling task on the desk when she comes in may prevent a lot of them.'

•  'Tell him about the substitute teacher first thing if you can. Surprises are what tip him over.'

•  'Giving him a job at transition time — handing out books — is a small thing that changes a lot.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Changing from one thing to another can feel wobbly. Your picture timetable shows you what's next, so there are no surprises.'

•  OLDER: 'Loads of people find the changes in the day hardest — the corridors, the bells. Let's work out which change is worst and plan for it.'

•  ASK: 'Which part of the day would you change if you could?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — leaving the building or absconding during transitions: a safety issue; ensure supervision and a clear plan with parents and principal.

•  WATCH — avoidance of specific corridors or times may indicate bullying: ask directly and follow anti-bullying procedures (Department of Education, Bí Cineálta procedures, 2024 — check current version).

•  WATCH — increasing distress at change combined with other features (social communication, restricted interests): consider whether a referral for assessment is warranted; describe rather than label.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'Won't a visual timetable make her dependent?' A: 'Most adults use calendars and reminders. It's a tool she can carry into adult life.'

•  Q: 'Should he leave class early? Won't others see that as special treatment?' A: 'It can be done discreetly, and fairness means each pupil gets what they need. It prevents incidents that cost far more time.'

•  Q: 'Is this autism?' A: 'Difficulty with ch

presentation.name: Behaviour system fit
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Part D's full wording: 'Behaviour system fit — is the system working for this pupil'. A question about the CONTEXT, not the child: does the school's or class's behaviour system (rules, rewards, sanctions, charts, points, detentions) actually change this pupil's behaviour — or does it repeatedly fail, or make things worse?

•  Part D lists it twice: here under 2.1 Behaviour in class, and as 'Context, not a diagnosis' among the systemic presentations. That is the point: the finding is about the system.

•  School-wide Positive Behaviour Support (Sugai & Horner, 2002) describes a tiered system: universal expectations for all, targeted support for some, individual plans for a few. A system that only has the universal tier will fail the pupils who most need it.

•  Common misfits: rewards a pupil never reaches; public charts (traffic lights, names on the board) that expose the same pupil daily; sanctions that remove the pupil from a task they wanted to escape (so they reward the behaviour); systems requiring skills the pupil lacks (waiting, self-monitoring). Greene (2008): 'kids do well if they can'.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a criticism of the school or teacher. Most systems work for most pupils; the finding is that this one needs adaptation.

•  NOT an argument to abandon consequences. Consistent expectations help most pupils; the question is fit and adaptation, not removal.

•  NOT a request for 'special treatment'. The code of behaviour should allow for individual needs — check the school's code and NEWB (2008) guidelines.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: star charts and 'time out' used with children who do not yet understand delayed rewards or reflection — the system asks for developmental skills not yet present.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: class-wide colour or points charts; the same pupil 'on red' daily loses motivation and becomes the class's identified 'bad child'.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: detention and suspension cycles; a pupil who wants to avoid class may be rewarded by removal. Part D: check the discipline record and whether it is all classes or some.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: course or workplace conduct procedures; the question is whether reasonable accommodations are in place.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: token economies and reward systems need to be individualised to the pupil's understanding and motivators; check staff consistency (Part D).

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  DLD

•  Intellectual Disability

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  MAP THE SYSTEM: what are the rules, rewards and sanctions? How is the pupil's behaviour recorded? Read the code of behaviour and any class systems.

•  COUNT: how often in a week does the pupil receive a reward vs a sanction? How often is feedback public vs private? Is praise specific? A pupil who never earns a reward is outside the system.

•  Look at the discipline record over time: are sanctions escalating without change in behaviour? That is data that the system is not working for this pupil (Maag, 2001).

•  Ask the pupil: 'What happens when you get a detention? What would make you want to earn the rewards?' — reveals whether the rewards are rewarding and the sanctions are aversive for them.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  ADAPT WITHIN THE WHOLE-SCHOOL CODE: an individual plan with reachable targets (shorter intervals, smaller steps), rewards that matter to this pupil, and private feedback — while keeping the same expectations.

•  STOP WHAT RE-TRIGGERS: remove the pupil from public charts or use a private tracking card; avoid sanctions that function as escape.

•  INCREASE SPECIFIC POSITIVE FEEDBACK: praise the targeted behaviour quickly and specifically. The often-quoted ratios of praise to reprimand are widely cited — check the evidence before quoting a figure.

•  BUILD SKILLS THE SYSTEM ASSUMES: waiting, self-monitoring, asking for help — teach them directly (Greene, 2008).

•  SYSTEM-LEVEL FEEDBACK: where several pupils are failing in the same way, raise it as a whole-school issue (Part D: whole-school policy and practice — a systemic change area) with the principal.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support for an individual plan within the system; consider staff training need identified through casework (Part D).

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'The school's system works well for most children. For him, it isn't working — he's on red most days and has stopped trying. We're going to adapt it so he can succeed within it.'

•  'Rewards only work if he can earn them and wants them. We'll ask him what matters to him.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Your system works for the class — the problem is he's never going to reach the reward at the moment, so it isn't motivating him. Can we give him a smaller target he can hit today?'

•  'Detention seems to be rewarding him with time away from Irish. Is there a consequence that keeps him in the lesson?'

•  'A private card on his desk instead of his name on the chart will get you the same information without the audience.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'We're making you a special card so you can collect stickers for the things you're getting better at.'

•  OLDER: 'The system in school doesn't seem to be working for you — you're getting more detentions and nothing's changing. Let's work out what would actually help.'

•  ASK: 'What would make it worth your while?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — escalating suspensions, repeated exclusion from class or open-ended reduced timetables: review whether the pupil's needs are being met and whether statutory guidance is followed (Education (Welfare) Act 2000; Circular 0047/2021 on reduced school days, which requires notification to Tusla — check for revisions).

•  WATCH — a pupil identified by peers as 'the bad one': risk of social exclusion and bullying; protect their standing.

•  BOUNDARY — your role is to consult and advise; decisions on sanctions and the code

presentation.name: Escalation and de-escalation pattern
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The predictable SEQUENCE a pupil's incidents follow, from calm through build-up to peak and back. Colvin and Scott (2015) describe seven phases: calm, trigger, agitation, acceleration, peak, de-escalation and recovery. Kaplan and Wheeler (1983) described a similar 'assault cycle' (trigger, escalation, crisis, recovery, post-crisis depression).

•  The key insight: what helps is DIFFERENT AT EACH PHASE. Reasoning works when calm; distraction and choices work in agitation; at the peak only safety matters; recovery needs low demand; and learning from the incident happens only when fully calm.

•  Each pupil's pattern has its own signs (going quiet, pacing, swearing under the breath, pushing work away) and its own timescale. Mapping the individual pattern lets staff intervene early, when the least intrusive response still works.

•  A descriptive presentation, not a diagnosis (Part D, 2.1 — added). It is a tool for planning, and applies whatever the underlying reason for the behaviour.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT 'out of the blue'. Incidents that seem sudden usually have earlier signs that were missed, or a setting event (bad night, row at home) that shortened the build-up. Ask what happened earlier.

•  NOT stopped by more words at the peak. Adult talking, questioning and demands during acceleration and peak commonly escalate further (Colvin & Scott, 2015).

•  NOT finished when the pupil is quiet. Recovery is fragile; pushing for a debrief or consequence too soon often triggers a second peak.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: tantrum cycles are developmentally typical; the pattern still helps adults co-regulate early and avoid prolonging the peak.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: incidents in class and yard with visible build-up (fidgeting, refusal, raised voice); SNA or teacher often able to intervene early if signs are known.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: faster escalation in front of peers; face-saving drives the acceleration phase — private, choice-based responses matter most. Physical size raises staff anxiety, which can escalate the adult too.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: self-knowledge of one's own pattern and early exit strategies are the main tools.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: incidents can be intense and frequent; a written individual crisis plan, staff training and post-incident review are essential. Behaviour against the setting baseline (Part D).

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Intermittent Explosive Disorder

•  Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder

•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  Autism

•  ADHD

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Incident timeline analysis: for three or four recent incidents, reconstruct minute by minute what the pupil did and what adults did — where did it turn, and what brought it down?

•  Staff interview: 'What are the first signs? What have you tried at each point? What made it worse?' Use Colvin and Scott's phases as the interview frame.

•  Pupil interview when calm: 'What does it feel like in your body at the start? What helps you come back down? What makes it worse?' — many pupils can describe their own pattern.

•  Frequency and intensity record over time (e.g., a simple 1–5 intensity scale) so the plan can be reviewed against data.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  WRITE A PHASE-BY-PHASE PLAN in the Student Support File: for each phase, what the pupil's signs are and what adults do. Share with every adult who works with the pupil.

•  EARLY PHASES (trigger, agitation): notice and name gently; offer a choice or a break; reduce the demand temporarily; move closer calmly; avoid public confrontation.

•  ACCELERATION AND PEAK: few words, calm tone, space; remove the audience (move other pupils, not the pupil) where safe; follow the school's crisis procedures. Physical intervention only as a last resort to prevent harm, in line with school policy and the Department of Education's Understanding Behaviours of Concern and Responding to Crisis Situations guidelines (12/12/2024 — check for update circulars); record and report every use.

•  DE-ESCALATION AND RECOVERY: low-demand activity, water, quiet; do not debrief or deliver consequences yet.

•  AFTER: a restorative conversation when fully calm; a staff debrief; update the plan. Staff wellbeing matters — incidents are stressful for adults too.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support Plus when incidents involve risk of harm; involve CAMHS or other agencies as indicated (Part D).

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Her incidents follow the same pattern each time — there are early signs we can spot, and what helps is different at each stage. We're writing a plan so every adult responds the same way.'

•  'What do you see at home before things blow up? That helps us catch it earlier here.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'At the peak, less is more — fewer words, more space. The talking and consequences come later.'

•  'His early sign is going very quiet and pushing his book away. That's the moment to offer the break — not when he's already shouting.'

•  'After an incident, give him twenty minutes of something easy before any conversation. If we push too soon, it starts again.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'When you get really cross, it's like a volcano. Let's work out what the rumbling looks like before it erupts, so we can help you cool it down.'

•  OLDER: 'Everyone has a pattern when they lose it. If we know yours, you and the teachers can stop it before it gets big. What does the start feel like?'

•  ASK: 'What's the one thing adults do that makes it worse?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — injury to the pupil or others, or use of restraint or seclusion: follow school procedures, record, inform parents, and review the plan urgently; check compliance with current Department of Education guidance.

•  RED FLAG — self-harm during or after incidents, or statements of wanting to die: same-day risk procedure; supervision follows action, never replaces it.

•  WATCH — incidents incre

presentation.name: Behaviour as communication of an unmet learning need
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.1 Behaviour in class)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  The hypothesis that a pupil's behaviour is — wholly or partly — a response to learning demands they cannot meet: disrupting to avoid reading aloud, clowning to deflect from not understanding, refusing to write because writing is exhausting. Part D's instruction: 'always test this hypothesis'.

•  Language is the most frequently missed need: Hollo, Wehby and Oliver (2014) found in a meta-analysis that a large proportion of children with emotional and behavioural disorders had language deficits that had not been identified (exact proportion — check before quoting).

•  Literacy difficulties are over-represented among young people in the youth justice system (Snowling et al., 2000) and pupils at risk of exclusion have high rates of language difficulty (Clegg et al., 2009) — the behaviour gets noticed, the learning need does not.

•  Greene (2008) frames it as 'lagging skills and unsolved problems': behaviour shows up where demands exceed skills. A descriptive presentation, not a diagnosis (Part D, 2.1).

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT an excuse for behaviour. The learning need explains it; it does not remove the need for expectations and consistent responses. Both are addressed.

•  NOT always the answer. Some behaviour is unrelated to learning — testing the hypothesis means being willing to reject it.

•  NOT confined to low-attaining pupils. Able pupils with a specific difficulty (e.g., dyslexia masked by strong verbal ability) or pupils who are under-challenged may also communicate through behaviour.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: behaviour often reflects language delay — frustration when not understood or when not understanding. Hearing checks and SLT referral are first steps.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: behaviour clustering in literacy or maths lessons, at reading aloud or writing tasks; work avoidance strategies (sharpening pencils, toilet trips, disruption).

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: subject-specific patterns (fine in PE and practical subjects, not in text-heavy ones); face-saving — being 'bad' is preferable to being seen as 'stupid'.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: disengagement from courses; unidentified literacy or language needs underlying dropout — ask directly.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: check that communication and learning demands match the pupil's level; behaviour may indicate a task is too hard or poorly understood, or that the pupil lacks a means to say so (AAC review).

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  DLD

•  Dyslexia

•  Specific Learning Disorder with impairment in mathematics (dyscalculia)

•  Intellectual Disability

•  ADHD

•  Hearing impairment (medical)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  THE ROUTINE CHECK: for every behaviour referral, screen literacy (e.g., WIAT-III UK reading and spelling), numeracy and language (receptive and expressive), and ask about hearing and vision checks.

•  Scatterplot and ABC data by lesson and task type: does behaviour cluster around reading, writing, listening to long explanations, or specific subjects?

•  Subject-teacher survey at post-primary (Part D): is it all classes or some? What distinguishes the classes where behaviour is fine?

•  Work samples compared with the class: can the pupil actually do the task set? Ask the pupil privately to read a passage from their textbook.

•  Pupil interview: 'What's the hardest thing about English? What do you do when you don't understand?'

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  MATCH THE TASK TO THE PUPIL'S LEVEL: differentiate so the pupil can succeed with effort; provide access supports (read-aloud, word banks, visual supports) — then review whether behaviour changes.

•  TEACH THE MISSING SKILL: targeted literacy, numeracy or language intervention at School Support; refer to SLT (Primary Care or CDNT) where language need is identified; audiology where hearing is in question.

•  SAVE FACE: avoid public reading aloud or board work without preparation; allow the pupil to rehearse; offer choices of how to show learning.

•  RECORD THE LINK in the Student Support File: behaviour targets and learning targets side by side, reviewed together.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support for targeted learning intervention; School Support Plus where outside agency assessment (SLT, NEPS assessment) is needed.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'His behaviour is worst in English and when he has to read aloud. When I checked, his reading is well behind — I think some of the messing is to avoid being seen to struggle.'

•  'That doesn't excuse the behaviour, but it tells us where to put our effort. If we help with the reading, the behaviour often settles too.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Can we check whether she can actually read the worksheet? If not, the behaviour makes sense — she's covering.'

•  'He's fine in woodwork and PE, and it goes wrong in the text-heavy subjects. That's a strong clue.'

•  'Try giving him the reading in advance, or reading it to the group, and see whether the disruption changes. That's a quick test of the idea.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Sometimes when work is too hard, people do other things to get away from it. Is that what happens for you sometimes?'

•  OLDER: 'A lot of people would rather get in trouble than let others see they're finding something hard. That makes sense. If the work was more doable, would things be different?'

•  ASK: 'What would you like teachers to know about how you learn?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  WATCH — a pupil with escalating behaviour who has never had a language, literacy or hearing assessment: this is a gap to close before behaviour-focused intervention continues.

•  WATCH — suspensions or reduced timetables that remove the pupil from the lessons where the learning need is greatest: the learning gap widens.

•  BOUNDARY — do not attribute all behaviour to a learning need without evidence; state the hypothesis and how you tested it.

11 · QUESTIONS YOU WILL BE ASKED — AND THE ANSWER
•  Q: 'He's just lazy — why test his

presentation.name: Harmful or sexualised behaviour in children
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Sexual behaviour by a child or young person that is developmentally unexpected, involves coercion, secrecy or an imbalance of power or age, or causes harm to themselves or others. Part D: 'Not a DSM diagnosis'. The term 'harmful sexual behaviour' (HSB) is used in UK and Irish guidance to describe behaviour, not to label the child.

•  Much sexual behaviour in children is NORMAL and HEALTHY for their age (curiosity about bodies, self-touching in young children). Hackett (2014) describes a continuum from normal through inappropriate, problematic and abusive to violent; the Brook Traffic Light Tool (Brook, 2012) gives age-banded examples of green, amber and red behaviours to support professional judgement.

•  NICE (2016) guidance on harmful sexual behaviour among children and young people emphasises a proportionate response, early help for lower-level concerns, and specialist assessment for more serious behaviour.

•  Children who show HSB may themselves have experienced abuse, neglect, trauma or exposure to sexual content — the behaviour can be both a risk to others and an indicator of harm to the child. Hackett (2014) reviews the evidence on this overlap. It is always a child protection matter as well as a behaviour matter.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a prediction of adult sexual offending. Research on young people who have displayed HSB reports that most do not go on to sexually reoffend (Caldwell, 2010 — check the rate before quoting). Avoid language like 'offender' or 'predator' for children.

•  NOT something the EP investigates. Establishing what happened is for Tusla and, where relevant, An Garda Síochána. The EP does not interview the child about the details of alleged incidents.

•  NOT the same at every age. Behaviour that is typical in a four-year-old (curiosity, showing) may be concerning in a twelve-year-old; context, age gap, coercion and persistence are what matter.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: touching own genitals, curiosity about others' bodies, playing 'doctors' with same-age peers are usually developmentally typical (green). Concerns: persistent behaviour despite redirection, sexual knowledge beyond age, coercion or distress.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: increased privacy is typical. Concerns: sexual behaviour with much younger children, force or secrecy, explicit sexual language or acts, simulating adult sexual activity.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: sexual interest and consensual relationships between peers are typical. Concerns: coercion, significant age gap, sharing intimate images (distributing an intimate image without consent is an offence under the Harassment, Harmful Communications and Related Offences Act 2020; any sexual image of an under-18 also falls under the Child Trafficking and Pornography Act 1998, as amended — treat as a child protection matter, not only a behaviour one), online exploitation.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: adult services and criminal justice frameworks apply; the EP role is limited to educational settings where relevant.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: pupils with intellectual disability or autism may show sexual behaviour in public due to limited understanding of social rules, and are also more vulnerable to abuse. Relationships and sexuality education adapted to their level is protective; assess understanding carefully.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Conduct Disorder

•  Intellectual Disability

•  Autism

•  ADHD

•  Post-traumatic stress disorder / trauma-related presentations

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  NOT an assessment of the behaviour itself — your role is to contribute to understanding the child's needs once child protection procedures are underway, and to support the school.

•  Use a shared framework (Brook Traffic Light Tool; Hackett's continuum) to help staff describe the behaviour and its context factually: age, developmental level, frequency, coercion, secrecy, age gap, response to redirection.

•  Record what was seen and said verbatim, with date, time and who was present; do not ask leading questions.

•  Once safe, and in coordination with Tusla/specialist services, contribute to understanding the child's learning, language, social and emotional needs (e.g., SDQ, BASC-3, adaptive measures where relevant).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CHILD PROTECTION FIRST: follow Children First: National Guidance (2017) and the Child Protection Procedures for Primary and Post-Primary Schools (Department of Education, 2017; revised 2023 — check current version). Inform the DLP; as a mandated person, report to Tusla as soon as practicable — telling the DLP does not discharge your duty.

•  SAFETY PLAN for ALL children involved — the child who displayed the behaviour and any children affected: supervision arrangements, toileting and changing, yard and transitions, online use at school.

•  SPECIALIST INVOLVEMENT: Tusla and specialist HSB services where available (availability varies — check locally); CAMHS where there are mental health needs.

•  EDUCATION: age- and developmentally-appropriate relationships and sexuality education and body safety teaching (e.g., the Stay Safe programme in primary; RSE within SPHE) — for the whole class, not singling out.

•  SUPPORT THE CHILD'S EDUCATION: keep the child in education with appropriate supervision; avoid exclusion unless safety requires it, and plan any restriction with the relevant agencies.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support Plus — this always involves outside agencies.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'I know this is very hard to hear. Some sexual behaviour is normal for children's ages, and some isn't — what's happened is beyond what we'd expect, so the school has to follow child protection procedures. That's a requirement, not a judgement of you.'

•  'Children who behave this way can be helped, and most do not go on to harm others as adults. The aim is to keep everyone safe and get the right support.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Write down exactly w

presentation.name: Adolescent substance misuse / dual diagnosis
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A description of a young person's use of alcohol, cannabis, nicotine/vapes or other drugs that is affecting school, relationships, safety or health. Part D lists it as 'Not a standalone diagnosis' — a Substance Use Disorder is diagnosed by CAMHS or addiction services, never by the EP.

•  'DUAL DIAGNOSIS' means a mental health difficulty and a substance use difficulty occurring together. Each tends to worsen the other, and young people often fall between mental health and addiction services — which is why it is named separately.

•  Hawkins, Catalano and Miller (1992) set out the risk and protective factors framework still used in prevention: early conduct problems, school failure, low commitment to school, peer use and family conflict raise risk; attachment to school and a warm adult lower it. Several of these are things a school can move.

•  For the EP the question is rarely 'is this addiction?' It is: what is the use DOING for this young person (coping, belonging, sleep, numbing), what is it costing in school, and is anyone at risk right now?

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT NEPS work to screen, assess or treat. Part D (Adolescent, 2.2): 'substance screening is not NEPS work — refer.' Your role is to notice, describe school impact, hold the safeguarding line and connect the family to the right service.

•  NOT simply a behaviour problem to be handled by the code of behaviour. Suspension alone can remove the one protective factor (attachment to school) the young person still has; the evidence on school connectedness points the other way.

•  NOT confidential between you and the student when there is risk. Use by a child is a welfare matter; significant harm triggers Children First (DCYA, 2017) and the Tusla route regardless of what was promised.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: not a presentation of the child. What you may see is the impact of a PARENT's substance use — neglect indicators, missed appointments, chaotic drop-off. That is a child protection matter (Children First; Tusla), not this presentation.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: use by the child is rare and is ALWAYS a welfare concern — ask who supplied it and who is supervising. Older siblings, exploitation and access at home are the usual routes. Tusla consultation, same day.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: the core band. Watch for a drop in attendance, a new peer group, lateness after lunch, sleep in class, money problems, and grades that fall across all subjects at once rather than one.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: usually adult addiction or mental health services; in further education, the EP's role is signposting and supporting course retention. Part D: 'Not typically a NEPS referral at this band.'

•  SPECIAL SETTING: young people with intellectual disability or autism may be targeted or exploited to carry or use substances; treat any indication as a safeguarding concern first.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Substance use disorders (alcohol, cannabis, opioid, stimulant, tobacco, inhalant, sedative, hallucinogen)

•  Conduct Disorder

•  ADHD

•  Major Depressive Disorder

•  Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

•  Gambling Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Gather the SCHOOL picture, not a drug history: attendance pattern by day and period, incident record, year-head notes, change in attainment across subjects, who the young person is with at break (Part D: corridor and break observation where possible · pupil interview · school incident record).

•  Pupil interview using a motivational interviewing stance (Miller & Rollnick, 2013): curiosity, not interrogation. 'What does it do for you? What does it cost you?' The young person's own account of the function is the most useful formulation data.

•  Screen for what sits underneath: low mood, trauma, anxiety, ADHD, an unidentified learning need. RCADS self-report or MFQ can describe mood; they do not assess substance use.

•  Establish RISK before anything else: self-harm, suicidal ideation, overdose, driving, exploitation, debt to dealers, sexual risk. Any one of these moves you to the same-day route.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  RISK FIRST: where there is immediate risk — overdose, suicidal ideation, exploitation, abuse — the same-day risk / child protection route applies. Report to Tusla as soon as practicable; telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's own duty (Children First Act 2015). Supervision follows the action; it does not replace it.

•  REFER through the family to the GP and to local HSE youth drug and alcohol / adolescent addiction services; for a co-occurring mental health difficulty, CAMHS. Service names and thresholds vary by CHO area — check locally before naming one in a report.

•  KEEP THE YOUNG PERSON IN SCHOOL: recommend the school weighs any sanction against the protective value of attendance and a trusted adult. A named key adult and a regular brief check-in are School Support Plus-level actions.

•  ADDRESS THE FUNCTION: if use is managing anxiety, sleep or low mood, recommend that the underlying need is supported in school (counselling, SPHE, student support team) while the specialist service works on the use.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: School Support Plus — outside agencies involved, a coordinated plan held by the student support team, with parents.

•  DO NOT give advice on medication or withdrawal, and do not agree to 'keep it between us'. DO NOT recommend drug-testing in school — that is outside the EP role and outside NEPS work.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'What we're seeing in school — the missed afternoons, the tiredness, the grades dropping everywhere at once — fits with what you've told me about the cannabis. I'm not the person who assesses the drug use itself, but I can help you get to the service that does.'

•  'Often the drug is doing a job for a young person — helping them sleep, or switching off worry. The service will look at both, and school will look at what's making the day hard.'

•  SIGNPOST

presentation.name: Unstructured time
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A pupil who copes in the structured classroom but whose difficulties cluster in UNSTRUCTURED time — yard, lunch, corridors, lining up, changing rooms, the bus queue. Part D names it 'Unstructured time — yard and corridor as the difficulty'.

•  The difficulty sits in the INTERACTION between the child and the demands of that time: no adult direction, fluid rules, noise and space, fast-moving peer negotiation, and less supervision. Blatchford (1998) showed breaktime is where much of children's social life — and conflict — happens.

•  The key finding is the CONTRAST: Part D (School Age, 2.2) — 'compare classroom vs yard — the difference is the finding.' A child who is fine at 10:45 and in trouble at 11:05 is telling you about the setting, not only about themselves.

•  Often the first place a social communication difficulty, a motor difficulty or anxiety shows, because the classroom scaffolds had been hiding it.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT evidence that the child is 'fine really and just choosing to misbehave at break'. The classroom supplies structure the child may rely on; its absence is the variable.

•  NOT solved by removing yard time. Keeping a child in removes exercise, peer contact and the chance to learn the skills; Baines and Blatchford (2019) report breaktimes have already been shortened in many schools — check your school's current times before assuming.

•  NOT automatically bullying — but check. Unstructured time is where bullying most often happens (Olweus, 1993), and a child reacting to provocation can look like the aggressor.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: free play and outdoor time in preschool. Snatching, running off and difficulty joining play are developmentally common — Part D: 'describe rather than classify'.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: the peak referral band. Games with shifting rules (tag, football), lining up, and the return to class after yard are the hot spots. Watch the first five minutes back in the room.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: corridors between classes, lunch, the canteen, toilets and the walk to and from school. More movement, less supervision, larger peer groups and online spill-over.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: canteen, common rooms and gaps in a college timetable; isolation is more common than conflict. Rarely a NEPS referral at this band.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: Part D — 'Break-time structure in the setting · supported vs unsupported time · staffing at transitions.' Compare the child in supported versus unsupported time.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

•  Developmental Language Disorder (DLD)

•  Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia)

•  Conduct Disorder

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Yard observation with event or frequency recording (Part D, School Age): what happens, where, with whom, how long into break, and what the adult on duty did. Observe more than one break — Monday and Friday differ.

•  A simple map of the yard or corridor with incidents plotted on it. Clusters by location (behind the shed, the stairwell) or by time point to setting changes.

•  Pupil interview with a map: 'Show me where break is good. Show me where it goes wrong.' Friendship mapping or a sociogram at School Age (Part D).

•  SDQ peer problems subscale (teacher and parent) for the social picture; incident log analysed by time of day and period.

•  Check for an unmet need the yard exposes: social communication (autism assessment route), motor skill in games (DCD route), language for negotiating rules (DLD), or anxiety.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  ADD STRUCTURE TO THE TIME, NOT THE CHILD: structured games or a games leader for part of break, a choice of a quieter zone (library, club, garden), a clear 'start and end' routine for yard.

•  PRE-CORRECTION AND ACTIVE SUPERVISION: a brief rule reminder before going out, and supervising adults who move, scan and interact. Lewis, Colvin and Sugai (2000) found pre-correction plus active supervision reduced problem behaviour at recess.

•  PLANNED TRANSITION BACK: a calm-down routine or a job on the way back into class; a key adult who meets the pupil at the door after lunch.

•  SKILL-TEACHING WHERE THE GAP IS: teach the specific game rules, joining-in phrases or conflict scripts in a quiet moment, then practise them with adult support in the yard.

•  CONTINUUM LEVEL: Classroom Support / School Support for most; School Support Plus if incidents involve injury or outside agencies. Put the break-time plan in the Student Support File, including who is on duty.

•  DO NOT recommend loss of yard as a standing sanction; if a quiet alternative is offered, it is a CHOICE with a planned return, reviewed after 4–6 weeks.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'In class, the teacher is running the show and he knows what's expected. At break the rules change every few minutes, and that's where he struggles. It's the setting, not a sign he's a bad child.'

•  'We're going to add some structure to his break rather than take break away. He needs the run-around and the practice with other children.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'Look at the incident log by time — nearly everything is at lunch or straight after. That tells us where to put the support.'

•  'He doesn't know how to join a game that's already started. Teaching him one phrase and having the yard adult help him use it is worth more than another sanction.'

•  'The five minutes after yard are when it spills over. A job to do on the way in gives him a landing strip.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Some children find the yard tricky because the games keep changing. Let's make a plan for what you can do at break.'

•  OLDER: 'Loads of people find the corridors and lunch harder than class — no one's telling you what to do and it's loud. Where's the easiest place for you to be?'

•  ASK: 'If break was perfect, what would you be doing, and who with?'

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED F

presentation.name: Supervision ratio and yard layout
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  A SYSTEMIC presentation: the difficulty is located in how break time is staffed and how the physical space is laid out, rather than in one pupil. Part D lists it under 2.2 so that the EP asks the question before formulating a child.

•  Covers: how many adults are on duty and where they stand; blind spots (behind buildings, toilets, bike shed, stairwells); crowding at pinch points (doors, the tuck shop, the one football pitch); whether zones exist for different activities; and how pupils line up and return.

•  Colvin, Sugai, Good and Lee (1997) showed ACTIVE supervision (moving, scanning, interacting) and pre-correction reduced problem behaviour at transitions — how adults supervise matters, not only how many there are.

•  It often explains why several unrelated referrals from one school all mention lunchtime.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a criticism of the staff on duty. Supervision is usually a rota squeezed between other duties; the EP's job is to help the school see the pattern, not to allocate blame.

•  NOT a matter with a single 'correct' ratio. No national yard supervision ratio is stated here — schools set supervision under their own policy and Board of Management arrangements. Check the school's policy rather than quoting a figure.

•  NOT a replacement for looking at the individual child. A systemic fix may resolve most incidents; a pupil who still struggles in a well-supervised yard needs their own formulation.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: preschool ratios are set by regulation for the setting as a whole (Child Care Act 1991 (Early Years Services) Regulations 2016, inspected by Tusla — check the current ratios before quoting); outdoor layout — bikes crossing the sandpit — matters as much as numbers.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: infants and senior classes sharing one yard; a single football pitch; lining up at one door. Staggered breaks and zoned yards are the common changes.

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: corridors, stairwells, locker areas and off-site lunch. Supervision is thinner and movement constant; toilets and the space between buildings are typical blind spots.

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: supervision is not the model; the issue becomes access to quiet spaces and social hubs. Rarely a NEPS question.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: Part D — 'supported vs unsupported time · staffing at transitions'. SNA deployment at break (often when SNAs take their own breaks) is frequently the gap.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  ADHD

•  Autism

•  Conduct Disorder

•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  Developmental Coordination Disorder (dyspraxia)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Walk the yard WITH a staff member during break and after it. Sketch the layout: entrances, zones, where adults stand, where incidents cluster.

•  Plot the school's incident log onto the map by location and time. Three incidents in the same corner are a layout finding.

•  Ask pupils (a class group or pupil council): 'Where is the yard good? Where do you avoid? Where do adults never go?' They know the blind spots.

•  Look at the rota: who is on duty, where, for how long, and what they are asked to do (e.g., also covering the canteen, also on their own lunch).

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  ZONE THE SPACE: separate areas for ball games, quiet play and structured games; rotate pitch access by class. Make the rules of each zone visible.

•  ACTIVE SUPERVISION: duty adults move on a route that covers the blind spots, scan, and interact positively; brief all duty staff on the pre-corrections for the hot spots (Colvin et al., 1997).

•  STAGGER AND SPREAD: staggered breaks or staggered lining up where pinch points are the problem; a second door in use at the end of break.

•  WHOLE-SCHOOL LEVEL: this is a whole-school recommendation, made in consultation with the principal and staff — frame it within the school's code of behaviour and anti-bullying procedures (Bí Cineálta, 2024).

•  INDIVIDUAL PLANS SIT ON TOP: for a pupil still struggling, a School Support plan names where they are, with whom, and which adult is nearby.

•  DO NOT quote a supervision ratio or a regulation you have not checked; DO NOT recommend CCTV or other surveillance — that is a Board of Management and data-protection question, not a psychological one.

7 · EXPLAINING IT TO A PARENT
•  'Most of the difficulties happen in one corner of the yard where adults can't easily see. The school is looking at how the yard is set up, which should help him and other children too.'

•  'This doesn't mean nothing is being done for him individually — we'll still plan for his break times specifically.'

8 · EXPLAINING IT TO A TEACHER
•  'When I put the incident log onto a map of the yard, nearly all of it was behind the prefab and at the back door when lining up. That's a layout problem we can fix more easily than a child problem.'

•  'Moving around and chatting to groups on duty seems to prevent more than standing at the door and responding — that's what the research on active supervision shows.'

9 · EXPLAINING IT TO THE CHILD
•  YOUNGER: 'Show me on this picture of the yard where you like to play, and where things go wrong.'

•  OLDER: 'If you were in charge of the yard, what would you change so fewer fights happen?'

•  ASK: 'Where do the teachers never go?' — the most useful single question in this presentation.

10 · RED FLAGS
•  RED FLAG — repeated injury, sexualised behaviour, or bullying in an identified blind spot: this is a safeguarding and anti-bullying matter, not only a layout issue — inform the principal and DLP, and where harm meets the threshold, report to Tusla as soon as practicable (telling the DLP does not discharge a mandated person's duty).

•  WATCH — children with physical or sensory needs in a crowded yard (a wheelchair user at a pinch point; a child with visual impairment near ball games): risk assessment by the school.

•  BOUNDARY — the EP advises; staffing decisions, rotas and physical changes belong to the

presentation.name: Group dynamics and peer influence
presentation.code: No DSM code — a description, not a diagnosis · 2. BEHAVIOUR (2.2 Behaviour during break times and around the school)
presentation.text:
1 · WHAT IT IS
•  Behaviour that is best understood at the level of the GROUP rather than the individual: a pupil who behaves differently depending on who they are with, a class or friendship group that escalates together, a role the pupil holds in the group (clown, enforcer, follower, scapegoat).

•  Salmivalli et al. (1996) showed bullying is a group process with participant roles — bully, assistant, reinforcer, outsider, defender, victim. Most children in a bullying episode are not the bully or the victim, and their roles can be changed.

•  Peer influence is strongest in adolescence: Gardner and Steinberg (2005) found adolescents took more risks in a driving task when peers were present, and the peer effect was larger for adolescents than for adults.

•  Dishion, McCord and Poulin (1999) showed that grouping young people with conduct problems together can INCREASE problem behaviour ('deviancy training') — directly relevant when schools set up behaviour groups.

2 · WHAT IT IS NOT
•  NOT a reason to stop at 'he's easily led'. Ask what the group gives him — belonging, protection, status — and what he would lose by stepping out.

•  NOT only negative. Peer influence also drives prosocial behaviour; defenders, buddies and peer mentoring use the same process.

•  NOT solved by splitting everyone up without a plan. Separating a group without giving each member somewhere to belong often reforms the group elsewhere.

3 · HOW IT SHOWS AT EACH AGE
•  EARLY YEARS 0–5: play groups form and change quickly; copying is how young children learn. Describe; do not attribute intent.

•  SCHOOL AGE 6–12: stable friendship groups from middle primary; exclusion and 'ganging up' appear, especially among the older classes. Friendship mapping is informative (Part D, School Age).

•  ADOLESCENT 13–16: the peak. Status, reputation and online groups (group chats) shape behaviour in and out of school; risk-taking rises in the presence of peers (Gardner & Steinberg, 2005).

•  YOUNG ADULT 17–26: peer norms in college, work and social life; relevant mainly for substance use, risk and belonging. Rarely a NEPS referral at this band.

•  SPECIAL SETTING: small class groups mean one relationship can dominate the dynamic; pupils with social communication difficulties may be set up by peers to break rules without realising.

4 · OFTEN SITS BESIDE
•  Conduct Disorder

•  ADHD

•  Oppositional Defiant Disorder

•  Substance use disorders (alcohol, cannabis, opioid, stimulant, tobacco, inhalant, sedative, hallucinogen)

•  Social Anxiety Disorder (social phobia)

5 · HOW YOU DESCRIBE IT — ASSESSMENT
•  Observe the pupil with different groups (class, yard, a structured group task). Record who initiates, who reinforces (laughs, films, watches), and who withdraws.

•  Sociometric or friendship mapping (Part D, School Age) — handled ethically and privately; never displayed. At adolescence, a pupil interview about who they spend time with and why.

•  Incident log analysed by WHO WITH, not only what and when.

•  Pupil voice: 'Who are you when you're with them? Who are you on your own?' Adolescents can often describe the role they hold.

6 · RECOMMENDATIONS — WHAT YOU WRITE
•  CHANGE THE ROLES, NOT JUST THE PERSON: work with bystanders and potential defenders — whole-class work on how to respond when something happens (Salmivalli et al., 1996).
