method.name: Classroom observation
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
Systematic classroom observation has two roots that were joined only in the 1970s–80s: the naturalistic tradition of child study, and applied behaviour analysis.

NATURALISTIC ROOT — BARKER & WRIGHT (One Boy's Day, 1951) recorded a single child's entire day as a continuous 'specimen record' at the Midwest Psychological Field Station, Kansas. Barker's later ecological psychology (1968) introduced the 'behaviour setting': that classrooms produce behaviour as much as children do. This is the direct ancestor of narrative (running record) observation.

BEHAVIOURAL ROOT — BIJOU, PETERSON & AULT (1968, Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis) set out how to integrate descriptive field observation with experimental analysis, including the antecedent–behaviour–consequence record. Interval and time-sampling methods were refined in applied behaviour analysis through the 1970s; POWELL, MARTINDALE & KULP (1975) showed that partial-interval and whole-interval recording are biased estimators and momentary time sampling less so.

SCHOOL PSYCHOLOGY — structured coding systems followed, such as the BOSS (Behavioral Observation of Students in Schools; Shapiro, 2011 edition of the Academic Skills Problems Workbook), which builds momentary time sampling and a peer comparison into one protocol. Volpe et al. (2005) reviewed seven such coding schemes.

IN IRISH AND UK EP PRACTICE observation is usually embedded in consultation and the NEPS Continuum of Support rather than used as a standalone test. Frederickson & Cline (2015) place it inside an interactive, ecological account. See Reference Part A row 31 for the full teaching.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
Classroom observation is DESCRIPTIVE MEASUREMENT, not a standardised test. Unless you use a published coding system, there are no norms. Say so in the report.

INTER-OBSERVER AGREEMENT can be good when operational definitions are tight. Report it where you have it: percentage agreement = agreements ÷ (agreements + disagreements); Cohen's kappa corrects for chance and is the better statistic (Reference row 31). On placement you rarely have a second observer — say that rather than implying reliability.

TEMPORAL STABILITY IS THE WEAK POINT. Hintze (2005, School Psychology Review) is the standard reference: a single session is a poor estimate of a child's typical behaviour and several sessions are needed. How many depends on the behaviour and setting — number not stated here, check Hintze before quoting one.

SAMPLING BIAS IS KNOWN AND DIRECTIONAL (Powell et al., 1975; Cooper, Heron & Heward, 2020): partial-interval over-estimates, whole-interval under-estimates, momentary time sampling is least biased for 'how much of the time'.

OBSERVER EXPECTANCY — you read the referral first, so you tend to find it. Mitigation: definitions written in advance, a comparison peer on the same schedule, description separated from interpretation.

REACTIVITY — your presence changes the room. Report it, do not pretend it away (Reference row 31).

STRENGTH: ecological validity. It is the only method that samples the place the referral is about.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: referrals in NEPS areas 1.1 (attention, concentration, work skills), 2.1 (behaviour in class), 2.2 (behaviour at break) and 4.1 (friendships); any referral where the teacher's account and the child's test performance do not fit; any time you need a baseline to evaluate an intervention later (CORU 3.8).

WHY IT IS NEEDED: everything a teacher tells you is mediated by their interpretation; a WISC-V shows a child in a quiet room with one adult. Observation is your one chance at unmediated data from the setting where any recommendation will have to work.

IT ALSO TESTS THE ENVIRONMENT: seating, task demand, instruction pace, adult prompting, transitions. Without this, you produce a within-child formulation by default.

WHEN IT IS NOT THE RIGHT CHOICE: when the question is purely attainment (use curriculum-based and standardised measures); when the pupil is old enough to know why you are there and will perform (think post-primary — see Adolescent); when the teacher already has good frequency data and a further morning only confirms it; when there is a safeguarding concern — that goes to the risk route, not to more data gathering.

UNDER 5 OR IN FREE PLAY — use Structured play observation (Part H) instead.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
A REFERRAL QUESTION you can answer in one sentence, agreed with the teacher. If you cannot define the behaviour tightly enough to record it, the question is not yet clear — go back (Reference row 31).

AN OPERATIONAL DEFINITION SHEET: behaviour · counts as · does not count as · minimum duration · method · interval · comparison peer · setting · date. 'Off task' must say what counts, e.g. not looking at the work, the teacher or a helping peer for more than three consecutive seconds.

THE METHOD, CHOSEN IN ADVANCE, with a reason: narrative, event, duration, whole-interval, partial-interval, momentary time sampling, or ABC. A pre-printed grid.

A TIMER with a silent interval prompt (a phone vibration app works; no sound).

CONSENT: parent consent for EP involvement covering observation (CORU 1.15; PSI 1.3.4–1.3.5), the principal's and class teacher's agreement, and an agreed, TRUE introduction for the class that does not single the child out: 'I'm visiting to see how the class works.'

THE LESSON WHERE THE DIFFICULTY IS REPORTED, not the convenient one. Ask the teacher which slot shows it best and which shows it least — ideally observe both.

A COMPARISON PEER, chosen by the teacher as typical (not the most settled child), same sex where possible, seated comparably.

TIME: 20–30 minutes of recording after a settling period; two settings or two occasions minimum where possible. Know the school's child protection and lone-working arrangements before you sit down.

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Agree the question an

method.name: ABC functional analysis
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
TERMINOLOGY FIRST: what schools call 'ABC functional analysis' is usually DESCRIPTIVE FUNCTIONAL ASSESSMENT — recording antecedents, behaviour and consequences as they happen. Strictly, 'functional analysis' means EXPERIMENTAL manipulation of conditions. Use the terms carefully (Reference row 31, Stage 4).

B. F. SKINNER (Science and Human Behavior, 1953) set out the three-term contingency: behaviour is shaped by its consequences in the presence of antecedent stimuli.

BIJOU, PETERSON & AULT (1968, Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis) formalised the ABC narrative record as a way of integrating field observation with experimental analysis.

IWATA, DORSEY, SLIFER, BAUMAN & RICHMAN (1982; reprinted 1994 in JABA) developed experimental functional analysis for self-injury: brief conditions (attention, demand, alone, play) compared to identify the maintaining consequence.

CARR & DURAND (1985) showed that teaching a communicative replacement for the same function (functional communication training) reduced problem behaviour — the link from function to intervention.

O'NEILL, HORNER and colleagues (1990; 3rd ed. 2015) produced the practical handbook of interview, observation and hypothesis statements used in schools. Positive Behaviour Support (Carr et al., 2002) built this into a values-based framework.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
EXPERIMENTAL FUNCTIONAL ANALYSIS is the best-validated method of identifying function, with a large single-case literature (Hanley, Iwata & McCord, 2003, JABA review). It requires specialist training and is not a trainee EP method in Irish schools.

DESCRIPTIVE ABC RECORDING AGREES WITH EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS LESS OFTEN THAN PRACTITIONERS ASSUME (Thompson & Iwata, 2007, JABA), partly because attention follows most problem behaviour in classrooms whatever its function. Write 'consistent with', not 'the function is' (Reference row 31).

INDIRECT MEASURES (rating scales such as the Motivation Assessment Scale, Durand & Crimmins, 1988; QABF; FAST) are quick but their reliability and agreement with experimental analysis are mixed — check the psychometrics of any scale before citing it.

FUNCTION-BASED INTERVENTIONS tend to outperform non-function-based ones in the single-case literature; exact effect sizes vary by review — check before quoting.

SCHOOL FBA (Gresham, Watson & Skinner, 2001) is most defensible when interview, ABC recording across settings and days, and a hypothesis-driven plan with outcome monitoring are combined.

LIMITS: it describes observable contingencies, not internal states; one week of data is a sample; teacher-kept records are affected by who is recording and when.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: NEPS area 2.1 or 2.2 referrals where the question is WHY a specific behaviour keeps happening; behaviour that is frequent, disruptive, dangerous or leading to exclusion or reduced timetables; behaviour in children with limited language (special classes, special schools, autism, intellectual disability) where the behaviour may be communication; before any behaviour support plan at School Support Plus.

WHY: plans that do not match function can make behaviour worse — e.g. time-out for behaviour maintained by escape from demands rewards it. Function-based planning moves from 'stop this' to 'what does this get or avoid for the child, and how else can they get it?'

WHY IN IRELAND: the NEPS BESD Continuum guidelines (2010) describe ABC recording and hypothesis-based planning at school level; Reference Part D lists 'Functional behaviour assessment (ABC)' for School Age behaviour referrals.

WHEN IT IS NOT THE RIGHT CHOICE: when the difficulty is an unmet learning need (assess attainment first); when behaviour signals distress, trauma, anxiety or possible abuse — the function frame can miss the child's experience and safeguarding comes first; when the behaviour is rare (a record may never capture it); when the question is emotional rather than behavioural.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
A TIGHT DEFINITION of ONE target behaviour: 'throws objects (any item leaves his hand towards a person or wall)', not 'aggressive'. One behaviour at a time.

A SHORT FUNCTIONAL INTERVIEW with the teacher (and SNA, parent): when, where, with whom, during what, what happens after, what has been tried. O'Neill et al. (2015) include a structured interview form; the FACTS is a shorter school version — check current versions.

AN ABC GRID: date · time · setting/activity · who present · antecedent (what happened immediately before) · behaviour (exactly what) · consequence (what happened immediately after) · outcome for the child. Plus a SETTING EVENTS column: sleep, hunger, illness, a hard morning at home, a change of routine.

WHO RECORDS: usually the teacher or SNA over 5 school days, plus your own observation. Agree a realistic plan — a grid they will not fill in is no data.

A SCATTERPLOT (time of day × day of week) if you need to see when the behaviour clusters (Touchette, MacDonald & Langer, 1985).

CONSENT from parents for EP involvement and for staff recording about the child (CORU 1.15; PSI 1.3.4). Explain what the record is for.

SAFETY: know the school's crisis/safety plan and child protection route before you start.

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Define one behaviour, in observable terms, with the teacher.

STEP 2 — Functional interview (20–30 min): conditions when it is most and least likely; setting events; what happens after; what has been tried and with what effect; the child's strengths and preferences.

STEP 3 — Record across 5 school days (teacher/SNA) plus at least one EP observation: every episode, A–B–C in the moment or as soon as possible after. Record neutral facts: 'asked to open maths copy' not 'asked nicely'.

STEP 4 — Analyse: count episodes by antecedent type (demand, transition, peer, adult attention withdrawn, unstructured time), consequence type (attention given, task removed,

method.name: Report writing
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
The psychological report grew up alongside mental testing, and most of its known problems were described within fifty years of its start.

EARLY TESTING — Binet's and later Terman's work produced reports that were essentially lists of scores for a teacher or physician.

KLOPFER (1960), 'The Psychological Report' — one of the first books to treat the report as communication rather than record-keeping. It asked who reads the report and what they need from it.

TALLENT (1958; 4th ed. 1993) — criticised reports built on generic statements true of almost anyone, which he called the 'Aunt Fanny' report. This connects to the Barnum effect (Meehl, 1956; demonstrated by Forer, 1949).

EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY — reports gradually moved from test-by-test to domain-based and referral-question-based structures, with a formulation section (Lichtenberger et al., 2004).

IRELAND — for years NEPS and private reports were the gateway to resource teaching hours. The 2017 Special Education Teaching allocation model (Circulars 0013/2017 primary and 0014/2017 post-primary) removed that link, so reports now mainly inform the Continuum of Support rather than unlock hours. Reports are still read by SENOs, the NCSE, CDNTs and the SEC. Check what each one currently needs before promising a parent that 'the report will get them' anything.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
There is no reliability coefficient for a report. The evidence is about whether readers can understand and use it.

READABILITY — Harvey (1997, 2006) analysed school psychology reports and found their reading level well above that of most parents and many teachers. Jargon, long sentences and passive voice were the main causes. Check her papers for the exact figures before quoting them.

WHAT READERS PREFER — Pelco et al. (2009) asked teachers to rate different report styles. Teachers preferred reports organised around questions and recommendations over reports organised test by test. Check the paper for the exact comparisons before citing detail.

THE REPORTING DEBATE — Groth-Marnat and Horvath (2006) reviewed the current controversies: length, how much to report scores, and writing for the professional versus the lay reader. Their conclusion was to write for the actual reader and link every finding to the referral question.

BARNUM EFFECT (Forer, 1949; Meehl, 1956) — people accept vague personality descriptions as accurate about themselves. A report full of such statements feels right to the reader and says nothing.

CONFIRMATION BIAS — once a hypothesis is formed, clinicians look for evidence that supports it. Naming the disconfirming evidence (Monsen & Frederickson, 2008) is the report-level safeguard.

HONEST SUMMARY: the evidence consistently favours plain language, a question-led structure, integration rather than a list of tests, and recommendations that are specific and addressed to a named role.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: after every individual assessment, and after consultations where the service requires a written record. Report types widen across the three years; UCD Table 3 expects seven categories (Reference, macro 34).

WHY: the report outlives you on the case. Parents, teachers, SENOs, CDNT clinicians and the next EP will read it, sometimes years later (Reference, macro 34). CORU 5.27 requires reports that are clear, concise, accessible and accurate, suitable for the intended audience, and that justify the professional opinions in them.

COUNTERSIGNING STANDARD: your supervisor must be able to put their name to your reasoning, not just to your arithmetic. That is a higher bar than 'accurate'.

WHAT A REPORT IS NOT:
— a transcript of everything you did
— a place for information not germane to the purpose (PSI 1.2.1)
— a place for a medical or psychiatric diagnosis the EP did not and cannot make (PSI 2.2.2)
— a route for child protection information, which goes through the Children First channels, not a document circulated to the school

WHEN A SHORTER FORMAT FITS: a consultation record, a review note or a letter can be the right product when no individual assessment was done. Check the service's templates for each.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
RAW DATA, SCORED AND CHECKED TWICE: ages calculated correctly, the right norm tables, scores transcribed without error. A wrong score in a signed report is a serious error, and 'no score or name errors' is a named pass test (macro 34, CORU 2.8).

THE REFERRAL QUESTION, re-read before you write the conclusion (macro 34).

THE SERVICE TEMPLATE AND HOUSE STYLE: ask for the current version. Read five reports written by experienced EPs in this service before your first (macro 34 Block 1).

THE FORMULATION, drafted as a separate document first, with a named framework (Monsen, Interactive Factors, or Carr's 4 Ps).

A LIST OF SOURCES WITH DATES: parent interview, teacher consultation, pupil interview, observation, tests, school records.

THE CHILD'S OWN WORDS, verbatim from the pupil interview (UNCRC Art. 12; macro 34 Block 3).

CONSENT ON FILE for each person who will receive a copy.

GUARDIANSHIP: if the parents are separated, check who is entitled to a copy before sending.

TIME: allow 2–3 hours per report at first (macro 34 Block 2). Send it to your supervisor with the raw data and scoring, not just the draft (macro 34).

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Reason for referral. Write the question actually being answered, in one or two sentences. If it changed during the work, say so.

STEP 2 — Background. Give only what is relevant to the question (PSI 1.2.1). Summarise each source briefly and date it.

STEP 3 — What was done, and why. List each method with its date, and give a rationale for each tool — why this tool for this question (CORU 3.2; macro 34 Block 2). Record any adaptation to standard procedure.

STEP 4 — Findings, by source or domain. Describe the performance, then give the score, then say what it means. Give c

method.name: Graduated return (EBSA)
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
School non-attendance driven by distress has been described for about ninety years, under changing names.

BROADWIN (1932) described a form of truancy driven by anxiety. JOHNSON et al. (1941) called it 'school phobia' and located it in separation anxiety between mother and child.

BERG, NICHOLS and PRITCHARD (1969) gave the criteria still quoted for school refusal:
— severe difficulty attending, often with emotional upset
— the child stays at home with the parents' knowledge
— no significant antisocial behaviour
— parents have made reasonable efforts to get the child to school

KEARNEY and SILVERMAN (1990s) moved the focus from form to function. They proposed four reasons a child might avoid school: avoiding distress linked to school; escaping social or evaluative situations; seeking attention; and seeking rewards outside school. Kearney's School Refusal Assessment Scale–Revised (2002) measures these.

HEYNE et al. (2019) proposed a shared typology: school refusal, truancy, school withdrawal (the parent keeps the child home) and school exclusion.

'EMOTIONALLY BASED SCHOOL AVOIDANCE' (EBSA) became the UK EP term through West Sussex EPS guidance (West Sussex County Council, 2018; updated 2022).

IRELAND — NEPS published 'Managing Reluctant Attendance and School Avoidance Behaviour' good practice guides for primary and post-primary schools, with parent versions. The primary guide's layout is dated 10/2023; check the publication date on gov.ie. The guides use 'reluctant attendance and school avoidance behaviour' and include a 'Steps in a Gradual Return' template. The workbook lists EBSA as a descriptive presentation, not a DSM diagnosis (Part D, 3.6).

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
INTERVENTIONS — Maynard et al. (2018), a Campbell systematic review of psychosocial interventions for school refusal, found a small number of trials, mostly CBT with a graded exposure component. They reported improved attendance, a less clear effect on anxiety, and low to moderate study quality. Check the review for exact effect sizes before quoting them.

CBT TRIALS — King et al. (1998) and Heyne et al. (2002) tested child- and parent-focused CBT with graded return, with positive attendance outcomes in small samples. The children were mostly primary and early post-primary age.

FUNCTIONAL ASSESSMENT — the Kearney–Silverman functional model is widely used. However, the fit and usefulness of the four functions have been questioned (Heyne et al., 2019). Treat functions as hypotheses, not categories.

GRADED EXPOSURE — the core of graduated return. It rests on a large exposure-therapy evidence base for childhood anxiety in general, rather than on trials of school return specifically.

IRISH GUIDANCE — the NEPS good practice guides and the West Sussex guidance are practice guidance built on the research and consensus. They are not trials. Cite them as guidance.

OUTCOMES WITHOUT INTERVENTION — follow-up studies link persistent school refusal with later difficulties in education and mental health (Elliott & Place, 2019, review). Check before quoting any rate.

HONEST SUMMARY: moderate evidence that structured, graded, multi-component plans involving the child, parents and school improve attendance. The evidence is weaker for which component matters, and thin for adolescents with long absences.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: when a pupil has been consistently absent, or attends only partially, and the absence is driven by distress rather than truancy, parental withdrawal or illness. The NEPS guides say the gradual return template 'should only be used with pupils who have been consistently absent'. For emerging reluctance, act quickly with the whole-school and classroom strategies first; a staged return is not the first response.

WHY: avoidance is negatively reinforced. Each day at home relieves the distress, which makes the next day harder (the NEPS guide's cycle figure, adapted from West Sussex). A plan that increases time in school in steps the child can manage breaks that cycle. Waiting for the child to 'feel ready' usually makes it stronger.

WHY THE EP: formulating why this child avoids school — function, risk and protective factors, unmet learning need, relationships — is what makes the steps the right steps. NEPS describes its role at every level of the Continuum, from whole-school consultation to direct involvement at School Support Plus (NEPS guide, Appendix H).

WHEN IT IS NOT THE RIGHT RESPONSE, OR NOT YET:
— a safeguarding concern explains the absence (bullying, harm at home or school, a young carer)
— untreated physical illness has not been ruled out
— significant self-harm, suicidal ideation, an eating difficulty or psychosis is present: that needs the GP or CAMHS route first
— the absence is truancy or condoned absence, which needs a different formulation and response (Part D, 3.6)

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
ATTENDANCE DATA: days attended out of days possible (the NEPS referral form asks for this), plus patterns — which days, which lessons, late arrivals, time of day. Get the school's actual register, not an estimate.

ACCOUNTS COLLECTED SEPARATELY from the parent, the pupil and the teacher. They usually differ (Part D, 3.6). The NEPS guide provides an 'Information Gathering: School and Parent/Guardian Checklist' (Appendix A) and 'My Views About School' for the pupil (Appendix B).

A KEY SCHOOL CONTACT: a named adult the pupil trusts, ideally chosen with the pupil (NEPS guide, Step 2).

A HEALTH CHECK: has the GP seen the child about physical complaints? A graduated return is not planned around undiagnosed illness.

A RISK SCREEN: self-harm, suicidal ideation and safeguarding, asked about directly in the pupil interview.

THE LEGAL AND REPORTING POSITION:
— Under the Education (Welfare) Act 2000, s.21(4), the principal must notify TESS when a pupil's absences in a school year reach an aggregate of 20 days or more. (The NEPS guide says 'mor

method.name: Solution-focused pupil interview
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
Solution-Focused Brief Therapy was developed by STEVE DE SHAZER and INSOO KIM BERG with colleagues at the Brief Family Therapy Center, Milwaukee, from 1978 onwards.

It grew out of the Mental Research Institute brief therapy tradition in Palo Alto and from the work of MILTON ERICKSON, but broke from it by abandoning problem analysis altogether.

The founding observation was empirical rather than theoretical: de Shazer's team noticed that clients who described exceptions — times the problem did not occur — improved, regardless of whether anyone understood the cause.

The MIRACLE QUESTION was reportedly developed after a client, asked what would need to happen, replied that it would take a miracle. Berg formalised it.

Its arrival in educational psychology is largely through UK practice in the 1990s and 2000s. RHYDDERCH and GAMESON built constructionist assumptions into COMOIRA (2008), which is on the UCD handbook's named framework list.

It is widely used in NEPS practice and is within trainee competence with supervision — unlike most therapeutic models.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
The evidence base for SFBT is moderate and growing, with most trials in mental health rather than education.

Kim (2008) meta-analysed SFBT outcomes and found small but positive effects, strongest for internalising problems.

Gingerich & Peterson (2013) systematically reviewed 43 studies and concluded SFBT is effective across a range of problems, while noting methodological weaknesses in many of the studies.

Bond et al. (2013) reviewed SFBT specifically with children and families and found promising but limited evidence — 38 studies, most of modest quality.

BE HONEST ABOUT THIS IN REPORTS. The evidence supports SFBT as a reasonable approach, not as an established treatment. PSI 4.2.2 requires you not to exaggerate effectiveness.

Its practical advantage in schools is fit rather than superiority: it is brief, it does not require a diagnosis, it does not require you to work outside trainee competence, and it produces goals the school can act on.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: when you need the child's own account and their view of what would help; when the adults around the child disagree and you need a route that does not require deciding who is right; when time is short; when the referral is about motivation, confidence or school experience rather than a specific skill.

WHY: it puts the child's construction into the formulation, which every named framework requires and which trainee reports most often omit.

WHEN IT IS NOT RIGHT: where there is risk or a safeguarding concern — stop and follow the protocol. Where trauma is disclosed — that is outside trainee competence and needs referral. Where the child is not ready to talk; forcing it damages the relationship the school has to maintain.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
WHAT YOU NEED: a quiet room the child is not in trouble in. Twenty to thirty minutes. Paper and pen for scaling, or a printed scaling line.

Consent from parent, assent from the child, and a clear sentence about confidentiality and its limits, said BEFORE you start: 'What you say stays between us, unless you tell me something that makes me worried you or someone else isn't safe — then I'd have to tell someone who can help, and I'd tell you first.'

Optional and often useful with younger children: Blob Tree, How Do You Feel cards, or a simple drawn scale.

Know your referral route before you go in, in case something comes up.

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Set up. Explain who you are, why you're here, how long, and what happens to what they say. Ask if they have questions. Wait.

STEP 2 — Problem-free talk. Two or three minutes about something unrelated — what they like, what they're good at. This is not small talk; it establishes competence before difficulty.

STEP 3 — Best hopes. 'What are your best hopes from us talking today?' This sets the agenda as theirs.

STEP 4 — The preferred future or miracle question. 'Suppose tonight while you're asleep, the thing that's been hard just stopped being hard. You wouldn't know, because you were asleep. What's the first small thing you'd notice tomorrow morning that tells you something's different?'

STEP 5 — Exceptions. 'When has a bit of that already happened, even a little?' Follow every exception with 'how did you do that?'

STEP 6 — Scaling. 'On a line from 0 to 10, where 10 is that morning you just described and 0 is the opposite — where are you today?' Then: 'What put you at a 4 and not a 2?' NEVER ask what would get them to 10. Ask what one point up would look like.

STEP 7 — Close with a compliment that is specific and evidenced from what they said, and one small next step in their own words.

STEP 8 — Record verbatim where you can. Their words go in the report, not your paraphrase.

6 · EARLY YEARS 0–5
EARLY YEARS 0–5 — not appropriate in this form. The language demands are beyond most children under 6.

Substitute: play-based observation, and the adults' accounts. Where a young child can indicate preference, use pictures or objects rather than scaling.

If you use any scaling at all with a 5-year-old, use three points with faces, not 0–10.

7 · SCHOOL AGE 6–12
SCHOOL AGE 6–12 — this is where it works best in school settings.

Concretise everything. Use a drawn ladder or a line on paper rather than an abstract 0–10.

Shorten the miracle question: 'If tomorrow was a really good day at school, what would be different?'

Use 'how did you do that?' relentlessly after any exception — children rarely attribute success to themselves and the question does most of the therapeutic work.

Keep it to 20 minutes. Younger children tire and start agreeing with you.

8 · ADOLESCENT 13–16
ADOLESCENT 13–16 — works well, but the set-up matters more.

Be explicit that you are not there to report back to the school on what they say, within the confidentiality limits you have stated.

method.name: Parent feedback session
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
Feeding back assessment findings to families has no single originator. It comes from three traditions.

BREAKING NEWS IN MEDICINE — Buckman (1992) and the SPIKES protocol (Baile et al., 2000): Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and Summary. It was written for oncology. Its central move carries over directly: ask what the person already knows before you tell them anything.

THERAPEUTIC ASSESSMENT — Finn and Tonsager (1992, 1997) and Finn (2007) treated feedback as a collaboration: the client helps interpret the findings. Findings are ordered by how close they sit to the person's existing story about themselves.

CONSULTATION IN EP PRACTICE — UK consultation models (Wagner, 2000) moved EPs from the 'expert' position to joint problem-solving. The feedback meeting became shared sense-making rather than delivery of results.

IRISH CONTEXT — the Continuum of Support treats parents as partners in the Student Support Plan. Many services feed back to parents before or alongside the written report. Check your service's current order (feedback then report, or report then meeting) with your supervisor.

The workbook teaches this skill twice: at macro 22 (Intervention) and at macro 32 (Working with Others). It is the same skill evidenced for two competencies.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
There is no norm table for a feedback session. The evidence is about what helps information land, and about when feedback itself helps.

RECALL — Kessels (2003) reviewed evidence that patients forget much of what clinicians tell them, that what they recall is often inaccurate, and that anxiety makes recall worse. Implication: give the headline first, keep to a few messages, and send a written summary. Check the paper before quoting any recall percentage.

TEACH-BACK — health-literacy practice asks the person to explain the information in their own words. 'Does that make sense?' is not a check (Reference, macro 32).

THERAPEUTIC EFFECT — Finn and Tonsager (1992) randomised college students waiting for counselling to receive collaborative MMPI-2 feedback or attention only. The feedback group reported less distress and higher self-esteem. Poston and Hanson (2010) meta-analysed assessment with personalised, collaborative feedback and found a meaningful positive effect. Both used mostly adult clinical samples, so be cautious about applying them to parents in schools.

PARENTS' REACTIONS — grief-like responses to a child's disability are well described. Olshansky (1962) called it 'chronic sorrow', and it recurs at transitions. The evidence does not support fixed stage models, so never tell a parent which 'stage' they are in.

HONEST SUMMARY: the evidence is good that structure, plain language and checking improve understanding. The evidence for a therapeutic benefit is weaker and comes mostly from adults.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: after every individual assessment, before the written report is finalised where your service allows it, so the parent hears the findings from a person first. Also at Student Support Plan reviews, after an intervention block, and whenever a finding changes the family's picture of their child.

WHY — THE ETHICAL CASE: PSI 4.3.1 gives clients the right to an explanation of assessment results in language they understand. CORU 2.1 requires assessment findings to be communicated in a way the service user can understand. A report posted home meets neither on its own.

WHY — THE PRACTICAL CASE: parents carry out the home recommendations. They take the report to the next school, the SENO, the CDNT or the GP, and they advocate for the child for years after you have gone. A parent who leaves confused cannot do that. A parent who leaves feeling judged disengages from the school (Reference, macro 22).

WHEN TO ADAPT OR DELAY:
— A child protection concern has come up: follow the risk route first.
— Parents are separated and in conflict: check guardianship, and decide with your supervisor whether to hold joint or separate sessions.
— A parent is acutely unwell or intoxicated: reschedule.
— An interpreter is needed but not booked: do not go ahead with a family member interpreting, and never a child.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
THE FORMULATION, FINISHED — the meaning, not the scores. If you cannot answer the referral question in two sentences, you are not ready to meet the parent.

THE FIRST THREE SENTENCES, written down (Reference, macro 22 Block 1).

THE THREE HARDEST TRANSLATIONS, rehearsed. Typically 'percentile', 'below average range' and 'working memory'.

ONE EVIDENCED STRENGTH, taken from the assessment. An invented strength sounds like consolation and undermines everything else you say (macro 32).

DRAFT RECOMMENDATIONS, each naming a Continuum level and who does what, so the parent can react to them before they are final.

DECISIONS AGREED WITH YOUR SUPERVISOR:
— whether the school is in the room, and for which part (CORU 2.14 on power and authority)
— whether the child attends any part
— who leads which section
— what you will do if the parent disputes a finding

PRACTICAL: 45–60 minutes in a private room where the Principal will not walk through. Tissues and water. A one-page plain-language summary to hand over. If an interpreter is needed, book and brief them, and allow roughly double the time (CORU 2.5).

CONSENT AND GUARDIANSHIP: check that consent to share the report with the school or another service is current. If the parents are separated, check guardianship before you send anything.

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Open and contract. Thank them, say how long you have and who is present, and state the purpose. Then ask: 'Before I start, what are you hoping to hear today, and what's worrying you most?' This is SPIKES Perception and Invitation, and it meets PSI 1.4.1.

STEP 2 — Describe the child without numbers, in two sentences the parent would recognise (macro 32 Block 2).

STEP 3

method.name: Group intervention
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
Group work with children has three separate lineages, and the one you borrow from shapes what you think a group is for.

GROUP PSYCHOTHERAPY — Yalom (The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy, 1970; Yalom & Leszcz, 6th ed. 2020) named the therapeutic factors of groups: universality ('I'm not the only one'), instillation of hope, imparting information, altruism, interpersonal learning, group cohesiveness, among others. These are why a group can do what individual work cannot. Tuckman (1965, Psychological Bulletin) gave the forming–storming–norming–performing sequence still used to plan session arcs.

EDUCATIONAL AND NURTURE GROUPS — Marjorie Boxall set up the first nurture groups in inner London (ILEA) in 1969-70 for children whose early experiences left them unready for class (Bennathan & Boxall, 2000). Circle of Friends came from North American inclusion work and was adapted in UK EP practice (Newton, Taylor & Wilson, 1996; Frederickson & Turner, 2003).

MANUALISED CBT AND SEL PROGRAMMES — from the 1990s: FRIENDS (Barrett, Australia), Zippy's Friends (Partnership for Children, UK), Incredible Years small-group Dinosaur School (Webster-Stratton). Durlak et al. (2011) consolidated SEL evidence.

IRELAND — NEPS has trained teachers in FRIENDS programmes and Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management; Weaving Well-being and Zippy's Friends are used in Irish primary schools. Check which programmes your service currently supports before you offer one (Reference row 78).

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
Uneven, and you must say which part of it you are relying on (PSI 4.2.2; Reference row 78).

UNIVERSAL SEL — Durlak et al. (2011, Child Development, 213 programmes) found modest but real gains in social-emotional skills, behaviour and attainment. Implementation problems weakened outcomes; fidelity is the variable that predicts benefit (Durlak & DuPre, 2008).

TARGETED ANXIETY AND DEPRESSION PREVENTION — Werner-Seidler et al. (2017, Clinical Psychology Review) meta-analysed school-based prevention: small effects for both depression and anxiety; for depression, targeted programmes outperformed universal ones. Effect sizes: check the paper before quoting.

WHO DELIVERS MATTERS — Stallard et al. (2014, PACES trial, Lancet Psychiatry): universal FRIENDS delivered by health facilitators reduced anxiety; delivered by school staff it did not differ from usual PSHE. Training and support of the deliverer is part of the intervention (see Staff training, Part H).

MINDFULNESS — Kuyken et al. (2022, MYRIAD) found universal school mindfulness no better than usual provision for adolescents. Do not present it as established.

SOCIAL SKILLS GROUPS — modest effects, weak generalisation (Gresham, Sugai & Horner, 2001).

HARM — Dishion, McCord & Poulin (1999) documented deviancy training in groups of adolescents with conduct difficulties. Read it before you run any group.

IRISH TRIAL — Clarke, Bunting & Barry (2014) evaluated Zippy's Friends in disadvantaged Irish primary schools; read the outcomes and the implementation findings before citing.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: the same need is shared by several children in one school (anxiety about transfer, friendship difficulty in one class, bereavement after a death in the community, emotional literacy in an infant class); consultation shows the school wants to build its own capacity; individual referrals in one area keep arriving (NEPS areas 3.1 anxiety, 4.1 friendships, 2.2 behaviour at break).

WHY: a group reaches eight children for the cost of one assessment, and Yalom's universality factor ('other people feel this too') is only available in a group. It also leaves something behind: a trained co-facilitator and a set of materials (CORU 5.40).

CHOOSE THE TIER FIRST (Reference row 78): universal (whole class), targeted/selective (children identified as at risk), indicated (individual). If a third of the class shares the difficulty, it is a classroom problem and a targeted group mislabels it as a child problem.

WHEN IT IS NOT THE RIGHT CHOICE: a child at current risk of self-harm or in acute distress — individual work and the risk route first; a child whose difficulty would be amplified by grouping (conduct difficulties with similar peers); a school that cannot give a stable room, time slot and co-facilitator for the full programme; a request after a critical incident for a single-session 'debriefing' group — NEPS critical incident guidance favours psychological first aid and monitoring, not compulsory debriefing (check the current NEPS Critical Incident guidelines).

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
A NAMED NEED AND A TIER, agreed with the school in consultation, with the reason it is a group need.

A PROGRAMME OR PLAN with a stated evidence base and its core components identified from the manual — what must not be cut (Reference row 78, 'Adapt delivery').

A CO-FACILITATOR from the school (class teacher, SET, guidance counsellor, SNA where appropriate) who commits to every session and will run it after you.

MEMBERSHIP SCREENING: who is in, who is not, and why. Mix of presentations (not all withdrawn or all externalising). Size typically 6–8 for a targeted group; check the manual. Any child you screen out needs an alternative, not just exclusion.

CONSENT from parents for a targeted group (it identifies the child), with a plain account of content, measures and what happens to data (PSI 1.3.4–1.3.5); child assent in their terms; opt-out arrangements for universal work.

A DISCLOSURE PLAN: what you will say at session one about limits of confidentiality, who the DLP is, who follows up a child who becomes upset.

PRE- AND POST-MEASURES chosen before session one: a brief validated child measure (SDQ, RCADS self-report where anxiety is the focus — check licensing and service approval), a fidelity checklist, and a staff view.

LOGISTICS: a fixed room and slot that does not take a child from a subjec

method.name: Transition planning
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
ECOLOGICAL TRANSITIONS — Bronfenbrenner (1979) defined an ecological transition as a change in a person's role or setting, and argued development is shaped by how well the settings (mesosystem) connect. Transition planning is the practice of building those connections.

SCHOOL START — Rimm-Kaufman & Pianta (2000) proposed the ecological and dynamic model of transition: outcomes depend on the relationships between child, family, preschool, school and community over time, not on the child's 'readiness' alone.

PRIMARY TO POST-PRIMARY — in Ireland, the ESRI study Moving Up (Smyth, McCoy & Darmody, 2004) followed first-year students and documented what eases or complicates the move; Growing Up in Ireland has since added national cohort data (check the relevant GUI reports). In England, Evangelou et al. (2008) identified features of a successful transfer.

POST-SCHOOL — Kohler's Taxonomy for Transition Programming (1996; 2.0, 2016) and Test et al. (2009) set out evidence-based predictors of post-school outcomes for students with disabilities. In Ireland, McGuckin et al. (2013, NCSE Research Report 14) studied transitions to further and higher education.

IRISH POLICY — NCCA transfer documents (Mo Scéal, 2018, preschool to primary; the Education Passport, from 2014, primary to post-primary); HSE New Directions (2012) for adult day services. Part D lists transition planning at every band as context, not a diagnosis.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
Transition planning is a PROCESS, not a manualised intervention; the evidence is mostly observational and qualitative. Say that (PSI 4.2.2).

SCHOOL START — Rimm-Kaufman & Pianta (2000) and later work support multiple, relationship-based transition practices (visits, information sharing, contact with families) over single events; causal evidence is limited.

PRIMARY TO POST-PRIMARY — Evangelou et al. (2008) found that most pupils settle well, and that successful transfer is associated with new friendships, confidence, settling into routines, interest in school and curriculum continuity; pupils with SEN and those bullied at school were more likely to struggle. Irish ESRI work (Smyth et al., 2004) reports similar themes; check specific proportions before quoting.

POST-SCHOOL — Test et al. (2009) systematically identified predictors such as work experience in school, self-determination, inclusion in general education, parental involvement and interagency collaboration. Correlational, US-based: use as a planning checklist, not as proof.

IRISH POST-SCHOOL — McGuckin et al. (2013) described uneven information, late planning and dependence on individual staff. Scanlon, Shevlin and colleagues have published further Irish work — check current NCSE research.

PRACTICAL LESSON across all three: late planning and information that does not travel are the commonest failures.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN: any child with SEN or significant wellbeing needs approaching a change of setting — (1) PRESCHOOL → PRIMARY (school start, including choice of mainstream class, special class or special school); (2) PRIMARY → POST-PRIMARY (Sixth Class to First Year); (3) POST-SCHOOL (further education, training, higher education, employment, HSE adult day or rehabilitative training services) — plus service transitions (CDNT to adult disability services; CAMHS to adult mental health services, usually at 18 — check local arrangements).

WHY: transitions concentrate risk. Supports held in one setting (AIM, SNA access, a trusted key adult, an informal understanding with a teacher) do not transfer automatically. Anxiety, school avoidance and deterioration cluster around them (Part D: 'Anticipatory anxiety about transitions').

THE EP ROLE: formulation and information that the next setting can use; advice on placement and supports (not the placement decision, which rests with parents, schools and the NCSE); linking agencies; the child's voice in the plan.

WHEN NOT: transition planning is not a reason to re-assess a child who has a current, adequate report; update the functional picture instead. It does not replace the school's own transfer process — support it.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
TIMING — start a year ahead: preschool → primary in the autumn before school entry; primary → post-primary from Fifth Class (school applications often close in the autumn of Fifth or Sixth Class — check local admission policies under the Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018); post-school by Transition Year or Fifth Year at the latest (Reference Part D: 'post-school transition planning starts here').

CONSENT — parental consent (and the young person's, increasingly, from 16; and theirs alone for decisions at 18+, see Assisted Decision-Making) to share reports and the Student Support File with the receiving setting (PSI 1.2.5).

THE CURRENT PICTURE — Student Support File and Plan, most recent psychological and CDNT/CAMHS reports, AIM supports in place (for preschool), current Continuum level.

THE PEOPLE — parents; the child or young person; current and receiving setting leads (SET coordinator, guidance counsellor, year head); the SENO (NCSE) where special class/school placement or SNA access is in question; CDNT key worker; for post-school, the HSE disability services contact and the guidance counsellor.

THE SYSTEM FACTS, CHECKED THIS YEAR: AIM levels (aim.gov.ie); NCSE processes; DARE/HEAR rules (accesscollege.ie); CAO dates; HSE school-leaver profiling arrangements in the local area. These change annually.

AN ADAPTIVE PICTURE for post-school planning with significant needs: Vineland-3 or ABAS-3 (adult forms where age-appropriate).

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — MAP: what supports exist now, which will not transfer, what the receiving setting offers. Write it as a two-column table: now / next.

STEP 2 — HEAR THE CHILD: what they know, fear and hope about the move (visual scale, solution-focused questions, a 'my profile' page

method.name: Staff training
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
EP-led training of teachers grows out of Caplan's (1970) idea of indirect service: reach the child through the adults who see them daily. Training is consultation delivered to a group.

JOYCE & SHOWERS (1980s; Student Achievement Through Staff Development, 3rd ed. 2002) studied which components of staff development transfer into classroom practice: theory, demonstration, practice with feedback, and in-classroom coaching. Their central finding, cited on Reference row 95: training alone rarely changes practice without follow-up coaching. (Specific transfer percentages are widely quoted from their work — check the source before quoting any figure.)

KIRKPATRICK (1959; Kirkpatrick & Kirkpatrick, 2006) set out four levels for evaluating training: reaction, learning, behaviour, results. GUSKEY (2000) adapted this for education, adding organisational support and student learning outcomes.

EVIDENCE SYNTHESES — Desimone (2009) proposed core features of effective PD; Kennedy (2016) and the EEF meta-analysis (Sims et al., 2021) shifted attention to mechanisms: building knowledge, motivating teachers, developing techniques and embedding practice.

IRELAND — NEPS has long delivered programme training to teachers (e.g. Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management, FRIENDS programmes); teacher professional learning is now largely provided by Oide (established 2023) and the NCSE Support Service. Check what they already offer before designing your own.

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
WHAT WORKS IN PD (the most useful summary for an EP): Sims et al. (2021, EEF systematic review and meta-analysis) found PD programmes that combine mechanisms from all four groups — build knowledge, motivate, develop technique, embed practice — are more effective. The EEF Effective Professional Development guidance report (2021) is the practitioner version (Reference row 95).

ONE-OFF SESSIONS — Kennedy (2016, Review of Educational Research) found that how PD is structured matters more than its duration or content label; programmes that prescribe without building teacher understanding show weaker effects. A single input session should be treated as awareness-raising, not intervention, unless followed up.

WHO DELIVERS AND HOW WELL — Stallard et al. (2014, PACES): the same programme delivered by trained school staff did not reproduce the health-led effect, which is an argument for better training and support, not against school delivery.

IRISH EVIDENCE — Hickey et al. (2017) evaluated Incredible Years Teacher Classroom Management in Irish schools in a group randomised trial; read it for effects on teacher and child behaviour before citing.

EVALUATION DATA ARE USUALLY LEVEL 1 — satisfaction forms tell you whether people liked it, not whether practice changed. Claim only what your level of evaluation supports (PSI 4.2.2).

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: a pattern across cases (three referrals in one school showing the same misunderstanding, e.g. 'he can do it when he wants to' about a child with working memory difficulty); a school implementing something new (a group programme, a Student Support Plan format, a restorative approach); after a critical incident, where staff need to know what to expect and what to do; a request for CPD on a topic within your competence.

WHY: it reaches more children than casework (Reference row 95) and is the most direct route to CORU 5.40 — building capacity among those who deliver interventions. It is also where the Year 1 review named a strength: interpersonal communication and delivery of training.

WHEN IT IS NOT THE RIGHT CHOICE: when the difficulty is a system or resourcing problem (timetabling, SET allocation) — training teachers will not fix it; take it to consultation with the principal. When the request is really for case advice about one named child — that is consultation, not training, and confidentiality forbids it in a staff room. When the topic is outside your competence (medication, diagnosis, specialist therapy): decline or co-deliver with the right professional (PSI 2.2.2).

WATCH FOR: training requested to show that something was done. Ask what the school wants to be different in a term's time.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
A NEEDS ANALYSIS — ask the principal and two or three staff: what they want to be able to do, what they already know, what they have already had (Oide, NCSE, NEPS inputs), and what would make it a waste of time.

AN OUTCOME AT KIRKPATRICK LEVEL 3 — what staff will do differently, e.g. 'every class teacher uses a visual schedule with the three pupils on School Support Plus'.

EVIDENCE for every claim you will make: search properly, appraise five sources, use three (Reference row 95, Block 1). Cite in plain language on the slide.

YOUR SUPERVISOR'S AGREEMENT to the topic and content; trainee-delivered training is under supervision.

PRACTICAL DETAILS: audience size and roles (teachers, SNAs, SET, leadership), time slot (Croke Park hours and staff meetings are short — plan for 45–60 minutes), room, technology, whether SNAs are paid to attend.

A ONE-PAGE HANDOUT with the actions; people keep one page (Reference row 95).

AN EVALUATION FORM (three questions: what will you do differently, what was most useful, what was missing) and a follow-up plan, ideally a check-in 4–6 weeks later.

CASE MATERIAL THAT IS FULLY ANONYMISED OR INVENTED — never a recognisable local child.

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Needs analysis and agreed outcome, in writing, with the principal.

STEP 2 — Build the content backwards from the action: for each action, the minimum theory that makes it make sense (Reference row 95: 'every section should end with what to do').

STEP 3 — Structure for adults (Knowles, 1980): start from their experience ('think of a pupil who...'), short input, a demonstration or video, practice (role-play, planning for one real pupil anonymously), then commitment.

STEP 4 — Rehearse o

method.name: Teacher consultation
method.text:
1 · HISTORY — WHO MADE IT, WHEN, WHY
GERALD CAPLAN (The Theory and Practice of Mental Health Consultation, 1970) defined consultation as an indirect service: the consultant works with the consultee (teacher), who works with the client (child). He distinguished four types — client-centred case, consultee-centred case, programme-centred administrative and consultee-centred administrative consultation — and insisted the consultee remains free to accept or reject advice. Nearly every later model keeps that stance.

BEHAVIOURAL CONSULTATION — BERGAN (1977) and BERGAN & KRATOCHWILL (1990) set out a four-stage problem-solving sequence: problem identification, problem analysis, plan implementation, plan evaluation. SHERIDAN & KRATOCHWILL extended it to Conjoint Behavioral Consultation (Sheridan & Kratochwill, 1992 paper; Sheridan, Kratochwill & Bergan manual, 1996; 2nd ed. 2008), bringing parents and teachers into one process.

PROCESS CONSULTATION — SCHEIN (1969; revisited 1999) emphasised helping the client see and act on their own situation rather than supplying expert answers.

UK EP PRACTICE — PATSY WAGNER (1995 onwards; Wagner, 2000, Educational Psychology in Practice) built consultation as a whole-service delivery model in Kensington and Chelsea, drawing on symbolic interactionism, systemic thinking and personal construct psychology. Her chapter in Kelly, Woolfson & Boyle (2008; 2nd ed. 2017) is the standard UK text.

IRELAND — NEPS delivers much of its service through consultation with schools within the Continuum of Support. The Irish standards fold consultation into other competencies; CORU 5.38 names it (Reference row 94).

2 · EVIDENCE — HOW GOOD IS IT
The evidence is moderate and mostly from US behavioural consultation; UK/Irish process-oriented models have less outcome research. Say that honestly (PSI 4.2.2).

Sheridan, Welch & Orme (1996, Remedial and Special Education) reviewed consultation outcome studies and found most reported at least some positive outcomes, with behavioural models best represented — check the exact proportions before quoting.

PROBLEM IDENTIFICATION PREDICTS OUTCOME: Bergan & Tombari (1976) found that reaching an agreed problem definition was strongly associated with plan implementation and success. This is why Reference rows 82 and 94 say the work is mostly in problem identification.

IMPLEMENTATION IS THE WEAK LINK: teachers' implementation of agreed plans tends to drop off after the meeting; follow-up with performance feedback improves it (Noell et al., 2005, School Psychology Review). A consultation with no follow-up plan is weaker by design.

CONJOINT BEHAVIORAL CONSULTATION has randomised-trial support in the US (Sheridan et al.; check the specific trial before citing effect sizes).

PROCESS MEASURES: Nolan & Moreland (2014, Educational Psychology in Practice) examined what EPs actually do in consultation — useful for describing process rather than outcome.

Bottom line: consultation is a reasonable, capacity-building delivery model with the best evidence where there is a clear problem definition, a written plan, and follow-up.

3 · WHEN AND WHY IT IS NEEDED
WHEN IT IS NEEDED: at the START of nearly every school referral (to turn a description into a question); after assessment (to turn findings into a plan the teacher owns); at review (to evaluate and revise). Also as the whole intervention where the difficulty is best addressed at classroom level.

WHY: one EP cannot assess every child; consultation reaches more children through the adults who see them daily (CORU 5.40, building capacity). The teacher holds the comparison data (how this child compares with thirty others) and the intervention history — without both, recommendations repeat what has already failed (Reference row 39).

IT FITS THE CONTINUUM OF SUPPORT: Classroom Support and School Support are delivered by teachers; consultation is the EP's route into both.

WHEN IT IS NOT ENOUGH ON ITS OWN: when the question requires individual assessment (a specific learning difficulty, a cognitive profile for NCSE or access arrangements); when there is risk or a safeguarding concern — that is not negotiated in consultation; when the teacher is not the right consultee (the issue sits with management, or the SET holds the intervention).

WHEN TO PAUSE: when the consultation is being used to build a case for exclusion, or the teacher is in acute distress — respond to that first.

4 · WHAT YOU NEED BEFORE YOU START
A MODEL, NAMED. Problem-solving (Bergan & Kratochwill), solution-focused, or Wagner's consultation framework. Learn one properly and name it in your notes (Reference row 94).

THE REFERRAL FORM and any Student Support File / Student Support Plan, with dates and review notes. Know the Continuum level the child is at.

PARENTAL CONSENT for EP involvement in relation to a named child (service policy; CORU 1.15). A general, un-named consultation about a class issue may follow different rules — check your service's policy.

TIME AND PLACE: 30–45 minutes, protected, not in the corridor or during yard duty. Ask the principal to cover the class if needed.

THE RIGHT PEOPLE: the class teacher, and the SET if they deliver support. Ask who knows the child best, not who is available.

A ONE-PAGE RECORD TEMPLATE: concern in teacher's words · agreed question · when it happens / does not · what has been tried and what happened · teacher's hypothesis · agreed actions (who, what, by when) · review date.

YOUR OPENING SENTENCE about purpose, time and what will be written down. Supervisor briefing if it is a first consultation.

5 · HOW TO ADMINISTER IT, STEP BY STEP
STEP 1 — Contract (2–3 min). 'We've about forty minutes. I'd like to understand what you're seeing, and work out together what might help. I'll take notes and send you a copy.'

STEP 2 — The concern in their words. 'Tell me about him.' Listen for strengths as well as concerns. Write their words down.
